All levelsBooks with pictures

Level Z1

80 books · 10 pages each

1. A King Found Beneath the Parking Lot

1A rough floor plan shows how Greyfriars Abbey may have looked. The plan marks trenches. It marks walls that were found. It marks walls that researchers only hypothesized. It marks a hypothesized bench. The abbey was destroyed about fifty years after Richard III died. This book begins under a parking lot. It tells what led the search. It tells the ancient history. It tells what modern science added. It tells about honors for a king. It asks whether he was a villain or a victim. Word meanings come last. A search team member uses ground penetration radar at the Greyfriars parking lot. The tool is called GPR. The team is trying to locate the grave of Richard III. Town center ground held an ancient skeleton. It was not in a coffin. It was not even in a cemetery. It lay beneath a parking lot. Dirt was gently scraped clear by an archaeologist. The dirt had hidden the skeleton's spine. The burial spot was strange. The spine was strange too, for two reasons. First, the spine was crooked. It had a striking curve in the shape of an S. Second, this spine belonged to a famous king. Researchers found the bones in the fall of 2012. The place was a parking lot in Leicester, England. Leicester is said LES-ter.

2The bones were those of King Richard III. More than 525 years passed while he lay hidden. How could the researchers be sure it was Richard? Ancient history led the way. Modern science followed. Finding the king's long-hidden body under a city parking lot was not an accident. Historical records pointed the way. Researchers knew what lay under that plain parking lot. The buried ruins of the Greyfriars Priory were there. It was a monastery. Catholic monks lived there from 1255 to the late 1530s. A medieval historian recorded Richard's burial. Battle death came first. Burial in the priory followed. The battle was at nearby Bosworth Field. The month was August. The year was 1485. Richard's side had lost the battle. His side had lost the throne. Claiming his body was probably a brave act for the monks. Signs show that he was buried quickly. His skull was jammed upright. That was so he would fit. The grave was slightly too small for his body. There was no coffin. The grave sat in a position of honor. It was near the church's high altar. Even so, it was unmarked. It was under the monastery floor. Just over fifty years later, the abbey at Greyfriars was destroyed. The year was 1538. Who won and who lost in 1485 led straight to that destruction.

3In time the town grew and covered the site. By the time modern researchers hunted for Richard, the church had been underground a very long time. Its time underground was almost as long as his. They consulted old maps. In the centuries after the abbey was destroyed, street names had changed. Finding the exact grave took careful detective work. Even after they found the site, almost nobody expected a skeleton inside. The archaeologists themselves did not expect one. Some ancient accounts said Richard's body had not been buried at all. They said it had been thrown in the River Soar. That was after the body was paraded through the streets of Leicester. The king's first burial, by monks, was under the monastery altar. As soon as the archaeologists found the skeleton, they were pretty certain whose it was. The bones expert saw a gash in the skull. Then she saw the twisted spine. She reported that the hair on her neck rose. This was King Richard III. King Richard hoped a brave charge would change the battle. He charged toward Henry. He hoped the charge would inspire his troops. He hoped they would renew the fight. He hoped they would defeat Henry's forces. Richard died in 1485.

4The place was the Battle of Bosworth Field. The field is a few miles from Leicester. He led a direct charge toward his enemy. The enemy was Henry Tudor. Slippery ground cost Richard his horse. Henry's soldiers overran him. He lost his life. His crown fell beside his body. Men he trusted betrayed him. Bosworth Field is where Richard III died. Writers of the time described the blows that killed him. Similar injury marks were on the skeleton beneath the parking lot. There were ten blows. Eight of them were to the skull. A large fracture in the skull was likely the killing wound. The fracture was behind his left ear. No later English king died in battle. Henry Tudor led the triumphant procession back into town. Richard's body was slung over the back of a horse. Two days in the town square was how long Richard's body was left. The display was proof that he was dead. It was proof that Henry was now the king. The disrespectful display also showed his crooked back. Everyone could see it. In the play Richard III, Shakespeare depicts Richard as a hunchback. The character has a raised right shoulder. A crooked spine would cause that. In the play, this deformity brings scorn more than sympathy.

5Real life is another matter. The skeleton of Richard III shows a clear curve in his spine. His spine began to bend when he was young. The bend probably started between the ages of 10 and 12. Doctors at the time may have known the cause. They certainly would not have known how to help him. Because of the crooked spine, he stood inches shorter than his true height. His true height was five feet eight inches. That was tall for a medieval man. As an adult he probably lived with pain that almost never stopped. Centuries later we know the name of his condition. He suffered from scoliosis. Archaeologists lifted the arms from the grave first. They lifted the legs. They lifted the skull. When they finally reached the torso, they saw the crooked spine. Then they knew they had found Richard. Everything ancient history could tell them pointed one way. Richard III was the man these bones belonged to. Confirmation would come from modern science next. They studied the bones. Soon they learned the bones came from a man about thirty-two years old. That was Richard's age when he died. They could also tell something about his food. The owner of the skeleton had eaten a high-protein diet. The diet was rich in meat.

6It was rich in ocean fish. In the fifteenth century, only the wealthy ate that well. A king would be one example. They used carbon dating tests on two ribs. The tests showed when the person died. The death fell between 1455 and 1540. Richard died in 1485. Michael Ibsen is a descendant of Richard III's sister. He is a seventeenth-generation descendant. Her name was Anne. Scientists also studied DNA. DNA is the information in our cells. It determines many of our traits. That same DNA type shows up in under 2 percent of people in England. Scientists took DNA from two living descendants. Those people descend from Richard's sister, Anne of York. The samples matched. One picture is the tomb of England's Queen Elizabeth I. She ruled from 1558 to 1603. She is considered one of England's greatest rulers. Tradition places British monarchs in tombs at Westminster Abbey. The abbey is in London. With Richard's bones recovered, some people were delighted. Traditional honors could now be part of a new burial for the long-lost king. The question was where to bury him. Within twenty-four hours of the DNA confirmation, two towns claimed his body. Officials in Leicester wanted the bones buried nearby. The spot would be barely 100 yards from where the bones were found.

7The place would be Leicester Cathedral. A center for visitors, focused on Richard, was part of their plan. Richard came from the northern city of York. York is 100 miles north of Leicester. Some people insisted he would have wanted burial there. Other people felt strongly about London. They said his disputed place in English history should not matter. He should have been reburied in Westminster Abbey. Other British monarchs lie there. After much thought and debate, officials decided. The reburial would be in Leicester Cathedral. March 2015 was when the public first saw the tomb. People do not agree about what sort of man Richard was. We know he met a violent end. The question is whether he deserved what he got. For centuries, almost no English king was hated more. Shakespeare's play Richard III depicts him in a harsh way. He is limping. He is deformed. He is haunted. Shakespeare never knew the king. More than a hundred years after Richard's death, the play was written. He wrote during the reign of the Tudors. The Tudors were Richard's enemies. Some people argue that the Tudors wronged Richard III. They argue that Shakespeare wronged him too. They say he was a victim of their propaganda. What they said and wrote made him seem worse than he was.

8A picture shows the playwright William Shakespeare. The picture he gave of Richard III may have been false. Certainty may stay out of reach. Here is what we do know. In 1483 Richard's older brother died. The brother was King Edward IV. He probably died of pneumonia. Loyalty to his brother had been Richard's habit. Before Edward died, he named Richard to a role. Richard would be the royal protector of Edward's eldest son. In time that son would have become Edward V of England. Instead, Richard ascended the throne. He began to consolidate power for himself. He imprisoned his brother's two sons in the Tower of London. The sons were Edward and Richard. After that, nobody saw the young princes. No one knows what happened to them. Two years into Richard's reign, a battle was fought for control of England. It was between Richard's forces and the followers of Henry Tudor. The place was Bosworth Field. Men he thought were his supporters betrayed him. He lost his horse. He fought desperately on foot. He was killed. Someone lifted the crown from the spot where it fell. On that battlefield, Henry Tudor received the crown of England. He became King Henry VII. Years later, in 1534, Henry's son broke with the Catholic Church.

9The son was Henry VIII. He dissolved the monasteries. That act led to the destruction of Greyfriars Priory. It led to the loss of the priory. Centuries later, Richard's skeleton was uncovered there. Clarity fades for the rest of the tale. After Henry VII took the throne, rumors spread. The rumors were about Richard. The talk concerned the possible fate of the two young princes held in the Tower. Their murder may have been Richard III's order. Maybe they lived through the two years he reigned as king. Maybe the new king, Henry VII, killed them later. Henry VII had killed Richard. A secret trip out of the country may have carried the princes to safety. Today, fans of Richard III hold a hope. They believe the discovery of his skeleton may change people's opinions. In their view he cared deeply about ordinary people's rights. They believe he established many principles of modern law. One idea says a defendant stays innocent unless guilt is proved. Another idea is that defendants have a right to bail. Another idea is that all laws must be known. They must be published. His story may be told differently because of what happens now. A saying puts it this way. Victors are the ones who write the history.

10He lost his life more than 525 years ago. He lost his throne then too. A significant victory may still be his. The victory comes from a shallow grave. The grave was hidden under a parking lot. These words have special meanings in this book. An archaeologist studies what ancient cultures left behind. Ascended means moved upward. It can mean rose in position or rank. Betrayed means hurt another person by being unfaithful, false, or disloyal. Carbon dating is a test used to determine age. The test measures certain kinds of carbon inside a very old object. A deformity is a body part or an object part that looks abnormal. Descendants are the later family of a person or group from earlier times. Despised means disliked very much. It means hated. DNA holds the genetic information of a living thing. The long name is deoxyribonucleic acid. Medieval means of or relating to the Middle Ages. That period in European history runs from the year 500 to the year 1500. Monarchs are rulers of a kingdom or an empire. Kings are monarchs. Queens are monarchs. Monks or nuns live and worship in the buildings of a monastery. Propaganda is news, arts, or other media. It often uses false or exaggerated information to influence people.

2. A Kingdom beside Two Seas

1The parts of this book come in this order. One part asks where the country is. Then come parts on people, land, and history. A part on animals follows. Food comes after the animals. A conclusion follows the food. A glossary closes the book. A map shows Spain, the Mediterranean Sea, and the Strait of Gibraltar. It shows Casablanca, Salé, and the Bou Regreg River. It shows the Atlantic Ocean, Rabat, and Algeria. It shows the Canary Islands, which belong to Spain. It also shows Mauritania and Western Sahara. Smaller marks place the region among Asia, Europe, and Africa. Where Is It? On the coast of northwestern Africa lies the country of Morocco. Its shores run along the Mediterranean Sea. Its shores also run along the Atlantic Ocean. Morocco is slightly smaller than Spain. Spain is a country in Europe. Inside Africa, Algeria lies to the east and the southeast. A territory called Western Sahara lies along the southern edge. The Strait of Gibraltar separates Morocco and Spain. That strait is a narrow channel. It connects the Mediterranean Sea and the Atlantic Ocean. Spain and Morocco are only about 13 kilometers (8 mi.) apart where the water is narrowest. The capital of Morocco is Rabat.

2Rabat sits on the Atlantic coast. It sits at the mouth of the Bou Regreg River. Its sister city, Salé, is right beside it. Rabat's history reaches back to the twelfth century. French and Islamic architecture stand mixed together in the city. That mix shows the city's past. Rabat is no longer a major port. Silt has built up in the mouth of the Bou Regreg River. For centuries, though, the city saw heavy sea traffic. Not all of that activity was legal. From the seventeenth century to the nineteenth century, Rabat and Salé were a hub for pirates. The pirates ranged the seas along Spain, Italy, and England. They also ranged along Ireland and Iceland. A picture shows a wall around a section of the capital known as Old Rabat. Another picture shows a musician performing on a street in Rabat. Music is important to life in Morocco. People Morocco's population is a little above 33 million. Sixty percent of them live in urban areas. Casablanca is the largest city. About 3.5 million people live there. Tourism gives work to more people than mining does. It also gives work to more people than manufacturing does.

3In rural areas, farming gives work to about one-third of Moroccans. Morocco has plenty of farmland. It also has a mild climate. Among its neighbors, Morocco stands out for its ability to grow crops. In cities, many men like to meet in cafes. They visit and watch soccer matches on television. Soccer has taken the place of traditional horsemanship contests. It is now the most popular sport in Morocco. In large cities, people also like to see movies. They eat in restaurants. They shop in stores or in open-air markets. They go to the beach. Most Moroccans come from Berber families, from Arabic families, or from both. Berber people are the native people of the region. Morocco has many young people. People younger than twenty-four make up almost half of the population. Religion has a very strong place in Morocco. Islam is the official religion. Ninety-nine percent of the people are Muslim. Moroccan law includes Islamic laws. It also includes secular laws. In 2004, Morocco changed its laws. The new laws gave women more rights. Those laws give Morocco one of the highest ranks for gender equality among Arab countries. People in Morocco speak Arabic. They also speak Berber.

4They also speak French. A sign for the Princess Lalla Meryem School uses three languages. The school is named after a daughter of a Moroccan president. A landform map marks the Mediterranean Sea and the Rif Mountains. It marks Merja Zerga and the Bou Regreg River. It marks Rabat and Ouzoud Falls. It marks the Atlantic Ocean, the Atlas Mountains, and Mount Toubkal. It also marks the Sahara Desert. Land Morocco has Atlantic and Mediterranean coasts. Even so, much of the land sits high above sea level. Two major mountain ranges cross the country. The Atlas Mountains stand in the middle. The Rif Mountains stand in the north. The tallest mountain is Mount Toubkal. It is 4,165 meters (13,665 ft.) high. The ranges get a lot of rain and snow. That water creates a large number of streams. The climate changes in a sharp way from place to place. Northern areas and the coasts have mild Mediterranean temperatures. The south has desert conditions. Coastal temperatures range from 18 degrees C to 28 degrees C (64 degrees F to 82 degrees F). Inland areas can be extreme. In summer, inland temperatures are often more than 35 degrees C (95 degrees F).

5In winter, they sometimes drop below freezing. A hot wind called the sharqi blows out of the Sahara Desert. The name is said shar-KEE. It blows in late spring or early summer. The sharqi raises the temperatures. It often brings heat waves as high as 41 degrees C (106 degrees F). The landscape of Morocco varies widely. It ranges from mountains and waterfalls to coastal beaches and desert. Forests cover the land where the weather is milder. In some high mountain areas, forests of argan trees grow. The argan tree grows only in Morocco. The Saharan part of Morocco is different from the milder areas. It has few plants, except in oases. In the oases, people grow date palms. Pictures show Ouzoud Falls, the Sahara Desert in Morocco, and the Atlas Mountains. History More than twelve hundred years ago, Islamic dynasties rose in the land that is now Morocco. Idris I came to the area from the Middle East. He was a descendant of the Islamic prophet Muhammad. Idris took control from the Berbers, the native people of the region. In later years, Muslim kingdoms held lands that now belong to Spain. Catholic rulers forced them out in 1492.

6Morocco had been independent for more than a thousand years. Then it came under the political powers of Europe. In 1884 Spain set up control along the Moroccan coast. Unrest inside Morocco led to French control of the rest of the country in 1912. The French promised to share their military strength. They promised to protect the standing of the Moroccan royal house. Morocco stayed under French rule until 1956. A king and a prime minister both lead Morocco today. In the 1970s Spain gave the desert of Western Sahara to Morocco and Mauritania. Since then, Morocco has fought armed battles over this land. The fights have been with Algeria. They have also been with Western Saharan groups. The area is a harsh desert. Under the bare land lie valuable minerals. The country that controls them could become very rich. Morocco claims most of Western Sahara. Morocco controls most of it too. Many people still question that claim today. A picture pairs a camel with a flamingo. Animals Morocco has an impressive variety of birds. Merja Zerga is a lagoon on the Atlantic coast. The name is said MUR-zhah ZUR-kah. Visitors there can see huge flocks of herons.

7They can see flamingos. They can see ducks. Winter is when these birds gather in the greatest numbers. Northern Africa is home to camels with a single hump. Those camels are called dromedaries. They thrive in Morocco. They play an important part in the tourist industry. Visitors can trek through the countryside on a camel. The Barbary macaque is another species that lives in Morocco. The name is said muh-KAK. It is a monkey that lives in the forest. Among macaques, Barbary macaques are interesting for a special reason. The male monkeys help care for the young members of their group. Across the Strait of Gibraltar, Barbary macaques live in Spain as well. They are the only monkeys living in Europe. A picture note says the large ears of the fennec fox help it let out body heat so it can stay cool. Other interesting animals live in the deserts of Morocco. Fennec foxes live in the Sahara in Morocco. They are the smallest type of fox in the world. They are active at night. Night activity helps them beat the desert heat. A spider with a very odd skill also lives in the desert of Morocco.

8If it feels threatened, the spider throws its body end over end. The move is like a gymnast's handspring. People call the move a flic-flac. The spider can flip forward. It can also flip backward. It can even use the move to travel uphill. While it flips, the spider can travel 2 meters (6.6 ft.) each second. That speed is twice as fast as its usual travel. A picture shows the Moroccan flic-flac spider tumbling down a sand dune. Food People around the world enjoy Moroccan food. The food holds parts of Spanish, French, Berber, and Arab cooking. One main dish is couscous. Couscous is a tiny round pasta. Meals come with bread, just as they do in other Arab countries. Moroccans cook many dishes in a special clay pot. The pot is called a tagine. The name is said tah-ZHEEN. The word tagine also appears in the names of dishes cooked in that pot. A picture shows chicken tagine. Meat is plentiful in Morocco. It appears in kebobs of many kinds. During Ramadan, people serve a lamb stew that features this meat. Another popular meat dish is b'stillah. The name is said buh-STI-lah. It is a pastry filled with pigeon meat.

9Sugar is sprinkled on top. People in coastal areas also eat fish regularly. Tomatoes, onions, peppers, and eggplant are hallmark vegetables of this cooking. Garlic, olives, and lemons often flavor the food. Saffron, cumin, coriander, and cinnamon often season the food as well. People often finish a meal with mint tea. They also drink black coffee. A picture shows the city of Casablanca shining at night. Conclusion Morocco is a land with an ancient history. Snowy mountains fill parts of it. Sunbaked desert dunes fill other parts. Inviting beaches fill still others. Many kinds of interesting animals live in the different areas. Because of where it sits, tourists find Morocco a bridge to Africa. They also find it a gateway to Europe. Morocco stands out in the region for a mild climate in the north. It stands out for a strong ability to grow crops. It stands out for reforms on gender equality. It stands out for a delicious cuisine that is famous around the world. Here are key facts about the country. The population is 33,322,699. The land is 446,300 square kilometers (172,317 sq. mi.). The capital city is Rabat. The primary languages are Arabic and Berber.

10The primary religion is Islam. The currency is called the dirham. These facts come from the Central Intelligence Agency World Factbook (2016). Glossary Islamic means of or about the faith of Muslims, a faith with one God. Architecture is the design of buildings and the work of putting them up. Cuisines are ways of cooking, or foods cooked in the styles of certain countries. A lagoon is calm, shallow water lying between a reef and the shoreline. Oases are fertile places with water in a desert. A descendant is the offspring of a certain person or group that lived in the past. In most countries with a parliament, the prime minister leads the government. Dynasties are lines of rulers from the same families in a country. Gender is the state of being male or female, or males as a group or females as a group. Secular means not religious and not tied to spiritual things. A handspring is a tumbling move. The tumbler jumps, lands on the hands, swings the legs up and over the body, and lands on the feet again. A strait is a narrow passage of water that connects two large areas of water.

3. A New Beat That Would Not Fade

1Bill Haley and the Comets made Rock Around the Clock, the earliest rock 'n' roll song to reach number 1. This book follows that song back to the blues. It follows the change from rhythm and blues into rock 'n' roll. It looks at teenagers, at racism, and at barriers that fell. It ends by showing why the music stayed, and it explains hard words. May 1955 brought the movie Blackboard Jungle into theaters. Its story was set inside a high school in New York City. As the movie opened, the room heard Rock Around the Clock, recorded by Bill Haley and the Comets. No rock 'n' roll song had been heard in a movie before. The tune was so catchy that teenagers danced in the theaters. Many adults were not pleased with this new music called rock 'n' roll. At best they called it a fad. At worst they called it a danger. The words often touched taboo subjects. Popular media usually stayed away from those subjects. So the music looked like rebellion. Adults labeled rock 'n' roll junk. They labeled it poison. They labeled it a disease. Many adults demanded a radio ban. They burned records. They smashed records. Blackboard Jungle helped launch the music.

2The anger did not matter. Rock 'n' roll had already arrived to stay. No single year marks the birth of rock 'n' roll. No single place marks it either. The music grew across time. Players all over the United States mixed styles. The mix drew on jazz and on swing, on gospel, on country-western, and on rhythm and blues. Rhythm and blues, called R&B, shaped early rock 'n' roll more than any other style. R&B itself grew from older music called blues. Blues began in the South near the end of the 1800s. Work songs and spirituals were its start. Enslaved people sang them on plantations. The music spoke the suffering of Black farmers in rural places. It also spoke their hope. From the 1920s on, millions of Black people left the South. They wanted to escape racism that was brutal. They wanted better jobs in cities of the North. Blues traveled north with the musicians. Bessie Smith was one artist who carried blues to a much wider public. City players later changed how they sang. They changed how they performed. New styles appeared, including Delta blues and urban blues. Electric guitars replaced acoustic ones. Electric sound could cut through a noisy room.

3Songs got faster. A heavier beat made dancing easy. That is how R&B was born. Sister Rosetta Tharpe came long before the famous rock 'n' roll stars of the 1950s. People now call her the Godmother of Rock 'n' Roll. She joined pieces of blues, jazz, and gospel. What she made was an early form of rock 'n' roll. She was a Black woman in a business run by white men. Barriers and hard trials stood in her way. She became a star anyway. Before she turned twenty-five, she played some of the country's most famous music rooms. Her voice and her guitar shaped famous rock players of the 1950s and the 1960s. The Hall of Fame for rock music took those players in many decades ahead of her. Her own induction waited until 2018. Forty-five years had passed since her death. A picture places LaVern Baker at the far right. She ranks among the most successful early artists of R&B. Fans stand with her. The year was 1951. Two small companies began to work as partners. Chess Records was in Chicago, Illinois. Sun Records was in Memphis, Tennessee. They searched for new R&B artists and recorded them.

4Some of the best-known R&B players reached a wider public through them. Stations across the country put the songs on the air. Players in the Mid-South heard that radio. Country-western music was already popular there, and they blended it with R&B. From country-western they took drums. They took a vocal twang. They took the steel guitar as the lead instrument. In R&B, the lead was usually a saxophone or a piano. The blend made lively music called rockabilly. Rockabilly was one of the first styles of rock 'n' roll. Early rock 'n' roll was fast. It was cheerful. A heavy rhythm made it good for dancing. Melodies stuck in the ear. Words were simple enough to sing along. Many of the first artists were young. Songs often talked about fun or about falling in love. Teenagers of the 1950s responded to all of that. In that same decade, Mexican American players in California and the Southwest mixed rock 'n' roll with Latin music. Chicano is a name sometimes used in the United States for people whose descent is Mexican. The music they made was called Chicano rock. Ritchie Valens carried Chicano rock to the whole country. He was seventeen when two songs became top hits in 1958.

5One song, La Bamba, came from an old Mexican folk song. Every word of it was Spanish. A few months later, while on tour, Valens died in a plane crash. Other Chicano rock players followed the path he opened. The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame inducted him in 2001. The American economy boomed in the 1950s. Pay was high. Few people were out of work. Earlier generations of teenagers often had to help support the family. Many teenagers of this time did not. Money they earned could stay with them. Parents were earning more, so allowances were common too. Teenagers had more spending money than ever. Two new inventions made fresh music easier to reach. The first was the 45. A 45 is a vinyl record with one song on each side. Older records were larger. A 45 was small enough to carry to school or to a friend's house. The price was low. Almost any teenager with an allowance could buy one. Jukeboxes were machines that played vinyl records. A transistor radio was the other new device. Before it, a radio was a big piece of furniture for the whole family. A transistor radio let teenagers hear favorite music while they were out.

6Parents' music and parents' programs no longer had to fill their ears. Stations saw teenagers as a new audience and built shows for them. The Moondog House was one of the most popular. Alan Freed, a host in Cleveland, Ohio, ran it. The show grew so popular that stations nationwide aired it. The name became Rock 'n' Roll Party. Freed did not invent the words rock 'n' roll. He was first to use those words for the style he played. Rock 'n' Roll Party was among the first radio shows made for both Black and white listeners. Deep segregation marked both society in America and its popular culture then. American Bandstand was a television show seen across the nation. Teenagers danced to rock 'n' roll on it. Every weekday, millions of teenagers could watch after school. They heard the newest hits. They learned new dances. Black teenagers had often danced those steps first. They danced them on another program, The Mitch Thomas Show. Black musicians did perform on American Bandstand. Black teenagers were often barred from dancing there. They were often barred from sitting in the studio audience. The show was never officially segregated.

7Even so, Black teenagers did not appear there regularly until 1964. The show had already been on the air for twelve years. When Freed's radio show began, R&B was called race music. Black artists made it, mostly for Black listeners. Mainstream radio mostly ignored it. White listeners mostly ignored it. Then shop owners who sold records noticed a change. Radio hosts noticed it too. White teenagers were growing interested in R&B. Jerry Lee Lewis sang songs first made by Black artists. Companies wanted the money in that interest. Companies thought a white teenager would usually reject the record after learning the singer was Black. So the companies hired white players to cover the songs. Black artists had written those songs and sung them first. The white singers usually softened the raw feeling in the voice. They rewrote some of the words. A broader audience was supposed to find the songs more acceptable. The watered-down copies often outsold the originals. Mainstream radio promoted them and played them. The Black writers were paid little. Sometimes they were paid nothing. Racism held back even the most successful Black artists. At a show in Alabama, the Flamingos were ordered not to meet the eyes of white people in the crowd.

8At a Tennessee concert, a white band took Chuck Berry's place. The organizer had learned that Berry was Black. In 1957 the first primetime television show of rock 'n' roll was taken off the air. Frankie Lymon, a Black singer of only fourteen, had danced with a white girl. Pat Boone and Elvis Presley were two leading white rock 'n' roll artists of the 1950s. Both grew famous by covering songs from Black artists. Boone softened the songs so white listeners would like them more. Presley kept the gritty, emotional sound. He kept the content too. Boone looked and sounded friendly and clean-cut. White parents approved. Those same parents saw Presley as wild and rebellious. That reputation is probably why teenagers wanted him. From 1956 to 1960, Presley had fifteen songs at number 1. Boone had five. Racism fed a fear. People feared rock 'n' roll would draw Black and white teenagers together. In some ways, that is what happened. The music crossed the racial split in popular culture. Shows by Black musicians and by white musicians usually drew a mixed crowd. Some shows began with the crowd split apart. A rope held the groups separate. People still crossed that line.

9By the night's end they were dancing together. The Staple Singers belong in this story. Soon rock players used songs to back equality in a direct way. Ray Charles refused segregated stages in the 1960s, and so did James Brown and the Beatles. Other artists wrote songs that called for racial justice. Chuck Berry did. The Impressions did. The Staple Singers did. Marchers and protesters for civil rights even sang those songs. By the 1960s, rock 'n' roll was popular around the world. Players began to treat it as art. It was no longer only popular entertainment. It became a force that could change society. Young players used it to protest war. They used it to protest injustice. The civil rights movement gained national notice. The Black Power movement did too. Frustration went into songs by Marvin Gaye, by Aretha Franklin, by Nina Simone, and by Sam Cooke. They put hope into music too. A picture shows folk singer Joan Baez at the March on Washington. That famous civil rights protest was in 1963. Four artists in one picture helped keep rock popular through the 1970s and the 1980s. Jimi Hendrix is at the bottom left. Joan Jett is at the top left.

10Tina Turner is in the center. Elton John is on the right. The 1970s and the 1980s brought many new forms of rock 'n' roll. Punk rock was one. Glam rock was another. Heavy metal was another. Today, dozens of smaller styles sit inside rock. New rock artists rise every year. Players who were famous decades ago still tour the country. Their shows still sell out. Rock 'n' roll was not the short fad many people in the 1950s expected. It was not the fad they wanted. Acoustic describes an instrument whose sound does not come from an electronic device. Allowances are sums of money given on a regular schedule. Appealed means caught someone's interest. Banned means not allowed. Catchy means pleasant, or easy to remember. A fad is wide excitement for something popular only a short time. Mainstream means the beliefs a society accepts most widely. Racism is unequal treatment based on a belief that some races are better. A rebellion is a fight against authority or power. Records are vinyl disks that hold recorded music. Segregated means kept apart by group differences such as race. Taboo means forbidden, or avoided, because it clashes with common social values.

4. A Palace, a Tower, and a Huge Bell

1Readers can use this book to learn who or what Big Ben is. Westminster's history comes next. The fifth of November has its own part. Fire and later reconstruction have a part too. Another part goes inside Westminster and Parliament. The towers of Westminster are described. Big Ben is shown as an icon. The closing part asks whether this landmark is indestructible. Hard words are explained in a glossary. Side to side, the great bell measures 2.7 meters (9 ft.). Its height passes 2.2 meters (7.2 ft.) by a small amount. A person of average size could fit in that space many times. Big Ben is a name people often give the historic clock tower. That tower belongs to Westminster Palace. People often give the same name to the giant clock. The enormous bell had the name before either of those. Clock faces stand in front of that bell. The faces are high at the tower's top. This bell is made of bronze. It hangs in London, England. Over 13 metric tons (14.3 t) is what it weighs. Think of two African elephants beside each other. Together they are about as heavy as the bell. One bell grew into an iconic landmark. The path to that fame is a long one. The 1830s brought plans for a rebuilt Palace of Westminster. The people of Britain were making those plans. For the new tower, the government would not accept just any old clock. In a single day, the clock was allowed to stray by no more than one second. A bell with a chime was required as well. Casting took place in East London. The date of the casting was April 10, 1858. That date opened Big Ben's path through history. People usually accept one of two stories about the bell's name.

2The first ringing came in 1859. Parliament then called a special meeting. The meeting was meant to agree on a name. Sir Benjamin Hall was a large man. Friends used Big Ben as an affectionate nickname for him. His speech at the meeting went on for a long time. Another member of Parliament spoke when the speech ended. That member proposed Big Ben as the bell's name. The bell carries an inscription of Sir Benjamin's name. The inscription adds credibility to this story. A second well-known story is about Benjamin Caunt. Caunt was a big man. In his day he was a heavyweight boxing champion. Big Ben was his nickname too. Because of that nickname, some people think the bell was named for Caunt. Nearly 4.2 meters (14 ft.) is the length of each minute hand. Follow one minute hand around the dial for a year. The distance equals 189.9 kilometers (118 mi.). A map can show the United Kingdom. Scotland, England, Wales, and Northern Ireland appear on it. The Atlantic Ocean is marked to the west. The North Sea is marked to the east. Glasgow and Edinburgh appear in Scotland. Belfast appears in Northern Ireland. Dublin appears in Ireland. London appears in England. The River Thames is marked at London. London is a name most people have heard. Hearing it can bring big red buses to mind. Black taxicabs can come to mind as well. So can fish and chips. So can guards at Buckingham Palace. Those guards wear enormous headgear. All of these things really are part of London. London offers still more. The city is now the capital of the United Kingdom (UK). Westminster Palace stands in that capital. Parliament meets there. The palace is the seat of the United Kingdom's government.

3Westminster Palace was not always the home of Parliament. Kings and queens of England chose it as their home for a long stretch of time. It began midway through the eleventh century. It lasted into the sixteenth century. Building of the original palace took place between 1097 and 1099. Westminster Hall was part of that original work. The hall still stands. King William II was reigning while it was built. In those years the palace lay outside London. The city later grew until the palace was surrounded. No documents that still exist show the exact early layout. Nothing on record shows the ceiling from King William II's time. Today's huge wooden ceiling was a later addition. The year of that addition was 1393. King Richard II had it added. A picture can show the Palace of Westminster in the sixteenth century. The Houses of Parliament can appear in that same picture in their sixteenth-century form. Under King Henry III, this palace grew into the place where government was centered. His reign ran from 1216 to 1272. Before that reign, government tended to follow the royal leader from place to place. King Henry VIII is famous because he had six wives. He is also famous because he beheaded large numbers of people. No monarch after him lived in Westminster Palace. A fire came in 1512. After the fire, Henry VIII moved away. His new home was Whitehall Palace. As years passed, the Houses of Parliament made Westminster Palace their permanent home. Of his six wives, King Henry VIII divorced two. He beheaded two others. His own reign ran from 1509 to 1547. A timeline can mark the main dates at Westminster. Westminster Hall was constructed from 1097 to 1099.

4In 1393, a free-standing roof took the place of Westminster Hall's original roof. King Henry VIII moved out in 1512. He was the last monarch who lived at Westminster. Guy Fawkes tried in 1605 to blow up Parliament. He also tried to kill King James. The year 1642 was when King Charles I entered the House of Commons. No monarch has done so since that visit. The 1834 fire ruined the Houses of Parliament. The old hall itself was spared. In 1940, during World War II, Nazi Germany bombed London across nine months. Many historic buildings in London were destroyed. The clock tower received an official new name in 2012. The name was the Elizabeth Tower. Intense German bombing in World War II did not destroy Big Ben. The bell went on chiming every fifteen minutes. An English folk verse of 1870 tells people to remember. The day to remember is the fifth of November. Guy Fawkes is named in the verse. His companions are named too. The verse recalls the Gunpowder treason and plot. It says there is no reason for that treason to be forgotten. The companions, the verse says, worked out a scheme. The scheme was to blow up the king and Parliament. Henry VIII had been gone for nearly one hundred years when a new plot formed. That plot nearly caused the demise of Parliament. It nearly caused the demise of King James I as well. During 1604, Guy Fawkes met with several other men. They discussed how to kill King James I. They also discussed when to do it. Elizabeth I had been the monarch before James. She decided that England's official religion would be Anglican. That church is the Church of England. Many people in the country still belonged to the Catholic Church.

5The conspirators were Roman Catholic. Freedom to follow their own religion was what they sought. For Catholics, conditions under Elizabeth were dreadful. Conditions under James were dreadful too. Unfair treatment fell on many of them because of what they believed. The conspirators devised a plan. They would blow up the Houses of Parliament. They picked a day when King James was sure to be present. November 5, 1605, was that day. The plotters' first step was to rent a house. The house was adjacent to Parliament. They started digging a tunnel from there. Later they managed to rent a cellar. That cellar sat directly beneath Parliament. Once the cellar was theirs, they dropped the tunnel. Barrels of gunpowder were smuggled into the cellar a little at a time. Guy Fawkes knew explosives. On the chosen day, lighting the fuse was his task. To light it would be treason. It would mean murdering the king. Officers found Fawkes in that cellar one night before the plot was meant to finish. Thirty-six barrels of gunpowder were there with him. Officers arrested him. He was put in prison. Later he was put to death. Guy Fawkes Day is observed every year. The observance spreads through the whole United Kingdom. They celebrate because the king survived. They celebrate because the Houses of Parliament survived. Bodyguards of the monarch still search the cellars under Westminster Palace. The search comes before opening day of a session of Parliament. More than two centuries after that plot, the year 1834 brought an enormous fire. The Houses of Parliament were all but destroyed. A competition to pick an architect was held six years after the fire. Charles Barry was the winner. Barry gave a confident estimate of six years for the building work.

6Work then started. The estimate was quite wrong. Thirty years passed before the palace was built. The cost rose far above the estimate. Barry brought in another architect, Augustus Pugin. Pugin made some drawings. He also gave advice on fittings and on furniture. People still argue about this majestic building. The argument is about who deserves more credit, Barry or Pugin. Neither man had the chance to see the finished palace. Death came for Pugin in 1852. Death came for Barry in 1860. Workers completed the palace ten years after Barry died. Saturday visits inside the Houses of Parliament can be arranged in any season. Weekday tours are possible while Parliament is in recess. Parliament in the United Kingdom now has two houses. One house is the House of Commons. The other is the House of Lords. Membership in the House of Commons is 650. The British people choose these politicians by democratic election. Debating laws is their responsibility. They also vote on laws that other members lay before them. Membership in the House of Lords does not stay at one number. Election is not how Lords gain their seats. Some lords hold titles they inherited. Some people hold a title a monarch has given them. Bishops and archbishops of the Church of England sit there as well. A bill needs approval from the Lords. It also needs approval from the Commons. After both approvals, the bill becomes law. Laws of that kind are called Acts of Parliament. Houses of Parliament can mean the building. The same name can mean the bodies that govern the United Kingdom. Barry and Pugin's buildings still stand. They rise on the banks of the Thames. Nearly 150 years have passed since those buildings went up.

7Inside them sits a much older hall. It is Westminster Hall, also called the Great Hall. More than nine hundred years have passed since that hall was built. Feasts and banquets have filled the hall over the centuries. Coronations have been held there. A coronation is the ceremony that crowns a new king or queen. Entertainment has used the hall. Political rallies have used it too. Tradespeople have set up stalls and stores inside it to sell goods. A wooden roof makes the Great Hall famous. Among medieval wooden roofs in Northern Europe, this one is the largest. April 1685 was when Queen Mary was crowned beside King James II. At that coronation, Westminster Hall saw 144 separate dishes served. Cooks did not stop at that number. Thirty more dishes were made only for the king and the queen to enjoy. Adding those dishes made a total of 174. The banquet for this coronation was an elaborate event. The king was James II of England. The queen was Mary. His reign ran from 1685 to 1688. On Parliament's opening day, Queen Elizabeth II sits at the center in Westminster Hall. An election comes before that opening day. No other day brings all three groups into one meeting. Commons members attend, Lords attend, and so does the king or queen. Curious rules have force inside the Houses of Parliament. An English king is not allowed inside the House of Commons. An English queen is not allowed there either. King Charles I was the last monarch to step inside that house. The year was 1642. A suit of armor may not be worn inside the Houses of Parliament. A person's rank in society does not lift that ban.

8An old belief says nobody is permitted to die inside Westminster Palace. The belief is about seven hundred years old. A person who starts to look unwell is supposed to be escorted out quickly. State affairs of high importance pass through a grand entrance at the Victoria Tower's base. After elections, the king or queen uses that entrance for the opening of Parliament. The Victoria Tower stands on the south side of this palace. Queen Victoria gave the tower its name. Her reign ran from 1837 to 1901. Of the towers, this one is the tallest. Its height is 98.5 meters (323 ft.). Completion came in 1860. For many years it was the world's largest square tower of stone. All the original documents of Parliament were meant to be kept there. Those documents are still kept there. Access is given to very few people. Height of the Central Tower is 91.4 meters (300 ft.). Smoke from palace fireplaces was meant to leave through this tower. It was designed as that chimney. The other two towers do not share its shape. This tower is octagonal. A spire rises from it. At the north end stands the Elizabeth Tower. Fame comes to this tower because Big Ben is housed there. Height of the tower is 96.31 meters (316 ft.). For a long time its only name was the Clock Tower. A new name, the Elizabeth Tower, was given in 2012. The change marked sixty years of Queen Elizabeth II as queen of England. One side of the tower sits lower than the other. Digging in a nearby street caused the tilt. Falling is not a danger, fortunately. A drawing of the Palace of Westminster can include the River Thames. The House of Lords and the House of Commons can be labeled on that drawing.

9So can the Central Tower, the Elizabeth Tower, and the Victoria Tower. Gardens around the palace are left out of one size measure. Leave the gardens out, and the building's own footprint is 32,374 square meters, or 348,480 square feet. That ground is in central London. Staircases inside number 100. Rooms inside number 1,100. A spiral staircase leads visitors up. The climb leaves them exhausted. At the top they see how the clock works, behind the scenes. Among landmarks in the United Kingdom, Big Ben is one of the best known. Each year, millions of visitors see it. Photographers in London single out the Elizabeth Tower more than almost any other sight. Many movies have shown the tower. A citizen of the United Kingdom can book a time to tour the tower. The climb to the top is 334 steps. The climb is difficult. Builders put in no elevators. Guests stand 62 meters (203 ft.) above the ground. From there, London spreads out in a spectacular view. A behind-the-scenes tour shows the giant clocks. It also shows the mechanisms that run them. Visitors can come close to Big Ben itself. Visits to the Houses of Parliament are open to people from around the world. A tour is one choice. Watching a debate is another. Afternoon tea is possible there as well. Across the world, Big Ben is easy to recognize. The Palace of Westminster is easy to recognize too. Both are among the strongest symbols of Britain. Monarchs have lived and worked in the structure. Politicians have done so as well. Destructive fires did not bring it down. Intense bombing did not bring it down. Today it still stands, proud, as a national monument.

10People who live in the United Kingdom know the chime of Big Ben's bell. Visitors know that chime too. Some television channels send the chime out live. They do this at midnight on every New Year's Eve. November 11 brings a stop across the whole country. The stop is two minutes of silence. At 11:00 a.m. that day, Big Ben rings. The ringing remembers people who lost their lives in wars. A chime comes from Big Ben every quarter of an hour. The sound reminds listeners that the bell is present. Perhaps that reminder will always come. From the year 2000 onward, millions gather along the Thames. They gather each New Year's Eve. A brilliant show of fireworks is the reason. Something adjacent is nearby. It may share a border. Money, property, or a title that is inherited comes to someone after a death. Conspirators join a secret plan. The plan is to do something illegal or harmful. A majestic thing is grand. It may also be dignified or impressive. Credibility is a quality of seeming true. It is also a quality of being believable, a kind of trustworthiness. Medieval refers to the Middle Ages. In European history, that period runs from AD 500 to 1500. A demise is an end. It can be a failure, or a death. A monarch rules a kingdom or an empire. A king or a queen is a monarch. Someone who escorted another went along. Protection was often the reason for going along. To observe can mean to celebrate a special time, a custom, or a ceremony. It can also mean to acknowledge that occasion. Iconic describes an important symbol. It also describes what is famous and recognizable. Rank is a position held inside a group.

5. A Tiny Life at the Center of the Sea

1This book opens with an introduction. It then explains the food web. Life in the sunlit zone comes next. The twilight zone follows. The midnight zone comes after that. A return to the top and a word list close the book. Let Me Introduce Myself. Where I live, the ocean is one huge buffet. Everything in the water can feed there. So can many animals on land, including humans. You might picture fierce great white sharks eating their prey. You might picture enormous blue whales taking in tons of krill. You might picture giant stands of seaweed being eaten by everyone, like a salad bar under the water. Here is a fact you may not know. In the end, other creatures of the sea consume over 90 percent of them. At some moment, another sea creature eats nearly every organism that lives in the ocean. Eating other sea creatures is also what nearly every sea creature does. No animal on Earth is larger than the blue whale. A picture shows microscopic phytoplankton called diatoms. Some very small organisms almost always get eaten. They do not actually eat anything themselves. No ocean species is more microscopic than they are. Even so, the ocean's food web has its center in them. Some people might think it is a raw deal to be food for everyone else. To me, the job is quite powerful. Let me step back and introduce myself properly. My name is phytoplankton.

2The word is said FY-tow-plank-ton. I am an algae. That is almost like a very tiny plant. Unlike plants, I have no roots. I am not attached to the ground or to the sea floor. I am free to float with the ocean currents. I prefer to stay near the surface of the sea. I am quite fond of sunlight. You can find me in every ocean on Earth. A note about plant cells says chlorophyll takes in the sunlight plants need. Plants use that light to turn nutrients into food. I make food the way plants do. The process is called photosynthesis. I do not eat my food. I use chlorophyll to capture energy from the Sun. That energy changes nutrients from seawater into food. Chlorophyll makes me green, just as it does in plants. I am so tiny that the color shows only when billions upon billions of us gather in one place. A photo taken from space shows a bloom of phytoplankton and zooplankton. The bloom appears as light streaks. Fortunately, there really are billions upon billions of us. One cup of seawater can hold thousands of phytoplankton. All of that photosynthesis does something large for the air. It supplies well over half of the oxygen in Earth's atmosphere. We are also a good sign of how healthy the ocean is. Scientists can see large patches of us from space. If we are struggling or dying off, scientists learn how polluted the water is.

3I think a different job matters most. For the entire ocean, the food web centers on us. We feed every ocean life form, either directly or indirectly. That includes the smallest creature and the largest. The Food Web. Here is how it works. Think about a simple tuna sandwich. Tuna are fairly large fish. They eat smaller fish called mackerel. About 10 kilograms of mackerel, or 22 pounds, had to be eaten to produce 1 kilogram of tuna flesh, or 2.2 pounds. That is 22 pounds. That mackerel, weighing 10 kilograms, had eaten 100 kilograms of herring, a fish smaller still. That is 220 pounds. Those 100 kilograms of herring ate a full 1,000 kilograms of zooplankton. That is 2,200 pounds. Zooplankton are microscopic animals. Krill are among them. Krill are tiny animals that look like small shrimp. Larvae are included too. So are the young of crabs, of jellyfish, of shrimp, and of other fish. Supporting those 1,000 kilograms of zooplankton took 10,000 kilograms of phytoplankton. That is 22,000 pounds. The chain is simple. Tuna eat mackerel. Mackerel eat herring. Herring eat zooplankton. Zooplankton eat phytoplankton. A picture is a cross section of the ocean. It shows the different zones. To show you how much life I support, I will take you through the ocean. We start at the surface, where I live. The trip ends at the deepest trenches of the seafloor.

4A note places otters in the sunlit zone, where they feed and where they live. Life in the Sunlit Zone. The top level of the ocean is the euphotic zone, also called the sunlit zone. The name is said yoo-FOE-tic. It reaches about 200 meters down from the surface. That is 660 feet. Plenty of sunlight is here. We phytoplankton love it. Ocean plants love it too. That sunlight is why most ocean animal species live in this layer. Much of the shallow floor here is covered by red algae and green algae. People also call them seaweed. Enormous giant kelp grow in thick forests. The forests are almost like forests on land. They give shelter to many sea animals. Protected water at the kelp's base is where sea urchins live. Sea otters feed on those urchins. Sleeping sea otters wrap long kelp strands around themselves. The kelp keeps them from drifting away. The euphotic zone supplies nearly all seafood that people eat. Shallow seafloors are home to clams, mussels, and oysters. Inside coral reefs, lobsters and crabs scuttle. They also scuttle among beds of seaweed. Most species of fish stay up in the sunlight. Salmon, tuna, mackerel, cod, and swordfish are among them. There is plenty to eat there. The light is good for hunting. Squid and octopuses do live in the deeper zones. Most of the ones humans eat still come from the euphotic zone.

5A note says most familiar fish, such as the hammerhead shark, live in this zone. Colorful coral reefs are the most popular areas of the sunlit zone. Coral reefs are also home to most of the ocean's plant species and animal species. These areas are fragile and beautiful. They form by the accumulation of skeletons from small animals called coral polyps. Clear tropical water with strong sun is where they grow. Many animals make the reef a colorful and busy place. They include sea fans, brain coral, clown fish, angelfish, and lion fish. They include moray eels, sharks, shellfish, crabs, and lobsters. Anemones are animals that look like beautiful flowering plants. They catch zooplankton with stinging tentacles. Jellyfish swarm in massive numbers. Sea turtles that like this meal are drawn in. Coral reefs also give a safe haven to the young of many creatures. Those young will live in the open ocean when they are adults. People especially enjoy a snorkel or a dive in this top zone. They especially love the waters around coral reefs. From these surface waters they take thousands of tons of fish. Some of the fish are food. Some become pets in tropical aquariums. Sadly, all this human activity threatens the well-being of coral reefs. Pollution adds to the threat. Other areas in the euphotic zone are threatened too. Coral polyps are often killed by pollution. Boat engines break them. Divers step on them.

6Once the corals die, every other kind of reef life suffers as well. Overfishing can drop whole populations of fish to a dangerously low level. A picture notes that boats, anchors, and divers can break coral. A visit to a tide pool may reveal a spiny sea urchin. One way to sample ocean life here does no harm. Look into a tide pool. When the tide leaves, a small pool of water can remain. That pool is a tide pool. Mussels and sea stars may be there. Urchins, clams, barnacles, and snails may be there too. You might even see an octopus. You might spot a hermit crab hurrying about in the shell of another animal. You do not even have to get wet. You can still see all the life that depends on me and on my fellow phytoplankton. Some of that life depends on us directly. Some depends on us indirectly. The Twilight Zone. Below the euphotic zone, the water starts to get darker. It gets colder. It gets heavier. This next layer is the twilight zone. It begins at about 200 meters, which is 656 feet. Its lower edge is about 1,000 meters down, or 3,280 feet. The pressure here would crush a person. Life that stays here has adapted so the pressure does not crush it. This zone is also called the disphotic zone. The name is said dis-FOE-tic. There is not enough light for photosynthesis.

7There is not enough light for plant life. Some animals do make their homes here. Whales are visitors. They come down from the euphotic zone. Permanent residents include octopuses and squid. Odd fish live here too, including the hatchet fish and the viperfish. Many fish in this zone often have huge mouths. The teeth are big and curved. Seeing is so hard that the fish do not hunt. They simply hold their fearsome mouths open. They wait for something to swim in. Black is a common color. Dark red is another. Those colors blend with the dark water. A note says this angler fish is small but scary. Sperm whales carry sucker scars from fights with giant squid. This zone is also home to the famous giant squid. For a long time, nobody had seen a living giant squid. Now and then a body washed up on shore. Bodies were also found in the stomachs of sperm whales. A few people have seen the squid at the surface. Inside the disphotic zone, a few scientists have watched it. Even so, the giant squid remains a mystery. A note says octopuses live in both the euphotic zone and the disphotic zone. Many animals here live on what scientists call marine snow. The pleasant name refers to phytoplankton and zooplankton that have died. After death, our bodies sink slowly from one ocean layer to the next. They fall the way snow falls through the air.

8So phytoplankton are eaten even in places where we do not live. Tiny bioluminescent animals glow in a beautiful way in the pitch-black depths. The Midnight Zone. This part of the ocean is totally dark. It holds 90 percent of the ocean's water. It holds almost none of the ocean's life. It runs from 1,000 to 5,000 meters, which is 3,280 to 16,404 feet, and it continues below that. Almost anything would be crushed by pressure this strong. Most submarines would be crushed. The temperature is near freezing. Some life is here if you look closely. This zone is also called the aphotic zone. The name is said ay-FOE-tic. Little lights run along the bodies of many tiny animals here. The lantern fish is one example. A special process called bioluminescence makes that light. Fireflies make light by the same process. Sunlight never arrives here. Jellyfish, squid, fish, and even bacteria still glow by bioluminescence. These lights let animals see. They let animals communicate with each other. Mates can be found with the lights. Food can be found with them too. The lights make them incredibly beautiful as well. Some oceanographers split the midnight zone into two more zones. They are the abyssal zone and the ocean trenches. The abyssal zone is totally dark. It covers much of the ocean floor. That floor includes vast plains, mountains, valleys, and canyons. A picture shows a chimney called a black smoker.

9It spews hot minerals. The warmth and the nutrients support crabs, tube worms, and other animals. Ocean trenches occur along faults. Faults are places where large plates of Earth's crust come together. The plates collide and create canyons and cracks. Those cracks can be up to 10,000 meters deep, which is 32,808 feet. Survival at a trench bottom seems impossible. Darkness, cold, and pressure are all extreme. Even so, openings on the trench floor pour out hot water. They also spew minerals from deep within the Earth. Warmth and nutrients here are used by the animals. Certain bacteria are able to live on these nutrients. They use them the same way phytoplankton use sunlight. Around those openings, also called chimneys, you can find tube worms. You can find shrimp and giant clams too. They feed on these bacteria. These chimneys were discovered only recently. Just a few submersibles, a kind of submarine, are strong enough to reach a trench bottom. The pressure there is enormous. A picture shows a submersible that can withstand that pressure. Back on Top. So you see the full picture. Phytoplankton live only at the top of the ocean. Even so, we sit at the center of the food web. We support all other life in the sea. Coral reefs may be the beauty that draws you to the ocean. You might enjoy the mystery of the abyssal zone. You might enjoy some tasty fish and chips.

10In every case, you have us phytoplankton to thank. Word list. Inside the aphotic zone, the abyssal zone takes in the deep ocean floor. Accumulation means a piling up of material over time. Anemones are plantlike marine animals. Their tentacles often look like flower petals. The aphotic zone is the bottom ocean zone, and it receives no sunlight. Bioluminescence is light, or the giving off of light, made by a biochemical process inside a living thing. Chlorophyll is the green substance in plant cells. During photosynthesis, plants use it to take in light energy for making food. The disphotic zone is the middle ocean zone. It receives very little sunlight. It contains no plants and few animals. The euphotic zone is the top ocean zone. Nearly all ocean life is found there. Faults are cracks in Earth's crust, and movement occurs along them. Photosynthesis is the process by which plant cells take in sunlight and use the Sun's energy. They turn water and carbon dioxide into food. A phytoplankton is a single-celled alga living in water. Snorkeling is swimming with a short, curved tube. The tube reaches above the surface so the swimmer can breathe while under the water. A submersible is a small craft that works underwater, above all in deep water. Trenches are cracks in the seafloor, like long ditches. A zooplankton is a microscopic animal that lives in water.

6. A Water Path Cut through Panama

1A picture shows ships passing the Gatun locks. East is the side of the Panama Canal where these locks stand. The book opens with an introduction. It then tells of dangerous crossings. It tells how the French took charge. It tells how the Americans took over. It tells of a battle against the mosquito. It tells of an order to make the dirt fly. An old waterway and its later years come next. A glossary explains hard words. A picture shows the ship Ancon. In 1914 that ship made the first trip through the Panama Canal. Most people thought this modern marvel would never be built. A dream became real on August 15, 1914. On that day the cargo ship Ancon sailed the new route. It moved through narrow channels. It moved around tall mountains. No ship had gone from the Atlantic to the Pacific by this canal before. The canal was newly open. For many people, the voyage of the Ancon was a day of triumph. Travel that had filled months now took only a few days. Human ingenuity was part of the reason. American technology was part of it. So was the sweat of thousands of laborers. The canal is fifty miles long. Building it was a colossal feat of engineering. The world had never before witnessed a work like it. Workers spent ten years cutting earth from the isthmus. They beat back obstacle after obstacle. The opening pushed global commerce forward. It also helped set the United States up as a world power. A century and more has passed. Thousands of ships still go through. The ships range from yachts to aircraft carriers. They cross from one ocean to the other. A map can compare two trips between San Francisco and New York.

2It can mark the United States, the Atlantic Ocean, and the Caribbean Sea. It can mark the Panama Canal, the equator, South America, and the Pacific Ocean. The trip through the Panama Canal is 5,300 miles (8,370 km). The trip around South America is 13,000 miles (20,900 km). A canal between the Atlantic and the Pacific was not a new idea. Explorers from Spain were the earliest people to dream of such a water route. The engineering technology it needed was not on hand in the 1700s. In the early 1800s, Britain made its own plans. France made plans on its own as well. Neither government carried the plans out. The year 1848 fixed a cross-isthmus canal in the public imagination. That year a ranch hand found gold. The gold was in a streambed in California. The find set off a major gold rush. Hopeful seekers of fortune came from the East. The country was still young. No transcontinental railroad linked the East Coast and the West Coast. No stagecoach route linked them either. Much of the land west of the Mississippi was wild, open country. The overland trek crossed mountains, plains, and deserts. It was dangerous. It was long. Many travelers chose the sea instead. The sea route was somewhat less hazardous. A boat from New York to San Francisco was safer than the land route. It also took much longer. Sea travelers had two choices. One choice was to sail to Panama. They then crossed the isthmus by land. A second vessel carried them on to California. The other choice was to stay on one ship the whole way. That ship had to round Cape Horn. Cape Horn is the southern tip of South America.

3Heavy winds made that rounding hazardous. Rough seas made it hazardous too. Crossing the isthmus took about a week. The week was far from comfortable. It was far from pleasant. Middle years of the 1800s brought a choice by a group of Americans. They would lay a railroad across Panama. They wanted an easier journey. By 1855, trains ran on a regular schedule. The rail line was 47 miles (75.6 km) long. It linked the Atlantic coast with the Pacific coast. A map can show the Caribbean Sea and Panama City. It can show the Panama Canal and the country of Panama. It can show the Gulf of Panama, Costa Rica, the Pacific Ocean, and Colombia. Panama is a curved ribbon of land. It connects Central America with South America. It is the narrowest strip of land between the Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean. The climate is hot. It is humid. Rain is common. The land is diverse. Thick jungles grow there. Many kinds of plants and animals live there. The railroad made the crossing easier. Many people still believed a canal would be the best way across the isthmus. Ferdinand de Lesseps was a Frenchman. He had supervised a successful canal in Egypt. That canal was the Suez Canal. It was 102 miles (164 km) long. A shorter canal across the isthmus seemed to need a leader like him. French businessmen joined together as a company during 1879. The company would dig a canal across Panama. De Lesseps headed the project. He was sure the shorter canal could be finished in ten years. Ten years was half the time the Suez Canal had taken. France first had to sign a treaty with Colombia.

4Colombia owned the isthmus. The work force was brought in next. De Lesseps led that move, with help from his assistant Philippe Bunau-Varilla. Armies of workers arrived. Heavy machinery arrived. De Lesseps was an enthusiastic manager of the project. He was not much of an engineer. He did not take in the difference between two landscapes. Central America was jungle. Egypt was sandy land. Some people warned that the jungle would doom the project. De Lesseps ignored those warnings. Digging began slowly. Workers carved only tiny slices out of the jungle. The tropical climate caused trouble for more than the workers. Equipment suffered too. Damp air in the Panamanian rainforest made steel construction tools rust fast. Rust limited how long the tools could be used. Day after day, workers labored in steady downpours. Week after week, the heat was stifling. Mudslides took many lives. Accidents took countless other lives. Diseases spread by mosquitoes took lives as well. After seven years the project fell apart. It crumbled the way the deadly mudslides had crumbled. De Lesseps had been the hero who conquered the desert. He left Panama as a failure. The investment was more than 287 million dollars. That sum is over 7 billion dollars in today's money. The money bought little more than a muddy mess. It also bought the loss of more than twenty thousand lives. For the next ten years, nobody moved to build a canal in Panama. Most countries refused the task after watching the French fail. Many nations saw a miserable swamp of death and disease. The United States saw something else. Its leaders recognized the many opportunities a canal offered. A timeline can mark the American years. On November 18, 1903, the United States signed a treaty with the new Republic of Panama.

5Panama was newly independent. The treaty was to begin work on the canal. On June 28, 1904, the first American workers arrived in Panama. On November 12, 1904, the first steam shovel arrived. On November 21, 1904, workers recorded the first case of yellow fever. On July 26, 1905, John Stevens arrived to take charge. On August 15, 1914, the canal officially opened. On January 1, 2000, Panama took control of the canal. The start of the twentieth century widened America's role in the world. The United States had a great deal to gain from a canal. Theodore Roosevelt became president in 1901. He believed a canal in Central America was the path to America's future. Commerce from America, as he pictured it, would move on that channel the way carts move on a highway. Firms in the eastern part of the United States could reach buyers they did not have before. Those buyers would be in Asia. It could also carry American warships. His administration was committed to building a canal. New obstacles still blocked the effort. The biggest obstacle was Colombia. The first American plan did not stay in Panama. It called for a new canal farther north, in Nicaragua. Bunau-Varilla had worked with de Lesseps. He advised against Nicaragua. He persuaded officials to start again on the French site. Panama was still part of Colombia. The United States signed a treaty with Colombia. Colombia's congress rejected that treaty. The congress called it unfair to their country. Roosevelt was not a man who accepted no. He decided to help revolutionaries from Panama. They would overthrow the government that had refused him. Rebels started taking hold of the region on November 3, 1903.

6The revolution was finished by sundown. Three days later, the United States formally recognized Panama. It recognized Panama's independence from Colombia. A picture from 1906 shows President Theodore Roosevelt. He is testing a steam shovel during the canal work. Soon thousands of workers poured into the new country. They brought giant steam shovels. Engineers set teams digging. The canal would run almost 50 miles (80.5 km). It would run from Colón to Panama City. Panama City is on the Pacific coast. Malaria did not let up for the Americans. Yellow fever did not let up either. The French had faced the same diseases. Treatment had reached over 85 percent of the people working on the canal by 1906. The illnesses included these two and other diseases that mosquitoes carry. A new case of yellow fever often threw the workers into panic. Roosevelt asked Doctor William Gorgas for help. Gorgas was an army doctor. His job was to stop diseases spread by mosquitoes. Mosquitoes lay their eggs in water. Gorgas organized teams of Panamanians. The teams walked the streets and emptied barrels that held standing water. He sent fumigators out in force. They sprayed homes with insecticides. He demanded netting over workers' beds. The nets would block bites during sleep. The ideas worked. By August 1906, yellow fever cases were down to just twenty-seven. By November the count was one. That patient was the last yellow fever victim Gorgas would see. Malaria was a greater challenge. Even there, the effort showed results. By early 1910, the death rate from malaria had fallen below 1 percent. That was a marked improvement from the project's start. A picture from 1913 shows workers and steam-powered machines. They are cutting through the mountains of Panama.

7The world watched construction that had begun in 1904. An experienced engineer named John Wallace was in charge. Roosevelt ordered Wallace to make the dirt fly. The order was hard to obey. Steam shovels did not lift dry dirt. They lifted thick, sticky mud. Almost as soon as a shovelful came out, more mud slid down. It filled the fresh trenches again. By June 1905, most of the American workers had left Panama. The task had overwhelmed them. The project was in peril. Wallace quit. A hard-driving engineer named John Stevens replaced him. Stevens arrived while morale sagged. Seventeen thousand workers wanted a new leader. They wanted direction. They wanted a reason to carry on. Stevens knew the troubles. He took time to review the situation. He planned with care. The mightiest steam shovel was useless if the dirt was not hauled away at once. He stopped all digging. He started building roads. He started refurbishing parts of the old Panama Railway. The roads and the railway would carry the mud out. He even built churches. He built hospitals, mess halls, and schools. The buildings were meant to lift worker morale. He also changed the plan for the canal. The first plan dug the canal at sea level. Workers would have had to dig through the mountains. That dig would have added years. The Chagres River was another obstacle. It ran high along the mountains. Stevens proposed a series of locks to solve these problems. Each lock would be longer than three football fields. The locks would carry ships over the mountains. He also decided to dam the Chagres River. The dam would create a huge lake. The locks would work like a staircase.

8A ship could scale the mountain. It could cross the new lake at the top. It could descend the far side. The lake would receive water from the locks. It would deliver water back to them. Digging was ordered to begin at each end of the place where the locks would stand. Stevens gave that order. The two digs would meet in the middle. Each lock was 70 feet (21.3 m) deep. Each lock was 110 feet (33.5 m) wide. Four years went into raising these huge locks. Stevens had been highly successful. Even so, he resigned without warning in 1907. Roosevelt then sent Major George Washington Goethals. Goethals belonged to the Army Corps of Engineers. He went to Panama as supervisor. He oversaw the building of the canal. Up to that point, much of Stevens's work had been preparation. Much of it had been excavation. Under Goethals, real construction could start on the locks. The canal would have three sets of them. Crews also began Gatun Dam. The dam crossed the powerful Chagres River. Workers finished the canal in 1914. The locks worked just as planned. The Panama Canal soon became an important route for navigation. Making Gatun Lake helped preserve the natural habitat around it. The lake gives a water route through the area. That route lessens the need for roads and other pathways. Those pathways could disrupt the ecosystem. Native wildlife in Panama continues to thrive. Human activity does not disturb it. A diagram can show how the canal's locks work. It can mark sea level and the height of Gatun Lake. It can show the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean. It can show Miraflores Lake and Gatun Lake. It can show the Gatun locks, the Miraflores locks, and the Pedro Miguel locks.

9The side view is seen from the north. It is not drawn to scale. A lock is a watertight chamber. Huge steel doors close each end. Engineers can raise the water in a lock. They can lower it too. A ship that wants to pass finds the front door open. The ship sails into the chamber. The door then closes. Engineers open valves. The lock that sits higher than the ship sends water down into the compartment. The water level rises. The ship rises with it, up to the next lock. Three locks lift the ship.
