The ship is then level with the lake that lies inland. On the far side, those steps go in reverse. Engineers drain water instead of adding it. The ship drops to the level of the next lock. One pictured step shows a ship moving into an open lock. The next step shows the gates shut while water fills the lock. The ship rises to the following lock. Further locks raise the ship to the height of Gatun Lake. The ship then crosses Gatun Lake. On the far side, the locks reverse the process. The United States controlled the canal through the end of 1999. Panama then took it over. A treaty agreement set that change. Age had become easy to see on the canal once the twenty-first century was only a few years old. More than fourteen thousand ships passed through its locks each year. So did three hundred million tons of cargo. A makeover was badly needed. Larger ships had to be able to pass. Traffic jams had to be solved. In 2006 the people of Panama voted for new construction. They voted for two new sets of locks.

10They voted for two new lanes of navigation. Those lanes would join the new locks to the channels already there. In 2016 the work was finished. Forty thousand workers had completed it. The cost was 5.4 billion dollars. The building had taken ten years. Much larger ships can pass the new locks. The amount of cargo the canal can handle each day is effectively doubled. The expansion is one more marvel of engineering. It joins a long history. A picture shows a tugboat helping a freighter. The freighter is making its way through the Panama Canal. A canal is a waterway dug across land. Ships use it for transportation. Channels are wide passages of water. They connect two larger bodies of water. Commerce is business or trade. To have contracted an illness is to have caught it or developed it. Engineering is the work of designing and building. Science and math are its tools. Ingenuity is cleverness or skill used to solve a problem or a challenge. An isthmus is a narrow strip of land. It joins two larger landmasses. Locks are gated sections in a river or a canal. Inside them, the water is raised and lowered so ships and boats can pass. Malaria is a dangerous tropical disease. Mosquitoes spread it. Morale is the confidence or enthusiasm of a person or a group. It shows while they work toward a goal. Refurbishing means changing or repairing something so it is better. To scale something is to climb what is high or steep. It can mean reaching the highest point. Transcontinental describes something that extends across a continent. A trek is a long, hard journey. It is often a journey on foot.

7. Across the Wide Russian Land

1Where Is Russia? Russia is a giant country. It begins in eastern Europe and keeps going until it reaches East Asia. That distance crosses eleven time zones. A time zone is a band of Earth that shares one clock setting. Eleven settings show how wide this land is. The area of Russia is 16,377,742 square kilometers. The same area is 6,323,500 square miles. That area is double the area of the United States. No other nation on Earth has more land. Seas meet Russia on two sides. Oceans meet it on those sides too. The Arctic Ocean is north of the country. Three seas lie to the east. Those seas are the Bering Sea, the Sea of Okhotsk, and the Sea of Japan. Finland shares a European border with Russia. Ukraine shares one too. So does Kazakhstan. More countries in Europe share borders with Russia as well. Maps of this region also name Estonia, Latvia, and Belarus. Three neighbors stand on the Asian side. Mongolia is one. China is another. Japan is a third. The Bering Strait separates Russia from Alaska. Alaska is a state of the United States. The farthest eastern tip of Russia lies only 88.5 kilometers from the west coast of Alaska. That gap equals 55 miles. All of these facts point to one idea. Russia stretches across Europe and Asia. It faces northern and eastern waters. It comes very near the United States. Eleven time zones and a land total of 16,377,742 square kilometers help explain that huge reach. What Will You See in Moscow? Moscow is the capital of Russia. A capital is the city where a nation's leaders carry out the main work of government. Moscow is large.

2It lies a short way in from the western border. Over twelve million people make their homes in that city. One famous site there is the Kremlin. In earlier times, people used the Kremlin as a castle. They also used it as a fort. A castle was a strong home for a ruler. A fort was built so people could defend a place. Those were earlier roles. Today the Kremlin is many buildings gathered at one place. Palaces are part of the group. Cathedrals are part of it. Government offices are part of it too. The government of Russia has its center in the Kremlin. The president's official home is inside it as well. A famous plaza called Red Square runs along one end of the Kremlin. A plaza is a broad public square. The Kremlin matters to people in Russia. Red Square matters to them too. Both places matter to people beyond Russia. Care for both places will not stop. Guards will keep them safe. Repair work will keep them standing. Saint Basil's Cathedral dates from the sixteenth century. Those years are the 1500s. It is a sight people around the world connect with this country. When darkness comes, modern skyscrapers in the capital shine with light. A skyscraper is a very tall building raised in modern times. Who Lives Here, and What Do They Speak? Russia covers more ground than any other nation. Even so, population tells a different story. This country ranks tenth for the number of people. About 142 million people live inside its borders. The United States has more than twice that many residents. A 2016 data list from the CIA World Factbook gives a sharper count.

3It lists 142,423,773 people. City life is common. About three fourths of the population live in cities. Language is varied, yet one language leads. About one hundred languages are used in communities spread across the land. Even with that variety, Russian is what most people speak. A country fact list names Russian as the primary language. Writing in Russian uses an alphabet called Cyrillic. Cyrillic comes from the Greek alphabet, but it was changed. Count the letters and you find thirty-three. Set that beside the alphabet used for English. Cyrillic has seven extra letters. These facts belong together. The land is the largest of all, but the population rank is tenth. Most residents choose city homes. They may know one of many local languages, yet Russian is the language that ties daily life and writing together. The thirty-three Cyrillic letters are the signs of that shared writing system. What Work Comes from the Land? A great share of jobs in Russia comes from natural resources. A natural resource is anything people find in nature that has value for humans. People can also use it to make a product. Minerals are one example. Forests are another. About a quarter of the forests on this planet stand in Russia. Because of that, few countries produce more lumber. Fishing is a busy industry with strong growth. Oceans lie along two borders, and that helps the industry. Crews of fishermen pull salmon up in nets. Buyers far away eat fish taken from waters off these coasts. Other resources are present in very large supplies. Coal is one of them. Oil is another. Natural gas is a third. Russia stands among the first three nations that produce oil.

4It holds that same place for natural gas. Put simply, forests, fish, coal, oil, and gas shape daily work. Lumber moves from those forests to buyers. Fish moves from coastal waters to tables in many lands. Oil and natural gas place Russia with the leading producers. The glossary idea of a natural resource fits each of these gifts of land and sea. How Do People Play, and What Art Do They Make? Soccer is a sport many people follow here. Ice hockey is another sport with a wide following. Outdoor pastimes belong to both the summer months and the winter months. Swimming is one pastime. Tennis is another. Volleyball is another. Snowmobiling is another. Ice fishing is another. Sledding is another. Some people also visit hot springs. Chess has deep roots in this country. A large number of the finest chess players anywhere first learned the game in Russia. The arts are strong and full of life. Well-known authors were born on this soil. Well-known poets were born here too. So were well-known writers of classical music. A composer is a person who writes music. Russia has had many composers. Ballet is a field where Russia leads other nations. Swan Lake may be the best-known ballet anywhere. The composer who wrote it is Tchaikovsky. His name is said chy-KAWF-skee. He is one of a long line of famous music writers from Russia. Dancers of the Moscow Ballet present Swan Lake. Play and art sit side by side in daily life. A winter crowd may watch hockey or ride sleds. A concert hall may offer music by Tchaikovsky. A stage may offer ballet. The same country that cheers for soccer also trains chess champions.

5What Shape Does the Land Take? The look of the land changes from one region to another. Russia is a vast territory. Three kinds of features stand out most. One kind is the plain. Another kind is the plateau. Another kind is the mountain. A plateau is flat land that has been lifted, and it covers a wide space. Maps of Russia name the Central Siberian Plateau as one of these high flats. The West Siberian Plain lies in the center of the country. Its area is greater than 2.6 million square kilometers. That is over 1 million square miles. Another plain shown on maps is the Russian Plain. Mountains cover a large share of the territory. In the west, the ranges include the Ural Mountains. More ranges rise across the south. More ranges rise across the east. The Sayan Mountains are one of those ranges. Maps also name the Kamchatka Peninsula. Water cuts through this land in many places. Rivers do that work. Lakes do it too. The depth of Lake Baikal is 1,620 meters, which is 5,315 feet. No lake anywhere is deeper than Lake Baikal. Plains, raised flats, and mountains are the backbone of the map. The West Siberian Plain alone is a huge piece of the center. Lake Baikal then drops farther down than any other lake on Earth. What Are the Wild Regions and the Weather Like? Russia holds several ecosystems. An ecosystem is a community of living things plus the habitat around them. A habitat is the home area those living things use. The north is covered by tundra. Tundra is flat land that stays frozen through the year.

6It accounts for about one tenth of the whole country. South of the tundra is the taiga. Taiga is evergreen forest. Spruce grows in that forest. Pine grows there as well. Those broad forests feed a very large lumber trade. People know this zone as the Russian taiga. Warmer districts grow different trees. Oak is one of those trees. Maple is another. Birch is another. Still farther south, the land opens into wide grasslands. The name for those grasslands is the steppe. The Kulunda Steppe is one named example. The climate is best called very cold. Even the most southern places in Russia sit as far north as Seattle, Washington, or farther from the equator. Most of the remaining country lies even more to the north. Oymyakon is a small village in Siberia. Of every place where people live year after year, it is the coldest. Its lowest recorded temperature is -71 degrees Celsius, or -96 degrees Fahrenheit. Frost leaves some areas for only two months or three months in a full year. Many areas still enjoy lovely summers. From frozen northern ground to southern grass, living communities change with the weather. The taiga supports lumber. The far south offers steppe. Cold rules most months, yet summer can still be pleasant. How Did Rule of the Country Change? The story of Russia is long. For hundreds of years, the rulers were czars and czarinas. A czar was a man who ruled before the revolution that arrived in 1917. A czarina was a woman who ruled in that older time. The word czarina can also mean a czar's wife. Rule by one person who was never elected is a monarchy. A king can be that person.

7A queen can be that person too. The czars belonged to this kind of rule. Until Peter the Great, Russia held little strength among the nations of Europe. He is also known as Peter I. He was ruler from 1682 to 1725. He made the military stronger. He made the economy stronger. His work modernized the country. It raised Russia to the same level as Europe's other powers. The eighteenth century brought Catherine the Great. That century is the 1700s. She is also known as Catherine II, and she ruled from 1762 to 1796. Russia gained important lands while she led. Parts of Poland came under Russian control. Parts of Turkey did too. Years of unrest followed. In 1917, revolution remade politics from top to bottom. That revolution ended monarchy in Russia. In 1922, a new state was formed. Its name was the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. A short name for it is the USSR. The USSR was the earliest country run by a communist government. The word communist fits a system in which government runs the economy, or it fits support for that system. Private persons may not own property under it. Communism aims to make people less unequal. Land would belong to the government. Housing would too. Companies would too. Wealth would be divided in equal parts among the citizens. Russia held control over the countries of the USSR. Ukraine was inside that group. Belarus, Georgia, Azerbaijan, and Armenia are names now used for other members. Azerbaijan is said a-zur-by-ZHAHN. More lands were members too. The capital city for the USSR was Moscow. The union suffered economic troubles and political troubles. Poverty was the result for many people.

8A scene from the 1930s shows poor women of the Soviet Union sharing one bowl of soup. The union had a flag of its own. On December 31, 1991, the USSR ended in an official act. From the next day onward, Russia was not under communist rule. The country now has more of a market economy. In that kind of economy, supply and demand decide prices. They also decide how much is produced. Control by the government is not what sets those choices. Businesses vie with one another. Government does not direct them. Near the time when the USSR fell, elected presidents began to lead. A parliament shares in that leadership. A parliament is a set of government officials. Those officials are able to create laws for a nation. They are able to revise laws as well. Which Holidays and Faiths Shape the Year? Russia has not chosen a single religion as the official one. The Russian Orthodox Church is still the main religious body. A fact list names two primary religions. They are Russian Orthodox and Muslim. Christmas is celebrated by many people here. In the Russian Orthodox Church, the date is January 7. The date is not December 25. Easter is a major holiday as well. Families usually bake goods for this day and pass them around to share. They also paint eggs that have already been boiled hard. Muslims form a large part of the population. A Muslim person is someone tied to the faith of Islam, or the word describes that faith. In Ramadan, which is a holy month, Muslim people do not eat until the sun has set. Two national holidays sit on the calendar.

9June 12 is Independence Day. May 9 is Victory Day. Victory Day recalls the moment World War II came to a close. Maslenitsa is an old holiday for winter's finish. Say the name MOSS-leenyit-sah. The star of the meal is a pancake. One pancake is a blini, and the plural is blinis. Say that word BLEE-nees. Each blini is a sign of the Sun. The usual topping is butter. Some tables add caviar. Some add berries. Some add sour cream. During a Maslenitsa celebration, a woman might be cooking these pancakes. Outdoor fun is part of the day. People go out on sleigh rides. People toss snowballs in friendly battles. Saint Petersburg has been the scene of one cheerful battle of that kind. In some communities, bears dance so the crowd can watch. Faith, national memory, and old seasonal custom all appear on this calendar. January 7, Easter eggs, Ramadan evenings, June 12, May 9, and pancake week each carry a different meaning. What Foods Do People Share, and What Lasts? Borscht is a soup loved in Russia and known far beyond it. Cooks build it from beets and from cabbage. They add further root vegetables. Onions are among them. Carrots are among them. Beets turn the soup red, and that color makes it easy to recognize. You may eat a bowl while it is hot. You may eat a bowl while it is cold. Some people mix a drink called kvass in their own homes. It is a traditional drink. The method follows a set order. Stale bread is soaked in water, and yeast is added. Raisins may be added at times. Mint may be added at times.

10The mix is then left to rest for several days. The result tastes sharp, with a sour edge. Kvass can also become the base of okroshka, another traditional soup. Cucumbers go into okroshka. Meat goes in, and sausages are one choice. Salami is another choice. Eggs that have been boiled go in too. This soup is put on the table cold. Summer is the season when people eat it. Before the twentieth century, most food had to be kept from going bad. It had to survive winters that were long and cold. Salt was one tool. Pickling was another tool. Drying was another tool. Some homes still use those methods. They do so in honor of custom. Restaurants in every region now offer meals drawn from many lands. The pattern is strongest in the major cities. Moscow is one such city. Saint Petersburg is another. The wider country holds many landscapes and many ways of living. One picture is busy Moscow. Another picture is forests that are huge and wild. One kind of work is mining for coal. Another kind is dancing ballet. Natural resources supply the base of many jobs in the economy. The currency of the country is called the ruble. History here has been long, and it has often been hard. In about one hundred years, rule passed from monarchy into a communist state. After that, it became a free market economy. Culture means the shared ideas of a group, along with the group's customs. Through every change, people here still take joy in old celebrations and in old foods. The culture of Russia keeps growing in a homeland that is beautiful and full of winter.

8. Beautiful Stones from Underground

1The parts of this book come in this order. An opening. How gems form. A try-it activity. How gems become jewelry. What makes gems valuable. Hardness and the Mohs scale. Some kinds of gems. A closing. A word list. Many people call gems the most beautiful thing Earth creates. Even a tiny piece of that beauty can cost them thousands of dollars. Sparkling gems are worn on fingers, on necks, and on wrists by people around the world. Families pass gems down through generations. Gems can be found on crowns that royalty wears. They can be found on sacred religious objects. Many gems decorate the most beautiful and the most valuable jewelry. Any beautiful stone fit for jewelry counts as a gem. Most gems sparkle, or they show beautiful colors. They are hard enough to stand up to daily wear. Gems fall into three major types. Minerals make up the first two types, which are crystals and stones. Minerals are the natural, nonliving substances that make up ordinary rocks. Crystals are very pure minerals. They form in tight shapes and in neat patterns. Stones are mixed minerals. They have beautiful colors and patterns, but they lack strict shapes. The third group, organic gems, comes from substances that living things make. A picture shows garnet, a crystal, at the top. Turquoise, a stone, is in the center. A natural pearl, an organic gem, is at the bottom. How gems form is the next topic. Some of the most famous and costly gems are crystals. Diamonds, emeralds, and rubies are examples. Crystals are extremely pure forms of minerals. Every mineral is made of millions of particles called atoms. Atoms are so small that the naked eye cannot see them. Ordinary rocks hold many kinds of atoms tossed together without a tight order. They have no pattern and no order. In crystals, the atoms are arranged very precisely.

2The patterns are neat and orderly. Crystals have flat sides called faces. The faces form shapes. Different kinds of crystals form in different shapes. Some of those shapes are shown here. Some crystals form cubes. Others form long columns with six sides. The shape names shown are trigonal, cubic, tetragonal, monoclinic, and hexagonal. A diagram of a volcano shows where diamonds form. They form deep inside Earth's mantle. Eruptions of volcanoes carry them up to the surface. Labels mark magma, pressure from gravity, layers of Earth's crust, the mantle, heat, and diamonds. Very special conditions far underground are where most crystals grow. Diamonds are one example. They grow when layers of rock squeeze the mineral, which means it is compressed. The compression forces the atoms into the smallest shape possible. Others, such as sapphires, form when a mineral inside Earth grows so hot that it melts. As it cools slowly, the atoms fall into place. They form a regular crystal pattern. Opals belong to a further group. They grow after minerals dissolve in water. Very slow drying of the water leaves mineral behind, and that mineral becomes a crystal. Try this, and make your own crystals. When salty seas dry up, they leave rock salt. Another name for it is halite. You can watch a much smaller version of that same process. You need only water and ordinary salt. Step 1. A cup of warm water gets one tablespoon of salt stirred in. Stir until the salt dissolves. Step 2. Add more salt in small amounts. Stop when no more salt will dissolve. Step 3. Put a clean toothpick in the water. Step 4. Place the cup somewhere warm in the sun. Crystals grow on the toothpick while the water dries away. They also grow on the cup's sides. Step 5. Look at the crystals under a magnifying glass.

3What do they look like? The minerals in stones do not form orderly patterns. Other minerals may be mixed in. Stones often form in layers. The layers make streaks and lines. That pattern is called the grain. Beautiful patterns and surfaces on stones come from the grain. Organic gems include pearls, amber, and coral. They come from living things. Pearls usually begin when something gets trapped inside an oyster's shell. The trapped thing may be a tiny worm or another living thing. It may be a broken bit of shell. The oyster covers it with layers of smooth nacre. Nacre is the same material the oyster uses to build its shell. A common wrong belief says pearls begin from grains of sand trapped inside. Oysters are actually quite able to push sand out of their shells. They create jets of water that shoot the sand out. Millions of tiny sea creatures leave skeletons, and those skeletons form coral. Those creatures are called coral polyps. Amber began millions of years ago. Sticky sap oozed from trees and hardened. Amber often holds the fossils of insects and of spiders that got caught in the sap. A picture shows a spider in amber. How gems become jewelry is the next topic. Most mineral gems are found deep inside Earth. People get them by digging mines. Because gems are so small and so rare, mining is often still done by hand. Workers chip and cut at the rock. They look for single stones set inside it. Finding gems takes a great deal of work. It is expensive. Value rises when a gem is rarer and when finding it is harder. Opals form when water rich in minerals evaporates from cracks underground. A streak of mineral crystal is left in the rock. Veins is the name given to streaks of crystal.

4Underground veins hold the world's best opals. The place is the Australian desert town of Coober Pedy. Coober Pedy, in the Australian Aborigine language, has the meaning white man in a hole. Opal mines are simple holes in the ground. A gem just dug up by a miner looks unlike the gem later set in a ring or a necklace. Rough edges are common on it, and the surface is often dull. Its shape is bumpy. Cracks are common in gems. So are dark marks, bubbles, and other flaws. Gem cutters are called lapidaries. They cut gems into regular shapes. The shapes highlight the best qualities and hide the flaws. Gem cutters once used saws and polishers edged with diamond. Recently they began using lasers to cut gems. A picture shows an uncut diamond that looks uneven and flawed. Flat surfaces called facets are cut on most crystal gems. Facets show off the gem's color and pattern. They let the gem sparkle with reflected light. Lapidaries cut different gems with several different styles. A picture shows a cut diamond reflecting a lot of sparkle. The cutting styles, shown from the top and from the side, are step, brilliant, carving, rose, and cabochon. These styles display each gem's best traits. Diamonds often receive the popular style called the brilliant cut. Diamonds have more sparkle than color. Light bounces off the gem from the many facets in this style. Deep green emeralds, by contrast, are often cut in a style called the step cut. That style has rectangular facets. It creates a wide, flat top of pure color. Another style, the rose cut, has a rounded top and triangular facets. It is most often found on older gems. The oldest style of cut is the cabochon, said KAB-uh-shon. It is simply rounded and polished. It is most often used with stones that are opaque or patterned.

5Small sculptures can be carved from other gems, including jade and coral. What makes gems valuable comes next. As a group, gems are valuable for two reasons. They are beautiful. They are rare. Gem prices shift over time. Certain gemstones have been called precious through the ages and in many cultures. Diamonds, for example, have always been seen as valuable. Their value has risen in a dramatic way in the last century. This happened even though the supply of diamonds grew a great deal in that same time. Several large finds in South Africa caused the supply to grow. Diamonds became more valuable in the last century partly because diamond engagement rings grew more popular around the world. Higher prices also come from global marketing by companies that sell diamonds. The value of one gem is set by the gem's hardness and by a system called the four Cs. The four Cs are cut, carat weight, color, and clarity. Cut means how well the gem is cut and polished. It can also mean how beautiful the natural gem is. Dullness or an uneven look can follow a poor cut. Carat weight is the size of the stone. One carat weighs about the same as a kernel of unpopped popcorn. Color, the next of the four Cs, is a major reason gems are seen as beautiful. Unlike regular rocks, gems have bright, pure, intense colors. The stronger and purer the color is, the more valuable the gem is. The same mineral can often form gems of different colors. Red rubies and blue sapphires contain the same mineral. Tiny bits of other chemicals, mixed into the main mineral, create the different colors. It takes only one different atom in a thousand to change a gem's color. Clarity means how free of flaws the gem is. Gems with dark marks, cracks, and bubbles are less valuable.

6Cloudy gems are less valuable too. Gems without these flaws are worth more. Even so, clarity is often not as important as the size of a gem or its rarity. Emeralds often have many flaws. A flawed emerald can be worth more than a flawless diamond, since emeralds are so rare. A picture shows an uncut emerald with many cracks and other flaws. Hardness and the Mohs scale come next. Hardness shows how pure and how tightly structured the mineral in a gemstone is. Daily wear is another test this measure gives for a gem. A geologist named Friedrich Mohs made a scale to test gemstone hardness. The test is simple. One gem is used to scratch another. A gem can scratch only gems that are softer than it is. The softest mineral is talc. Talc cannot scratch anything else. Talc is a 1 on the Mohs scale. Diamonds are the hardest substance on Earth. They are a 10 on the Mohs scale. A diamond can scratch anything. Only another diamond can scratch a diamond. Jewelry needs most gems to score 5 or higher, so they stay strong enough. On the scale, 1 is talc. 2 is gypsum. 3 is calcite. 4 is fluorite. 5 is apatite. 6 is orthoclase. 7 is quartz. 8 is topaz. 9 is emerald. 10 is diamond. The Mohs scale measures how hard various gems are. A fingernail, for comparison, measures 2.5 in hardness. A penknife measures 5.5. Some kinds of gems come next. Diamonds form very deep in the ground. The depth is generally 140 to 190 kilometers, or 90 to 120 miles, beneath Earth's surface. Huge pressure and high temperatures create them. Volcanic pipes let magma carry diamonds up near the surface. In a few cases, diamonds have also been found in deposits left by melting glaciers.

7The diamonds that reach Earth's surface may be up to three billion years old. No natural substance in the world is harder than diamonds. Flawed diamonds, and ones that are not attractive, often go onto saws and onto drill tips. They can cut metal, stone, and anything else. Most diamonds are almost colorless. An intense yellow is possible in very rare diamonds. So is an intense red, or an intense blue. Diamonds are most often found in Russia and in Canada. They are also found in several African countries, including Botswana, Angola, and South Africa. Engagement rings use diamonds more than almost any other stone. One of the most famous diamonds is the Hope diamond. It is not famous for its size. It is famous for its intense sky-blue color. A long history of theft, and of ownership by royalty and by wealthy people, gave it a reputation for being cursed. The largest diamond ever found was found in South Africa. It is the Cullinan diamond. It weighed over 3,100 carats. It was as large as a pineapple. It was cut into nine gems. One of those gems, the Greater Star of Africa, weighs 530 carats. A picture shows the Hope diamond, one of the most famous diamonds in the world. Pencil lead, called graphite, is the very same mineral that forms diamonds. In graphite, the atoms sit in loose layers. Those layers make graphite very soft. It is so soft that rubbing it on paper breaks atoms off. The broken atoms leave a pencil mark. In diamonds, those same atoms have been squeezed together very tightly. Nothing except another diamond can scratch them off. Corundum, also called aluminum oxide, is the mineral in both rubies and sapphires. Rubies are one of the rarest gems on Earth. To be classed properly as rubies, they must be truly blood-red or pink.

8Ruber, a Latin word for red, is where the name ruby comes from. Chromium, an element, causes the famous red of rubies. Any other form of the mineral corundum is considered a sapphire, no matter the color. Sapphires are known mainly for their deep blue color. One feature can occur in both rubies and sapphires. It is an asterism. An asterism is a bright star-shaped pattern inside the stone. Titanium oxide causes it by reflecting light in a very brilliant way. Star sapphires and star rubies are highly valuable. Few gems anywhere are wanted more than these. A picture shows a red ruby and two sapphires, one blue and one yellow. Among crystals, no family is more common than quartz. Quartz is found all over the world. It comes in all the colors of the rainbow. Nearly anyone can pay for most quartz, because it is so common. About 6 meters, or 20 feet, was the length of the largest quartz crystal ever found. It weighed more than 44,000 kilograms, or 48 tons. That is more than a loaded truck with eighteen wheels. Opal, a stone of many colors, is the quartz worth the most. Opal shimmers with white, with blue, and with red-orange. Australia is where opals turn up most often. A picture shows quartz crystals, which are common and can grow very large. An incredible green is what emeralds are known for. Emeralds of gem quality are rare and usually small. Egypt is where emeralds were first found, several thousand years ago. Colombia is where the finest emeralds are found today. Beryl is the same mineral that forms emeralds. It also forms a blue-green stone called aquamarine. Few stones are prized more than jade. It occurs in lavender, in white, and in almost every shade of green. Green is the most valuable. Jade is incredibly tough.

9Even so, it is easy to carve along its grain. Beautiful knives, swords, and axes were made from jade by many civilizations, especially in Asia. Pictures show a jade figurine and a person carving jade. Turquoise is often speckled and striped with black. Blue-green turquoise comes from the deserts of Iran, of Tibet, and of the southwestern United States. Pretty spots often run through this stone, and so do streaks. Much of the world's turquoise is set in silver. The Navajo Native Americans traditionally wore it that way. The Navajo believed turquoise was pieces of the sky that had fallen to Earth. Natural pearls are strangely shaped. They are extremely rare. An oyster needs two or more years to create a pearl. Jewelry stores sell beautiful round pearls that are almost all cultured. Cultured means made with human help. Pearl farmers insert a round bead of shell into an oyster's shell. The oyster covers the bead with nacre. Some types form a perfectly round pearl in six months. Other types need several years. Cultured pearls come in every color of the rainbow. Creamy white is one color. Pink, yellow, green, and even black appear as well. Gemologists are scientists who study the chemical makeup of gemstones. Sometimes a gemologist is an expert in one gemstone, such as diamonds or rubies. Gemologists who work in the laboratory can often tell which area of the world a gem came from. They do this by examining its chemical makeup. They can also tell natural gems from synthetic gems. They study clues inside the gems. Those clues give information about how the gem formed. A picture shows that natural pearls are rare and oddly shaped, while cultured pearls are round. A picture shows a strip mine clearing an immense area of land. Beautiful gems can be found around the world. Many gems stand for power and for wealth.

10For centuries, people have killed for them and have died for them. Blood and violence still fill the gem trade in some places, including West Africa and Colombia. Mining gems with dynamite and with strip mines is often dangerous. The work damages both humans and Earth. Scientists can grow gems in the lab. Those gems are identical to the finest natural gems. They cost a thousand times less. In the future, created gems might help fill our wish for the beauty of gemstones. At the same time, they might help protect Earth and its people. Word list. Grain is a noun. Grain means the lines and patterns that mineral layers leave in a stone. An asterism is a noun. It is a star-shaped reflective pattern inside a gem. Atoms are a noun. They are the smallest units of a chemical element. Lapidaries are a noun. They are gem cutters. Magma is a noun. It is melted, liquid rock beneath Earth's surface. Crystals are a noun. They are minerals formed in regular, tight patterns. Cultured is an adjective. It means made with the help of human beings. Nacre is a noun. Oysters build shells from nacre. They also build pearls from it. Embedded is an adjective. It means buried in, or surrounded by. Opaque is an adjective. It means not see-through. Facets are a noun. They are the flat surfaces of a cut gemstone. Organic gems are a noun. They are gems made from substances that living things created. Fluctuate is a verb. It means to change, or to shift back and forth, or up and down. Polyps are a noun. They are small sea invertebrates, such as coral. They have a tube-like body and a mouth with tentacles. Gemologists are a noun. They are scientists who study the chemical makeup of gemstones.

9. Black Cavalrymen Known as Buffalo Soldiers

1A memorial stands in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. It honors Black soldiers. Every war of the United States is part of what it honors. This book tells how a new army formed. It tells why men joined. It tells about duty out west. It tells how a reputation grew. It tells about later service. It tells how discrimination went on. It tells what the buffalo soldiers left behind. Word meanings come last. The Revolutionary War effort of the United States included help from more than 5,000 Black soldiers. They helped the country gain independence from Great Britain. Nearly a hundred years later, another large group served. The Northern Union Army had help from more than 170,000 Black soldiers. They helped win the Civil War in 1865. Only after that war could Black men join the United States Army in peacetime. The Army Reorganization Act became law in 1866. Black soldiers received their first peacetime regiments from that act. Many Black men who joined had served in the Union Army. Others had formerly been enslaved. The first all-Black units were infantry regiments. They were the 38th through the 41st. The 9th Cavalry Regiment was also among the first. So was the 10th Cavalry Regiment. Infantry soldiers fought on foot. Cavalry soldiers rode horses. Native peoples of the Great Plains gave a name to the men of the 10th Cavalry. They called them buffalo soldiers.

2Soon the name was used for all the men who served in these regiments. A picture shows the 10th Cavalry in 1898. Sharecropping was the work of many Black people once the Civil War ended. A sharecropper is a farmer who rents land from the owner. The farmer also rents supplies. In exchange, the owner receives part of the crop. New laws came from white lawmakers in the South once slavery ended in the United States. The laws greatly restricted the freedom of Black people. People called these racist laws the Black codes. Employment was required of Black people. They also limited the kinds of jobs Black people could hold. The jobs were usually farming. They were usually service positions. Black people had to sign work contracts every year. The pay was very low. If they did not sign, they would be arrested. For a time they would have to labor without pay. The labor might be in prison. It might be for a white employer. Union Army fighters from the Civil War appear in a picture. Equal salary for every soldier began in the army in 1864. Race did not change the pay. White workers earned much more than Black workers at most jobs. Fair pay was rare for a Black man outside the army. Army pay beat what most of them could earn in other work. They also received food.

3They received clothes. They received medical care. They received shelter. Many of these men had been enslaved. They had been kept from a formal education. The army gave them a chance to learn to read. It gave them a chance to learn to write. Black soldiers still faced severe racial discrimination. Service by Black soldiers was opposed by most white soldiers. Most white officers thought the same. At first, Black soldiers could not rise to the ranks of commanding officers. White officers always led their regiments. Command of Black regiments was refused by many white officers. White civilians showed racism too. They did not want armed Black soldiers near their communities. That is why most Black soldiers were posted far off. They went to the Great Plains. They went to deserts on the western frontier. Women were not allowed to enlist in the United States Army until 1943. Even so, every American war has included important work by Black women. During the Civil War, spies collected information for the Union Army. Mary Jane Richards was one. Harriet Tubman was another. They passed that information along. Guide was another role Tubman took on. She acted as a scout. She went with Union soldiers on raids. The raids were on plantations in the South. She led hundreds of enslaved people to freedom. World War II espionage against the Nazis included actress Josephine Baker.

4She passed information in secret messages. The messages were written in invisible ink. War efforts have received the work of thousands of Black women. They have served as spies. They have served as scouts. They have served as guides. They have served as nurses. They have served as doctors. They have served as soldiers. They did this while facing discrimination based on gender. They also faced racial discrimination. A picture shows Maj. Charity A. Earley inspecting her troops. During World War II she was the highest ranking Black female officer. In the 1800s the United States government wanted to expand the country's borders. The expansion would go west. The government signed many treaties with Native leaders. A treaty is an agreement. The treaties set borders between United States territory and Native territories. The government broke these treaties again and again. The breaks let white pioneers settle on land that belonged to Native peoples. Decades of war followed. The war was between the United States Army and Native peoples. Those peoples were defending lands they had lived on for thousands of years. The Native peoples included the Apache. They included the Comanche. They included the Cheyenne. They included the Kiowa. Others were involved too. As years passed, the army pushed growing numbers of Native peoples from the lands of their ancestors. The people were pushed onto reservations. The land set aside as reservations was small.

5They were usually the poorest farming lands available. They were usually the poorest hunting lands too. A picture shows members of the Lakota Nation. They camp near the Pine Ridge Reservation. The place is South Dakota. The year is 1891. A picture from the 19th century shows a battle. Buffalo soldiers fight Native peoples of the Plains. The year of that battle is 1868. Government officials encouraged a mass killing of buffalo. Settlers took part. Soldiers took part. Officials knew Native peoples depended on the buffalo. Buffalo were crucial to the diet on the Plains. They were crucial to the way of life there. Hunger to the point of starvation was usual on the reservations. Disease spread quickly. The communities were crowded. Many Native peoples resisted the move onto reservations. They fought back against the army. Black soldiers were sent west to fight them. Protection of white settlers was another job given to Black soldiers. The West was vast. It was hard to enforce laws as more white settlers arrived. Outlaws rode freely. They stole cattle. They stole horses. They robbed banks. They robbed stagecoaches. Stagecoaches brought important supplies. They brought mail. Black soldiers were sent to protect settlers from these thieves. They were sent to protect stagecoaches. They were sent to protect railroad crews. Black soldiers were given the hardest duties. They were given the most dangerous duties.

6Some of the country's roughest terrain lay on their route. They searched for water. They built roads. They mapped lands that white settlers had not explored. Summer brought extreme heat that they had to bear. They endured freezing temperatures in the winter. They received old horses. They received supplies that were not adequate. They received damaged equipment. White settlers they were there to protect also showed them hatred. They met violence. Sometimes that violence was deadly. Despite all of this, the troops did their duties well. In time they earned a reputation. People saw them as brave. People saw them as hardworking. People saw them as talented soldiers. Native peoples they fought on the Plains gave them the name buffalo soldiers. Those peoples may have been the Cheyenne. A link to buffalo, many people think, is why Native peoples chose the name. Buffalo fur coats on the soldiers are one suggested source of the name. Others believe the soldiers got the name because they were brave in battle. They were fierce, like the buffalo. Evidence for this belief has not been found. Many Native leaders today challenge the idea. Cathay Williams is known as the one woman who served as a buffalo soldier. The 38th Infantry Regiment took her in during 1866. Women were not allowed to serve as soldiers then. A man's disguise hid who she was.

7She used the name William Cathay. She served for nearly two years. A doctor discovered she was a woman during a hospital visit. She was discharged in 1868. An artist made a picture of her. Buffalo soldiers served in the West through the decades of that war. The war was between the United States Army and Native peoples. Eighteen buffalo soldiers received the Medal of Honor between 1870 and 1890. No United States soldier's award ranks higher than the Medal of Honor. As the wars in the West ended, many Black soldiers were sent to a new fight. They fought in the Spanish-American War. The conflict in 1898 lasted ten weeks. Five more Medals of Honor went to buffalo soldiers. After that war ended, hundreds of buffalo soldiers took a different job. They worked as park rangers in California. They worked at Yosemite National Park. They worked at Sequoia National Park. Between 1899 and 1904 they oversaw the building of roads. They oversaw the building of trails. They fought forest fires. They stopped people from hunting animals. They stopped people from stealing timber. A picture shows buffalo soldiers at Yosemite National Park. In the 1890s the army asked a question about bicycles. Could bikes replace horses? Bikes were cheaper. They were easier to care for. The buffalo soldiers rode 1,900 miles on that test. The distance is 3,057 kilometers. They rode from Missoula, Montana.

8They rode to St. Louis, Missouri. They crossed mountains. They crossed rivers. They crossed shifting sandhills. They still averaged 50 miles a day. That average is 80.4 kilometers. Before long, motorcycles replaced the bikes. A picture shows buffalo soldiers with their bikes. The place is Yellowstone National Park. The year is 1896. The buffalo soldiers had a strong reputation. They had many achievements. Black soldiers still experienced discrimination. White citizens of Brownsville, Texas, brought an accusation in August 1906. They accused buffalo soldiers stationed nearby. They said the soldiers had killed a white man. They said the soldiers had hurt another person. Proof that the soldiers did this was missing. Bed was where the officers said the men were when the shots were fired. President Theodore Roosevelt still gave an order. The order removed 167 Black soldiers from the army. Leaving the army caused them to lose their pensions. A pension is a payment a person receives after army service ends. A new investigation came in 1972. Only then were the soldiers found innocent of the crime. World War I lasted from 1914 to 1918. President Woodrow Wilson followed racist policies. Those policies kept Black soldiers from a role in Europe. They could not join white United States soldiers in battle there. Command over them went to the French army instead. A picture shows Black soldiers arriving home after service in World War I.

9World War II included the United States starting in 1941. Those regiments, called buffalo soldiers, had already been broken up. They had been reorganized. Black soldiers and white soldiers stayed separated until the 1950s. When Black troops finally joined white regiments, racism did not stop. They endured it from fellow officers. They endured it from fellow soldiers. Three men stand out among the buffalo soldiers. Lt. Henry O. Flipper was the first Black graduate of the United States Military Academy. No Black student had graduated before him. The academy is at West Point in New York. Command of Black soldiers by a Black officer began with him. Lt. John Hanks Alexander took command of the 9th Cavalry in 1887. No other Black officer then held a commission to lead troops in combat. He was commissioned to lead troops in combat. Col. Charles Young was a commanding officer of the 9th Cavalry. The first Black national park superintendent was his role starting in 1903. Since the Revolutionary War, every major American conflict has included Black soldiers. The buffalo soldiers of the original 9th Cavalry are perhaps the best known. The original 10th Cavalry is just as well known. People have written books about them. People have made movies. People have made television shows. People have even written songs. People have built museums in their honor. People have built monuments.

10The monuments stand in Kansas. They stand in Alabama. They stand in Texas. Buffalo soldiers faced severe racial discrimination. Sometimes it was fatal. The discrimination came from inside the army. It came from outside the army too. Even so, leaving their units was rarer for them than for other soldiers. They showed incredible courage. They faced fierce combat. They faced deadly violence. They faced harsh living conditions. United States history includes their service as an important part. A monument honors their memory. It is the Buffalo Soldier Monument. It stands in Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. These words have special meanings in this book. Ancestral points to family or tribal generations that lived earlier. Contracts are formal or legal written agreements. They are between two or more people. A disease is an illness. Evidence is something that supports a theory or a claim. Fierce means very powerful, forceful, or violent. Regiments are military units. Each one holds at least two large groups of soldiers. Reputation is the general way that other people think of a person or a thing. Restricted means limited or controlled. A salary is set pay for work, usually figured by the year. It is usually calculated per year. Severe means extremely harsh or unpleasant. Starvation is extreme hunger. It can mean death because of a lack of food. Terrain is the natural form of a piece of land.

10. Brazil across a Wide Continent

1Brazil sits in the eastern part of South America. Nearly half the continent is taken up by this one country. The whole United States is only a little larger. Brazil’s eastern half reaches into the Atlantic Ocean. Size is the reason the Atlantic shore runs so far. Measured along the Atlantic, the shore passes 7,400 kilometers. That length is 4,600 miles. Crossing the entire United States is a shorter trip. Brazil’s shore is almost twice that distance. A map around Brazil also marks Guyana, Venezuela, Suriname, and French Guiana. It marks Colombia, Peru, and São Luis. It marks Brasília, Bolivia, and the Pacific Ocean. Rio de Janeiro is marked on that map. So is the city of São Paulo. Paraguay is marked too. It marks Argentina, Uruguay, North America, and South America. Many smaller countries share Brazil’s western border. Venezuela is one of them. Colombia is one. Peru is one. Bolivia is one. Paraguay is one. Argentina is one. Uruguay is one. Every other country in South America touches Brazil except two. Ecuador is one exception. Chile is the other. For many years the capital was Rio de Janeiro, on the eastern coast.

2Say Rio as REE-oh DAY, then zhuh-NAIR-oh. A new capital was chosen in the 1950s. Builders placed Brasília near the country’s center. Say Brasília as bruh-ZIL-yuh. Clearing a huge wild area was part of the giant job. Roads had to connect Brasília to other parts of Brazil. An artificial lake was in the plan, and it had to be dug. The official capital changed to Brasília in 1960. Planners expected only a few hundred thousand residents. Residents passed two million early in the present century. Problems nobody had fully planned for followed that growth. The artificial lake grew dirty. A plant was required to clean the water. The web of highways now puts wild places at risk. The Amazon rainforest is one of those places. Brazil, like many countries, mixes many ethnic groups. European descent accounts for about half the people. Portuguese ancestors are the largest European share. Say Portuguese as POR-chuh-geez. Spanish ancestors are part of the mix. Italian ancestors are part of it. German ancestors are part of it.

3Polish ancestors are part of it. Portugal held Brazil as a colony for three hundred years. Portuguese is the country’s main language. Other Brazilians descend from people of Angola and of the Congo. They were enslaved and shipped in as laborers. Big farms used that labor. Mines used it too. Still others descend from Native peoples who lived in South America first. In every group of ten Brazilians, about four have mixed ancestry. Industry is concentrated in the big city of São Paulo. Say it SOW, then POW-loh. Brazil’s residents number more than two hundred million. Eight out of ten of them live in cities. No city in South America is larger than São Paulo. City growth over the past sixty years has been rapid. Problems have come with that speed. People with little money have had to settle on vacant ground beside the cities. Homes there are built from whatever materials can be found. Service work employs some people, including banking. Construction is another service field. Education is another. Health care is another. Coastal hotels and restaurants employ people as well.

4Away from cities, mining provides jobs. Oil work provides jobs. Farmers raise sugarcane. They also raise a large share of the world’s coffee. Agriculture matters greatly to the country. Oranges are produced. Soybeans are produced. Pork, cattle, and chicken are produced. Lumber is produced. Ranching in the far south has a long history. Ranch cowboys known as gauchos were at work by the 1500s. Say gauchos as GOW-chohz. Cattle were in their care. Sheep were in their care. Horses were in their care. Clothing, songs, and dances of their own grew up over the centuries. Ranches in southern Brazil still employ modern gauchos. Landform maps show the Guiana Highlands and the Amazon River. They show the Amazon Basin and the Brazilian Highlands. They show Brasília and the Pantanal Wetlands. They show the coastal lowlands, the Pacific Ocean, and the Atlantic Ocean. The Amazon River and the Amazon rainforest, both inside the Amazon basin, are what Brazil is famous for. This rainforest is the world’s largest tropical rainforest. Its nickname is lungs of the planet. Oxygen used around the world gets about 20 percent of its supply from those plants.

5Highlands appear in two regions. Mountain ranges fill the far north. Steep cliffs are there. Waterfalls are there. Deep valleys are there. Southeast Brazil holds the larger highlands, with both hills and low mountains. The capybara, native to the Pantanal, is the world’s largest rodent. The Pantanal, in central Brazil, is one of the largest freshwater ecosystems on Earth. Its reach can pass 210,000 square kilometers. That area is 81,000 square miles. Rivers flood the land in the wet season, from October through March. Waters then rise several meters. Later the waters recede. An amazing variety of life is supported. Downstream places are protected from floodwater during the wet season. The dry season brings a steady release of water downstream. Pollutants are removed, so the region works like a giant water treatment plant. Transportation uses its waterways. Earth’s water cycle depends on the region in an important way. Sandy beaches along the eastern coastal lowlands draw many tourists. The Guarani were among the first known peoples. The Yanomami were among them too.

6Rainforests are still home to some of these groups. The Amazon’s shores are still home to some of them. Portugal conquered the area in the early sixteenth century. At first the land was used to collect a wood called pau brasil, or brazilwood. Say it POW, then brah-SEEL. Native peoples were enslaved by the Portuguese. Huge fields of sugarcane were the forced workplace. Later, millions of African people were enslaved and brought over. Coffee plantations used their labor. Diamond mines used their labor. Gold mines used their labor. Added together, the Caribbean and North America received fewer enslaved Africans than Brazil did. Independence came in 1822, under Emperor Pedro I. Slavery ended in 1888. In 1889 the military forced Pedro II to step down. Dictators led the country for the next hundred years. Turmoil and uprisings filled those years. Democracy arrived in 1985. Serious challenges remain. Poverty presses on the people. Unemployment presses on them. Deforestation threatens the natural environment. Carnaval fills Rio’s Sambadrome with singers and with dancers. They ride elaborate floats. The dance they perform is the samba. Religion shapes many holidays.

7The Catholic faith is the religion of most people in Brazil. The Portuguese brought that religion. Carnaval lasts four days and leads up to Lent. It is the largest holiday. It is also the most popular. Streets fill with crowds for parades and for dancing. Elaborate costumes are worn, with masks and with headdresses. Preparation lasts all year. Rio de Janeiro has samba schools. Dancers there practice all year. Enslaved African people brought the samba many years ago. The planet’s widest mix of living things is here. Thousands of insect kinds live in the Amazon rainforest by itself. Thousands of kinds of fish live there. Thousands of kinds of birds live there. Reptiles live there in huge variety. Amphibians do too. Mammals do too. Some are beautiful. Some are dangerous. A toucan, said TOO-kan, is easy to know by its bill. The bill is brightly colored and almost as long as the body. Black shows in the feathers. White shows in them. Green shows in them. Yellow shows in them. Red shows in them. Toucans are heard constantly. Sightings are rare.

8The birds keep to the treetops. The rainforest’s bright frogs are beautiful. Few creatures anywhere carry a stronger poison. Touch alone can kill, for some species. Many of these frogs get their skin poison from the harmful foods they eat. Red-bellied piranhas, said pi-RAH-nuhz, hunt in the Amazon River. A pack may hold one hundred of these fish. Some packs are even larger. Teeth on these meat-eaters are very sharp. Their jaws are strong. Animal flesh is their food. Humans are rarely attacked. Dead animals are the usual meal. Hyacinth macaws and the giant anteater live in these lands. A snakelike fish in the river can shock. It is the electric eel. Length can reach almost 2 meters, or 6 feet. Weight can reach almost 22 kilograms, or 48 pounds. Prey is stunned by a strong electric shock. Enemies are stunned by it too. The Pantanal holds fascinating animals as well. Storks build nests in its swamps. Herons build nests there. Parrots of many colors pass in the sky. On the ground, giant anteaters wander. Jaguars roam it. Deer roam it.

9Habitat loss could erase some animals of the Amazon rainforest and of the Pantanal from Earth forever. A destroyed share of the Amazon rainforest already stands above one fifth. The loss cannot be undone. Saving what remains is shared work for many groups and for Brazil’s government. Futebol, also called soccer, is a sport many Brazilians love to watch and to play. Say futebol as FOOT-bohl. The World Cup is the world’s largest soccer tournament. Brazil has won it more often than any other country. The most famous player from this country is Pelé, and the world knows his name. He led Brazil to World Cup victory three times. The years were 1958, 1962, and 1970. Land, animals, and people of many kinds give Brazil its color. Life of many kinds fills the Amazon River. It fills the Amazon rainforest. It fills the Pantanal. People here are diverse. The culture is vibrant. Celebrations are amazing. No other place feels quite like it. Population is 211,049,527. Land area is 8,458,417 square kilometers. The same area is 3,265,813 square miles. Brasília is the capital.

10Portuguese is the primary language. Catholic is the primary religion. The currency is the real, said ray-AHL. Figures come from the Central Intelligence Agency in 2019 and from the World Bank. A basin is a low place, a depression, in Earth’s surface. Highlands are lands full of mountains, set high above the sea. The word Catholic points to the Roman Catholic Church. That church is one branch of Christianity. A plantation is a large farm with many workers. Samba is a rhythmic Brazilian dance that began in Africa, and it is also the music for that dance. Deforestation means clearing trees and other plants out of an area. Sugarcane is a tropical grass, and sugar comes from it. A dictator holds complete power. Force is the usual way that power is kept. Toxic means poisonous and dangerous to life. An ecosystem is living things together with the places they inhabit. The water cycle is water’s path, and the changes it passes through, as it moves in the environment. Gauchos are cowboys of the grassy plains of South America.

11. Cars Powered by Electricity

1The parts of this book come in this order. Caught in traffic. What an electric car is. The first electric cars. Steam, electricity, or gas. Why the electric car faded. A return of interest. Another return. What may come next. A word list. Teens get on a school bus in Miami, Florida. You grab your lunch and your backpack. Then you head out the door. Before you see the bus round the corner and turn down your street, you hear its engine rumble. It is the school bus. The other kids on your block already wait at the bus stop. You run and join the line just as the bus pulls up. You wait while schoolmates board ahead of you. Heat from the exhaust warms your legs. Fumes reach your nose and your mouth, and you taste them. At last you climb aboard. You find your favorite seat. You glance out the window as the bus speeds away from the curb. Only a moment seems to pass before the bus stops. A look out the window shows why. Cars, trucks, and motorcycles are everywhere. None of them are moving. You are in a traffic jam. The kid across from you cannot be heard, because the noise is so loud. The end of the racket is what you start to wonder about. Surprisingly, smelly and noisy traffic could have ended long ago. That could have happened if the electric car had grown more popular early on. A picture shows school buses moving through traffic in Toronto, Ontario. What is an electric car? The 1830s brought the first electric cars, through Robert Anderson, a man from Scotland. The first carriage that ran on electricity was his invention. A fellow Scot, Robert Davidson, and an American, Thomas Davenport, built electric vehicles in 1842.

2Those vehicles used electric cells as a power source. The cells could not be recharged. The power source had to be replaced often. Two Frenchmen created a better store of power, and then improved it. Gaston Plante did this work in 1865. Camille Faure did it in 1881. Their source could hold more electricity, and it could be recharged. It was the lead-acid battery. A picture shows Gaston Plante, a French physicist, with his lead-acid battery. In 1899, Jenatzy, a famous race car driver, went faster than 100 miles per hour in an electric car. That lead-acid battery marked a huge breakthrough. Makers build these batteries with sulfuric acid and lead. When the acid eats at the lead, a chemical reaction occurs. An electric charge is created. This charge powers the motor until the battery needs a recharge. After the lead-acid battery was invented, electric cars grew more popular. France and Great Britain, for several years, were ahead of the world in building electric vehicles. The United States did not join in until 1891. That year, A. L. Ryker built an electric tricycle. William Morrison built an electric wagon for six passengers. Suddenly, America was hooked. Early test models of electric cars were built in large numbers. New York City, in 1897, purchased a whole fleet of electric taxis. The seller was the Electric Carriage and Wagon Company of Philadelphia. The taxis looked almost like horse carriages, except the horse was gone. They cost nearly 2,000 dollars each. That would be at least 50,000 dollars today. A picture shows an advertisement from 1903. By steam, by electricity, or by gas is the next question. By the start of the twentieth century, cars had grown far more popular in America. More and more people were moving to cities. They wanted greater mobility.

3Inventors answered the demand quickly. They took up different technology. They devised many new and original ways to power vehicles. This led to cars powered by steam and by gasoline, along with electric cars. Sales of electric cars soared in 1899 and in 1900. The main reason was that rivals lacked what electric cars offered. Electric cars did not shake the way gasoline cars did. Their motors did not make the sharp smell and the loud noise of gasoline cars. Gear changes on gasoline cars turned out to be a bother as well. Drivers were often seen struggling with the gear shifter. Electric vehicles did not need a gear change. Steam vehicles did not need one either. Steam cars, however, took a long time to start. The wait was sometimes as much as forty-five minutes. Cold mornings made the wait especially long. Gasoline cars also took time to start. Drivers had to turn a hand crank. Range, meaning the distance traveled, was a problem for these early cars. Steam cars could go only a short distance before they needed more water. Electric cars had the advantage. On a single charge they could travel farther than steam cars. At that time, the best roads were in cities. Most travel was local. That situation made electric cars popular. They could ride smoothly and quietly for short distances. A standard electric car cost a little less than 1,000 dollars. Makers of electric vehicles wanted to reach richer buyers. Designers created huge, ornate carriages. The showy interiors used costly materials. Those changes pushed the price to almost 3,000 dollars by 1910. The higher price would haunt the electric car for years. In 1911, Rauch and Lang, a vehicle maker in Ohio, offered one of the highest-priced electric vehicles for sale. A picture shows the Lohner Porsche Mixte of 1900.

4Hybrid cars were invented too, a bit more than one hundred years in the past. A car is a hybrid when it runs on two different energy sources, such as electricity and gas. The first hybrid car came from Ferdinand Porsche in Germany, and the year was 1898. Generators were spun by a gasoline engine in his design. The electricity produced went to the electric motors that powered the car. After the first rush of interest in electric vehicles for short trips in town, production and sales dropped fast. The high price was not the only cause. By the 1920s, cities in the United States had expanded their road systems. Motorists could travel between cities on good roads. This change created a need for vehicles that could go greater distances, like the gasoline car. An important breakthrough was Charles Kettering's invention of the electric starter. The starter used electric power. Gasoline cars no longer needed that difficult hand crank. Oil was found in Texas around that same time. Gasoline became easier and cheaper to produce. It became much more affordable for the average driver. A picture shows cows in Texas fields that now also held oil rigs. Many cars sat unused in 1973 because gas was short. Other drivers waited in long lines to buy what gas was available. In time, Henry Ford's assembly lines allowed gasoline cars to be made in huge numbers. As a result, Ford could sell his vehicles cheaply. At the start, the price ran between 500 and 1,000 dollars. Gasoline cars became cheaper and cheaper to make and to sell. At one point in 1912, an electric car with fancy designs sold for about 1,750 dollars. A gasoline car went for about 600 dollars. Electric vehicles had nearly vanished by 1935.

5They would not be built again until the 1960s. People had learned the heavy cost gasoline cars put on the environment. Vehicles kept releasing harmful gases. That release pushed Americans to demand vehicles that were kinder to the environment. Buyers also wanted fuels other than gasoline. They wanted to depend less on oil from other countries. Interest returned. An electric truck was created late in the 1960s by a company called Battronic. It could carry 2,500 pounds. It could go 25 miles per hour. General Electric needed utility vehicles for short moves inside its plants. The vehicles had to carry a considerable weight. In the mid-1970s, GE asked Battronic to build 175 electric vans and 20 electric buses. Seeing fresh interest in electric vehicles, Sebring-Vanguard built about 2,000 CitiCars. One charge carried these electric cars for 55 miles. They could go as fast as 44 miles per hour. The Elcar Corporation followed with the Elcar. It went slightly faster, at 45 miles per hour. It went a bit farther, at 60 miles, than the CitiCar. In 1975, the United States Postal Service saw the promise of electric vehicles. A test order for 350 electric delivery jeeps went to the American Motor Company. These jeeps had a top speed of 50 miles per hour. They could go only 40 miles before they needed a charge. Two electric cars were in use by the London Metropolitan Police in 2002. Their range was 53 miles. Their top speed was 56 miles per hour. In 1990 and in 1992, the United States government passed two laws. They were the Clean Air Act Amendment and the Energy Policy Act. A few states also created policies to cut toxic emissions. These laws limited the emissions cars could put into the air. They also limited how much gasoline could be used.

6As a result, car companies worked with the United States Department of Energy. They converted some gasoline cars into electric cars. Examples include the Chevrolet S-10 pickup truck and the Geo Metro. Soon after, other car makers created their own electric cars. General Motors produced the EV1, a sports car for two passengers. It could go from 0 to 50 miles per hour in less than 7 seconds. Its top speed was 80 miles per hour. It could travel 80 miles on one charge. Other electric cars included a sport utility vehicle, Toyota's RAV4. They included Honda's EV Plus sedan. They included Chrysler's EPIC minivan. A picture shows a driver and a passenger supporting electric vehicles like the Toyota electric RAV4. Despite this progress, history seemed ready to repeat. An average buyer could not afford this new group of electric cars, as had happened almost one hundred years before. The price ran from 30,000 to 40,000 dollars. Makers hoped to cut these high prices. They planned to improve how they built the cars and to build more of them. A picture shows a Nissan Altra EV electric station wagon plugged in to recharge in 1999. Some pluses of electric cars come next. They do not produce emissions the way gasoline cars do. Their motors create about the same horsepower no matter the speed. They speed up faster than gasoline cars, and they do it more quietly. It is possible to recharge their batteries with renewable energy, such as solar power or wind power. Some minuses come next. Batteries often contain toxic chemicals. Those chemicals can pollute if people throw the batteries away in the wrong way. Some electric cars need special electrical sockets for recharging. Recharging batteries can take many hours. Batteries have a limited life.

7They are expensive to replace. A picture shows a center in France that recycles old car batteries. Electric cars took another huge leap near the end of the twentieth century. Part of the leap came from the lithium-ion battery. That battery has mostly replaced the lead-acid battery as the power source for electric vehicles. Lithium, a type of metal, is what lithium-ion batteries are made with. They cost more than lead-acid batteries. Even so, they can store quite a bit more electricity. In electric cars, that higher storage lets drivers travel more miles before a recharge. Lithium-ion batteries also last longer. More of their stored energy is available for use. Lithium-ion batteries were first used in a vehicle by the tzero, a sports car. The new technology let it reach 60 miles per hour in less than 4 seconds. Its price, roughly 220,000 dollars, put it far beyond most people. A picture shows a Tesla Roadster. Tesla Motors was established in 2003. It promoted the tzero and lithium-ion technology in general. New ground was broken in 2008 by the Tesla Roadster, a sleek sports car. It was the first electric vehicle made in large numbers that used lithium-ion batteries, that ordinary buyers could get, and that was designed for legal use on public roads. One charge carried the Roadster farther than 240 miles. It could go from 0 to 60 miles per hour in less than 4 seconds. It turned public opinion toward electric cars. Even so, the cost of 109,000 dollars was out of reach for most people. As lithium-ion batteries grew more affordable, new kinds of electric cars appeared. In 2011, Nissan brought out the Leaf. It was an affordable hatchback with five doors, for city travel and for highway travel. The Leaf was popular.

8More than 300,000 had sold by early 2018. Sales were higher for other electric cars, among them the Tesla Model 3 and the Chevrolet Bolt. Even so, the Leaf greatly helped electric cars seem reachable for many more budgets. In recent years, electric trucks have started to appear as well. The Rivian R1T came out in 2021. It can reach 60 miles per hour in only 3.3 seconds. One charge can carry it farther than 300 miles. Even so, a price of about 80,000 dollars is too steep for many people. The Slate Truck, a more affordable electric truck, is set to go on sale in 2027. Hybrid cars use two sources of power. They are another kind of car that is kinder to the environment. Though first invented in 1898, they grew more common only late in the twentieth century. A hybrid vehicle has a gasoline engine and one or more electric motors. Which power source does more work depends on the hybrid type and on the driving conditions. These cars were developed partly to answer a worry. The worry was running out of electricity while away from home. Hybrid owners need not worry. They can always fill the gas tank if they must drive farther. Some hybrid cars can even run on alternative fuels that come from plants. Rising gas prices helped hybrid cars sell. Toyota's Prius sedan was one of them. More than one million of these vehicles had sold by 2007. A picture shows the Honda FCX Concept, a hydrogen fuel cell. Fuel cells are another power source for electric cars. Most fuel cells make electricity by splitting hydrogen atoms. They then combine those atoms with oxygen atoms from the air. The electricity from this chemical reaction charges a battery. The oxygen and the hydrogen join to make water, written H2O.

9That water is the only thing that comes out of the car's exhaust. Hydrogen cars use fuel cells to create electricity. They can be fueled quickly. A single tank can take them farther than 300 miles, as a gasoline car can. In the past, their popularity was limited by worries. People worried that hydrogen was dangerous. They worried it was hard to store safely in a car. As technology has advanced, both their safety and their popularity have grown. The Toyota Mirai, available since 2014, was the first hydrogen car made in large numbers. More of them have come on the market since that first one. Many new hydrogen cars are being developed as well. Electric cars are here to stay. Fossil fuels such as gasoline will not last forever. As long as electricity can be made for them, these cars can keep running. Rising gasoline prices also raise demand for electric cars. So do worries about air pollution and about climate change. Motors in coming years may draw electricity from many sources already known. It may also come from totally new sources not yet discovered. The possibilities seem endless. The energy situation keeps changing. The next time you are stuck in traffic on the way to school, you might start thinking. You might think of new, efficient ways to travel that people can afford and that treat the environment kindly. A picture shows a team of high school students. Each gallon of gas takes their hybrid vehicle 1,610 miles. Word list. Alternative is an adjective. It means available as a different choice or possibility. Atoms are a noun. They are the smallest units of chemical elements that can still keep the properties of those elements. A breakthrough is a noun. It is an important event, or an advance in knowledge, that moves technology, science, medicine, and similar fields forward.

10Capacity is a noun. Capacity means the largest amount, or the largest number, a thing can hold. A chemical reaction is a noun. A chemical reaction turns one group of chemical substances into a different group. Dangerous is an adjective. It means having the potential to cause harm. Efficient is an adjective. It means able to work well while making little waste, or no waste. Eliminated is a verb. It means removed, or taken away. Emissions are a noun. They are things produced and given off as part of a process. Environment is a noun. It means all the conditions that affect an organism in a set area. Those conditions include plants, animals, water, soil, weather, landforms, and air. Exhaust is a noun. Exhaust means waste gases released during a process. Flamboyant is an adjective. It means showy or fancy, or brightly colored. Generation is a noun. It means types of objects that have changed when set beside earlier versions. Hybrid is an adjective. It means made from a variety of different things. In automobiles, the word often refers to the power sources. Methods are a noun. They are planned or orderly ways of doing things. Mobility is a noun. It means the ability to move from place to place. A nuisance is a noun. It means an annoying person or an annoying thing. Production is a noun. Production means resources are joined so a product can be sold. Prosperous is an adjective. It means having success, or being well off. Prototypes are a noun. They are original models used to form later things of the same type. Pungent is an adjective. It means having a sharp flavor or a sharp smell.

12. China from the Himalayas to the Sea

1Skyscrapers, tall apartments, and crowds fill Beijing, the capital of China. The country’s official name is the People’s Republic of China. It is one of the largest countries on Earth. A significant share of Asia lies inside its borders. Square kilometers of land pass 9.5 million. That area is 3.4 million square miles. The whole continent of Europe is only a little larger. Many countries line the borders. Russia is one. India is one. North Korea is one. Vietnam is one. Coastline totals about 14,500 kilometers, or 9,000 miles. The East China Sea borders the eastern edge of the mainland. The South China Sea borders the southeastern edge. A regional map also shows Mongolia, Kazakhstan, and Myanmar, also called Burma. It shows the Yellow Sea, Shanghai, and Hong Kong. Hong Kong, Beijing, and Shanghai are among China’s large cities. Beijing has stood for more than three thousand years. That age makes it one of the oldest cities anywhere. Ancient and modern sit side by side. Skyscrapers give the city a modern face. Subways do too. Fast-food restaurants do too. Temples, monuments, and courtyards are the ancient neighbors. The Forbidden City is a massive palace from the fifteenth century.

2Emperors made it their home across hundreds of years. A strict rule gave the palace its name. Every room could be entered only by the emperor. Visitors now walk the palace as they would a museum. A bridge near Beijing carries the name of Marco Polo. He was an Italian explorer. His book about the journey to China dates from the thirteenth century.
