The East China Sea is the water beside Shanghai. It is China’s largest city. It is the country’s largest industrial center. It is one of the largest ports on Earth. Great numbers of workers move there each year. The population is more than twenty million. In its busiest section, each square kilometer may hold 50,000 people. That density is 125,000 people in each square mile. New York City’s busiest district is less packed. Set against New York’s busiest district, the ratio is greater than one and a half. China’s population is more than 1.3 billion, the largest of any country. The United States, by comparison, holds about 316 million. That is about one fourth of China’s population. Towns and villages are home to more than half of China’s people.

3Rural people often grow crops. They often raise livestock. Town and village people may manufacture goods. They may do other jobs as well. Large cities hold many people too. Those cities are centers of trade and of business. Mandarin is what most people speak. The name means common language. Regions may use dialects of Mandarin. Many other languages are spoken, including Cantonese. English is spoken as well. Cell phone users in China outnumber those of every other country. A cell phone is in the hands of about 75 percent of residents. Mandarin characters can stand for English ideas such as fire. A character can stand for mountain. A character can stand for forest. A character can stand for woman. Some characters look like the thing they mean. English uses an alphabet for separate sounds inside words. Chinese writing uses characters for whole words, or for parts of words. Experts place the start of this writing around 2000 bc. That age makes it one of the oldest writing systems. Draw the peaks of a mountain, and you have nearly drawn that character.

4An educated person knows about four thousand characters on average. The full language holds tens of thousands. School is required for nine years. After that, students may go on to secondary school. Job training may follow. University may follow. Admission to a university is very difficult. Each year, admission goes to just a few students. Landform maps show the Zunghaer Basin and Beijing. They show the Gobi Desert and the Turfan Depression. They show the Tarim Basin and Shanghai. They show the East China Sea and the Tibetan Plateau. They show the Himalayan Mountains and the Sichuan Basin. They show Hong Kong and Mount Everest. Many kinds of landforms fit inside a country this vast. Southern mountain ranges are among the most outstanding features. About one third of the land is mountainous. The Himalayas hold many of the world’s highest peaks. The tallest is Mount Everest. Its height is 8,850 meters, or 29,035 feet. The peak stands on the border China shares with Nepal. Western areas also have mountains. Plateaus rise there too. The east is lowland, with forests and with wetlands. China’s large cities sit in that eastern lowland.

5A huge desert crosses about 1,600 kilometers of the north, a distance of 1,000 miles. The Gobi Desert meets Mongolia. Waterless place is what the name Gobi means. Like every desert, the Gobi gets little rain. Yearly rain in the west can be as low as 5 centimeters, or 2 inches. In the northeast it can reach 20 centimeters, or 8 inches. People still manage to live in this harsh place. They are nomadic herders. Underground water lets them raise cattle. They raise sheep. They raise goats. They raise camels. Wild camels live in the Gobi too. Gazelles live there. China’s rare wild horses live there. Thousands of rivers cross China. The longest is the Yangtze, said yank-SEE. It runs 6,300 kilometers, or 3,915 miles. People and goods both travel on it. People call that basin the granary of the nation. About half of the country’s farming sits in that basin. Rice farming there is the country’s largest amount. Barley is grown in the basin. Wheat is grown there. Corn is grown there. Birth weight for a giant panda is typically only about four ounces. The mother is far larger.

6Fame follows the giant panda more than almost any other animal in China. It belongs to the bear family. It is very rare. Wild pandas, scientists think, number only about 1,600. The drop came after habitat disappeared. Those lost forests were in central China’s mountains. Forests are the panda’s home. Bamboo is its only food. Many bamboo forests were cleared. Agriculture took the land. Timber took it. Fuel took it. Special nature reserves were created to save the giant panda. Breeding pandas away from the wild has been attempted by scientists. Some of those scientists work in China. Some work in other countries. Births are uncommon once pandas leave the habitat they come from. Only in recent years have babies been born in captivity. Only two alligator species exist in the world. China’s alligator is included in that pair. It is smaller than its American cousin. Native habitat follows the Yangtze River. Habitat loss has cut its numbers sharply, as with the giant panda. Wild numbers are down to a few hundred. Breeding in captivity has gone very well. Scientists are working with farmers beside the Yangtze. Safety in the home habitat is the aim of that work.

7Seeing a golden snub-nosed monkey is a surprise. Golden fur is not the oddest part. The blue face is. Forests of central China are its home. Habitat loss hurts this primate too. Reserves have been set aside so some habitat remains. The monkeys are also bred in captivity. Groups are large. Four hundred or more may live in one group. China is among the world’s oldest civilizations. Evidence from science places some of the earliest humans here. The dates run from about 770,000 years ago to about 230,000 years ago. Emperors ruled for thousands of years. A single family might hold power over parts of the land for hundreds of years. Those stretches of rule are called dynasties. Written history begins with a dynasty called the Shang. The start sits around 1600 bc. Further dynasties came later, including the Zhou, said JHOW. They include the Qin, said CHIN. They include the Han, said HAHN. They include the Jin. They include the Tang, said TAHNG. They include the Song, said SUNG. They include the Ming. The Qin Dynasty added several important pieces to China’s history.

8Shi Huangdi, said SHI HWAHNG-dee, was the Qin emperor. His years of rule were 259 to 210 bc. A wall against invaders was built on his order. Building continued under later emperors. Ming rulers did much of that later work. The work went on for nearly 2,000 years. People now call it the Great Wall. It is really a series of walls. The walls run through northern China and through Southern Mongolia. One section runs about 8,850 kilometers, or 5,500 miles. Across, the section measures 5 to 8 meters. That width is 15 to 25 feet. Great advances and many inventions came from ancient China. The abacus was an early tool for complex mathematical calculations. The magnetic compass was invented there and helped early sailors find their way. Gunpowder was invented to blast rocks apart. It was also used to make fireworks. Fabric made from silk was first made by the ancient Chinese. No export was more popular than silk. Buyers came from distant lands. Their route was called the Silk Road. Silkworms spin cocoons, and silk fibers are taken from those cocoons. Pulling the fibers free was a skill the ancient Chinese learned.

9Spinning turned the fibers into thread that was strong. Weaving turned that thread into beautiful cloth. Massive change came in 1912. War with Japan, plus strife inside the country, ended the Qing Dynasty. China became a republic. Politics stayed stormy, and conflict continued, for years after that. Government power passed in 1949 to the Chinese Communist Party, known as the CCP. Food baskets hang from a farmer’s shoulders in Yangshuo. Crowds visit a shopping district in Shanghai. Ancient and modern meet in China. Rural life and urban life meet there too. The world still feels the effects of this long past. Diverse peoples show that history in cultures that are unique and interesting. The land stretches across much of Asia. Breathtaking mountains are part of the landscape. Huge deserts are part of it. Ancient rivers are part of it. Amazing structures draw visitors from all over the world. A visitor has many choices for a first stop. Population is 1,355,692,576. Land area is 9,569,901 square kilometers. The same area is 3,694,959 square miles. The capital is Beijing. The primary language is Mandarin. Daoism is a primary religion.

10Buddhism is a primary religion. The currency is the yuan, said yoo-WAHN. Figures come from the Central Intelligence Agency in July 2014 and from the World Bank. Agriculture means the science or the practice of farming and of raising livestock. Long leaves and woody stems that stretch out mark the bamboo plant. A dialect is a form of a language used in a certain region or by a certain group. A dynasty is a line of rulers from the same family. An export is a product sent or sold out of a country or a region. Grain is kept in a building called a granary. Industrial describes the making of goods in factories, the goods themselves, or the people who make them. Nomadic means moving from place to place with no lasting home. A plateau is a large, raised stretch of flat land. Rain on a river basin runs off into that river. It may also run into streams that feed the river. Silk is strong thread made by a spider or by a silkworm. A temple is a building used as a place of worship.

13. Cities of the Two Rivers

1A clay tablet kept a record of food shares and goods. A sharp tool cut the pictures into the clay. A map of this old land shows the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea. The Fertile Crescent is marked on that map. Akkad is marked there too. The Tigris River runs through the mapped land. The Euphrates River runs through it as well. The map names the cities Mari, Babylon, Umma, Ur, Lagash, and Uruk. The Mediterranean Sea is shown to the west. Europe and Africa lie past that sea. This book begins with the first people who farmed the river land. It then tells how Uruk became the first known city. Later pages tell how city-states went to war. They also tell of a richer time of new tools and ideas. The story closes when the empire falls. A word list comes at the end. About 6,000 years ago, the earliest civilizations started to form. Cities are home to at least some people in a civilization. Those people do specialized jobs. A civilization has a government. Writing often belongs to a civilization. Arts often belong to one too. Science often belongs to one too. Trade often belongs to one too. Monuments often belong to one too. Ancient Mesopotamia is one of the earliest civilizations. The land takes in what is now Turkey. It also takes in present-day Syria, Iraq, and Kuwait. Many historians see this land as the place where civilization was born. The name Mesopotamia means land set between a pair of rivers. The Tigris is one of those rivers.

2The Euphrates is the other. The heart of this old civilization lay in the Fertile Crescent. That heart sat between the Tigris River and the Euphrates River. The first people to live in Mesopotamia settled the far southern part of the crescent. That southern part is now Iraq and Kuwait. Modern archaeologists worked at a site called Tell al 'Ubaid. Say that name TEL EL oh-BAYD. The site lies near the Euphrates River. They uncovered ancient stone tools. They uncovered bricks. They uncovered pottery. Those artifacts were the only clues to how these people lived. The items show farming settlements as early as 5000 bce. Those settlers are called the Ubaid. Their name was taken from that find-spot. A small mosaic box may have held a musical instrument. The box shows scenes of life in early Mesopotamia. Sumer was first farmed and developed by the Ubaid. Earlier, Ubaid groups and other Sumerian tribes hunted and gathered while moving camp. They moved from place to place. Weather decided where they went. The supply of food and water decided it too. In time, the Ubaid found ways to stay in one place. They drained marshes. They grew crops in the rich soil. They built irrigation canals. The canals carried water to drier ground. They made pottery from river clay. They wove baskets from reeds. Those reeds grew in shallow water. Copper lion heads were common guardian figures. People set them on Mesopotamian buildings for protection. The river supplied what families needed. It also supplied goods to trade with travelers. Major trade routes ran from Asia and from Europe.

3Those routes crossed the rich plains of Sumeria. If the Ubaid could neither grow an item nor make it, traders supplied it. Cedar from Lebanon was one item they wanted badly. Metals from other regions were wanted badly too. Over the years, more Sumerian settlements rose in the Fertile Crescent. A number of those settlements grew into true cities. Some of the cities became city-states. The most influential city was Uruk. Uruk is modern-day Warka, in Iraq. Between 4100 and 3000 bce, authority in the area centered on Uruk. It was also the center of trade. Uruk's population once reached as many as eighty thousand. Uruk spread across over 2.6 square kilometers, or 1 square mile. Huge buildings of mud bricks stood in the city. A multitiered ziggurat, or temple, stood there too. People used the ziggurat for worship. They also sacrificed animals and crops there. Painted clay mosaics decorated the ziggurat and other important buildings. Relief carvings decorated them as well. A drawing shows a rebuilt ziggurat from ancient Mesopotamia. The stone base of Uruk's ziggurat still stands at the original site. Mesopotamian pictographs showed up first in Uruk. This early writing grew because Uruk was a center of commerce. Workers marked plain pictures onto tablets of clay. The marks tallied workers' food shares. They also recorded goods. During the following thousand years, those pictures grew into the writing called cuneiform. This was a first in human history. Symbols now stood for sounds. They did not stand only for objects. Any language could be written with those symbols.

4An account of monthly grain shares was written in cuneiform. That account sits on a clay tablet from around 2350 bce. This phonologic system had advantages over a pictographic system. Writers could shuffle one symbol set and spell many different words. Because of that, fewer symbols were needed. The system also made abstract ideas easier to express. Those ideas would be hard to draw as pictures. Clay tablets carry wedge-shaped cuneiform symbols. The tablets tell about Sumerian life in that period. People in Uruk and in other Sumerian city-states lived in structured societies. At the top was a priest-king. He led other ranked officials. One official was a leader of the plow. Another was a leader of the law. There were still more officials of this kind. Mesopotamian society had three main classes. One class was free. Another class was semi-free. A third class was enslaved. Daily life for Sumer's lower classes is mostly unknown. Wives and mothers made up most of the women in Sumer. Home and family care filled their days. School was closed to most girls. Girls from a wealthy family were the exception. Women in Sumer held more rights than women did in later cultures of Mesopotamia. They could own property. They could run businesses. They could act as judges. They could act as witnesses in court. They could become priestesses, scribes, and physicians. One of the most famous rulers was King Gilgamesh. In Sumerian his name is Bilgames. His rule over Uruk is placed near 2700 bce. The Early Dynastic Period ran from 2900 to 2350 bce.

5Song and legend turned him into an epic hero. His reign of 126 years was the subject of poems. Stories called him a demigod. His father was said to be King Lugalbanda. His mother was said to be the Sumerian mother-goddess Ninsumun. Credit for Uruk's huge protective wall goes to Gilgamesh. That wall still stands today. Ancient poems from Mesopotamia make up the Epic of Gilgamesh. The poems tell an ancient king's battles, struggles, and achievements. He works to gain immortality. Many people also believe this epic is history's oldest literary work that still survives. Stone tablets with single poems date back to about 2100 bce. A total of twelve tablets tell the tales. Gilgamesh builds the great wall of Uruk. He battles the wild man Enkidu and later befriends him. He fights the monstrous demon Humbaba. In the tale, lion skins cover Gilgamesh, and he is the one who slew those lions. Around 600 bce, a carving shows Gilgamesh fighting. His opponent in the carving is the wild man Enkidu. Modern archaeologists have long worked to sort fact from fiction about Gilgamesh. A reign longer than a century is not likely. A German team of archaeologists has found support for details in the ancient poem. The poem is The Epic of Gilgamesh. In 2003, the team said they had found the tomb of Gilgamesh. The tomb lay beneath an ancient bed of the Euphrates. Certain buildings named in the epic poem were among the finds. The discoveries show that Gilgamesh was a real person.

6Growing Sumerian city-states started to rival one another. Every city-state sought power in the region. Battles grew steadily more common. One battle is the first Sumerian war described in detail. Lagash fought Umma in the year 2525 bce. Pictures and writing were cut into a tall stone pillar. That pillar is a stele (STEE-lee). The pictures show infantrymen in copper helmets. The soldiers bring swords. They also bring spears and shields. Wheeled carts carried the military leaders. Pairs of onagers pulled the carts. An onager is a native species of donkey. Historians rank this stele fragment among the oldest documents of past events. War scenes on it involve Lagash and Umma. Trade routes were vital. They brought the materials needed to make the tools of war. Blacksmiths had learned something important about two soft metals. Smelting could join copper with tin. Together they made a fairly hard substance. This alloy is called bronze. Bronze was well suited for swords and spear tips. Tin, however, was rare. Traders from central Asia were one source. Traders from Europe were the other source. Feuding city-states often tried to break trade routes. They knew a shortage of smelting materials would hurt the other army. In one scene, a priest of Sumer points at a stele. Umma and Lagash used that stele to mark their border. The two city-states argued constantly over who owned the land. The Sumerians' constant fighting ended under a new king. About 2340 bce, Akkad's King Sargon seized the region. Akkad lay in southern Mesopotamia. That victory fused the city-states. The new realm was the Akkadian Empire.

7Sargon kept order by putting trusted allies in powerful posts across the kingdom. Sargon's descendants kept up this practice. A map of Sargon's Akkadian Empire shows the Caspian Sea. It also shows the Mediterranean Sea, Syria, Akkad, and Egypt. By 2150 bce, the Akkadian Empire was finished. Westward, the realm met the Mediterranean Sea. It reached Arabia in the south. It reached Iran in the east. Northward, it met the Anatolian Peninsula. Sumerian was not the Akkadian spoken language. They did adapt the Sumerian cuneiform script. They used it to write their own language. Only scholars and literary scribes still used the Sumerian language. They used it in official and religious ceremonies. Enheduanna is the first poet in world history with a known name. She was Sargon's daughter. Ur was the city where she served as high priestess. The goddess Inanna is praised in many of those poems. No deity in Mesopotamia was more popular than Inanna. People in Mesopotamia placed a high value on literacy. Mari's large library is proof of that value. Cuneiform tablets in that library numbered over twenty thousand. The Akkadian years of peace changed Mesopotamia. The first postal system was a Mesopotamian creation under Akkadian rulers. Cuneiform messages were cut into clay tablets. Each tablet was then wrapped in a clay envelope. A mark on the envelope was the sender's seal. It was also marked with the name of the person who should receive it, and with the place it should go. Only the recipient could read the message. Someone had to break the clay envelope before the inside could be read.

8A centralized government was set up. Laws and regulations were enforced. Trade networks grew. Commerce boomed. Personal property carried relief figures. These ornate images did much more than decorate. Cylinder seals made the figures. A cylinder seal was a carved tube. People pressed it into clay to show who owned an item. Cuneiform script covers a clay tablet that is a letter 2,300 years old. Every Sumerian used a cylinder seal from ancient Mesopotamia as a signature. The seals showed property rights. Daily business in the empire also depended on those seals. People approved documents and transactions by pressing a seal into the clay. The Mesopotamians also developed numerical place value. Their counting system was base sixty. Another name for it is a sexagesimal system. The way we measure time uses this same system. The way we calculate angles uses it too. The system began thousands of years ago. Certain objects are counted with numerical base systems. Eggs counted by the dozen use base twelve. Twelve eggs equal one dozen. Time is counted in base sixty. The ancient Mesopotamians devised that system. One minute holds sixty seconds. There are sixty minutes in one hour. Historians are not quite sure why the Mesopotamians used base sixty. One theory says sixty can be split evenly in many ways. That made math easier in a world without calculators. The earliest pottery wheels have been found in Sumer. Sumer has also yielded the oldest wheels used to move loads. Modern life still depends on wheels.

9Near 3500 bce, Sumerian workers started to use a flat round machine. They used it to make clay bowls. An axis held the potter's wheel in a flat, level position. Spinning let the potter form a bowl whose edges and surfaces stayed even. After another three hundred years, wheels took on a new Sumerian job. Wheels made it easier to move objects. They also made it easier to transport people. Many trials led the Sumerians to a fresh layout. A single axle got one wheel on the left and one wheel on the right. Loads became easy to haul with this device. Little effort sent the cart rolling over the ground. The design may have been copied by other civilizations. Soon wheels were used around the world. About 2150 bce marks the end of the Akkadian Empire. A severe drought was one cause. Gutian invaders (GOO-tee-uhnz) were the second cause. These Gutians were nomads. Their home was the mountain country to the north. Bands of Gutian fighters often struck the kingdom's outer lands. As a result, trade slowed. Fields lay untended. Shar-Kali-Sharri was Akkad's ruler then. He struggled to keep control as the Gutians pushed farther into Mesopotamia. Akkad eventually fell to the Gutian nomads. The Akkadian Empire collapsed. An ancient statue shows Gudea. He was a Gutian prince. Lagash was under his rule from 2144 to 2124 bce. Sumerians pray to their gods. Their prayer asks the gods to let them win against the Gutians. Running a society this complex was new to the Gutians. They were poor administrators.

10They let the canal network fall into disrepair. A terrible famine followed. A grim time in Sumer followed that rule, and the rule lasted 125 years. People later called that time Mesopotamia's Dark Age. Mesopotamia did not regain its place as a thriving empire until later. The change came in the seventeenth century bce. King Hammurabi was the ruler then. The empire was called Babylonia. Hammurabi, king of Babylonia, set down a law code. Many later civilizations used that law code as their model. An alloy is a metal made by combining two or more metals. Nomadic describes moving from place to place with no lasting home. City-states are cities that act as independent countries. Phonologic means related to speech sounds inside a language or among languages. Civilizations are organized societies with steady food, government, social structure, culture, writing, and religion. Pictographs are pictures or symbols that stand for words or ideas. Smelted means melted or fused with extreme heat. Commerce means buying goods and selling them. People also call this business or trade. A stele is a tall rock slab, or a rock column set on end. It is usually carved with designs or words that honor a person or an event. Another spelling is stela. Cuneiform is a writing system of wedge-shaped marks. People in some areas of the old Middle East used this script. A ziggurat is a rectangular building of ancient Mesopotamia. Steps climb its sides, and a temple sits at the top. In myth, a demigod has one human parent and one divine parent.

14. Cities That Live with Water

1Twelve water places appear in this book. They are Venice in Italy, Amsterdam in the Netherlands, and Reine in Norway. Singapore is on the list. So is Palm Jumeirah in Dubai. Ganvié in Benin and Fadiouth in Senegal are on the list too. The Uros Floating Village in Peru is included. Mexcaltitán in Mexico is included. Auckland in New Zealand, Sausalito in California, and Manarola in Italy close the list. The chapters move from living near water to Europe, Asia, and Africa. South America, North America, and Oceania follow. A chapter on people and water comes next. A word list ends the book. Boats cross the Grand Canal, Venice's main waterway. They carry people and goods among the many islands the city stands on. Visitors from every part of the globe come to Venice, Italy. They come to see its famous canals and bridges. Builders set Venice on over one hundred islands. Venice is the water city people know best. It is not the only water city. A water city is a place built on water or beside it. Some are tiny communities. Others are huge urban areas. Oceans hold some of them. Seas, bays, lakes, and rivers hold others. Some sit in those waters.

2They appear on every continent except Antarctica. People built them for many reasons. Each city has a story worth hearing. Europe holds more than one famous canal city. Amsterdam, in the Netherlands, is another. Amsterdam is the capital of the Netherlands. It is also that country's largest city. Roughly one-third of Dutch land lies below sea level. Polders make up about 17 percent of the Netherlands. A polder is a wide stretch of land people took back from water. The water came from lakes and from the North Sea. People pumped that water out. Amsterdam itself sits about 2 meters below sea level. In feet, that depth is 6.6. The city began in the late twelfth century. It started as a fishing village. In the seventeenth century it became an important seaport. Today it is one of Europe's largest seaports. More than 1,200 bridges cross its web of canals. A picture of the city shows that web. A moat ringed Amsterdam from 1480 to 1585. In the 1600s the population surged as the city grew. Workers drained swampland. They built three more canals in half circles. Those canals share one center. They wrap the downtown area. The four waterways served transportation. They also served defense.

3They served water management too. About 160 more canals run through the city, beyond the main ones. Together they stretch over 100 kilometers (62 mi.). Those canals split Amsterdam into nearly 100 little islands. Over 1,200 bridges join those islands. For centuries the canals were the main routes for getting around. Today smaller barges and boats are the main users. The canals still shape the city's special character. Reine is a tiny fishing village in Norway. Reine lies more than 100 kilometers above the Arctic Circle. In miles, that distance is 62. A nickname calls it the world's most beautiful place. Its shore belongs to one island in the Lofoten group. Visitors can fish, kayak, ski, watch whales, and hike. Gorgeous beaches are there as well. The village is also a fine spot for striking views of the northern lights. Singapore is one island, yet it is a city and a country at the same time. It is the world's only island city-state. It is not only one of Asia's busiest port cities. Few port cities anywhere are busier. The country is made of sixty-three islands. It has few natural resources. It must bring in almost everything from outside. Projects that started in the 1960s grew its land area.

4The gain was almost 25 percent. Amsterdam made new land by taking seawater away. Singapore did something different. Rocks went into the water, and sand went in too, so the shore moved outward. A project begun in 2016 will pump water out to make polders. That method matches Amsterdam's. As the city grew more urban, the government planted greenery. The goal was a city set in a garden. Parks and nature reserves now cover close to one-tenth of the land. Inside the United Arab Emirates, seven political territories exist. One of those seven has Dubai as its capital. Oil found in the 1960s made the country rich. The economy now centers on tourism. Real estate matters too. So do other industries. Dubai is full of building projects. One project is the Palm Islands. These are three human-made islands shaped like palm trees. Workers build them along the coast. They pile up huge amounts of sand and rock. The islands add hundreds of miles of shoreline to the city. They also add homes for many thousands of people. Building started in 2001. The first island was finished in late 2016. A crescent-shaped breakwater wraps the island. It guards the island from strong waves and storms.

5Palm Jumeirah belongs to the Palm Islands. It lies on the Persian Gulf. Among artificial islands, few in the world are larger. From above, it was planned to look like a palm tree. People sometimes call Ganvié the Venice of Africa. Benin, in Africa, is its country. Nearly every building in Ganvié stands on stilts over the water. Ganvié looks nothing like the modern cities of Singapore and Dubai. No stilt village in Africa is larger. Lake Nokoué holds the village at its center. Say the lake name NOHK-we. Benin is the country. About twenty thousand people live in Ganvié. The village has three thousand buildings. Only the school stands on land. A cemetery that is only partly built stands on land too. Ganvié began during the West African slave trade of the seventeenth century. A powerful tribe called the Fon captured people from other tribes. The Fon sold those people into slavery. Fon religion did not allow them to chase people who lived on water. The Tofinu were another tribe. They escaped by going to Lake Nokoué. They wanted to avoid capture. They founded the stilt village. The way of life they built still thrives. Their success shows in the village name.

6The name means we survived. Fishing is the main way villagers earn a living. Underwater fences hold fish and let the people breed them. Grass patches grow in the water. Chickens live on them. Goats live on those patches too. Their boats are long and narrow. Those canoes are called pirogues. Fadiouth, also called Shell Island, is in Senegal. Say the name fad-YOOT. The people there live on an island made only of clamshells. For more than three centuries they have eaten clams. They reuse the shells. Shells form buildings. Shells form streets. Shells form the land itself. Tree roots and reed roots hold the shells in place. The Uru people live in the Uros Floating Village on Lake Titicaca, in Peru. Reeds grow along the lake shore. The Uru turn those reeds into canoes. Those canoes are how they travel. Like the Tofinu, the people of Uros moved onto water to stay safe. The Uru fled to Lake Titicaca more than five hundred years ago. The Inca and the Colla had taken their land. The lake is now home to about two thousand Uru. They use about seventy floating islands. Totora reeds form the islands. Thickness runs from 1.2 meters up to 2.4 meters.

7In feet, that span is 4 to 8. The islands break apart from the bottom. People keep adding fresh reeds on top. The Uru also use the reeds for canoes. They use them for homes. They use them for furniture. Fishing and the sale of handicrafts provide their living. Old traditions remain. Some modern amenities are part of life too. A radio station serves the community. Some residents have solar panels. Some have motorboats. Mexcaltitán sits on a lonely sand bar off Mexico's Pacific coast. The bar stretches 400 meters. In feet, that length is 1,300. The Aztec people ruled wide parts of Mesoamerica. Their rule ran from the fourteenth century to the sixteenth century. Legend says their first home was Aztlán. Say that name ahst-LAHN. Stories describe Aztlán as an island of myth set in a lagoon. Northern Mexico may be where that real place stood. Then their gods told them to find a new homeland. They founded Tenochtitlán. The trip there lasted two hundred years. That city was their capital. Spanish conquerors took it in 1521. After that, Tenochtitlán was known as Mexico City. Some historians think Aztec civilization began at Mexcaltitán. Say that name mes-kahl-tee-TAHN.

8It is a small island people made near Mexico's Pacific coast. Old manuscripts show the early Aztecs traveling by canoe. The canoes look like the ones people in Mexcaltitán still use. A map from 1579 puts Aztlán and Mexcaltitán in the very same spot. Mexcaltitán measures about 350 meters by 40 meters. In feet, that is 1,150 by 130. About eight hundred people live there now. Their houses have tile roofs. Adobe forms the houses. Brick forms them too. Cement forms them too. Many people earn a living by catching shrimp. Local restaurants buy the shrimp. People sometimes call this water town the Mexican Venice. In summer, the rainy season floods the streets. Boats are then the only way to move through town. Local children play a game they call water soccer. They play it on the island's only soccer pitch. That pitch lies under water. During flood season, people boat through the streets and swim in them. Auckland is not the capital of New Zealand. It is the country's largest city. This modern city has 1.5 million people. New Zealand's North Island is where the city stands. That island is in the South Pacific Ocean. Two large harbors flank the city. The city sits on an isthmus.

9At its narrowest, the isthmus is less than 2 kilometers across. In miles, that width is 1.2. One harbor opens to the Pacific Ocean on the east. The other opens to the Tasman Sea on the west. People call Auckland the City of Sails. About one-sixth of the people who live there own a boat. The city has hosted the America's Cup yacht race two times. Residents and visitors enjoy thousands of beaches. Water fun includes kayaking and parasailing. It also includes swimming, surfing, boating, and fishing. Diving and horseback riding on the beach are part of it too. The water cities already described are not the only kind. A picture set shows California, Italy, and an aircraft carrier. Manarola, in Italy, is a tiny fishing town. Brightly colored homes are piled together there. They cling to steep, rocky cliffs. Sausalito, in Northern California, is a floating community. Its houseboats are fancy, simple, and vintage. Aircraft carriers are huge ships built to launch aircraft. They house thousands of military people for months at a time. Water means different things to different people. For people in water cities, it may mean play. It may mean a link to nature. It may mean a way of life.

10It may mean safety. It may mean survival. It may mean a needed link to the rest of the world. Water cities around the world differ in remarkable ways. That variety shows how people adapt and invent. Adaptability is the skill of changing to fit a new place or situation. Innovation is a new idea, product, or method, or the act of bringing new things in. Amenities are features that add ease, comfort, or pleasure. An isthmus is a narrow land strip that joins two larger land areas. A breakwater is a wall built in the sea. It shelters a harbor or a coast from waves. Reclaimed means taken back or improved so people can use it. A seaport is a town or harbor used by ships that sail the sea. Concentric describes things that share one center. Disintegrate means something breaks down into tiny pieces. A stilt is a post that holds a structure above ground or water. The same word can mean one of two long poles for walking high up. Diversity is a wide mix of many different things. Urban is a word for city life and town life, and for the people there.

15. Cloth Made on Every Continent

1The parts of this book come in this order. An opening. How weaving began. North America. Latin America. Europe. Asia. Africa. Oceania. A closing. A word list. The art and craft of weaving give our world an amazing variety of objects. Everyday items include clothing fabric, sheets, blankets, and towels. Fine museum tapestries and other works of art belong on the list too. Woven fibers are strong. Our earliest ancestors found a difference in fishing. Woven nets caught more fish at one time than hooks or spears did. Woven ropes made it easier to pull large objects or to carry them. Woven leather strips could be shaped into vests. They could also become belts or bags. Weaving is the process of making fabric by lacing two sets of threads together. The warp is a set of threads held in position by tension. A device called a loom can hold them. Gravity can hold them too, with help from a weighted object such as a rock, a board, or even a tree branch. The weft is a set of threads the weaver laces over the warp and under it. The weaver then packs those threads tightly together. A diagram labels warp threads and weft. From the earliest days of human history, people have had woven items. Every area of the world developed its own weaving style. Each style has its own materials, patterns, and colors. Weavers have always used whatever materials were nearby. Those materials include yarn, string, wool, silk, cotton, plants, and grass. A picture shows a vertical loom modeled on an ancient Viking loom. Our earliest ancestors gathered natural resources for food, for shelter, and for clothing.

2Then one day someone felt moved to try something new. Perhaps that person noticed the elaborately woven nests of the weaver bird. Those nests protected the eggs. Taking a nest apart may have shown that person how the nest was made. Or the person saw wind mat blades of grass together after a storm. Or the first tries at weaving came after someone saw how snugly the fingers of two hands can braid. Uses for weaving grew quickly after people started to experiment. The first woven objects were meant to make life easier. People bent grasses and reeds and added leaves. They made simple mats. Mats could serve as floors, as roofs, or as walls. Mats could also carry things. Over time, people built skills and weaving traditions. Those traditions passed from generation to generation. Weaving techniques took an important leap 20,000 to 30,000 years ago. People learned they could make fine string. They twisted thin bundles of plant material together. This step was the foundation of sewing and of spinning. It was also the foundation of more advanced weaving. The earliest simple looms appeared in the span from 8,000 BCE to 3,000 BCE. Warp threads stayed firm in the loom frame while weft threads crossed them. A picture from 1879 is an engraving of a weaver in India. A picture shows an antique wooden loom. On early looms, weft threads went over the warp and under it in turns. One early loom used poles set in the ground. The warp was tied onto those poles. Another loom style used weights of clay or of stone to make warp tension. People kept using these simple methods for thousands of years.

3They made cloth for use at home. Weaving then changed in an important way. A more complicated loom was invented. The new weaving technology appeared in China during the Shang period, said SHAHNG. That period ran from 1766 to 1122 BCE. Someone thought of feeding the threads through separate devices like needles. Those devices were attached to crossbars. A lever worked by foot or by hand controlled the bars. A shed opened when some warp threads were lifted and others were not. A shed is an opening between groups of warp threads. A spool of thread could now travel between groups of warp threads, which had not been possible before. The weaver no longer had to lift the threads one at a time. This change mechanized weaving enough for a new result. Weavers could produce much larger amounts of cloth than earlier looms allowed. All modern looms rest on this loom design from China. Later changes in loom design allowed intricate patterns. They also allowed even more efficiency and higher productivity. During the Industrial Revolution, from the late 1700s to the early 1800s, cloth weaving became a mechanized industry. New loom technology greatly increased how much cloth could be made. The spinning industry grew so it could meet the greater demand for yarns. Fabric is still made at the American Textile History Museum on a loom from about 1890. A world key links places to cloth traditions. Asia, Europe, North America, Africa, South America, and Australia appear on the map. The named traditions come in this order. First is Guatemalan backstrap weaving. Next is Harris tweed. Then comes Kente cloth.

4Then come kilims and carpets. Then come Navajo rugs. Last is raranga. Today, automated machines make most textiles. Handlooms and small weaving shops around the world still keep many artisans at work. These people keep alive the tools, the skills, and the craft traditions of weavers from long ago. Let us look at some cultures that create works of great beauty with traditional weaving. In North America, the focus is Navajo rugs. More than 600 years ago, the Navajo made their home in lands that are now northern Arizona and New Mexico. A nomadic life grew up among them in this dry land of mountains and open country. That life centered on raising sheep for food, for wool, and for clothing. In the mid-nineteenth century, Europeans killed and relocated the Navajo. The Navajo were pushed onto reservations. Those reservations cover parts of Arizona, Utah, and New Mexico. Contact with Pueblo tribes in the 1600s is how Navajo weaving got its start. Those tribes lived just east of the Navajo. In Pueblo culture, weaving was a man's task. Among the Navajo, it became a specialty of women. For two centuries, weavers made practical clothing such as ponchos and belts. They used patterns from their own basketry. They also borrowed designs from other tribes. No other Native tribe in the United States is larger than the Navajo Nation. It has more than 330,000 members. A picture shows Navajo textiles. A picture shows a Navajo woman weaving a rug. In the late 1800s, European, Mexican, and American settler-colonizers pushed more contact onto the Navajo. They were taking nearby land and settling on it. New techniques, yarns, and dyes then influenced Navajo weavers.

5More contact also meant more trade. It meant greater demand for items and patterns that buyers liked. Weavers answered by making wall hangings and decorative rugs, and they made less clothing. Weaving styles have changed through the years. Even so, Navajo weaving remains some of the finest cultural artwork in the world. The tribe also earns income from this work. In Latin America, the focus is Guatemalan backstrap weaving. The Mayan civilization reached its peak around 300 to 900 CE. It was centered in Guatemala, a country in Central America. Close to half the people in the country today descend from the Mayas. Fairly isolated villages in the mountains are home to many of these people. Guatemalan weavers have made brightly colored textiles on the backstrap loom since before European settlers arrived in the 1520s. One end of this loom is anchored to a tree or to a wall. The other end is anchored to the weaver's body. The weaver leans forward to loosen warp tension and to lift warp threads. The weaver leans back to tighten the warp and to pack down the weft. A picture shows a Guatemalan woman weaving on a backstrap loom. Mastery of the more complex patterns can take many years. Besides bright colors, this Guatemalan weaving is known for animal motifs and for nature motifs. It is also known for geometric patterns that are unique. Backstrap weaving is a women's tradition. Mothers and grandmothers teach it to girls when the girls reach the age of seven or eight. Women and girls show their artistry through the weaving. They also show their dedication to cultural traditions.

6Woven cloths become blouses, shawls, belts, and bags. They become all-purpose cloths for carrying babies or goods. They become other items too. In Europe, the focus is Scotland and Harris tweed. Picture a string of remote northern islands. They have rugged coastlines, hills without trees, and sheep in numbers too great to count. Few woolen textiles in the world match the quality of Harris tweed. Dyeing, spinning, and weaving of the wool all happen on islands off Scotland's northwest coast. The islands are called the Outer Hebrides, said HEH-bruh-deez. The islanders keep their Gaelic culture and their Gaelic language. Many have not left the islands for decades. Long ago, weavers used an early loom worked by hand. Advances in technology around 1900 had an important effect on Harris tweed. Until then, women had done most of the weaving. The new loom was heavier. It took greater strength to operate. Making Harris tweed became mostly a men's activity. As technology kept developing, weavers began to produce larger amounts of textiles. A picture shows a man weaving Harris tweed. A picture shows a traditional Harris tweed loom in the 1980s, and a handbag made with Harris tweed. Around the same time, people began to inspect Harris tweed. A certification process built confidence in its quality. Sales rose. Advances over the years have let weavers make their product more efficiently. Even so, the island tradition of weaving Harris tweed by hand is centuries old. It has stood against the trend on the Scottish mainland to mechanize. In Asia, the focus is Turkish and Persian kilims and carpets. These rugs are known worldwide for amazing beauty and for intricacy.

7This tradition goes back to 7,000 BCE, and maybe earlier. It has grown into many weaving styles and patterns. Each style is tied to a specific region. The Ottoman Empire once had its center in this part of the world. That empire was one of the largest ever known. The area includes a rich mix of people, races, languages, religions, and cultures. They have intermingled for many centuries. This mix shows in the variety of weaving traditions. The work has generally been an activity of women. A picture shows two women in Turkey making carpets. A picture shows carpets for sale in Morocco. Kilims, said kee-LEEMZ, and carpets use two different weaving methods. Kilims are flat weaves. They use a basic mix of warp threads and weft threads. The mix creates intricate geometrical patterns. For centuries, villagers and tribal members have made kilims for everyday needs. The uses include decoration, wrapping, room dividers, and floor coverings. Carpets are raised weaves. They combine weaving and knotting. The result is a densely packed rug that is thick and heavy. Many carpets have floral patterns or other patterns from nature. Traditionally, people have used carpets for floors, for beds, and for prayer. Cultural origins and traditions show up in the motifs of kilims and of carpets. The rugs are symbols of heritage. They are also useful and decorative. In Africa, the focus is kente cloth, made by Asante and Ewe weavers of Ghana. Kente, said KEN-teh, is a ceremonial cloth. It is made in Ghana and in Togo by the Asante, said ah-SAHN-teh, and the Ewe, said EH-weh. Men in particular make it. It is meant to be worn at special social events and at religious events.

8The cloth is bright and bold in color and in design. Weavers make it in strips from three to eight inches wide. The strips are cut into shorter lengths. They are sewn together to make larger pieces. Kente cloth is more than fabric for clothing. It represents the culture, the spiritual beliefs, and the traditions of the Asante and the Ewe. Each warp thread pattern has a name and a meaning. Each weft design does too. The meanings reflect beliefs, historical events, social organization, or other parts of the culture. Long ago, only royalty wore kente cloth. Over time it has become available to everyone. Cultural pride has an important symbol in this cloth. A picture shows kente weavers wearing examples of their work. Pictures show different types of kente cloth on display. An inset shows a weaver working on a length of kente cloth. In Oceania, the focus is raranga, the flax weaving of the Maori. Raranga, said RAH-rahng-ah, is a traditional Polynesian weaving method. It belongs to the Maori, said MOU-ree, the Native people of New Zealand. People call the method flax weaving. The plant, called harakeke, said HAH-rah-keh-keh, is actually a lily, not flax. Harakeke is an exceptionally strong material. The Maori have used it for at least one thousand years. They make mats, baskets, clothing, and other items. Maori weaving has always been mostly an art of women. Men, however, have developed ways to use harakeke for building. They also use it for hunting and fishing, for example to make ropes and fishing lines. A picture shows a Maori cloak made from harakeke in the early 1800s.

9The cloak feels silky and soft. Another picture shows a Maori trap for eels. More weaving traditions you might want to learn about include these. Indonesian ikat, said EE-kaht. Japanese kasuri weaving, said kah-SOO-ree. Nepalese inlay weaving. Peruvian tapestry weaving. Ie-Toga, said EE-eh-TOHN-gah, which is Samoan fine mat weaving. Silk weaving in India, in France, and in China. You can also search the internet for weaving traditions or for traditional weaving. The Maori, along with other traditional Polynesian peoples, hold a belief. They believe the gods express creativity through individual artisans. Raranga therefore has a spiritual side as well as an everyday use. This weaving tradition has also been passed down from Maori ancestors. It is a strong symbol of tribal traditions. The British oppressed the Maori with violence during colonization. They stole Maori land. Raranga is living proof that Maori culture has survived. This weaving tradition stands for the unity of the Maori people. It also stands for the wholeness of all creation. The cultures and weavers in this book are only a few of the vast number of weaving traditions in the world. Each tradition reflects a people's native materials, daily needs, and cultural symbols. When you see hand-woven items in a museum, an art gallery, or a shop, remember something. Each piece tells a story about the long traditions of the weaver's culture. Many of these cultures continue to thrive, even while the world modernizes. As you go through daily life, notice the woven items you use. Imagine what you might wear if cloth for clothing did not exist. Imagine life without sheets, blankets, or towels. Even cloth from automated looms tells a story.

10The story is about creative people who invented ways to turn plant fibers into fine fabrics. A picture shows a weaving machine that can weave complex patterns quickly. Word list. Artisans are a noun. They are people skilled at a craft or a trade who create items by hand. Mechanized is a verb here. It means machines were brought into the way things are produced. A backstrap loom is a noun. It is a hand-weaving loom anchored to a tree or a wall at one end and to the weaver's body at the other end. Motifs are a noun. They are stories or decorative themes told through designs or patterns. Raised weaves are a noun. They are woven items made with threads and with knots together. Diversity is a noun. It means variety. Flat weaves are a noun. They are woven items made with warp and weft threads, and without knotting. A shed is a noun. A shed is the opening in the warp threads that lets the weft pass. Intermingled is a verb. It means mixed together. Spinning is a noun. Spinning means raw fibers are turned into thread or into yarn. Intricate is an adjective. It means very detailed or complicated. Textiles are a noun. They mean cloth, or woven fabric. Warp is a noun. It means the vertical threads that form the foundation of a woven piece. Tweed is a noun. It is a woolen cloth with a rough surface and with flecks of color. Weft is a noun. It means the horizontal threads added to create a woven piece. Pictures show jeans, placemats, and bags.

16. Computer Worlds You Can Step Into

1A heads-up display of augmented reality shows weather and traffic. This book covers types of digital reality. Gaming and entertainment come next. Learning by viewing and by doing follows. Work and daily life come after that. A closing section is called brave new realities. A word list ends the book. Types of Digital Reality. Reality is the life we live while we do ordinary things. Getting on the bus is one of those things. Setting the table for dinner is another. Workers in this field sometimes say IRL for life away from computers. The letters mean in real life. Digital realities are different. They are environments built with computer hardware and software. They let users interact with computer programs in new ways. Digital reality tech falls into three main groupings. They are virtual reality, augmented reality, and merged reality. Virtual reality builds an environment that is completely artificial. To enter it, people wear special headsets. The headsets have goggles and speakers that shut out the real world. Computer software supplies everything the person sees and hears. The user treats the surrounding virtual world as if it were real. Augmented reality does not shut out the real world. It adds information or images on top of that world. A user might wear see-through glasses or goggles. A user might use a smartphone instead. The person can still see what is happening nearby. At the same time, the application, or app, puts useful information on the screen. A live map while you walk down the street is one example.

2A chart compares the three types. In virtual reality, users are inside a fully digital environment. The real world drops out of their awareness. In augmented reality, users stay in the real world while digital information lies over it. In merged reality, users are in a mixed setting. Virtual objects and real objects can affect each other. A picture shows an augmented reality app on a mobile phone. The app displays how a new chair would look in an empty corner of a room. Merged reality, also called mixed reality, is similar to augmented reality. The large difference is that virtual objects and real objects can interact. A room, and every object in that room, can be mapped by the technology. It can also track how users move. Goggles or glasses let users see objects from both worlds. With their real hands, users can push virtual buttons. They can bring real objects into the virtual world. They can also make virtual objects seem to sit in a real place. A person might pick up a real book, and that book then appears in the virtual world. Two people might play virtual chess on a real table. These technologies are getting better at a rapid rate. Many kinds of people are finding new uses. Game designers, doctors, architects, and teachers are among them. Their goal is to improve work and daily life through virtual reality, augmented reality, and merged reality.

3Gaming and Entertainment. Most video games are about leaving ordinary life behind. Combat games do this. Fantasy adventures do it too. Players jump into other worlds and other lives. Digital realities let a player enter a scene and stand in the middle of the action. A player's senses are taken over by the virtual world. Gamers wear headsets that cover the eyes and the ears completely. Everything they see and hear belongs to the game. What the player does is folded into the game. The experience can feel more intense than earlier digital play. A picture shows a young gamer in virtual reality goggles. The gamer plays in a mock city at a virtual reality park in Dubai, in the United Arab Emirates. Sensors track how players move and show those movements in the game. A controller in each hand is what most systems require. The controllers send movements and actions into the virtual environment. Some users even feel motion sickness. The game fools both the brain and the body. Some gamers now squeeze into full-body suits and gloves. The gear lets them feel what happens in the virtual environment. Pushing open a door is one example. Being grabbed by a virtual opponent is another. Those feelings come from electrical currents that stimulate muscles. A picture shows a researcher demonstrating a special glove. The glove is designed to give feedback inside a virtual reality environment. A picture shows a mobile game adventure.

4A virtual character appears in a real-world place. These adventures twist reality by another method. They use augmented reality out in the real world. Some of the games run on smartphones. They rely on GPS, the Global Positioning System, which pinpoints where players are as they wander. When a player reaches a set spot, the game reveals characters and situations the player must handle. In one popular game, players hunt virtual creatures in the real world. When they find a character, they play on the phone. They throw balls at the character in order to add it to a collection. Merged reality mixes pieces of virtual settings and real settings. It is not the same as augmented reality. Players wear special headsets. Through the headsets, virtual objects appear in the actual room. Players can interact with them. The hardware scans the room and builds a 3D map of it. Software in the headset shows a hologram of the game laid over the real room. Players can use voice commands. They can use their own hands and their own movements. A merged-reality version of the creature game would let players throw virtual balls with their real hands. They would not be limited to throwing balls only inside a phone game. Other entertainment is taking up these technologies too. Makers of film, television, and video want virtual reality to wrap audiences in the action. Fans of theme parks may wear a headset on a future roller coaster. Parks are adding virtual storylines.

5Superheroes and other elements are part of those storylines. The goal is to put even more excitement into the ride. Tracking is what makes users feel they are inside another world. There are three types. Head tracking watches how the head moves. Parts inside the headset can tell if you look up. They can tell if you turn to the side. They can tell if you tilt your head toward one shoulder or the other. The computer then changes the images on the view screen by itself. Motion tracking uses base stations. Sensors on those stations are placed around a room so the room can be mapped. Lasers follow your position and your movements. Eye tracking reads the direction of a person's gaze. It then changes the focus of the image so the view feels more natural and more realistic. This technology is still being developed. A picture shows merged-reality smart glasses. The user sees pieces of a virtual world and still sees the ordinary world around them. Learning by Viewing and Doing. During first-period social studies, a walk through the Acropolis lets you lean close to a statue. Is the figure the Greek goddess Artemis, or is it Athena? Science class can send you inside a cell that exists only as a digital model. It feels like a visit to an alien world. In the afternoon art class, you paint a life-sized jungle in three dimensions. Learning can surround a student completely when virtual reality is used.

6Students never have to leave the school building. Headsets let them step into other worlds and interact there. Studies indicate that the brain treats virtual action as if it were really happening. Research also shows a difference in memory. People keep more of what they learn by doing a task, or by simulating it, than by reading about it or hearing about it. Virtual field trips fit this technology in a natural way. The Acropolis has been turned into virtual lessons. Lessons also exist for the Great Pyramid of Giza. Machu Picchu has lessons too. Many further sites do as well. Educational companies that work on digital reality made those lessons. Natural wonders can be visited in a fully surrounding way. The Great Barrier Reef is one. Sequoia National Park is another. Even the surface of Mars is not too far for a journey in virtual reality. Digital reality is also finding room in science class and in math class. In biology, students use these apps to study human anatomy. Software designers are building programs for chemistry and for physics. The aim is a lab lesson in which young scientists can run experiments. They would face no risk of slicing a finger. They would face no risk of starting a fire. In math, the three kinds of digital reality help students grasp geometric shapes and other ideas. Students work with those ideas inside a digital landscape. Art students can spread colors in three dimensions.

7The results bend the mind. They sit somewhere between sculpting and painting. Other people can see the artwork if they put on their own goggles and enter the artist's virtual studio. Teachers and students will also like the easy cleanup. Paint cannot spill in a virtual world. A picture shows painting programs that let users make works impossible in the normal world. A picture shows a therapist testing waterproof goggles. The goggles give disabled swimmers a virtual experience of swimming with wild dolphins. Students who face learning challenges can find new kinds of support in this technology. Many students with autism feel overwhelmed by sights and sounds around them. They may also struggle to read social cues, such as the look on a face. Virtual reality can let them practice skills. One skill is telling whether someone is happy or upset. There is another side as well. The National Autistic Society made a virtual reality film called Too Much Information. It gives people who are not autistic an immersive look at life for their friends with autism. Experts in educational technology believe this technology holds great potential for schools. People do not all learn the same way. Students who learn best by moving and by doing may see their school performance rise. Students and educators can both take an active role. They can search for classroom uses that work. Along the way, they may build new digital experiences for other people. A picture shows a second grader in virtual reality goggles.

8The trip on the headset goes to the Grand Canyon. Work and Life. Businesses and professions are shaping the technology around the work they do. Manufacturers are trying it as a way to streamline how products are developed. Clients and customers can be reached in new, engaging ways through the same tools. Among carmakers worldwide, Ford stands near the front. At its facility in Dearborn, Michigan, it has a virtual reality laboratory. The lab is changing how the company designs vehicles. The lab is called FIVE, which stands for Ford Immersive Vehicle Environment. Designers and engineers can develop virtual vehicles there, inside and out. They wear headsets in a room fitted with cameras that record how they move. With this tech, they can use 3D sketching. Rough concepts turn into finished designs. They can walk around the virtual vehicles. They can climb inside for a closer look. A picture shows car designers studying a virtual model of a car. The model is projected in a special room. Makers such as Ford are finding that virtual reality can save time and money. Decision makers can find problems and fix them before plans become prototypes. Architects are also designing buildings with help from this technology. Virtual tools or augmented tools let them see a new office building or a new house in its future location. They can do that before they ever break ground. They can also tour clients through a virtual building while the project is still being planned.

9Designers of the Atlanta Braves baseball stadium used the technology while the park was still being developed. Builders could see the field from any seat. They could enter changes on the computer. Concrete did not have to be ripped out once building was underway. A picture shows architects talking over a building model rendered in augmented reality. Health care is another field where the technology is already in use. Surgeons practice procedures in virtual simulations before they work on real patients. Soon a checkup might include a doctor or a dentist wearing augmented-reality glasses. Health records would appear on a screen. The doctor or dentist could review them while talking with you. A picture has two parts. On top, a doctor in a merged-reality headset operates on a patient's spine. The lower image is the surgeon's merged view. Vertebrae are marked in color, and extra information is shown as help. Brave New Realities. The border between real things and digital things grows less clear because of these three technologies. They also give people more natural ways to bring computing power to their work and to daily life. Billions of dollars are being invested by large computing companies. They want the technology's promise fulfilled. Headsets and other hardware cost less than they once did. More people, more schools, and more workplaces can afford them. More software engineers are writing better software. That software uses abilities the technology keeps gaining.

10Designers are also finding cheap ways to make content, programs, and apps. A smartphone can be paired with goggles made from cardboard. Digital reality is no longer only for games and for gamers. It is on the verge of changing how we live, how we learn, and how we work. A picture shows a sailor aiming a tablet at a page in a technical manual. A three-dimensional digital model of ship equipment appears from that page. Word list. An application is software, or a software program, with one particular purpose. People also call it an app. Merged means blended or joined into one. Potential is the chance that something may develop or may happen later. Augmented means made larger, better, or different by adding something or by changing something. A prototype is an original form used as a model for later production. Digital reality is an environment or an object made by a computer that interacts with reality. A sensor is a device that detects a physical change around it, such as a change in touch, light, or heat. Enhance means to raise or improve value, quality, or amount. A hologram is a special image that looks three-dimensional. Simulating means modeling something, or imitating how it looks or what condition it is in. Immersive describes an experience of being fully surrounded, or of being deeply involved. Virtual describes something created or felt in a digital world rather than in the real world.

17. Copying the Tricks of Living Things

1A male peacock spreads his feathers so mates will notice him. A peacock's feathers hold little color of their own. The special shape of the feathers bends light. That bend makes the feathers look colored. Locusts never crash into one another. A special part of a locust brain notices something in front of it. That part reacts much faster than a human brain can. Living things of this kind fill nature in vast numbers. Each one has abilities that help it survive. For many years, humans have studied nature. We have studied how nature works. A science called biomimicry is now growing. It looks at lessons from nature. It asks how we can use those lessons in our own lives. This book asks what biomimicry is. It shows inventions that began with a surprise from nature. Velcro is one example. Road reflectors are another. Screens that cut glare are another. Paint and roof tiles that clean themselves are another. A fast train in Japan is another. Swimsuits are another. Ways to cool a building are another. Materials for building are another. The book asks why this science matters so much. It looks ahead. Artificial leaves are part of that look ahead. Spider silk is part of it. Fish antifreeze is part of it. Natural plastics are part of it. Medicine is part of it. A closing thought comes near the end. Word meanings come last. In Florida, a biologist is shown studying a manatee. Two older words were joined to make biomimicry. Bio means life. Mimic means to copy. People also call this field biomimetics. It is the science of copying life. That can sound simple. The idea behind the science is pretty simple. Organisms in nature have faced many different challenges. Living things have adapted across many thousands of years.

2Adapted means they have changed. The changes help them survive better in their environments. Biologists study those changes. So do other scientists. So do designers. So do engineers. So do other people. They look at how organisms solved the challenges they face. Then they look at the challenges humans face. They ask how nature's adaptations can help us find answers. Biomimicry does not use living things. It learns from them. The idea is not new. For hundreds of years, people have turned to nature to solve problems. Leonardo da Vinci was a scientist. He was an inventor. He was an artist. He lived from 1452 to 1519. He designed many flying machines. He based them on what he saw birds do. Every one of those machines failed. You can see the same kind of copying in the shape of boats. It also shows up in places that may surprise you. A famous drawing by da Vinci shows one of his flying machines. Janine Benyus stands among the earliest modern experts on this subject. She and her peers say the field asks two main questions. One question is how nature solves a problem. The other question is which problems are worth solving. Watching animals deal with problems is what these scientists recommend. Humans can then use what they see. They can use it on similar human problems. Teaching biomimicry to more people is one goal Benyus holds. Several awards have recognized her work. A close view shows hook-and-loop fabric. A small picture shows a burr. Another picture shows a boy in a suit of that fabric, hanging on a wall covered with it. In 1941 a Swiss engineer took an autumn hike. His name was Georges de Mestral. His dog went with him through a meadow.

3Prickly seeds called burrs stuck in the dog's fur. He looked at the burrs under a microscope. Little hooks covered parts of every burr. The hooks could catch on fibers. Hair is one kind of fiber they catch. From that look, he created Velcro. One fabric has hooks. The other fabric has loops. Together they hold things for a while, then let go. The same adaptation lets those little seeds travel far. People have used the idea in hundreds of ways. Those uses have made daily life easier. The idea even helped people go to the Moon. A cat's eyes shine when light hits them. A small picture shows a road marker in Yorkshire, in the United Kingdom. At night, light bounces off plastic pieces set along roads. The pieces sit in the middle of the road. They also sit along the sides. Markers like these are common all around the world. The first version was Percy Shaw's invention. One night in 1933 he was driving in fog. Suddenly a pair of cat eyes shone back in his headlights. A highly reflective layer of cells sits at the back of a cat's eye. That layer is what makes the eyes glow when light hits them. That glow was all Shaw needed. He created a marker he called the Cat's Eye. It uses two highly reflective spheres. The spheres are set into the center of a road. The marker has changed over the years. Even so, the idea from those two shining eyes has helped countless drivers. It has helped them get home safely at night. It has helped them in fog too. A tiny view shows the surface of a moth's eye. That surface cuts down reflection. Scientists have studied insects for many years.

4In the 1960s they found something about a moth's eye. The surface reduces reflection. The eyes of certain kinds of flies do the same thing. Almost forty years passed. Then human tools were ready. Lasers could make screens that copied a moth's eye surface. These new screens are often found on computers. They greatly reduce glare. Working becomes much easier on our eyes. Playing becomes easier on our eyes too. Tiny views also show self-cleaning paint. The paint copies the surface of a lotus leaf. Water beads up on it. The water rolls off. A lotus leaf can do something pretty amazing. Lotus plants grow in ponds. They grow in rivers. Dirt can cover them easily. Mud can cover them easily. A lotus leaf may get very dirty. A light sprinkle of rain still cleans the surface completely. When water lands on the leaf, the special surface makes the water bead up. The beads roll off. As the water rolls, it picks up the dirt. The leaf ends up clean. A group of scientists noticed this feature. Engineers noticed it too. They made paints with a surface like the lotus leaf. They made roof tiles with that kind of surface too. Rain then cleans the outsides of houses that use these paints. It cleans houses that use these tiles. A kingfisher is a small bird. In 2010 a Shinkansen train pulled into a station in Tokyo. Japan's Shinkansen is also called the bullet train. It used to have a rounded nose. That nose worked well until the train entered a tunnel. Its speed reached as high as 320 kilometers per hour. That speed is 199 miles per hour. When the train left the tunnel, the air around it was under great pressure.

5The pressure made a booming noise. Designers looked to the kingfisher to fix the problem. The bird's beak has a unique shape. Its head has a unique shape too. Those shapes let it dive for fish without a big splash. The designers based a new train nose on a kingfisher's beak. The new nose solved the noise problem. It also made the train faster. It made the train more efficient. A swimmer models a swimsuit made to work like a shark's skin. A close picture shows shark scales. A great white shark is shown as well. Ocean sharks were already swimming before dinosaurs lived. They are well adapted to moving in water. Their skin is strong evidence of that. The skin looks smooth. A hand run across it would feel sandpaper-rough. A shark's skin is made of tiny grooved scales. The special shape of the scales helps the shark. The shark moves through the water more easily. It also moves faster. At the 2000 Olympic Games in Sydney, a number of companies showed new swimsuits. The suits were designed to work like a shark's skin. Of the swimmers who wore those suits, 80 percent won medals. The Eastgate Centre lets hot air out through vents. The vents run along the sides of the building. They also run along the top. The cooling plan works like a termite mound. Some kinds of termites build huge mounds to live in. Biologists found a surprise about those mounds. Outside, the air might be very hot. Inside, the temperature stayed steady. It stayed cooler. The termites cool the mound with a complex set of tunnels. Vents are part of that set. Tunnels link the deep ground with the mound's top. Warmer air rises. Hot air leaves the mound through the top.

6Air from lower down comes up cooler. The mound stays at a steady temperature. The Eastgate Centre stands in Harare, Zimbabwe. Builders used these same ideas there. The building uses materials that resist heat. Special vents at the top help keep the large building cool. It stays cool without air conditioning. An ordinary building of the same size would need ten times as much energy as this one. The Moss Landing power plant is in California. It was one of the first plants to turn carbon dioxide into cement. The process is similar to one that corals use. Greenhouse gases include carbon dioxide. Those gases cause climate change. We burn fossil fuels to make electricity. We burn them to drive cars. That burning puts more and more carbon dioxide into the air. Some living things use carbon dioxide to build structures. Coral is one of those living things. Scientists studied how these living things use carbon dioxide. Then they found a way to copy the process. Some of the carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels can now be used. It can be made into materials similar to concrete. We can build new things with those materials. Making what people want is something humans do well. We are great at making the things we need. Our species has been here for many thousands of years. In that time we once lived in caves. We had to hunt for food. We had to gather food. Now we sleep in homes. We shop at stores. Our recent growth has forced us to face some tough challenges. One challenge is how we produce all the things we use. We make food. We make homes. We make plastic bottles. We make cars. We make video games.

7Those are only a few examples. We use great quantities of resources to make them. Waste materials come from us in large amounts too. We produce pollution. Often the energy that makes these things comes from fossil fuels. The energy that runs them often comes from fossil fuels too. Greenhouse gases collect in the air because of fossil fuels. We also create many artificial chemicals. Those chemicals may harm the environment. When we finish using things, they often end up in landfills. The buildup of greenhouse gases is starting to cause problems. Garbage is part of that problem. Other waste materials are part of it too. Pollution is causing the climate to change. We are running out of fossil fuels. We are running out of other resources. Our garbage is contaminating Earth in a variety of ways. Other waste materials are contaminating Earth too. Garbage pours from a truck into a landfill. A small village in the United Kingdom sits near the landfill. One thing we can do is learn from nature. Nature is great at making what it needs in order to survive. It does this in a very simple way. It does this with little waste. A clam makes its shell from seawater and food. It needs nothing else for that shell. Water travels a long way inside the world's tallest tree. The water goes from the roots to the top branches. The energy comes from the Sun. The tree uses no water pump. Another organism can use any waste as a resource. A dead tree can become food for hundreds of living things. It can become shelter. It can become energy. An ecosystem's parts all work as one. They work in a sustainable way. They do not use up resources. They do not damage resources.

8These sustainable environments took many thousands of years to form. Each living thing plays a certain role. Its adaptations play a role too. Mushrooms grow on a fallen tree. Moss grows there too. Biomimicry gives us a chance to see how these environments keep going. We can see how the organisms in them work together. Through them we can learn. We can change how we live. We can change how we make the things we use. That can help solve our challenges. It can help us live in more sustainable ways. A design called Solar Ivy acts like artificial leaves. It turns sunlight into energy. A tree does that too. Sunlight is what trees use when they make energy. The process is called photosynthesis. Scientists are working on artificial trees.
