The leaves would use sunlight to produce electricity. They would use wind as well. One day these trees might make enough energy for a change. We could burn less fossil fuel. A tiny view shows a spider spinning silk. A funnel spider builds its web in the larger picture. Have you ever walked into a spider's web by accident? If you have, you know the silk is sticky. You know it is strong. Scientists have proved a comparison. Compared with steel, spider silk is about three times stronger. Now they are trying to learn how a spider makes silk. The process is not simple. Then they want to create the silk themselves. Artificial spider silk would be a fabric. It would be incredibly strong. It would be light. It would be natural. It could have many different uses. Antarctic ice fish live in water that is below freezing. A natural antifreeze in their blood lets them survive. Oxygen can enter through their skin as well.

9Many kinds of fish can live in temperatures below freezing. Some live in the Antarctic. Some live at the bottom of the ocean. That extreme cold would kill most creatures. These fish survive because of antifreezes in their bodies. The antifreezes are of different kinds. Scientists are trying to learn how these antifreezes are made. They are trying to learn how they work. If they succeed, they may find a variety of uses. Organ transplants are one possible use. Ocean exploration is another. Tiny views show two kinds of microorganisms. Those microorganisms make natural plastics. Each year, people go through tons of plastic. Great amounts of energy go into the usual way of making plastic. It creates huge amounts of waste. Scientists have found something in some microorganisms. Those tiny living things make the building blocks of plastics. They make them inside their cells. Scientists want to learn how that making begins. If they can, they can copy the process. Plastics could then be made with less energy. They could be made with much less waste. A chimpanzee eats medicinal plants. Her baby eats them too. Other animals have survived in the wild for thousands of years. Sickness happens to them sometimes, as it does to us. Even so, treating their illnesses seems to be something they know. They use native plants. They use minerals. Many people around the world have used natural remedies too. They have treated illnesses this way for thousands of years. They have treated injuries this way too. Two children look closely at a dragonfly. Nature still has a lot to teach us. We can learn how nature helps us make new things. We can learn how it helps us make better things. We can learn how it helps sustain life.

10That includes our life. It includes every other life-form on Earth. Humans as a species face many challenges. Some of those challenges are easy. Others are very difficult. As we try to solve these problems, a look outside might help. You might be playing in a park. You might be walking in a forest. You might be doing anything in nature. Stop and look around. Look at how many living things share your world. A special role belongs to each one. That role helps every part of the environment work. You have a role too. The most interesting solutions to our challenges may be very close. The most efficient solutions may be close too. They may be waiting to be found through the science of biomimicry. These words have special meanings in this book. Adapted means changed to fit a new situation or a specific environment. Fossil fuels are energy sources taken from the ground. Coal is one. Oil is one. Natural gas is one. An antifreeze is added so a substance freezes only at a colder point. Glare is a bright light. It is usually light reflected off something. Greenhouse gases are gases in Earth's atmosphere. They trap heat. They contribute to global warming. Biologists are scientists who study living things. Contaminating means making something unusable or unsafe. A harmful or unwanted substance is added. Microorganisms are microscopic organisms. Viruses are examples. Single bacterial cells are examples. An ecosystem is living things plus the habitat they share. Resources are supplies of very useful or valuable things. Efficient means making good use of time or resources. Sustainable means something can be used without using a resource up completely. It also means use that does not cause permanent damage to a resource.

18. Courts That Explain the Nation's Rules

1Nine seats, one per justice, fill the highest court's courtroom. This book starts with a section called the referee. It then links the Constitution to the judicial branch. Organization and daily work of that branch come next. Courts in action follow, with three famous cases. Checks and balances come after that. A section on Lady Justice and a word list close the book. The Referee. Black parents in Topeka, Kansas, sued the school district in 1951. They sued for their children. One child was third grader Linda Brown. Schools in Topeka were segregated. White children and Black children were kept in separate schools. The case was Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka. The dispute climbed to the highest court in the United States. No court in the country ranks above it. In 1954, the court voted unanimously to end legal school segregation across the country. For Black Americans seeking greater equality, the ruling was a major win. A photo shows a mother and her daughter on the Supreme Court steps. They celebrate because public-school segregation has ended. The case helps show the judicial branch at work. Courts and the legal system are under this branch. It manages the legal process. It tries to interpret laws fairly. You can think of this branch as a referee. It explains the rules that guide government and society. It also enforces those rules. A caption dates the signing of the Constitution by American leaders to September 1787. The Constitution and the Judicial Branch. American leaders gave the Constitution their approval in 1788. Laws and principles for governing the young country were set down in that document. The system has changed over time. It is still in effect today. The Constitution is a blueprint for the government.

2It divides that government into three branches, or parts. The president leads the executive branch. Most government operations and departments are managed there. The legislative branch is the U.S. Senate and the House of Representatives. It considers laws, makes laws, and represents citizens. The judicial branch oversees the justice system through its courts. Sometimes the branches cooperate and compromise. At other times they oppose one another. What happens depends on the circumstances. Seven articles, or sections, make up the Constitution. They give the basic guidelines for government. The first three articles split the government into three branches, and one of those is the judiciary. The reach of the judicial branch, especially the federal courts, is set out in Article III. The opening line says judicial power of the United States is placed in one Supreme Court. It also says Congress may create lower courts from time to time. In short, Congress, which is the legislative branch, may set up lower federal courts to handle legal cases. Control of the federal courts sits with the Supreme Court. It does not sit with Congress. The Constitution limits the kinds of cases federal courts may hear. They take cases for the U.S. government and cases against it. They take cases between states. They handle cases about violations of the Constitution. They handle cases about breaking federal laws. Bankruptcy, copyright, patent, and maritime law are covered by federal courts as well. For the most part, federal courts are separate from state courts. State courts have wider jurisdiction. They hear a greater variety of cases. Robbery, traffic violations, and family disputes are all in that range. If a state case involves federal law, or raises a question about the Constitution, federal courts may step in.

3Federal laws cannot be defied by state governments. State courts may not defy them either. Two Kinds of Law. Legal systems at the state level and the federal level deal with two areas. They are criminal law and civil law. Criminal law deals with criminal acts. Theft, assault, and vandalism are examples. Prison is a possible sentence after a guilty finding in a criminal court. Civil law covers cases in which a person, a business, or an organization feels harmed. The harm may also be a feeling of being taken advantage of by another party. A civil case may end in a money settlement or in some other resolution. Nobody in a civil case risks prison. A trial never happens in most cases. That is true for criminal matters and for civil matters. How a Case Reaches the Supreme Court. A chart shows two paths. On one side are the lower federal courts. There are 94 U.S. federal district courts. Above them are 13 U.S. federal courts of appeals. Above those is the U.S. Supreme Court. On the other side are state courts. Local trial courts sit at the bottom. A state appeals court is above them. The highest state court of appeals is above that. A case can climb the federal side to the Supreme Court. A case can also come from state courts if it deals with a federal law. Organization and Operation of the Judicial Branch. The judicial branch is the national system of federal courts. It includes district courts, U.S. courts of appeals, and the Supreme Court. A judge or judges manage each court. Behind the scenes, many administrators, lawyers, and assistants keep the system running as smoothly as they can.

4The Federal Judicial Center also serves the federal courts. Congress established it in 1967. Federal judges and the court system can use its research. They can also use its teaching materials. There are eighty-nine U.S. district courts across the United States. Every state has at least one. Five more district courts sit in districts and territories that the United States controls. Puerto Rico is an example. Those five bring the total to ninety-four. Each district has one judge at its head. As a rule, federal cases are first heard at the district level. Some cases become jury trials. Groups of citizens hear the case and make a judgment. Other cases are bench trials. In a bench trial, the judge acts as both judge and jury. After a ruling, the side that lost may ask a court of appeals to look at the decision. That request comes if the loser thinks the district court ruled wrongly or mishandled the case. A note says jurors are U.S. citizens chosen at random. Attorneys for both sides appeal to the jury when they argue. A picture shows U.S. Court of Appeals judge Neomi Rao being sworn in. Thirteen U.S. courts of appeals exist. Two are in Washington, D.C. Eleven serve other geographic regions. Three federal judges sit together to hear an appeal. The appeals court does not hold the trial over again. The judges review what the district court decided. They decide whether the case was handled fairly and properly. They also decide whether the court made mistakes in reading the law or in managing the case. Their findings may lead them to leave the ruling in place. They may overturn it. They may send it back to the lower court for a new trial.

5How many times a person may appeal depends on two things. The state that hears the case is one factor. It depends on the level of the court system where the case was first heard. The Supreme Court of the United States is the last appeals court. Each year, thousands of people ask it to hear their appeals. Very few requests are accepted. The court has nine judges called justices. Eight are associate justices. One is the chief justice. A case is heard only if four or more justices vote for it. When they do, they grant a writ of certiorari. Those Latin words mean to be more fully informed. The writ asks lower courts to send the records of the first trial and of its appeals. The justices study the case. They attend oral arguments. They listen to lawyers for each side. They ask questions. Later they vote. The vote decides which side wins. A math note uses two figures. In a typical year, this court is asked to take up roughly 7,500 cases. The court usually hears fewer than 150 of them. Using 7,500 and 150, the share of cases the court actually hears is 2 percent. Notable Justices. Nine justices serve on the Supreme Court today, and one of them is the chief justice. Important justices of the past and present include these people. John Jay served from 1789 to 1795. He was the first chief justice. John Marshall served from 1801 to 1835. He was the longest-serving chief justice in the court's history. He helped set early American law in place. William Howard Taft served from 1921 to 1930. He had been president. He is the only person who has held both offices.

6Earl Warren served from 1953 to 1969. Under his leadership, the court oversaw wider civil rights and wider federal power. Thurgood Marshall served from 1967 to 1991. He became the first Black justice. Sandra Day O'Connor served from 1981 to 2006. She was the first woman on the nation's highest court. Ruth Bader Ginsburg served from 1993 to 2020. Workers' rights and equal treatment of genders were backed by her rulings. Sonia Sotomayor has served from 2009 to the present. She is the first Hispanic justice of the Supreme Court. The hardest and most complicated legal cases often come before this court. Its decisions become precedents. A precedent is a legal decision that later cases can use as an example. A Supreme Court decision can affect the U.S. government in a large way. It can affect American society as a whole. The Courts in Action. Most Americans see the courts mainly on television. Few real cases and trials are that dramatic. Most never go to trial. Some take years to resolve. A legal fight may not be exciting. It can still matter. Some cases have changed American society in a large way. That is especially true of cases that reach the Supreme Court. Three landmark cases follow. The case is known as Tinker versus the Des Moines Independent Community School District. Parents of three teenagers brought a suit in 1965 against an Iowa school district. School officials had suspended the students. The reason was black armbands worn at school. The black bands protested the part the United States was taking in the Vietnam War. The students argued that suspension took away their free-speech right. The students won at the Supreme Court in 1969.

7The decision said students have a right to free expression in school. The expression must not be disruptive. A picture shows Mary Beth Tinker and her brother John. The photo is from 1968, after the Supreme Court agreed to take the case. The two hold up the armbands. Gideon v. Wainwright. In 1961, Clarence Gideon was arrested in Panama City, Florida. He was accused of breaking into a pool hall and stealing. He could not afford a lawyer. He asked the court for one. The request was rejected. Gideon was found guilty. He was sentenced to five years in prison. He sent a letter to the Supreme Court while he was locked in jail. He argued that his constitutional rights had been violated. He pointed to the Sixth Amendment. That amendment says an accused person shall have the help of a lawyer for his defense. The Supreme Court heard the case. In 1963 it ruled for Gideon by a vote of 9 to 0. Gideon got a new trial. He was found not guilty. The case set a precedent. Every U.S. court must provide a lawyer for a defendant who cannot pay for one. Because of his efforts, thousands of convicted people in Florida got a second trial or were freed. Gideon himself was among them. Massachusetts v. Environmental Protection Agency. Massachusetts, joined by other states, asked the Environmental Protection Agency in 2003 to put controls on carbon dioxide. They also asked it to regulate other gases that add to global warming. Gases from motor vehicles were included. The agency refused. Massachusetts sued. Massachusetts argued that the Clean Air Act required the agency to control these gases. Congress passed that pollution-control law in 1963. The agency said these gases were outside that law.

8The court ruled for the states by a narrow vote of 5 to 4. The agency was therefore required to monitor these gases and to regulate them. The agency reported a 2010 figure. Transportation, including cars and trucks, produced 14 percent of greenhouse gas emissions worldwide. Checks and Balances. The leaders who wrote the Constitution feared one person or one group might rise and take control of the government. To guard against that, they built checks and balances into the ties among the three branches. The executive branch, the legislative branch, and the judicial branch each have ways to limit the others. Two main checks on the judicial branch come from the executive and legislative branches. The first check is a power the Constitution grants. Congress may set up courts below the Supreme Court. Second, and most directly, judges and justices are nominated and then confirmed. As head of the executive branch, the president nominates federal judges. Presidents usually name judges who share their views. The Senate of the United States must then confirm the nominee, which means approve that person. That vote lets the Senate block the president's choice. The same process shows the legislative branch checking both the judicial branch and the executive branch. A picture shows President Obama with Sonia Sotomayor, whom he named to the Supreme Court in 2009. After confirmation, federal judges serve for life. Supreme Court justices do too. No one in the executive branch or the legislative branch can fire them. A lifetime appointment checks the other two branches. It stops leaders from replacing judges for political reasons. The U.S. Senate can still impeach a judge and remove that judge for illegal or unethical behavior.

9That power is another check on the judicial branch. Only fifteen federal judges have been impeached. One of them was a Supreme Court justice. Eight of the judges were in the end convicted and removed from office. A picture shows U.S. District judge Harry Claiborne, who was impeached for tax evasion in 1986. Another power held by this branch is judicial review. It keeps the other two branches from stepping past their constitutional roles. Courts may review laws passed by the legislative branch. They may review actions taken by the executive branch. Courts can cancel a law or an action that breaks the Constitution. Lady Justice. One symbol of the judicial branch is Justitia, also called Lady Justice. She carries a set of scales. She wears a blindfold. She bears a sword. She stands for weighing the facts. She stands for a search for truth that prejudice does not mislead. When it is necessary, she stands for taking action so that justice is done. Management of the legal system belongs to this branch. It interprets the laws. The people who wrote the Constitution knew a strong justice system mattered. It was an important piece of a more just society. People and institutions gained ways to settle conflicts because of it. They do not have to turn to intimidation or force. Lady Justice comes from Roman mythology and from Roman art. The judicial branch also works as a counterbalance. It steps in if the executive branch or the legislative branch drifts from the principles of the Constitution. It protects freedoms and rights of Americans. Those include freedom of speech and religious freedom. They include the right to organize. One of those rights is safety inside a person's own home.

10Plenty of faults remain in this justice system. Critics can easily point to ways wealthy people use money to avoid legal punishment. Hiring a good lawyer often decides whether someone is found guilty or not guilty. Sometimes criminals escape punishment because of constitutional protections. Even so, the principles of the judicial branch rest on a firm base. When they are applied well, they can produce true justice. A note explains that the public may attend oral arguments in the Supreme Court courtroom. Seats go to people who arrive first. Word list. Jurisdiction is the area, or the limit, inside which someone has power to make decisions or laws and to enforce them. An appeal is a formal request that a higher court change a legal decision made in a lower court. A landmark is a major event. It marks a change, or it marks a new stage. Confirming means making a person's appointment to a job official. A lawsuit is the legal path a court uses when people or groups disagree. A defendant is who a court case accuses of doing wrong. The accused may be a person or a group. Federal describes the central government. Power is shared with the states or with regions. To regulate is to hold steady an amount, a rate, a speed, or a behavior. The aim is proper working, or obedience to laws and rules. Impeached means a leader or official was charged with wrongdoing and might be removed from office. A ruling is an official decision a judge makes in court. Judicial describes the branch charged with checking that laws fit the Constitution. A violation is an act of breaking a law or of not following a rule.

19. Crowds, Costumes, and Comic Gatherings

1A contents list opens this book. A welcome to comic con comes first. An origin story follows. Then the book follows the rise of an art form. Big cons and small cons are described. Cosplay has a section. Celebrity appearances have a section. The exhibit hall has a section. Growing pains and other issues come next. Pushing the boundaries is the part after that. A glossary closes the book. Robin, the Joker, and Batman share some quality time during New York's comic con of 2014. They are Robin, the Joker, and Batman. Picture a seat in an auditorium packed with thousands of other fans. The wait for stars to reach the stage feels impatient. A Chewbacca costume makes the wait warm. Two rows down, another person wears a helmet. Inside that helmet, the heat must be even greater. The character under the helmet is hard to place. A better view means craning your head. All at once the audience is up and cheering. You jump up with them. Robert Downey Jr. is striding onto the stage. He arrives as Iron Man himself. You see him just as the moment starts. The Avengers panel is underway. Comic cons form a colorful world. That world is crowded. Fans of pop culture are the people it is built for. Someone who collects comic books can find a place in it. Someone who watches cartoons can too. So can someone who goes to the movies. So can someone who plays video games. These fan gatherings are called cons for short.

2They take place all over the country. Some cons are huge. Thousands of attendees may show up. The events may run for several days. Other cons are very small. A small con may last only a day. It may last only an afternoon. Events and attractions exist for every kind of fan. Young children come. Adults come. Hardcore gamers come. Obsessive readers come. People who fall between those groups come as well. Shel Dorf was among the first people to organize comic book conventions. Dorf worked as a comic book artist. During the 1960s he set up small gatherings of comic fans. Those gatherings were in Detroit. He went on to found a convention now called Comic-Con International (CCI): San Diego. The year of that founding was 1970. San Diego's opening year brought about 100 fans. It has grown into the largest comic con in the nation. Over 130,000 people have come to its events in recent years. Stan Lee was a legendary writer. He was also an editor and a publisher. Comic cons were a frequent stop for him. Lee helped create many of the most popular superheroes at Marvel Comics. He died in 2018. San Diego's success was followed by hundreds of other comic cons. Each year a con with huge stars meets in New York. Seattle hosts one too. Denver and Phoenix do as well. Those cons use huge venues. Their attendance numbers are huge too. Cons are held on every continent except Antarctica. Tickets for these events can sell out months before the doors open.

3Some fans camp at ticket booths. They may camp for days to be sure of getting in. An explosive growth needs a cause. The first cause is a rise in the popularity of comic books. During the 1930s and the 1940s, a period called the Golden Age, comics already had many readers. After about 1950, and through the rest of that century, comics lost much of that popularity. Some people in that period treated comics as low-quality literature. Others treated comics as kid stuff. That perception is no longer true. It may not have been true even then. Series near the end of the 1980s and the start of the 1990s opened fresh paths for this art form. The Sandman was one of those series. Watchmen was another. They drew devoted readers. They also drew critical acclaim. In that Golden Age, few comic books outranked Superman in popularity. Since those years, far more people have cared about comic books. Writers still explore new topics. Artists still explore new styles. The range of comic books today is wider than ever. One comic made now might follow a classic superhero plot. It might tell a story about war. It might tell a story about family drama. Graphic novels are a spin-off of comic books. Young adult fiction now counts them among its favorite forms. Graphic memoirs are another popular spin-off. Adult nonfiction has these memoirs out on its newest edge. Art Spiegelman created Maus, a work that is both graphic memoir and novel.

4He built it from interviews with his father. His father was a survivor of the Holocaust. Maus was given the Pulitzer Prize. That prize is one of the country's highest literary awards. Comic topics grew. Audiences grew with them. Fans of every gender can find a comic they relate to. Fans of every color can do the same. So can fans of every age and every nationality. Comic con attendance has risen sharply as a result. A picture can show Art Spiegelman speaking about Maus. The place is the International Berlin Comic Festival. Hollywood supplies a second cause of the growth. Films that use characters from comics have succeeded enormously in recent years. Many more people came to comic cons because of those films. New Spider-Man films made during the 2000s pleased large audiences. Iron Man, released in 2008, was a favorite too. The Dark Knight, also from 2008, was a favorite. Wonder Woman, from 2017, drew audiences. Black Panther, from 2018, drew audiences as well. New fans arrived with these movies. Movies now fill a large share of comic con programming. Famous actors from comic-book movies appear regularly on panels. Writers from those movies appear too. Directors appear as well. The panels draw huge crowds. Movies are only a beginning. Comic cons around the world now include video games. They include novels. They include television shows. The audience grew so large that some fans broke away. Those fans formed conventions focused on specific genres. A blockbuster film in 2002 put Spider-Man on the big screen for the first time.

5Anime and manga have gatherings devoted to them. Anime means animated films from Japan. Manga means comic books from Japan. Many fans go to those gatherings. Other cons welcome fans and collectors of classic comics. Science fiction has cons of its own. Fantasy fiction has cons too. Steampunk, horror, and humor each have fans and cons. Many further kinds exist. A picture can show two fans wearing manga-style costumes. Cities all over the world host comic cons. San Diego and New York hold the huge conventions. Outside those two cities, the crowds are smaller. The enthusiasm of the fans is still huge. A local newspaper can tell you if a comic con is coming to a nearby town. An online check can tell you the same thing. The find may surprise you. Smaller cons often put local fans in the same room as famous cartoonists. They also mingle with movie stars. In this country, a comic con of any size might include the star of a favorite show. It might include the writer of favorite books. Local artists are likely to be there too. New friends are likely as well. Many fans use comic cons to display creativity of their own. Cosplay is the tradition they use. In cosplay, fans dress as characters. The characters may come from comic books. They may come from anime or manga. They may come from other fantasy genres. For fans around the world, cosplay is serious business. A costume can be bought from a provider of costumes.

6It can be custom-built. It can be made by hand. A character's weapons may show up as realistic copies in a cosplayer's hands. They carry reproductions of accessories too. Some cosplayers behave like a favorite character while the costume is on. A costume may be simple. It may be incredibly detailed. For many fans, most of the fun is solving the costume, whether they sew it or construct it. Around the world, comic cons give cosplay a central place. Vendors sell costumes in the exhibit halls. Hundreds of fans in costume fill the audience. Cosplay contests are held at many conventions. There, cosplayers can pose for photos. They can also act in skits built on their characters. One pictured fan is dressed as Deathwing D.Va. That character is from Heroes of the Storm. A panel brings Danai Gurira together with Michael B. Jordan. Both are actors from Black Panther. San Diego's comic con of 2017 was where that panel was held. Comic cons let fans meet creators on a personal level. A huge share of the appeal comes from panels. Writers appear on those panels. Artists, actors, and directors appear on them too. Audience members can hear favorite stars speak. Stars describe what it was like to create the comics, the films, and the shows. A direct question from the audience is sometimes allowed. A photo with a celebrity is sometimes possible. An autograph is sometimes possible. Many fans treasure these personal moments as memories. Celebrities often say their own comic con memories are positive.

7They often mention how warm the fans are. They mention how friendly the fans are. They mention how devoted convention fans tend to be. A picture can show attendees flowing through a giant exhibit hall. The hall belongs to the New York Comic Con. The city is New York City. For most comic cons, the exhibit hall is the center. People mingle in that hall. They talk. They shop. Goods tied to comic books are on display. So are goods tied to movies, television, games, and other pop culture. Comic books can be bought here. They can be traded. Other merchandise is sold as well. Action figures are part of that merchandise. Toys are part of it too. A collector with experience can hunt rare editions. Unique editions can be found too. A new collector can get a head start. An area for author signings is often set up in the hall. Fans meet artists and writers there. A visitor who buys nothing still has plenty to see. Cosplayers wander past in colorful costumes. Movies play on a regular schedule. Movie trailers play too. A celebrity sighting is always possible. Colorful merchandise sits ready for browsing in an endless supply. Fan contests in cosplay draw huge audiences. Panels draw them too. So do movie screenings, shopping, and conversation. Comic cons have become an enormous draw for people worldwide. They count as entertainment in their own right. The growth has not been free of controversy. Some readers of comic books feel the bigger cons have grown much too large.

8They feel the focus has drifted too far from comic books. Fans of movies now fill the events. Fans of television, books, and games fill them too. The comic book fans say the original inspiration can get lost in that mix. Pop culture convention would be a more accurate name for many of these meetings. Comic book convention would fit less well. The audience for the books and the cons has changed. In earlier years, readers and attendees were largely male. About forty percent of recent attendees at CCI: San Diego are female. Some statistics look at attendees under thirty. About half of that younger group are women. Younger fans, a full generation of them, are discovering these cons. More than half the people at recent cons are under twenty-nine. Larger crowds come with this wider mix of people. Most fans welcome that change. Comic cons can also host talk about larger controversies. The comic book form has made a comeback. Authors now take on topics that are serious and highly charged. Race is one of those topics. Gender is another. Politics and war are others. These comics are not to every reader's liking. Some comics become targets of banned book campaigns. In that kind of campaign, a community asks a library to remove a book from its shelves. A school may be asked to do the same. Spider-Man comics have been challenged in some communities. Batman comics have been challenged as well.

9Adult language is one reason given. Adult themes are another. Readers have discussed censorship on panels. Teachers and librarians have joined those discussions. The panels have been part of several recent comic cons. One result is the rise of two labels. The labels are graphic novel and graphic memoir. They name comic books intended for adult audiences. Children remain the audience for some comics. Taken as a whole, comics are no longer for kids only. Some comics are fictional. Some are not. Some are educational. Some are meant for entertainment. Some deal with adult themes. Others give an escape into fantasy worlds. Because comics differ so much, a question comes up. Should all comics share the same shelves in libraries and schools? A further question asks what role comics play in the larger society. Panels at comic cons return to these questions often. Widening what comics can cover is sometimes difficult. Even so, this is an exciting time for comic cons. Comics available today show huge diversity. That spread has produced bigger audiences for comics. It has produced more diverse audiences for conventions too. A fan of any age can find a comic that shows someone like them. A fan of any gender can do the same. A fan of any nationality can do the same. One hero might look like Superman. Another might be a young girl from Botswana. Another hero might be a person reporting from Bosnia itself. Nothing in a comic book has a set limit. Its heroes have no set limit either.

10People come to comic cons because of that open range. The cons build worlds. The fictional stories behind the cons build worlds too. Inside those worlds, ordinary people can turn into heroes. Dressing as a favorite character lets a person sink into possibility. Trading books with fellow fans does the same. Trading trivia questions does the same. Shaking an artist's hand does the same. Many people come back to that experience again and again. A picture can show a young girl in costume. Her costume is a pink stormtrooper outfit from Star Wars. She is at CCI: San Diego. Censorship means cutting or hiding some or all of a publication, a play, or a film. Merchandise means goods that people buy or sell. A panel is an invited group. Listeners sit before the group while a subject gets discussed. The speakers are expected to know that subject well. A controversy is a dispute about an issue. Conventions are large gatherings. At them, people talk about their work. They also talk about an interest they share. Pop culture is popular ideas and entertainment. Mass media is how those ideas travel. Critical describes careful judgment made for a review. A screening is an organized showing. The showing may be a movie or a television program. Diversity means many different things gathered together. Themes are the chief ideas inside artistic works. A memoir is writing that retells what a person has lived. A venue is a place where an organized event is held.

20. Earth's Eight Billion People

1A picture notes a coming change. No country on Earth will soon have as many people as India. This book opens with a giant mystery. It asks how many people are too many. It asks whether the problem is recent. It describes a growth spurt. It tells how technology came to the rescue. It shares some good news. It looks at an uncertain future. It asks whether there can be enough for everyone. It ends with an island in space. A glossary explains hard words. Giant statues stand on Rapa Nui. Their weight made carrying them impossible. How anyone moved them is the mystery. Dutch explorers first reached Rapa Nui in 1722. The island is also called Easter Island. It lies in the South Pacific Ocean. The explorers were amazed. Hundreds of colossal stone statues ringed almost the whole coast. Every statue faced inland. None faced out to sea. One statue was more than 32 feet (9.7 m) long. It weighed 164,000 pounds (74,389 kg). The islanders had only ancient tools. No large trees remained to make rollers. The giant carvings are called moai. The name is said as MO-eye. How could these people have carved the huge stones? How could they have hauled the stones across the island? Centuries later, experts learned something new about Rapa Nui. The island had once been heavily forested. A group of people settled there almost eight hundred years ago. They cleared trees for homes. They cleared trees for fields. Fish, wildlife, and crops were plentiful. The population grew until about 1680. Then the carving stopped. The population dropped. What happened? One popular theory looks at resources. As the population grew too large, the people used up many of their resources. Resources are raw materials in the environment that help us live. Food is a resource. Clean water is a resource. Energy is a resource. At one time the island could feed a small population. It could supply water. It could supply wood for building. In time the population grew too large. Not everyone could get what was needed. The forests were all gone. Many of the people died. They had used up their resources. Many people today look at the eight billion humans on Earth. They think those humans are using up the planet's resources. The pattern may match what the people of Rapa Nui did. Will Earth's people meet the same fate? A picture can ask what 8,000,000,000 looks like.

2Eight million is a smaller count than the people of New York City. That city has 8,930,000 people. Los Angeles holds about half of eight million people. Los Angeles has 4,097,000 people. Germany's people number roughly eighty million. It is about twice the population of California. A giant gingerbread figure can stand for eight billion humans. Smaller gingerbread figures can stand for eight million and for eighty million. Those smaller counts are still huge. Set beside them, eight billion is colossal. Look around, and Earth may not seem crowded. Empty houses stand here and there. Empty fields and forests do too. Even New York City has open park space. The city averages 29,729 people per square mile. In fact, every person on Earth could fit inside the city limits of Los Angeles. They would have to be packed into skyscrapers. The fit would not be very comfortable. Lack of space is not what overpopulation means. It is a problem of whether resources are available. Overpopulation means people have gone past the carrying capacity of their environment. The biggest population a place can hold is called its carrying capacity. Once the number is passed, the resources needed for survival get used up. Scientists estimate Earth's carrying capacity at somewhere between two billion and forty billion people. The estimate swings so widely for a reason. Each person's use of resources changes how large that capacity can be. Suppose everyone on Earth lived as most Americans live. Earth could then support only about two billion people. High-income countries use most of the world's resources. The United States is one of those countries. Countries in Western Europe are too. Only a small part of what the world provides is used by people in countries with low incomes. Three-quarters of the world's people live in middle-income countries. In those countries, more and more resources are being used. China is an upper-middle country on that scale. India is a lower-middle country. Each has a population greater than one billion. Each uses more resources as it develops. Wealthier places enjoy a certain ease of life. These countries want an ease that matches it. To reach that goal, they invest in infrastructures. They expand industries. Suppose people on Earth consumed only what they need to stay alive. The planet could then support about forty billion people. Other species would be pushed to extinction. Life for the species that remained would be hard. A chart can show a growing global footprint.

3Global material footprint means all the raw materials taken out to meet what humans consume. The footprint is expected to grow faster than population. It stood at 43 billion metric tons in 1990. By 2060 it is estimated at 190 billion metric tons. That rise is 442 percent. A figure of 92 billion metric tons is also shown between those two. The figures come from a 2019 report. The report is from the United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs. Is the problem a recent one? Jared Diamond is a well-known scientist. He wrote about the decline of the Rapa Nui. The book came out in 2004 and was a best seller. Its title is Collapse: How Societies Choose to Fail or Succeed. Some experts before him thought the same thing he thinks. Rapa Nui probably held ten thousand residents once, or a number even higher. Europeans arrived in the eighteenth century. By then the island could barely support two thousand people. The forests were gone. The best farming soil had washed away. The people of Rapa Nui had gone past the carrying capacity of their island. Experts suspect this kind of collapse has struck many civilizations. The span covers millennia. In the Middle East, farming began about ten thousand years ago. An area there was called the Fertile Crescent. The name fit because the land could grow so much food. Irrigating crops made food supplies larger. Populations soared. Irrigation can erode soil. It can also leave enough salt and other minerals to kill crops. That harm is avoided only if the soil is flushed often. Heavy downpours can do the flushing. A flooding river can do it too. Clearing trees can cause erosion. Plants die when salt in the soil climbs too high. In this case, clearing trees for farming let salt out of the soil. The salt ruined the land. The Tigris River flooded each spring. The Euphrates River flooded too. The waters brought new topsoil that gave life. The floods were not the same every year. In some years, so much water came down from the mountains that whole villages were washed away. Fields were washed away too. The theory says the land wore out over time. The floods grew less and less regular. More salt could build up. The carrying capacity of the land fell. The ancient civilizations disappeared. When a population passes its carrying capacity, several results can follow.

4Starvation can follow. Disease can spread. The environment can be destroyed. Wars can start as people fight over resources that are running out. If they are able, some people leave to find new resources. The people of Rapa Nui could not leave. Their nearest neighbors lay several thousand miles across the ocean. No wood was left for boats. They could not reach other islands. They could not reach the mainland of South America. Europe's population boomed in the 1800s. Those people could move to other continents. The Americas were among the places they went. Australia was another. Hundreds of years must pass before rich soil for farms is even a few inches deep. That same soil can be blown away in a few years. It can be washed away just as fast. A growth spurt can be marked in dates. In 1800, one billion people lived on Earth. Humans had taken 120,000 years to reach that number. By 1927, only 127 years later, the number had doubled. Thirty-three years after that, the year was 1960. The count had tripled, to three billion people. In 2022 the eight billionth person was born. The population is still growing. The rate is 200,000 people each day. Charts can show world population growth through history. Doubling a small number again and again soon means doubling a huge number. That pattern is exponential growth. It is a rate of growth that gets faster and faster. Some populations are still growing at that exponential speed. One set of figures comes from world population projections for 1990 to 2150. Another set comes from long-range projections made in 1991 by the United Nations. Three estimates of the future world population can be compared. All three start at 5 billion. Later, the numbers move far apart. Across sixty years, fewer births change the total a great deal. New machines and methods are where the sudden rise in population started. That technology belonged to the Industrial Revolution. The years were 1760 to 1850. In agriculture, new tools appeared. New farming practices appeared. Fertilizers appeared. Farmers could work the land more easily. They could produce larger amounts of food. They could produce kinds of food that were more nutritious. In manufacturing, steam power took the place of water power. It also took the place of power from livestock. Machines could work faster. They could work longer. They needed less human oversight. Railroads lowered the cost of moving goods and materials.

5The way people lived changed. Better food, and better ways to distribute it, meant more children lived through the diseases of childhood. People were healthier. Farms needed fewer workers. More people moved from farms to cities. They went to work in factories. At the same time, scientists found the causes of many diseases. They urged better hygiene. In 1796 Edward Jenner discovered the smallpox vaccine. It was the first of many vaccines. Those vaccines saved thousands of lives. Cleaner and healthier children were more able to reach adulthood. More adults were then alive to have still more children. The human population boomed. A picture shows a girl who is seven months old. She breathes in penicillin that has been turned to vapor. Penicillin was discovered in 1928. No antibiotic came before it. The lives it saves cannot be counted. Technology has been offered as a rescue. Thomas Malthus raised an alarm about overpopulation in 1798. He did it in an essay. The essay is called Essay on the Principle of Population. Geometric increase in the number of humans was the growth he described. He argued that the power to produce food was growing arithmetically. In other words, people were increasing faster than the food that could feed them. He warned that hunger would spread over the whole world unless families had fewer children. In his time, the world held about eight hundred million people. Malthus did not know what the next two hundred years would bring. Advances in technology would let farmers grow more food. The Green Revolution began in the 1940s. Scientists developed special seeds. Norman Borlaug was one of those scientists. He worked with farmers in Mexico. The seeds let farmers produce more food. The scientists also developed pesticides. They developed herbicides. The chemicals were meant to control insects and plant diseases. Land once unfit for farming could now grow food. Chemical fertilizers made that possible. Irrigation made it possible too. The new farming technology spread across the globe. Mexico could grow more food. India could grow more food. Countries in the Middle East could grow more food. Mexico grew more than its own people needed. It became an exporter of foods. The new techniques tripled food production. Some people believed human ingenuity of this kind would let population grow forever. The new technology also brought new problems. Irrigation demanded more water. Herbicides and pesticides polluted supplies of food.

6They polluted supplies of water. They poisoned the environment. Rachel Carson published a landmark book in 1962. The book is called Silent Spring. It drew attention to these problems. Her scientific view taught chemists something. Human activity has an impact on the environment. Some people realized a hard fact. We were destroying the planet that our lives depend on. Some resources, of course, are renewable. New trees can be planted. The sun offers a huge supply of energy. Wind does too. In 1.5 hours, Earth receives enough solar energy for a whole year of the planet's energy needs. That is true if people can learn how to harness the energy. Water is renewed all the time. The path is the hydrologic cycle. The cycle is evaporation, then condensation, then precipitation. Most of Earth's water is salt water. Only 2.5 percent is fresh. Of that small fresh share, two-thirds is frozen in glaciers. Fresh water that people can use is less than 1 percent of all the water on Earth. A chart can show one region's water table from 1945 to 2005. Tucson, Arizona, once relied on water under the ground. Population growth drove the water table downward by 170 feet. Recent decades have seen Tucson choose water from other places. The Colorado River is one of those sources. Fresh water is not spread evenly over the planet. One quarter of people lack a safe source of drinking water. Most of those people are in Africa and in parts of Asia. At the same time, people waste a great deal of fresh water. Seventy percent of the fresh water that is available goes to irrigation. Fields in the American West receive water pumped up from below the ground. The pumping is faster than the water can be replaced. The mighty Colorado River may only trickle to the sea. Sometimes it fails to reach the sea at all. So much of its water is taken for irrigation and for cities. Scarcer water will change much of the cropland that feeds people into desert. Some of Earth's resources are finite. They are nonrenewable. Coal is one. Copper and other metals are others. These resources take millions of years to form. Once they are used up, they cannot be replaced. China consumes the most coal. It consumes far more than other countries. The United States consumes the most oil. It uses more than its share. It has less than 5 percent of the world's people.

7It uses 20 percent of the world's oil. An ecosystem is another resource that is nonrenewable. Health of the planet depends on jobs that ecosystems carry out. Swamps clean water. Estuaries clean water too. They also reduce flooding. Plants that grow in them act as filters. Grasslands form rich soils. Savannas do the same. Grasses grow and then decay, and the soil builds. Forests balance the atmosphere. They take up carbon dioxide. They emit oxygen. Heavy use of wood is destroying many important ecosystems. Heavy use of farmland is destroying them too. Nearly two-thirds of Earth's tropical rainforests are gone. Those forests are the most diverse ecosystems. Thousands of plant species become extinct each year. Thousands of animal species do too. We cannot bring them back. China's fast industrialization pressed hard on the baiji. The baiji was the country's freshwater river dolphin. Water pollution killed many of them. Lethal fishing nets killed many. Noise pollution killed many more. Boat propellers killed many more. The baiji had lived on Earth for more than twenty million years. It is now extinct. July 2021 brought heavy rains to Germany. The rains brought deadly floods. More people then noticed how dangerous a shifting climate can be. One palm that once grew on Rapa Nui was the biggest of its kind ever known. That palm no longer exists. Perhaps the people cut the trees down to help move the moai. Whatever happened to the trees, losing them cost the islanders their fuel. It cost them materials for building. It also cost them the forest ecosystem. That ecosystem had protected the topsoil from erosion. It had kept the soil healthy. It had given habitat to mammals and birds. It had stored water. It had recycled waste. Their tiny island was changed forever. Our planet is changing too. Burning fossil fuels lets carbon dioxide out into the atmosphere. Oil is one of those fuels. Coal is another. The gas traps more heat at Earth's surface. Our planet is getting warmer. Ecosystems around the world are changing. Polar ice caps have already shrunk. Deserts have grown in size. Weather has grown more dramatic. These trends cannot be turned around easily. There is good news as well. By 2010, the global rate of population growth had slowed. It had been as high as 2.2 percent a year. It had fallen to 1.1 percent a year. Growth of population has halted in many countries where incomes are high.

8In some it has reversed. The result is negative population growth. Their birthrate now sits below the replacement rate. The replacement rate is 2.1 children per woman. Across years, that average number of children for each woman holds a population steady. More people are learning that Earth has limited resources. Renewable energy is being developed. Wind power is one kind. Solar power is another. Many countries have passed laws to protect the air. They have passed laws to clean the air and the water. They have passed laws to protect many ecosystems. Since 1985, water use per person has fallen in the United States. Most of the drop comes from farming and industry using water more efficiently. Forests have increased. Even with new trees, the living systems of old-growth woods are often gone. New trees may be planted, and the old complexity is still missing. An old-growth ecosystem can take a long time to become established. The future is still uncertain. Despite the good news, the world's population keeps growing. Most of that growth is in lower-income countries. A forecast from the United Nations puts the world near ten billion people in 2050. By most estimates, that number is almost twice what Earth can support in a lasting way. Whichever estimate a person believes, one point is now shared. The human population cannot grow forever. Forever growth would destroy the planet. China's population is almost 1.5 billion. It is the largest population in the world. A rule of one child per family began there in 1979. The aim was to control population growth. Under that rule, a second child was illegal for many couples. The policy is estimated to have lowered China's population by 400 million. It was controversial. Late in 2015, China relaxed the policy. Couples could have two children. In 2021 the country announced a further change. A couple may now have three children. Schooling is the main key. Education for women matters most in bringing birthrates down. Equality for women matters most too. Birth numbers in many Arab countries have dropped sharply over recent years. Several steps can push birthrates downward. The first tool is also the most effective. Educate women. When women are educated, they often choose fewer children. The same choice is common when they receive the same opportunities as men. It is common when they control the decision about family size. The second tool is health care for children.

9Clean water helps more children reach adulthood. Healthy food helps. Quality health care helps. Parents who trust their children will live usually raise smaller families. The third tool belongs to governments. They can support people who are elderly. They can support people who are sick. That support encourages smaller families. Big families in some regions are a choice with a purpose. They want someone who will care for them when they are old or sick. Is there enough to go around for all people? An ecological footprint belongs to the United States. The measure is how much land must supply the resources that country uses. The footprint is much greater than the land the country occupies. The country has gone past its carrying capacity. Its citizens must import resources from other countries. The imports keep up their standard of living. Eight billion people live on Earth. If all of them lived as most people in the United States live, many more planets would be needed. High-income countries can share Earth's resources more fairly. Fairer sharing can help lower the global birthrate. A 2022 chart asks how many planets we would need. The chart looks at what would happen if everyone lived like a resident of certain countries. The figures come from accounts of national footprint and biocapacity. Food enough for every person alive is possible if one condition is met. People in high-income countries must eat smarter. They must waste less. Around the world, a third of the food that is produced is wasted. That wasted food is enough to feed 2 billion people. Grain is the world's most important source of food. Meat production has boomed in high-income countries. It has boomed in middle-income countries too. Livestock receive one third of the grain raised around the world. Making 1 pound (0.45 kg) of meat takes a lot of grain. It takes even more water. Eating less meat leaves more grain for people in low-income countries. It leaves more water for them. It also protects valuable grasslands. China passed the United States in total energy use in 2009. Average Americans use more food than they need in order to survive. They use far more water than they need. They could shrink their ecological footprint. Eating smarter would help. Buying less would help. Conserving energy would help. Americans are the world's biggest consumers. They could become the world's most efficient consumers. Intelligent choices about how to live would do it.

10The COVID-19 crisis in 2020 cut carbon dioxide emissions. The yearly drop was the largest since the Second World War. The drop was about 6 percent. By December 2020, emissions had climbed again. They stood above the levels from before the crisis. Earth is an island in space. Carved tablets carry records the people of Rapa Nui left behind. No one has yet been able to translate that ancient language. We might never know for sure what happened. Some experts hold a belief about the years of overcrowding. Tribes fought over resources. The moai were toppled. Thousands of people died. Later, Europeans brought diseases. Those diseases killed still more people. Only 111 people were left when 1877 arrived. Today the population of Rapa Nui is growing again. Workers have put some of the moai back in place. Most of the native plants have become extinct. Most of the native animals have become extinct. The ancient culture of the people is lost. The story of this little island can teach a lesson, if we let it. We can learn to protect the limited resources of Earth. Earth is our own little island in space. Hydrologic describes the science of how water is spread and how it circulates on Earth. Arithmetically describes a change that stays at a constant rate. Babies born to a group of people in a chosen span of time make up the birthrate. Infrastructures are the frameworks of public structures and systems. Regions depend on them in order to function. Roads and utilities are examples. Carrying capacity is the greatest population an environment can support. The support has to last indefinitely. Middle-income countries are a varied set. On average, their people have incomes that are neither very high nor very low. Consumed means ate, bought, or used. An ecological footprint measures how living things affect the environment. It especially measures the natural resources used to sustain them. Millennia are thousands of years. A place is overpopulated when too many people live there. Too many other living things can crowd it as well. Emitting means sending something out. Estuaries are parts of rivers. There, fresh water mixes with the salt water of the ocean. Oversight means supervision. Standard of living is the level of material comforts and wealth. A person, a community, or a country may have that level. Geometrically describes a change that keeps a constant ratio.

21. Experts Who Help the President

1Fort Knox, Kentucky, is the home of the United States Bullion Depository. This book opens with an introduction. The next part is about rules for a new nation. After that, the book turns to the cabinet. A later part looks at a country whose needs kept growing. Openness and official power come next. A closing section and a word list finish the book. One picture shows the founding fathers drafting the Declaration of Independence. A new house calls for workers who each have a special skill. Carpenters raise the wall frames. Roofers put the roof in place. Plumbers lay the pipes that bring water. Electricians run the wires that deliver power. Every one of these workers is an expert. Their work gives the home systems that people can depend on. When the United States first became a nation, about 2.5 million people lived there. Citizens needed systems they could depend on. A house needs the same kind of care. The founders understood that need. They designed a plan so experts would watch the nation's many systems. The president would have their help in running the country. Rules for a New Nation. American leaders approved the United States Constitution in 1788. That paper listed the principles and the rules for governing the young country. The same principles and rules still guide the country.

2Three branches, or parts, share the government under the Constitution. One part is the legislative branch. It contains the U.S. Senate and the House of Representatives. Lawmakers there study proposed laws and pass laws. They also speak for the constituents who elect them. Another part is the judicial branch. Its courts watch over the justice system of the United States. The third part is the executive branch. The president leads it. Most government operations and departments are managed there. A chart names each branch and its job. Making laws belongs to the legislative branch, which holds the Senate and the House of Representatives. Carrying out laws belongs to the executive branch, which holds the president, the vice president, and the cabinet. Deciding how laws can and should be used belongs to the judicial branch, which holds the Supreme Court and the other federal courts. An elected president, and the executive branch around that office, worried the founders a great deal. A monarchy was not what they wanted. Daily work for the whole nation would fall to the president as chief executive. One person could not handle a job that large. George Washington said this even before he held the office. In his words, a single man could not get through all the great business of the state.

3A portrait shows George Washington. Rulers in earlier times often kept a small circle of advisors beside them. The Constitution borrowed that practice. Expert advisors called secretaries could head executive departments. Together, those advisors are known as the president's cabinet. Their help keeps the country's systems working well for citizens. The Cabinet. Congress had created three executive departments by 1788. The three names were Foreign Affairs, War, and the Treasury. A separate Office of Attorney General appeared in 1789. That office was not yet a department. Washington entered office in 1789. He selected secretaries and asked the Senate to approve them. The men he picked were the most qualified he could find. They came from both political parties of the day. They also came from different parts of the country. His aim was to help unify the nation. February 1793 brought the first meeting of the cabinet. Thomas Jefferson served as secretary of foreign affairs. He and Treasury secretary Alexander Hamilton clashed again and again over where the country should go. A strong federal government seemed best to Hamilton. Washington shared that view. Jefferson held a firm belief in the rights of the states. Jefferson left the cabinet in December 1793. Separate pictures show Thomas Jefferson and Alexander Hamilton.

4Washington drew a lesson from those clashes. He said he would stop choosing cabinet members who fought the way he wanted to govern. Later presidents mostly followed the same habit. They filled the cabinet with people who would back the president's position. That habit was one of several principles that turned into traditions. A second tradition requires Senate approval for cabinet members. After that vote, they answer to the president alone. They do not answer to Congress. Congress has no power to dismiss a department secretary. Asking a cabinet member to resign is a step only the president can take. No cabinet member holds power alone. Presidential authority is not shared with them. Advice is something they may offer. The president's directions are what they must follow. An early picture lines up the first cabinet from left to right. George Washington stands first. Henry Knox, of War, is next. Alexander Hamilton, of the Treasury, follows. Thomas Jefferson, of State, comes after him. Edmund Randolph, the attorney general, is last. The Growing Needs of a Growing Country. Cabinets grew larger as the nation itself grew. The earliest departments and offices changed over the years. Their number also rose. Presidents kept naming more experts to help run the country. A modern cabinet holds an array of departments.

5Each one has its own set of duties. Foreign Affairs later became the Department of State. Building good ties with other countries is its main mission. That work is called international diplomacy. Inside those countries, ambassadors and diplomats act for the United States. Some State Department work stays inside the United States and does not concern other lands. More than fifty bureaus, also called agencies, now sit inside the department. Their topics run from passports and stopping terrorism to food security around the world and cultural affairs. Washington, D.C., holds the main offices. More than 190 countries host over 300 of its embassies. The department also issues passports. An American citizen needs that legal paper before travel outside the United States. In 1947, Congress voted to join several fighting forces into one department. The U.S. Army, the Navy, the Marines, and the Air Force became the Department of Defense. Its headquarters is the Pentagon, in Washington, D.C. Command of the armed forces still belongs to the president, who is commander in chief. The forces needed to fight a war are managed by the Defense Department. So is the work of protecting the nation's security. No other cabinet department is close to its size. Service personnel number over 1.3 million. Civilian employees number 742,000. A picture shows the Pentagon.

6Banks, taxes, and money all fall under the Department of the Treasury. It regulates the nation's banks. It collects taxes. It prints the national currency. Washington, D.C., is where this department sits. Most duties first given to it in 1789 are still its work. A few duties moved. Until 1829, the Postal Service was under Treasury direction. Business matters later went to the Department of Commerce. A picture shows the Treasury Building. The attorney general's office grew into the Department of Justice in 1870. This department takes every legal matter that belongs to the federal executive. Enforcement of every federal law is supervised by this department. The Federal Bureau of Investigation takes part in that work. So do U.S. marshals and U.S. attorneys. Civil rights violations are investigated there as well. Immigration concerns and the management of federal prisons are also part of the work. The Drug Enforcement Agency sits under the Justice Department too. This department belongs to the executive branch, as the other cabinet departments do. It does not belong to the judicial branch. In practice it acts much like a local police force, because its job is to enforce the law. A different job belongs to the federal courts. Those courts decide if the laws being enforced agree with the Constitution.

7They also decide if the Justice Department is reading those laws the right way and enforcing them the right way. A picture shows the Robert F. Kennedy Department of Justice Building. A newer department appeared in 2002. It is the Department of Homeland Security. Keeping citizens safe inside the borders of the United States is its task. Among cabinet departments, it ranks third in size. Almost a quarter of a million people work there. Several well-known services sit inside it. The services include the Coast Guard of the United States. They include the Secret Service. They include the Transportation Security Administration. They include Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Residents are to be shielded from many dangers. Cyberattacks are one danger. Smuggling or an invasion by sea is another. Airplane sabotage and natural disasters are others. A picture shows the Coast Guard. Homeland Security now controls the Coast Guard. That service is one branch of the United States Armed Forces. Law on the oceans and the seas is its to enforce. Both domestic waters and international waters are under its official control. Defense never included the Coast Guard. The Treasury Department was its first manager. In 1967 it moved to the Department of Transportation. A picture shows a Coast Guard boat of the United States in New York Harbor.

8Mapping the country's lands has been work of the U.S. Geological Survey since 1849. That agency belongs to the Department of the Interior. The department itself was set up in 1849. People often call it the housekeeper of the nation. Caring for natural resources, and managing them, is its central duty. Two services sit inside it. One is the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. The other is the Bureau of Indian Affairs. Direction of the National Park Service is also its job. Other public lands are maintained and managed by this department as well. Ten further cabinet departments were also part of running the government as of 2018. Energy is one of them. Transportation is another. Agriculture and Labor are two more. Every department secretary talks with the president on a regular basis. The talks cover what is going on inside that department. The president also gives input on which policies ought to be used. Transparency and Authority. Growth in the cabinet departments has worried some people. Questions of transparency and of authority have come from their size and their reach. Transparency here means knowing what a vast web of departments actually does. Without that tracking, wasteful work can spend government money. Taxpayers pay for that waste too. Authority here means the limits of a job.

9Even so, some officials have taken on large powers that the Constitution does not spell out. At times they decide things and write rules in ways that are not allowed. Sheer size can leave some of that activity unchecked. In 2018, both worries reached the Supreme Court. The Court's decision urged reform of the expanded cabinet in the executive branch. Officials in the departments were encouraged to follow the Constitution. They were told not to step past their authority. A picture shows the U.S. Supreme Court. Presidential Succession. A chart dated as of 2018 shows the immediate line if the president can no longer serve. First is the vice president. Next is the Speaker of the House. Then comes the president pro tempore of the Senate. After the president pro tempore of the Senate, the successors are the department heads. The cabinet sets the order of who takes office if something should happen to the president. Conclusion. Four departments stood at the start. The cabinet now employs over four million people. That growth has helped the United States keep working while times changed. It has also helped while the country grew.

10Inside the departments are many offices, agencies, or bureaus. The cabinet has shifted and adjusted as the years passed. Its importance has stayed the same. People with expert skills in these departments try to do great good. They serve the president. They serve the citizens of the country as well. Word list. An advisor is a person who gives suggestions or guidance on one subject. An agency is a part of a government, a company, or another group that supplies a particular service. An array is a big number of things, or a wide mix of them. A constituent is a citizen with the right to vote who is represented by a particular official. Currency is money in any form people accept, used to stand for what goods and resources are worth. Executive refers to the branch that leads a nation and puts the laws into action. Federal describes the central government. That government shares power with the states or with regions. Ratified means approved in an official way. Reliable means able to produce a steady result, and so dependable. Security is being protected from danger, from loss, or from a threat. Transparency is being open, honest, and easy to understand. To unify is to join separate things so they become one whole.

22. Feathers Left in Stone

1A fossil shows the flightless bird Diatryma. The parts of this book come in this order. An opening. What fossils can tell. Birds of prehistoric times. Did birds come from dinosaurs? A closing. A word list. An index. Most animal species that have ever lived on Earth meet extinction. The environment can change. The climate may cool. The amount of food may drop. A whole species can die out when it cannot adapt to conditions that are new. Paleontologists have learned about many such extinct organisms from fossils. A fossil is evidence of prehistoric life kept in rock or in other material. Some fossils are simple marks an animal made while moving. Footprints are one kind. Trails left in the ground are another. Other fossils are hollow impressions of a whole animal body, pressed into rock. Still others are preserved body remains, such as bones or shells. These fossil remains of a prehistoric bird hold many secrets of the past. Fossils show how new kinds of species developed across eons. For example, scientists have found fossils that lead them to a belief. More than 150 million years ago, they believe, reptiles gave rise to birds. Those reptiles may have been dinosaurs.

2What fossils can tell us comes next. When almost all animals die, bacteria and fungi break the bodies down. That decomposition makes the bodies slowly disappear. If conditions are suitable, though, a dead animal may turn into a fossil. The fossil leaves clues about the animal's body and about how it lived. Usually, an animal that becomes a fossil is buried in sediment right after death. Sediment can be mud or sand. Burial of that kind is more likely in rivers, in the sea, or near other bodies of water. Water carrying minerals, such as calcium, then soaks into tiny spaces inside the bones. More and more bone tissue dissolves and decays. More and more minerals take the place of the bone. In time, a rocky copy of the skeleton remains. John Day Fossil Beds in Oregon is a typical place where fossils are found. When the body decays completely, impressions of the body form. Those impressions can show features such as feathers or scales. All that remains then is the hollow space where the body was. Sediment surrounds that space. A picture sequence shows the steps. An animal dies near water. The water rises not long after the animal dies.

3Skin and other soft tissues decay away. Sediment carried by the water buries the skeleton. Minerals replace the bone. The bone decays away. Scientists learn an animal's looks from its fossil bones and from other features. Those features also let scientists compare the animal with species alive today. Likenesses and differences may reveal how the extinct creature behaved. For example, fossil bones may look like bones in bird wings today. Maybe that animal could keep flying for a long time. Such traits may also show that modern birds are related to this extinct animal. Paleontologists use different procedures to learn how old a fossil is. That means learning when the animal caught in the fossil lived. Sediment piles up year after year. Fossils in deeper sediment are older than fossils closer to Earth's surface. Scientists get their best age estimates by studying certain chemicals in the rock that holds the fossil. Paleontologists find fossils, study them, and sometimes help museums display them. They have dug up many fossils of extinct prehistoric birds. The earliest known bird fossils belong to a primitive bird that was like a reptile. Its name is Archaeopteryx, said AHRkee-OP-tuhr-ihks.

4It lived about 150 million years ago. These fossils give strong evidence that birds came down from reptiles. Fossils of Archaeopteryx, including one shown here, rank among the most important fossils ever found. How old is that fossil? The main chemical method paleontologists use to estimate fossil age is called radioisotope dating. The method rests on a fact. Chemicals called radioactive isotopes break down into other chemicals. They do this at a known rate as time passes. Scientists compare how much of the radioactive isotopes remain in a fossil with how much of the breakdown products are present. From that comparison they calculate how long the decay has been going on. That calculation tells them how long ago the fossil formed. Fossils of Archaeopteryx show a crow-sized animal. Some of its traits looked like birds. Other traits looked like reptiles. Like modern birds, it had feathers, wings, and a wishbone. A wishbone is a forked bone in the upper chest. Teeth and a long bony tail made it like a reptile. Each wing also had three fingers, and the fingers had claws. Archaeopteryx probably flew rather poorly. Scientists base that conclusion on the sternum, or breastbone, seen in the fossils.

5Flat is the shape of the Archaeopteryx sternum. Modern birds have a sternum with a part that sticks out. Strong muscles used in flight attach there. Without a sternum like that, Archaeopteryx would have lacked powerful flight muscles. Beside insects, this animal was one of the first flyers. A fossil of Hesperornis shows that bird probably could not fly. Paleontologists have found several fossils younger than those of Archaeopteryx. Those fossils show other birds. They reveal how birds gained more modern traits as time passed. Hesperornis, said hes-pur-OR-niss, and Ichthyornis, said ik-thee-OR-niss, were two kinds of water birds. They lived about 90 million years ago. Fossils of Hesperornis show a bird that looked like a large loon. Big webbed feet helped it swim. A beak lined with tiny teeth helped it catch fish. Its wing bones were only rudimentary, so flight was impossible for it. Ichthyornis looked like a gull. Its wings were long and pointed. It was probably an excellent flyer. It dived into the sea to catch fish. By about 35 million years ago, fossils show, many chief bird types known now were already here. Those types included birds that looked like modern chickens, doves, ducks, parrots, penguins, owls, and songbirds.

6Did birds come from dinosaurs? Paleontologists theorize that bird fossils with reptile-like traits are signs of a link. The signs say birds developed from reptiles. Scientists have also found fossils of dinosaurs that had feathers and other traits like birds. Evidence in these fossils points to dinosaurs as the reptiles that gave rise to birds. Meat-eating dinosaurs called coelurosaurs, said sil-YUR-uh-sorz, resemble birds in many ways, fossils show. Scientists still class them as true dinosaurs. The most birdlike members of the coelurosaur group left fossils about 155 million to 135 million years old. The fossils show animals that were small for dinosaurs.
