On a summer afternoon in 1973, teen Cindy Campbell asked Clive, her older brother, for help. She wanted him to DJ, or work as a disc jockey, at a back-to-school party.

2Home for the party was their neighborhood, the South Bronx of New York City. Most people in that community were Black or Puerto Rican. Five years before, the Campbell family had moved from Jamaica to the United States. Clive's childhood in Jamaica included local parties. DJs there spoke over the records. His nickname was Hercules. He performed under the name DJ Kool Herc. He did not have fancy equipment. He chose some records from his collection. He hooked two turntables to a guitar amplifier. Both turntables carried the same record. He moved back and forth between them. That trick stretched the percussion breaks, the best part of the song for dancing. A picture shows DJ Kool Herc performing in England in 2000. The party succeeded beyond expectations. By the next day, Clive was famous all through the Bronx. He did not know what the coming decades would bring. Music that started in the South Bronx that day would later inspire people worldwide. Looking back, DJ Kool Herc said nobody knew they were making history. Nobody knew they were starting a cultural revolution. A future title, Father of Hip-Hop, was not something he expected. From Griot to Rapper. During his performances, DJ Kool Herc drew on a Jamaican tradition called toasting. Toasting means talking or chanting over a rhythm. It became popular in the 1950s. Jamaican toasting grew out of an even older oral tradition of West African griots. The word is said GREE-ohz. A griot may be a storyteller, a poet, a singer, or a historian. Many hip-hop fans see rappers as griots of the present day. Rappers, in the griot tradition, narrate what their community has lived.

3They record struggles and triumphs in a way that entertains and also informs. By doing that, they help shape the history and culture of their community, and they help preserve both. A picture shows a griot from Mauritania performing in New York City. The Four Pillars of Hip-Hop. Hip-hop is more than music. It is an entire culture. At the start, the community had no clubs for shows. It had no stages for dance. It had no galleries for art. The street became the place where these artists showed their ideas. The culture has four pillars, or key elements. Those elements are the DJ and breaking. They are also graffiti art and the MC. The DJ. A DJ's job is to keep the music flowing. When one turntable's song is ending, the other turntable brings the next song in. The music therefore keeps going without a break. Scratching is among the sounds people most link with hip-hop. The scratchy noise comes from sliding the record forward and back during play. A picture shows Grandmaster Flash with DJs at an event in 2002. Crowds, early DJs saw, loved the break beat more than other parts of a song. In that part, every sound except the drums drops out. Grandmaster Flash and other early hip-hop DJs put one record on two turntables at once. They did it so they could repeat the break beat again and again. With these techniques, hip-hop DJs were making new music out of old music. The idea proved influential beyond hip-hop. It would inspire music makers for years. A picture shows a DJ performing in Denmark in 2018. Breaking. Some people call this dance break dancing.

4The first street dancers preferred another name. They called what they did breaking. Their own names for themselves were b-boys, b-girls, or breakers. A picture shows b-boys performing during a competition in 1984. Breakers danced to hip-hop. They danced to funk. They danced to breakbeat music as well. While the break beat played, they showed skills they made up in the moment. They usually used six types of movement. Top-rock is fast footwork that takes skill. The breaker does it while standing. Down-rock uses the feet while both hands and both feet stay on the floor. Power moves are acrobatic. They call for speed, agility, and strength. Freezes are sudden stops. All movement halts while the breaker holds one position, usually an unusual or difficult one. Popping moves the arms and the legs in a smooth flow. In locking, limbs snap into a pose and stay there, often at sharp angles. Dance battles were common. Two breakers, or two dance crews, took turns showing their best moves. Audiences formed a circle around them and judged creativity and skill. Breaking became famous for a style all its own. Movies featured it. Television shows featured it too. Hip-hop fans all over the world took it up and loved it. Graffiti Art. Painted words or pictures on public property are called graffiti. By the early 1970s, hip-hop culture had taken graffiti in as a major piece. Graffiti artists did not use a canvas. They painted on buildings, subway cars, trains, and bridges. Part of the thrill was knowing thousands of people would see the work every day. A picture shows Lady Pink at work on a painting that honors women in hip-hop. Defacing public property is against the law.

5A lot of these painters were glad to be known as outlaw artists. People outside hip-hop culture saw the work as pollution of the environment. Inside hip-hop culture, graffiti was a form of art. Later, galleries around the world showed work by many of them. Classic hip-hop graffiti has also been kept in museums and in art books. A picture shows artwork by Jean-Michel Basquiat hanging in a gallery. Some of the best-known graffiti artists are Sandra Fabara, known as Lady Pink, and Fred Brathwaite, known as Fab 5 Freddy. Jean-Michel Basquiat is another. So is Donald Joseph White, known as Dondi. The MC. Early on, the word for a rapper was MC. Those letters stand for master of ceremonies. The DJ kept dance music flowing so the party would not die. The MC then took the mic. The MC used call-and-response to energize the crowd and to pull people in. Soon MC'ing grew into talking and rhyming in time with the music. Rappers are judged on content, on flow, and on delivery. Content covers a wide range of subjects. Clever expressions of self-confidence are part of it. Social opinions and political opinions are part of it too. Flow is strong when the lyrics stay locked to the beat. Rappers hit one syllable harder so their rhythm matches the music. Good delivery means a voice people can recognize. It means words said clearly. It means breathing that does not break the flow. A picture shows rapper Dumbfoundead performing in California in 2019. The Fifth Pillar of Hip-Hop. Many fans count knowledge as a fifth pillar. Legendary MCs such as KRS-One say knowledge ties the other four elements together. To be great, artists must know their own history and identity.

6They must know the history of their community. They must also know the history, the values, and the ideas of hip-hop culture. With that knowledge they can grow. They can also find fresh ways to speak through art. The same knowledge turns their art toward changing society. Women in Hip-Hop. From the start, women helped shape hip-hop culture. One of the earliest was Sharon Green, or MC Sha Rock. People count her as the earliest woman to rap. She began as a b-girl at age fourteen. She quickly built her skills as an MC. A record deal in 1979 made her the first woman in rap to sign one. She did so with her group, Funky 4 + 1. National television hosted this group in 1981, a first for any hip-hop act. Sylvia Robinson is sometimes called the Queen of Rap. She is sometimes called the Mother of Hip-Hop. Few music producers have shaped the field as much as she did. In 1979 she founded Sugar Hill Records, the first record label of hip-hop. Some of the most famous early hip-hop records had her help in production. One song was Rapper's Delight. The Sugarhill Gang performed it. It was the first hip-hop hit across the nation. People across the country met hip-hop through that record. At the time, the music was largely unknown outside New York City. A picture shows Sylvia Robinson. Men dominate the hip-hop industry. Men dominate the music industry in general. Female hip-hop artists have faced sexism from the beginning. Later hits by male artists often used words that showed disrespect toward women. A group of rappers changed hip-hop. The list includes MC Lyte and Queen Latifah.

7It includes Salt-N-Pepa and Lady B. It includes Lauryn Hill and Roxanne Shante. Hip-hop became their way to strengthen themselves and to strengthen other women. They used rap as a platform. They talked about how women were treated in hip-hop and in mainstream culture. A picture shows Lauryn Hill. Roxanne's Revenge. Lolita Shante Gooden was only fourteen, yet she already ranked with the best rappers then working. She is better known as Roxanne Shante. Her 1984 release carried the title Roxanne's Revenge. It was about the sexism women experience. Listeners made the song a major hit. A year later she reached the finals of a freestyle contest. Its name was the MC Battle for World Supremacy. In the last battle, her win looked clear to the crowd. One judge still marked her low on purpose, and that mark made her lose. Years later, that judge, himself a well-known MC, told her why. He did not want a girl to win. In his view, a win by a young girl would make people doubt hip-hop as serious art. Shante lost the battle. She still went on to release two rap albums. Young women making hip-hop later found a mentor in her. Rapped in Controversy. Hip-hop began as party music. Even so, the earliest artists took up serious social issues and political issues in their songs. Grandmaster Flash was among the first, through a song titled The Message. Poverty and misery in New York City streets were what the song described. Public Enemy used music to communicate Black pride. The group also addressed racism that Black people experience. Lana Michelle Moorer, known as MC Lyte, put several harms into her songs. She discussed racism.

8She discussed sexism. Drug use, and the damage it did in her community, was one subject. A note calls Public Enemy one of the top hip-hop groups during the 1990s. In the 1990s, a style called gangsta rap began to dominate hip-hop. Its lyrics often included words some people considered offensive. As this style grew more popular, the music industry promoted it above other styles. Many Black artists were not given record deals unless their music fit this type. As gangsta rap rose, outsiders began treating every kind of rap as offensive. Many other people have seen rap as a form of poetry. Rap and traditional poetry share many elements. Expert use of rhythm is one. Rhyming is another. Storytelling is another. Maya Angelou, among the most celebrated poets, also heard poetry inside hip-hop. Some of history's best-known rap artists worked with her. She inspired them as well. A photo shows Maya Angelou speaking a poem at President Bill Clinton's inauguration. Poetic Roots. Rap had a path cleared by spoken-word poetry of the 1960s. The Last Poets, based in New York City, spoke poems over a beat. The Watts Prophets, from California, did the same. The beat might be a bongo drum or jazz music. Social messages and political messages filled their poems. The messages were about Black pride, racism, poverty, and justice. People often treat these poets, and the work they made, as hip-hop's forerunners. A picture shows the Last Poets. The Golden Age of Hip-Hop. Hip-hop music spread across the country in the mid-1980s and the early 1990s. That spread transformed the culture. New artists brought new musical influences. They brought greater diversity. They brought innovation in style. Local radio stations and club DJs wanted more new hip-hop.

9Demand grew. Mainstream popularity shot upward. Record companies began spending a lot of money to produce new hip-hop albums. Different cities grew distinct styles. New York City produced hardcore rap and boombap. Los Angeles, California, produced G-Funk and gangsta rap. Run DMC and other newer artists started blending hip-hop with different genres. De La Soul used pieces of jazz and blues to create jazz rap. An upbeat style from Salt-N-Pepa got two names, pop rap and hip pop. One defining feature of this era was sampling. A sample is a part of one song reused in a different song. Artists took samples from many genres, including jazz, blues, soul, and rock. Movie sound clips were sampled by some artists too. Hip-Hop Goes Global. Nearly 9,000 miles, or 14,484 kilometers, separate the Bronx and New Zealand. Hip-hop music crossed that distance in the early 1980s. Māori listeners took it up eagerly. They are the indigenous Polynesian people of New Zealand. Many Māori lived in communities with few advantages. Black residents of the South Bronx in the early 1970s had faced the same kind of hardship. They faced greater financial struggle. They faced higher levels of crime. They faced poor access to health care and to education. They felt mainstream New Zealand culture did not represent them. They identified strongly with hip-hop. Bands including Upper Hutt Posse and Third3ye made hip-hop their own music. The musicians were Māori. A picture shows Upper Hutt Posse. Hip-Hop Does Not Stop. Worldwide popularity turned hip-hop culture into a movement that crossed borders. France took it in. So did Mexico, New Zealand, and South Africa. Films made the world notice break dancing.

10Wild Style, from 1982, was one. Breakin', from 1984, was another. Japan, Germany, Russia, and South Korea took up the dance in a special way. Incredible graffiti can be seen on city streets from Brazil to Morocco to China. Pictures show three scenes. Graffiti decorates a building in Brazil. In Hungary, a b-girl who comes from Japan competes. England is the stage for one member of a Muslim hip-hop pair. A 1973 street party thrown by a young girl in the South Bronx grew into a sensation across the globe. Thin resources pushed people toward musical inventions that rank among the twentieth century's most creative. It also led to powerful forms of artistic expression. Popular culture in many countries still shows hip-hop's influence. It has left a lasting mark. Word list. Agility is the ability to move quickly and easily. A ceremony is a formal event held for a special occasion. Culture means one society, with ideas and customs of its own. Distinctive means having a quality that is different and notable. Economic relates to the buying and selling of goods and services. Encircled means formed a circle around something. A genre is a category of writing or art. Style, form, or content sets it apart. Improvisational means performed or created without preparation. Innovation is the act of introducing new things or inventing them. A revolution is an overthrow of earlier ideas or of earlier ways of doing things. A sensation is someone or something that causes great excitement. Sexism is the belief that one sex or gender falls short of the other in strength, intelligence, or ability. Most often it says girls and women do not stand as equals of boys and men.

30. Hockey's Top Prize

1Jordan Nolan plays for the Los Angeles Kings. During 2012 he carried the great prize through the town where he grew up. The town is Sault Ste. Marie. Ontario is the province. Canada is the country. This book tells what the prize is. It names the man behind it. It follows the long road to a win. Famous moments from 1928, from 1942, and from 1970 come next. An octopus legend follows. An Oilers run follows. A closing cheer and a word list finish the book. A photo from 1996 shows Red Wings player Dino Ciccarelli, number 22. He is being pushed into Blues goalie John Casey. It is the seventh game. The series is the Western Conference final. Hockey's greatest prize. The year is 1996. The match is the seventh one. This series decides the West. Detroit's Red Wings face St. Louis. The other club is called the Blues. Whoever wins moves on. The next stop is the final round of the National Hockey League playoffs. People shorten that league name to NHL. The score is tied at 0 to 0. The period is the second sudden-death overtime. Tension could not be higher. Detroit captain Steve Yzerman takes the puck. His name is said EYE-zur-mun. He picks it up at center ice. He races to the blue line. Without warning comes the crack of a slap shot.

2The shot booms past the St. Louis goalie. Air seems to leave Detroit's Joe Louis Arena. Red Wings supporters, in the tens of thousands, burst into cheers. Plenty of fans rank that score among hockey's greatest thrills. Lord Stanley's cup. October is when the skilled athletes of the ice lace their skates. One aim fills their minds. They want the greatest prize in men's hockey. That prize is the Stanley Cup. April ends the regular season. Then the real season starts. For fans, the playoff weeks are the most thrilling of the year. Players skate. They shoot. They save. They check. They fight. All of it is for the cup they covet. The name honors Lord Stanley of Preston. Canada's Governor General is the post he held. The years ran from 1888 through 1893. In 1889 he watched ice hockey for the first time. The place was Montreal's Winter Carnival. Love for the game hit him immediately. He decided the top team should receive a trophy. Craftsmen finished the trophy in the year 1892. Its first name was the Dominion Hockey Challenge Cup. Canada's best amateur ice hockey club received it. His full name was Lord Frederick Arthur Stanley. Birth came in 1841. Death came in 1908. In 1915, two pro hockey groups made a deal. Each league would send its best club.

3Those two clubs would contest the trophy. Later years brought new leagues. Some leagues shut down. Some leagues joined together. A new title, the Stanley Presentation Cup, arrived in 1926. Another change came in 1947. From then on, people said Stanley Cup. The NHL then had only six teams. One club was in Toronto. Another was in Montreal. Detroit had a club. Chicago had a club. New York had a club. Boston had a club. All six still play in the NHL. The label historians use is Original Six. The reason is that more teams entered the league afterward. With all five bands in place, the cup stands 35.25 inches tall. That height is 89.54 centimeters. The first cup was silver. It stood 7.2 inches tall, or 18.5 centimeters. Its diameter was 11.4 inches, or 29 centimeters. The year 1963 is when the first cup entered the Hockey Hall of Fame. What players lift today is a stand-in. Among major sports in North America, only hockey skips a brand-new trophy every year. Champions hold the trophy only until the following season is finished. Five bands circle the cup. Winners' names are shown on the lowest band. When that band is full, the top band moves to the Hall of Fame. The other bands shift upward. A fresh band takes the bottom spot.

4A 2019 chart maps the conferences on the road to the cup. The chart labels the quarterfinals of each conference. It labels the semifinals. It labels the conference finals. It labels the Stanley Cup finals. Eastern clubs named on the chart include Tampa Bay, Columbus, Boston, and Toronto. Washington, Carolina, and New York appear too. So do the NY Islanders and Pittsburgh. Western clubs named include St. Louis, Nashville, Dallas, and Winnipeg. San Jose, Calgary, Colorado, and Vegas appear as well. The chart states that St. Louis won 4 to 3. The road to the cup. That road is long. It is difficult. Fans would not want an easier path. Thirty NHL teams play now. They split into two conferences. One conference is the Eastern. The other is the Western. Inside the East are the Metropolitan Division and the Atlantic Division. Inside the West are the Central Division and the Pacific Division. Each division sends its first, second, and third clubs straight into the playoffs. Other spots remain. Those spots go to the next two highest teams in each conference. Four rounds follow, and each round is a best of seven. First come the conference quarterfinals. Then come the conference semifinals. Then come the conference finals. Last come the Stanley Cup finals. The Eastern champion meets the Western champion there. The Los Angeles Kings player Willie Mitchell raises the trophy.

5Mount Benedict, in Canada, is under his feet. Imagine if the trophy could speak. These playoffs rank among the most competitive in sports. No wonder the winners get wildly excited. They get silly too. Odd stories fill more than a century. One New York Islanders player, Clark Gillies, let a dog feed out of the trophy. Andre Roy of Tampa Bay used the cup to carry an engagement ring. Three separate teams tossed the cup into a swimming pool. They wanted to know if it would float. It does not float. New York mayor Jimmy Walker handed the cup to the 1928 champions. Those champions were the New York Rangers. Famous moments. The year 1928, and a coach in the net. The Rangers were playing the Montreal Maroons. It was Game 2 of the finals. New York goalie Lorne Chabot got hurt. He had to leave. A spare goalie was rare in those days. Coach Lester Patrick scrambled for a last-minute fill-in. He asked the Maroons' head coach for a favor. Star Ottawa goalie Alec Connell was sitting in the stands. Patrick wanted to use him. Eddie Gerard coached the Maroons. Gerard refused. He wanted to keep his team's large edge. Patrick's players offered another plan. They asked their own coach to take the net. They promised harder play if he was the one in goal.

6A picture shows Lester Patrick, number 9. Across a career of twenty-four years he played for nine different teams. The Rangers were one of those teams. Moments later Patrick skated out. He wore a full set of goalie gear. He was forty-four. He was a retired defenseman. Goaltending experience was very thin. The cup was on the line. He had no other choice. Before he stepped on the ice, he spoke to his players. He asked the boys not to fail an old man. The result was remarkable. He stopped nineteen shots. He let in only one goal. The Rangers won in overtime. New York went on to take the Stanley Cup. Count his age that day as 44 years. Add three months. Add nine days. No older person has ever played in a Stanley Cup final. The record still stands. So does the story of that game. The year 1942, Maple Leafs against Red Wings. Original Six hockey had not yet held a cup final before this one. Toronto faced the worst odds. Detroit had already won the first three games. Game number 4 forced a jolt. Hap Day, coaching the Leafs, supplied it. He sat two star players down. Rookies took their places. He wanted the team to work harder. The plan succeeded.

7The Leafs won the next four games. The comeback was amazing. No club had ever erased a three-game hole in the Stanley Cup finals before. Someone asked Gaye Stewart, a Leafs player, what the series meant. A single word was his answer. That word was phenomenal. Beating Detroit in 1942 ended a dry spell for the Maple Leafs. Nine years had passed without a cup. A later Bruins win over the Blues returned the cup to Boston. Boston had waited twenty-nine years. The year 1970, and Bobby Orr's famous flying goal. It was overtime in Game 4 of the finals. The Boston Bruins were chasing a 4 to 0 result against the St. Louis Blues. The net of St. Louis was where captain Bobby Orr found himself. Derek Sanderson, a teammate, had just received a pass from Orr. Sanderson passed it straight back. Orr shot at the loose puck. He watched it cross the goal line. At that moment a St. Louis defenseman tripped him. The trip mixed with his excitement. Up he went, the way a comic-book hero might. Ray Lussier, a photographer, caught the moment. Hockey fans often name that picture the sport's best-known photograph. Orr is in the air. His arms are stretched out. He is celebrating a cup win. The Red Wings of Detroit added a habit in the year 2008.

8A giant inflatable octopus opened their games. The octopus legend. Hockey has some very strange traditions. None is stranger than the octopus story. Detroit is where it started. The date was April 15, 1952. The Red Wings were in a Stanley Cup playoff run. Only six teams existed then. A champion had to win two series. Each series was a best of seven. That meant eight wins in all. One night, a pair of local fans flung an octopus onto the rink. The animal had come from a seafood shop. Eight legs stood for the eight wins the team needed. Detroit won the cup that year. People treated the octopus as good luck. Year after year, Detroit kept the habit. A single game in 1995 saw thirty-six of the animals hit the ice. A second playoff night that same year brought a heavier animal. Two fans supplied it. The weight was 38 pounds. That weight is 17.2 kilograms. Twelve months later the ice received an octopus of 50 pounds. That weight is 22.7 kilograms. The habit still goes on. Twenty seasons in the NHL were Gretzky's career. A dynasty in Edmonton. From 1983 to 1990 the Edmonton Oilers looked like an All-Star team. Wayne Gretzky led them. Fans called him the Great One. His name is said GRET-ski. The club won five Stanley Cups in those years.

9He was that dominant. Terry O'Reilly, who coached the Boston Bruins, once spoke about him. O'Reilly called him the best. He joked that a league rule should send Gretzky to a different team each year. Gretzky was not the only star. The Hall of Fame also took in six more Oilers from those seasons. Official Dynasty status came from that Hall at a later date. Wins had piled up, and the span of years was fairly short. Since that award, the Hall has given Dynasty status to nobody else. Women's hockey has a second great trophy, called the Isobel Cup. The names are Isobel, Constance, and Mary. The family name is Gathorne-Hardy. The title is Lady. She is the person behind the trophy's name. She was Lord Stanley's daughter. Early women's hockey counts her among its first leaders. Amateur clubs were the first winners. The change arrived in 2016. From then on it honored the top pro women's club on this continent. A celebration photo shows the Boston Pride. The prize is the NWHL Isobel Cup Championship. March 27, 2021, is the day of that party. A game worth naming the best. Each year, hockey fans worldwide hunger for one picture. The dream is a favorite NHL club with the Stanley Cup in its hands. Players have chased that dream for over a century.

10They have scored. They have made saves. They have checked. They have fought. The reward is a drink from hockey's greatest prize. Playoff hockey can surprise anyone. Whichever club lifts the cup, the real winners are the fans. Those fans live all over the world. Words to know. Sudden death is an extra period after a tie. The first team to score in that period wins. A goalie is the defender who must keep the puck out of the net. A slap shot is a hard swinging hit that drives the puck with great force. A dynasty is a team, or a family, that stays successful or powerful for a long time. A semifinal round is a pair of games among four teams. The two winners move on. A deficit is a shortage, and the word is often used for money. Quarterfinals are four games among eight teams. The four winners move on. A conference is a group of sports teams. They play one another inside a larger league. A puck is the hard rubber disk used in hockey. To check is to stop a player who has the puck, or to take the puck away. Benched means kept out of the game. A playoff is a set of games after the regular season. Those games decide a champion.

31. How a Bat-and-Ball Game Won the World

1A match in Mumbai, India, stops for a short rain delay. Fans use the pause to wave the national flag of India. The pages ahead follow one path. They begin with the sport’s rise around the world. They then tell how the game grew. A middle section shows cricket as it is played now. Another section explains a match, from the throw to the run. Later pages name players who stood out on the oval. The finish looks at fair play. A word list comes last. The action is easy to picture. The batter’s tool is a bat with a wide, flat face. In size, the ball nearly matches a baseball. Few sports have a bigger following. Cricket belongs in the top five. One source counts two billion to three billion fans worldwide. The crowd did not appear overnight. In the sixteenth century, the players were children. The pastime grew into a sport that whole countries follow. England is the birthplace. The story starts in that country. A written record first mentions a cricket game in 1598. The spelling “creckett” sits inside a legal paper. The paper concerns a dispute over land. A witness said that he and his schoolmates once played on the plot in question. The document shows that the players were children.

2Other papers show adult games as well. Rival villages met rival towns. Early in the 1700s, wealthy patrons built the first paid teams. Each of those teams faced sides backed by other rich men. Modern teams grew from that start. One team’s rules did not always match the next team’s rules. In 1788, noblemen of the Marylebone Cricket Club wrote the “Laws of Cricket.” Officials have altered parts of those laws since then. Players still use them hundreds of years later. A picture from 1743 shows a game in London. People call the nineteenth century “the Golden Age of Cricket.” The sport’s modern shape formed in those years. Bowling rules changed in 1864. Until then, a bowler could pitch only underarm. The new law allowed an overarm pitch. The ball gained speed. It also gained spin. Batters answered with complex new techniques. During those years the game spread through lands held by the British Empire. Canada took it up. Australia did too. So did India. South Africa followed, and so did New Zealand. The Caribbean did as well. Professional sides played the first long Test-level matches in 1877. A Test can last many days. Those long games settle important championships.

3International cricket still treats a Test as its highest level. When the nineteenth century closed, women’s clubs were already active in several countries. In the twentieth century, many fresh ideas came from international teams. Players from the West Indies built the modern aggressive way of bowling. A photo shows C.P. Cumberbatch, from the West Indies, throwing during a match. People play cricket in many countries today. The strongest following remains in the United Kingdom. It is also strong in lands that Britain once ruled. A national side must hold Test status before it can play at the top. Twelve national teams held that status in 2024. Below the Test level, matches range from casual community games to paid contests. Women play for national sides and in international Tests. Some leagues, and some special matches, use their own extra rules. The sport appeared at the Olympic Games once. That was the second Games, held in 1900. It has stayed off the program ever since. Fans still lobby for a return at the Summer Games. Twelve teams hold Test status, in this order. England comes first, then Australia, then South Africa. Next are the West Indies and New Zealand. Then come India, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka. Zimbabwe, Bangladesh, Ireland, and Afghanistan complete the list.

4Players on the West Indies side come from sixteen separate countries and colonies. A new watcher may think the game is baseball. Early cricket helped shape baseball. The two sports are not the same. Their fields are not the same either. Cricket uses an oval ground. A small rectangle in the middle is called the pitch. Each side has eleven players. The sides take turns with the bat and with the bowl. To bowl is to throw. Runs come when the batting side hits the ball and runs up and down the pitch. The bowling side tries to dismiss each batter. A dismissal can come when the ball strikes three posts. Ten dismissals, out of eleven batters, end the innings. The sides then trade jobs. The bowlers go in to bat. The batters go out to bowl and to field. A few cricket phrases now live in everyday British English. If someone says a thing is “not cricket,” the meaning is unfair play or poor manners. Players call a wet or muddy ground a “sticky wicket.” Away from the field, that phrase means a hard situation. A 1984 photo shows Joel Garner bowling for the West Indies. An Australian wicketkeeper waits behind an Indian batter, ready for a catch.

5A ball can fly at about 95 to 100 miles an hour. That is 152.8 to 160.9 kilometers an hour. Baseball uses a pitcher and a catcher. Cricket uses a bowler and a wicketkeeper. The wicket is made of three short posts set in the ground. Those posts are the stumps. Two small pieces of wood lie across the tops. Those pieces are the bails. One bowling-side player takes the bowler’s job and throws. Another stands behind the wicket as wicketkeeper. The captain places the other nine players around the ground. Two batters walk out. They stand at opposite ends of the pitch. The batter who faces the ball is the striker. The partner is the nonstriker. The bowler aims at the wicket and tries to dismiss the striker. A legal overhand bowl keeps the elbow straight. If the bails fall off the stumps, the striker is out. A new batter comes in. Grounds are not all one size. A full-size ground covers at least 16,000 square yards, which is 13,378 square meters. The pitch measures 22 yards, or 20.12 meters. One marked width is 12 feet, or 3.66 meters. A field diagram names the pitch, the bowling crease, and the return crease.

6It also names the popping crease, the boundary, and each wicket. The same diagram marks the bowler, the striker, and the nonstriker. It marks nine field players, two umpires, and the wicketkeeper. The striker guards the wicket with the bat. The striker also tries to hit hard enough for runs. After the hit, both batters run. Each heads for the other end. They pass in the middle of the pitch. The popping crease is the line drawn just before the wicket. A run is scored when the runners cross that line and trade ends. Batters keep running, end to end, for as many runs as the hit allows. The fielding side tries to “run out” the striker during those runs. The striker must be safe behind the popping crease. If not, a fielder can use the ball to knock the bails off the stumps. That dismissal ends the striker’s turn. A catch can also end the turn. The catch counts if a fielder holds the ball before it hits the ground. Suppose the running ends and the striker has not been dismissed that way. Whoever now stands at the striker’s old end takes over as striker. Safety gear covers the legs, the chest, and the arms.

7Players also wear a face guard and gloves, and they carry a bat. The set of gear includes bails, a wicket, a ball, and stumps. The wicketkeeper and the striker are part of that picture too. Only one striker faces the bowler, yet the pitch has two wickets. Here is how the second wicket comes into play. A bowler delivers six times. If those six balls bring no hit and no dismissal, the bowler swaps with a teammate. The new bowler aims at the batter who had been the nonstriker. That batter is now the striker. Runs can also come as “extras.” A hit that crosses the boundary in the air, with no bounce, stops the running. The striker is given six runs. A fumble by the wicketkeeper can also give the striker a run. An ordinary match has two innings. Each side bowls once and bats once. The day can end the game as well. Whichever side scores more runs takes the win. Sometimes the day ends before both innings are finished. The result is then a tie, also called a draw. A side that is ahead may close its own innings on purpose. That choice can stop a draw. A Test uses four innings. It is a long test of stamina.

8Play can run for five days. Each day holds about six hours. The sport sets a high value on sportsmanship. A few rules are used only when the two sides cannot settle a question. One case is a ball stopped by the batter’s body rather than the bat. The umpire decides only if the teams still disagree. The disagreement is whether that ball would have hit the wicket. W. G. Grace lived from 1848 to 1915. He worked as a doctor, and cricket counted him as an amateur. He still reshaped the sport. Many rank him among the greatest players ever seen. He built a batting style that could adapt. He could use it from more than one stance. The style folded in many different strokes. Kumar Shri Ranjitsinhji is pronounced koo-MAR SHREE rahn-JEET-seeng-jee. People called him “Ranji.” His years were 1872 to 1933. He is a standout from the years people call “the Golden Age of Cricket.” He ruled Nawanagar, an Indian region under British control. Judges of the game placed him with the best batters. At home in India he became an icon. India’s national championship, the Ranji Trophy, uses his name. Politics mattered to him as well. He spoke for India at the League of Nations.

9That league came before today’s United Nations. Sir Donald Bradman lived from 1908 to 2001. Australians know him as the finest Test batter in history. His Test average was 99.94. He almost never failed. The next-best average in the record is 60.97. After World War II he captained Australia. The side’s nickname was “the Invincibles.” Their tour of England broke records. They stayed unbeaten across thirty-four matches. The tour lasted 144 days, and they played on 112 of those days. Each year since 1889, the cricket paper Wisden has chosen five Cricketers of the Year. Claire Taylor, born in 1975, was the first woman to receive that honor. The year was 2009. At college she played with the men. Her batting grew closer to the men’s style than to the style common in the women’s game. She then joined professional women’s cricket. Few batters in the sport’s history rank above her. What turned cricket into an international phenomenon? The story of the British Empire is part of the answer. New styles of play, still being invented, are another part. Two features of the game may matter even more. A batter at the crease is judged as a player, not by name.

10Birthplace does not decide the contest either. On the field, the players meet as equals. Tradition also says that every player is owed the same respect. Those two values, equality and respect, are values people everywhere can share. That sharing may explain the sport’s hold on players and on spectators. Young players build skill using the bat, the ball, and the wicket together. A photo shows boys in northern India starting a game of their own. The word list follows. Adaptable describes something that can change to fit a new setting. Aggressive describes a person ready to attack, or a force that is too strong. A dispute is an argument. To field means to catch the ball and throw it, whether the game is baseball or cricket. Incorporated means brought in and blended with the rest. Innovations are new ideas, new products, or new methods. To lobby is to press decision-makers for what you want. Officials are people trusted with special duties or with authority. A phenomenon is a striking event, or a person famous for a rare gift. Spectators watch and do not join the action. Sportsmanship covers fair play, respect, and obedience to the rules. Techniques are skilled ways of getting a job done.

32. How a Loose Union Became One Nation

1The Liberty Bell can be pictured at the start of this book. Another picture shows colonists in a fight with British soldiers at the Battle of Lexington. The story moves from the Articles of Confederation to the Treaty of Paris. Money troubles and the Constitutional Convention come next. Then come fights over land, the Louisiana Purchase, exploration, and war. Hard words are explained at the end. The year was 1776. North America's thirteen British colonies put their names on the Declaration of Independence. They said they were free from rule by Great Britain. They said they were independent. In the same moment they called themselves a union of states. The name they chose was the United States of America. That union then needed a system of government. People from the first thirteen colonies, by then called states, started writing a plan. Those people were delegates. War with Great Britain had not ended. Because the war went on, five years passed before the plan was firmly set in the new union. Forty more years would pass. Another war with Great Britain would come. Only then would the new union feel truly united. The year was 1777. Each state had named delegates to the Second Continental Congress. Those delegates agreed to send the new government plan to the states. The states would review it. The paper that laid out the plan became the Articles of Confederation. It refused the word nation for the United States. Its own phrase was a firm league of friendship. Thirteen states were in that league. A weak government for the whole country was set up. Strong governments for the states were set up. States liked the authority they held under the Articles. They liked the freedom too. Every state wrote a constitution of its own. Every state printed money of its own. A map of those first thirteen states shows Indigenous peoples on the surrounding lands.

2The names include the Algonquins, the Abenaki, the Ottawas, and the Chippewas. They include the Iroquois, the Hurons, the Illinois, and the Miamis. They include the Pottawatomies, the Delaware, the Powhatan, and the Shawnee. They include the Cherokee, the Chickasaws, the Creek, the Choctaws, and the Seminole. The Mississippi River is on that map. The first thirteen states were founded inside areas where Indigenous peoples lived. Those same areas bordered the states. Under the Articles, the federal government had no authority. It had no freedom to act. War had left the United States with debts. Congress was the only federal branch the Articles created. Congress could not tax anyone to raise money for those debts. No power to tax would prove a fatal flaw in the Articles of Confederation. Other flaws sat in the document too. No one executive stood in charge. A president was chosen to watch over the meetings of Congress. That president could not decide anything. Congress also could not change the Articles when the states found a part of the plan failing. Nine states out of thirteen had to agree before a change could happen. Several years after approval, the flaws finally showed. Indigenous peoples were pushed off their lands by the first thirteen states. A pattern began there. The same pattern returned in the westward expansion of the 1800s. Indigenous peoples resisted European colonists with diplomacy. They also resisted with warfare. Epidemics held their efforts back. The sicknesses came from diseases Europeans had brought. Almost five years passed before all thirteen states agreed to the Articles of Confederation. Major fighting in the Revolutionary War stopped in 1781. U.S. General George Washington defeated British General Charles Cornwallis. The place was Yorktown, Virginia. Two more years passed before the war was officially finished. Peace terms were discussed in Paris, France. The talkers represented the United States and Great Britain. Talks began in the middle of 1782.

3Talks closed on September 3, 1783, the day the Treaty of Paris received its signatures. That signature is what officially closed the war. Two important ideas were written into the peace treaty. The new United States was recognized as independent from Great Britain. Boundaries of the new country were set. Its land began at the Atlantic Ocean and reached west as far as the Mississippi River. New Orleans was left out. The Floridas were left out. Spain controlled both. The northern edge was set at the Great Lakes. It also followed the borders of Quebec and of Nova Scotia. Both of those places belonged to Canada, which Britain controlled. A map of this settlement can show Canada under British control. It can show land claimed at once by Great Britain and by Spain. It can show the Great Lakes, the Mississippi River, and U.S. states and territories. It can show New Spain, the Atlantic Ocean, and New Orleans. A wish for wealth drove most European colonization of North America. In the 1500s, trade paths between Europe and Asia were badly broken. The Ottoman Turks were fighting various groups. Lost profits pushed many European powers to seek new sea paths west toward Asia. From 1565 to 1625, colonies in North America were planted by Spain, Britain, France, and the Netherlands. The Treaty of Paris in 1783 closed the American Revolutionary War. Land was split between the United States and Great Britain. Rights of Indigenous peoples were ignored. Those peoples had lived on the lands since before recorded history. After the Revolutionary War and the signed Treaty of Paris, money troubles hit the United States hard. Soldiers went home poor and tired. The government held no money. It held no power to tax. Many soldiers therefore went unpaid. A larger money headache waited. That headache was the debt from the war. The nation owed more than 76 million dollars.

4Foreign countries were owed part of it. Individual Americans were owed part of it. State banks were owed part of it. Leaders had no clear way to pay debts that large. In Massachusetts, money pain at home set off a rebellion. Some farmers had fought for independence and then lost their farms. Prison took them because the debts could not be paid. The year was 1786. Daniel Shays had been a captain in the Revolutionary War. He marched with about a thousand farmers and other workers. They marched on Springfield, Massachusetts. Then they went toward Boston. There the U.S. Army traded gunfire with them. Some workers were tried and hanged. Others received no punishment. Shays' Rebellion convinced many citizens, and many leaders, that the federal government must be stronger. A picture shows a gold U.S. Half Eagle dated 1795. Fifty-five men came to Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, to face the country's many problems. The meeting place was Independence Hall. The month was May 1787. Their aim was to alter the Articles of Confederation. A stronger federal government was the goal. They would draft a constitution. An executive would lead the union. Congress would gain the power to tax. A way to change the governing paper would be created. Delegates came from twelve of the thirteen states. Each man was an influential leader at home. The men most involved in building the new union are sometimes called the founders. Every delegate was a wealthy, educated white man. That fact matched another fact of the time. In most states, the vote belonged only to white men who owned property. George Washington was elected to preside. The meeting took the name Constitutional Convention. It would run for several weeks. Tempers rose in debates about changing the Articles of Confederation. Two issues concerned power in the new government. Representation was the first issue. More seats in Congress would mean more power. Two plans were put forward.

5One plan tied representation to population. States with more people would get more representatives. The second plan gave every state the same representation. Slavery was the second issue. The people held in slavery were Black, taken from Africa, or born to people who had been taken. They were treated as property. Freedom was denied to them. Conditions were often terrible. They had to work, and they were not paid. Southern states wanted to keep slavery as an institution. They also wanted enslaved people counted when representation was set. Those people had no rights. They could not vote. George Washington, like many founders, gained because enslaved people labored on his estate. Southern delegates hoped a count of enslaved people would lift their states. They wanted footing closer to that of the Northern states. The Northern states had more people. Out of this came the Three-Fifths Compromise. It dealt with representation and with slavery. Congress would have two houses. The Senate would represent every state equally. The House of Representatives would follow population. On slavery, Congress was barred for twenty years from any change meant to control it. Each enslaved person would count as three-fifths of a person. That fraction would set how many representatives a state received. How much power a president should hold was debated too. The answer was a system called checks and balances. A power handed to one branch would be matched by equal power in the other two. Three branches were proposed. The legislative branch would hold two houses of Congress. The executive branch would hold a president. The judicial branch would hold courts that enforce laws. A method for changing the Constitution was written into the document itself. The date was September 17, 1787. Thirty-nine convention delegates signed the Constitution. It went out to the states for a vote. Across the country, people argued over whether the plan was a good one.

6The Federalists liked the Constitution. They worked so states would ratify it. The Antifederalists did not like it. They worked to keep it from becoming the law of the land. No democracy then existing in Europe could serve as a model. None existed. Delegates instead looked at some Indigenous nations. One example was the Haudenosaunee Confederacy. People sometimes call the Haudenosaunee the Iroquois. They had built a complex government for a confederacy of six nations. That government showed how ideas the delegates wanted might work in real life. A picture shows an Osage warrior, a Haudenosaunee man, and a Pawnee woman. The first U.S. presidential election came in 1789. In most states, the voters were only white men who owned land. After the Civil War, the Constitution was amended. The vote was widened more than once. People of every ethnicity can vote now. Women can vote now. Any citizen older than eighteen can vote now. Many people say voting-rights laws still discriminate. They say the harm falls unfairly on people of color. They say the problem is still serious in many parts of the country. Abigail Adams supported women's rights in America at an early time. Antifederalists said the Constitution must list rights that belong to the people. Government must not be able to take those rights away. The two sides later agreed. All thirteen states voted yes on the Constitution. The deal between Federalists and Antifederalists added ten changes. Those changes are the Bill of Rights. Free speech was guaranteed. Religious practice was guaranteed. Freedom from a religion run by the state was guaranteed. Other rights were guaranteed too. George Washington became president of the United States of America under the new Constitution. He took office on April 30, 1789. A great leader is what many people believed him to be. He served two terms. Each term lasted four years. His presidency ran from 1789 to 1797.

7In the first term he named Alexander Hamilton secretary of the treasury. Hamilton's fix for the nation's money problems included taxes on imports. It also included the first national bank. Faith in the government seemed to return. The economy grew. When Washington's second term ended, John Adams was elected president in 1796. Adams served from 1797 to 1801. Thomas Jefferson came next, in 1801. Jefferson served from 1801 to 1809. Another problem waited. What should be done with the huge lands won in the Revolutionary War? State governments claimed land to the west. Indigenous peoples had lived there since before recorded history. Some tracts were claimed by more than one state at the same time. The Land Ordinance of 1785 explained the split of this property. It would be split into townships and sections. Settlers would buy the sections. Some sections were reserved for the government. Some were reserved for public schools. In 1787 a Virginia delegate, Thomas Jefferson, designed the Northwest Ordinance. It gave rules for making new states inside the Northwest Territory. The United States would not hold colonies. Britain had held the thirteen colonies. The new country would not copy that pattern. Tecumseh led the Shawnee. They fought American settlers who were moving into the Northwest Territory. Homes went up as settlers moved west. The Land Ordinance and the Northwest Ordinance prepared a huge westward move of settlers. That move came in the early 1800s. Roads were built so the expansion could happen. Canals were built. Railroads were built. Growth was fast. The new government seemed able to match the pace. Debts were being paid down. Power in the new government was divided. The grim mood after the war had lifted. Prosperity and growth led leaders to make new plans. France now held ground that started at the Mississippi River and reached the Rocky Mountains. France also held New Orleans. Westerners in the United States could not send crops down the Mississippi for trade.

8They could not use the port of New Orleans for that trade either. The United States went to Napoleon Bonaparte, emperor of France. The hope was to buy New Orleans. Bonaparte had suffered major setbacks in a European war. He needed soldiers and cash. To pay for his war, he offered more than the city. He offered all of the Louisiana Territory. The price was 15 million dollars. In October 1803 the United States paid France's price. The nation doubled in size. Added land came to 800,000 square miles, equal to 2.07 million square kilometers. The added people numbered 200,000. Land area of the United States was nearly doubled by the Louisiana Purchase. Westward expansion was pushed farther. In many cases Indigenous peoples were destroyed or driven from their homes. May 1804 was when President Thomas Jefferson sent two army officers west. Their names were Meriwether Lewis and William Clark. A further group of 45 people went with them. They were to find a route across the continent. They were to explore the Louisiana Territory. They were to come back and report. Sacagawea, a girl of the Lemhi Shoshone, worked as an interpreter. Her help let the expedition succeed. More than two years of travel ended with their return. They carried journals. They carried drawings. They carried hundreds of plant and animal samples. The expedition prepared the way for taking land in the West. Many Indigenous groups already living there would be hit hard. A picture shows Lewis and Clark's group moving through the Louisiana Territory. While they explored, an old ally was fighting. France was in a raging war with Great Britain. President Jefferson hoped the United States could stay out. James Madison became president in 1808. He hoped for the same staying out. Staying out proved impossible. British ships seized U.S. ships and searched them. French ships did the same.

9Each side wanted to stop supplies from reaching its enemy. Britain also took the sailors off the captured ships. Those sailors were forced to serve Britain. Citizens of the United States had won independence from Britain. Now they were under Britain's tyranny again. In 1812 President Madison warned Great Britain. Searching and seizing of U.S. ships had to stop, or war would follow. The answer did not satisfy him. He declared war on Great Britain on June 18, 1812. During the War of 1812, the United States lacked a navy that could fight Britain at sea. An invasion meant to conquer Canada, then under Britain, failed. The failure showed that the army could not face that giant nation again. The war lasted two and a half years. A peace treaty was signed by the two countries on December 24, 1814. The U.S. ship Constitution grew famous in that war. It won a battle against the British ship Guerriere. The war was officially over. The United States still fought Britain once more. On January 8, 1815, Americans won a clear fight called the Battle of New Orleans. General Andrew Jackson led them. He did not know peace had already been signed. British dead numbered almost three hundred. U.S. dead numbered less than twenty. The win made something plain. The western part of the country was truly under the United States, not under Great Britain. Citizens felt as if the War of 1812 had been won. In truth, neither side had victory. The late win may have mattered most for another reason. The new United States of America felt, at last, like one united nation. A timeline of the American Revolution opens with the French and Indian War. That war is also called the Seven Years' War. It ran from 1754 to 1763. The years 1764 and 1765 brought the Sugar Act, the Quartering Act, and the Stamp Act.

10The year 1767 brought the Townshend Acts. The year 1770 brought the Boston Massacre. The year 1774 brought the Coercive Acts, also called the Intolerable Acts. The First Continental Congress met in 1774. The Revolutionary War began in 1775. The Second Continental Congress met in 1775. The Declaration of Independence was signed on July 4, 1776. The Revolutionary War ended in 1781. All thirteen states approved the Articles of Confederation in 1781. Shays' Rebellion came in 1786. The Constitutional Convention was held in 1787. All states ratified the Constitution in 1791. The Bill of Rights was ratified in 1791. War with Britain began again in 1812. The Treaty of Ghent, signed in 1814, ended the War of 1812. Authority is power to govern, to give orders, or to decide. Checks and balances split power among branches so no single branch can dominate. A compromise is a decision in an argument where each side gives something up. A constitution holds the basic laws that say how a state or a nation is governed. Debates are talks between people or groups who disagree on an issue. Debts are things owed to someone, and they are usually money. Executive describes the branch that leads a nation and carries out its laws. Expansion is growth in size, amount, volume, or scope. Guaranteed means promised, or made sure. Judicial describes the branch that checks whether laws agree with the constitution. Legislative describes the branch that makes laws. Prosperity means success, wealth, or good fortune. To ratify is to give official approval. A rebellion is a fight against authority or against power. Representatives are people picked to speak, to vote, or to act for someone else. Seizing means taking control by force. A treaty is a formal peace or friendship agreement between nations or groups. Tyranny means cruel or harsh acts done by someone, or by a group, that holds power.

33. How Congress Makes the Nation's Laws

1This book moves through the power of Congress. It then explains the Constitution and the legislative branch. Structure and duties of Congress come next. The path a bill follows is after that. Later parts show Congress at work, including committees, elections, speeches, and votes. Checks and balances follow. A closing part is called a great responsibility. A word list ends the book. The Power of Congress. In the summer of 1964, Congress was debating a new law that caused strong disagreement. The Civil Rights Act would put an end to segregation in public places. Schools, libraries, and swimming pools were among those places. Businesses were included too, such as movie theaters and restaurants. The House of Representatives had already passed the act. It still needed a yes vote from the other half of Congress, which is the Senate. A group of senators tried to delay that vote. They gave very long speeches on the Senate floor. That delay is a filibuster. Some people call the tactic talking the bill to death. Senator Robert Byrd of West Virginia spoke for fourteen hours and thirteen minutes. His speech gave reasons the Senate should refuse the Civil Rights Act. A 1964 photo shows Senator Byrd packing a briefcase after he finished speaking on the Senate floor. Not long after Senator Byrd finished, most senators voted to stop the filibuster. Nine days after that, the Senate passed the Civil Rights Act. President Lyndon Johnson then signed it into law. A note says Thomas Jefferson, the third president of the United States, held a contest to choose the design of the Capitol Building. The same note appears again beside a picture of that building.

2The Civil Rights Act shows one way the U.S. Congress does its work. Congress is the main body of the legislative branch. Its members come from the Senate and from the House of Representatives. Their workplace is the Capitol, located in Washington, D.C. They speak for the American people inside the government. Writing laws is their duty. Amending laws is their duty as well. They have other important duties besides those. The Constitution and the Legislative Branch. Leaders adopted the Constitution in 1788. It works as a blueprint for the government of the United States. It splits that government into three parts, or branches. The president leads the executive branch. Most government operations and departments are managed there. The legislative branch has two chambers. They are the U.S. Senate and the House of Representatives. That branch represents citizens and also makes laws. The judicial branch oversees the courts of the justice system. At times the branches cooperate and reach a compromise. At other times they stand against each other. What they do depends on the situation. Article I of the Constitution gives lawmaking to the legislative branch alone. Only that branch may create a new law. Only that branch may change a law that already exists. Congress also has the right to borrow money. The money may come from businesses, from state governments, or from other countries. Taxation is under Congress as well. Congress decides what people and businesses must pay the government. That money supports public services. Schools and roads are examples. Military funding is controlled by Congress too.

3No other branch may declare war. A note from 2018 says the yearly pay for a U.S. senator was $174,000. The Structure and Responsibilities of Congress. Both the Senate and the House act for the American people. The two bodies do not have the same number of members. Each state gets two senators. The size of the state does not change that number. Population does not change it either. The Senate's full membership is one hundred. A senator's term lasts six years. After that, the senator must run again to stay in office. Treaty-making is another Senate duty, beyond writing laws. The Senate ratifies treaties with other countries. The Senate must also approve some people the president names to jobs. Judges on the Supreme Court are one example. The House of Representatives has 435 members. Each one is elected for a term of two years. The fifty states share those members according to population. California has the largest population in the United States. It also has the most representatives in the House. States with smaller populations sit at the other end. Montana is one of them. Delaware is another. Each of those states has only one seat. Representative Lisa Blunt Rochester is the only House member from Delaware. The 435 voting members are not the whole House. Six more representatives are elected, and they do not vote. They come from U.S. territories. The six places are the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico. They also include American Samoa and Guam. They also include the Northern Mariana Islands and the Virgin Islands of the United States. Members of the House choose their own leader.

4That leader is the Speaker of the House. If the president could not do the job, and the vice president could not either, the Speaker would become president. That possibility makes the Speaker a powerful post in government. Representatives act in government for their constituents. Citizens who dislike how the country is run have a way to respond. A public database lists contact information for elected officials. A citizen can use it to reach a representative. People may also go to town hall meetings led by national politicians. At those meetings, government matters can be discussed in the open with the representatives. A photo shows a college student speaking. A senator and a representative are with the student at a town hall. The Legislative Process. A new law takes many steps. Writing the bill is the first step. Any person may write one, including a member of the public. Individuals and organizations may go to their elected officials with an idea. They might want an old law changed. They might want a brand-new law. A member of Congress must then present the bill in an official way. That member is the sponsor. The bill may be presented to the Senate, to the House, or to both chambers. Other members who back the bill are called cosponsors. Next, the bill goes to one or more committees in the Senate or the House. Those committees review it. Members of a committee research the proposed bill. They decide which laws should be looked at. They recommend what to do next. Hearings are part of committee work. At a hearing, the committee asks experts about the bill.

5The committee tries to find answers to problems that might come up. After that, a subcommittee reviews the bill. The subcommittee looks deeper and looks at more specific points. It then holds a hearing of its own. When most subcommittee members vote to recommend the bill, it goes back. The full committee receives it again. The full committee holds a hearing and a vote. A picture shows hundreds of thousands of protesters. They marched on Capitol Hill in March 2018 at a rally against gun violence. If most members of the full committee will not recommend the bill, talk about it ends. Members of Congress can bring the same bill back. They often do bring bills back more than once. Support from most of the full committee puts the bill on the official calendar of one chamber. Bills that matter most are decided right away. Other bills may sit for months. Many bills are never taken up at all. Dead Bills. A term of Congress lasts two years. When the term ends, any bill that did not pass is treated as dead. That includes a bill passed by the Senate or by the House, but not by both. It even includes a bill passed by both chambers if the president never signed it. An image made in the early 1860s shows House members in debate. When a bill's day arrives, that chamber holds more than one debate. They may change the bill while they debate. Then that chamber votes. Approval by a majority sends the bill to the other chamber of Congress. There it is debated again.

6It may be amended again. Sometimes the two chambers pass different versions. A conference committee is then created. Its members come from both chambers. The committee works out the differences. It writes a bill that is a compromise. Each chamber must approve the revised bill. After a majority in each chamber says yes, the bill is sent at once to the president. The president has a few choices. A signature turns the bill into an official law. There is a second path to becoming law. The president may let ten days go by. If there is no signature and no veto in that time, the bill becomes law on its own. A veto means the president rejects the bill. The bill then goes back to Congress. Congress looks at the reasons the president gave. A bill may become law even when the president withholds approval. That happens if two-thirds of the Senate and two-thirds of the House vote to override the veto. Most bills that are proposed never become laws. In the span from January 2011 to January 2013, Congress put forward 6,845 bills. Just 561 of them passed and turned into laws. The number that did not become law is 6,284. A picture from 1936 shows a representative placing a bill into the hopper. The hopper is a special bin for bills on the House floor. Congress in Action. A typical member of Congress has a very full schedule. Most of the time goes to legislative work. Time also goes to work for constituents. What follows is a look at a few parts of that work.

7Committees. Committee work matters a great deal in both chambers. Senators and representatives are placed on committees and on subcommittees. Some committees are permanent. Education and the workforce is one example. Agriculture is another. The budget is another. Permanent committees are called standing committees. Other committees are called special or select committees. Those are temporary. They look into one particular problem. A committee may form a subcommittee to handle certain tasks. In the Congress of 2017 to 2018, the Senate had sixteen standing committees. It had sixty-eight subcommittees. It had four select committees. Standing committees in the House numbered twenty. It had ninety-seven subcommittees. It had one select committee. A picture shows a scientist speaking at a hearing of the Senate Intelligence Committee. Campaign money in 2016 was large. A typical senator's spending was $10.4 million. A representative spent $1.5 million. Those figures are for their election campaigns. Getting Elected. Members of Congress put a lot of time into campaigning. They put a lot of money into fund-raising as well. Representatives face the voters every two years. Fund-raising matters if they want to keep the job. The money pays for campaign staff. It pays for travel and for advertisements. It also pays for posters, stamps, and stickers. In an election year, a representative might use a quarter of work time on fund-raising. Phone calls, speeches, and interviews are tools members use. They talk about what they have already done for the people they represent. They also talk about what they plan to do. Winning the votes of the American people is what gets a member elected. Speeches. A senator's remarks on a bill have no fixed stopping time.

8That freedom ends if a time limit has been set. While that talk goes on, the floor often holds only a handful of senators. The others are busy with committees or busy in their offices. Bells and lights tell senators when to come to the floor. The signal means it is time to vote. The House has far more members than the Senate. Because of that, rules limit how long a representative may speak on a bill. The rules also limit how many changes may be made to a bill. A picture shows reporters interviewing Representative Nancy Pelosi. She had just spoken for eight hours. Her eight-hour speech in 2018 was an attempt to filibuster on the House floor. Voting. A member of Congress must be inside the Capitol Building in person in order to vote. The House uses an electronic voting system. A representative puts a card into a machine. There are forty-seven voting stations around the House. The member then presses a button. Green means yea. Red means nay. Yellow means present. A yellow vote is not a yes and not a no. It does count toward the smallest number of representatives who must be there for a vote to happen. Senators have three ways to vote. In a roll call vote, a clerk says each name. The senator answers yea or nay out loud. In a voice vote, names are not counted. Exact totals are not counted either. The presiding officer judges, as well as that officer can, whether more senators support the bill or do not.

9In a division vote, also called a standing vote, those voice votes are counted one by one. A picture shows the electronic system the House has used since 1973. Checks and Balances. The framers of the Constitution wanted no branch to misuse its power. That includes the legislative branch, the executive branch, and the judicial branch. Checks and balances in the Constitution spread power in a fair way across the three branches. The legislative branch checks the executive branch in two ways. It approves people the president picks for certain government jobs. It also approves treaties made with other countries. The president's judge picks must be approved by the legislative branch. That approval checks the courts. Congress may also propose amendments to the Constitution. Those amendments can overturn decisions of the courts. The other two branches can check Congress in return. The judicial branch uses judicial review. The Supreme Court can throw a law out. It may do that when the law, already passed by Congress and signed by the president, conflicts with the Constitution. The president's veto is a check by the executive branch on the legislative branch. The president can block a bill that most of Congress has already accepted. Congress may still vote to override that veto. The override keeps a balance of power. A Great Responsibility. A statue named Freedom stands at the top of the Capitol dome. The figure is a woman. She wears a military helmet. Her right hand holds a sword that is still in its sheath. Her left hand holds a laurel wreath. She wants peace. She is also ready to fight if that is what it takes to protect her country's freedom.

10The statue stands for the pillars the country was built on. It reminds the politicians who represent the American people. Freedom is made of bronze. It weighs around 15,000 pounds, which is 6,804 kilograms. Writing laws and changing laws are powers of the legislative branch. Those powers make the branch an integral part of the government of the United States. Senators and representatives are meant to give every citizen a voice. They are meant to see that citizens are represented fairly. Word list. Amending means making a change in order to improve something. The House of Representatives is a lawmaking house inside Congress. Population decides how many members each state sends. A committee is a group of people who look at a plan or decide what action to take. A constituent is a citizen who may vote and who is represented by a particular official. Integral means needed if something is to be complete. Legislative describes the branch of government that makes laws. Disperse means to break something up or to scatter it. A filibuster is a long speech in a government meeting, used to delay a vote or to block one. Override means to take over, to cancel, or to replace something else. The Senate is the other lawmaking house of the U.S. Congress. It has two members for each state. Funding is money a group or a branch of government gives to support a purpose. A sponsor is a person who backs another person, an idea, or a thing, and who accepts responsibility for it.

34. How Flu Germs Invade and How We Fight Back

1This book explains what the flu is. It explains how viruses change and how the body fights. It explains how to block the virus, how to treat the flu, and how flu has moved through history. A short close and word meanings come last. A water bottle and a blanket are useful helpers during the flu. Chills may make you shiver. A fever may make you burn. Your throat may hurt. Your nose may feel stuffed. Your head may pound. Your muscles may ache. You may feel deeply fatigued right after waking in the morning. Symptoms like these can mean flu germs have entered your body. Learn what the flu is. Learn what causes it. Learn the symptoms. Learn the treatment. Then you can push back against the illness and stay healthy. Another name for the flu is influenza. A virus is the cause. That virus can move quickly from one person to another. A virus is a tiny microorganism. It is a microbe, which means a germ. The naked eye cannot see it. Inside a virus sits a little genetic material. A hard shell of protein wraps that material and guards it. Viruses are submicroscopic. Only extremely powerful microscopes let scientists see them. Even then, the image must be magnified to one thousand times the virus's real size. Hundreds of thousands of viruses can sit on a pin's head. A picture shows the avian influenza virus. Viruses are all around. Some never bother you. Some are dangerous, and some can kill people or other animals. In the northern hemisphere, flu season runs from October through May.

2Viruses are widespread in that season. Like many living things, a virus needs a certain kind of home if it is to survive and reproduce. For people and for other animals, that home is sadly inside us. Viruses behave as intracellular parasites. They can exist on their own for a while. Sometimes that while lasts years. In the end they must find host organisms. They must enter the cells of those hosts before they can reproduce. After a virus infects a person, its hard protein shell punches a hole in a cell. The virus then goes in. Inside the host cell, the virus puts its own genetic information into the cell. Copies of the virus are made very fast. Symptoms may start one to four days after infection. The host may feel sick. Spread inside the body follows steps. A virus enters a cell of a human body. It takes the cell over and builds copies. Those copies burst out. They begin to enter other cells. A breathing diagram names the nose, the mouth, and the pharynx. It names the windpipe, also called the trachea. It names the larynx and the lungs. The respiratory tract is what flu viruses attack. Flu comes in many kinds. A specific virus causes each kind. The types differ, yet the symptoms look much alike. Flu infects the respiratory tract. You usually feel achy, feverish, congested, and fatigued. Your stomach may feel sick. Three basic types exist. They are Influenza A, Influenza B, and Influenza C. Influenza A can make humans and other animals seriously ill.

3Large outbreaks usually come from it. Influenza B is milder and causes smaller outbreaks. It affects only humans, and mostly children. Influenza C usually brings only a mild illness in humans. Every type can pass from a sick person to a healthy one through the air. Passage can also happen by touching objects such as utensils for eating or drinking. Saliva from a sick person's mouth often carries the virus. So do mucus droplets coughed or sneezed into the air. Cover your mouth and your nose whenever you cough or sneeze. Wash your hands after you use the bathroom. Wash them before you eat or prepare food. If you are infected, staying home is the best step. Keep away from other people so your germs do not travel. A sneeze fills the air with tiny drops of saliva and of mucus. Viruses often move from wild birds to chickens on farms. Those chickens meet people more often. Viruses can change. That change is called mutation. Among all viruses, flu viruses change as much as any. A virus that mutates out of another is called a strain of the first virus. Many influenza viruses begin in wild animals. Birds are the most common start. Farm ducks and farm chickens can catch strains that mutated from those viruses. After farm birds are infected, further mutation can happen. New strains can infect pigs. They can infect humans. On farms, chickens, pigs, and humans stand close together. That closeness can make the mixing and spreading of viruses deadly.

4The animal chain from wild animals to humans is not the same for every virus. One chain may hold animals as unlike as dogs and whales. A virus sometimes skips steps in the chain. The avian virus of 1997 did that skip. It went straight from birds to humans. One sample chain runs from a wild duck, to a chicken, to a pig, and then to a human. A body-fight picture shows a cell holding flu virus, plus white blood cells, antibodies, and viruses. The human body can fight an invasion by flu viruses. The immune system guards against harmful microbes. It makes chemicals called antibodies. Those antibodies ride in the blood. They move through the body looking for invaders. Each antibody is set to destroy one specific kind of microbe. When an invasive microbe is found, antibodies strike. They destroy cells that hold the virus. Mutation lets influenza become a terrible enemy. Your body may beat a virus, and the virus may still change into a new strain. You may have no immunity against that new strain. The body must begin again. It must learn, at the level of cells, how to fight the new strain. Scientists keep fearing that the next strain will kill more people than earlier ones.
