White blood cells are made to guard you from infectious diseases. Invading microbes in the blood can be noticed by the body. Antigens sit in the proteins of these diseases. Special immune cells, such as T helper cells, can sense those antigens. They sense them in small bits of virus that stick out of your cells.

5Finding an antigen opens many ways to attack. T helper cells order other cells to make antibodies. They also call phagocytes, cells that eat microbes. Or they call killer T cells. A killer T cell can destroy a cell that a virus has infected. An artist's picture shows killer T cells striking a virus. Memory is one of the immune system's best gifts. A microbe fought once will be remembered. The body will know how to fight that microbe again. You may gain immunity to one particular microbe. The fight can grow so strong that a virus is fully destroyed before you feel sick. These are only some of the striking ways the body holds invaders off. Many kinds of cells are produced. The kind depends on the microbe that was found. Most of the time the body knows the right fight for an invading microbe. A weak immune system lets viruses take a stronghold. They then copy themselves faster than they can be destroyed. Flu symptoms follow. Without medical care, those symptoms worsen quickly. Scientists look for ways to help the body fight flu. Commonsense steps can keep a flu virus from getting in. Plenty of rest is one of the best ways to stay healthy. Eating well is another. Stay away from cups and utensils used by infected people. Wash your hands often. Keep fingers out of your mouth. These steps matter because a person can be contagious before any symptom shows. That person may not know about the exposure.

6Sickness may be about to start, and the person may not know it. People who sneeze or cough should be avoided. That avoidance helps keep the virus away. Frequent hand washing also helps you avoid the flu. Caution does not save everyone. Infection can still happen. Medical scientists did find a way to stop a flu virus from taking the body over. The way is vaccines. A vaccine holds flu viruses that are weakened or dead. It is injected before the person gets sick. The weakened viruses push the body to make antibodies. Those antibodies attack the weak or dead germs and destroy them. Once those antibodies exist, the body stays on alert. Stronger viruses that arrive in flu season can then be attacked. Every strain needs its own vaccine. Some flu vaccines hold several strains at once. Each injected strain makes the body build a matching antibody. Meeting many strains gets the immune system ready. The body can then face many virus forms that doctors expect in a given flu season. The first vaccine came from British physician Edward Jenner in 1796. He injected patients with cowpox virus. His aim was protection from smallpox, a similar virus that was far more dangerous. For most viral strains, vaccines prevent illness eighty percent of the time. That means immunity, and no sickness, in eighty of one hundred cases for a strain in the vaccine. The rate is high, yet it is not perfect. A vaccine does not guarantee that flu will stay away. If you did get the vaccine, the illness should be milder.

7Aches should be lighter. You should not feel so hot. A strain missing from your flu shot can still make you sick. Scientists must act like detectives. Each year they must guess which strains belong in the shot. Risk is not the same for every person. Some people become much sicker than others. The very young and the very old face a greater risk. People who already have diabetes or heart disease face a greater risk too. Flu cannot always be prevented. After viruses are inside you, several steps can still help. Pharmacies sell many over-the-counter medicines. Those medicines can ease flu symptoms. They can quiet aches in the head and in the muscles. They can bring a fever down. Lots of fluid helps, including water and fruit juice. Rest helps the body fight viruses inside its cells. Picture the work an immune system does during an infection. Pain and exhaustion make sense. A war is underway in the bloodstream. Water and rest let the body do that work. Most people get over the flu with no special medical treatment. Very serious cases can be treated with medicines doctors have. Antibiotic drugs do nothing to viruses. Some antiviral drugs do aim at flu viruses. A drug that beats one strain may fail against another. The same is true of other medicines. Over time, viruses can grow resistant to drugs. They can even grow immune to drugs. A picture shows a doctor in 1941 giving vaccine shots to children. History holds many influenza outbreaks. Some were mild and stayed limited.

8Others were severe, traveled the world, and killed millions. A new flu virus that infects a few people can spread fast. It can become an epidemic. Evidence suggests flu epidemics go back hundreds of years. They may go back thousands of years. Each one has killed thousands of people, or more than that. Late January and early February of 1918 brought severe sickness to Haskell County, Kansas. Soon after, soldiers at Camp Funston, an Army base in Kansas, showed the same symptoms. In a single week the Army hospital treated more than five hundred sick soldiers. Spring's end left forty-eight of those soldiers dead. At first the cause was unknown. Doctors did not know it. Scientists did not know it. Later, doctors traced the illness to one strain of influenza virus. That strain is called the 1918 flu. It killed more than six hundred thousand Americans. Worldwide, it killed twenty-five to forty million people. An outbreak of that size is a pandemic. A pandemic races around the world. A picture shows 1918 flu patients filling a makeshift ward. The 1918 pandemic was not history's only major influenza outbreak. About seventy thousand people in the United States died in the pandemic that ran from 1957 to 1958. It showed up first in China. It reached the United States in June 1957. A different flu strain was first found in Hong Kong, China. In 1968 that virus set off another pandemic. Deaths in the United States alone reached 34,000. A small city holds about that many people.

9H1N1, called swine flu, was in 2009 the first influenza pandemic for forty-one years. People in more than seventy countries were infected. A map can mark Russia, Mongolia, China, Japan, India, and the Pacific Ocean. Such a map can show how a pandemic may travel from one region to many. The flu of 1957 to 1958 is an example. Some influenza outbreaks caused wide worry without becoming pandemics. The Russian flu of 1977 is one. Avian flu in 1997 and in 1999 is another. Both avian strains began in parts of China. They then reached other countries. Doctors keep watching for the next major influenza outbreak. They believe speed of detection matters. Fast detection can stop an outbreak from becoming a flu pandemic across the world. A mask over mouth and nose cuts the chance of catching the virus. It also cuts the chance of passing the virus on. Influenza has existed for hundreds of years. Flu viruses can change into new strains. Because of that change, influenza may never be erased. If you have the flu, caring for yourself comes first. Keeping the illness from other people comes with that care. Drink water the way a camel drinks. Sleep the way a hibernating bear sleeps. Take a vaccine when one is available. Above all, fight back. Good food and rest give healthy cells a chance to win. Antibiotic describes medicine that fights body infections from certain microbes. Fatigued means tired or weary from work of the mind or of the body. Genetic material is the cell part that holds basic facts about an organism's traits.

10Antibodies are body chemicals that attack germs coming in. Antigens are substances that set off immune responses. Germs are microorganisms that often bring disease and sickness. Congested means filled or blocked, as when mucus fills the nose and throat. Hosts are organisms that other organisms live in or on. Immunity is a body's ability to resist infection. Contagious means able to pass from one organism to another. Intracellular means found inside cells. An epidemic is a disease outbreak that spreads fast through a group of living things. Invasive describes a move into a new area or body that harms or disrupts. A microorganism is alive but microscopic, for example a virus or a single cell of bacteria. The respiratory tract is the nose, mouth, throat, and lung passages that air uses during breathing. Mutating means changing into another form. A strain is a group of microbes that share a type. A pandemic is a disease spreading fast across the world. Submicroscopic means too small for an ordinary microscope. Parasites live inside other organisms and take nourishment from them. Vaccines are medicines built from weak or dead viral strains. The body learns from them how to fight a stronger virus of the matching type. Phagocytes are cells that eat microbes invading the body. A virus is a microorganism that enters a body, enters cells, copies itself fast, and causes illness. The word virus can also mean the illness that virus causes. Protein is a needed nutrient found in the cells of every living thing.

35. How New York's Line of Towers Changed

1A picture from 1930 shows a construction worker perched on a beam. He is bolting the framework of the Empire State Building. Another picture shows a policeman of the Port Authority. He monitors traffic from an electric patrol car. The place is the Holland Tunnel in New York City. This book opens with an introduction. It tells how the big city grew. It tells how skyscrapers were built. It tells how twin giants rose and then fell. It tells how a new tower rose from the ashes. A glossary explains hard words. Think of Paris with no Eiffel Tower. Think of Dubai with no Burj Khalifa. Cities all over the world are known by a silhouette. Structures reach skyward and form that skyline. Architecture and skylines identify places. They do this the way fingerprints identify you. Each set is one of a kind. Fingerprints stay the same. Skylines do not stay the same forever. They change. A set of labels can name Dubai, Paris, and New York. Manhattan in New York City shows change of more than one kind. Skyscrapers there have risen. They have fallen. They have risen again. The place began as an indigenous homeland. The Dutch later colonized it. It is now a major hub of the world. New York's skyline has evolved. The changes reflect the changing times. An illustration from 1884 shows Lower Manhattan Island.

2Little of the city's structure and skyline was developed then. New York City was not always a towering metropolis. Indigenous tribes lived there before Dutch settlers arrived. The settlers came in the seventeenth century. Henry Hudson, exploring for the Dutch, brought his ship into a river mouth in 1609. The ship was the Half Moon. That river would later bear his name. He called the port New Amsterdam. The British later took New Amsterdam. They renamed it New York. The British port kept expanding well into the 1700s. By the start of the American Revolution, southern Manhattan Island was tightly packed. Four thousand buildings stood on its streets. The nineteenth century brought further expansion. New York became a major American city. Its population grew more diverse. Its skyline grew quickly too. The Civil War ended in 1865. Formerly enslaved people then came north in droves, looking for work. Immigrants from Ireland followed. Immigrants from Poland followed. Immigrants from Italy followed. The growing city became more diverse still. Many refugees and immigrants seeking opportunity made homes on Manhattan Island. Late in the 1800s, no city in the United States packed people in more tightly than New York. In 1925 no city anywhere packed its people more tightly. New residents needed places to live. They needed places to work and to shop. The city's borders crept north little by little.

3New stores, factories, and homes were built. Manhattan Island covers only about 23 square miles (59.6 sq km). Sites where people could still build soon grew scarce. At ground level, the city had no more room to expand. The only direction left was skyward. New ways of building were required. Until then, traditional methods used walls to hold a building's weight. Walls on the first floor had to carry every floor above them. They had to carry the roof as well. Those walls had to be especially sturdy. Height was limited as a result. No practical method could make walls strong enough for a building of many floors. A list can name buildings in the New York City skyline. In 1899 the Park Row Building rose 391 feet (119 m). It had 29 stories. In 1908 the Singer Building rose 670 feet (204 m). It had 37 stories. In 1909 the Met Life Tower rose 700 feet (213 m). It had 50 stories. In 1913 the Woolworth Building rose 792 feet (241 m). It had 55 stories. In 1930 the Chrysler Building rose 1,048 feet (319 m). It had 77 stories. In 1931 the Empire State Building rose 1,454 feet (443 m). It had 103 stories. In 1970 the World Trade Center's North Tower rose 1,727 feet (526 m). It had 110 stories. In 2014 One World Trade Center rose 1,776 feet (541 m).

4With its spire, the height is 1,792 feet (546 m). It has 104 stories. A newer method used a steel frame, not walls, to hold a structure up. Enormous steel beams were joined into a skeleton. Walls were then hung from the beams. The hang was like curtains on a rod. The bottom of each wall was attached to the floor. Walls of upper floors no longer pressed down on the walls below. Most of their weight spread along the steel beams that held them. Steel frame construction let buildings reach new heights. Around 1900, several huge structures already stood in New York City. People dubbed them skyscrapers. Soon skyscrapers rose one after another. Builders and architects competed. Each wanted the world's tallest building. The Chrysler Building is a skyscraper in the Art Deco style. Automobile tycoon Walter Chrysler funded it. By the late 1920s, New York City's skyline had climbed to new heights. Two of the city's most famous landmarks were built in that period. In 1928 the Chrysler Building was under construction. It was seventy-seven stories tall. It was locked in a duel, floor by floor, with another building going up nearby. The prize was the title of world's tallest. Competition grew so sharp that a tall spire was hidden, then set on the Chrysler top. The secret plan worked.

5The Chrysler Building became the world's tallest structure. Nothing else then stood above 1,000 feet (305 m). Pictures can show the Empire State Building while it was being built. They can show it finished. Workers added four and a half stories each week. The Chrysler Building's reign did not last long. Just blocks away, a behemoth of steel frame was rising. World's tallest would soon be a title belonging to the Empire State Building. Workers broke ground in January 1930. Amazingly, the building was done only 410 days later. More than 3,000 workers supplied skill and labor. The building has 103 stories. Steel and granite form it. It stood over 1,400 feet (427 m) tall. Sixty-four elevators carried people upward. A ride starting at ground level reached floor 80 before one minute ended. An observation deck outside sits on the 86th floor. An inside deck sits on the 102nd floor. Both offer panoramic views of the city. New York City gained a widely loved symbol in that tower. A list called the Seven Wonders of the Modern World included this building. Many books and movies featured it. It kept the crown of world's tallest for nearly forty years. Twin giants rising downtown then took the crown. New York and New Jersey share a body called the Port Authority. The year 1921 was when this body was created.

6Developing places for trade is part of its job. Transportation places are part of that job too. It also modernizes them and operates them. The facilities are in New Jersey and in New York City. A large share of the World Trade Center complex is still the Port Authority's property. The same body still runs it. That complex covers 16 acres (64,750 sq m). Charge of the George Washington Bridge project belonged to the Port Authority. The bridge connects Manhattan and New Jersey. After the Empire State Building, skyscraper construction fell into a slump. A struggling American economy was the cause. The city's skyline did not grow taller again until 1970. In the 1960s, city officials considered a world trade center. It would be a hub for international commerce. The site would be Lower Manhattan. Direction of the project sat with the Port Authority that New York shares with New Jersey. Architect Minoru Yamasaki proposed twin towers. He was a Japanese American born in Detroit. The towers would be part of a complex of many buildings. Offices and storefronts would fill that complex. The towers would be 110 stories tall. They would include some structural innovations. A side story asks who Elisha Otis was. People needed a way to reach the upper floors of a skyscraper. Climbing hundreds of stairs was not realistic. Elevators were needed.

7Early elevators were not as safe as they should have been. Elisha Otis resolved that problem. In 1854 he designed the first safety elevator. If the cable broke, the platform would fall only a few inches. Engines able to drive the elevator were another design of his. Tall buildings needed his invention. Look around the next time you ride an elevator. There is a good chance the name Otis appears somewhere inside. More than 3,500 workers helped build the twin towers. That number was the peak of construction. One innovation used tube-frame construction. It did not use steel frame construction. Each tower would resemble a hollow square pipe. Vertical columns would stand close together along the outside perimeter. Main support columns around the edge cut the number of supports needed inside. Much more of each floor could be used. Another innovation was the sky lobby. Height decides how many elevators a building needs. People and freight both have to move. The towers were so large that Yamasaki proposed a special elevator plan. He modeled it on the city's subway lines. An express elevator could go straight to a sky lobby on a high floor. It would bypass the floors below. Riders would then transfer to a local elevator. Ten floors just above the sky lobby would each receive a stop from the local car. The system was an ingenious way to move people vertically.

8It was efficient. Fewer elevator shafts were needed. Work on the towers began in 1966. The North Tower was completed in December 1970. At the tip of its spire it measured 1,727 feet (526 m). The Windows on the World restaurant stood on the top floor. Diners there got a breathtaking view. The South Tower reached 1,362 feet (415 m). It was finished seven months later. Under both buildings lay a parking garage. A railroad lay there too. Subway stations lay there as well. The Twin Towers made a striking addition to the skyline. They stood some distance from the city's other tall skyscrapers. They dwarfed the buildings around them. For thirty years they were the tallest structures on Manhattan Island. They were also the most prominent. Then disaster struck. Two planes were flown into the Twin Towers by terrorists on September 11, 2001. That morning, hijackers flew two passenger jets into the towers. The South Tower started to fall before a full hour had passed from the attack. It crumbled to the ground. Thirty minutes after that, the North Tower fell as well. New Yorkers watched in stunned disbelief. The enormous structures became heaps of burning rubble. Nearly three thousand people died because of the attack. The World Trade Center tragedy devastated New York. It devastated the rest of the country too.

9New Yorkers mourned neighbors they had lost. They mourned their landmark. They vowed to rebuild. The new World Trade Center site would be even bigger and better. Digging out the ruins of the old towers took time. Plans for the site took years. Ideas and opinions about what to do were many. Many designs were submitted. The controversy was considerable. At last the Port Authority unveiled a design for the new complex. A park of memory was given a place of its own. It remembers the people who lost their lives that day. The ground where the original buildings stood is now reflecting pools. Cascading waterfalls fill those pools. A memorial museum holds historical artifacts from the old towers. A new tower of 104 stories has been built nearby. People nicknamed it the Freedom Tower. It rises 1,776 feet (541 m). That number stands for the year the United States became independent from British rule. The new tower is taller than either of the original towers. Glass panels cover it. Its shape is a twisted octagon. A reflective surface mirrors the changing light around it. A spire stands at the top. The spire carries a beam of light. The beam can be seen for miles. The tower's name is One World Trade Center. Several other high-rise buildings are being built at the site as well.

10Six new towers were planned for the World Trade Center complex. By 2021, four of those six were complete. The memorial was complete too. So was the museum. New York's skyline keeps changing. It reflects a resilient spirit. The city continues to adapt. It continues to grow. The World Trade Center Memorial has two reflecting pools. A picture can show one of them. Both pools hold the largest waterfalls made by humans in the United States. A behemoth is a person or a thing of immense size or power. A complex is a group of buildings close together. They serve a common purpose. To have dwarfed something is to have made it seem smaller or less important. Ingenious describes cleverness, skill, or intricacy. Innovations are new ideas, new products, or new ways of doing something. Landmarks are important historical buildings or sites. They can also be objects on land that mark a place. Panoramic describes a complete view in every direction. Perimeter means the distance around an outer edge. That edge may belong to an area or to a surface. Prominent means easy to see, standing out, or important. A silhouette is a solid dark shape. Light surrounds it, or it sits against a light background. A skeleton is the frame that holds a structure up. A building can have one. Vertically means straight up and down.

36. How Steroids Harm Athletes and Teens

1Police found anabolic steroids in someone's house. This book tells what steroids are. It tells their history. It tells how they can be bad medicine. It tells how athletes got caught. It tells about teens who use them. A closing thought comes near the end. Word meanings come last. Lance Armstrong is shown on the bike during the Tour de France. In the world of cycling, he seemed to fit the role of a real-life superhero more than anyone. A single bound over a tall building was beyond him. On a bike, though, his skill was clear. He won the Tour de France seven times. The wins came between 1999 and 2005. That race is the world's most grueling cycling race. No rider before him had managed a feat like that. Few sporting events demand as much as the Tour de France. Almost superhuman fitness is required of these cyclists. They must cover a course of 2,173 miles. That distance is 3,497 kilometers. The course crosses the mountainous French countryside. His feat was even more remarkable for another reason. He had earlier won a life-and-death struggle with cancer. The sports world had him at its peak. He had money. He had fame. He had medals. He had trophies. Then it all collapsed. His reputation was ruined. He was a cheater. He had illegally used steroids. The drugs improved his performance. They gave him an unfair advantage.

2The advantage was over cyclists who did not use steroids. For years he denied that he took them. In 2013 he admitted the truth. He called that mythic, perfect story one big lie. Days later, the honors were gone. The sport he once led later cast him out. He was also participating in blood doping. Blood doping increases the oxygen carried by the body's red blood cells. Extra oxygen lets a body run with greater efficiency. One method starts before a competition. Athletes remove some of their blood. They freeze it. By race time the body has naturally replaced the missing red blood cells. As the race is about to begin, they put the stored blood back. The body then has extra red blood cells. It has extra oxygen for game day. A picture can compare doped blood with normal blood. It can show red blood cells inside a blood vessel. Ben Johnson was first in that Olympic 100-meter race in 1988. A later test showed steroids in his body. He had to return his gold medal. The word steroids can refer to different things. Some steroids are made by the human body on its own. It does this as it develops. It does this as it goes through puberty. These natural steroids affect bone growth. They affect muscle growth. They play a role in many other changes. These steroids stay in a delicate balance inside the body.

3Other kinds of steroids are sometimes ordered by doctors. They treat health problems such as asthma. They treat skin disorders. These steroids can also help people who have cancer. They can help people with other serious diseases. They should be used only under a doctor's careful supervision. They can be very dangerous. The steroids some athletes use have a long name. They are anabolic-androgenic steroids. People shorten that name to AAS. Anabolic means they affect how the body builds tissue. Muscle is one kind of tissue. Body development is what androgenic refers to. That includes reproductive organs. It includes facial hair. People often call these drugs anabolic steroids for short. They are similar to the hormone testosterone. The human body produces testosterone naturally. It produces it in small amounts. Hormone balance in the body shifts when artificial steroids are used. The imbalance can help people become better athletes in the short term. Serious health problems can follow as well. When people exercise, their muscle fibers develop tiny rips. They develop tiny tears. The body repairs those tears in a natural way. The cells become larger. Muscles grow. Muscles become stronger. More exercise means more torn fibers. Then they are repaired. Repair goes faster when steroids are used. Strength comes faster for users than for people who skip those substances. An old engraving shows the Olympic Games in ancient Greece.

4Lance Armstrong is only one athlete in a long line. Many have tried to gain an unfair advantage with special substances. A special concoction was the drink of the first Olympians in ancient Greece. They believed it made them stronger. Roman chariot racers drank an herbal drink. The drink supposedly increased their stamina. Performance-enhancing drugs entered their modern era in the 1950s. John Ziegler was an American physician. He was also a weight lifter. He learned something about weight lifters from the Soviet Union. They were using artificial steroids. Those drugs helped them dominate international competitions. A synthetic steroid of his own was Ziegler's creation. Popular magazines for bodybuilders carried his account of the discovery. The steroid craze began. Soon athletes began using these substances. Other people began using them too. Major sports have rules about steroid tests and penalties. MLB uses tests for steroids. NBA uses tests for steroids. NFL uses tests for steroids. A first offense in baseball brings a suspension of 5 games. A first offense in basketball brings a suspension of 4 games. A first offense in football brings a suspension of 50 games. The football suspension is without pay. A second offense in baseball brings a suspension of 10 games. A second offense in basketball brings a suspension of 6 games. A second offense in football brings a suspension of 100 games. That suspension is without pay.

5A third offense in baseball brings a lifetime ban. A third offense in basketball brings a suspension of 25 games. A third offense in football brings a suspension of at least 1 year. So many athletes were using steroids that a ban followed. The International Olympic Committee organizes the Olympic Games. It banned steroid use in 1975. Today steroid use is banned in every major sport. The United States has passed laws against anabolic steroids. Many other countries have passed such laws too. The laws make use illegal. They make possession illegal. They make sale illegal. The chance of going to jail does not stop some people. They keep using anabolic steroids in spite of the risks. Recent years have made this much easier. Designer steroids have been developed. These specially made steroids are built so a drug test will miss them. Sports organizations then find it difficult to catch cheaters. Muscles may look larger after a person takes steroids. They may perform better than before. These artificial hormones still have a big impact on the body. They have a big impact on the mind. Short-term side effects can include bad breath that will not go away. They can include acne. They can include swelling of the legs and feet. Long-term use can ruin a person's life. It can even end a life. Blood cholesterol levels can shift because of steroids. Cholesterol is a fatty substance.

6Blood-vessel walls can collect this substance. A broken-off piece of this substance can block a blood vessel. That can cause a stroke. It can cause a heart attack. One large muscle is the heart. Steroid use can cause serious heart problems. Steroids can also destroy a person's liver. The liver helps remove waste from the bloodstream. If the liver is not working properly, waste builds up in the blood. That buildup can cause serious illness. Steroids can disrupt the brain's ability to function. A person may see sights that are not real. They can cause panic attacks. They can cause depression. They can cause an overly aggressive behavior. People informally call that behavior 'roid rage. Steroids can bring many harmful effects. Aggressive behavior is one. Severe acne on the face is one. Severe acne on the back is one. High blood pressure is one. Heart disease is one. Stroke is one. Blood clots are one. Nausea is one. Bloating is one. Aching joints are one. Liver damage is one. Urinary problems are one. Bowel problems are one. A higher risk of tendon injuries is one. Hormone levels can shift a great deal because of steroids. Women who take them may grow facial hair. They may develop a voice that is permanently deeper. Men who take them can develop noticeable breast tissue. Adolescents who use them can have severe side effects.

7Stunted growth is one of those effects. Quitting after steroid use has begun can be very dangerous. The body's chemical messaging system is thrown off completely. When a user stops the drugs, severe withdrawal can follow. Depression is one withdrawal effect. Muscle aches are another. Nausea is another. Irritability is another. Those are only a few. Muscles shrink within weeks after stopping. Strength diminishes within weeks too. The year 1998 was one for the record books. Two baseball sluggers battled each other. Mark McGwire played for the St. Louis Cardinals. Sammy Sosa played for the Chicago Cubs. Each hoped to break baseball's record for home runs in a single season. The 1961 record belonged to Roger Maris of the New York Yankees. He hit sixty-one home runs. McGwire broke that record. He slugged seventy home runs. The following season Barry Bonds hit seventy-three. Bonds played for the San Francisco Giants. The season looked spectacular at the time. It would soon be tainted. Sosa became mixed up in a huge steroid scandal. McGwire did too. Bonds did too. Other big-name players did too. Sports has rarely seen a steroid scandal so large. In the early 2000s, baseball officials revealed test results. They had tested 1,438 major-league players for drugs. Five percent of those players took steroids. Because of the link to steroids, some stars have been refused a high honor. The Baseball Hall of Fame has refused to induct McGwire.

8Bonds has been refused too. Refusal has also met other top stars. The Hall of Fame is the highest honor in the game. Each of these players has been branded a cheater. Their legacies are stained forever. Olympic athletes can have a legacy tainted by anabolic steroids too. The harm reaches athletes around the world. A world record in 1997 belonged to Chinese swimmer Wu Yanyan. The record came at the Chinese National Games. A test was taken at the Chinese Olympic trials. Anabolic steroids showed up on Wu Yanyan's test. Both she and her coach were fined. They were dismissed from the Chinese national swim team. A picture shows her after that positive test in 1997. World swimming rules required a suspension. She had to stay out of competitive swimming for four years. At that time she ranked among the world's best swimmers. The suspension kept her out of the Olympic Games in 2000. Human growth hormone is also called HGH. As the name suggests, it helps the body grow. Artificial HGH is injected every day by some people. Proper growth needs more of the hormone than their bodies make. Some athletes abuse HGH. They believe it increases muscle mass. They believe it makes them stronger. Researchers dismiss these claims. They say HGH is dangerous when it is abused. Teens using steroids has become a major problem.

9One study offers numbers. The study's figure for high school boys is 4.9 percent using anabolic steroids at least one time. It suggests that 2.4 percent of girls have done so. That is 375,000 young men. That is 175,000 young women. Caught teens usually lose the right to play sports. School can even expel them. This one poor choice can happen in middle school. It can happen in high school. It can cause problems for a person's entire future. Community members hold a memorial service in one picture. The service is for two young athletes. Those athletes died from steroid use. Researchers say teens take steroids for a reason linked to media. They are influenced by the media's idea of what a body should look like. They also take steroids because school sports are highly competitive. Many students in sports hope a steroid edge will bring a win. They are trying to enhance how they look. Or they are trying to enhance what their bodies can do. The sad result is harm to the body they hoped to improve. They damage their bodies. A picture shows professional baseball player Mark McGwire. He is sworn in before he testifies about steroid use. Steroids change who you are. A person may want a competitive edge. A person may want only larger muscles. The body transforms. The mind transforms. A price comes with this change. Athletes at all levels run a risk if they use steroids.

10They risk being labeled cheaters. They tear apart their bodies to earn an artificial victory. They tear apart their minds. Terrible side effects are what remain for them. Those effects may never subside. They are also left with a hard truth. The whole achievement was one big lie. These words have special meanings in this book. A cheater is someone who breaks rules for personal gain. A side effect is an extra result of a drug or treatment, and it is usually harmful. They go beyond the desired effect. Competitive means related to a rivalry. The rivalry can be between individuals, teams, or businesses. Stamina is the energy that lets a person keep going. A hormone is a chemical that steers how a body grows. Steroids are drugs that make body tissue grow. Athletes sometimes use them illegally to enhance performance. Illegally means in a way that a law or a rule forbids. Puberty is the stage when adolescents become physically mature. They become capable of reproduction. Stunted means limited in growth or development. Synthetic describes a thing people make by joining substances. It does not occur in nature. Reputation is the general way that other people think of a person or a thing. Scandals are behaviors, actions, or events that seem shocking or bad. They damage the reputations of the people involved.

37. How Women Fought for the Vote

1Election Day is when voters cast their ballots. In 1872, Susan B. Anthony stepped into a voting office. Rochester, New York, was the city. The presidential election was the contest she voted in. Arrest followed two weeks after that vote. A woman’s vote was illegal in most states at the time. Anthony knew the law was being broken. Unjust was her judgment of that law. Decades of effort for women’s rights already stood behind her. Harriet Tubman shared that effort. Lucretia Mott shared it. Sojourner Truth shared it. Marching was one of their tools. Protest was another. Congress felt their pressure. Anthony hoped a ballot would pull attention toward women’s suffrage. Suffrage means the right to vote. Notice did follow her act. Almost fifty more years still passed before the Nineteenth Amendment won approval in Congress. Women with U.S. citizenship gained the vote through that change in law. For most women of color, nothing ended there. U.S. citizenship did not close their struggle. That moment sat midway in a far longer suffrage battle. A 1913 parade shows a group of suffragists on the march. The United States adopted its Constitution in 1787. Voting rights were not set out in that document. Each state was left to decide who could vote. By 1807, the vote belonged only to free white men. Women remained unable to vote. Some rights still matched men’s rights for certain unmarried women. Marriage was the choice most women made.

2A wife had no legal voice in government. She had no legal voice in her own family either. Property she owned passed to her husband. Wages she earned passed to him if she held a job. Only the father had a claim to children she bore. Women who were enslaved held no legal rights at all. Marriage did not grant those rights. July 1848 brought about three hundred people together in Seneca Falls, New York. Women’s rights were the topic they met to discuss. That gathering is called the Seneca Falls Convention. Many historians treat it as the suffrage movement’s starting point. A model of equal rights for women stood close by. Artwork shows Elizabeth Cady Stanton addressing the Seneca Falls Convention. That town stood on ancestral land of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy. Few rights, and sometimes none, belonged to most women in the United States then. Inside their own nation, Haudenosaunee women held wide political power. A chief had to be a man. Choosing him was women’s work. Advising him was women’s work. Removing him was women’s work. Every government decision included women’s help. Any act of war could be blocked by women. Land stayed under the control of Haudenosaunee women. Food sources stayed under their control. Economic power followed from that control. Marriage did not strip their rights. Their property stayed theirs after marriage. Early suffragists took this as proof. Men and women could live as equals inside one society.

3Ideas from the Haudenosaunee inspired white suffragists. Most of those suffragists still did not demand U.S. voting rights for Indigenous women. Indigenous suffragists labored alongside white suffragists. One was Zitkála-Šá, said zit-KAH-lah-SHAH. Another was Marie Louise Bottineau Baldwin, said BOT-in-oh. Laura Cornelius Kellogg was another. White women’s voting rights stayed the aim of the mainstream movement. The early 1900s made Zitkála-Šá widely known. Her nation was the Yankton Dakota Sioux. Activism for Indigenous people and for women both carried her name. Music was part of her life. Teaching was part of her life. Writing was part of her life. National magazines ran her stories about Indigenous people. They also ran her articles. Washington, D.C., became her home in 1917. Protecting traditional Indigenous ways of life was her work there. She argued for U.S. citizenship for Indigenous people, so that voting could follow. The year 1926 was when she founded National Council of American Indians. She led the group as president. Indigenous people gained a shared front in the suffrage fight through her work. She helped them sign up as voters. Advocacy for Indigenous rights continued until her death in 1938. Women’s suffrage grew from abolition work that had begun in the 1830s. Speaking against slavery was how many early suffragists began. Writing against slavery was another start. Organizing against slavery was another. The year 1865 brought the end of slavery. Abolitionists then aimed at the vote for white women and for every Black person.

4A split soon opened among suffragists. The Fifteenth Amendment was the point of disagreement. Black men would gain the vote under that amendment. Support for the amendment was the view of Frederick Douglass. Lucy Stone shared that view. Both still meant to keep working for women’s suffrage. Anthony would not back an amendment that left women out. Elizabeth Cady Stanton would not back it either. They opposed giving greater power to Black men they regarded as uneducated. They opposed the same shift for immigrant men. Passage of the Fifteenth Amendment came in 1869. Many Black men still found voting nearly impossible under some state laws. The South was where that barrier was sharpest. Artwork shows a celebration by men in Baltimore, Maryland. The year of that celebration was 1870, after the amendment had passed. Women of color were shut out by Stanton and by other leaders inside the movement. Black women faced that exclusion most of all. Racism was a problem Black suffragists wanted named. Sexism was a problem they wanted named too. Addressing racism did not interest many white suffragists. They feared politicians would step away. They feared white women in the South would step away. Important leaders in the vote fight still included many Black women. Mary Church Terrell was among them. Ida B. Wells was among them. Nannie Helen Burroughs was among them. They saw the vote as a route to laws shielding Black Americans from racial violence.

5Demonstrations were organized by them. Women’s clubs were founded by them in cities nationwide. The East held many of those clubs. The Midwest held many of them. Black suffragists could be mobilized through the clubs. In the 1900s, Nannie Helen Burroughs was widely known as a suffragist. She was an educator. She was a speaker. She was an activist for women’s rights. Alice Paul, a suffragist, helped plan a march for women’s suffrage in 1913. Washington, D.C., was the setting. The date was the day before Woodrow Wilson became president. More than sixty years of suffrage work already lay behind women. A national event for the movement had not happened before that march. Streets filled with more than five thousand marching women. Men in the crowd tripped the marchers. Some of those men were police. Marchers were grabbed. Marchers were shoved. Marchers were spat on. Marchers were insulted. The country paid attention. A new generation of activists drew energy from the day. Tougher tactics in the suffrage fight became easier to imagine. Mexican Americans in the Southwest faced limits from racial violence. Segregation limited them as well. Spanish-speaking women were rallied by bilingual leaders. In New Mexico, Nina Ortero-Warren spoke in Spanish. She also gave out fliers in Spanish. California heard the same kind of work from Maria Guadalupe Evangelina de Lopez. Texas journalist Jovita Idár printed articles that favored suffrage.

6Those articles ran in newspapers written in Spanish. Work of this kind was crucial to passage, in 1920, of the Nineteenth Amendment. Literacy tests were later used by some lawmakers to block women of color. Poll taxes were used for that same block. Decades of shared work with white suffragists did not prevent a new isolation. Suffragists of color then had to seek their own voting rights without that partnership. August 26, 1920, was the day the Nineteenth Amendment became law. No Indigenous person could cast a ballot in a U.S. election then. U.S. citizenship was not granted to Indigenous people. A 1924 law changed that status and granted citizenship. Indigenous women gained the vote with citizenship. State officials still shut many Indigenous voters out for decades. Living on a reservation was treated as proof someone was not a state resident. Belonging to a tribe was treated the same way. Asian American women born inside the United States did receive the vote in 1920. Immigrants who were the first Asian generation in their families did not. Older laws remained active. Nearly every Asian immigrant was blocked from U.S. citizenship by those laws. Voting rights did not exist without citizenship. Years of work for women’s suffrage still left some Asian American suffragists unable to vote. Dr. Mabel Ping-Hua Lee was one such suffragist. The year 1920 did not include a ballot for her. A law in 1952 lifted that limit.

7Asian immigrants could then obtain both U.S. citizenship and the vote. Barriers kept being built by many lawmakers. Even women of color who already held U.S. citizenship were stopped by those barriers. Poll taxes were one tactic. Tests were another. Intimidation was another. Threats were another. Violence was another. A 1963 march showed activists demanding voting rights. Before 1965, one common tactic was a poll tax. The tax was a fee due before a person could vote. A literacy test was another common tactic. Passing it was supposed to prove a voter could read. The tests were written, on purpose, to confuse people. Failure was easy. A citizenship test demanded proof that a voter understood government. A voter might have to recite from the Constitution of the United States. A voter might have to write pieces of it. A voter might have to explain those pieces. Voters of color were the people these tactics were built to hinder. A grandfather clause opened a way around the requirements. The way opened if a grandfather had held voting rights before 1867. Most places allowed only white people to vote before that year. White voters who could not pay a poll tax could still vote under the clause. White voters who could not pass a test could still vote under it too. True suffrage was still being fought for in the 1960s. Fannie Lou Hamer worked without rest for stronger protection of voters of color.

8Ella Baker did that work. Diane Nash did that work. President Lyndon B. Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act in 1965. The act banned tactics aimed at blocking voters who were people of color. Further protections arrived in a 1975 amendment. People facing voter discrimination because English was not their first language gained those protections. Annie Devine, Fannie Lou Hamer, and Victoria Gray were civil rights activists with a crucial part in this work. Voting rights for people of color were better protected because of them. Devine appears on the left of a well-known picture. Hamer appears in the center. Gray appears on the right. Hawai‘i was a kingdom for a long time before 1900. In that year it came under the United States as a territory. A monarchy ruled the kingdom. Americans overthrew that monarchy in 1893. A new government was set up by them. Women were barred from voting under the new government. Before the overthrow, women had held wide political power. Families looked to them as important leaders. Communities looked to them as important leaders. The kingdom looked to them as important leaders. Work to win women’s votes back began at once. Clubs were founded by Hawaiian suffragists. Speeches were made. Rallies were held. Articles were written for newspapers in the Hawaiian language. Articles were also written for newspapers in English. By 1919, the wait felt far too long.

9Wilhelmina Kekelaokalaninui Widemann Dowsett led the protest. Say the long middle of her name as keh-keh-lou, then kah-lah-nee-NOO-ee. Five hundred suffragists followed her. Their banners read Votes for Women. They walked onto the floor of Hawai‘i’s House of Representatives. The next year, the Nineteenth Amendment brought women’s suffrage back. Full voting rights for Hawaiians waited until statehood in 1959. An important piece of the Voting Rights Act was removed by the U.S. Supreme Court in 2013. Before that removal, certain states needed permission from the federal government. Any new voting law required that permission. Those states had discriminated against voters of color in earlier years. Harmful laws could be stopped before damage was done. Each year, stickers reading I Voted are placed on the grave of Susan B. Anthony. The stickers honor her work. New voting laws have appeared in many states since 2013. Advocates say the laws lower the risk of voter fraud. Voting is made harder by some of the laws. People of color carry the heavier burden. One example is a smaller number of voting stations. The cuts fall in areas where residents are mostly people of color. Lines grow long at the stations that remain. The wait to vote can stretch a long time. Sometimes that wait passes ten hours. Women still meet voting barriers across wide stretches of this country. The Nineteenth Amendment did not finish the fight for women’s suffrage.

10The Voting Rights Act did not finish it either. Large progress has still been made. Suffragists and civil rights activists produced that progress. The record runs from the first meeting in Seneca Falls, New York, up to the present. An advocate is a person who works openly for a cause. A movement is many people organized to reach a goal or to cause a change. The people and groups inside that effort are also called a movement. An amendment is a change added to a document or to a law. A barrier is a rule, an obstacle, or a problem that stops progress. Suffrage is the right to vote. A suffragist supports giving the vote to people who lack it. The Constitution is the written set of rules and principles under United States law. A convention is a political meeting of delegates. Plans are formed there. Goals are set there. People are chosen there to run for office. Unjust means unfair. It can also mean undeserved. It can also mean dishonest. Wages are the regular pay a worker earns. The amount of time worked sets that pay. Discrimination means treating someone, or a whole group, in an unfair way. Race can be the basis. Age can be the basis. Sex can be the basis. Religion can be the basis. Other differences can be the basis. An election is the act of picking someone for government office by voting.

38. Japan, a Chain of Islands

1In Kagoshima, Japan, women dance for the Ohara Matsuri Dance Festival. Japan is an archipelago, which means its land is a chain of islands. The chain runs more than 2,400 kilometers, a distance of 1,500 miles. Asia’s eastern shore is nearby, and the islands sit in the Pacific Ocean. The country does not take up much space. California covers more ground than Japan does. Four large islands form the core, and thousands of small islands join them. China is one close neighbor. North Korea is another. South Korea is another. So is Russia’s Siberian region. The Sea of Japan separates Japan from Asia. People also call that water the East Sea. The East China Sea lies off the southwest. Open Pacific water lies off the eastern side. Maps of this part of the world also show the Yellow Sea, the city of Tokyo, and the continent of Asia. Tokyo’s busiest station is crossed by bullet trains full of riders. The biggest island is Honshu, pronounced HON-shoo. Honshu is home to more than 80 percent of the people. Hokkaido ranks as another main island. Shikoku ranks as another.

2Kyushu ranks as another. Honshu holds the biggest cities. The east coast is where nearly all of those cities stand. The capital is Tokyo, pronounced TOH-kee-yoh. Tokyo stands on Honshu as well. Residents of this sprawling metropolis number more than thirty-two million. They make their homes there, and their jobs are there too. Business and trade reach Tokyo from many countries. Few cities on Earth hold more people. The districts around Tokyo hold millions more. Greater Tokyo is a common name for that wider area. Commuters ride bullet trains, which are very fast, in from those districts. They also ride trains that are slower. They also ride subways. For transportation, Tokyo is the country’s main hub. A railway station called Shinjuku, pronounced SHEEN-ju-ku, stands in Tokyo. People say no other station on Earth has more travelers pass through. The population tops 127 million even though the country is small. Cities and towns hold over 90 percent of residents. Service jobs are common, including work in banks. Restaurants employ many city people. Hospitals do too. Other service trades do too. Factory work is another path.

3High-tech electronics come from those factories, including cell phones. Computers come from them. Televisions come from them. Motor vehicles come from them. Machines come from them. Electronics production is a field where Japan leads. Fishing is a massive industry in coastal cities. The fleet of fishing ships is one of the world’s largest. A cell phone goes by the name keitai, pronounced KAY-i-tie. Tall apartment buildings house many people because cities are crowded. Suburbs more often have houses and shorter apartment buildings. Some homes, where room exists, have Japanese gardens kept with great care. Thick mats woven from rice straw cover floors in some homes. The mats are called tatami, pronounced tah-TAH-mee. Shoes come off at the door. That custom is widely kept. Sleep, for some people, is on a thin bed called a futon, pronounced FOO-tahn. The bed is unrolled onto the floor. Rooms in some houses are split by screens, not by solid walls. The screens are thin paper or bamboo. Rules of manners cover many situations. One set of rules covers greetings. Another covers how guests are served. People bow to greet each other.

4They do not shake hands. Social status decides the number of bows. It also decides how deep each bow goes. The main language is Japanese, and the writing system is very complex. Hiragana is one script. Katakana is the other. About fifty symbols sit in each script. Each symbol stands for a sound. Kanji are used too. Those characters were borrowed from Chinese writing. Letters of the Latin alphabet, the same letters English uses, show up as well. A kanji picture can suggest fire. Another can suggest a mountain. Another can suggest rain. Landform maps label Kyushu and Hokkaido. They label the Hidaka Mountains and the Ryukyu Islands. They label Honshu and the Ou Mountains. They label the Sea of Japan, also called the East Sea. They label the Pacific Ocean, the Japanese Alps, and Tokyo. They label the Chugoku Mountains and Mount Fuji. They label the Izu Archipelago. They label the Shikoku Mountains, the island of Shikoku, and the Kyushu Mountains. Rugged land, high mountains, and surrounding water define the country. Mountains cover most of it. Flat coastal ground is therefore where nearly every city stands.

5A few islands are too steep and too dangerous for anyone to live on. Mount Fuji is the tallest peak. Honshu’s south coast is where that volcano stands. Geology here is among the least stable on Earth. More than seventy volcanoes are active. About one thousand earthquakes strike each year. A quake under the sea can build a huge wave. The wave is a tsunami, pronounced tsoo-NAH-mee. Harbor wave is the Japanese meaning of the word. Fast rivers drop from the mountains onto the flats. Rice farms on the coastal plain draw water from those rivers. Some lakes sit near the ocean. Other lakes sit inside volcanic craters called calderas. Rain has filled those craters over time. Monsoons steer the climate and bring strong winds. The winds may be stormy and wet. The winds may be dry. Heat and cold differ a great deal from place to place. Cooler weather belongs to the north. Warmer weather belongs to the south. A similar spread of temperatures appears along the eastern side of the United States. Fall is the rainy season, and typhoons are a threat then.

6Northeastern Honshu includes the city of Ishinomaki. Pronounce it ih-SHIH, followed by noh-MAH-kee. The 2011 tsunami left that city in ruins. Temples of Buddhism and shrines of Shinto are found in many places. Nippon is what the Japanese call their country. Sun’s origin is what the name means. An old belief said the Sun’s first rays fell on Japan. Land of the Rising Sun is another name. The civilization goes back thousands of years. Strong influence came from Asian neighbors to the west. Crops are one place that influence shows. Some historians think the skill of growing rice arrived from China long ago, measured in thousands of years. In the sixth century, Buddhism spread into Japan from Korea. Unique customs grew inside Japan as well. Shinto stands as one of the main religions. Plenty of people keep Shinto customs and Buddhist customs together. Shrines for Shinto are spread through the land. Temples for Buddhism are spread through it too. Fights over land were common in the past. Fights over power were common too. The Yamato dynasty is the family that has supplied every emperor.

7That line has lasted more than two thousand years. No other monarchy has run so long without a break. Control shifted in the twelfth century when a warrior took the country. That warrior was the first shogun, a kind of military king. Rule by shoguns lasted for centuries. Emperors from the imperial family were still allowed to serve. Their real power was scant. Samurai belonged to the same age, and the word is said SA-muh-rye. They were fierce in war. Honor, under a strict code, guided them. Skill in fighting was another mark of the samurai. Feudalism organized society then. A lord owned a piece of land and held power over its residents. Staying on that land meant peasants had to labor for the lord. Democracy arrived in the nineteenth century. Voters chose leaders for the parliament, which is called the Diet. An emperor remains in place today. After World War II ended, his role became ceremony, not politics. The calendar holds many holidays and festivals. Rice planting is celebrated. Harvest is celebrated. Children’s health is celebrated. Ancestors are honored. January 1 is New Year’s Day.

8A full week of celebration, among the biggest holidays, leads up to it. House cleaning is a common task in that week. Debts are paid off. Cards wishing good luck are sent. Special toys go to children. Kimonos, the traditional robe, are often worn on January 1. Foods prepared for the day are eaten. Prayers for luck in the coming year are offered at a shrine nearby. Summer brings Obon, also called the Lantern Festival. Families use Obon to honor ancestors. Lit lanterns are placed on rivers. Lit candles are placed on lakes. The lights drift slowly off. People believe those lights lead the souls of ancestors home to rest. Rice matters greatly in daily meals. Small round cakes of rice are called mochi, pronounced MOH-chee. People eat mochi as a snack. Food also comes heavily from the sea around the islands. Many dishes include fish. Many dishes include other seafood. City fast food often means sushi, pronounced SOO-shee. It often means sashimi, pronounced sah-SHEE-mee. Raw fish is in both. Looks matter as much as flavor, in the view of many people.

9Several small dishes usually make up a meal. Soup is a frequent dish. Noodles sometimes appear. Chopsticks are the usual tools, as they are for neighbors in China. Wood is the material, and the sticks are long and thin. A sushi roll often wraps sticky rice around raw fish and around vegetables. Strict rules shape how some foods are cooked and how they are set out. Tea is the focus of one old ceremony. Every step is ordered, and the style is elegant. A room built for nothing else usually hosts the ceremony. Tokyo’s Imperial Palace has modern buildings pressed along the edge of its grounds. Mountains cover this small country of islands. Crowded cities still bustle with high-tech industry. Earthquakes shake the land. Volcanoes blow. Typhoons storm through. People continue to thrive. Long centuries taught them to use both soil and sea fully. Small fields yield tons of rice. The ocean yields large catches of fish and of other seafood. Ancient custom sits beside the newest machines. The old world and the modern world are both at home here. Population stands at 127,250,000.

10The land area is 364,485 square kilometers, or 226,480 square miles. Tokyo is the capital. Japanese is the main language. Shintoism and Buddhism are the main religions. Yen is the currency. The Central Intelligence Agency gave these figures in July 2014, as did the World Bank. Buddhism is both a faith and a philosophy, drawn from Siddhartha Gautama, who taught in ancient India. A kimono is a Japanese robe or gown, often chosen for formal events. A metropolis is a city that is huge or especially important. A monsoon is a storm tied to the season, sometimes with heavy rain. Shinto is Japan’s traditional faith, honoring many nature gods. In early Japan, a shogun was the ruler who held military power. A shrine is a holy or special place set up to honor a god or a person. A tsunami is an ocean wave big enough to destroy. The cause may be a quake under the water, a slide of land, or a volcano. A typhoon is a spinning storm, fierce with wind and rain, near the Indian Ocean or the western Pacific.

39. John Muir and the Wild Land

1This book follows a love of nature, then an early life, then a break into freedom. It moves to the High Sierra, to writing and public action, and to the Sierra Club now. A word list closes it. Settlers began, long ago, to colonize land. That land is the west of what we now call the United States. Many of them talked about conquering nature. Indigenous peoples in that region had cared for the land and guarded it for thousands of years. The settlers wanted the land cleared. They wanted natural resources used with no limit. John Muir walked in nature to draw nearer to what he called the world's heart. Few settlers shared his wish to keep nature safe. That love pulled him away from crowded places. For years he lived in cabins far from towns. It also pulled him to walk across huge parts of California. He traveled to many other places in the world as well. His picture of a clean, untouched wilderness shaped what he thought about nature. He strongly backed protection of the environment. He backed the idea of setting land aside so national parks could be made. He was an eloquent writer. He was an eloquent speaker too. He used those skills to move other people into the conservation movement.

2That movement could harm Indigenous peoples. John Muir's birthplace in Scotland is a museum now. The museum is about his life and his work. April 21, 1838, was his birthday. The town was Dunbar, in Scotland. Daniel, his father, worked in business. Daniel had also been a soldier. His mother, Anne, kept the home. She painted, wrote poems, and loved nature. John was the oldest son. The family had eight children. In 1849 John was eleven. Wisconsin became their new home inside the United States. Daniel wanted a farm and more money. Daniel was a strict disciplinarian. He made John and the other children work long hours at farm labor. They were allowed only one small meal each day. Their health suffered because of that. During those years John had no formal schooling. He still hungered to learn. Each morning he got up at 1:00 a.m. He was thrilled. Those hours gave him five extra hours every day for his own interests. On his own he studied literature and philosophy. He also studied mathematics and geometry. Daylight that was free was spent outdoors near the farm, among trees and open ground. In his teen years he became a skilled inventor. Some of the early-morning time went to his inventions.

3Those included water wheels and tools for reading the weather. A later invention was a rough alarm clock. At the set time, the machine got him up. The clock was also a desk. It was fixed to a bed that could collapse. At the chosen moment the machine lit a lamp. Then it set John down on the floor with a gentle drop. Young adulthood left Muir restless. He wanted to follow his loves and get off the farm. A neighbor had an idea when Muir was twenty-two. Muir should show his inventions at a fair. Its name was the Wisconsin State Agriculture Fair, and the year was 1860. The city was Madison. The inventions were a huge hit. The alarm clock stood out most. Jeanne Carr was one of the judges. She would later be his mentor. She gave him a cash prize. For the first time, Muir had some independence. He did not go home. He stayed in Madison and went to college. Jeanne Carr was a writer and an amateur botanist. Ezra Carr was a professor of geology. Both became Muir's friends and teachers. In the fall of 1860, his new life was going well. He studied botany, the science of plants.

4He later wrote that this study sent him rushing into woods and meadows, full of wild excitement. He also studied geology and chemistry. He did not finish a degree. A picture shows him as a young man. In 1863 he left Madison. He said he was going to the University of the Wilderness. He walked around Canada. He walked through parts of the northern Midwest. He watched nature closely. Odd jobs paid his way. In 1866 he took work as a mechanic. The city was Indianapolis, in Indiana. The next year an injury at work hurt his eye. For a time he could not see. He feared the blindness would last. Sight came back over about a month. Once he could see, he understood something. Inventing was keeping him from the thing he loved most. He quit the job. His promise was simple. The years ahead would be lived outdoors. Muir set out on September 1, 1867. He walked about 1,000 miles toward Florida. In kilometers, that distance is 1,609. In his writings he recalled the route he chose. It was the wildest path, the leafiest path, and the path with the fewest feet on it. Each day he walked 20 miles or more. In kilometers, a day was at least 32.

5He took detailed notes on plants during the trip. A map of the 1867 journey marks Indianapolis. It shows travel by train, by foot, and by boat. The map names Ohio, West Virginia, Indiana, and Kentucky. It also names Virginia, North Carolina, Tennessee, and South Carolina. Alabama, Georgia, the Atlantic Ocean, Florida, and Cedar Keys are on it too. The Sierra Nevada region is marked as well. He reached the Gulf Coast in a little more than seven weeks. A few days later he became very sick. He had caught malaria while crossing the swamps of Florida. The next January he was only partly well, and his health was still poor. He boarded a ship for Cuba. He hoped to reach the Amazon later and study the plants that grow there. He went to San Francisco instead. He arrived on March 28, 1868. He asked a person to point out the nearest way out of town. The man asked where Muir wanted to go. Muir answered that any wild place would do. On foot, he headed for California's Sierra Nevada. The beauty of that country filled him with awe. He was lonely without other people. He was still ecstatic to be among woods and fields. If he had to choose people or nature, nature usually won.

6A map shows California, San Francisco, and the Pacific Ocean. It also shows Ahwahnee, also called Yosemite Valley. His first trip into the High Sierra was short. He came back the next year. For a short time he worked as a shepherd. Then he ran a sawmill near Yosemite Falls. Say the place name yoh-SEH-muh-tee. Free hours went to exploring the land and to celebrating nature. Ralph Waldo Emerson's books gave him ideas. Emerson was a famous writer and lecturer. He often wrote about why people should connect with nature. In the early 1870s, Muir offered a theory that caused argument. He said moving glaciers had carved Yosemite Valley. Glaciers fascinated him, so he went far into the mountains seeking proof. An article on glaciers came from his pen. The month was October, and the year was 1871. The New York Tribune printed it. Over time, people confirmed his theory. Readers and scientists were starting to notice Muir and what he saw in nature. His Yosemite cabin drew other naturalists who wanted to meet him. Emerson came in 1871. Settlers used the name Yosemite for a place that already had a name. Ahwahnee Valley means a place like a gaping mouth.

7Say it ah-WAH-nee. It is the homeland of several Indigenous tribes. Those tribes include the Ahwahneechee, the Miwok, and the Paiute. A militia band drove out many Indigenous people by force. Yosemite, as a name for the area, came from that band. El Capitan is one feature of the valley. Yosemite Falls is another. Once Muir knew Yosemite so well, he gave more time to writing about what he had lived. Oakland, California, became his home in 1873. Magazine articles from there made him famous across the United States. He wrote with passion. He wanted readers to care about natural places. In April 1880 he married Louisa Strentzel. People called her Louie. He moved to her family's fruit ranch. The town was Martinez, California. He was a devoted husband. He was unhappy with the work the ranch demanded. He still longed for far-off places. With Louie's encouragement, he traveled again. A trip to Yosemite in 1889 led to two articles that many people read. The articles described the area's beauty. They also argued for keeping it safe. Other people helped by urging Congress to protect Yosemite. Those efforts built public support for conservation, and they worked. The next year Yosemite became a national park of the United States. It was the third.

8Yellowstone was earlier. Sequoia was earlier too. Muir and other conservationists saw a need. Yosemite needed a group to defend it. So did the rest of the Sierra Nevada. Muir helped start the Sierra Club in 1892. He became its first president. The club's purpose now includes guarding nature areas and wildlife across the United States. President Theodore Roosevelt wanted a meeting with Muir. The year was 1903. Roosevelt wanted to understand what far-off wild areas in the West needed. Muir felt honored. He took Roosevelt camping in Yosemite. Muir used the trip to argue for setting natural land aside as named parks. Because of that trip, more of Yosemite joined the national park. Roosevelt also protected many other natural places. Crater Lake National Park was one. Wind Cave National Park was another. Writing about where he had traveled filled more of his later years. Four universities gave him honorary degrees. One picture gathers him, Louisa, and the couple's two daughters. He also led a fight that lasted twelve years. He wanted to stop a planned dam from flooding Yosemite's Hetch Hetchy Valley. People tried to stop the project. Muir wrote a letter to Congress. Even so, the project was approved in 1913. The fight still woke the public to the need to protect natural land.

9It also helped bring about the National Park Service in 1916. That service gave stronger management to every national park in the United States. December 24, 1914, was the day John Muir died. He was already dead when the National Park Service began. His work still helped make that service real. A picture shows him as an older man. The word wilderness can suggest a natural place that nobody cares for and nobody lives in. Many places Muir called wilderness had people in them. Indigenous peoples had lived there and managed them since before written history. Muir did not always understand Indigenous ways of caring for land. He did not always agree with them. Indigenous peoples had used controlled burns for thousands of years. A controlled burn is a planned fire that keeps a forest healthy. Muir believed the only protection was to stop every fire. Evidence now shows that controlled burns work and that they matter. Many nature places carry John Muir's name. So do other establishments. Muir Woods National Monument is one example. It lies north of San Francisco. Environmental conservation in this country owes a great deal to John Muir. His drive to protect natural places helped create national parks.

10Those parks still keep beautiful land safe for people not yet born. Today the Sierra Club works on many kinds of environmental problems across the United States. It also works on climate problems around the world. The group works with Indigenous communities. Together they protect land and animals. The aim is to keep loved places safe and healthy for years ahead. To advocate is to support something or to recommend it. Speech or writing that is eloquent stays simple. It is also strong and elegant. Avid means showing a strong interest or a strong wish, and it can mean eager. Glaciers are large bodies of ice and packed snow that stay all year and creep downhill. Conservation is the protection of wild land and of the living things there. A mentor is an experienced teacher and adviser. Controversial means causing a lot of disagreement. A naturalist studies nature and its history. Plants and animals are the usual focus. If something is designated, people have marked it, named it, or picked it for a special job. Passion is intense enthusiasm or strong feeling. Ecstatic means feeling huge happiness, excitement, or delight. Remote means far away or cut off, and it can also mean in the distant past.

40. Kenya from Highland to Coast

1Five countries border Kenya, a nation on the continent of Africa. North of Kenya is Ethiopia. South of Kenya is Tanzania. Say Tanzania as tan-zuh, then NEE-uh. West of Kenya is Uganda. The northwest border is with South Sudan. East of Kenya is Somalia. Southeast, the shore meets the Indian Ocean. Kenya is crossed by the equator. Temperature does not swing enough to mark the seasons. What changes instead is how much rain falls, and how long it falls. Place still changes the temperature. Higher mountains are the cooler spots. Lower places are warmer. Nearby labels on a map include Lake Turkana, Lake Victoria, Nairobi, and Mombasa. A wider map also takes in Europe, Asia, and the rest of Africa. The capital is Nairobi. Say it nie-ROH, then bee. Railway builders created the town as a station on the new rail line. Today the city holds more than three million residents. Industry for the whole country centers here. Clothing comes from its factories. Furniture comes from them. Bread comes from them. Cornmeal comes from them. Other processed foods come from them. East African farms sit close enough that raw crops reach the food plants without a long haul. A wildlife park in the backyard is rare for a capital. Nairobi National Park is that park, and it is a large game reserve.

2The park begins just 8 kilometers out, a trip of 5 miles. Lions can be seen there. Giraffes can be seen there. Reptiles and birds can be seen there. A hotel close to Nairobi offers something unusual. Breakfast at Giraffe Manor may be shared with Rothschild’s giraffes. Dinner may be shared with them too. This rare giraffe has a large sanctuary, and the hotel sits on it. Windows are no barrier. The giraffes push their heads inside. Visits often come in the morning. Visits often come again in the evening. People in the nation number more than forty-five million. That count places Kenya thirty-first among countries. Tribes, meaning ethnic groups, number more than thirty. African ancestors are the background of nearly every Kenyan. Each tribe has its own language, and people speak it. A national language is spoken as well, at least one of them. English is a national language. Swahili is the other, said swah-HEE-lee. English is the language of government. It is the language of higher education. It is the language of large business corporations. Swahili is the language of primary schools. It is also used in many smaller businesses. Only a few Kenyans have ancestors in the Middle East, in Europe, or in Asia.

3Soccer, which many also call football, is a sport people love to watch and to play. International races have made Kenyan runners renowned. Olympic gold medals have been won by those runners. Young and old both play bao. The game uses a wooden board. Small cups in the board hold seeds or stones. Board is the Swahili meaning of bao. Fibers come from sisal after the plants are crushed and then dried. Weaving joins those fibers. Countryside life is the pattern for about 75 percent of the people. Farming is how most of them earn a living. Family meals come from food they grow. Crops are also raised to sell. Tea is one sale crop. Coffee is another. Corn is another. Sweet potatoes are another. Wheat is another. Flowers are grown as well. A natural insecticide is made from many of those flowers. Sisal ranks as another major crop. Ropes and mats are made from its strong fibers. Income also comes heavily from tourism. Yearly visitors number over a million. Clothing such as the kanga is made from cotton, another important crop. A kanga is a large cloth full of color. Women use it as a shawl. They use it as a headscarf. They use it as a skirt.

4A child can be carried in a kanga. A proverb is printed on many kangas. One of them warns that digging a well can leave the digger inside it. Mapped landforms include Lake Turkana and the Chalbi Desert. They include the Great Rift Valley, Mount Kulai, and Mount Elgon. They include the Merti Plateau and Mount Kenya. They include Lake Victoria and Nairobi. They include the Loita Hills and the Yata Plateau. They include the Chyulu Range and the Nyiri Desert. They include Mount Kilimanjaro, the Indian Ocean, the Taita Hills, and Mombasa. Western Kenya is highland country. Those highlands are split by the Great Rift Valley. Earth’s crust is cracked there for 6,437 kilometers, or 4,000 miles. Width of the crack runs about 50 to 130 kilometers, or 30 to 80 miles. The floor holds lakes. It holds volcanoes. It holds deserts. Escarpments, which are cliffs, form the walls. Height of those walls reaches 2,700 meters, or 9,000 feet, above the floor. Farming rain falls in the highlands. Only one other area gets enough rain for crops. The highlands are therefore home to most Kenyans. Inside the highlands, Mount Kenya outranks every other peak. Farming rain also falls on the coastal lowlands. Coconuts thrive in that coastal belt.

5Cashews thrive there too. Beaches of white sand follow the shore. Forests of mangrove follow it too. The Sahara is larger than the deserts of northern Kenya. They are not as large as other deserts in Africa. Nomadic tribes, few in number, live in these dry lands. Sheep and goats are their main herds. The deserts’ western edge holds Lake Turkana. Fossils found there belong to the earliest humans. Lake Rudolf was the lake’s former name. No desert lake on Earth is larger. The savanna is a landscape Kenya is known for. Wildebeests graze in large herds. Zebras graze in large herds. Gazelles graze there, along with other animals. Grass on the savanna can reach 1.5 meters. That height is 5 feet. Flat-topped acacia trees, thorny ones, are scattered across the view. Say acacia as uh-KAY-shuh. Grasslands lie on both the western side of the highlands and the eastern side. Early humans from this region did not all stay. Some left and settled in other places. Those who remained were largely cut off from the wider world until the first century ad. Trade in East Africa was then opened by people from the Middle East. People from Asia opened trade there too. Hundreds of years of coastal trade included enslaved people.
