6Ivory was traded. Other goods were traded. Elephants are one source of ivory. Hippos are another source. Selling ivory is banned by many countries today. The late 1400s brought people from Europe. British Empire rule became official in 1920, when Kenya was made a colony. Anger followed when much native land was handed to white settlers. Some of those settlers came from Great Britain. Others came from South Africa. Independence became the fight in 1952. British rule ended in 1963, and the country was free. Presidential power was very large for a few decades after that. The government had a single political party. An end to that inequality was what many Kenyans wanted. Less power for the president, and more for the people, came with a new constitution in 2010. Safari vans, with guides, carry tourists who search for animals to watch and to photograph. Rare animals are part of why the wildlife is famous. Protection comes from more than fifty parks and reserves. Safaris draw millions of tourists each year. Rhinoceroses are among the animals they come to see. Lions are among them. Leopards are among them. Hippos are among them. Elephants are among them. Elephants here come in two kinds. Highland rainforests are home to the forest elephant.

7Many settings, deserts included, are home to the savanna elephant. Rhinoceroses also come in two kinds. One is called the white rhino. The other is called the black rhino. Gray is the real color of both. Eyesight is poor. The sense of smell is sharp. The sense of hearing is sharp. Weight averages about 3,600 kilograms. That weight is 8,000 pounds. Running speed can reach 45 kilometers in an hour. That pace is 28 miles in an hour. Grazing animals, including zebras and gazelles, crowd the savanna. A yearly trek of wildebeests and zebras is among the most amazing sights in Africa. Wildebeests on the move number about 1.5 million. Zebras on the move number about 300,000. Distance covered is more than 1,600 kilometers, or 1,000 miles. The path leaves the Serengeti Plain and reaches Kenya’s savanna. Say Serengeti as ser-en-GEH-tee. Food is the goal. Water is the goal. Hardship marks the journey. Deaths among wildebeests reach about 250,000 a year. Hunters follow behind the herds. The followers include lions. They include leopards. They include cheetahs. They include hyenas. They include wild dogs. Few sights match the herds as they cross the Mara River. Hippopotamuses live in the Mara and in rivers like it. A hippo moving in water can seem serene.

8It can seem harmless. Human deaths in Africa are caused more often by hippos than by lions. Aggression and a strong sense of territory define them. Water is where they stay for most hours. Night is when they leave the water to feed. Grass is eaten. Other plants are eaten. Crops are sometimes eaten, and people then come into conflict with the animals. Danger is increased by the size of their teeth. Wildlife is not limited to the savanna. Lake Nakuru, inside the Great Rift Valley, draws flamingos. Both greater flamingos and lesser flamingos come. Counts reach the thousands. Counts sometimes reach the millions. Heads go down into the water as these wading birds feed. Tiny plants are the food. Tiny animals are the food. Most hours of a flamingo’s life are spent in water. Land is the only home of a different African bird. No bird on Earth is larger than the ostrich. No bird lays a larger egg. An egg may weigh 1.35 kilograms. That weight is 3 pounds. Stretching flat on the ground is one way an ostrich hides from predators. Running is another way. Speed can reach 70 kilometers in an hour, or 43 miles in an hour. Powerful kicks are the defense if hiding and running both fail.

9Large predators in Kenya are several, and they are dangerous. Humans are harmed most by two animals that are actually tiny. A share near one third of Kenya is infested by the tsetse fly. Say tsetse as TSEE-tsee. The mosquito infests that same portion. Malaria is a disease these insects carry. Sleeping sickness is the other disease they carry. The name sleeping sickness comes from a symptom. Deep sleepiness takes hold of a sick person. A bite transfers a very small organism. Disease follows from that organism. Severe illness follows from malaria. Severe illness follows from sleeping sickness. Government buildings are numerous in Nairobi. Museums are there. Several universities are there. Fame rests on safaris and on the savanna, but Kenya holds much besides. Life fills the valley, and the Great Rift’s cliffs rise above it. Some animal species here are found in no other place. Industry for the entire country centers on the capital. Exports leave that city for markets around the world. Natural beauty is found in abundance. Fascinating cultures are found in great number. The population figure is 52,573,973. Area of the land is 569,140 square kilometers. The same area is 219,746 square miles. Nairobi is listed as the capital. Swahili is listed among the primary languages.

10English is listed among them too. Christianity is listed as the primary religion. The Kenyan shilling is listed as the currency. Both the Central Intelligence Agency, in 2019, and the World Bank are the sources of these figures. Moving about with no lasting home is what nomadic means. Small yellow flowers, or white ones, mark the acacia, a tree of warm climates. Wild plants and wild animals are protected inside a reserve. Halfway between the North Pole and the South Pole, an imaginary line circles Earth. That line is the equator. Searching for wild animals is the purpose of a safari. Two levels of land can be split by an escarpment, a steep slope or cliff. A sanctuary is a place of safety. Tusks of elephants, and of other animals that have tusks, are made of a white material called ivory. Few trees stand on a savanna, which is flat grassland. Ropes use the strong fibers of sisal leaves, and the plant is grown for those leaves. Shallow salt water or swamps are where a mangrove, a tropical tree, can grow. Branches of a mangrove send out roots. Living things that move in a regular, predictable way, from one location to another, are on a migration.

41. Lakota Life on the Great Plains

1The Dignity of Earth and Sky statue stands in Chamberlain, South Dakota. It honors Dakota women and Lakota women. This book begins with the Oceti Sakowin Nation. It then looks at the head of the family. Skilled warriors and traders come next. A section follows the places where bison roamed. Important ceremonies come after that. War and resistance follow. The closing parts are the resilience of the Lakota, a conclusion, and a word list. The Oceti Sakowin Nation. In the United States, the Great Plains reach from the Rocky Mountains on the west side to beyond the Missouri River on the east side. They run from Canada in the north to nearly Mexico in the south. The Lakota are part of the Oceti Sakowin Nation. The name is said oh-CHEH-tee shah-KOH-wee. They have a long history on the Plains. Among Native nations in the United States today, this one is among the biggest. Three distinct groups make it up. The groups differ in language, in culture, and in geography. They are the Lakota, the Dakota, and the Nakota. Each of those is split further into smaller bands. The Lakota are the largest group inside the Oceti Sakowin Nation. Before the 1800s, Native peoples were a majority of the people on the Plains. Village life, with crops in the fields, was the way for some. Others were nomadic. They moved often, following the paths bison took as the herds migrated. Few nomadic tribes were larger than the Lakota. A picture shows the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation in 1891.

2It is a reservation of the Oglala Lakota. What's in a Name? The Oceti Sakowin once lived farther east. Those lands are now part of Minnesota and Wisconsin. In the 1700s another Native group, the Ojibwe, pushed them west. The Ojibwe name is said oh-JIB-way. Outsiders often call the Oceti Sakowin the Sioux, said SOO. That word may come from an Ojibwe term meaning snake or enemy. Members of the nation call themselves Lakota, Dakota, or Nakota. Each of the three names carries the idea of allies, of friends, or of people joined together. The Head of the Family. In Lakota society, men and women traditionally had different duties. Both sets of duties were equally crucial to survival. Women were in charge of the family. They were also in charge of the group's overall well-being. They played an important part in decisions made for the good of the tribe. Women owned all the household goods. They owned the animals. They owned the tipis, a word said TEE-peez. Setting the tipis up was their job. Taking them down when camp moved was their job too. Women cooked food and preserved it. They collected water and firewood. They made pottery and clothing. They raised the children. Often they supplied most of the group's food by gathering wild plants and berries. After a hunt, they skinned the bison and cut up the meat. A picture from 1908 shows a Lakota woman drying meat, which is one way to preserve it.

3People admired Lakota women for their art. They were highly skilled at making clothes, shoes, and tipis. They used hides of bison, elk, and deer. They made bison robes with rich decoration. Paint, porcupine quills, and shells went into the designs. Later, beads did too. The robes took great skill. European traders came to want them very much. Home on the Plains. Tipis were once the homes of the Lakota, as they were for other nomadic Native peoples on the Plains. The structures suited life on the Plains. They could stand up to strong winds. They stayed warm in winter. In summer, air could flow through. The cone shape came from wooden poles. Walls were hides of bison, sewn into one cover. The design let people take a tipi down quickly and carry it to a new place. A picture from 1891 shows a Lakota girl sitting outside a tipi. Skilled Warriors and Traders. Lakota men were highly skilled with horses. They could handle them and ride them well. That skill helped give them a reputation as fierce warriors. Before the 1700s, the Lakota traveled on foot and hunted on foot. Trade and raids brought them horses. By the late 1700s, horses had become an important part of Lakota culture and of the Lakota way of living. A picture from 1907 shows Lakota men acting out a war party. Brave deeds could bring a Lakota man wealth, honor, and higher status in his group. Success in warfare could do the same.

4Touching an enemy first in a battle, for example, brought great honor. Taking a horse from an enemy counted as a great deed too. The Lakota were talented merchants and traders as well. They helped build a strong economy on the Plains. They knew the land. They knew how bison moved. Because of that knowledge, Lakota hunters could get animal hides and furs faster than European traders could. They could get them more easily too. They held fairs. At the fairs they traded bison robes to Europeans. What came back included tools and beads. Fabric and weapons came back as well. Where Bison Roamed. Tatanka, said tah-TAHN-kah, means bison. Bison are sacred animals to the Lakota. They were crucial to the traditional Lakota way of life. The Lakota used every part of the animal. Bones became tools, weapons, and everyday items such as paintbrushes. Horns became cups, spoons, toys, and headdresses for ceremonies. Hair and fur went into pillows, headdresses, and ropes. Hide became robes, blankets, tipis, and many other things. Bison were also the main source of meat. In the years before guns, some Lakota hunts for bison used bows and arrows. The Lakota were very skilled bison hunters. Before they had horses, one method was to lure a herd over the edge of a cliff. The animals fell to their death. The method was very dangerous. It called for great skill, bravery, and teamwork. Today bison are still very important to Lakota religion and culture.

5Gifts made from bison products are prized possessions. Nearly every religious ceremony still uses a bison head or a bison symbol. Important Ceremonies. Ceremonies first performed centuries ago are still held. They may have changed over time. A leading ceremony is the Wiwanyang Wacipi. Say it wee-WAHN-yahng wah-CHEE-pee. It is the Sun Dance. It is held once a year in late spring or early summer. It lasts four days. The Lakota build a hocoka, said hoh-CHOH-kah, which is a ritual circle, on sacred ground. They place a tree in the middle. The tree stands for the Great Spirit, also called the Great Mystery. It also stands for the center of the universe. Dancing in the circle runs from sunrise to sunset. As they dance, the participants look at the sun. During those days the Lakota renew their bond with the land. They renew it with all beings too. Another important ceremony is Hunkapi, said hoon-KAH-pee, or Making of Relatives. Its first use was making ties and alliances with other Native nations. Today it joins two people and their families. A family may also use it to adopt a child in a formal way. The Lakota have performed these ceremonies, and others, for centuries. There was a time when such ceremonies were forbidden. War and Resistance. All through the 1800s, the U.S. government tried to destroy Lakota culture and religion. It tried to force the Lakota to take up the lifestyle and customs of European settlers. The government outlawed religious ceremonies.

6Boarding schools were created, and Native children had to go. Officials knew bison were crucial to Lakota life and to Lakota spiritual practice. Officials urged people to kill the animals in huge numbers. Millions of bison were killed by white settlers and by soldiers. They took the parts they thought were valuable. They left the bodies to rot and go to waste. Around thirty million bison had lived in the United States. By the close of the 1800s only a few hundred remained. Boarding Schools. From 1860 onward, boarding schools for Native children were opened by the government and by Christian missionaries. Lessons pushed the customs and beliefs of white Americans. They were forced to go. The schools were often far from home. Children were not allowed to speak their own language. They were not allowed to wear traditional clothing. They were not allowed to practice their people's customs. They were punished if they did. Many children did not see their family for years. A reunion with family never came for some of those children. A picture shows Native children in a math class. Many treaties, meaning agreements, were signed by Lakota leaders and the government. The treaties set borders between U.S. territory and Lakota territories. The government wanted the country's borders to move west. Again and again it broke the treaties. Land owned by the Lakota was opened to white pioneers. Reservation land for the Lakota kept shrinking. War between the Lakota and the army lasted for decades because of those actions.

7One of the greatest Lakota victories against the army in this period was the Battle of the Greasy Grass. Gold was discovered in 1875 on lands sacred to the Lakota. The army ignored earlier treaties and invaded the area. Thousands of Lakota left the reservations because the betrayal angered them. In Montana they joined Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse. In June 1876, Native leaders learned that U.S. troops were coming to attack the camp. About three thousand warriors went with Crazy Horse to defend the camp. The troops were outnumbered. They were quickly overwhelmed. Within an hour, more than two hundred U.S. soldiers were dead. Skilled leadership helped the Lakota win many battles. So did the strength and dedication of their people. Even so, war did not stop. Death tolls were high. Crucial resources were lost. Defending the land grew harder and harder. Lakota leaders saw that survival meant accepting peace. It meant accepting the terms of surrender, including a move onto reservations. Even then, the Lakota kept working to preserve their way of life. They passed traditions and beliefs down through oral history. They hid children so the children would not be sent to boarding schools. They held religious ceremonies in secret. Those efforts went on until 1978. The American Indian Religious Freedom Act became law that year. Open practice of Lakota religion and customs was allowed once more. A picture shows a Lakota boy in traditional clothing. He dances at a powwow in South Dakota. Notable Lakota.

8William Mills, also called Billy Mills, has the Lakota name Tamakoce Te'Hila. His years are given as 1938 onward. He is a retired Olympic athlete. In 1964 he set a world record. No American before him had won gold in the 10,000-meter race. Eagle Woman, whose Lakota name is Wambli Autepewin, lived from 1820 to 1888. She was an activist, a diplomat, and a translator. She is the only woman recognized as a Lakota chief. Luther Standing Bear, whose name is also given as Óta Kté, lived from 1868 to 1939. He was a musician and an actor. He helped film studios hire Native actors. He worked to improve how movies showed Native culture. Mary Brave Bird, also called Ohitika Win, lived from 1954 to 2013. She was an activist and an author. She belonged to the American Indian Movement. That movement helped raise awareness about how Native peoples were treated. Dr. Beatrice Medicine, whose Lakota name is Hinsha Waste Agli Win, lived from 1923 to 2005. She was an anthropologist, an educator, and an activist. She spoke up for the rights of Native peoples. Tokata Iron Eyes was born in 2003. She is an environmental activist. Her travels cross the whole country so more people learn about climate change. The Resilience of the Lakota. Today the Lakota still gather for festivals and ceremonies. They celebrate and honor their heritage. Each year brings contests and performances of traditional dances. Lakota organizations have also brought back ceremonies that were once forbidden, so new generations can know them.

9In the 1990s, the Isnati Awica Dowanpi was restored with help from the Brave Heart Women's Society. Say the first part eesh-NAH-tee. Say the middle ah-WEE-chah. Say the last part doh-WAHN-pee. It is the First Moon Ceremony. It is a coming-of-age ceremony for Lakota girls, and women of the community lead it. The four days teach girls their culture. They also teach the role of women. They take part in traditional activities. The Lakota are also working so younger generations learn their Native language. In 2007, Red Cloud Indian School joined with Indiana University. The school is a Lakota school in South Dakota. Together they created the Lakota Language Project. The program encourages people to learn the Lakota language and to use it, both in school and in the community. The Lakota are also helping to raise the number of bison on the Plains. The same effort includes over sixty other tribes. Those tribes come from nineteen states. The tribes joined to create the Intertribal Buffalo Cooperative. Their goal is to restore bison so the land can heal. Healing the spirit of Plains Native peoples, for generations still to come, is another aim. The group began in 1991. Since then the bison count has climbed past twenty thousand. A set of pictures shows three scenes. In 2019 a young Lakota woman addresses the United Nations Youth Climate Summit. Learners practice putting Lakota words on paper. President Barack Obama meets young people from the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe.

10Conclusion. War did not end the Lakota people or their culture. They have survived discrimination. They have survived a campaign of two hundred years that tried to destroy their way of life. Today they still protect their ancestral land. They are increasing bison populations. They organize to resist building projects that would hurt the environment. They work to teach younger generations about their history, their language, and their traditions. They teach non-Native peoples as well. Lakota people keep giving to the wider world in many roles. Those roles include teaching, medicine, activism, art, and politics. They contribute to their own community. They contribute to the world. Word list. Ancestral describes something linked to earlier generations of a family or a tribe. Annually means once a year. Crucial means extremely important and essential. Distinct means different enough to be noticed. Elaborately describes work full of parts and details. Luring means drawing someone or something toward a place that is dangerous, unwanted, or surprising, often by offering a reward or bait. Merchants are people who buy goods, trade goods, or sell goods. Plummeted means fell or dropped quickly. Sacred describes something linked to a god, a religion, or a spiritual purpose. Spiritual describes something related to a spirit, a soul, or a divine being. A tipi is a tentlike home of Native peoples who lived on the Great Plains. Traditionally means according to a ritual, an action, or a belief passed down year after year and generation after generation.

42. Learn to Weave by Hand

1The parts of this book come in this order. What weaving is. A mat made of paper. A bracelet for a friend. Other kinds of weaving. A closing. A word list. Weaving is the process of making fabric. The maker laces two sets of threads or fibers together. This art and this useful craft go back tens of thousands of years. People today still weave many kinds of fibers. They make clothing, rugs, and much more. A picture shows weaving with natural materials. Two sets of threads must be ready as a base before a new woven pattern starts. The warp is a set of vertical threads. Tension holds them in place, usually over a frame. The weft is one horizontal thread, or more than one. The weaver laces the weft over the warp and under it. The weaver packs the weft down. The threads then fit closely and form a fabric. This book introduces weaving through two fun projects. One project is a paper mat. The other is a friendship bracelet. Each project teaches a different way to weave.

2Gather the supplies and begin. The materials are these. Construction paper that is 9 inches by 12 inches. Use one whole piece. Cut a second piece into strips that are 1 inch by 9 inches. Also gather a pencil, a ruler, scissors, and a glue stick. The first project teaches the basics of weaving through paper. Paper weaving can make placemats. It can make book covers. It can make colorful designs for a bare spot on a wall. Step 1. Choose one piece of paper. It will be the warp, the foundation of the project. Fold it carefully in half. Draw a straight line 1 inch from the long open edge. Step 2. From the fold to the line you just drew, mark ten to twelve lines. The lines may be straight, curved, or a mix of both. Do not draw lines too close to the edges of the paper. Also avoid complicated shapes, because those shapes make the weaving too hard. Step 3. Keep the paper folded. Cut along the lines from step 2. Start at the fold.

3Stop at the straight line. Do not cut on that straight line. Gently unfold the paper. Lay it flat on the table. Place the cuts so they run up and down. Step 4. Pick up a strip that is 1 inch by 9 inches, in a different paper color. This strip is the weft. Insert it crosswise, over one warp and under the next. If you are right-handed, start on the right side. If you are left-handed, start on the left side. Keep weaving over one strip and under the next until you reach the far edge. Move this weft strip gently until it reaches the top edge of the warp. Stop at the horizontal line. Step 5. Start a new row with another strip of the same size. The row before began by going over one. Start this row by going under one. Keep adding weft strips. Switch the start of each row, first over one and then under one. Gently slide each weft strip up so it sits right beside the one before it.

4Be especially gentle with the last strip so the paper does not tear. Step 6. When the weaving is finished, use a glue stick on the loose edges of the weft strips. Turn the weaving over and glue those edges too. You have just finished your first weaving. You can vary the project in several ways. Try warps and wefts of different thicknesses so new patterns appear. Wrapping paper is one paper you can try. Origami paper is another. Handle thin paper with care so it does not tear. Curves, rather than straight lines, can be the shape of the weft cuts. Insert the weft strips in the same order as the cuts so the pieces will lock together. Using a different paper color, cut a shape from the center, such as a heart or a butterfly. Cut the weft and the warp so the shape you cut stands out. A picture can be painted or drawn on paper first. That same paper can then serve as the warp. The next project uses these materials. Embroidery floss in various colors.

5Round toothpicks. Masking tape. Small beads, if you want them. This project takes the skills from the paper weaving and uses them in a thread craft. You can make friendship bracelets with this finger-weaving method. Step 1. Cut four to six warp threads of embroidery floss. Make each thread 1 foot long. Also cut one weft thread 4 feet long. Line up one end of all the threads so the ends match. Tie an overhand knot 3 inches from that end. A small diagram shows how to tie an overhand knot. A diagram labels the weft and the warps. Step 2. The tails at the knotted end get taped down on your work table. Keep that tape a few inches back from the table edge nearest you. Step 3. Pull the long thread, the weft, away from the warp threads. Decide the order you want for the warp threads. Smooth them flat. Near the table edge, tape the threads so the order you chose stays put. Step 4. Insert a toothpick crosswise just under the knot.

6Go over one warp thread and under the next. Continue the toothpick over one thread and under the next until the far side is reached. This toothpick stays in place until the weaving is finished. Tape both ends of it to the table. Step 5. Use another toothpick to lift every other warp thread. Lift the threads that are opposite the ones the first toothpick lifted. After the toothpick is woven through, lift it enough to open a space. That space is a shed. It lies between the lifted warp threads and the threads that stay flat on the table. A label marks the shed. Step 6. Send the weft thread through the whole space. Pull it gently across. Slide the toothpick up. Pack the weft firm against the top of the weaving with that toothpick. Take care not to pull the taped warps loose. Step 7. Keep lifting every other warp thread with the toothpick. Feed the weft thread through. Pack it tightly. You may need to move the weaving and tape it again several times as it grows.

7If the weft covers the warp threads, tighten the warp threads. Add more tape at the end closest to you. Step 8. If the weft thread is about to run out, cut another piece. Use a square knot to join it to the piece you already have. Try to place the knot in the middle of a row so it stays hidden. A diagram shows the new thread woven in, the threads tied, and the square knot. Step 9. Stop when the weaving is as long as you want. Remove the tape at the bottom. Tie an overhand knot so the last weft row stays secure. Cut the tails to 3 inches so they match the other tails. Gently remove the tape from the top. Remove the toothpick too. Step 10. Finish the fringe by braiding, or by tying an overhand knot on each piece of embroidery floss. You can also add decorative beads if you like. A diagram shows how to braid, with the strands labeled a, b, and c in a repeating order. Step 11.

8Use an overhand knot to tie the bracelet in place, or to attach the weaving to something. Use the tails for that knot. Do not use the woven area. More variations are possible. Try different color patterns. You might switch warp colors in turns. You might make a stripe in the middle. Other patterns are possible once the warp count is six or higher. Two of those patterns go over two and under two. For these patterns, start with an even number of warp threads. Do not count the thread that becomes the weft. Pictures show three helpful tools. One is a creative weaving tool made at home. One is a small plastic tool from a craft store. One is an inventive way to anchor the work without tape. If weaving paper and thread by hand is fun, you might like other kinds of weaving too. Many kinds use a loom. While a weaver works, a loom keeps yarn or thread from slipping. Looms come in many shapes and sizes. Hand looms are common. So are frame looms, backstrap looms, and floor looms.

9There are even small looms for friendship bracelets, so you do not need tape. Pictures show a frame loom, a backstrap loom, and a floor loom. One picture shows the weaving of a Peruvian friendship bracelet. People all over the world have used the art of weaving for centuries. They make rugs, clothing, accessories, and more. Weaving has deep and meaningful roots in many cultures. We can still learn about it and enjoy it today. These projects give only a small sample of the weaving you might try. You have learned the basic principles of weaving. You have experimented by using your imagination. You have tried different materials, patterns, and colors. Many other kinds of weaving can use these same ideas and techniques. Have fun. More books to explore come next. One is Weaving Around the World, by Kira Freed, from 2007. Another is Weaving Without a Loom, by Veronica Burningham, from 1998. Another is You Can Weave! The rest of that title is Projects for Young Weavers. The authors are Kathleen Monaghan and Hermon Joyner.

10The year is 2000. On the web, you can find directions for many weaving projects that need no special equipment. Try searching for the words finger weaving. Also try the words card weaving. A picture shows a hand loom. Word list. Alternating is a verb. It means occurring in turns, or switching between things. Complicated is an adjective. It means complex, or having many parts. Horizontal is an adjective. It means across, from left to right. A loom is a noun. A loom can turn yarn into fabric strips. It can do the same with thread or with other soft materials. Previous is an adjective. It means earlier, or the one before. A shed is a noun. A shed is the opening in the warp threads that lets the weft pass. Vertical is an adjective. It means up and down. Warp is a noun. It means the vertical threads that form the foundation of a woven piece. Weft is a noun. It means the horizontal threads laced between the warp of a woven piece.

43. Learning the Work of Astronauts

1The parts of this book come in this order. The introduction is called From Space Camp to Space. Then comes Space Camps Around the World. Going to Space Camp follows. Astronaut Training comes next. That part includes the Multi-Axis Trainer and the 1/6 Gravity Chair. It also includes the Space Shot and the G-Force Accelerator. Simulated Missions come after the trainers. Astronauts of the Future? comes near the end. A glossary closes the book. Introduction: From Space Camp to Space In the summer of 1990, a sixth grader named Kate Rubins went off to camp. The camp was in Huntsville, Alabama. It was not a place for singing around a campfire. It was not a place for paddling a canoe. This was space camp. It was an in-depth program. The program went deep into the science of space exploration. It also went into the excitement of that exploration. She had told her parents about her dream. She wanted to become an astronaut, and a biologist, and a geologist, in that order. She jumped with enthusiasm into the science activities at the camp. She jumped into the engineering activities too. She was thrilled to take part in real astronaut training. She was thrilled to join the teamwork of simulated space missions. A picture shows the entrance and the habitat where campers stay. The place is United States Space Camp in Huntsville, Alabama. A picture shows Takuya Onishi, Anatoly Ivanishin, and Kate Rubins.

2They fly to the ISS in July 2016. Move ahead twenty-six years to 2016. Young trainees walked into an IMAX theater at the very same camp. They sat in their seats. They watched in awe. A real liftoff played on the theater's live video feed. The rocket was a giant Russian rocket. On board were fresh supplies for the International Space Station. Crew members were on board too. The short name of the station is ISS. The ISS orbits more than 322 kilometers (200 mi.) above Earth. Watching the launch was especially special for these trainees. One of the three astronauts on board was Dr. Kate Rubins. She was a graduate of space camp. For years she had worked as a biologist. Then she began to train with the National Aeronautics and Space Administration. The short name of that agency is NASA. Now she was blasting off. She would serve on a four-month mission on the ISS. She would act as the mission's flight engineer. She would conduct biology experiments. As this former space camp trainee rocketed into orbit, she met her childhood dream. She became an astronaut. A picture shows the Pathfinder. It is a model of a space shuttle. The model stays on display for good near Alabama's space camp. Space Camps Around the World Space camps let people dive into space-related science through many activities. Multimedia programs teach the exciting history of space exploration.

3Hands-on projects focus on the robotics used in the field. They also focus on the technology. Campers test the equipment that real astronauts use to prepare for missions. Sometimes trainees must practice teamwork in simulators. A simulator is a machine built to imitate how a real spacecraft operates. Space camps now run in many locations. The camp in Huntsville, Alabama, sits near the United States Space and Rocket Center. There, trainees can see the giant rockets that helped NASA astronauts reach the Moon in 1969. They can see the space capsules too. Attendance at Alabama's space camp has passed 750,000 trainees. The camp opened in 1982. Every one of the fifty states has sent campers to this camp. They have come from more than sixty other countries. During summer breaks, some universities in the United States run space camps. Some museums do too. The Frontiers of Flight Museum in Texas offers space camp for children. They can attend Florida's Camp Kennedy Space Center. Several summer day camps are offered by the Smithsonian Association in Washington, D.C. The camps offer space-related activities. Children as young as kindergarten age can join. These programs feed children's fascination with science. They feed fascination with technology and engineering. They even feed fascination with science fiction stories about space exploration. Popular space camps exist in other parts of the world too. In Quebec, Canada, the Cosmodome hosts three-day camps. It hosts a variety of other space-related programs too.

4Space Camp Turkey is in Izmir. Izmir is one of Turkey's biggest cities. Russian Space Camp is at the Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Center. Lectures there cover the country's amazing past in space exploration. The center's name honors Yuri Gagarin. In 1961 he became the first human to fly into space. A world map of space camps marks six places. They are Dallas, Texas, USA, and Huntsville, Alabama, USA. They are Merritt Island, Florida, USA, and Laval, Quebec, Canada. They are Izmir, Turkey, and Star City, Russia. The map also marks North America, Asia, Europe, the Atlantic Ocean, and Africa. Going to Space Camp Space camp programs serve a wide range of interests. At some camps, younger children can take part with their family. Camps for older children are grouped by age. Trainees with special needs can join sessions at some space camps. Those needs include visual impairments. They include hearing impairments. Many programs offer scholarships. Scholarships give every eager space fan a chance to attend. A picture shows rockets built at space camps. The rockets can be powered by water. A Day at Space Camp The list below shows one sample day for a space camper. From 8:00 to 9:00 am, campers get ready and eat breakfast. From 9:00 to 10:00 am, they ride simulators. From 10:00 to 11:30 am, they do leadership and team-building activities. From 11:30 to 12:00 noon, they eat lunch in the crew galley.

5From 12:30 to 1:30 pm, they use an astronaut training simulator. From 1:30 to 3:00 pm, they do rocket construction. From 3:00 to 4:00 pm, they watch a movie. From 4:00 to 5:00 pm, they do simulated mission training. From 5:30 to 6:00 pm, they eat dinner. From 6:30 to 7:30 pm, they learn about spaceflight history. From 7:30 to 8:30 pm, they join an engineering workshop. From 9:00 to 10:00 pm, they call home and prep for bed. Space camps generally concentrate on three things. Those things are the history, the science, and the technology of space travel. At many space camps, trainees study rocketry. They build their own model rockets. They launch those rockets. At other camps, they study spacecraft design. Then they design their own ship for a space mission. Programs that emphasize robotics are common as well. Robotics has grown into an important piece of space exploration as technology moves ahead. For example, the Opportunity rover has explored the surface of Mars. The Spirit rover has done so too. Both are robotic rovers. Robotics trainees engineer robots. They program robots to solve real-world problems. Teams may meet in a lively robotics contest when camp ends. A picture shows a NASA astronaut and an educator. They test-drive a robotic rover built in a space camp program. The food astronauts eat is dehydrated. Drying the food cuts its volume.

6It also makes packing easier. The process helps the food stay fresh longer. Alabama's space camp has a weeklong aviation program. Attendees can learn about flight. They can learn about military aircraft. Military test pilots were the first jobs of all the earliest NASA astronauts. Even while eating, space campers may have unusual experiences. Even while sleeping, they may have them too. Trainees at Quebec's Cosmodome tie themselves into sleeping bags. The bags simulate how astronauts sleep on the ISS. Other camps let trainees try the specially packed meals that astronauts eat in space. Children are not the only ones having fun. Adults from many countries attend plenty of space camps. Some science teachers attend. They want to leave with new ideas. They want creative lessons that can energize the next generation of space explorers. Astronaut Training Simulators are among the most popular activities at some space camps. Before astronauts ever step into a spacecraft, they must practice. They practice for every situation they might meet. The simulators let trainees feel some of the challenges astronauts face. While trainees are on the equipment, camp counselors watch over them with care. The Multi-Axis Trainer The Multi-Axis Trainer is called the MAT for short. Testers used it on the first astronauts in the early 1960s. It helped them practice getting command back. The practice was for a space capsule tumbling out of control. The MAT is a big metal ring set inside a larger ring.

7The trainee is strapped in the center ring. Then the two rings spin wildly. They spin in different directions. The design of the MAT should keep trainees from feeling nauseated on the ride. They should not become dizzy either. The 1/6 Gravity Chair The 1/6 Gravity Chair lets trainees feel what it is like to bound around on the Moon. Gravity there is one-sixth of Earth's gravity. The simulator helps trainees get used to moving. Their bodies feel much lighter than normal. Here is a math minute. What would someone weigh on the Moon if that person weighs 27 kilograms (59.5 lb.) on Earth? The answer is 4.5 kilograms (10 lb.). The Space Shot and G-Force Accelerator The feeling from these simulators will be known to anyone who has been on a roller coaster. Riders on the Space Shot are sent upward at four g's. Four g's means four times the force of Earth's gravity. The upward rush feels so quick that your stomach seems to stay behind. If you weigh 23 kilograms (50.7 lb.), the ride changes how heavy you feel. On the Space Shot, you seem to weigh 92 kilograms (202.8 lb.). The G-Force Accelerator is a spinning ride. It produces a high-pressure force. The force comes from the fast speed of the spin. Three times the pull of Earth's gravity is the force reached by the G-Force Accelerator.

8That force is three g's. Astronauts feel the same force during a rocket launch. A picture shows some trainees working inside the simulators. They operate controls as if they are flying a shuttle. Simulated Missions Another highlight at many camps is simulated space missions. Some simulations work much like video games. Teamwork is an important quality in real astronauts. Leadership is important too. Mission simulators let trainees hone these skills. One mission has participants launch the space shuttle. They fly it to the International Space Station. They dock the craft. Team members perform a variety of duties. They must communicate on their headsets. Just like a real crew, they run through checklists. The lists make sure they remember their tasks exactly. The lists also make sure they stick to the schedule. Some trainees serve as astronauts. Others work in Mission Control. Mission Control is the command center back on Earth. Some simulated missions include practice voyages to the Moon. Others take place on models of a space station. Others take place on models of other spacecraft. The crew must be ready to think fast. The simulator may create an emergency for them. One example is a simulated engine problem. Another example is a sudden meteor shower. A few space camps built future simulations for older trainees. One future mission is a trip to Mars. Crews work together aboard life-size models. The models are of the Orion capsule and the Mars lander.

9This training is at the space camp in Alabama. On the planned trip to Mars, real astronauts will live aboard Orion. They will live on it during the voyage back. The landing module will carry them down to the surface of Mars. They will use it to return to the Orion. The Orion will remain in orbit around Mars. A picture shows campers repairing a model of the Hubble Telescope during a simulation. Space Camp Heroes Here are a few astronauts and scientists. They have graduated from space camps, or they have supported programs that help young people learn about space. Dr. Leroy Chiao is a veteran NASA astronaut. He now leads the Houston Association for Space and Science Education. Students and trainees around the world receive live-stream visits from Chiao. Bobak Ferdowsi is an aeronautical engineer. He is also an astronautical engineer. Ferdowsi is planning a future mission. The mission would send a robotic probe to Europa. Europa is one of Jupiter's moons. Samantha Cristoforetti was a space camp trainee. She became a fighter pilot for Italy's air force. In 2014 and 2015, Cristoforetti served on the ISS for 199 days. Robert Gibson is also known as Hoot Gibson. He is a big supporter of space camps. Five space shuttle missions in the 1980s and 1990s are part of his record. Michael E. Lopez-Alegria served on four space shuttle missions. Space Camp Turkey has also had him as a speaker.

10Astronauts of the Future? Much like Dr. Kate Rubins, today's trainees may be the astronauts of tomorrow. Those trainees come from space camps around the world. NASA is working with other space programs. Together they plan a mission to Mars. They want the mission to begin as early as the 2030s. If plans work out, some people on Orion could be today's space camp trainees. The soil of the Red Planet could hold their footprints, among the first ever made there. In that way they would continue humanity's reach for the stars. Glossary Aeronautics is the science and practice of flight. A rover is a vehicle that explores surfaces in space, including planets and moons. Aviation is the flying of aircraft. Simulated means modeling or imitating how something looks or the condition it is in. Counselors are people who supervise at a camp. Exploration is a journey through unfamiliar territory in order to learn more about it. A spacecraft is a vehicle used for traveling in space. Technology is scientific knowledge, or tools, used to make or do something. G's are units of force. The pull of gravity on an object at Earth's surface is equal to one g. Trainees are people who are being taught a particular job. Hone means to sharpen or improve. Mock means not real. It describes something done for practice or as a simulation.

44. Leonardo of Vinci, Maker and Questioner

1This book follows a prankster who never had an ordinary class. It tells his childhood, his many skills, and his questions. It tells what he invented, how he learned by looking, and how notebooks were lost. Hard words are explained at the end. Leonardo was born in 1452. The place was Vinci, a small village in Italy. He liked pranks. Curiosity sent him on adventures even while he was small. Once he shaped bizarre creatures from soft wax. He filled them with air. He set them loose in a garden. The people there were surprised and frightened. Another time he painted a monster on a wooden shield. He hid the shield in a dark room to scare his father. Father walked in. Window light fell only on the monster. Father believed the monster was alive. He fled. One picture is a self-portrait of da Vinci. His life lasted 67 years. Other children his age were not like him. Charm was one difference. He was gentle. He was handsome. Animals were dear to him. He loved them so much that meat stayed off his plate. Vegetarians were very rare then. People found his refusal of meat strange. Other differences showed too. Math ideas far beyond his years made sense to him. Even as a child, his music already sounded adult. His art already looked adult. Home, in childhood, was with his grandparents and his uncle.

2His father, Ser Piero, was a businessman with big plans. Most of Ser Piero's time was spent 40 miles away, in Florence, Italy. Visits to the family home near Vinci were rare and short. With father gone so often, Leonardo stayed with Francesco, his father's brother. The uncle let him roam fields and woods by the farm. Francesco was patient. He tried to answer every question. He taught plant names and herb uses. He taught signs that weather was coming. He taught how local wildlife behaved. Reading, writing, and basic math came from the village priest. All of this left Leonardo thirsty for still more knowledge. A picture shows markets on the Ponte Vecchio Bridge. It also shows a view from the Duomo in Florence. Teenage Leonardo went to Florence so he could live near his father. The father had just married. Florence held a major place in Europe's rebirth. People called that rebirth the Renaissance. The Renaissance took place in the sixteenth century, from 1485 to 1603. The city held artisans and sculptors, and it held poets and musicians, all living and working there. Leonardo wanted the life of an artist. Father agreed he could serve a local artist as an apprentice, which means an assistant. The shop belonged to master Andrea del Verrocchio.

3There Leonardo learned many methods of painting and of sculpting. He even mixed his own paints from pigments and egg whites. He rose to head assistant. Soon his painting passed Andrea's. Respect as an artist followed. Painting pleased him. People in Florence sent many commissions, meaning requests, for portraits. Some complained that he did not treat the jobs as serious. They said one task could not hold him long enough to finish. Customers grew upset while paintings sat unfinished. Leonardo was unbothered. New projects filled his mind. Art was only one of his gifts. Solving problems was another. Uncle Francesco had taught him to ask questions and hunt for answers. If trouble appeared, a solution should be hunted too. Leonardo followed that teaching. Painting brought problems, and he set out to solve them. Candlelight and oil-lamp light were too dim for the work. He built a new lamp. Water in the lamp magnified the flame. Light then filled the whole room. A sketch shows that oil lamp. Fine detail strained his eyes and hurt his sight. He changed his eyeglasses so he could see better. Other inventions answered other problems. He made pliers. He made a wrench. Larger projects had parts that needed tightening and loosening. The new tools did that work. No one had seen either tool before his time. He designed a clock that showed minutes, not hours alone.

4The clock would keep him on schedule. The prankster in him also built a very funny alarm clock. Here is the way it worked. A rope was tied to a sleeper's ankles. The rope's other end held a bucket hung from the ceiling. Overnight, water slowly filled the bucket. A full bucket was heavy enough to yank the sleeper's legs straight up. Waking up was certain. What he made was often written, described, and drawn in notebooks. The notebooks open a window on his thinking. They show his way of solving problems. A picture shows a replica of the alarm clock. Problem-solving was a great strength. Curiosity is what made the strength so great. The childhood wish to explore never left him. He had explored that way in fields and woods by his uncle's farm. Study delighted him. Once he wanted a tree's age. He studied the tree. He found that rings in the trunk can tell anyone how old the tree is. Another time he asked whether solar power was possible. Concave mirrors bounced sunlight and heated water. Flight stayed a lifelong question. Birds were among his favorite notebook subjects. He studied them and sketched them. If he could grasp how a bird flew, he thought the knowledge could be used. A machine might then let a person fly.

5Sketches of an early helicopter followed. A child's toy was the base of those designs. He also drew a machine like a bird. That machine would have been far too heavy to leave the ground. A parachute was sketched too. His best flight design was a hang glider. The hang glider appears in his books. Some people think he really tried a flying machine on January 2, 1496. The Wright brothers' first flight came four hundred years later. An early sketch shows the hang glider. Not every invention was built. Ideas were drawn with care in the notebooks. Precise details and instructions were written for each one. He believed a drawing was the fullest way to understand a thing. So he drew objects from many angles. Forms showed in the drawings. Functions showed too. Some sketches are so careful and so beautiful that books today use them as examples. Learning never stopped being a passion. He read every book he could reach. He borrowed books. Libraries held him for hours. Unknown words were written down while he read. He could learn them afterward. One notebook held over nine thousand words. The words ran backward, in his own mirror writing. Some experts think the backward hand kept ink from smearing. He was left-handed. No teacher forced his other hand to do the writing.

6Some left-handed people did face that force. He simply wrote in the way that felt easiest. Every study opened more questions. It opened more interests. Light, and the way light lets a person see, led him to the human eye. The eye led him to the human body. Birds led him to flight. Mathematics led him to mechanics. Currents of air and of water led him to power and to energy. Each new fact made him want another. Why and how were favorite questions after he finished a book. The questions started fresh thinking. They sent him toward new interests. People still study the notebooks. Modern builders have made prototypes, meaning models, from those notes. A number of the prototypes really work. A museum of his work might show a prototype of the clock. It might show a miniature replica of a cathedral design. It might show a small helicopter model. It might show the many hydraulic machines, meaning machines run by water, that he drew. The drawings in the notebooks are careful and faithful. One picture is a cathedral design. In 1993, and in later years, scholars gathered to test the hang glider designs. The prototypes flew beautifully. Modern materials that are light made them work especially well. People of the 1400s could hardly imagine many of his inventions. Today a door that opens by itself is ordinary.

7In the fifteenth century, a door yanked open without warning would have been a novelty. His design used ropes and weights for that pull. It might even have felt a little scary. He could throw an object's image onto a wall. He needed a box, plus a small lens and a candle. People were amazed. His camera obscura let images be caught on paper. Feats like these led some of his own students to accuse him of witchcraft. The ideas were so unfamiliar that the work turned controversial. Probably for that reason, the pope in Rome would not commission anything from him. As a master craftsman he signed on with the guild. He then trained apprentices of his own. Students often finished paintings he had left undone. The arrangement suited him. He would rather invent gadgets and improve them. He would rather study what he loved. Painting portraits all the time did not appeal. When he was not painting and not inventing, he was watching. Birds, water, people, and anything else of interest held his eye. He believed knowledge comes from knowing how to see. His ideas were not always right. Wide watching of how the world works still produced creations. For his time, those creations were amazingly accurate. He also drew animals that lived only in his imagination. Some ideas stayed private.

8Submarine designs were among them. He feared a submarine might be used to kill people who had done no wrong. Much of his knowledge was shared anyway. For years, one theory carried the name Leonardo's law. His theory said a thing stays unmoved unless another thing moves upon it. Sir Isaac Newton later wrote a mathematical formula for the same principle. He did that work in the seventeenth century. People then called it Newton's first law of motion. A picture can show Isaac Newton. Leonardo meant to publish his writing as an encyclopedia. He stayed so busy that the book never appeared. Death came on May 2, 1519. He was 67. Count Giovanni Francesco Melzi was a devoted student. Melzi inherited the notebooks and the documents. He inherited many other belongings too. He tried to sort thousands of papers into the books his master had dreamed of. Only one book was finished. Its title was A Treatise on Painting. It held Leonardo's thoughts about art and about the artist. Publication came many years after Leonardo's death. When Francesco Melzi died, the papers went to his son. The son cared nothing for them. They sat in the younger Melzi's attic for years. Later he gave much of the work away or sold it to collectors. The papers scattered across the world. A picture shows a page from A Treatise on Painting.

9For a long time, most people knew Leonardo da Vinci only through his art. The Last Supper was one masterpiece. La Gioconda was another. Americans more often call La Gioconda The Mona Lisa. Nothing pushed people to see him as more than a wonderful painter. The only book of his in print was about art. During the Industrial Revolution of the 1880s, the documents began to surface again. People met ideas that were new and original. Many creations of his had, by that point, been built again by later people. Other people received the credit. Fields of study could have moved ahead centuries sooner because of his ideas. That chance was lost. Research and drawings filled 13,000 pages, and half of those pages had disappeared. Famous people have studied the art and the notebooks, or written about them. The playwright Oscar Wilde is one. The poet William Butler Yeats is one. The psychologist Sigmund Freud is one. The scientist Albert Einstein is one. The artist Andy Warhol is one. A biographer wrote that Leonardo has always been studied more than he has been understood. Journals say little about his private life or his feelings. Most works and notebooks carry no date. So the timing of events in his life is confused. The reasons for those events are confused too.

10The biographies disagree with one another. Fascination with his life and his discoveries still continues. He made over 1,500 careful drawings of the human body. That output was a great achievement. His gift to science through anatomical pictures alone cannot be priced. His life was a hunt for knowledge. He took on problems and solved them himself. One of his sayings shaped that life. The saying was that knowledge of all things is possible. Anatomical means related to how a body is built. An apprentice is a beginner who learns a skill or a trade from a master. A camera obscura is a dark, closed space. Outside images pass through a small lens and land on a facing surface. Commissions are jobs someone asked for and paid for. A guild is a group of people who share a trade. It is a union. Hydraulic means run by water. The Industrial Revolution shifted how goods were made. Hand work based in homes gave way to large factory production. Innovative means new and original. A novelty is something new and unusual. Prototypes are first forms used as models for later making. The Renaissance was a historical time marked by a return of classical art, literature, and architecture. A replica is a copy of a work of art, often smaller than the original.

45. Lincoln's Short Speech at Gettysburg

1Only one version of the Gettysburg Address carries President Lincoln's signature. It is the fifth version. This book begins with brother against brother. It tells about President Lincoln and the Civil War. It asks what the president said. A closer look follows. Life after Gettysburg comes next. A glossary explains hard words. Fights between siblings are so common that people barely notice them. Imagine a war in which you fight on one side. Your brother or sister fights on the other. One country divided into two sides and fought for a long time. People call that fight the American Civil War. Soldiers sometimes knew the person they faced. Men from the same town fought on opposite sides. Men from the same family did too. Many officers had trained together in an earlier conflict. They had fought on the same side then. Some had been close friends before this war. The Union was made up of the Northern states. The Confederacy was made up of the Southern states. The Civil War raged from 1861 until 1865. It cost the lives of 620,000 men. The Battle of Gettysburg was one of the war's most famous battles. Lewis Armistead and Winfield Scott Hancock had been close friends before the Civil War. During the war they served as generals. They served on opposite sides. Both were wounded at Gettysburg. Hancock lived. Armistead died. The battle's first morning was July 1, 1863. Rudolf Schwarz served the Union. He watched captured Confederate men being marched off. To his dismay, his own brother was among them. The Schwarz brothers embraced. They were happy to see each other. They had not met since they left Germany for the United States. Guards led the Confederate brother off, and the brothers' meeting ended. They never met again. That same afternoon, Rudolf died while fighting. How did the United States reach a war of brother against brother? Why is the Battle of Gettysburg famous? Why is a speech of 272 words about that one battle even more famous? A map can show slavery in the states and territories in 1860.

2Abraham Lincoln ran for president in 1860. The country then had thirty-three states. Slavery was legal in the fifteen Southern states called slave states. It was illegal in the eighteen Northern states called free states. Many enslaved people tried to escape to the North. Lincoln was against letting slavery spread past the Southern states. That stand upset many people in the South. They believed a President Lincoln would in time abolish slavery in every state. Many Southerners earned their money from agriculture. Their huge farms were called plantations. Those farms required a great deal of labor. Plantation owners thought enslaved workers were the best way to fill that need. They thought an end to slavery would destroy their way of life. The Northern economy was different. The South had far fewer factories. Making goods in factories was much more common up north. Those factories did not use enslaved labor. Many people in those states thought slavery should end. Lincoln was elected in 1860. Over the months after the election, eleven slave states announced a break. They were leaving the United States. They formed the Confederate States of America. A map can show that confederacy in 1861. Four slave states did not join it. They were Missouri, Kentucky, Maryland, and Delaware. The eleven that did join can be listed. They were Alabama, Arkansas, North Carolina, and South Carolina. They were Florida, Georgia, Louisiana, and Mississippi. They were Tennessee, Texas, and Virginia. West Virginia formed during the Civil War. It is the only state formed by seceding from a Confederate state. That state was Virginia. March 1861 was the start of Lincoln's time in office. One month after he took office, fighting started between the two sides. Confederate soldiers were called rebels. They were also called Johnny Reb. People who lived in the Southern states fought hard for independence. The Northern states supported Lincoln and the United States. They were called the Union. Their dedication was to hold the country in one piece, so the name Union matched.

3Northern soldiers were nicknamed Yankees. They were also called Yanks. Many Northerners wanted slavery to end. They fought with passion in a war they called the War of Southern Rebellion. Men, and sometimes boys, put on uniforms. Blue was the color for the North. Gray was the color for the South. They left jobs, farms, and families in order to fight. Many thought the war would end quickly. Two years of Lincoln's time as president had passed when Gettysburg was fought. Confederate General Robert E. Lee had won many victories. He had led troops north into Pennsylvania. The route went through Virginia and Maryland. The Union had suffered losses. Even so, Lincoln had kept the nation together. Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, saw more than 93,000 Union soldiers arrive on the march. The Confederates marched more than 71,000. Fighting stopped three days later. Dead soldiers, wounded soldiers, and missing soldiers added up to nearly 51,000. Death or injury came to thirty percent. The Battle of Gettysburg stopped Lee's advance toward the north. Both armies suffered devastation. The town suffered it too. Public buildings were used as hospitals. Private homes were used as hospitals too. Every farm became a graveyard. The war went on for another year and a half. More men died at Gettysburg than in any other battle of the Civil War. Four months after the battle, a cemetery was ready. It was the Soldiers' National Cemetery at Gettysburg. It would be dedicated as the first national cemetery. The date was November 19, 1863. An invitation asked President Lincoln only for a few fitting remarks. He was not the main speaker. The formal speech belonged to Edward Everett. Few speakers of that time were more popular. That speech lasted two hours. The crowd that day already knew Everett well. He had been a congressman of the United States. He had been a senator. He had plenty of practice speaking to an audience. Gettysburg gave him still more practice. He spoke for two hours. That is longer than many movies last today.

4A speech of that length may sound overwhelming to us. It may sound boring. In the 1860s it was common. The crowd applauded. Everett wrote to the president the next day and praised the short speech. He said he would be glad if his own two hours had come as close to the day's central idea as the president's two minutes had. Lincoln wrote back. Word that the speech had not wholly failed left him glad. Days before the event, President Lincoln spoke to a journalist. He said the speech would be short, short, short. He wisely kept his word. Brevity often moves people more strongly than a long, drawn-out speech. Two hours of talking is unnecessary if two minutes will do the job. A modern phrase, less is more, carries the same idea. The power of that brevity cannot be overstated. It is surely part of why people still value the speech. The speech was concise. Lincoln still gave his words careful thought. Witnesses describe him writing on the train to Gettysburg. They describe him writing on the morning of the ceremony. The writing went on until the hour came to leave for the cemetery. A picture shows President Abraham Lincoln in August of 1863. August fell one month after the fighting at Gettysburg. That fighting turned the direction of the war. Not many people saw that until much later. Even four months afterward, few people understood what the battle implied. Confederate leaders treated their loss as a defeat. They did not treat it as a disaster. Weariness with the war had reached some people in the North. They wanted to let the South go. Lincoln could not tell them that victory was close. He knew it was not. On that day at Gettysburg he needed more than a good speech. He needed a great one. The speech had to keep the Union strong. It had to keep the Union in the fight. Today the Gettysburg Address is counted among the most inspiring speeches in American history.

5Lincoln spoke before recording machines existed. No recording can prove his exact words. People reporting from the scene set down the words they had heard. They sent those words by telegraph to newspapers. Five copies written in Lincoln's own hand still exist. Each copy is slightly different from the others. Because the speech was given in 1863, no sound recording survives. Many witnesses and reporters still wrote about how he sounded. They say he spoke loudly. They say he spoke clearly. They also say he spoke slowly and with care. The slow pace may have been for effect. It may have shown how serious and solemn the words were. A short set of remarks may also explain the slow pace. Sickness was already coming over him, as people learned later. The sickness was serious while he gave the address. Most people who saw him that day call his manner fittingly sad. They call it mournful. Lincoln's secretary spoke of his color. The secretary called it ghastly. The secretary called his face haggard. The president spoke of weakness. He spoke of dizziness on the day of the speech. He had felt it the morning before as well. By the time he boarded the train home, he was feverish. He had a severe headache. Doctors later diagnosed smallpox. Of every version of the Gettysburg Address, readers turn most often to the last copy. Lincoln signed that version. He also gave it a title. Those marks are why this copy is reproduced most often. People consider it worth almost half a million dollars. The White House keeps the original paper in a room named for Lincoln. The words of that version can be retold this way. Eighty-seven years earlier, the speakers' fathers had started a new nation on this continent. A score is twenty, so four score and seven names that same count of years. Liberty was the idea in which the nation was conceived. The nation was dedicated to one proposition. The proposition is that all men are created equal. A great civil war was now under way.

6The war was a test. It asked whether a nation born that way could last a long time. It asked the same question of any nation with that birth and that dedication. The crowd had met on a great battlefield of the war. They had come to dedicate a portion of the field. The portion would be a final resting place. It was for the people who had given their lives there. They had done so in order that the nation might live. Doing this was altogether fitting. It was proper. In a larger sense, the living could not dedicate the ground. They could not consecrate it. They could not hallow it. Brave men had struggled there. Some of those men were still living. Some were dead. Those men had already consecrated the ground. Their act stood far above any poor power of the living to add to it. It stood above any power to detract from it. The world would little note the words spoken there. It would not long remember those words. What the soldiers did there could never be forgotten. The task of the living was different. They were to dedicate themselves to work that was still unfinished. The people who fought there had carried that work forward in a noble way. The living were also to take up the great task still ahead. From the honored dead they would draw a deeper devotion. The cause was the one for which those dead had given devotion's last full measure. The living would highly resolve that these dead had not died in vain. The nation, under God, would have a new birth of freedom. A government belonging to the people must not vanish from the earth. The same people must be the ones who run it. It must exist for them. A closer look can take the address idea by idea. Four score and seven years ago is Lincoln's count. Score means twenty, and he uses that count four times. He then adds seven more years.

7The year of the speech was 1863. Eighty-seven years earlier was 1776. That was the year the Declaration of Independence was signed. Lincoln pauses to remind the listeners of the nation's birthday. More important, he reminds them why the nation was born. People were to escape the constraints of an old political system. They were to enjoy the freedom of a new democracy. They were to enjoy its opportunity. When he says our fathers brought forth a new nation, he means the Founding Fathers. Thomas Jefferson was one of them. Lincoln points toward words Jefferson set down in the Declaration of Independence. The line calls certain truths self-evident. One truth is that all men are created equal. Glaring inequality marked how the South treated its people during 1863. Lincoln quietly reminds the audience of a duty. They are to uphold equality. Equality was the cornerstone of the country's founding. He then moves from the past into the present. The painful Civil War, he explains, is a test of the country's values. It is a test of the country's fortitude. The test asks whether the nation truly holds that all men are created equal. It asks whether people ought to be treated as equals. The North had been moving to make this value a political reality. That move put the nation under great strain. The nation was divided unto itself. The crowd stood on a great battlefield of the war. Gettysburg was among the bloodiest battles of the long war. Confederate leaders still showed no sign of giving up. Lincoln knew the war was far from over. The people had come to dedicate a portion of that field. It would be a final resting place. It was for those who gave their lives there so the nation might live. Gettysburg National Cemetery is a final resting place. Union dead from the battle, more than 3,500 of them, rest in that ground. During the 1870s, Confederate dead numbering 3,200 were moved toward the South. They went to cemeteries in the South.

8A few Confederates do remain at Gettysburg. Soldiers from later wars lie there too. Lincoln says the soldiers gave their lives. He does not simply say they died. The wording stresses the sacrifice they made for their country. He was trying to unite mourners from both sides. The reason was the sake of the country. He says it is altogether fitting and proper to do this dedication. First he says it is right to set aside part of the battlefield as a national cemetery. Then he repeats himself in order to make a stronger point. He uses other words for dedicate. Hallow means to honor something as holy. Consecrate means to make something sacred. The president has not changed his mind. He is not deciding that there can be no cemetery. He means the soldiers' deaths have already made the ground sacred. They have made it as special as it can be. He says the world will little note what is said there. He says the world will not long remember those words. He says the world can never forget what the soldiers did. In a way, he is saying that actions speak louder than words. In the second part he changes will to can. That change strengthens the claim. Forgetting the battle of Gettysburg is not even possible. The living, he says, must dedicate themselves on that spot to unfinished work. The people who fought there have so far advanced that work in a noble way. The living must also dedicate themselves to the great task still in front of them. From these honored dead, the living take a greater devotion. The cause is the one for which the dead gave devotion's last full measure. The living make a strong promise. These dead must not have lost life for nothing. Under God, freedom in this nation would begin again. Government of the people must not perish. Government by the people must not perish. Government for the people must not perish from the earth. Lincoln fills his listeners with respect for the fallen soldiers.

9He describes those soldiers as noble. He describes them as honored. Giving their lives is what devotion's last full measure describes. They have nothing further to give. He uses that respect to inspire the listeners. They are to commit again to their nation. They are to commit again to its freedoms. They are to commit again to the great task ahead. That task is winning the war. It is ending slavery. It is saving the United States of America. The speech closes on its most famous idea. A government of the people must not disappear from the earth. It is a government by the people. It is a government for the people. Here Lincoln uses repetition again. This time he does not swap in synonyms. He keeps one phrase and changes only simple prepositions. Listeners are pointed back to one idea. In the United States, government exists for people. A tablet can be seen in a detail of a mural. The mural is Elihu Vedder's work called Government. It dates from 1896. Washington, D.C., keeps the mural inside the Library of Congress. The tablet carries Lincoln's famous phrase. Copies of the Gettysburg Address in Lincoln's handwriting are treasures of the nation today. Carved letters of the speech cover part of the Lincoln Memorial. That memorial stands in Washington, D.C. Visitors draw inspiration from it every day. Even so, no one is certain what the audience thought of the address in 1863. The Lincoln Memorial was designed to resemble a Greek temple. It opened in 1922. Martin Luther King Jr. stood on those steps to speak once another forty-one years had passed. The speech was called I Have a Dream. Leaders as great as Lincoln and King have shown something about America. Words and speeches have power to inspire change. A statue of Abraham Lincoln sits in the memorial's central hall. The statue is 19 feet tall. Stand that same figure up, and the height would be 28 feet. The crowd's reaction to Lincoln's speech was quiet.

10Some say the applause was delayed and scattered. It was barely enough to be polite. One newspaper's editorial spoke against the speech. It called the president's remarks silly and said it would pass over them. For the nation's credit, the editorial wanted a veil of oblivion dropped over those remarks. It wanted the remarks neither repeated nor thought of again. Other accounts describe a hushed scene. They describe a dignified silence. Some historians say there was no applause for a different reason. The audience was deeply impressed by the president's words. In just ten sentences he had summed up the war. He had summed up the spirit of a nation. The battle's importance became clear only as time passed. Respect for Lincoln's speech has grown in the same slow way. People revere the speech today for a clear reason. He kept alive a vision of a nation founded on equality. The nation was also dedicated to equality. He rescued more than the war effort. He rescued the ideal those men died for. Americans have drawn inspiration from that vision ever since. Lincoln was the sixteenth president of the United States. For many people today, he is the most beloved president of all. An address is a formal speech. Oblivion is the state of being completely forgotten or unknown. Brevity is the quality of saying something in few words. It can also mean lasting only a short time. To perish is to die. The death is often sudden, violent, or unexpected. Conceived means thought of, or imagined. A proposition is an idea to be considered, explored, or proved. Concise describes wording that uses as few words as possible. It means brief. To revere is to respect someone or something deeply. It is to hold that person or thing in high esteem. Constraints are limits on actions or ideas. They are the state of being restricted. Secession is the act of formally leaving a government or another organization. Devastation is great damage or destruction. Fortitude is strength. It is endurance.

46. Living and Working Far Above Earth

1Astronaut Robert L. Curbeam Jr. smiles for the camera. He is aboard the International Space Station. The smile comes after a successful space walk. This book tells about weightless living. It tells about the race to space. It tells about space stations. It tells about an astronaut's life. It tells about sleeping. It tells about eating. It tells about using the toilet. It tells about bathing and cleaning teeth. It tells about free time. It tells about exercise. It tells about the return to Earth. Word meanings come last. Sunrise is the moment you wake. Earth spreads outside a small window. It is a bright blue sphere. It takes a moment to get free of the sleeping bag. The space around you is small. You open the door. You grab a handle. You flip yourself over. A gentle push sends you flying. The push carries you across the room. Another crew member floats by. The crew member hands you a packet of coffee. The greeting is good morning, spoken in Russian. You thank the crew member. You yawn. You are tired because you have not slept much. Your stomach has not adjusted yet. The cause is the lack of gravity. You are also incredibly excited. A space shuttle is shown docking with the International Space Station. You are about to begin your first full day of work aboard that station.

2You have trained for years. Even simple activities are complicated without gravity. Eating is one of them. Bathing is one of them. Going to the bathroom is one of them. It is almost as if you must learn them all over again. The transport back to Earth is not coming for another six months. Starting now is the sensible choice. The race toward space took off in the 1950s and the 1960s. The first person in space was a cosmonaut from Russia. His name was Yuri Gagarin. Russia was then part of the Soviet Union. He orbited Earth once. He landed safely after 108 minutes. The day was April 12, 1961. In August of that same year, another Soviet cosmonaut flew. His name was Gherman Titov. He orbited Earth more than 17 times. The flight lasted about 25 hours. Technology advanced quickly. People could go farther. They could stay longer. In 1968, United States astronauts aboard Apollo 8 orbited the Moon. The flight was a success. Apollo 11's crew set foot on the Moon on July 20, 1969. Technology kept advancing. Space programs built vehicles that let people stay in space for days. Some stays lasted weeks. Scientists were also working on something more lasting. They wanted a structure in space where people could live for months.
