3They wanted stays that could last years. The Soyuz spacecraft were first created in the 1960s. They are still used to carry people to the International Space Station. They also carry people home. 1971 was the year the Soviet Union sent up the first space station. It was called Salyut 1. Three cosmonauts stayed aboard for three weeks. It spent 175 days in space. Then it fell out of orbit. It burned up while reentering Earth's atmosphere. Skylab went up from the United States in 1973. Skylab supported three missions. It was abandoned in 1974. Its fall back to Earth came in 1979. A picture shows a space shuttle docking with Mir. Mir's first piece went up in 1986 from the Soviet Union. Mir is said MEER. Only then did a space station keep working for more than a few years. Fifteen years was how long Mir circled Earth. That was three times longer than first planned. It hosted scientists from many different countries. Russian scientist Dr. Valeri Polyakov spent 438 days in space in a row. The stay covered 1994 and 1995. He lived on Mir during that record stay. He orbited Earth 7,075 times. His record still stands. Work on a newer station was already underway before Mir's 2001 fall.

4The new station would be larger. Countries from all over the world worked together. The United States was one. Russia was one. Japan was one. Canada was one. Orbit received the station's first section in 1998. People call the station the ISS. Later years brought more sections. Future plans call for still more sections. By 2012 its length was 357 feet. That length is 108.8 meters. It weighed almost 1 million pounds. That weight is 453,592.3 kilograms. It is the largest human-made object in space. People can see it in the night sky. They do not need a telescope. People have stayed on the ISS without a break since November 2, 2000. Over the years, more than 240 people have visited. They came from nineteen countries. The station has more living space than the average house with five bedrooms. The time an astronaut spends there varies. Many stay for about three to six months. That can mean six months of living without gravity. It means six months of working without gravity. The space is enclosed. Three to six other people share it. Crew members might come from different countries. They might speak different languages. They still have to work together as a team. This can be extremely stressful for the mind. It can be extremely stressful for the body.

5An astronaut practices a repair on an underwater model of the ISS. Space walks are practiced ahead of time by working underwater. Astronauts attend school for many years before training begins. They often earn the highest degree in their field. Physical training includes a special airplane flight. The flight simulates weightlessness. A space suit can be on them for as long as seven hours. They work underwater in a huge pool. The pool holds 6.2 million gallons. That volume is 23.5 million liters. They work on life-size models of space vehicles. Once they are on the ISS, they still must adjust. Life there is completely weightless. When astronauts first arrive, bodies need time to adjust. Minds need time too. Illness hits some people because of the change. The ISS comes with special bags for that purpose. One side of the bag is cloth for wiping up. An extra bag is attached. That bag can be sealed for easy disposal. Without gravity, astronauts cannot jump into bed. They cannot curl up under a pile of blankets. The ISS has six small sleep pods instead. Each pod contains a sleeping bag with armholes. Each bag is tied securely to the wall. The tie keeps the astronaut from floating away while asleep. The lack of gravity often causes a certain kind of dream.

6Astronauts dream of falling. Because of the station's orbit, the crew sees many sunrises. They see many sunsets. The number is sixteen of each every day. Night is the usual time for people to sleep. They are used to being awake during the day. The extra sunrises and sunsets can cause serious sleep problems. The station has a shades-down period. During that time it is dark. It is quiet. The quiet dark lets the astronauts get the sleep they need. A picture shows astronaut Alvin Drew getting ready to sleep on the ISS. Another picture shows breakfast on the station. The meal is eggs and sausage on a tortilla. Coffee is part of it. Early astronauts ate gels. They ate pastes. They ate freeze-dried food. The food had the nutrition they needed. It did not taste very good. Today astronauts eat many foods that most people enjoy. Chicken is one. Fruits are one. Peanut butter is one. Brownies are one. The ISS has no refrigerator. All food must be packaged so it will not spoil. An oven is available on the station. Some food can be eaten as it is. Peanut butter is an example. Other food needs water added. Spaghetti is an example. Salt comes in liquid form. Pepper comes in liquid form too.

7Dry particles would float away. They could damage the delicate equipment. Once the food is ready, swallowing still feels strange. Astronaut Piers Sellers compared it to eating while lying on one side. Things float around in space. The bathroom is not simple to use. Toilet use takes special training for astronauts. Two parts make up each ISS toilet. A tube with a nozzle handles liquid waste. For solid waste, they must stay in place. Foot straps help. Handles help. They position themselves over an opening that is 4 inches wide. That width is 10 centimeters. An average toilet on Earth has a much wider opening. The opening is 12 to 16 inches. That is 30.5 to 40.6 centimeters. The space toilet uses light suction. The suction moves the waste from the opening or the tube. The waste goes to storage in another part of the station. Liquid waste goes into a tube on the wall. Solid waste goes into a base set on the floor. The ISS has two toilets. They have stopped working more than once. Earth has to send the parts before a toilet can be fixed. Those parts can take months to arrive. Hair washing on the ISS is demonstrated by astronaut Karen Nyberg. Astronauts wash their bodies with water and special soap on a cloth.

8The hair shampoo they use needs no water. They clean their teeth with toothpaste they can swallow when they finish. Earlier stations had an actual shower. Skylab was one of them. An enclosed space was where those astronauts stepped in. A tube squirted water. Soap and a cloth were used for the wash. A second tube pulled the dirty water away. Free time is very scarce for astronauts on the ISS. They still find ways to entertain themselves. They might play cards. They might read. They might write. They do other things too. Keeping in touch with loved ones is important. Astronauts can make calls. They can use video chat. Sometimes they hold live video chats. Questions from students worldwide are answered by the crew. They give tours of the station. When they have nothing else to do, many simply look out the windows. They take photos. The view is pretty amazing. It is hard to blame them for looking. A guitar is played on the ISS by astronaut Chris Hadfield. During his last visit he even made a music video. For astronauts, exercise matters a huge amount. On Earth, bones and muscles must work against gravity during exercise. That work makes them stronger. In space there is almost no gravity. It takes very little strength to move things.

9Those same things might be extremely heavy on Earth. It takes very little effort. Because movement is so easy, bones weaken over time. Muscles weaken too. Daily workouts are required if the decline is to slow. The workout lasts at least two hours. The ISS gym has special equipment. Straps on a treadmill tug the runners downward. Other equipment uses resistance. The resistance helps them stay strong. Most astronauts still lose muscle after that hard daily workout. Muscle mass drops by 20 to 30 percent. The loss comes during a six-month stay. A picture shows astronaut Sunita Williams. She exercises on a treadmill on the ISS. Coming home from the ISS does not end the work. Recovery from a long time in space takes a long time. A six-month stay calls for about six weeks of rehabilitation. The goal is to regain lost muscle. Bones can take a whole year to fully recover. Astronauts must endure hard work. They must endure inconvenience. They still know the time in space is worth it. They know the work there is worth it. A 2021 picture shows Japanese astronaut Soichi Noguchi with his thumb up. He has just returned to Earth. His spacecraft home was a Crew Dragon capsule. During the time in space, scientists monitor the astronauts.

10They monitor them during rehabilitation too. They watch physical health. They watch mental health. The information has already helped astronauts live healthier lives. It has helped them live happier lives. We are looking farther into space. Some places may take months to reach. Some may take years. Some may take decades. This vital information might mean success for future exploration. It might also mean failure for future space exploration. These words have special meanings in this book. Astronauts train for travel and work off Earth. Orbited means revolved around another object. A cosmonaut is trained for space travel and space work. The word is Russian for astronaut. Rehabilitation is the process of restoring health or normal activity. Gravity is the natural force that pulls objects toward each other. One example is the pull toward the center of Earth. Resistance is a force that slows motion. Simulating means modeling or imitating how something looks or what condition it is in. A space station is a spacecraft where people can live for a long time. It is used for scientific research. Grueling means extremely difficult. It means exhausting. Launched means used force to start something moving. Technology means using science or tools to make things or get work done. Operational means a thing is ready to work.

47. Lost Ships and Sea Secrets

1A map of lost ships marks North America, Europe, and Africa. It also marks the Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean. The numbered wrecks are Antikythera, HMS Victory, and Mary Celeste. They also include HMS Erebus, HMS Terror, and SS Valencia. USS Cyclops and SS Edmund Fitzgerald complete the list. The map key shows three kinds of marks. One mark is the place of a wreck. One mark is the last known place of a missing ship. One mark is a sighting of a ghost ship. The parts of this book come in this order. First is Marine Mysteries, Lost and Found. Then come Mystery of Antiquity and Long Lost Victory. Next is Ghost Ship: Mary Celeste. Then comes the long hunt for HMS Erebus and HMS Terror. Terror on the Rocks tells about SS Valencia. Gone Without a Trace tells about USS Cyclops. There and Gone tells about SS Edmund Fitzgerald. The Sea Keeps Many Secrets comes near the end. A glossary closes the book. Marine Mysteries, Lost and Found The United Nations estimates a huge number of shipwrecks. More than three million wrecks litter the world's coastlines and seafloors. Marine archaeologists study some of those wrecks. Some wrecks are hundreds of years old. Some are thousands of years old. Treasure hunters search for other wrecks. They hope for riches that stories say sank with the ships. In some cases, ships have simply vanished. They left no clues that might suggest what happened. A picture shows a wreck on the bottom of the Red Sea in Jordan. Every shipwreck holds some kind of mystery. People ask what the ship was carrying. They ask where the wreck ended up. They ask what happened to the people on board. The mystery that grabs curiosity the most is another question. What really sent the ship to its doom?

2Stories of shipwrecks are often dramatic. They tell of danger, death, sunken treasure, and intrigue. Clues can help people solve mysteries. In most cases, though, the sea hides the clues. It may hide them for years. Sometimes it hides them forever. Mystery of Antiquity In 1900, divers found a shipwreck near the Greek island of Antikythera. The name is said an-ti-ki-THEER-uh. They had not even been looking for it. Shifting sands partly buried the wreck. It lay 55 meters (180 ft.) beneath the surface. No one knew how the ship got there. Greek archaeologists soon saw a more interesting question. They asked when it got there. A picture shows a diver recovering a bronze spear from the wreck. People think the spear was part of a large statue. The Richest Wreck A British warship sank the Spanish galleon San José in 1708. Gold went down with the ship. Emeralds went down too. Those riches were meant to pay for Spain's war against Great Britain. For three hundred years, no one knew where the wreck lay. The mystery lasted until recent years. Searchers located it in 2015 off the coast of Colombia. Spain and Colombia have long disputed who owns the wreck and its treasures. Estimates put the worth of the cargo as high as $17 billion. That amount places the wreck among the world's most valuable. A picture shows a piece of the world's oldest computer. The device is known as the Antikythera Mechanism. It is displayed in a museum in Athens. As divers brought artifacts to the surface, researchers began to fit a historical puzzle together. The ship was ancient. It was more than two thousand years old. It had been loaded with an amazing hoard of art. Luxury goods were on board too. One item has been described as the earliest known computer.

3It was a mechanical device. Gears inside it calculated the precise positions of the stars and the planets. It may have been used for navigation. More than 120 years after the wreck was found, research teams are still diving on it. They are still studying it. A painting by Thomas Butterworth shows HMS Victory sailing through rough seas. Long Lost Victory HMS Victory was the finest ship in the formidable navy of Great Britain. The ship was launched in 1737. It was armed with 110 cannons. That armament made it the biggest military monster of its time. Early in October 1744, Victory led its fleet on the return to Britain. A fierce storm caught them in the English Channel. The Victory became separated from the other ships. The great warship disappeared. Some 1,150 people disappeared with it. On that fateful night, people on nearby islands heard a steady booming of cannons. The sound was a maritime cry for help. The seas were far too treacherous for any rescue attempt. A picture shows a bronze cannon and other artifacts from HMS Victory. A salvage company discovered them. Days later, some wreckage from the vessel washed ashore. Some wreckage reached the rocky islands where people had heard those calls for help. The main body of the ship was nowhere to be found. That main body was the hull and the decking. It was as though the storm had swallowed the ship. The loss of such a massive ship baffled investigators. The puzzle lasted more than 250 years. Modern technology helped solve the mystery of the final resting place. A marine salvage company searched across a wide area in 2008. The search used sonar and other advanced equipment. The remains lay 100 kilometers (62 mi.) from the place where people first thought the ship had sunk.

4The salvage company and the British government worked together. They retrieved valuables from the wreck. HMS Victory is the name of the oldest naval ship still in commission today. Ghost Ship: Mary Celeste Not every lost ship ends on the bottom of the sea. Some meet a fate that is even more mysterious. The Mary Celeste is one example. The cargo ship left New York City, in the United States, on November 7, 1872. It was bound for Genoa, Italy. The vessel was 30.1 meters (100 ft.) long. It had a crew of seven. Captain Benjamin Briggs was also on board. His wife, Sarah, was with him. Their daughter, Sophia, was two years old. An 1861 illustration shows Mary Celeste entering the port of Marseille, France. A month after that, a vessel was spotted by the British ship Dei Gratia. The vessel was drifting in the Atlantic Ocean. It was the Mary Celeste. A boarding party found no one on the ship. A lifeboat was missing. The ship's navigation equipment was missing too. There were no signs of violence. The crew's personal gear was stowed. All the cargo was still in the hold. The last entry in the captain's log showed nothing wrong. Captain Briggs was never seen again. His family was never seen again. The crew was never heard from again. Investigators later examined the Mary Celeste. They found few clues. They could not tell why a seasoned crew would leave a seaworthy ship. Even so, some unknown cause seems to have pushed them away from Mary Celeste. The intrigue has led to many made-up accounts of the mystery. Those stories usually feature rebel crew members. They feature murder. They even feature sea monsters. The Fraidy-Cat of Empress of Ireland People regarded Emmy as the cat of the Empress of Ireland.

5Emmy ran away from the passenger ship on the day before it left Canada. People carried her back aboard. She escaped again. People read her actions as a sign of coming trouble. On the following day, another ship was struck by the Empress of Ireland. It sank in just fourteen minutes. More than one thousand people died. The sinking is the deadliest wreck in Canadian history. A painting by François Etienne Musin shows HMS Erebus stuck in the ice. The Long Hunt for HMS Erebus and HMS Terror In 1845 the British navy mounted the Franklin Expedition. The goal was to search for the Northwest Passage. People hoped this new route across the Arctic Ocean would be a shortcut. The shortcut would help shipping between Europe and Asia. The expedition was named for its commander, Sir John Franklin. It included 129 people. The ships carried three years' worth of supplies. There were two ships, HMS Terror and HMS Erebus. The pair had been designed as sturdy warships. They had been refitted for the fearsome conditions of Arctic exploration. Two whaling ships saw Terror and Erebus on July 26, 1845. The sighting was in Canada's Baffin Bay. A year passed with no word from Franklin. Then two years passed. Officials feared for the safety of the explorers. The public feared for them too. What had really happened went beyond their fears. Search and rescue ships slowly found abandoned gear. They found graves. They found notes that desperate crew members had left on islands where no one lived. Pack ice had closed around both ships in September 1846. Sir Franklin died the following June. For two years the sailors waited. They were sick and dying. They waited in vain for the ice to let the ships go.

6Finally, in April 1848, the survivors tried a desperate hike. They headed south to reach the Canadian mainland. Local Inuit, in 1855, described a group of Europeans to investigators. Those Europeans had starved to death along the coast. Evidence showed that the group had turned to cannibalism. They did it to try to survive. The doomed expedition has never stopped fascinating adventurers. Sonar on a ship located the wreck of Erebus in 2014. The wreck was well preserved. It lay in 12 meters (40 ft.) of frigid Arctic water. Its partner ship stayed missing until September 2016. Then the preserved remains of HMS Terror were found. The remains rested on the bay floor off King William Island. A picture shows a diver exploring the remains of the Erebus. Terror on the Rocks: SS Valencia Few shipwrecks were more terrifying than the SS Valencia. The passenger steamer left San Francisco for Seattle in January 1906. It had 173 people on board. Its iron hull struck the ground near midnight on January 22. The grounding was near Vancouver Island. Pounding waves trapped the ship. Escape was nearly impossible. The crew lowered lifeboats. Most of the boats flipped in the churning seas. A boat that flips in this way has capsized. People were tossed into freezing water. They drowned there. High winds hampered rescue efforts. High waves hampered them too. About thirty-six hours after the stranding, people on shore watched in horror. A huge wave swept over the upper deck. Dozens of passengers there were holding on for their lives. In total, only 37 of 136 passengers survived. A picture shows a Valencia lifeboat escaping the violent seas. The boat carries some of the few survivors. Another picture shows Valencia leaving San Francisco. That departure was eight years before the tragic sinking.

7How, why, and where were not the mysteries of this wreck. Investigations concluded that the captain had made bad decisions. The crew had made bad decisions too. Those decisions put the ship and its passengers in danger. Most of the mysteries came later. They inspired tales of the supernatural. In 1910, for example, newspapers reported a strange sight. Sailors said they had seen a ghostly Valencia sailing near the wreck site. A rumor also spread about a lifeboat. The story said the boat held eight skeletons and was found in a nearby cave. The story was never confirmed. In 1933, a lifeboat from Valencia seemed to arrive out of earlier years. That was twenty-seven years after the disaster. The boat was discovered in a nearby bay. British Columbia's Maritime Museum now shows the boat's nameplate. Gone Without a Trace: USS Cyclops The USS Cyclops was a supply ship of the U.S. Navy. In Brazil, during World War I, the crew took on a load of heavy ore. While there, Captain W. Worley reported to his superiors. He said one of the engines needed repairs. That engine was not operational. The order was to repair it after arrival in the United States. On February 22, 1918, the ship left Brazil. It had a crew of 309. The Cyclops disappeared somewhere in the Atlantic Ocean. Not one piece of wreckage has ever been found. At the time, people guessed that a German submarine had sunk the ship. Some naval officials wondered about Captain Worley. He had been born in Germany. They wondered if he had secretly handed the ship over to the enemy. There was no proof of that. The loss of USS Cyclops remains the largest loss of life in U.S. naval history in an event not tied directly to combat.

8A picture shows the ship. Some ships have been sunk on purpose in the Bermuda Triangle. The goal is to create artificial reefs. Those reefs promote sea life in the area. Another theory notes where the Cyclops vanished. It disappeared in the Bermuda Triangle. That area of the Atlantic Ocean has a reputation for swallowing ships. Most naval experts think more than one problem was at work. The ship lacked full engine power. It was also overloaded and unstable. They say a violent storm on March 10 may have caught the ship. That storm could have sent the ship to the ocean floor. The Bermuda Triangle An area of the Atlantic Ocean is known as the Bermuda Triangle. Bermuda, Puerto Rico, and the tip of Florida roughly set its three corners. A map of the area also shows the United States and the Caribbean Islands. According to legend, a high number of ships and aircraft vanish there without explanation. Those stories lead to rumors of supernatural powers. The rumors say those powers sink ships or snatch them. Researchers have determined something different. Ship disappearances are not more common there than in other busy routes for shipping. There and Gone: SS Edmund Fitzgerald The SS Edmund Fitzgerald was a huge freighter. On November 9, 1975, the ship left Superior, Wisconsin. It was fully loaded with iron ore. Ernest McSorley was the captain. A storm was forecast. The veteran captain was not concerned. On the afternoon of November 10, the U.S. Coast Guard sent a warning. It told all ships to seek shelter. Whitefish Bay, Wisconsin, was the place the Edmund Fitzgerald aimed for. Around 7:00 p.m., McSorley said water was coming into the ship. He radioed, "We are holding our own." From bow to stern, the Edmund Fitzgerald measured over 213 meters (700 ft.).

9It was the largest vessel ever built for the Great Lakes. It was also the longest. A picture shows Coast Guard officers looking at life rings recovered from the wreck. A short time after that report, the freighter vanished. The ship dropped off the radar screen. No lifeboats were launched. Searchers found none of the twenty-nine people in the crew. Within a few days, the Coast Guard found the wreck on the bottom of the lake. The freighter had broken into two parts. A run of three rogue waves is what investigators think may have sent the ship down. The ship went down so fast that no distress call could be sent. Rogue Waves Researchers suspect rogue waves in some shipping disasters that have no clear explanation. These waves are dangerous because they cannot be predicted. They are also dangerous because of their size. They are dangerous because of their power. A rogue wave comes out of nowhere. It is much bigger than the waves around it. A powerful mix of strong water currents and high winds creates it. This usually happens far out at sea. A sharp rise in wave height can turn big freighters over. The Slave Wrecks Project Between the 16th and 19th centuries, many ships that carried enslaved people were lost at sea. The number may have been as high as 1,000. Most of those shipwrecks remain undiscovered today. They also remain undocumented. Organizations are working to find those lost ships. They also want the historical information the ships contain. The Slave Wrecks Project is one such group. It was founded in 2008. In 2014 the project made its first major recovery. The sunken ship is called the São José. It lies near the coast of Cape Town, South Africa. The Sea Keeps Many Secrets Sailing the seas has always held an element of danger.

10The oceans stretch across vast distances. Weather can turn treacherous in a sudden way. Threatening reefs hide along coastlines. Rocks hide there too. Modern equipment makes shipping safer than ever. Even so, dozens of shipwrecks still take lives. About two thousand people die in them every year. Working on a ship remains one of the most dangerous jobs in the world. Sailors trust their lives to their knowledge. They trust their skills. They trust the ships they serve on. Sometimes their fate comes down to luck. Every shipwreck leaves mysteries behind. Some of these mysteries can be explored. They can eventually be explained. Older wrecks may give us a glimpse into the past. Often, however, these secrets stay hidden in the ocean. Glossary Aground means on or onto the shore, or on the bottom of a body of water. Maritime means of or about the sea, sailing, or activities done on the sea. Artifacts are objects that humans made or used long ago. Navigation is the act of steering a course toward a destination. Capsized means turned over in the water so that the bottom or a side faced up. Salvage is property saved from damage or destruction. The word also means the recovery of a wrecked ship or its cargo. A fleet is a group of ships or vehicles traveling together under the same command. Seaworthy means safe or ready for travel on the sea. A hull is a ship or boat's main body, taking in the bottom, the sides, and the deck. Shipwrecks are ships that have sunk or been destroyed. Investigators examine details carefully so they can find out the facts. Supernatural describes something that science or the laws of nature cannot explain.

48. Mexico from Shore to Highland

1North America’s southern lands include the country of Mexico. The United States stands on its northern side. Central America stands on its southern side. A shared border runs between Mexico and the United States. Guatemala shares a southern border with Mexico. Belize shares a southern border with Mexico too. Some islands belong to Mexico. Those islands sit along the western coast. Other islands sit along the eastern coast. West of the mainland is the Pacific Ocean. East of the mainland is the Gulf of Mexico. A second gulf lies between the main body of land and a long, fingerlike stretch. That second gulf is called the Gulf of California. That stretch juts out from the northwest coast. It is called the Baja Peninsula. A map of the region also marks the Yucatán Peninsula. Mexico City is marked as well. Honduras appears on the wider map. El Salvador appears there too. South America appears beyond the southern neighbors. Mexico City’s center holds the Metropolitan Cathedral. Builders began the cathedral in the late 1500s. Few cities in North America are older than Mexico City. It is Mexico’s capital. More than nineteen million people live in it. Mountains ring the basin where the city rests. A lake bed once covered the ground under the city.

2That lake was drained so building could go forward. Old structures and new ones stand side by side. The mix gives the city both a historic face and a modern one. Hundreds of buildings fill the center. The oldest among them come from the 1500s. Floating gardens are part of the city. They are islands people made, not islands nature made. The Aztecs, an ancient Indigenous people, built those islands. Corn was one crop grown on them. Beans were another. Beautiful parks also fill Mexico City. Alameda Park is the oldest of them. Its creation dates to 1592. Chapultepec Park is the largest. Fountains are found there. Museums are found there. A zoo is found there. Lakes are found there. For thousands of years, thriving Indigenous civilizations lived on land that is now Mexico. Spanish explorers colonized Mexico in 1521. About two thirds of the people descend from both Indigenous ancestors and European ancestors. Mestizos is the name for these people. Latin America has few Indigenous populations more diverse than Mexico’s. Indigenous groups still form about one sixth of the population. The country now holds more than 120 million people. Spanish is the language most Mexicans speak. No other country has more Spanish speakers. Indigenous languages are spoken by some people.

3Náhuatl, said NAH-wah-tuhl, is one of those languages. Three fourths of the people in Mexico, plus still more, live in cities. Art in Mexico reaches far back and runs deep. Stunning art was made by ancient Indigenous peoples. Temples and other buildings wore that art. In the middle of a Mexico City museum stands a god carved long ago by the Aztec. Painting, sculpture, and architecture still carry older traditions forward through modern artists. The mural ranks among Mexico’s best-known art forms. Beautiful jewelry was also made by ancient Indigenous peoples of Mexico. Gemstones went into that jewelry. Precious metals went into it too. The craft of making jewelry has lasted into modern times. Mexico leads the world at producing silver. Many jewelry artisans today shape that precious metal. Sports in Mexico have a long history, and the history is a serious one. People today use a short name for one of Mexico’s oldest sports. They call it the ball game. The invention dates back over two thousand years. Stone courts used for the game still stand in some places. Soccer draws crowds in Mexico today. Baseball draws crowds too. Fronton draws crowds too. Fronton resembles handball. A Mexican soccer player is shown getting ready to put the ball in the goal.

4Mexico’s land is full of geographic contrasts. Mountains rise here. Canyons cut here. Deserts spread here. Rainforests grow here. There is mainland. There are islands. The west holds mountain ranges. The east holds mountain ranges. The south holds mountain ranges. An unstable zone called the Ring of Fire runs along Mexico’s edge. Volcanoes make up some of its mountains. The country’s highest mountain is itself a volcano. It reaches 5,700 meters. That height is 18,701 feet. Terrible disasters can follow earthquakes around the Ring of Fire. September 1985 brought an earthquake to Mexico City. More than nine thousand people died. Eruptions came from volcanoes in the 1990s. Eruptions came again in the 2000s. A landform map names the Sonoran Desert. It names Copper Canyon. It names the Chihuahuan Desert. It names the Baja Peninsula. It names the Sierra Madre Oriental Mountains. It names the Gulf of California. It names the Mexican Plateau. It names the Gulf of Mexico. It names the Yucatán Peninsula. It names the Pacific Ocean. It names Mexico City. It names Pico de Orizaba. It names the Sierra Madre del Sur Mountains. Canyons and gorges cut the other way from the mountains. They slice deep into Earth’s crust. Copper Canyon, in northern Mexico, is known as larger than the Grand Canyon.

5Depth in places reaches 1,400 meters. That depth is 4,600 feet. Northern Mexico is crossed by the Sonoran Desert. The Chihuahuan Desert crosses it too. Native vegetation in the Sonoran Desert comes in more types than in any other desert of North America. The count is about two thousand species. California would fit inside the Chihuahuan Desert. No North American desert covers more ground. Dry weather marks the north. Wet weather marks the southeast. Thousands of animal species live in the rainforests there. Thousands of plant species live there too. East of the mainland coast, two islands rise from the sea. One island is Cozumel. The other is Isla Mujeres, said EES-lah moo-HAIR-es. Bright tropical fish, full of color, live in the ocean around both islands. Two peninsulas push into the oceans on Mexico’s two sides. The Baja is one. The Yucatán is the other. Limestone forms the Yucatán Peninsula. Over thousands of years, that limestone has dissolved in places. Water-filled caves are the result. The caves are called cenotes, said sih-NOH-teez. The first people on this land were Indigenous. Advanced civilizations grew among several groups. The Maya were one group. The Aztec were another. Great cities rose under them.

6Beautiful works of art were made. Their calendar was accurate. It showed when crops should be planted. The Maya are the people who developed that calendar. About 700 years ago, Aztec people reached central Mexico. Lake Texcoco held an island, and the capital stood there. The capital’s name was Tenochtitlán, said tay-nohch-teet-LAHN. Water entered the city by aqueducts. Aqueducts are waterways. Canals joined every part of the city. By 1519 the Aztec empire was huge. Five to six million people lived in it. Life, the Aztec believed, was the most precious thing a person had. To their gods, a human life was the gift with the deepest meaning. People were sacrificed to those gods because of this belief. Experts think the sacrifices may have numbered in the thousands each year. Hernan Cortes, a Spanish explorer, reached Tenochtitlán in 1519. Within two years, Aztec enemies joined the Spaniards. Together those forces conquered the Aztec. Mexico became a colony of Spain in 1521. Conquerors arrived in Mexico in the 1500s. Spanish calls them conquistadores, said kohn-kees-tah-DOH-res. Smallpox came with them. Measles came with them. Indigenous peoples had never met these diseases. The effect was devastating. Scientists think about twenty million people lived in Mexico when Spain conquered it. By 1600, barely one million people remained.

7Spanish rule lasted the next few hundred years. Independence from Spain came in 1821. Years of war led to that win. Fair treatment did not reach every Mexican person just because the country was free. Farming was the work of most people. Farmers held hardly any of the land. Poverty was the condition of almost all farmers. Rights for them were few. Improvement began with the Mexican Revolution. The years of that revolution were 1910 to 1920. Mexico today is a democracy. Life has improved for many people. Two main social classes still divide the country in a general way. The rich form one class. The poor form the other. Pancho Villa led in the Mexican Revolution. Emiliano Zapata led as well. Villa is pictured on the left. Zapata stands to Villa’s right. Tourists from around the world favor Mexico as a place to travel. Ancient ruins let a visitor walk back through the history of Mexico. The best-known Mayan ruin is Chichén Itzá, said chee-CHEN eet-SAH. Southeastern Mexico is where it stands. Two large cenotes mark the site where Chichén Itzá was built. Religious offerings were thrown into those cenotes. Precious gems were among the offerings. Metals were among them too. The gifts honored the Mayan god of rain.

8Building of the city began around the 500s. A finished city held an observatory for studying stars and planets. It held a ball court. It held temples. It held a pyramid now called El Castillo. El Castillo, also called the Castle, rises 24 meters. That height is 79 feet. Ninety-one steps run up each of the four sides. Added up, the steps come to 364. A full orbit of Earth around the Sun is counted here as 364 days. The Maya had already left Chichén Itzá by the time the Spanish reached Mexico. Jungle hid the city across the three hundred years that followed. People found the city again in the 1800s and began to study it. Another name for El Castillo is the Pyramid of Kukulkán. The Maya knew this snake god by that same name. Palenque, said pah-LEN-keh, is a Mayan ruin that looks over the jungle around it. A mountain forest is its setting. Toucans are among the wildlife that live in that forest. Monkeys live there too. Architecture at Palenque is remarkable. Sculpture there is remarkable. Wall carvings there are remarkable. Tombs of ancient rulers are there. A water system is there as well. Scientists learned the city’s history from writing cut into tombs and into buildings.

9Carved symbols helped too. Teotihuacan, said tay-oh-tee-wah-KAHN, stands near Mexico City. Scientists do not know where its people lived before the city was built. They do know the city ranked among the world’s largest at the time of building. Two main pyramids rise at Teotihuacan. The larger pyramid carries the name Pyramid of the Sun. Its pair, called the Pyramid of the Moon, does not rise as high. Great temples stand in the city. Palaces stand there. Apartment complexes stand there too. Study of the site shows a practice shared with the Aztec and the Maya. The builders sacrificed people to their gods. Visitors notice the Sun pyramid before any other feature at the site. Across Mexico, many people enjoy folk dancing as a pastime. Traditional clothing is often what the dancers wear. Mexico’s story moves from Native civilizations to conquest by Spain. It moves on through revolution and into democracy. The history is rich. Artistic traditions tell that long, fascinating story. Ancient ruins tell it too. Geographic contrasts mark the land as well. Desert is here. Rainforest is here. Mountain is here. Canyon is here. All of them belong to this amazing country. The population count is 127,575,529. Land covers 1,964,375 square kilometers. That area equals 758,450 square miles.

10Mexico City is the capital. Spanish is the primary language. Roman Catholic is the primary religion. The currency is the peso, said PAY-soh. Figures come from the Central Intelligence Agency for 2019 and from the World Bank. An aqueduct is a channel people built so water can travel from one place to another. An artisan is a person with skill in a craft or a trade. A basin is a low spot, a depression, in Earth’s surface. A cenote is a deep well made by nature. It appears when limestone at the surface falls in and groundwater shows. Conquistadores is Spanish for conquerors. They seized land for Spain during the sixteenth century in both North America and South America. A gorge is a long, deep valley with higher land around it. Indigenous describes what is native to a given region. A mestizo is a person whose ancestors are both European and Indigenous. A mural is a large artwork, usually painted, made right on a wall. A peninsula is a long arm of land with water around nearly all of it. The Ring of Fire borders the Pacific Ocean. Active volcanoes and frequent earthquakes mark that region. Ruins are what remains after something has been destroyed.

49. Objects That Travel Around Other Objects

1Eight planets travel around the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Each of those planets is a satellite. Any object in space that travels around another object is a satellite. Orbiting means revolving around that other object. Two kinds exist. One kind is natural. The other is made by people, and that kind is called artificial. The Moon is natural, and it revolves around Earth. The Sun is orbited by every planet in our solar system, so each planet is a natural satellite. Humans build the artificial kind. The pages ahead explain what satellites are, how they are built, and the paths they follow. They show the work satellites do, the first ones ever launched, the International Space Station, rescues, and what happens when a satellite's life ends. A word list closes the book. A picture of our solar system puts the Sun in the middle and the eight planets around it. The Moon travels with Earth. Natural satellites were already moving through space before any person built one. Artificial satellites came later, shaped for work people needed done. This book stays with both kinds. It explains an orbit. It looks at the parts of a machine above Earth. It follows the paths those machines take. It describes their jobs, from carrying messages to watching weather to looking far outward. It tells how the earliest ones left the ground. It visits the station where crews live in orbit. It tells how a damaged satellite can be reached, and how an old one at last comes down. Tools of high technology, built by people, circle Earth. They work like robots in space, taking on jobs people cannot do. We often forget they are there. Even so, they have mattered in daily life ever since Sputnik I went up in 1957. Cell phones depend on them. So does the choice of TV programs from hundreds of channels, both at home and from other countries.

2Ship captains use them to find a route. Meteorologists use them to forecast where a dangerous storm will go. Thousands now circle Earth. Space probes are similar, though their usual targets are other planets, moons, or asteroids inside our solar system. The far reaches of space are within reach of some probes. Valuable information comes back from them. A drawing places Saturn, Earth, Jupiter, and Mars near a probe, and the drawing is not to scale. Builders shape each satellite for one kind of job. From the outside, the shape may recall a barrel. It may instead recall a windmill. Paddles may stick out from it. Solar panels may too, or sails. Inside sit scientific instruments chosen for that mission. The payload is the set of tools the satellite needs, such as sensitive antennas, cameras that show fine detail, and electronics for communication. Carrying the payload is the bus's job. It holds the pieces together. Computers get electrical power from the bus. Communication gear gets power from it too. So does the push that moves the satellite forward. Energy from the Sun runs the equipment. Solar cells can cover the flaps, the wings, the panels, or the outer shell. Those cells turn the Sun's energy into electricity. No satellite ever pays an electric bill. A satellite can turn gathered information into a radio signal and send it earthward. That step is called downlinking. The signals cross space and arrive at an Earth Station, which is a dish. Uplinking is the name for signals sent upward to a satellite. Earth Stations are grouped so they can catch those signals. Computers act as the satellite's brain. Information comes in. The computers interpret it. Messages then go back down to Earth. Advanced digital cameras act as eyes. Sensors are important too. Light and color are things sensors can recognize.

3Heat is another. So are water, minerals, and gases. They record changes in whatever is being watched. Radios on the satellite send the information down, and antennas on Earth receive it. In mid-2010, researchers presented the first global model of gravity based on data from the GOCE satellite. GOCE can map tiny variations in the pull of Earth's gravity. Artificial satellites stay in orbit by using gravity. Earth's gravity draws every object inward, toward the middle of the planet. Staying in orbit means the speed has to change whenever the pull changes, even by a tiny amount. Speed pushes back against gravity just enough. The satellite does not shoot off into space, and it does not fall back down. Rockets carry satellites to different kinds of orbits and to different heights, matched to the job. Closer satellites are in low-Earth orbit. That height can be 200 to 500 miles, or 321 to 804 kilometers. Nearer Earth, gravity is stronger. These satellites therefore need a speed of about 17,000 miles an hour, which is 27,358 kilometers an hour. Otherwise they fall. Satellites farther out can travel more slowly, because the pull is weaker. A space shuttle in low-Earth orbit once struck a fleck of paint. A window took a pit from that fleck. The pit was nearly a quarter of an inch across, or 6.35 millimeters. Space can look empty. What is really there is an orbiting dump of garbage. Leftovers from early missions include gloves, lens caps, bolts, and rocket motors. Meteoroids are out there too. These objects hit spacecraft at 170,000 miles per hour or more, which is 273,588 kilometers per hour, and the damage is serious. Known pieces of space junk now on the charts number more than 370,000. Satellite missions helped build that count. NASA did that charting. After six years in space, some satellites came home full of pits, cracks, and holes from debris.

4Some satellites follow a lopsided path that is elliptical, meaning oval, so they can get a closer look at Earth. Polar orbit sits at 540 miles up, or 869 kilometers. Their route runs from one pole to the other. A single day holds eighteen loops around Earth. A different group orbits above the equator, at 22,300 miles, which is 35,888 kilometers. Earth's turning speed is the speed they match. Their orbits are called stationary. The satellite takes 24 hours to circle the planet. A full spin on Earth's axis takes 24 hours. Because the times match, the satellite seems to hover over a single spot. The job decides the path. One choice is a polar route. Another is low-Earth. Another follows the equator. Scientists build satellites to gather many kinds of information, and they choose the orbit to match the data they want. Comsats is the short name for communication satellites. Cell phones depend on them. So do emails and faxes sent around the globe. Television and radio can be broadcast worldwide because of them. Phone calls from an airplane in flight are possible too. With satellite TV, a home can pull the signal straight down. Telstar, an experimental satellite, carried the first live broadcast over the Atlantic Ocean. The year was 1962. Before that, news traveled by telegraph, by telephone, or by cables. Now a signal can bounce across several satellites and reach the most remote places. Environmental satellites watch the effects of deforestation, and they watch sediment that clogs rivers and harbors. Temperature is one fact these Earth observational satellites collect. Oceans are another. Wildfires, animals, and even volcanoes are on the list too. Sometimes those are called environmental satellites too. They record changes in Earth's surface and in the atmosphere, including pollution and the destruction of forests by human activity.

5Powerful cameras take pictures with light rays, with X-rays, and with radio waves. The value of this information keeps rising for environmentalists. Farmers see that value too, and so do miners and fishermen. Military satellites, also called spy satellites, have photographed Earth since 1960. Reconnaissance satellites is the official name. Spysats is the short one. Other nations are what they watch. Coded messages are relayed by them. Nuclear weapons are watched. Enemy armies are observed. Many kinds of electronic communication can be eavesdropped on. In 1983, Ronald Reagan, then president of the United States, announced research into a defense system based in space. The name was the Strategic Defense Initiative, or SDI, and it was also called Star Wars. Enemy missiles would be spotted by a network of defense satellites. The hope was to destroy those missiles before they left the air. Work on the system never reached completion. Technology built for spysats has been stretched to other jobs. Sites that might hold oil, or minerals, are hunted with imaging satellites used by industries. Places growing illegal drugs are something law enforcement looks for with these satellites. Pollution has been followed, by satellite, back to the people who caused it. Finer detail than ever before is now possible on maps of Earth, thanks to research satellites. One program tracks meteors that come too close to Earth. Tests are underway on ways to turn those meteors aside, or to destroy them, before a collision with the planet. The same program watches those tests. A research satellite has taken an image of New York City. Both communication satellites and military spy satellites matter in major emergencies. Disasters often wipe out every means of transportation and every other kind of communication. Satellite signals are not affected. Mobile dishes serve as ground stations for radio stations and for TV stations. Up goes a signal, to a communication satellite.

6From there it may be beamed around the world. It may instead be bounced onward to a second satellite. Satellites can show how far a major disaster area spreads. Weather satellites predict storm systems and track them around the world. They save lives. Weather systems are monitored. So are wind speeds and rainfall, along with much besides. Hurricanes are one kind of dangerous storm they warn about. Typhoons are another. A warning that comes sooner, plus information that is more accurate, gives people time. They can prepare, or they can leave. Earth's atmosphere is a subject for meteorologists, who are scientists. Weather is another subject. Climate is a third. Satellites help them make better forecasts. Cameras on weather satellites, and tools that measure temperature in the atmosphere, do much of that work. Ships at sea get help when the satellites detect snow and ice. Meteorologists combine orbits to see more clearly. Over the poles, two weather satellites make their circle of Earth. Another set orbits at the equator. GPS began as a tool for the military. People across the globe now use it to learn where they are. Small monitors for GPS ride in many cars. A driver can learn the way from one place to another. GPS is not perfect. Electrical storms can disturb it. So can solar flares, a computer failure, or a power failure. Without navigational satellites, large ships lose the ability to hold a course. Large planes do too. GPS stands for Global Positioning System. Radio signals from three satellites are what it uses. An exact spot, anywhere, can be pinpointed that way. Astronomical satellites have the widest view of the universe. Deep space is where they look. The Moon is in view, and so are the Sun, planets, stars, and galaxies. Waves moving through space are one thing scientists study with them.

7Particles are another. The hope is a better understanding of the universe. Infrared satellites probe the darkest corners and send back images of objects no one could see before. Among astronomical satellites from the United States, none is more famous than the Hubble Space Telescope. People called it the ultimate telescope. It was launched into low-Earth orbit in 1990. Twenty years of work went beyond every expectation, and the last mission in a series of refits gave it a final tune-up. New cameras went in. New batteries went in. New gyroscopes went in. A Cosmic Origins Spectrograph went in as well. Hopes rose that it might take pictures in deep space for perhaps another ten years. Its speed around Earth stays at 17,000 miles each hour. Eyes on the universe is the role of its reflecting telescopes. High-powered cameras share that role, along with sensors and other tools. Those eyes, across the first twenty years, recorded over 45 terabytes of data. About 5,800 DVDs would be needed to hold it. Hubble helped scientists understand how stars are born and how they die, and it helped them study black holes and the way galaxies change. The famous scientist Isaac Newton first imagined an artificial satellite in 1687. The Moon stays in orbit, he realized, because Earth's gravity holds it there. Nearly 300 years passed. Then the former Soviet Union acted on the idea. Sputnik I was the first object sent into space. In size it was close to a basketball. Four antennas sent out radio signals. One loop around Earth took 98 minutes. The path was an ellipse. Americans were surprised by the launch. Between those two countries, a race into space began at that moment. Six months later, Sputnik I drifted downward and burned away in the atmosphere. Was survival in space possible for a living thing? Proof was what the Soviet Union set out to find.

8In 1957 a dog named Laika rode the second satellite, Sputnik II. No living traveler had gone to space before her. Sadly, Sputnik II was not built to come home, and Laika died. Space stations let astronauts live and work while they orbit Earth for long stretches. The first crew went aboard in 2000. The station's name is the International Space Station, shortened to ISS. Nothing in space then was newer, and nothing was larger. Mir, a Russian station, held the record before the ISS. It was the largest space station yet built, and the most famous. Weight came to 130 tons. Time in space came to 15 years. At full size it was about 98 feet from end to end and 45 feet across. Six components made it up. Growth by 2010 left the ISS about four times as big as Mir. Its living and work space equaled that of a 747 jumbo jet. Power comes from solar panels covering almost an acre. Sixteen countries share the work. The United States is one. Canada, Japan, and Russia are others. Eleven countries come through the European Space Agency, called ESA. Brazil is a partner too. Each partner contributes important pieces. Canada built a robotic arm that can maneuver with great skill. Low-Earth orbit is the ISS path, about 250 miles above the ground, or 402 kilometers. That height lets launch vehicles ferry people and equipment back and forth. Russia's Soyuz rocket is one such vehicle. The U.S. space shuttle was another. Eighty-five percent of the globe passes under the station on this path. Earth can be watched very well from there. It holds the most advanced laboratory in orbit. Discoveries that help people everywhere are what scientists hope to make, and they hope for many of them. One planned study looks at what long-lasting low gravity does to humans.

9Another looks at bone loss that spaceflight causes. Another watches Earth's environment over a long time. Astronauts in the space shuttle have adjusted the Hubble Space Telescope while it orbits. After the space shuttle Columbia launched in 1981, missions to rescue satellites grew easier. Technology aboard the shuttles improved the chance of success. A chair with no legs is what a Manned Maneuvering Unit resembled. It was strapped onto an astronaut's back. Outside the craft, astronauts could move freely. No tether held them to the shuttle. A robotic arm could grab a satellite and haul it inside, ready for use on a different path. Shutdown of the United States shuttle program came in 2011. Since then, NASA has tested and studied new methods and new equipment, so that other ways remain to repair satellites in orbit. Busyness fills space. Junk is a big part of it. So are thousands of satellites growing old in low-Earth orbit. No international law currently says an old satellite must be taken out of orbit. Thousands of years can pass before an object comes down, if it orbits higher than 500 miles, or 804 kilometers. Some orbits slowly lose their satellites, which are tugged back into the atmosphere of Earth. Most often they burn up before they reach the ground. Fresh ideas for clearing old traffic in orbit are being developed by NASA and by other agencies. Nothing suggests satellites will leave our lives. Their technology keeps changing, and it will keep changing our lives. One recent step is Internet Routing In Space, or IRIS. Voice can move to remote areas more instantly. Video can too, and so can data. Herd animals can be tracked by imaging programs researchers have built. Water supplies can be watched, and so can levels of irrigation. Better satellite technology adds a great deal to what science knows. Quick delivery of information, to people everywhere, is something satellites make possible.

10Their images help us find better ways to protect the planet. Our galaxy will keep being probed by research satellites. The mysteries of the universe will keep being unraveled with their help. Russia's launch in 1957 opened the space race. On the right is Sputnik I. Its size was close to that of a basketball. Sputnik II appears on the left. These words may help. Human-made objects that travel around other objects in space are called artificial satellites. Low-Earth orbit is a path close to Earth, 200 to 500 miles high, or 321 to 804 kilometers. Waves in deep space, and particles there, are monitored by astronomical satellites, which are a kind of research satellite. Atmosphere, climate, and weather on Earth are what meteorologists study. They are scientists. Ships learn their position with help from navigational satellites. Planes do too. The bus is the body of a satellite, holding basic functions and equipment. An orbit is the path of one object around another. Sound signals are picked up by communication satellites. Picture signals are too, and so are telephone signals. The payload is the part that carries tools. Environmental satellites monitor how Earth is changing. North pole and south pole both lie under a polar path. Information about other countries is what reconnaissance satellites gather. The letters GPS stand for Global Positioning System. Locations get pinpointed from radio signals that satellites send. Weather satellites monitor weather. Gravity is Earth's force pulling everything toward its center. Other topics in the book include Mir and the Moon. They include the space shuttle Columbia. They include downlinking and uplinking. They include Earth observational satellites, an Earth Station, and an elliptical orbit. They include solar energy, Sputnik I, and Sputnik II. They include the Strategic Defense Initiative, the Hubble Space Telescope, and the International Space Station.

50. Painters of a Passing Moment

1A painting called Boulevard des Capucines was made by Claude Monet in 1873 and 1874. This book starts with new art for a changing Paris. It then tells how painters rebelled against old habits, changed their subjects, and tried new methods. It looks at pictures and cameras, then closes with a word list. Paris, France, was changing in the middle of the nineteenth century. Its art world was changing too. A group of artists chose to rebel against the art scene that was already in power. They did not want formal paintings in the realistic style people preferred then. They wanted brief moments from ordinary days. A map places Paris in France, with the Atlantic Ocean, Europe, the Mediterranean, Asia, and Africa around it. Art was shifting while the city itself was being rebuilt and modernized. Paris had stayed much the same since the Middle Ages. The city had grown more and more crowded. Narrow streets wound through it. Those streets were filthy. Disease was everywhere. As the city changed, streets too narrow for carriages were taken out. Long boulevards lined with trees replaced them. Builders added cafés. They added theaters. They added parks in the open air, and they added squares. They also added a grand opera house. Wealthy people came to enjoy this new Paris.

2Paris was a major home of culture. Many artists lived and worked there. Collectors liked to search its galleries and build art collections. Each year Paris hosted an art event. No show of art anywhere in the West drew more people. People called it the Salon. It was an exhibition. Paintings covered the walls from the floor all the way to the ceiling. Work shown in the Salon was wanted by collectors at once. The artists who picked the Salon art were conservative. They especially liked formal portraits. They also liked subjects from history, myth, and religion. One favored kind of picture is the Princesse de Broglie. Say that title PRAHN-sess DU BROY. It is a portrait of a wealthy woman from France. Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres painted it in 1853. The sounds of his name start ZHAHN oh-GOOST. Then comes doh-mee-NEEK AN-gruh. Fine brushwork and sharp detail make it realistic. People prized that style then. Another picture, by Renoir, is Luncheon of the Boating Party, from 1880 to 1881. People of different classes pass time in a café. Paris had been made over. Many young artists wanted people's ideas about art made over too. They did it by challenging old traditions. They left behind styles they felt were out of date.

3The Salon did not often pick their work. When it did, the pieces were often hung so poorly that nobody noticed. That was frustrating. The young artists hoped rich people would become their patrons. A patron gave an artist money. Then the artist did not need another job. The artist could focus on making art. A patron could also present an artist to other people who collected art and had money. Thirty artists who were struggling joined together. Claude Monet was one. Say his name moh-NAY. Edgar Degas was another. Say his name du-GAH. Mary Cassatt was another. Say her name kuh-SAT. They wanted to change the Salon's settled art scene. In 1874 they held their own exhibit. Their subjects included sunlight striking water at one time of day. They also showed people laughing while they ate with friends in a café. Monet's exhibit piece was a painting. Its name was Impression, Sunrise. He had made it in 1873. A small rowboat sits in it. Behind the boat, ship masts and smokestacks appear in a haze. One reviewer attacked the lack of detail. He said the work offered nothing beyond simple impressions. Monet did not paint the scene exactly as it looked. He painted the personal effect the sunrise had on him.

4The reviewer's cutting words stuck. The artists in the group did not all paint the same way. Together they became known as the Impressionists. They would define a new movement in art. Impression, Sunrise helped start that new movement in art history. Style was only one challenge to old ways of painting. Many Impressionists refused the usual subjects. They stepped away from scenes of history and religion. They stepped away from realistic portraiture too. They wanted the world as their own eyes saw it. They wanted their own points of view. They wanted both the beauty and the flaws of ordinary life. Portraits and religious scenes no longer boxed them in. Subjects could come from a wide range. Landscapes of countryside in France were a frequent subject for Camille Pissarro. Say his name pi-SAR-oh. Alfred Sisley often did that too. Say his name SIS-lee. Pierre-Auguste Renoir focused on sunlight. Start his name pee-AIR. Finish it oh-GOOST ruh-NWAH. He studied how that light fell on flowers and on figures. He also made informal portraits. One example is a picture from 1892. Its title begins Two Young Girls. The rest is at the Piano. It shows that a portrait, an old kind of picture, could be painted in a new way.

5In that painting Renoir caught a moment that was already passing. Short-lived moments had to be painted fast, so the Impressionists learned speed. Monet used a method called wet-on-wet. He put a new layer of color on top of another layer. He did not wait for the lower layer to dry. Older painters had to wait. Each layer had to dry before more color could go on. Oil paint can need a full day to dry. A large painting could then take months. It could even take years. The Impressionists did not lay down wide strokes of color. They tried small touches of paint. Those touches held the color and light they saw. They used pure pigments. A pure pigment is paint that has not been mixed with another color. They set these colors next to each other. They mixed them as little as they could. The contrast made each color look bolder and more vivid. One 1899 picture of that subject begins with the words Bridge Over a Pond. The rest is of Water Lilies. Monet made eighteen paintings of it. The River Thames in London was another subject. He made over one hundred images of it. Many of them show the Houses of Parliament. Many Impressionists, Monet among them, painted en plein air.

6Say that phrase ON PLEN AIR. It means outdoors. Before this era, working outside was uncommon. Artists had usually worked in indoor studios. Indoors, they could control the light more easily. Outside, they could watch natural light and color and play with both. Some painters returned to one scene many times. Each visit caught a different moment of light, color, and time. The British Houses of Parliament became a series in Monet's hands. That series is one example. He worked on it for three years. Different hours of the day appear in those views of the building. He also showed it in different weather. Some Impressionists, Edgar Degas among them, liked to paint indoors. They still showed moments of daily life. His paintings featured ordinary people of Paris. Restaurant diners appear. Musicians appear. Ballerinas appear. He often sketched ballerinas backstage in their dance halls. He also sketched them in his studio. After many sketches of the same pose, he was ready to paint. He used the sketches. He used what he had learned by watching how the dancers moved. Those figures were reshaped into a scene ready for paint. In The Ballet Class, made from 1871 to 1874, no one person stands out as the subject.

7The picture feels spontaneous. The ballerinas are backstage, practicing. Some stretch. Some chat. They are caught in an ordinary moment of their lives. They are not posing. They seem to have no interest in the artist. They do not even look out of the canvas. The painting shows how well Degas could catch a gesture that lasts only a moment. In the middle of the 1800s, modern photography was growing. As the new tools improved, more people had a photographer take their portrait. A photograph took less time than a painted portrait. It cost less. It could match a person's looks more closely. The Impressionists did not try to beat photography at its own job. They wanted viewers to see a kind of work a camera could not replace. At the same time, photography inspired them. By the 1880s, cameras were easier to carry. Photos became more candid. A photo could freeze a spontaneous moment. Painters tried to do that too. A subject might be ordinary. People waiting on a train is one example. It might be people resting in a park. Édouard Manet was never an official member of the Impressionists. Say his name e-DWAR ma-NAY. Some of his paintings still show their influence. The Railway, from 1873, is one.

8Cameras also taught artists to frame a scene in a striking way. That method is called cropping. In a photograph, an artist could cut off the edges to frame the subject better. The Impressionists understood cropping. They used it when they composed their own works. Their pictures show a strong debt to photography. From 1881 to 1886, Renoir painted The Umbrellas. People carrying umbrellas fill the group. Rain is falling as they move along a street. The edge of the canvas cuts off many figures. The center does not hold a single focal point. The viewer's eye jumps from place to place. It moves to the woman on the left. It moves to the girl on the right. Both of them look out of the canvas. X-rays show a later change. The left-side figures were painted again later, and the new handling is crisper. Degas's painting Waiting, from around 1882, holds many contrasts. Young meets old. Light meets dark. Glamour meets dreariness. In art history, Impressionism had a wide influence. When these painters began, people did not take their art seriously. The Salon rejected them. Acceptance was hard to win. They left traditional realistic styles behind, and that let them chase new ideas. They focused on moments that flee. They worked en plein air.

9They used some methods from photography. They kept a style of their own. Buyers now pay millions of dollars for pictures by Monet, by Degas, and by other painters from this group. People call them masterpieces. Art museums around the world display them. These painters broke the rules of traditional art. That break opened a road for later movements. Because of their work, artists still experiment. They still make us question what we think art is. Each art movement builds on movements that came before. By challenging old painting styles, the Impressionists opened a door. Other artists could keep experimenting. After the Impressionists, some artists tried to put deeper memories and feelings into their work. Color and shape carried those feelings. This was Post-Impressionism. Vincent van Gogh was a famous Post-Impressionist. Say his name VAN GOH. The Starry Night is one of his paintings. In the middle of the 1880s, Neo-Impressionism appeared. Georges Seurat was one of these artists. Say his name ZHORZH su-RAH. He used a new method called pointillism. The paintings were made of dots, or points, left by a brush. This work took time. It was not spontaneous the way Impressionist work was. One such painting is titled A Sunday. The rest of the title is on La Grande Jatte.

10Say the place name GRAHND ZHAT. Expressionists did not try to copy the natural world. They tried to catch emotions. Edvard Munch painted The Scream in 1893. It is among the best-known pictures of that time. A screaming figure stands on a bridge. The figure carries intense anxiety. Conservative means traditional and slow to change. To have criticized something is to have found fault in it, or to have judged it with disapproval. Depicted means showed or portrayed something. An exhibition puts artwork, or other interesting things, on show for the public. A focal point is the place that holds the center of attention. In art, an impression shows the basic features of something. It often aims to suggest a feeling or an effect. Modernization updates something. It can also make that thing fit newer technology, ideas, or style. A portrait can be a drawing of a person, a painting of a person, or a photograph of a person. Something realistic looks like real life, or it is accurate. A person who rebels actively fights an authority that is already in place, including a government. Sketched means made a rough drawing or an outline. Spontaneity means something happens on its own, or springs from a sudden impulse.

51. Printing Objects, Not Just Pictures

1This book starts with a first look. Later parts cover stamps and laser light. Flat sheets become solid forms. A new method spreads. Hearts and livers can be printed. One house is unlike the rest. The last parts look ahead and list words. Joseph Gutenberg takes a test sheet off the press. A picture shows shoes planned for one person and built by a printer that makes solid objects. A first look. A designer who plans goods for industry is deep in work on a computer. She is shaping a shoe no shop carries. Her eyes stay on the screen. A program made for this job lets her adjust the shoe's shape. She uses the same program to set the shoe's size. The design now satisfies her. She tells the machine to begin. On the other side of the room, the printer comes alive. A whirr fills the air. A hum follows. The result is more than a flat picture of footwear. A shoe you could hold is what the machine builds. You have entered three-dimensional printing. A shorter name for it is 3D printing. It is the newest way to form a model of nearly any object a person can picture. Such a model is called a prototype. The object that leaves a 3D printer is not like the sheet that leaves an ordinary computer printer. The two machines still rest on one shared idea. They add material one coat at a time. People call that method layering. Layering is what finishes the product. From stamps to lasers.

2Ask most people what printing is, and they picture words. They also picture pictures. The marks lie on something smooth. Paper is one such surface. Cloth is another. Ink, laid on as a coat, makes the marks. A hand can spread that ink. A machine can spread it too. History holds many ways of putting ink on a surface. Xylography goes back about two thousand years. People in Eastern Asia were the ones who used it. Another name for xylography is woodblock printing. The work began with a drawing on wood. Carving came next, and the carvers removed wood from around the drawing. Ink then covered the raised part that was left. That inked part was pushed onto a flat surface. Up came the block. What remained was a thin ink coat shaped like the raised picture. A stamp pad and a rubber stamp do this same job. Anyone who has stamped ink has tried xylography. Covering a whole page with many stamped pictures would eat up the hours. A machine invented in 1450 ended that long wait. The machine was the printing press. Its inventor was Johannes Gutenberg. His trade was blacksmithing, and his country was Germany. For the first time, books could be printed in huge numbers. One picture shows a lithographic press moving images onto the pages of a book. The new press did not stamp a page one mark at a time. Pieces of type, which are many small stamps, sat together in a tray. Paper met that tray under pressure.

3A single push put inked type across every part of the page. Copy after copy of one page became far simpler to produce. Hundreds of years passed, and printing kept changing. Lithography is one later method. Water plays a part in it. Oil plays a part too. On a lithographic press, images move onto the pages of books. Picture areas and blank areas share one flat plate. They sit at the same level. A treatment on the plate makes the picture area pull in inks made with oil. Water stays apart from oil. Because of that split, the blank areas drive the ink off. The year 1796 is when this lithographic method was worked out. Magazines still come off such presses. So do many books. The 1950s brought the earliest printer that could work at high speed. It was paired with a computer named UNIVAC. Data for that computer sat on reels of magnetic tape. A typewriter, changed for the job, was hooked to the reels. Words stored on the tape came out through that typewriter. Numbers came out the same way. No person could match that speed. By the 1980s, computers sat on desks in many homes and offices. Inkjet machines let those desk computers put digital pictures on paper. The computer sends facts about each shape. The printer reads those facts. Heating comes first, inside a cartridge packed with ink. Warm ink raises the pressure in the cartridge. Ink then bursts out through an opening called a nozzle. Jet is another name for that opening.

4Coat after coat of ink lands on the sheet. Work on laser printing began in the 1970s. Homes could not buy those printers until 1984. A laser printer resembles lithography. One big difference sets it apart. Oil is not painted onto the surface. Instead, a laser strikes the paper and leaves an image that carries an electric charge. Particles of dry ink move across the sheet. The charged image pulls those particles in. A roller then squeezes the particles against the paper. The page is printed. Flat sheets become solid forms. Charles Hull, in 1984, created a method he named stereolithography. That method is what people now mean by 3D printing. His job was design engineer. Long waits made him angry at his work. Plastic prototype parts took weeks to develop. Testing them took months. Redesign took still more time. He went looking for a fix. Prototypes, he believed, should be ready much sooner. A stack of layers, he realized, could grow into a solid thing. From that idea, 3D printing started. A picture shows Charles Hull. Stereolithography takes tools from inkjet machines. It also takes tools from laser machines. Those tools build objects with height, width, and depth. They do not stop at a flat picture. Software on a computer draws the image first. The drawing is saved as data. That file travels to the 3D printer. Think of the file as a map of roads. The map guides a part called the print head. The print head looks like a very small box.

5A nozzle, also called a jet, sticks out from the box. Metal bars form a grid, and the print head hangs on them. Some bars run the length of a platform. Other bars run across it. That platform is the print bed, and the object grows there. A diagram points to the bed, to the material, to a nozzle, and to the moving head above them. Plastic thread is the stuff this printer lays down. Small objects grow from that thread. Above the bed, the head slides forward and back. It also slides left and right. Material leaves the nozzle in a narrow stream while the head travels. Plastic is a common choice for that stream. The stream drops onto the bed. Instructions come from the image file on the computer. Those instructions stack the material in layers too thin to see one by one. People call those layers microlayers. Up and down goes the bed as the stack grows. A fresh layer lands. Heat from a laser meets that layer. The heat sticks it to the layer already there. Little by little, a solid prototype climbs off the bed. Each added coat brings it closer to done. Look at the monitor, and the rising object matches the picture there. Names and dates in printing. Bi Sheng, a printer from China, made the earliest known movable type. The time was about the year 1040. His letters were formed from clay. Gutenberg's press arrived in 1450. He was the German blacksmith already named in this book.

6Printed books could then be turned out in great numbers. Alois Senefelder brought lithography into the world in 1796. He wrote, and he also acted, in Germany. Plays were what he hoped to print without high cost. Lord Stanhope, a scientist from Britain, finished a press of cast iron in 1800. No cast-iron press had come before his. Richard Hoe, an inventor from America, built the cylinder press in 1846. Eight thousand sheets could leave that press in a single hour. Ottmar Mergenthaler invented the Linotype machine in 1886. He was born in Germany and later lived as an American. Before the Linotype, no device could line up a full row of type for the press. Chester Carlson invented electrophotography in 1938. Xerox is the other name people use for that invention. Carlson studied physics in America. He also worked as an attorney. Remington-Rand, a firm in America that made office machines, built a fast printer in 1953. That printer served the UNIVAC computer. It was the first printer of its speed for that machine. Gary Starkweather, an engineer from America, made a laser printer for sale in 1976. His was the first laser printer that businesses actually used. In 1984 Hull both built stereolithography and took out a patent on it. He was American. Design engineering was his field. The patent covers the method we call 3D printing. A new method takes off. Once the twenty-first century was young, factories chose stereolithography first. They used it when a prototype part had to be made.

7Design, building, and testing could all finish inside hours. Sometimes the work fit inside a few days. The old pace had been weeks. Sometimes it had been months.
