Plastic was the usual stuff in those early solid prototypes. Better machines arrived later. Ceramics joined the list of materials. Metals joined it too. Seoul, a city in South Korea, hosted a design show. There, a 3D printer formed a shape like a sculpture. More materials meant more things a printer could attempt. Workers in many jobs saw a shortcut to custom pieces. The wait shrank. A designer might form a jewel that exists only once. An artist might form a solid sculpture no one had shaped before. The price stayed fair. Only the material inside the object gets used. Nothing extra is poured away. Photos follow Beauty, a bald eagle, from before a new beak to after it was fixed on. Printing for the birds. Custom solid objects, made at a price people can pay, have found surprising jobs. One engineer walked into a place that nurses hurt wild animals. Beauty, the bald eagle there, stopped him cold. Her upper beak was gone. A hunter's shot had taken it. Hunting was impossible for her. Eating was impossible. Preening her own feathers was impossible. He thought a printed part could answer her need. An X-ray of her head was his starting point. On a computer he drew a plastic stand-in for the beak she had lost. The printer turned that drawing into a solid beak.

8Surgery locked the new beak on for good. Drinking is possible for her now, as it is for any healthy eagle. Eating is possible too. So is washing her feathers. Have a heart, or have a liver. Real human organs are the new goal for some engineers. Scientists share that goal. Living cells can be fused by the same layering used for plastic. The fused cells become human tissue. Cells taken from one patient go into a gel. Layers of that gel copy the organ's shape. Time in an incubator lets the cells grow up. They fasten to each other as they mature. Ears have already been grown this way. Lungs have been grown. Livers have been grown. A heart is the project on the bench now. Natural tissue would be part of it. Artificial material would be the other part. Rejection is the trouble many transplant patients face. An organ from a printer might spare a person that trouble. Put something foreign into a body, and the immune system sees a danger. It fights the newcomer. Medicine after a transplant tells the immune system to hold back. Without that medicine, the new organ would be destroyed. The medicine has a cost. Infection becomes more likely. Cells from the patient change the odds. An organ grown from those cells is less likely to be rejected. Less medicine may be enough. The body can mend faster. Fewer extra problems show up during recovery. Medical classes use a solid model of a human heart made by this method.

9Amsterdam, in the Netherlands, is home to the 3D Canal House. A printer made one block for that build. The left-hand picture shows the block in the walls. The right-hand picture is a drawing of the house when the work is done. One house stands apart. Some engineers have aimed 3D printing straight up. The height is real, not a figure of speech. Architects in Amsterdam run a printer big enough to move from place to place. Their project is a plastic house. It will stand three floors high. Melted plastic, laid in coats, hardens into bricks. The bricks lock into one another. Thirteen rooms will be built from those bricks. Three years is the planned build time. Ordinary houses go up faster than that. The team wants the trial to change how people think about homes. Factory methods, including this kind of printing, might shape the next house. Move clockwise, and the first object is a work of art. Next comes a lollipop made of chocolate. Then a lamp. Last, a dinosaur's head. A 3D printer made each of them. The years ahead. No one can count every use still waiting for this technology. People can already tailor goods to one user. Braces for teeth, formed from plastic, are one good. Furniture big enough for a whole apartment is another. A full building is another. The machines keep getting better. Odd settings may be next. A trip through space that lasts a long time is one odd setting. The craft could carry a printer.

10A broken part could be replaced on the spot. New tools could be drawn up out there. Those tools could be built to make life in space possible. Staying alive on a strange world might depend on this invention. Words to know. Call something customized when it is made for one person alone. Call a thing innovative when it is new and when it did not copy an older idea. A laser is a tool that throws a tight, strong beam. Waves in that beam are alike. Data means facts, including sizes and counts, that help a person study a problem or make a plan. A particle is a speck of matter. Digital means the facts are saved as ones and zeros in a row. A computer, or a similar machine, can read that row. A prototype is the first form of an object. Later copies follow that first form. Stereolithography names a way of printing. A digital plan goes in, and a solid object comes out. An engineer designs machines. An engineer may also design a building, a bridge, or some other structure. Building and repair can be part of the same job. Technology means using what science knows, and the tools science builds, in order to make something or carry out a task. Industrial points to the making of goods. Machines often do that work. Automation and other technology often do it too. Three-dimensional describes an object that has height. It also has width. It also has depth. The short label is 3D.

52. Samuel de Champlain and the French Start in the North

1A picture made in 1613 shows St. Croix Island. Samuel de Champlain drew that picture. St. Croix Island was the earliest French settlement in Acadia. Acadia is now part of Maine. This book tells how the English held Champlain as a prisoner. It tells who he was. It follows his first journey to North America. It follows his search along the St. Lawrence. It tells of bitter days in Acadia. It tells how Quebec began. It tells of his final trip back to New France. It tells what remained after his life. Word meanings come at the end. A map marks Indigenous lands on his path in 1629. The Labrador Sea is on that map. Hudson Bay is on that map. Canada is on that map. The Wabanaki Confederacy is on that map. The Atlantic Ocean is on that map. Four Indigenous nations formed the Wabanaki Confederacy. Each of those nations had its own system of government. Nitassinan was the homeland of the Innu people. The Montagnais in the south belong to the Innu. The month was July. The year was 1629. The place was Quebec. Quebec was a trading settlement. Samuel de Champlain had started that settlement. He started it on the river he called the St. Lawrence. He stood at the edge of the region he called New France. New France was a huge area. People later called that area Canada. He also stood at the edge of the Wabanaki Confederacy. He stood at the edge of Nitassinan. Those places were long-standing homelands of different Indigenous peoples. This part of North America was land France hoped to possess. England wanted to own it too. English ships rode at anchor in the river next to the fort. David Kirke was in command of the vessels. He was a private English sea captain. He was also an adventurer. His brother Lewis was with him. The Kirke family had five brothers in all. England had chosen the brothers to seize New France.

2The siege of Quebec was one piece of a larger war. France and England were fighting that war. Five hundred years of off-and-on fighting lay behind the two countries. Now the fighting had spread into North America. Both countries were trying to lock down control of Indigenous nations' lands. The Wabanaki Confederacy was one of those nations. The Haudenosaunee Confederacy was another. England wanted quick wealth from those lands. France wanted that wealth too. The wealth they sought was timber. It was also furs. It was also minerals. Champlain had tried to hold a French foothold. That foothold sat in Wabanaki lands. It sat in Wyandot lands. It sat in Innu lands. He could see that hope was gone. Fewer than one hundred people were in the fort. Fighting men among them numbered no more than eighteen. Almost every bit of food was gone. The people defending the fort were starving. The day was July 16. Champlain handed over the fort. He did it so the suffering would stop. David Kirke was asked for leave to sail the colonists home to France. Kirke refused that request. The captain made Champlain a prisoner instead. Champlain and the other French colonists were put aboard the English ships. Those ships set sail for England. A true likeness of Champlain was never made. Most drawings of him come from a portrait of a different French official. That portrait was made in 1654. The drawing on this page is one of those later pictures. What we know about Samuel de Champlain is incomplete. The early years of his life are the least clear. Brouage is the town of his birth. Brouage lies near the western coast of France. His birth was sometime around 1567. His father was a sea captain. Ocean navigation was a skill his father taught him. Several sea trips took Samuel out with his father. He also sailed with his uncle.

3His uncle was another seaman in the family. Those trips helped him polish his navigational skills. During the same years he became an expert mapmaker. Army service in France filled most of his twenties. In 1598 he began long voyages with his uncle. Those voyages went to Spanish territories in North America. Those territories are now the Caribbean. On every trip he sketched local plants. He sketched local animals. He wrote notes that described what he saw. He was back in France in 1602. He gave King Henry IV a book of sketches and descriptions. The king was impressed with the young sea voyager. Henry believed Champlain could help make France stronger in North America. The king wanted more colonies. More colonies would keep French access to the riches of the continent. French people would populate the colonies. Military force would hold the colonies against other nations. The French king also wanted Indigenous peoples converted to Christianity. He wanted their lands seized for the Crown. That pair of goals was a common strategy of colonization. Champlain could draw with skill. He was a cartographer as well. His sketches show Indigenous peoples of North America. The year was 1603. The trip to New France was ordered by King Henry. Champlain went with a group that wanted to trade with Indigenous peoples. The trade they wanted was in furs. Getting furs was a leading reason for posts in North America. Beaver pelts were the main fur they sought. For centuries, people in Europe had prized beaver pelts. Hats made from those pelts were popular fashion items. By the early 1600s, beavers in Europe had been nearly wiped out. The demand for beaver hats had caused that loss. North America still had huge numbers of beavers. King Henry told Champlain to find a good site. The site would be for a fur-trading colony. Henry gave him a second task as well. Champlain was to search for the Northwest Passage.

4That passage would be a water route through North America. It would be a shortcut to Asia. By the early 1500s, explorers had learned something important. The Americas formed one unbroken land mass. The land stretched from the Arctic down to South America's tip. For Europeans, the best path west toward the Pacific Ocean would pass through North America or above it. The same path would lead on to Asia. Many explorers hunted for a water route across the continent. The route stayed unfound. It did not exist. Many European explorers wanted a northern sea lane toward Asia's markets. People called that lane a Northwest Passage. Ships from western Europe usually reached Asia by rounding the Cape of Good Hope. It also went around the southern tip of Africa. The path around Africa was long. Huge waves in the southern latitudes made it very dangerous. Merchants had long wanted a shorter route to Asia. They wanted a safer route too. In 1492 Christopher Columbus was searching for such a route. He ran into the Americas instead. If someone had found the route, the finder would have kept it. It was not something to share. It was something a country would seize for its own exclusive use. About four hundred years later, melting Arctic ice opened a real Northwest Passage. Ships can use that passage during the summer months. Champlain's group left in two ships. They set sail in March 1603. Violent storms tossed them during a voyage of ten weeks. Then they entered a wide river. That river is now known as the St. Lawrence. A harbor is where the ships stopped. The harbor is where the St. Lawrence meets the Saguenay River. Saguenay is said SAG-uh-nay. The next day Champlain met Indigenous people of the area for the first time. About a thousand people had gathered. The far bank of the Saguenay River was where they stood. They sang.

5They played music. They were celebrating a victory. The victory was over a shared enemy. That enemy was the Haudenosaunee. People commonly called them the Iroquois. Iroquois is said EER-oh-kwaw. Champlain crossed the river to meet the group. This was not their first meeting with Frenchmen. In 1534 another French explorer had claimed lands to the north for France. His name was Jacques Cartier. Cartier is said kar-tee-YAY. Cartier tried to found a colony in New France. That attempt failed. He did open the French fur trade. One tribe is not what the Haudenosaunee are. In that era the league held five nations. Later the league had six nations. They spoke related languages. They had formed an alliance with the English. When Champlain arrived they numbered about 12,000. Smallpox took at least half their people by the 1640s. Indigenous peoples in this land were skilled at trapping animals for fur. They traded those furs with the Europeans. The Europeans wanted more than money from the fur trade. They wanted to seize Indigenous land. They wanted to convert Indigenous peoples to Christianity. They wanted to block the English from moving farther into the area. Before this, Europeans were still new to most Indigenous peoples. They had little immunity to European diseases. Many Indigenous people died. Those huge drops in population helped European colonizers. Lands once full of Indigenous people now had fewer living there. An Indigenous man who spoke French aided Champlain. With that help, Champlain met an Innu chief. The southern Innu people are the Montagnais. Montagnais is said mon-ten-NAY. In French the name means mountain people. The chief's hope was French help to vanquish that enemy. That enemy was the Haudenosaunee. Champlain saw that an alliance with these tribes offered great possibilities. He might side with them against the Haudenosaunee. In return they might help him grow the fur trade. They might help him explore this land. In time they might help him acquire it for France.

6A picture from 1777 shows Indigenous men trading furs. They are trading with European sailors. Champlain's men explored much of the Saguenay River. After that they set out to explore the St. Lawrence Valley. A stop came at one spot as they traveled upriver. The Montagnais called that spot Kebec. Kebec means where the river narrows. To the French, the place became Quebec. An Indigenous town had once stood there. A French settlement, he believed, fit that spot perfectly. On several later expeditions he went on exploring the St. Lawrence. He ventured some 2,500 kilometers. That distance is 1,550 miles. He was sure the rivers and lakes of New France held a water route to the Pacific Ocean. That route would be the Northwest Passage. He could not find such a route. He never would. In mid-August of 1603 he set sail for France. He arrived in late September. He traveled to Paris. He made his report to King Henry. The king was pleased. Henry's trust showed when he gave Champlain the title Vice Admiral of France. At this time Champlain published a book. Three more books about his time in New France would follow this first one. In 1604 he returned to New France. About eighty male colonists came with him. The group included laborers. It included doctors. It included carpenters. It included missionaries. The missionaries hoped to persuade Indigenous peoples to give up their faith traditions. They also hoped Indigenous peoples would give up an entire way of life. The colonists settled in an area the French called Acadia. Acadia is present-day Maine. The Mi'kmaq lived in much of that area. Mi'kmaq is said MIG-maw. The Mi'kmaq are one nation in the Wabanaki Confederacy. Sainte-Croix was the name the French gave their chosen island. Sainte-Croix is said sawnt-KWAW. They built a storehouse. They built homes. They built other buildings. Then they settled in for a hard winter. Firewood was in short supply.

7Water was in short supply. The men ate dried foods. They ate salted meat. Fruits were missing from their diet. Vegetables were missing too. That lack made them sicken with scurvy. Missing vitamin C is what brings on the disease scurvy. Spring arrived. By then, thirty-five of the men had died. Citrus fruits can prevent scurvy. In the Canada of the 1600s, citrus fruits were impossible to get. In winter, scurvy was the most common disease among the Haudenosaunee. Boiled pieces of the eastern white cedar were their cure. People came to call that tree the tree of life. The colony then moved to a place on the coast. That place is modern-day Nova Scotia. They named it Port Royal. Winter scurvy hit this settlement too. The survivors held on. Farming at Port Royal turned out well. During the summers Champlain started exploring again. His ship followed the coast toward the south. He went as far as the place now called Cape Cod. Cape Cod is in the state of Massachusetts. Champlain came back to the St. Lawrence Valley in June 1608. Thirty-two colonists were with him. July was the month they anchored at Quebec. Here he planned a permanent settlement in the valley. He also planned a fur-trading post. He put the colonists to work at once. They began building a group of houses. They built other buildings too. He called the group the Habitation of Quebec. As the work went on, several tribes visited the settlement. The visitors included the Wyandot, also called the Huron. They included the Anishinaabe, also called the Algonquin. They included the Montagnais. His promise was what they brought up to Champlain. He had promised to help them fight the Haudenosaunee. A drawing of the Quebec settlement comes from Champlain's own sketches. Winter came early that year. It was a bitter winter. Illness started spreading among the men inside the Habitation. Scurvy struck many of them, as it had before.

8Twenty-eight colonists stayed for the winter. Twenty of them died. Spring came. It was time for Champlain to keep his promises to his allies. In July 1609 he and his men joined the Indigenous nations. They carried early firearms called arquebuses. Arquebuses is said ar-kway-BOOS-es. Together they raided the Haudenosaunee. They defeated them that time. A long lake appeared on this journey south. He named the lake for himself. Today that lake is a natural border between New York and Vermont. People still call it Lake Champlain. In later years Champlain and his men joined their Indigenous allies in other battles. Those battles were against the Haudenosaunee. The Haudenosaunee were allies of the English. The Indigenous nations at war shared far more than they differed. The French and the English were enemies too. They also had more in common with each other. The Europeans wanted to own the land. They wanted to exploit it. North America would change hugely under that view of nature. Unlike Europe, North America had stayed largely intact up to this time. Champlain went back to France often. He reported on his work in Quebec. He recruited new colonists. The title governor of New France came to him in 1620. Under his administration, Quebec grew. Quebec prospered. He wanted the settlement's defenses to be stronger. He built a fort on Cap Diamant. Cap Diamant is a rocky cliff. It overlooks the Habitation. A few years later he knocked that fort down. He built a larger fort in its place. The new fort was stronger. In 1629 he and his fellow colonists were in that fort. There they finally surrendered to the Kirke brothers. The Kirkes had taken Champlain prisoner. He landed in England in mid-October 1629. He then heard news he had not expected. France and England were no longer at war. A peace treaty between the two nations was already six months old.

9That meant the Kirke brothers' conquest was illegal. The conquest covered Quebec. It covered other parts of New France. Any territory the Kirkes won after the treaty was signed would go back to France. King Charles of England agreed to a return. Quebec should be given back to France. Other territory the Kirkes now ruled should be given back too. From the Indigenous point of view, both European claims were illegal. Indigenous laws said the same thing. King Charles accepted another treaty in March 1632. That treaty returned all of New France to the French. Champlain was free at last to go back to Quebec. He returned the following year. He took up his duties as governor of New France again. He was now in his sixties. He was tired. He was feeling his age. Two years later he suffered a stroke. One month after that stroke, he died. The day was Christmas Day. The year was 1635. Champlain traveled through lands that are now six Canadian provinces. He also traveled through lands that are now five American states. He had founded a little settlement where the river narrows. That settlement became Quebec City. The Canadian province of Quebec has Quebec City as its capital. He had hoped New France would last as a French colony. That hope did not come true. From 1689 to 1763, about seventy-five years passed. In that time France and England fought four more wars. They fought for control of New France. After 1707, England was part of Great Britain. France lost when the fighting ended. Its territories in North America came under British rule. Official rule put Quebec inside the British Empire. Even so, many French ways have lasted to the present day. In Quebec City, shoppers pass shops with signs in French. They pass other businesses with French signs too. Indigenous people live on there as well. The Montagnais are among them. The Montagnais are part of the Innu Nation.

10They were traditionally nomadic. Government policies later forced them to move. They had to settle in permanent places. Those policies did not recognize their title to ancestral lands. The losses have weighed on the Innu for generations. Even today, colonization still threatens to destroy their culture. Their culture adapts. Their culture lives on. A modern Innu man, a Montagnais man, hunts in traditional dress. These words have special meanings in this book. Administration means management. Appointed means chosen by one person or a group to do a job. Colonists are people who live in a colony. They can also be people who founded a new colony. Conquest is the act of invading another area or group. It includes taking over. It includes ruling. Convert means to change from one religion to another. It can also mean a change of belief or view. To exploit is to use a person or a thing for gain. It can mean making use of someone or something. A habitation is a home or a living space. Indigenous means native to a particular place. Missionaries go to another place so they can spread a religion. Navigate means to find one's way over a long distance. It also means to steer a course toward a destination. Populated means that people were added. A settlement is a new place where people live. In a siege, an enemy is surrounded and held that way for a long time. During a siege the enemy is kept from food and other supplies. A site is the ground where something is found or happens. It can be the place where something was found or happened. A treaty is a formal agreement of peace or friendship. It is made between two nations or groups. Vanquish means to defeat in battle. Ventured means dared to go to a dangerous place. Voyages are long trips or journeys. They are especially trips on a ship.

53. Seeing What Eyes Miss

1A credit card has a raised number. Magnification shows tiny flaws in that number. This book starts with things barely visible to the eye. It then tells how the first simple microscopes worked. Next it explains compound microscopes. Later pages step through stronger views. One step is twenty to thirty times. Another is fifty to two hundred times. A further step runs from two hundred times up to fifteen hundred times. One page reaches one million times. A closing page and a word list finish the book. A green blowfly's body would look strange if you could shrink yourself very small. Measure a human hair and the width is about a tenth of one millimeter. In inches, that width is 0.0039. A hair that thin is among the smallest things a human eye can see. Picture yourself shrunk until the hair looks as thick as your arm. In a second picture, that same hair is as thick as a tree trunk. What would meet your eyes? Hairs on a fly's legs would seem like huge spikes. The fly would seem like a monster with giant eyes. A microscope gives that kind of close view.

2It changes the way we see the world. People have spent thousands of years wanting to inspect their world more closely. The ancient Greeks filled glass globes with water. Objects seen through that water looked bigger. Roman makers, during the first century ce, found a new trick with glass. The useful glass was thicker at the center than at the rim. Things looked larger through it. That glass was the first magnifying glass. In Europe in the 1600s, people learned to make better glass lenses. The microscope was invented then. At the start, a microscope was only a fancy magnifying glass. One glass lens sat above a holder for specimens. Most magnifying glasses make objects look about five to ten times larger. People write that power as 5–10×. The first simple microscopes had that same power. A simple microscope from 1780 folded into its case. A person could carry it in a pocket. A modern compound microscope has named parts. They are the eyepiece lens, the body tube, and the objective lens. This kind of microscope has three objective lenses, each with a different power.

3It also has a focus knob, a stage, a mirror, and a base. Early users learned they could line up two magnifying glasses. The second lens enlarged the image that the first lens had already made. That step multiplied the power. Two lenses in one instrument created the compound microscope. Multiply the two lens powers and you get the total magnification. Picture a first lens at ten times, written 10×. Picture a second lens at forty times, written 40×. The specimen is then seen at four hundred times its real size, written 400×. Today a compound microscope can make an object look up to fifteen hundred times larger than it is. People write that power as 1,500×. Some views are only twenty to thirty times life size, written 20–30×. Robert Hooke, a British scientist, was among the first people to use early microscopes. He improved the early compound microscopes. Those tools could enlarge objects only about twenty to thirty times their real size. He was also among the first to write careful notes on what he saw. In 1665 he published those notes in a book called Micrographia.

4No scientist had written a book about using a microscope before this one. Hooke's Micrographia includes drawings of a louse up close and a flea up close. He drew a fly's compound eyes with more detail than anyone had shown before. He sketched the separate hairs that cover a fly's body. He sketched the delicate antennae. He sketched the complicated mouthparts. A detailed flea drawing from that 1665 book is one picture from his work. Plant sections and seed sections were in his sketches too. He looked at a thin slice of cork. He found that the cork was made of hundreds of tiny chambers. He called those chambers cells. Monks lived in small rooms inside a monastery. Those rooms came to his mind. Those rooms were called cells too. Later, people used cell for the tiny blocks that build every living thing. A magnified slice of cork still shows those many tiny cells. Today, thin plant slices show how seeds form. They show how cells build the veins and tissues of leaves. They show the cells that let water and nutrients move in stems.

5From that view, we can see how a plant stays alive and how it grows. Stronger views reach fifty to two hundred times life size, written 50–200×. Historians believe Hooke's Micrographia stirred another early user, Antonie van Leeuwenhoek. Say his name LEY-vun-hook. He was a Dutch cloth merchant. He was not a trained scientist. He used magnifying glasses to study the fabrics he bought and sold. Hooke's drawings of the tiny world moved him to grind lenses himself. He found a way to make better lenses. An object under his microscopes could look over 200 times as large as it really was. People write that power as 200×. He built more than five hundred microscopes. That work happened in the late 1600s and the early 1700s. With these stronger tools he found red blood cells. He also found tiny living things called microorganisms. They lived in lake water. They also lived in scrapings from a person's teeth. Before his time, nobody knew microorganisms existed. They are living things too small for the naked eye. Microscopes showed that these tiny lives are everywhere. Pond water, seen through a lens, can show them.

6A classroom microscope today likely enlarges about as much as his early tools did. Two hundred times may not sound huge. It is still enough to show details the naked eye misses. Even sand looks new under a lens. Without magnification, sand looks plain. Magnified sand from the ocean's edge holds microscopic shells. Pieces of shells are in it. Coral is in it. Volcanic rock is in it. Ordinary beach sand is really many tiny pieces with color. Still stronger views run from two hundred times to fifteen hundred times, written 200–1,500×. Early compound microscopes had a problem. Their lenses often bent the picture into distortions. It was very hard to know which part was the real image. The rest could be a false effect. Light passing through the lenses caused that effect. Joseph Jackson Lister solved this in the early 1800s. He was a scientist from Britain. He built a new kind of lens. His lens fixed the distortion problem. His work made microscopes stronger and more reliable. Older microscopes could stretch a picture the way a funhouse mirror does. After the fix, microscopes opened new finds in science and in medicine.

7Louis Pasteur, a biologist from France, worked in the mid-1800s. He found what made some drinks spoil. Say his name pass-TUR. Microorganisms in the air could get into beer or milk and spoil it. Around the same time, better microscopes let doctors see microorganisms inside sick people. Scientists linked microorganisms to disease for the first time. That link changed how medicine was practiced. Photos made by Snowflake Bentley in 1902 show another discovery. Each snowflake has its own beautiful shape. The early compound microscope helped prove that no two snowflakes match. Wilson Alwyn Bentley was an American photographer. People called him Snowflake Bentley because of his snowflake work. He fastened a camera onto his microscope. The years were the late 1800s and the start of the 1900s. He photographed more than five thousand separate snowflakes. He showed that a snowflake mirrors itself in six directions. Salt forms very specific crystals. Sugar does too. So do some other materials. Compound microscopes showed this. Salt contains only two kinds of atoms, spaced in a regular way. Because of that, salt forms cube-shaped crystals that repeat.

8Sugar, also called sucrose, is built from two simpler sugars that are not the same. Its crystals slant at each end. They are more oblong than salt crystals. Sugar crystals take a regular rectangular form. Natural hooks on a cocklebur gave people a model for a fastener. The fastener is called Velcro. Tiny details can show how things work. George de Mestral was an engineer from Switzerland. Cockleburs made him curious. The burrs stuck to his clothes and to his dog's fur. He wanted to know why the grip was so firm. He put the burrs under a microscope. He saw tiny hooks. The hooks caught loops in the cloth of his pants. Nature's hook-and-loop fastener gave him the idea. He tried to copy that design in fabric. Years later, Velcro was the result. Velcro uses two cloth pieces. Thousands of tiny hooks cover one piece. Thousands of tiny loops cover the other. The hooks and loops let the two pieces zip together. A tiny dust mite is another magnified subject. Flakes of skin from people are its food. Light itself sets a limit on how far a compound microscope can enlarge.

9During the last century, scientists built microscopes that light a sample in new ways. One way uses ultraviolet light. Another sends energy beams made of particles called electrons. A microscope that lights a sample with electron beams is an electron microscope. Electron microscopes enlarge more than any other kind now in use. They can enlarge a sample up to one million times. People write that power as 1,000,000×. A fish scale under the microscope shows details the naked eye cannot catch. Each step up in magnification shows more about the tiniest structures. Those structures belong to plants, animals, and materials. Nearly every science field has gained countless finds from microscopes. They turn the invisible into something we can see. They let us explore the world in a wholly new way. Plenty of cells are transparent. Other small objects are too. Transparent means see-through. That makes them hard to see under a microscope. Since the 1800s, stains and dyes have helped. They make an object stand out from what is behind it. The object is then easier to see.

10Stain on a sick human liver, seen up close, shows a change. Healthy cells, colored orange, are being replaced. Damaged cells, colored purple, take their place. Some animals have thin feelers on their heads. Those feelers are antennae. They help those animals touch and smell. An electron is a particle in an atom. It orbits the nucleus and carries a negative electrical charge. Artificial means human-made, not found in nature. A microorganism is a living thing so small it takes a microscope to see. Viruses fit this word. Bacterial cells fit it too. Compound means made of two or more parts. A microscope is a device for viewing tiny objects. To contaminate is to add something harmful, or something unwanted, so the item is no longer safe or usable. Living things need nutrients if they are to stay alive, keep healthy, and grow. A crystal is a solid whose atoms sit in a regular, tight pattern. In math, multiply two or more numbers and the answer is the product. Specimens are examples kept for comparison, study, or display. Distortions are twisted or untrue pictures of something.

54. Seven Emirates on the Gulf

1A family is shopping inside a mall in Dubai. The parts of this book come in this order. The first part asks where the country is. The next part is about people. Then comes a part about the land. A history part follows the land. Landmarks come after the history. A conclusion follows the landmarks. A glossary closes the book. Where Is It? The United Arab Emirates is a country in the Middle East. People often use the short name UAE. The Middle East sits where three continents come together. Those continents are Asia, Africa, and Europe. Most countries of the Middle East lie wholly in Asia. Some countries lie wholly in Africa. Some countries lie wholly in Europe. Some countries lie only partly in Africa or in Europe. The UAE lies wholly in Asia. The country covers about 83,600 square kilometers (32,278 sq. mi.). That land is part of the Arabian Peninsula. The UAE shares a border with Saudi Arabia. The UAE also shares a border with Oman. Most of the coast runs along the Persian Gulf. People in the region call the Persian Gulf the Arabian Gulf. The gulf flows outward to the Indian Ocean. A small part of the eastern coast lies right on the Gulf of Oman. In all, the coast measures 1,318 kilometers (819 mi.). Seven independent Arab states join to form the UAE federation. The states are Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Sharjah, Ajman, Umm al Quwain, Ras al Khaimah, and Al Fujairah.

2Sharjah is said SHAR-juh. Ajman is said ej-MAHN. Umm al Quwain is said OOM AHL ky-WAYN. Ras al Khaimah is said RAHS AHL KY-muh. Al Fujairah is said AHL foo-JY-ruh. Each state has its own capital city. The capital carries the same name as its state. Abu Dhabi is the capital of the federation. The capital lies on an island in the gulf. Abu Dhabi is the second-largest city in the UAE. The city dates back to 3,000 bce. Today Abu Dhabi mixes an ancient culture with buildings of the present day. Stately mosques with white domes stand in the city. Shining skyscrapers stand there as well. The largest city is Dubai. Dubai stands northeast of Abu Dhabi. Dubai serves as a center for trade. Dubai also serves as a center for tourism. Both cities show their wealth. Dubai shines in an especially bright way. The tallest building in the world is in Dubai. The only hotel rated with seven stars is in Dubai. One of the largest islands made by people is in Dubai too. Here is something to know. Dubai is among the fastest-growing cities in the world. In 1968 the whole city had just thirteen cars. Planners today are building roads with two decks. The roads are meant for 1.4 million vehicles. A picture shows a modern roadway in Dubai.

3People Millions of people live in the UAE. Most of them are not citizens. Immigrants make up most of the population. Most immigrants come from other Arab countries or from South Asia. They moved here so they could work. Citizens are called Emirati. Emirati people descend from Arab tribes. Those tribes settled the region long ago. The tribes have a history of rivalry. Many of them still share certain traditions. Most citizens prefer traditional Arab clothing. Men wear a garment that is long. The garment is white. The garment is made of cotton. The garment reaches the ankle. Men also wear a covering for the head. A light scarf goes with that covering. The scarf may be white. The scarf may be red with a check pattern. Women have two kinds of dress. At home, a woman might wear a dress together with loose pants. Outside, women must dress in a modest way. Outside, they usually wear a dark cloak. A scarf covers the head. At times women cover their faces too. The scarves carry a religious meaning. The scarves also give protection from the sun. A picture shows a UAE family posed for a portrait. Children wear traditional clothing on more formal occasions. Islam is the most common religion in the UAE. In 2005, Muslims were the majority of the population. Most people in the UAE speak Arabic.

4Arabic is the official language of the country. In school, students learn Modern Standard Arabic. Most Emiratis also speak dialects from nearby countries. English is also used by many of the people. The biggest businesses are oil and construction. Those industries have long been led mostly by men. Many foreign workers who come for jobs are young men. Those young men often arrive without families. Foreign workers make up so much of the population that men outnumber women. Men are two-thirds of all the people. A picture shows a construction worker on a skyscraper in Abu Dhabi. A landform view shows that almost all of the UAE is desert. Land Along the coast, the UAE is hot. The coast is also humid. Swamps and marshes cover the coastal land in a thick way. Shoals and islands dot the coastline. Eastward, the Hajar Mountains reach 2,000 meters (6,500 ft.). The country gets very little rain in a year. Yearly rainfall is only 10 to 15 centimeters (4 to 6 in.). The small amount of rain falls in the cooler mountain areas. The mountains are only a small part of the country. Inland desert makes up most of the land. In the desert the sun feels even hotter than on the coast. Desert temperatures can climb as high as 49 degrees C (120 degrees F). At times, northern winds throw dust and sand over the region.

5That dust and sand may travel for miles. These winds help form some of the largest sand dunes in the world. Most of the desert cannot support daily life. Oases give some relief. An oasis is a fertile spot in the desert. Plants can thrive in an oasis. Some animals can thrive there too. Al Ain is the fourth-largest city in the UAE. From Abu Dhabi, Al Ain is about 160 kilometers (100 mi.) to the east. More than 614,000 people live in Al Ain. The largest oasis in the UAE sits in the middle of that city. The oasis is also called Al Ain. Fruit trees grow in the Al Ain oasis. Out in the desert, plant life is limited. Desert plants there are grasses and thorny bushes. In the oases, people harvest date palms. They also harvest alfalfa. They also harvest mangoes. They harvest other crops as well. Desert wildlife includes the Arabian oryx. It also includes Gordon's wildcat. It also includes the sand fox. It also includes sand gazelles. Too much hunting has put some species in danger. The Arabian oryx was threatened with extinction. People rescued the oryx by taking animals into captivity. They placed the animals in breeding groups so the species could continue. Pictures show an Arabian oryx, Gordon's wildcat, a sand fox, and a sand gazelle. History People have made homes on the Arabian Peninsula for thousands of years.

6Wandering groups settled in the area. Around 600 ce those people adopted Islam. Across several centuries, the gulf grew into a major path for trade. The route linked Europe to Asia. In the 1600s England became one of the strongest powers in the region. In the 1700s the Arab states of today's UAE began to form. They formed as sheikhdoms. A sheikhdom is an area ruled by a leader called a sheikh. The sheikhdoms fought one another for control of the region. In the early 1800s Britain took control of trade routes there. In 1820 Great Britain signed a peace treaty with the sheikhs of the coastal tribes. A peace treaty of this kind is a truce. Later the states signed more truces. The sheikhdoms then came to be called the Trucial States. In the mid-1900s the sheikh who controlled Abu Dhabi made an agreement. He let British-owned oil companies look over the land. The search went on for several decades. In 1958 the oil company Abu Dhabi Marine Areas found a large oil deposit. In the years after that, oil was also found in Dubai. Oil was found in Sharjah as well. Drilling started quickly once oil companies from other countries arrived in the Trucial States. The economy of the UAE then improved in a dramatic way. The improvement came quickly. Great Britain ran into money problems.

7It could no longer pay to keep soldiers in the region. In 1968 Great Britain announced a plan to leave the gulf. The Trucial States decided to form a federation. Qatar and Bahrain joined that plan. They talked together about what the Trucial States would become. Qatar later chose to be its own country. Bahrain also chose to be its own country. Six of the Trucial States joined as the UAE in 1971. A seventh state joined in 1972. That seventh state was Ras al Khaimah. At that point every state was independent from Britain. Together they were the UAE. Membership in the Gulf Cooperation Council includes the UAE as well. The short name of that group is GCC. Kuwait is a member too. Bahrain, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and Oman are members as well. The GCC works together on security projects. It also works together on economic projects. One example is stronger military cooperation among the member countries. A picture shows Emirati girls carrying the national flag in a parade. The parade is on National Day. National Day is December 2. Each year the UAE marks its independence on that day. Landmarks The Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque stands in Abu Dhabi. It is one of the largest landmarks in the country. It is also one of the most famous. The mosque honors Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al-Nahyan. He helped build a strong economy for the UAE.

8At the same time he worked to keep Islamic culture. The building keeps the traditional domes of Islamic mosque style. The mosque stands for Islam's focus on respect. It also stands for love. It also stands for peace. A picture shows the Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque. Emirates Palace Hotel is another landmark of Arab culture. Royalty does not live in that hotel. Abu Dhabi is known for luxury hotels. Even among them, the palace stands out. The palace sits on 85 hectares (210 acres) of landscaped gardens. It also has 1.3 kilometers (0.8 mi.) of private beach. The palace has 348 luxury rooms. It has 14 restaurants of world-class rank. Visitors can enjoy many other offerings there too. The Burj Khalifa is a skyscraper in Dubai. Its height is an incredible 830 meters (2,723 ft.). It holds the record as the tallest building in the world. The Grand Mosque is not a fully modern building. Emirates Palace is not a fully modern building either. The Burj Khalifa is an entirely modern construction. For a growing UAE, it stands for the future of Dubai. Workers spent six years building the Burj Khalifa tower. The tower opened in 2010. Palm Jumeirah is another record-breaking landmark in Dubai. It is one of the largest islands made by humans. Seen from above, the design looks like a palm tree.

9It was first presented as the eighth wonder of the world. This top tourist spot holds four thousand luxury villas and apartments. Some people have made those homes their permanent homes. In most places, parks and ski resorts are ordinary tourist spots. In the desert country of the UAE, their presence is unusual. Their huge size makes them landmarks worth notice. A huge indoor theme park in Abu Dhabi is called Ferrari World. The park covers 86,000 square meters (925,696 sq. ft.). It was the first park built on a Ferrari theme. Visitors enjoy fast thrill rides there. They also drive miniature cars. Ski Dubai has slopes. It also has slides. It also has jumps. The snow there is made by machines. The snow park covers 3,000 square meters (32,292 sq. ft.). Conclusion The UAE has a long history. The history is interesting. Oil companies uncovered vast reserves. After that, the UAE began to flourish in its economy. Jobs and chances there drew immigrants. Immigrants are still moving to the UAE. Because of that, the culture keeps changing. The country holds on to its Arabic past. Modern citizens stay ready to build the UAE bigger. They also stay ready to build it better. Bright days appear to lie ahead for the UAE. Mosques that are hundreds of years old often stand among modern skyscrapers. That mix creates a beautiful contrast in the UAE.

10Here are key facts about the country. The population is 5,927,482. The land is 83,600 sq km (32,278 sq. mi.). The capital city is Abu Dhabi. The primary language is Arabic. The primary religion is Islam. The currency is called the UAE dirham. These facts come from the CIA World Factbook (2016). Glossary A mosque is a place of worship in the Islamic faith. Architecture is the design of buildings and the work of putting them up. Negotiated means people talked in order to reach a formal agreement. A dialect is a form of a language used in a certain region or by a certain group. Reserves are supplies set aside or stored for later use. An economy is the movement of money through industry, trade, and finance in a country or area. Rivalry is the state of competing, often for a prize or a higher standing. A federation is a large political group made of smaller groups joined by one shared goal. A shoal is high ground under the water that is dangerous to boats. Fertile describes land that produces many plants or that is able to do so. A species is a group of living things that are alike in body and can reproduce. Immigrants are people who come to live in a new country, above all so they can settle. A truce is an agreement not to fight.

55. The Award Alfred Nobel Left Behind

1No arts, science, or culture award in the world is more distinguished than the Nobel Prize. Even a nomination is treated as a once-in-a-lifetime honor. December 10, 1901, was the day the first prizes went out. Five years had passed since Alfred Nobel died. From 1901 through 2015, the winners included 874 remarkable people, called Nobel Laureates, and 26 organizations. For years, five prizes went out each year. Physics was one field. Chemistry was another. Physiology or medicine was included. Literature was included. Peace was included. Economics joined as a sixth prize in 1968. All of this came from the vision of one unusually gifted person, Alfred Nobel. Every medal shows his face on the front. The back changes with the category. Peace has its own back. Physics and chemistry share a design. Economics, literature, and physiology or medicine have their own images too. The pages ahead tell his uncommon life, the way winners are chosen, famous recipients in the sciences, in economics, in literature, and in peace, and the arguments that have followed the prize. A closing word list comes last. Alfred Bernhard Nobel was born in Stockholm, Sweden, on October 21, 1833. Caroline and Immanuel Nobel had four sons, and Alfred was one of them. Immanuel worked as an engineer and as a businessman.

2The family left Sweden for St. Petersburg, Russia, and was there by 1842. The schooling Alfred and his brothers got in that city was first-class. At seventeen his languages numbered five. They were Swedish and Russian. They also included French, German, and English. Chemistry interested him as well. Paris was where his parents sent him in 1850. The subject was chemical engineering. There he worked with nitroglycerine, a liquid that explodes with great force. It had been invented not long before. At the time, people thought it was too dangerous for practical use. The family went back to Sweden in 1859, and Alfred kept experimenting. His brother Emil also experimented with explosives. A tragic accident in 1864 killed Emil. Alfred did not quit. Soon he was making nitroglycerine in large amounts for sale, and he kept trying to make it safer. In 1866 he found a method. He mixed the liquid with very fine sand and got a paste. Packed into rods, that paste became a new explosive called dynamite. Riches and fame came at once. Tunnels, canals, roads, and railways could be built in a new way because of dynamite. War changed because of it too. Nobel thought of himself as a pacifist. The irony was sharp. He saw his own invention used in the Franco-Prussian War, fought from 1870 to 1871.

3The plan for the prizes appeared in his will, revealed after he died in 1896. The will set up a foundation to manage his fortune, invest it, and give the prizes. His family was not pleased. Lawsuits tied the will up for five years. The family lost. The Nobel Foundation was then established. The path to a prize follows a calendar. September is for getting ready to receive nominations. February is the deadline for sending them in. March through May is for building a short list. June through August is for review by advisers. October is when the laureates are chosen. December holds the award ceremony. The great honor of these prizes rests on how much research goes into the choice. Every year brings a new set of prize committees. Scholars known around the world sit on them. So do academics and scientists. Past winners sit on them too. Thousands of leaders, in every field, are invited each year to put names forward. The vote is top secret. December 10 is the day the prizes are handed over, every year. The date is the yearly remembrance of the day Nobel died. Selection and awarding, for economics, for literature, and for the sciences, are handled by three separate institutions, all in Sweden.

4Norway's own committee handles the Peace Prize. Every part of the world has sent winners. Ages vary from young to old. Men and women are both among them. Many cultures are represented. What follows is only a sample of the hundreds of winners since 1901. The first woman ever handed a Nobel Prize was Marie Curie. The year was 1903, and the field was physics. Poland was her birthplace. Most of her life was spent in France, where she worked as a researcher in science. Pierre, her husband, shared that award. Henri Becquerel shared it too. Their work was on radioactivity. A second win came in 1911. The field was chemistry. The reason was her discovery of two elements unknown before. Only two people have ever won Nobels in two different fields, and she is one of them. Her daughter also won in chemistry. No other mother and daughter have both received the prize. They were the first such pair, and they remain the only one. Few women have been awarded Nobels, especially in the sciences. Women in science, in earlier years, faced a limit on how high they could climb. New studies show that qualified women scientists are still under-represented. The picture is changing. Three science prizes in 2020, for example, went to women.

5E = mc2 is the formula. It belongs to the theory of relativity, the work of Albert Einstein. It changed the way people think about the physical world. Einstein was born in Germany. He received the prize in 1921 for work in theoretical physics. Winning let him continue a brilliant academic career. Many leading thinkers of the twentieth century felt his influence. Medicine's prize in 1945 went to Sir Alexander Fleming, who was from Scotland. The discovery was penicillin. Medicine was changed forever. Many lives were saved, and human suffering was eased around the globe. The 2015 prize in physiology or medicine went to Tu Youyou. Say the name TOO, then YOYO. She was the first scientist from mainland China to win a science Nobel. Ancient Chinese medical texts guided her work. Malaria is a deadly disease, and mosquitoes carry it. A cure came out of those old texts. The disease had grown resistant to other treatment. She tested the cure on herself before she gave it to patients. Millions of lives have been saved by what she found. Economics gained its second woman winner in 2019, Esther Duflo. No younger person had ever taken that prize. Abhijit Banerjee shared the prize. So did Michael Kremer. Their work takes on many forms of poverty around the world.

6As a team they break that complex problem into specific issues, into field experiments, and into interventions. Literature's 1993 winner, Toni Morrison, was the first African American woman to take that prize. She was also the first Black woman in the world to do so. The citation spoke of novels with visionary force and poetic import. The citation's words were these: she gives life to an essential aspect of American reality. Colombia was the birthplace of Gabriel Garcia Marquez. His voice as a writer was remarkably his own. He won in 1982. The committee praised a style in which the fantastic and the realistic are combined in a richly composed world of imagination. Influential authors have received many literature awards. These two are only examples. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. is one very famous Peace Prize winner. Mother Teresa is another. Nelson Mandela is a third. Political injustice and economic injustice were what they fought. Their aim was a better life for the people who suffered them. Dr. King's fight put civil rights at the center. He also fought so that people in the United States would be equal, whatever their color. The Peace Prize of 1964 honored that fight. A lifelong struggle brought Nelson Mandela the prize in 1993. He had opposed the repressive political system in South Africa.

7Three women shared the 2011 prize. They were Ellen Johnson Sirleaf and Tawakkol Karman. The third was Leymah Gbowee, said BOH, then ee. Liberia's president at that time was Ellen Johnson Sirleaf. Before she held office she resisted dictatorships that had ruled the country. Equality was one of her fights. Democracy was another. Leymah Gbowee is a social worker who educated herself. Women in Liberia were mobilized by her to demonstrate for peace. The country was living through years of civil war, and the wars were bloody. The journalist Tawakkol Karman is from Yemen. Demonstrations, sit-ins, and protests were the tools she led. Democratic rule was one goal. Free expression was another. Malala Yousafzai is the youngest laureate. The name is said in two beats: muh-LAH-lah, then YOO-suf-zy. Seventeen was her age in 2014, the year she received the prize. Pakistan is her home country. The Taliban had seized control in some parts of it. Education for girls was outlawed. Hundreds of schools were destroyed. Equal chances at education for women were what she fought for. The Internet was her platform. A soldier of the Taliban attacked her in 2012. The attack nearly killed her. She recovered, and she continues the fight for girls today. Some winners stir controversy. An American president, Theodore Roosevelt, got a Peace Prize in 1905.

8He had helped end a war. The two sides were Russia and Japan. Many people objected, including some members of the committee. Military power, in their view, had been used to lock in U.S. control. The places were the Philippines, Cuba, and Panama. That record, they felt, should have blocked the award. America's Secretary of State, Henry Kissinger, got the prize in 1973. He had negotiated a cease-fire while the Vietnam War was still being fought. Cambodia was not a country the United States was fighting. Critics said Kissinger had a part in bombing it in secret. His co-recipient from North Vietnam, Le Duc Tho, said LE DUK TAH, turned the prize down. He did not want to be linked with Kissinger. Questions also followed the Peace Prize given to Barack Obama. The year was 2009. Electing a Black president was groundbreaking. Critics still thought the prize came too soon after the election. He accepted the prize. The $1.4 million went to charity. Some people think the way winners are chosen is itself controversial. Norwegian politicians make up the committee that awards the Peace Prize. Critics say that makeup could bias the committee against diverse nominees from many countries and many fields. Other experts would be a better fit, critics say.

9Historians are one example. People who study politics are another. So are people who research peace. The members are politicians. Some people ask if that could tilt the prize toward anyone who might help Norway in politics. Race is another area of argument. Nobels have gone to 954 people. Asian winners number only 70. Black winners number only 17. Look through every science prize up to 2022. No Black person has received one. The award ceremony is held at the Stockholm Concert Hall. Cash is part of the reward. A diploma is another part. A gold medal, stamped with Alfred Nobel's image, is the third. An individual prize in 2015 came to eight million Swedish kronor. In U.S. dollars that was just under one million. If several people share a prize, that sum of eight million Swedish kronor is split equally. Stockholm City Hall is where the Nobel Banquet is held. That is where the prizes are given. Speeches fill part of the evening. There is dancing. There is a full concert. There is a fancy dinner. Controversy has followed the prize, yet its influence on the world has been lasting and positive. The awards put a light on the work and the dreams of great thinkers from every part of the world.

10Fame and cash let these extraordinary people keep going. Freedom is one thing the prizes honor. Peace is another. So is the commitment to better lives for humankind. A few words belong with the story. Laureates are people honored with a prize for creative or scientific achievement. Committees are groups that consider a course of action or decide on one. When people disagree about an idea or an issue, that disagreement is a controversy. A pacifist is a person against war and violence. Diversity is the quality of including many cultures or many kinds of people. Matter, motion, and energy are what physics studies, as a science. How living things work, and how their parts work, is the subject of physiology. Goods and services, and how they are made, sold, and used, are what economics studies. Radioactive waves or particles can be given off. That release, or the property of sending them out, is radioactivity. Designing machines is one job of an engineer. Building them is another, and so is repair. Buildings, bridges, and other structures fall under the same work. Afghanistan and Pakistan are the base of the Taliban, a fundamentalist Islamic group. Donated money supports a foundation. It is an organization set up to help society, or to help one particular cause.

56. The Banker Who Sent the Children to Safety

1The year on the map of Europe is 1939. This book begins with a girl who leaves home. It tells how a British banker came to Prague. It tells about Hitler and his plans. It tells how the banker asked the world for help. It tells about the trains he arranged. It tells how a secret was found. It ends with his own words. Word meanings come last. German soldiers rode military motorcycles into Prague in 1939. Prague was the capital of Czechoslovakia. Czech people stood stunned. They watched in silence. The German army's invasion is a day Vera Gissing still remembers. The day was March 15, 1939. Vera Gissing was Jewish. She was still young. She woke to the sounds of tanks. She woke to German soldiers marching through the streets. Soldiers even took over rooms in her family's home. They ordered the family to speak only German. Her father refused. A soldier spat in her father's face while she watched. It was bad. It was only the beginning. The Eberstark girls left the Prague train station that day. They never saw their parents again. Vera Gissing's story was like theirs. The day her parents sent her off is still in her memory. They hoped the trip would save her life. The day came shortly before her eleventh birthday. Dozens of other children went with her. Her best clothes were what she wore. A numbered tag hung around her neck. They stood at Prague's main train station. Engine steam rose and wrapped the families. Parents hugged their children. They kissed them. They whispered words of love. They whispered words of hope. In 2002 Gissing spoke about that morning. It was sixty-three years earlier. She said she would never forget the anguished look on her parents' faces. A 1938 picture shows a German Jewish girl holding a small bag. She clutches a doll too. She has just arrived in England. The children got on a train next. The train was bound for England. As it pulled away, Gissing tried to keep her eyes on her parents' faces. She did not know then that she would never see them again.

2She did not know that her parents would soon be sent away to die. The same fate waited for most other parents there. She also knew nothing of a stranger from Great Britain. He opened his heart to save her. Nearly fifty years passed with his actions kept secret. In 1938 Nicholas Winton was a banker in London. He was twenty-nine years old. He had big plans for his Christmas holiday. He was going to ski in the Alps. His good friend Martin Blake was going with him. The pair never reached the Alps. Blake's request to switch the trip to Prague came just before Winton left England. Organizations in Prague were where Blake was working. Those groups were giving food to thousands of Jewish families. They were giving other kinds of help too. The families had fled their homes. Germany had taken over a part of northern Czechoslovakia. That part was known as the Sudetenland. Christian organizations worked beside Jewish organizations. Youth Aliyah was one of the Jewish groups. The Children's Aid Society was another. The Kindertransport was another. They all worked to provide aid. Winton later explained why he went. He and others had talked a great deal about events in Europe. They had talked about it almost daily. The last thing he thought was that he was going there to work. This work was personal for him. He was of German-Jewish descent. His parents had decided to move to England. They had converted to Christianity. Without those choices, he and his family could have been in a desperate situation. The takeover of the Sudetenland was part of a secret plan. The plan belonged to Germany's leader, Adolf Hitler. Hitler had once been a soldier in the army. Germany's loss in World War I left him angry. That loss came in 1918. Part of the blame, in his view, sat on the Jewish people. He also blamed Black people. He blamed disabled people. He blamed LGBTQ+ people. He blamed Roma people. Jewish people were an inferior race in his belief. He believed they needed to die so they would be removed from society.

3Hitler took part in forming the Nazi Party once the war ended. That group wanted to restore Germany's power in the world. Hitler was an emotional speaker. He could excite a crowd. He became a popular leader. In time he and the Nazis grew so powerful that he was named Germany's leader. Control of the government passed into his hands. Then he started to build up the military. He also made a secret plan. His plan was to regain land taken from Germany after its loss in World War I. A picture shows him in Austria in 1938. He shouts. He gestures with great energy as he speaks to a crowd. Some people in the Sudetenland welcomed the German troops. They greeted them with a salute when the troops entered. Fear drove others out of the area. Hitler put his plan into motion in 1936. Austria was under his control by 1940. Land once given to France was now under his forces. Leaders in other European countries objected both times. No one moved to stop him. After taking Austria, he wanted the Sudetenland. That area lies along the border of Germany and Czechoslovakia. Many German-speaking people lived there. To get it, he met with leaders in 1938. The leaders were from France. They were from Great Britain. They were from Italy. All three countries were friends of the Czechs. They were allies. They had promised to protect the country. They did not like Hitler's actions. They also feared another war. His demands were met. Many people distrusted Hitler. A wider takeover of Europe was what they thought he planned. Jewish people were frightened. Germany, under Hitler, wrote many laws that targeted them. Lawyer was no longer a job Jewish people could hold. They could no longer work as doctors. They could no longer work as journalists. Those jobs are examples. Public hospitals were closed to them. They could not go to public schools after age fourteen. Marriage to a person who was not Jewish was blocked by other laws. Many photos from World War II show Jewish people wearing six-pointed stars on their clothing.

4Men wore them. Women wore them. Children wore them. The star is often made from two interlocking triangles. Another name for it is the Star of David. Judaism has used it as a symbol for thousands of years. During World War II the Nazis made a rule. The stars were required for every Jewish person. Then non-Jewish people could identify them easily. Shame was the purpose of those stars. They were meant to encourage discrimination against Jewish people. The rule applied to every Jewish person over the age of six. It applied in any country Germany controlled. Next, Hitler ordered the army to gather Jewish people who had been born in Poland. He ordered the same for Jewish people born in Russia. They were to be removed from Germany. Homes were taken from Jewish people by force. They could take only the belongings they could carry. They were loaded onto trucks. They were loaded onto wagons. They were driven to the border. They were left there. Soon after, the army kidnapped 30,000 German Jewish people. They removed them by force. They placed them in Nazi concentration camps. Prison is the closest word for what the camps were. Jewish people were sent there to live. They were sent there to work in torturous conditions. Then Hitler ordered their execution. A picture shows a family sitting in a wagon. They wear armbands that mark them as Jewish people. The removal shown here is from Krakow, Poland. These events frightened Jewish people across Europe. Leaving home was the choice many people made. They were trying to escape the danger. City camps in Prague held Jewish citizens of Czechoslovakia. The camps were short-term shelters. Rounding them up was easy for the Nazis because of that. The Nazis could take them to concentration camps. A school in Czechoslovakia was used as housing. Refugee families from the Sudetenland stayed there. Winton saw that conditions for Jewish people were terrible. New homes for Jewish people were the aim of some aid groups. He noticed where their focus sat. It sat on elderly people.

5It sat on sick people. The Jewish children of Czechoslovakia had no one working for them. Winton decided he would try to save them. In a 2002 film about his life, he described the situation. He said it was bad. The refugees felt the days were numbered. The helpers felt that too. They expected the Germans to arrive in the rest of Czechoslovakia. The people asked how they could save themselves. They asked what they could do. They asked where they should go. They were stuck. He began by basing himself in a hotel. The hotel was on Prague's Wenceslas Square. A dining-room table was his seat every day. Parents seeking safety for their children met with him. Safe homes for the children were the heart of his plan. The homes would be with families outside Czechoslovakia. A program in Germany was already using trains. The same program ran in Austria. It was called the Kindertransport. It took thousands of Jewish children to safety. Winton thought he could copy that program. Then he could save thousands of Czech children too. Word spread quickly about the Englishman of Wenceslas Square. Hundreds of Czech families arrived at the hotel. They sought his help. He hired two helpers to work with the families. Then he returned to England. Living places for the children still had to be found. He needed to raise money for their travel. In London he began writing letters. Governments in many countries received the letters. He asked them to take the children. Many countries refused. Children without parents were barred by those laws. In the end, only two countries agreed to help. One was Sweden. The other was Great Britain. England still had strict rules about bringing the children in. Winton had to find a family to take each child. The British government also said he must pay a fee. The fee would cover a later trip home for the children. That would be when they could return to Czechoslovakia. The fee was fifty pounds per child. Back then, such a fee was a small fortune. To find families, he placed ads in newspapers across Great Britain.

6He talked with churches. He printed pictures of the children. He sent the pictures all over the country. He hoped families would want to help once they saw the children's faces. At the same time he worked on permission. He needed the German government to let the children enter England. He needed the British government to allow it too. Sometimes the governments moved too slowly. Then Winton and a small team of helpers made fake permits. He said they only sped the process up a little. The pound is Great Britain's form of money. It is the currency. Fifty pounds counted as a small fortune in 1939. Fifty pounds then had a value above $3,400. In 1939, seven trainloads of children left Prague. They traveled to the coast of Holland. There they boarded a ferry. The ferry crossed the English Channel. Then they boarded a second train. That train took them to London. Winton's hard work paid off on March 14, 1939. That is when the first fifteen children left Prague. They left for Great Britain by airplane. Seven trains packed with children departed across the next six months. They left from Prague's Wilson Railway Station. Holland was where those trains carried the children. They reached the coast. There the children boarded a boat. The boat crossed the English Channel. The journey ended in the arms of new families. That meeting was at a London train station. A smiling Winton looked on. A 1939 photograph shows him holding one of the young children. He had rescued that child from Czechoslovakia. Safety was reached by 669 children in all. Some carried keepsakes from home. Some carried letters of thanks. Parents wrote those letters for the new families in Britain. Families took in most of the children. A Czech boarding school became home for many of the others. The school was in Wales. An eighth train was in Winton's plans. September 3, 1939, was the planned departure from Prague. It would carry 250 more children. On that day Hitler's army invaded Poland. All borders under German control were closed.

7The train disappeared. No one saw those children after that. A horrible military struggle came next. It lasted nearly six years. Nations around the world were pulled in. It became known as World War II. A barbed-wire fence splits male prisoners from female prisoners. The place is a German concentration camp. A guard is posted there to watch. In 1941 Hitler decided that all Jewish people must be killed. That decision was part of his war effort. Concentration camps were where millions were forced to go. Work continued until weakness killed them. Later the Nazis judged death in the camps too slow. They began murdering them instead. People call Hitler's effort to wipe out all Jewish people the Holocaust. Shoah is another name some Jewish people use. Shoah is a Hebrew word. It means a whirlwind of destruction. The camps were the place where six million Jewish people were murdered. More than a million of them were children. Non-Jewish people were murdered there too, in the millions. Among human crimes, the Holocaust stands as one of the most atrocious. The war brought a sudden end to Winton's rescue mission. Other ways to help were what he looked for. His first role was with the Red Cross. That group is a relief organization. The Royal Air Force was his next service. He became a pilot. After the war he went back to banking. He got married. He had a family. The children he had struggled to save never came up in his talk. Then, in 1988, his wife found his secret by accident. Her name was Grete. In the attic one day she came across a dusty leather briefcase. She opened it. Inside was a worn old scrapbook. It was filled with pictures of the children. Beside each photo was the child's name. There was information about the child's family in Czechoslovakia. There was a note of the British family who had taken the child in. The scrapbook also held letters. It held other papers. The papers described the work Winton had done. His story came out because Grete pressed him to speak.

8Soon a newspaper ran a story about him. That same year a British television show did a program about him. The show was called That's Life. As a surprise, rescued children were in the audience. More than two dozen of them had come to thank him. That emotional reunion included Vera Gissing. She is an author. A biography of Winton is one book she later wrote. She has written a book about her own experience. She was a child who lived through the war. She has said most Jewish children of her generation in Czechoslovakia owed their rescue to him. Very few of them met their parents again. The parents perished in concentration camps. If the children had not been spirited away, they would have been murdered alongside their parents. Descendants of those 669 children now number as many as 5,000. Those children rode his trains to safety in 1939. The children are now old. Many still call themselves Winton's Children. A picture shows some of them at a London train station. They have come to meet their rescuer. The day marks the 70th anniversary of their evacuation. In 2002 Winton got down on his knees. He was receiving one of his country's highest honors. The honor was knighthood. Once, knighthood was an honor and a title reserved for soldiers. In modern times it recognizes achievements of many kinds. Artists can receive it. Athletes can receive it. Politicians can receive it. Humanitarians can receive it. Inventors can receive it. Scientists can receive it. Other people can receive it too. The monarch performs the ceremony. Another member of Great Britain's Royal Family may perform it instead. Recipients kneel in front of the monarch at the ceremony. A sword taps each shoulder. They are also given a medal. They are given a title. Citizens of Great Britain receive a special title. The title sir is given to men. Women are given the title of dame. Winton's work has earned him many honors. The honors come from the government of Great Britain. They also come from the government of the Czech Republic. In 2002 Queen Elizabeth II made him a knight.

9That award is given for acts of bravery. It is given for service. It is given for success. A picture shows him with the medal from his knighting ceremony. Winton stands beside a train in one picture. The train repeated the last leg of the historic trip from Prague to London. In 2009 people marked seventy years since his last train. A trip repeated the journey his children had made. The path ran between Prague and London. The same path was the one that train used. Many of the people he had saved were on board. He greeted the group himself. The place was London's Liverpool Street station. He greeted them with open arms. The trip came a few months after his 100th birthday. From childhood, Vera Gissing thought of him as her savior. She just did not know who he was. For many years he felt he had not done anything that special. He felt it was not important. Only after he met Gissing did that view start to change. He met some of the others he had saved. Only then did the size of what he had made possible become clear to him. In 2002 she co-authored a book. The title is Nicholas Winton and the Rescued Generation. In it she writes about a chain of ifs. War clouds were gathering. Her parents needed courage to send their only children away. They needed strength. The children would go to unknown people in a foreign country. British families had to be found to take them in. Without those pieces, hopes and efforts would have been fruitless. Willingness to help would have been fruitless too. Nicholas Winton was the piece that made the rest matter. Because of him, she can sit in her garden. She watches her grandchildren playing. She listens to their laughter. She hears her daughter's voice calling them in for tea. It is an everyday family scene. It is a scene she can never take for granted. A candid photo shows Gissing and Winton together. Winton laughs with a boy in one picture. The boy is the grandson of a girl he saved.

10That rescue was 70 years earlier. After his secret was revealed, he spoke often. Saving the Czech children was a choice he talked about often. Nothing special was what he said he had done. He claimed that he did nothing heroic. He said that is why he never talked about it. He once said he only saw what was happening. Then he did what he could to help.
