Some of the people he saved wanted to thank him. They gave him a ring. A line is inscribed on the ring. The line comes from a book of Jewish laws. That book is known as the Talmud. The line says that to save one life is to save the world. July 1, 2015, was the day Sir Nicholas Winton died. That day was the 76th anniversary of a train journey. More children left Prague on that journey than on any other. The number was 241. These words have special meanings in this book. Inferior means lower in quality or rank. Anguished means filled with grief or pain. Jewish describes the people, the culture, or the religion. Atrocious means extremely bad, evil, or cruel. A concentration camp holds people who cannot choose to leave. The conditions are usually harsh. People are held because they belong to a specific ethnic group. They may be held as a minority. They may be held for political reasons. A keepsake is saved so an event, a person, or a place will be remembered. Perished means died. The word is used especially for a sudden, violent, or unexpected death. A generation is all the people born and living at about the same time. The word can also apply to other animals. A refugee has fled war, famine, persecution, or a natural disaster. They often have no definite place to go. Hebrew relates to the earlier people of today's Jews. Those ancestors lived in the area around Jerusalem. Spirited means smuggled or carried off secretly. During World War II the Nazis carried out the Holocaust, a planned killing aimed especially at Jewish people.

57. The Biggest Fish in the Sea

1Inside: a huge fish, a spotted pattern, life at sea, tiny meals, giant babies, staying alive, one more meeting, and words to know. A fish bigger than you expect. Picture yourself in the water off western Australia, with a snorkel on. A dark mass rises out of the deep. Closer now, the shape is clear. The animal is a shark. A school bus would match it for size. Your heart hammers. Fear is the wrong response. The shark in front of you is a whale shark. No fish on Earth grows larger. Size, for this animal, is not the same as danger. People swim next to whale sharks and come to no harm. The sharks are that calm. Swimmers speak of them as elegant. Majestic is another word swimmers use. One fact still stands. Among animals, whale sharks count as giants. How large is one? Length can reach 40 feet, which is 12.2 meters. Weight can reach 40,000 pounds, which is 18,144 kilograms. Set a person beside that shark for scale. The person in the chart stands 6 feet, or 1.8 meters. The same person weighs 175 pounds, or 79.4 kilograms. A giant checkerboard. See a whale shark once, in the sea or in a photo, and you will know it again.

2Other fish do not share this look. The head is wide. The head is flat. The snout is blunt. The mouth is huge. Swimming often happens with that mouth held open. Spots and stripes on one shark never match another shark exactly. Scientists tell individuals apart by that pattern. Rough skin is a shark trait, and whale sharks have it. Sharp scales cover them. The scales are dermal denticles. Those words mean skin teeth. Dark color covers the back. Blue can be the dark shade. Gray can be the dark shade. Brown can be the dark shade. Pale spots cross that dark back. Pale stripes cross it too. Some people compare the pattern to a checkerboard. Others compare it to a domino. Why the pattern exists is still unknown. Sunlight at the surface may be too strong, and the pattern may act as a shield. That is one idea. Camouflage is another idea. Adults grow so large that hunters seldom threaten them. Young whale sharks may still need the pattern. Blending into the water around them could keep the young ones safer. What puts a whale shark in the fish group? The whole body pushes this shark forward. Other sharks rely more on the tail and the rear of the body. A tall fin rises from the back.

3The tail fin is large as well. Each side of the body carries five wide gill slits. The mouth opens at the front of the head. On other sharks the mouth sits under the snout. Cartilage, not bone, forms the skeleton. Every shark is built that way. Most fish share a backbone. Most fish take oxygen through gills. Most fish spend their lives in water. Most fish have a tail. Most fish have fins in pairs. Most fish are cold-blooded. Most fish wear scales. Most fish lay eggs. Away from shore, and near it. Warm seas are home to whale sharks. Tropical water suits them. Warm temperate water suits them too. The Atlantic holds them. The Pacific holds them. The Indian Ocean holds them. Open water is one place they cruise. Water close to land is another. Watchers often find them at the surface. They also drop as far down as 6,000 feet. That depth is 1,829 meters. Strength is not in doubt. Speed is another matter. The shortfin mako is the fastest shark. A mako can pass 30 miles in an hour. That pace is 48 kilometers an hour. A whale shark is slow beside a mako. Long trips are still possible. The cruising pace is 2.4 miles an hour, or 3.9 kilometers an hour.

4A whale shark usually travels alone. Remoras often ride along anyway. A remora is a fish with a pad like a sucker. The pad grips the shark's body. Other big fish sometimes share the route. Those companions eat in a similar way. Parasites are fewer when remoras stay attached. The remoras gain a meal for their work. They also gain safety. Where these sharks live. A map marks Europe, Asia, and North America. It marks the Pacific and the Atlantic. It marks Africa, the equator, and the Indian Ocean. It marks South America and Australia. Shading shows where whale sharks live. Shading also shows how far they migrate. The journeys cover great distances. Nobody is sure why they go. Breeding may be the reason. Food may be the reason. Other needs may send them off as well. A common trip runs past 1,240 miles. That is 2,000 kilometers. One tracked shark covered 8,077 miles. That is 13,000 kilometers. More than three years passed during that trip. Gathering places are scattered worldwide. Scientists call them aggregation sites. The biggest site is the Afuera. Spanish speakers use that word for out, or for outside. Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula has this site off its coast. Counters once found over 400 of these sharks in that one place at a single time.

5Fish eggs, in huge amounts, were their food that day. Another big gathering showed up beside reefs. That water is called the Red Sea. These meetings are a classroom for scientists. Behavior is what they hope to read. Feeding grounds are one question. Breeding grounds are another. A huge body, a tiny meal. Most sharks chase prey. A whale shark does not. Predator is the wrong label for it. Plankton is the meal. Those are ocean plants and animals too small to see. They drift rather than swim hard. Micronekton is a second menu. Those animals are still tiny, but they can swim. Krill ranks as a favorite. A krill looks a bit like a shrimp. Small fish can enter the diet. Squid can enter it. Plants can enter it. Fish eggs can enter it. Now and then a bigger fish, such as a tuna, is eaten too. The feeding method has a name: filter feeding. The mouth opens. Seawater streams in and brings food with it. Flow continues toward the gills. Five pairs of pads, soft like sponges, catch the tiny plants and animals. Water then leaves by the gill slits on the outside of the body.

6A bit of food only 0.08 inches across can still be caught. That width is 2 millimeters. The pads do the catching. Gill slits let the water back out. Two main styles of filter feeding are known. One style is passive feeding. Ram feeding is its other name. The shark stays calm. The mouth stays open while it swims. The head swings from one side to the other. Whatever drifts in gets swallowed. Trash in the ocean gets swallowed too. The stomach can be turned inside out. It comes out through the mouth. That is how the trash leaves. Suction feeding is the second style. During suction feeding the gills pump. During passive feeding they do not. Think of a vacuum cleaner. Great gulps of water are pulled in. A thick cloud of food makes this style useful. Too much food can arrive at once. A cough may follow. Extra bits piled on the pads get cleared by that cough. Hard to believe. An open mouth on this shark can span 5 feet. That span is 1.5 meters. A person could fit inside that opening. The longest whale shark on record measured 66 feet. That is 20 meters. Line up a school bus and add half of another, and you match that length.

7Filtering power is just as startling. One Olympic pool holds 650,000 gallons of water. The same pool holds 2,460,517 liters. This shark can strain that much water in four hours. Feeding groups show up at the surface when the sun is setting. They also show up after dark. Plankton is abundant then. Smell is the likely guide to food. Scientists reached that view by studying where the nostrils sit. They also studied where the eyes sit. The nostrils sit high, close to where the mouth begins. Food passes close to that spot. The eyes are small. They sit farther back on the head. A placement like that hints at a smaller job for sight during feeding. Three hundred rows of tiny teeth line the mouth. Eating does not use those teeth. Young and grown. A newborn's length, multiplied by twenty-five, can equal an adult. Pups of giant size. Egg-laying was the old guess. The year 1995 changed the story. Live birth is what whale sharks do. A female died while she was pregnant. Inside her were more than three hundred young. People call the young pups. Each growing shark measured somewhere from 16 inches to 24 inches. That range is 42 to 63 centimeters. Some pups were further along than others.

8The further-along pups would have been born first. Human birth and whale shark birth differ in a key way. No shared blood supply links a pup to its mother. Nutrients do not pass straight from her body into the pup. An egg case wraps each baby. Yolk inside that case is the food supply before birth. The pup grows until it is ready. It breaks the case. Birth follows that break. A newborn can live without help. It is ready for the sea at once. A pup is a small copy of the adult. The pattern and the shape already match. Only size sets them apart. No scientist has watched a birth. Guesswork is all anyone has. Open ocean is the suspected birthplace. Shore water is not the leading guess. A newborn adds length faster than an older juvenile does. A female adds length faster than a male. Full-grown females are the larger sex. Maturity arrives around age thirty. Lifespan is a blank. Sharks in general last a long time. This species is enormous. A century of life is what some scientists expect from that size. Mexico's Sea of Cortez holds a scene of two snorkelers. They glide beside a young whale shark. West Papua, in Indonesia, holds another scene.

9A whale shark skims the surface and takes in plankton. The fight to survive. Hunters want the meat. They want the skin. They want the fins. They want oil from the liver. Surface swimming makes the hunt easy. Ships hit these sharks for the same reason. Nets set for other fish catch whale sharks by mistake. Dirty water is a further danger. Lost habitat is a further danger. Climate change adds more danger. Endangered is not the label yet. Vulnerable is the label. That word means the species could become endangered. A few countries cap the number that hunters may take. The cap is meant to slow the drop in numbers. Ecotourism adds another kind of help. It shows people why these animals matter. They are treasures of the planet. Small baitfish pack into a tight ball around a whale shark. Predators are the threat they are trying to dodge. A fish this large. The snorkel goes on again. This time the water is the Gulf of Mexico. A whale shark of great size comes near. Fear stays away. Wonder takes its place. The mouth opens. A bicycle, set on its length, would match that opening. Seawater rushes in. Huge gill slits pump as you watch. Tiny food is what those slits are gathering.

10Elegance shows even in a body this big. A close look at such a gentle giant feels like a privilege. Luck and local names. Japan treats the whale shark as a sign of good luck. Vietnam's name for it is Sir Fish. People there pray to the shark and ask for protection. Mexico's name is domino. Spots on the body are the reason for that name. Madagascar's name means many stars. Words to know. An aggregation is a crowd of many things, or of many animals, gathered in one place. Distinctive describes a trait that stands out and is easy to notice. Endangered describes a living thing that might vanish completely. To migrate is to leave one home region for another. The move comes at the same season each year. Passive describes something that is not taking action. Plankton are very small plants and animals. They live at the ocean surface or just under it. A predator hunts other animals and eats them in order to live. Reproduction is how living things make young. A snout is the nose and mouth together on an animal's face. Solitary describes one animal on its own. Temperate describes a place with mild weather. Vulnerable describes something that can be harmed with ease.

58. The Black Death Crosses Europe

1A map shows how the Black Plague spread by year. The places marked include Lubeck, Amsterdam, London, and Danzig. They include Paris, Kiev, Vienna, and Nuremberg. They include Venice, Bordeaux, Marseille, and Genoa. They include Ragusa, Barcelona, Valencia, and Naples. They include Rome and Constantinople. The map also marks the Atlantic Ocean, the Black Sea, and the Mediterranean Sea. The year bands are 1347 CE, 1348 CE, 1349 CE, 1350 CE, and 1351 CE. Some places are marked as mostly unaffected. The parts of this book come in this order. First is The Plague Ships. Then come The Fleas of Disease and Death Stalks Europe. Panic and a Prayer follows. Then come The Aftermath and Rebirth. A glossary closes the book. The Plague Ships The scene must have been staggering. The smell must have been staggering too. A dozen trading ships entered Messina's port in October 1347. Messina is in Sicily, part of modern-day Italy. The ships had made a long voyage across the Black Sea. Ships like these often carried news from the East. They often carried exotic goods too. Their arrival likely caused excitement around the docks. The people who greeted them got the shock of their lives. They may also have met the cause of their deaths. Most of the crew on the ships were dead. The sailors still working the ropes and sails were in agony. Pus and blood oozed from black boils on their skin. The citizens of Messina had heard rumors. The rumors told of a terrible disease spreading in Asia. These ships and sailors brought a deadly cargo to Europe.

2The cargo was invisible. It was the plague. This outbreak was later called the Black Death. It spread rapidly across Europe. It also spread across North Africa. Strangers passed it to strangers without knowing. Friends brought it to friends. Ships carried it to ports that did not expect it. There it found fresh victims. Tens of millions died from it. Rich people were not safe. Poor people were not safe. Royalty was not safe. Peasants were not safe. History records few disease outbreaks that were worse. The Fleas of Disease In the 1300s, no one had yet linked germs with illness. People did not know that bacteria could cause a cold, the flu, or other sickness. They did not know that viruses could do so either. No one had linked the plague with fleas. The link came only in 1894. That was almost 550 years later. Scientists identified the likely culprit. It was a bacterium called Yersinia pestis. These bacteria enter the digestive tract of a kind of flea. That flea feeds mainly on the blood of black rats and other rodents. Many historians believe the bacteria began killing the rodent colonies they normally lived in. The fleas then had to look for other warm-blooded creatures to feed on. Humans were among those creatures. A step chart shows how rats and fleas helped spread the plague. First, a rodent is infected. A flea bites the rodent. Plague bacteria multiply in the flea's gut. The flea bites a person. The person is infected.

3Poor public sanitation in the 1300s did not help. Poor human hygiene did not help either. Cities were overcrowded. Human waste was often dumped in the streets. Garbage was dumped there too. Bugs were regular guests in houses. Flea bites, and bites from other pests, were an unpleasant part of daily life. Some researchers doubt that fleas alone caused the Black Death. Some are not convinced fleas were even the main source. Many other diseases could cause deadly outbreaks. Cholera was one. Typhus was another. Some researchers argue that the 1347 outbreak spread too fast. They argue that it killed too quickly to be Yersinia pestis. They wonder if the Black Death was a deadlier microbe. That microbe, they say, has not been identified yet. Even so, Yersinia pestis remains the leading suspect. The case rests on descriptions of the symptoms written by people of the time. Archaeologists have also found the DNA of these bacteria. The DNA was in mass burial sites from the mid-1300s. People clearly began to give this deadly disease straight to each other. A person's pus could infect others it touched. Blood could infect others. Saliva could infect others. A simple cough could pass the sickness to the next victim. A handshake could do so too. Once contact between people began spreading the disease, it became all but unstoppable. Death Stalks Europe No treatment then worked against an illness as serious as the plague. After infection, three to five days passed before the bacteria showed themselves. As the illness ran its course, victims had headaches.

4They had fever and chills. They had diarrhea and vomiting. They had swelling and intense pain. They might die quickly. They might live another three to five days. Historians think just one person in five lived after the symptoms appeared. The plague was so deadly partly because it could appear in more than one form. Bubonic plague begins when Yersinia pestis bacteria strike the lymph nodes. The nodes are in the neck, the groin, and the underarms. Lymph nodes are vital organs of the immune system. They let the body battle disease. In response to the attack, the lymph nodes swell. They blacken with poisoned blood and pus. They become boils called buboes. The infected blood and other fluids eventually poison the victim. Then they kill the victim. Pneumonic plague also seems to have been a form of the Black Death. Victims of pneumonic plague do not develop buboes. Instead, bacteria attack their lungs. The lungs bleed heavily. That heavy bleeding is called hemorrhage. Tiny drops of blood or saliva can also carry pneumonic plague. Those drops become airborne when infected people cough. Some experts wonder if this is the form that let the Black Death spread so fast. People with bubonic or pneumonic plague could also develop septicemic plague. The word is said sep-teh-SEE-mik. In that form, bacteria multiplied in the blood. This form poisoned the victim's bloodstream. It was almost always fatal. The Black Death moved through Europe by 1348. Travelers carried it to new areas. Traders carried it. Trading ships carried it.

5Weeks often passed before a sick village, town, or city saw how terribly wrong things were. Action was no longer possible by that point. By 1351 the Black Death had arrived in nearly every part of Europe. A picture shows filthy, crowded medieval towns. Those conditions let the plague spread very quickly. Panic and a Prayer Once people realized the plague had reached their community, many panicked. Terrified families abandoned loved ones who were sick. Shopkeepers shut their doors. Doctors fled the places and people they served. Clergy fled too. Officials fled as well. City people escaped to the countryside. They thought it would be safer there. By fleeing, they often helped spread the disease. No one understood the causes of the Black Death. Because of that, few people had effective ideas about how to fight it or control it. Desperate people tried useless cures. Some strapped a skinned chicken to the buboes. Some drank potions made from unicorn horn. Swindlers sold those potions. Some burned incense. Some wore flowers to purify the air. Hoping to be saved, many people looked to their faith. Flagellants, who were bands of Christians, went from one town to another. They bloodied their backs with spiked whips. They prayed that their actions would prove something to God. They wanted God to see that they were sorry for their sins. They hoped to be forgiven. They hoped to be spared. A very different view of fate was taken by other Europeans. Some people lost hope of living, with so much sickness and death around them.

6Eating, drinking, and parties filled their days, as though the world were about to end. Some were sure that it was. Christian groups in many places falsely held Jews responsible for the plague. Many Jewish communities were attacked. Their people were driven off or killed. Pope Clement VI was the head of the Catholic Church. He issued a declaration. It made clear that Jews were not at fault. It said they should not be victimized. Even so, Europe lost more than two hundred Jewish communities in the mid-1300s. A few cities used common sense instead. They tried to control the disease. Port cities soon saw that arriving ships could carry contagion. They began to block ships that came from areas infected by plague. Some port authorities set rules. Ships had to wait forty days before they could dock. The waiting period is called quarantine. It was meant to confirm that the crew was free of plague. Only then could the crew meet local residents. Leaders in some areas also figured out a key point. The best chance to slow the spread was to stop people from moving. Families who were infected could not leave their homes. Officials set limits on travel to and from their cities. They set limits on trade too. Work crews hurried to bury victims as soon as possible. Burials were often in mass graves. People feared that the corpses could infect others. The Aftermath Picture a town or city with half its people missing. Imagine shops closed. Imagine stores empty of food.

7Many survivors of the Black Death's worst years lived through that kind of loss. That period ran from 1347 to 1353. Record-keeping in medieval Europe was spotty. Historians can only estimate the death count. Europe held about eighty million people before the Black Death arrived. Experts figure that a shocking 40 to 60 percent of them died. The death rate varied greatly by location. In Spain, 75 to 80 percent of the people may have died from the plague. In southern France, the rate may have been the same. In Germany, the rate may have been closer to 20 percent. England's rate may also have been nearer to 20 percent. Cities were usually the hardest hit. The disease spread easily in crowded, dirty neighborhoods. Nearly 60 percent of Londoners died. Half the residents of Paris died as well. After 1351 the outbreak eased. Scholars are still investigating the reasons. Survivors may have built up immunity to the disease. The bacteria may instead have changed into a form that was less deadly. For the next five hundred years, plague returned many times. None ever matched the devastation of the Black Death. Europe was a very different place after the mid-1300s. Workers were missing in very large numbers. Skilled artisans were absent. Laborers were absent too. That absence caused a crisis in manufacturing. Workers could therefore ask for better pay. They were able to demand better treatment. There were not enough peasants to work the fields. Crops were left unplanted. Crops were left unharvested. Livestock died from the plague.

8Livestock also died from a lack of tending. As a consequence, Europeans suffered widespread food shortages. They suffered starvation. Even so, peasants gained more power to bargain. Some moved away from their home villages. They went where they were offered better opportunities. The aftermath of the Black Death also changed how survivors thought. It changed their views of society. It changed their views of the meaning of life. Many questioned their belief in religion. They questioned the church. Some challenged their leaders. They challenged their lords. They challenged their kings. The authority of powerful people had proved useless. Those people had not protected the people they controlled and ruled. There were many examples of important progress in Europe after the plague. Agriculture improved. Farmers tried better practices. They tried better equipment. The goal was to grow more food with fewer hands. Public health saw positive changes. Medicine saw positive changes too. More communities saw the importance of sanitation. They put in place better ways to limit outbreaks. They put in place better ways to treat them. A picture shows the invention of the heavy plow. The heavy plow helped end food shortages after the plague years. It let farmers till fields much faster. Horses pulled the plow. Horses, rather than oxen, pulled the plow. Rebirth Another Black Death outbreak is all but impossible because of modern science. Modern medical care has done so too. Plague bacteria are still out there. They live in the fleas of some rodent colonies. Antibiotics can quickly stop most cases. Antibiotics are medicines designed to kill harmful microbes in the body.

9Modern sanitation also helps control the spread of most forms of disease. Public health programs help as well. A picture shows Alexander Fleming. Antibiotics: The Miracle Drug Antibiotics are a recent development in human history. Before the mid-1800s, some healers recognized a useful fact. Certain plant molds and other fungi attacked bacteria. Further study in the 1800s brought clearer knowledge. People learned more about the link between microbes and disease. Then, in the 1920s, Alexander Fleming made an accidental discovery. This Scottish biologist found a plant mold. The mold destroyed a dangerous form of bacteria. Out of his research came the wonder drug penicillin. Penicillin can kill many forms of bacterial infection. In 1945 the Nobel Prize in Medicine went to Fleming. The prize honored his breakthrough work. The Plague Population Crash Europe's population needed two hundred years to recover after the plague. A chart shows European population in millions. The years on the chart run from 1000 to 1700. The steps are 1000, 1100, 1200, 1300, 1400, 1500, 1600, and 1700. The chart marks the start of the Black Death. It also marks the time when the population recovers. The data source is William Langer, The Black Death, 1964. In the mid-1300s, the mystery of the Black Death terrified many Europeans. The horror terrified them too. Many came to believe the end of the world was upon them. No event in European history killed more people, if death rates are the measure. Some historians also connect that ruin with the Renaissance.

10The Renaissance period soon followed. It lasted from the late 1300s until the 1600s. The Renaissance was a huge cultural shift in Europe. It inspired great advances in medicine. It inspired great advances in science. It inspired great advances in art. It inspired great advances in philosophy. Renaissance means rebirth in French. After the horror of the Black Death, Europe needed a period of rebirth. That is precisely what the Renaissance was. Glossary The immune system moves antibodies through the body to fight infection. Bacteria are tiny living things made of one cell, and they sometimes cause infection and disease. Infect means to spread a disease-causing organism to another person, animal, or plant. Contagion is an illness spread by direct or indirect contact. The word also means the process by which such an illness spreads. A microbe is an organism so small it can be seen only with a microscope. Digestive describes the action of breaking down food for the body to use. Sanitation means the work and the tools used to keep a place clean or to take waste away. DNA is a code holding the genetic information of a living thing. The letters stand for deoxyribonucleic acid. Symptoms are specific signs of illness or injury. Exotic means different because of a mysterious or unusual quality. It can also mean from another country or a faraway place. Viruses are microscopic organisms that infect the body. The word also means diseases caused by a virus. Hygiene is cleanliness for the purpose of staying healthy.

59. The City Where the Gods Were Made

1A map places Teotihuacán in Mexico, in North America. The map marks the United States and the Gulf of Mexico. It marks the volcanoes Xitle and Popocatépetl. It marks Belize, Mexico City, and Guatemala. It also marks South America and the Pacific Ocean. The Pyramid of the Sun is one of the two biggest structures at Teotihuacán. The Pyramid of the Moon is the other. The parts of this book come in this order. First is Inspiring Awe. Then comes The Americas' First Great City. After that part, the book turns to the Pyramid of the Sun and the Pyramid of the Moon. Solving the Mysteries follows. Then come Centuries of Greatness and Collapse. Teotihuacán Today comes next. Discoveries Continue follows that part. A glossary closes the book. Inspiring Awe Almost two thousand years ago, an ancient people built the great pyramids of Teotihuacán. The name is said tay-oh-tee-wah-KAHN. They built them where modern-day Mexico is located. The people who built these huge structures are still unknown. What is known is that the site was planned to fill people with awe. It has done so for over a millennium. The Avenue of the Dead leads to the pyramids. The avenue is as wide as a highway with eleven lanes. Massive stone temples stand on both sides of the avenue. Palaces stand there too. In 1320 the Aztec people came upon the ruins. They named them Teotihuacán. The name means the place where the gods were created. Later, the Spanish were the first of their people to gaze upon the pyramids. They asked who had built them. Locals said a race of giants had built them. The locals said the giants came from the heavens long ago. To this day, tourists examine the pyramids of Teotihuacán.

2Scientists examine them too. They wonder about the creators. Teotihuacán's Ceremonial Center The base of the Pyramid of the Moon covers 20,280 square meters (217,686 sq. ft.). The pyramid rises 43 meters (141 ft.). Nearby stand the Palace of the Quetzalpapalotl and the Plaza of the Moon. Quetzalpapalotl is said ket-sahl-pah-PAH-loht-l. The center also holds the Pyramid of the Sun and the Plaza of the Columns. Some parts of the Avenue of the Dead are 95 meters (312 ft.) across. Among old pyramids, the Pyramid of the Sun ranks third for size. Other places in the center are the Yahualo Palace and the Zacuala Palace. The San Juan River crosses the area. The Citadel measures about 400 meters (1,300 ft.) on each side. The Temple of Quetzalcoatl stands there too. Quetzalcoatl is said ket-sahl-KOH-aht-l. Visitors at the top of the Pyramid of the Moon can look out over the long Avenue of the Dead. The Aztecs named that avenue. They mistook the structures beside it for tombs. The Americas' First Great City Teotihuacán is known around the world for its massive pyramids. This old city was among the early places where many people lived close together. At its zenith it was one of the biggest. Its population was one hundred thousand to two hundred thousand people. It was the largest city in the Americas. It was probably the sixth largest city on Earth. A grid sets the line of every building in this carefully planned city. Every avenue, road, and plaza is aligned to that grid too. The builders even shifted the path of the San Juan River. They set the river to cross the Avenue of the Dead at a right angle. The change made the river fit the grid.

3Teotihuacán was a religious center. It was a trade center too. Its new ideas in agriculture influenced Mesoamerica for centuries. Its ideas in art, architecture, and housing did so too. Even its ideas in fashion did so. Pyramid of the Sun The base of the Pyramid of the Sun is about 220 by 230 meters (720 by 760 ft.). The height is more than 66 meters (216 ft.). It is the largest structure in the ancient city. It is the third-largest ancient pyramid in the world. The builders placed it at an exact point on the horizon. That point is where the Sun sets on August 13. That placement sets the pyramid 15.5 degrees east of true north. The Avenue of the Dead was built with that same orientation. The whole city was built that way too. Why the builders made this choice is still unknown. One theory says the builders wanted to line the structures up with the movements of the Sun. Archaeologists found a cave under the pyramid in 1971. Evidence suggests a belief held by the people of Teotihuacán. They believed caves were where the gods were born. Artifacts found in the cave showed an earlier use. The cave was a sacred shrine before the pyramid was built. Around 100 ce is a possible start for work on the Pyramid of the Sun. The work took more than one hundred years. Workers hauled 764,000 cubic meters of heavy rock and other materials. That amount is about 1 million cubic yards. They hauled it by hand. They had no wheelbarrows. They had no animals to help. They used the material to build the stepped platforms. Thousands of people gathered broken pottery.

4They gathered other rubble too. They filled the core of each platform with rubble. They sealed the walls with clay bricks. On the surface they laid stone blocks. They covered the blocks with a thick layer of plaster. At the end, artists covered the pyramid with bright murals. No other site in Mesoamerica has more temples and palaces than Teotihuacán. A close look at the Palace of Quetzalpapalotl shows how intricate the carvings are. The Great Goddess Statue is linked with rainwater. It first stood in front of the Pyramid of the Moon. Today the statue is kept at the National Museum of Anthropology in Mexico City. Pyramid of the Moon The Pyramid of the Moon is not far from the Pyramid of the Sun. It is the second-largest structure in Teotihuacán. A rise at the head of the Avenue of the Dead is where this pyramid stands. Cerro Gordo frames it from behind. Cerro Gordo means Fat Hill. It is an oversized hill. Streams from the hill were important sources of precious water. That water kept the city going. In front of the pyramid is a huge plaza. Platforms flank the plaza. Temples once stood on those platforms. Thousands of the city's people could fit easily in the Plaza of the Moon. Local leaders could watch ceremonies in grand comfort from the many temple platforms. Visiting leaders could do so too. No records of the ceremonies have been discovered. Archaeologists have uncovered the remains of people buried inside the pyramid. The people were bound. They were sacrificed. They were buried with valuable objects made of jade. They were also buried with objects of obsidian. Obsidian is a volcanic rock that looks like glass. People used it to make sharp blades for tools and weapons.

5Researchers also found the remains of sacrificed animals. The animals were ones respected as powerful killers. They include pumas, rattlesnakes, and a wolf. Birds of prey were buried there too. Those birds include eagles, a falcon, and an owl. Evidence suggests a belief of the people of Teotihuacán. They believed the gods would send rain if these sacrifices were offered. How the Pyramid of the Moon Grew Archaeologists found that the Pyramid of the Moon was built again many times. It may have been rebuilt eight times. The first structure was begun around 1 ce. It was just a small platform. After 350 years it had become a stepped pyramid. It was about 46 meters (151 ft.) high. A temple stood on top. Solving the Mysteries The people who planned Teotihuacán are a mystery. The people who built it are a mystery too. Today we call those people Teotihuacanos. The Aztecs used that name as well. We do not know what the people called themselves. We do not know what they called their city. We do not even know what language they spoke. We do not know where they were from. We do not know the names of any of their rulers. Teotihuacanos used glyphs to name people and places. Glyphs are a form of picture writing. No one has yet figured out how to read them. No one has figured out how to interpret them either. Instead, archaeologists have studied the structures. They want to learn about the people who lived there. One mural at the site pictures a rain god together with a priest. The first Teotihuacano settlers arrived around 400 bce. Their community stayed small for hundreds of years.

6Teotihuacán lies in the northeastern part of the Basin of Mexico. That location was good for farming. The basin is wide and flat. It has good soil. Water comes from the mountains around it. These factors made ideal conditions for growing food for a rising population. The crops were corn, beans, and squash. They were also tomatoes, avocados, and chili peppers. The city's location was also great for trade. A break in the nearby mountains let merchant caravans pass in and out of the basin. Teotihuacán's people traded goods with the great Maya civilization to the south. They exchanged goods with the Gulf Coast cultures to the east. Merchants traded cotton and shells from those other regions. In return they offered valuable obsidian from Teotihuacán. These advantages let Teotihuacán grow. The growth was slow. Then, in the first century ce, the nearby volcano Popocatépetl erupted. The name is said poh-poh-kah-TEH-pet-l. The eruption caused tens of thousands of people to move. A large share of those people moved north and settled in Teotihuacán. A second great wave of immigrants came later. It followed the eruption of nearby Xitle around 320 ce. Xitle is said SHEET-lay. The population grew with these waves of immigrants. The newcomers brought unique skills. They brought unique cultures. Those skills and cultures enriched the city further. Evidence about farming suggests another practice. Teotihuacanos turned nearby wetlands into farms with raised beds. Canoes used the channels between the beds. The canoes carried produce into the city. The ruins of Teotihuacán include stone walls of temples. They include stone walls of other buildings too. Centuries of Greatness By the year 200 ce, the population was very large. A massive building program began. The program was innovative. The plan included more than two thousand apartment compounds.

7All of them were built along the city grid. These new structures were built for everyone. Farmers lived in them. Merchants lived in them. Laborers lived in them, including immigrants. They were not only for the wealthy. The compounds were large. They were spacious. They were expertly built of stone. They were painted with bright murals. The compound wall had only one grand door. Inside were beautiful courtyards. Inside were communal kitchens. Inside was a temple. Inside were fifty or more rooms. Those rooms housed between sixty and one hundred people. Fresh water was brought in from a reservoir. Drains took wastewater away. In Teotihuacán, daily life for ordinary people was very good. As the city grew, more immigrants came. Some evidence suggests that potters came from southern Mexico. They lived and worked in one neighborhood. Skilled textile workers came from the Gulf Coast. They settled in another neighborhood. A neighborhood of Maya people stood there too. All the neighborhoods competed. They tried to make the finest goods. They tried to offer the rarest imports. Part of a mural from a compound shows a chanting priest. A carving of a warrior was found at Teotihuacán. Sculptors carved stone heads that weigh 4 tons (3.6 metric tons). The heads are on a temple built in 200 ce. Some of the immigrants brought feathers to Teotihuacán. They brought shells. They brought incense. They brought cacao beans for making chocolate. The city became a center for art. It became a center for luxury goods of all kinds. By 500 ce the area of Teotihuacán was 20 square kilometers (8 sq. mi.). Trade roads from the city went as far as the Honduras of today. They reached Guatemala too.

8Teotihuacán was a wealthy city. Archaeologists found no signs of military structures. Their first question was whether this kingdom might have been peaceful. Today we know a different story. Murals show that warriors were plentiful. The murals show that the warriors were effective. Both commoners and wealthy men took part in battles. They did so in large numbers. They had deadly weapons. They had large shields. They dressed as deadly animals. A picture from 1895 shows the ruins overgrown with plants. That was before excavation began. Collapse The city had thrived for more than 650 years. Then a hard period may have come. There may have been long droughts. There may have been crop failures. There may have been hunger among poor people. The result may have been a drop in population. Researchers think the Teotihuacanos may have used up resources such as wood. Then, in 550 ce, outsiders attacked. They burned the temples and the palaces. Statues that stood in the city's ceremonial center were broken. Invaders may have been to blame. There may instead have been a rebellion from within. People still lived at Teotihuacán after that. It was only a much smaller town. The great pyramids were nearly completely abandoned. The temples were abandoned too. They fell into ruin for more than a thousand years. Teotihuacán Today Archaeologists began a major restoration of Teotihuacán in 1905. Tons of dirt and weeds were cleared from the Pyramid of the Sun. Through the 1900s, other major structures were slowly restored. Today, millions of visitors come every year. They explore the ancient city. Climbers go up 248 steep steps to reach the top of the Pyramid of the Sun. The view from the top is thrilling. For safety, tourists may no longer go past the first platform of the Pyramid of the Moon.

9Even that platform gives a grand view. The view looks down on the plaza. It looks along the length of the Avenue of the Dead. People walking the site may notice archaeologists busy with their work. The work of excavation continues. The work of preservation continues too. So far, careful digging by scientists has opened only 5 percent of the city. In 1987 Teotihuacán was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Today it is the most studied site in Mesoamerica. About 30 centimeters (1 ft.) is the rise of every step on the Pyramid of the Sun. In the museum, visitors can see beautiful artifacts that were dug up at Teotihuacán. One example is an incense burner. Millions of visitors hike to many ruins in and around the city. They also hike to archaeological zones there. All that traffic causes a lot of wear on the site. Natural forces cause wear too. Rain is one. Wind is another. New developers are another threat that can destroy parts of the site. In 2004 one developer got permission to build. The ground had once been part of the great city. By law, the company had to report any artifacts dug up during construction. It found artifacts. It did not report them. Instead, the company used heavy machines to dig. It threw away priceless artifacts in order to save time. Years of legal battles followed. A picture shows an archaeologist looking at an image. A small robot took the image under a temple. Discoveries Continue In 2013 archaeologists sent a robot through a small tunnel. The robot carried a camera. The tunnel led to a chamber under the Temple of Quetzalcoatl.

10The robot went there to take pictures. Hundreds of spheres filled one chamber, as the photos showed. A mineral powder covered the spheres. The powder gave them a golden glow. The whole chamber glowed like gold too. That glow was on the walls. It was on the ceiling. Long ago, everything in the chamber would have looked brilliant under torchlight. Masks were there too. Crystals and jade covered the masks. Archaeologists were stumped about the purpose of the golden chamber. They keep exploring the many tunnels under the pyramids. They keep finding new artifacts. The finds include a collection of obsidian knives. They include carvings of coiled jaguars. Perhaps one day archaeologists will finally learn who lived in ancient Teotihuacán. They may also learn who ruled there. Glossary Aligned means lined up with something, or arranged in a line. Mesoamerica is the region of Mexico and Central America that native civilizations occupied before Columbus arrived and before European colonization. Archaeologists are scientists who study the remains of ancient cultures. A millennium is a period of one thousand years. Artifacts are any objects that humans made or used long ago. Oriented means set in relation to something else, such as a direction on a compass or a landmark. Caravans are lines of people traveling together, often with vehicles or animals. A rebellion is a fight against authority or power. It is an uprising. Excavation is the process of uncovering something or digging it out. Restoration is the act of returning something to its original condition. Innovations are new ideas, new products, or new ways of doing something. Zenith means the highest point. It is the time when something is the greatest or the most successful.

60. The Corps of Discovery Heads West

1Canada, the United States, and Mexico all appear on a map of this journey. So do the Atlantic Ocean and the Gulf of Mexico. Missouri is the state where St. Louis marks the start. Fort Clatsop marks the far western camp. The way west belongs to the years 1804 and 1805. The way home in 1806 did not follow one single path. Borders of today's states can be drawn on that same map. The opening of this book is the start of the journey. Later parts take up the many nations of North America. The Louisiana Purchase comes next, and so does Jefferson's plan. Then come the Corps of Discovery, the Great Plains crossing, and the winter stop. A short close and some word meanings finish the book. The date was May 25, 1804. Travelers known as the Corps of Discovery went past the edge of the United States. Lands governed by Indigenous peoples lay on the other side. White men in the group numbered about forty. An enslaved Black man traveled with them. Later, people gave the journey the name Lewis and Clark Expedition. About two years passed before the trip was done. The miles they traveled numbered more than 8,000 (12,875 km). St. Louis, Missouri, was the starting city. The Pacific Ocean was the far point. After that, the travelers turned around and came back. More than fifty Indigenous tribes met them on the way. Notes were kept about the land.

2Notes were kept about plants. Notes were kept about animals. To the U.S. government, the trip was a bold look at land soon to be opened for settlement. For Indigenous peoples, what followed was nearly a century filled with invasion, with war, and with forced assimilation. Exploration made the expedition an adventure. Science made it a survey. The army made it a military mission. In later years that mission helped the United States push farther west. A new chapter of colonization began. Indigenous nations named for this story can be placed on a map. One name is Jiwére, also called Oto. Numakiki, also called Mandan, appears with Kaw, also called Kansa. Hiraacá, also called Hidatsa, is on the map. So is Apsáalooke, also called Crow. So is Niutachi, also called Missouri. Oceti Sakowin, also called Sioux, includes the Dakota, the Lakota, and the Nakota. Tsitsistas, also called Cheyenne, is named as well. Canada, the United States, and the Atlantic Ocean frame the map. Borders of today's states can be shown too. Lands long used by these nations often lay on top of one another. Those lands also moved as years passed. By 1803, North America's political map was not the map we know. The United States then covered only a little more ground than the first thirteen colonies. Other nations stood along its edges. British colonies called the Canadas lay straight north. Only the southeasternmost part of modern Canada was inside those colonies.

3Indigenous peoples still held the rest. Nations now called the Five Tribes bordered the United States to the south and the southwest. The five were the Cherokee, the Chickasaw, the Choctaw, the Muscogee, also called Creek, and the Seminole. Parts of European life had been mixed into their own ways. Those parts were European government, money, religion, writing, and slavery. Hundreds of other Indigenous nations lived to the west, and each was independent. Each one had a political system of its own, and those systems were complex. The French Empire claimed the eastern half of this huge region governed by Indigenous peoples. The claimed region carried the name Louisiana Territory. Europeans had settled only a tiny share of it. Most of that land was still home to Indigenous peoples. A second map can show the United States before the Louisiana Purchase. It can show the land added by that purchase. Borders of today's states can sit on it too. Control over Indigenous nations in the West was what U.S. President Thomas Jefferson wanted. He was afraid France would stand in the way. He hoped to cut some of France's power in North America. His question to France was about one city. Would France sell New Orleans, the key port, to the United States? France came back with a larger offer. The whole Louisiana Territory was for sale. The price was 15 million dollars.

4In today's money that price is about 310 million dollars. Enslaved Black people had just won a revolt. That revolt pushed France out of the land now called Haiti. France had almost no money left. Cash mattered more to France than land did. Indigenous peoples were living on the land that was sold. They did not accept France as the owner. France's real offer was a promise. France would not step in when the United States tried to take control of the Indigenous nations there. Jefferson did not wait to plan a look at the new territory. Money for the Lewis and Clark Expedition was approved by Congress before the purchase was even finished. The approved path ran all the way to the Pacific Ocean. That ocean sat well outside the Louisiana Territory. Taking Indigenous land in the West would be easier after this expedition. The men had orders to hunt for a water path. That path would join the Atlantic Ocean with the Pacific Ocean. Careful maps were also required. Plants they met had to be written down. Animals they met had to be written down. Congress wanted to know how the lands might earn money. Congress also wanted those lands for U.S. settlement. Jefferson had one more aim. He wanted Indigenous peoples to start coming under the control of the United States. At each new meeting, the men said the people must obey the laws of the Great Father.

5The Great Father was their name for the president of the United States. Gifts were handed out. Guns were then fired into the air so military strength would be plain to see. Coins called Jefferson Peace Medals went from the corps to Indigenous leaders. Jefferson's way of dealing with Indigenous peoples shaped these orders. He hoped talk would lead Indigenous peoples to give their lands up for U.S. settlement. He also hoped they would leave traditional cultures behind. European Christian customs were what he wanted in their place. In private he spoke of the army. If they resisted, the army would drive them off their lands or kill them. The gifts had a purpose of their own. Jefferson wanted Indigenous peoples to see good in goods made in the United States. He hoped they would then let trading posts into their communities. Those posts were a trick that pulled Indigenous peoples into debt. Officials at the posts let Indigenous customers take goods. Payment could wait, the customers were told. Later the officials said the sums owed were huge. The army then forced the debts to be cleared. The payment demanded was land, which had to be given to the United States. Jefferson picked his own secretary to lead. That man was Captain Meriwether Lewis. The group he led would be known as the Corps of Discovery. Lewis asked Captain William Clark to lead beside him.

6Clark was a friend, and he had once commanded Lewis. Both men had already fought Indigenous peoples. Those fights were wars to take more land after the United States broke free from Britain. The expedition was organized like an army mission. Soldiers and hired boatmen made up the members, with one exception. The exception was York, a Black man. Clark held York in slavery. Military uniforms stayed on every enlisted member for the whole trip. Lewis chose only men who were not married. He chose men whose health was good. He chose men who could stay alive in wild country. To get ready, Lewis studied medicine, astronomy, plants, and animals. York's parents were enslaved on a plantation in Virginia. He was born there in the late 1770s. In 1799 the legal claim to York passed to Clark. Claims to other enslaved people passed to Clark in that same year. York had to join the Corps of Discovery. His job was to serve as Clark's body servant. He was the expedition's only Black member. Hostility and aggression from the other men were regular parts of his days. Even so, the trip opened chances other enslaved people did not get. Training with firearms was one of those chances. At first meetings with Indigenous peoples, York often stood as a representative. Louisville, Kentucky, is where a statue of York stands. Camp Dubois in Illinois was the official starting camp.

7The date was May 14, 1804. Boats headed up the Missouri River. Eleven days later, the farthest west U.S. settlement on the river was behind them. Indigenous lands lay ahead. Bad behavior showed up in the early days. Some men slept while they were supposed to be on duty. Some men tried to run off. Order was kept with harsh physical punishments from Lewis and Clark. In the first months, the nations they met already knew white people well. Those white people were usually trappers or merchants. Many people there understood English. Little of note happened at those meetings. The lands they passed belonged to the Kaw, the Jiwére, the Niutachi, and the Dakota. Dakota lands meant the corps had entered Oceti Sakowin territory. Two-thirds of the Great Plains, on the northern side, lay inside that confederacy. Deeper in those lands, Teton Lakota leaders asked for a toll. The toll was the price of crossing their territory. Payment was refused by Lewis and Clark. The Lakota also had a suspicion. They thought the corps meant to sell firearms to Lakota enemies farther upriver. An argument followed. Weapons were drawn on both sides. Calm returned because of Lakota chief Black Buffalo. Three days passed with the corps among the Lakota. An agreement then let them continue up the river. Oceti Sakowin means The Seven Council Fires. The Lakota, the Dakota, and the Nakota make up this confederacy. Outsiders often use the name Sioux Nation.

8When Lewis and Clark traveled, this confederacy was one of the Great Plains' strongest powers. The strength was political, economic, and military. Their life followed bison herds that moved with the seasons. Across North America, few riders matched their skill or their fame. In the United States today, the Oceti Sakowin ranks among the largest Indigenous nations. Their languages are still kept. Their cultures are still kept. They still care for lands that have always been theirs. One picture shows a Lakota boy. He is protesting building work on sacred Lakota land. A month after the Lakota meetings, the corps reached two allied nations. Those nations were the Numakiki and the Hiraacá. A huge trade network had its center there. Its reach started at the East Coast and continued past the Rocky Mountains. White traders who brought enslaved Black people were already a familiar sight. The Numakiki and the Hiraacá treated the corps in a friendly way. Winter was close. The corps chose to stay until spring. They built a stronghold and gave it the name Fort Mandan. At that fort, Lewis and Clark asked what the river ahead would be like. They asked the Numakiki and the Hiraacá. They learned the shape of the upper Missouri River country. They learned that English would probably not be spoken in the lands ahead. French would probably not be spoken there either. Help with talking to later Indigenous peoples came from a hired man.

9His name was Toussaint Charbonneau. He was a French fur trader who lived in the Numakiki town. Later it became clear that his languages were only English, French, and a little Hiraacá. Clark's journal says Charbonneau had two Indigenous women. The journal says he had purchased them. One was a girl of 17. Her name was Sacagawea. The language she spoke was Newe. She would matter a great deal in the rest of the expedition. Before the corps left Fort Mandan, she gave birth to a son. The boy's name was Jean Baptiste Charbonneau. No one on the expedition was younger than he was. Fame may put Sacagawea on the same level as Lewis and Clark. Even so, little about her life is sure. Shoshone people say her birth nation was the Lemhi Shoshone. Most historians who are not Indigenous say the same. They say a Hidatsa raid took her when she was 12. Many Indigenous people do not accept a hero story in which she helped the United States grow. A traitor is what some of them see. Others see an enslaved woman who did what she could for her people. By then the distance traveled was 1,500 miles (2,414 km). Harder country still lay ahead. Only the Great Plains had been crossed so far. The Rocky Mountains would come next. The Great Basin would come after that. Forests of the Columbia River Basin would come too.

10In the months ahead, death would come close to the Corps of Discovery many times. Each time, Indigenous peoples would pull them back from that danger. Those peoples would care for them until they were well. Sacagawea was not the only reason the Pacific Ocean was reached. Every Indigenous people Lewis and Clark met helped make that arrival possible. A second book tells the rest of the journey. Assimilation means taking on a country's main culture, or being forced to take it on. Cultures are the ideas and customs of particular groups. A debt is something owed, and it is usually money. Colonization means taking a new territory for one's own use. Encountered means met suddenly or by chance. A confederacy joins people, organizations, states, or countries for a shared purpose. Enslaved means kept in slavery, owned by someone, or forced to work for that person. To conquer is to take control, usually by force, of a person, a group, a place, or a thing. An expedition is a group that goes on a journey or a voyage. Indigenous describes the earliest peoples of a place, or something related to those peoples. The Corps of Discovery was a unit of the U.S. Army. Meriwether Lewis and William Clark led it. From 1804 to 1806 it explored land gained in the Louisiana Purchase. A stronghold is a place with strong protection.

61. The Fight That Built a Nation

1A timeline of the quarrel runs through several famous events. It includes the Boston Tea Party and the passing of the Townshend Acts. It includes the French and Indian War. That struggle was one piece inside Europe's Seven Years' War. It includes the Sugar Act, then the Quartering Act and the Stamp Act. It includes the Boston Massacre and the Coercive Acts, also called the Intolerable Acts. It includes the meeting of the First Continental Congress. On April 19, 1775, war began. A shot at Lexington and Concord later gained a famous name: the shot heard around the world. The United States did not begin as a country. It began as thirteen colonies under Great Britain and under the English king, George III. Britain taxed the colonists and enforced new laws they hated. The colonists objected. Their demand was a known line: no taxation without representation in the British Parliament. The disagreements only grew. King George III tried to master the colonists with harsher taxes and with threats of military force. Those events led to a clash on April 19, 1775. British soldiers and colonists met at Lexington and Concord, two towns in Massachusetts. Shots crossed the village green at Lexington. Nobody knows who fired first. That opening shot started the war. Britain and the thirteen colonies were the two sides. A third group already lived on the land both sides were fighting over. For thousands of years, Native peoples had already lived in that region. Millions of Native people were dead by 1775 because Europeans had arrived. In the century that followed, millions more would die. From one coast to the other, more of their land would be seized. When King George refused to cancel the taxes, the colonies could see that independence would have to be won by fighting. Patrick Henry went back to Virginia once the First Continental Congress ended. There he gave a speech. He shouted seven famous words. Give me liberty or give me death! Later, Patriot fighters shortened the cry to Liberty or Death! Independence Hall in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, held the Second Continental Congress.

2The date was May 10, 1775. Fifty-six delegates were there. They chose George Washington with one voice. Washington came as a delegate from Virginia. Earlier he had served as an officer in Britain's army. Command of the troops went to him. Up to that point, people had called those troops the New England militia. Congress voted to rename those troops the Continental Army. Its ranks would be filled by volunteers, and every one of the thirteen colonies would send some. Washington's task was hard. His soldiers were a ragged mix of farmers, carpenters, and blacksmiths. They had few weapons and little training, sometimes none. Against them stood Britain's military, powerful, trained, and well supplied. Washington expected to fail. He told Patrick Henry, a Virginia lawyer, a bleak forecast. From the day I enter upon the command of the American armies, I date my fall, and the ruin of my reputation. He still believed deeply in American independence. He took the command. Pay was something he refused to take. Not every colonist wanted to leave Britain. Washington set off to lead the new troops. His road led toward Concord and Lexington, close to Boston. Back in Congress, the delegates still hoped to settle matters with Parliament. The delegates sent King George III a petition. They asked again for rights, and they asked him to call the colonists loyal English subjects. The king refused even to receive the petition. The charge he made was blunt. The colonists, he said, had proceeded to open and avowed rebellion. The Revolutionary War cut deep into Native life. King George III had tried to separate Native peoples from colonists. He hoped that distance would stop violence between the two. Britain reserved some lands for Native peoples. Colonists disliked that decision. As time passed, some Native peoples took the Patriot side. Others joined the British. Sometimes a nation, or an alliance, split, with members on both sides. When Britain lost, it handed the United States a huge stretch of land. Native peoples had lived on that land for centuries.

3They lost more than ground. They lost cultures, and they lost countless lives. Native peoples had also resisted the British before the American war. A picture shows the Ottawa leader Pontiac visiting the British in 1763. Soon afterward Pontiac would try to push the British out. Nearly every tribe around the Great Lakes gave him support. The fight called Pontiac's War ran from 1763 to 1766 and was named for him. Congress was still sitting in Philadelphia when colonial soldiers won a fight. The British garrison lost the fort. The place was Fort Ticonderoga. The colony was New York. Ethan Allen, a rough farmer from New Hampshire, had joined other local farmers in a band called the Green Mountain Boys. The fort Britain held on Lake Champlain was the target. Congress asked Allen's band to take it. Another soldier, Benedict Arnold, was also ordered to attack the same fort. Connecticut had given Arnold an official commission. His orders were to seize the fort from Britain. Both men wanted to lead. They argued the whole way to Ticonderoga. On May 10, 1775, they still managed to take the fort together. The next day Allen and Arnold captured a second British fort, at Crown Point. The wins lifted the soldiers' morale. They also announced that the war had truly started. Colonists now had to choose. Loyalists wanted to stay part of Britain. Patriots wanted independence. There was no middle ground. After Lexington, where the shot heard around the world opened the American Revolution, British soldiers fell back to Boston. Major John Pitcairn led them. Colonial soldiers camped outside the city and gathered strength. In time about 16,000 Patriot troops ringed Boston and cut the British supply line into the city. General Thomas Gage, commanding the British, feared what might come next. Gage feared the hills on the far side of the Charles River. Patriot troops might dig in there, opposite Boston. Charlestown held both hills. One hill was called Bunker Hill. The other was called Breed's Hill. A map shows the British retreat.

4After the defeats at Lexington and Concord, British troops fell back to Charlestown, crossed the river, and entered Boston. The Atlantic Ocean lies to the east of that coast. General Artemis Ward gave an order after dark on June 16, 1775. Patriot soldiers were to dig trenches. The hill he named was Bunker Hill. The soldiers misunderstood. They went instead to Breed's Hill, which stood closer to the British. Morning showed a hill crowded with soldiers. Trenches covered it too. British troops crossed the Charles River by ship, cannons firing. The advantage did not lie with the Patriots. Their training was poor, and they faced professional soldiers. They also had very little gunpowder. Officers gave a strict order so ammunition would last. The order was this. Wait until you see the whites of their eyes. Soldiers followed it, and the plan worked. British soldiers came rushing uphill. The Americans did not shoot until the last moment that was still safe. Many British soldiers died. More troops landed and attacked. The Americans again waited, then shot. Three waves of attack came. When the gunpowder was gone, the Americans had no choice but to pull back. Both hills then fell to the British. Breed's Hill was taken, and Bunker Hill was taken too. A map of the fight shows the Mystic River, Breed's Hill, Bunker Hill, Charlestown, the Charles River, Boston, and Copp's Hill. Patriot soldiers held one set of positions. British soldiers held another. Britain gained the two hills, and the price was high. British losses passed 1,000, counting both the wounded and the dead. The Patriots lost 441 men. Even in defeat, Patriot morale rose. They had shown they could stand against a larger body of professional soldiers and still fight a war. Most of the action happened on Breed's Hill. Even so, the fight came to be called the Battle of Bunker Hill. July 1775 was the month George Washington reached the army. For nearly a year his troops held the British inside Boston, unable to get out. Canada was another target.

5He sent troops to invade it. His hope was simple. If Britain could not land in Canada, it could not march south into New York. Montreal fell to the Patriots. The month was November, and the year was 1775. The city of Quebec was attacked under Benedict Arnold's lead. Severe December weather made the attack fail. Through the winter, Patriots turned captured British cannons on the soldiers inside Boston. On March 17, 1776, British soldiers left the city. Thousands of Loyalists left with them. Washington's troops marched into Boston in triumph. Those cannons, taken from the British, were the guns the Continental Army used against them. People still tell someone to sign a paper with a certain phrase. Put your John Hancock right here. People have used that phrase since 1776. John Hancock signed the Declaration of Independence in a bold, large hand. His signature nudged the other 53 signers to add their names. A pamphlet titled Common Sense came from the Patriot writer Thomas Paine. In it he said independence was the only right choice for the colonists. He challenged Britain's right to rule. He used plain words, the kind most people could follow. Within a few months, buyers had taken 150,000 copies. It pulled many Loyalists over to independence. June 1776 was when Congress picked a committee. The group was to write down the colonists' claim to govern themselves. Thomas Jefferson was picked as the actual writer because people knew his skill with words. July 4, 1776, was the day Congress said yes to the Declaration of Independence. Each of the thirteen colonies still had to pass it. When they did, the document brought the United States of America into being. Dark days followed. Defeat followed defeat for the Patriots. General William Howe waited only a month after the signing. Then he shipped Britain's army into New York Harbor. He had 30,000 soldiers. Three days was the length of the Battle of Long Island. The Patriots were outnumbered. At last they fell back, going south through New Jersey until they reached Philadelphia.

6New York City fell under British occupation. Another fight went Britain's way as well. Patriots handed over the post called Fort Washington. Nathan Hale is honored by a statue. Hale taught school, and he was 21. He volunteered for a spy mission against Britain's troops inside New York City. Capture came, and then a hanging. What he said at the end is famous. I regret that I have but one life to give for my country. Brave as he was, General Benedict Arnold felt mistreated. He blamed both Congress and the Continental Army. West Point was a fort on the lower part of the Hudson River. In 1779 Washington gave Arnold command of it. Arnold planned to sell that fort to the British. The scheme was revealed. Arnold then switched sides and entered Britain's army as a traitor. In October 1776, Arnold's Patriot gunboats lost a fight at Lake Champlain in Canada. The Patriots fought so hard that the British grew uneasy. Beating the rebels might be harder than they had thought. Trenton, New Jersey, lay across the Delaware River. December 24, 1776, was the date of the crossing. Ferries carried the soldiers, with George Washington in command. One night was enough to move 2,400 Patriots. They crossed an icy river while sleet and snow fell. The fight at that town was over in under an hour, and the Patriots won it. It was the war's first major victory. Princeton, New Jersey, was the next British defeat. It came only a few days later, under Washington. Those wins brought Patriot morale back to life. A picture shows Washington accepting the surrender of troops at Trenton in 1776. Britain struck back in June 1777. General John Burgoyne led a large army south from Canada. Albany, New York, was the point he wanted on the Hudson River. Taking it would slice New England and New York away from the rest of the colonies. On the way he recaptured Fort Ticonderoga. October brought the Battle of Saratoga. Patriot soldiers halted his advance there.

7Burgoyne surrendered about 6,000 men. A map of his march south from Canada marks Burgoyne, Lake Champlain, Fort Ticonderoga, and the British leaders St. Clair, Riedesel, and Phillips, along with British troops. Saratoga was a turning point. It showed France, and other countries in Europe, that the Patriots might actually win. France entered the war in 1778. Its old enemy was Great Britain. Supplies from France went to the Continental Army. Spain would soon declare war on Britain as well. Food was often missing for Continental soldiers. So were clothing and shelter. Troops needed supplies, so Congress looked for allies. France was one. Valley Forge, Pennsylvania, was where Washington's men spent a winter. They were cold and hungry until supplies finally came. Words from Washington are cut into a memorial arch at that camp. Naked and starving as they are, we cannot enough admire the incomparable patience and fidelity of the soldiery. In June 1778, after that awful winter, Washington attacked the British at the Battle of Monmouth. General Henry Clinton now commanded the British army. Neither side won. No later battle in the northern colonies matched it in size. It also showed that Patriots could fight as well as the British. Army service was closed to women. They still found other ways to help the war. One way was making homespun, cloth made at home. The Stamp Act became law in 1765. After that, many women showed support for the revolution by turning away goods from Britain. They made their own instead, a household act of protest. Public spinning was one of their acts. The women who did it called their group the Daughters of Liberty. Women made bullets. They sewed blankets and uniforms. They raised money. Inside the camps they cooked and cleaned. They nursed people who were hurt or ill. They also hunted for food. Carrying water out to troops under fire put some women's lives at risk. Mary Ludwick Hays took her husband William Hays's place when he was wounded. The name history gave her is Molly Pitcher. Monmouth was where she hauled water.

8Soldiers drank it, and the cannon crew used it too. That labor produced the nickname. Savannah, Georgia, fell to British forces. The month was December, and the year was 1778. Charleston, South Carolina, was attacked next and then captured. That happened in May 1780. August 1780 brought another British win, this time at Camden, South Carolina. Casualty counts in those three fights were the worst of the whole war. Many colonists in the South were Loyalists. Britain was winning there, but the Patriots would not quit. October brought a Patriot win at King's Mountain in South Carolina. The fight was over in a quick sixty-five minutes. Few battles in the war involved no British soldiers. This one did not. Patriots fought Loyalists. Patriots then won again at Camden and at Cowpens. British General Charles Cornwallis was the next man they drove. They pushed him north, into Virginia. Cornwallis had helped Britain win at Long Island, and the southern command was now his. Help from France started to show results. Soldiers from France helped keep the British from breaking through. They fought beside colonists in the force Washington led into Virginia. Black people joined the fighting in the thousands. Their choices of side were not all the same. Enslavement was the condition of most of them. Freedom looked more likely on one side or the other, and that hope guided most of their choices. Great Britain received the service of more than 20,000 Black fighters. On the Patriot side the number fell in a range, from 5,000 up to 8,000. Decades would pass before many enslaved Black people were free. James Armistead stands as one American hero of that fight. Before the war he was enslaved in Virginia. During the war his work was spying for both sides. He was good at it. His disguise was a runaway who had taken Britain's side. Before long the British were using him to watch the Patriots. What they never learned was the other half. The Patriots were using him to watch the British.

9British battle plans reached General Lafayette through Armistead. Those details were what the Patriots needed at Yorktown. Winning there meant winning the war. When the fighting was finished, a law called the Act of 1783 took effect. It freed enslaved soldiers who had fought on the Revolution's side. Because Armistead had been a spy, he did not benefit. He went back to life as a slave. Freedom came years afterward, with help from the French commander he had served. He joined Lafayette to his own name. It was thanks, and it showed the tie between them. A painting from 1824 shows James Armistead Lafayette. A picture shows Cornwallis surrendering to Washington at Yorktown. Ahead lay the battle that mattered most in the whole war. Yorktown sits on the Virginia coast. Ships from Britain arrived, hoping to save Cornwallis along with the men under him. French ships drove those rescuers away. The French fleet also brought more soldiers for the fight on land. Into Yorktown came troops from France together with Patriot troops. For three weeks they held the British army under siege. The British surrendered on October 19, 1781. With that surrender, the Revolutionary War came to a close. Victory belonged to the Patriots. They were independent from Britain. Official independence from Great Britain arrived with the Peace of Paris. The year was 1783. These colonies were used to another country's support. Now they had to pull together and form a nation of their own. The main figures of the war can be listed in a few lines. Command of the Continental Army belonged to George Washington. In later years he became the first president of the country. British troops in the colonies were under Thomas Gage. After Lexington and Concord, that army was stuck inside Boston. John Burgoyne commanded the British northern army. He captured Fort Ticonderoga and was defeated at Saratoga. Great Britain gained King George III when he was twenty-two. Keeping the colonies mattered to him no matter the cost. The Declaration of Independence was Jefferson's writing. Thomas Jefferson held the pen.

10Thomas Paine wrote the booklet Common Sense, which moved many colonists to choose independence. From 1775 until 1778, command of Britain's army in North America belonged to William Howe. Howe's replacement arrived in 1778. The new British commander was Henry Clinton. Charles Cornwallis was a British general under Henry Clinton. The South was his command. Surrender came at Yorktown. The date was October 19, 1781. A young man from France, Marquis de Lafayette, commanded troops under Washington. He was instrumental in getting the French military help that contributed to victory. Important places on the map include Quebec and Ticonderoga. Concord and Boston are marked too. So are Long Island and Valley Forge. Yorktown appears, along with King's Mountain, Camden, Charleston, and Savannah. The Atlantic Ocean lies beside them. These words belong with the story. Allies are people or groups that join for a shared cause. Morale is the confidence or enthusiasm a person or a group feels while working toward a goal. Amends are acts meant to make up for a harm or a loss. During the American Revolution, Patriots were those who wanted the thirteen colonies to be independent. A casualty is a person hurt, killed, or missing in a war, an accident, or a disaster. A petition is a formal written request, often carrying many signatures. A commission is an official order that authorizes someone to do a duty. Rebellion is a fight against authority. Delegates are chosen people who represent others and act for them. To have retaliated is to have struck back after being attacked. Independence is freedom from another power's control, influence, or support. A self-governing people may write laws and carry them out. No outside power may step in. Colonists who kept their loyalty to Great Britain, all through the American Revolution, were the Loyalists. In a siege, one side surrounds an enemy and stays there a long time. Attacks are common. Essential supplies are kept from getting through.
