Momentum is what keeps a thing in motion, or keeps it increasing, as time passes.

62. The Green Heart of the Imperial Palace

1The parts of this book come in this order. First is A Green Oasis. Then come The Heart of Tokyo and the History of the Imperial Palace. Construction of the Palace follows. Then come The Palace Grounds and The Imperial Palace Today. A Site of Tranquility comes next. A glossary closes the book. A picture shows a fortress on the palace grounds. The old fortress stands in stark contrast to Tokyo's modern skyscrapers. A Green Oasis Tokyo is a sea of towering skyscrapers. It is also a sea of glittering lights. A green oasis sits in the middle of this modern city. The oasis has manicured gardens. It has wooden buildings. Traditional stone walls surround it. This place is the Tokyo Imperial Palace. Few pieces of real estate on Earth are worth more than the palace grounds. The palace is the home of the emperor of Japan. It is the home of the empress too. They belong to the world's oldest monarchy. The Heart of Tokyo The city of Tokyo lies along the Pacific coast of Honshu. Honshu is the main island of Japan. The Tokyo Imperial Palace is in the heart of Tokyo. It is not far from an inlet of Tokyo Bay. It sits near many important cultural sites. One of them is the Japanese National Theatre. It also sits near tourist attractions such as Tokyo Disneyland. Thirty-five million people make their homes in Tokyo. No metropolitan area in the world is bigger. The National Diet Building stands very near the Imperial Palace. Japan's parliament meets in that building. Japan's government is a constitutional monarchy.

2That means the emperor shares his power with parliament. The country's laws are made by the members of parliament. The emperor holds a role that is more symbolic. His role is ceremonial. The current palace stands on the site of the former Edo Castle. Japan's imperial family lives in this place. History of the Imperial Palace Emperors of Japan did not always live where the Imperial Palace stands now. Shoguns, the military leaders, held most of the power to rule for hundreds of years. The emperor held very little power. In the early 1600s a shogun named Tokugawa Ieyasu began major improvements to Edo Castle. His name is said ee-e-YAH-soo. The castle stood where the Imperial Palace is today. The magnificent Edo Castle was the shogun's home. It was the largest castle in Japan. A terrible fire destroyed the main tower in 1657. The shogun reigning at that time did not have the money to rebuild it. The base of that grand tower is still whole on the Imperial Palace grounds. The reign of Tokugawa Ieyasu lasted more than 260 years. The reign of his heirs lasted through that same span. People in Japan call this part of their history the Edo period. In 1868 a political revolution gave the power back to the emperor. The revolution ended the reign of the shoguns. After the revolution, Emperor Meiji made a decision. His name is said MAY-jee. He decided to move the imperial residence. It had been in Kyoto for almost one thousand years. He shifted the residence to the grounds of Edo Castle in Tokyo.

3A new palace for that site was what Emperor Meiji ordered. The building project faced many challenges. Earthquakes were one challenge. Budget problems were another. Fires destroyed work too. Workers finally finished the new palace in 1888. That was twenty years after construction began. On the outside, the new palace looked like a traditional Japanese building. Its interior decorations included several Western elements. This was revolutionary. For much of its earlier history, Japan stayed fairly apart from the Western world. In traditional Japanese society, tables were low. People sat on the ground. They also sat in special legless chairs called zaisu. Zaisu is said ZY-soo. In the new palace, the emperor requested imported chairs from Germany. The chairs were for Western-style dining tables. The new palace had Western curtains. It did not rely on thin paper screens to cover windows. It had carpets. It had French-style wooden floors. It also had tatami. Tatami are straw mats. They were the traditional flooring material in Japan. Other breaks from the traditional Japanese style included fireplaces. Chandeliers were another break. Emperors of Japan lived in this palace until World War II. During the war, the United States firebombed Tokyo. The bombing was in April of 1942. The United States did not aim its bombs straight at the Imperial Palace. Areas next to the palace were hit hard. Fires moved from the areas around the palace onto the grounds. The fires significantly damaged the main palace building. A picture shows the new Imperial Palace dining room. It had Western-style tables and chairs. A second view shows the traditional Japanese style.

4After World War II, Japan rebuilt the palace. Workers completed the reconstruction in 1968. They used modern building techniques. They used modern supplies. They were still able to keep its historical appearance. Because of this history, some structures on the grounds are only a few decades old. The palace itself is one of those newer structures. Other structures have been there for centuries. That stone base under the old main tower of Edo Castle dates from the Edo period. Some sections of the stone walls around the castles are from that period too. Some wooden guard houses from the Edo period have survived. Some bridges from that period have survived too. The Imperial Household Agency Workers raised the Imperial Household Agency building on the Tokyo Imperial Palace grounds in 1935. After World War II, the royal family lived there for a time. They stayed while the new palace was being constructed. Construction of the Palace Workers built the original stone walls around the palace grounds during the Edo period. They used a construction method that was already centuries old. The method is called kirikomihagi. The name is said kee-ree-koh-mee-HAH-gee. The method began by forming the earth into a narrow shape like stairs. Next, builders set down a layer of small rocks. The rocks let rainwater drain. After the ground was ready, workers stacked the stones to form the walls. The workers left mortar out when they set the stones together. They had the technology to use mortar. They left it out on purpose. Empty cracks between the stones let rain drain out of the walls.

5If the water could not drain, Japan's heavy rains would have damaged the walls. Japan also has many earthquakes. The technique without mortar made the walls better able to stand through them. A slight lean was built into the walls by the workers. Because of that lean, enemies found the walls easier to climb. The slope also made the walls more proof against earthquakes. The walls at the Otemon Gate were built with the kirikomihagi method. That work was done in the Edo period. Japanese buildings were traditionally made of wood. The Suwano-chaya Tea House on the palace grounds is one example. Its name is said su-WAH-noh-CHAH-yah. Emperor Meiji thought about stone when he planned his palace. People even tried to put up a dining hall of stone on the grounds. An earthquake caused that structure to crack. After the crack, the project was abandoned. The incident was evidence of a useful fact. Where earthquakes come often, buildings of wood proved more reliable. Wood was what Emperor Meiji chose for building his palace. He chose the traditional Japanese style. After World War II, workers rebuilt the Imperial Palace with a different material. They used concrete reinforced with steel instead of wood. Even so, the palace still looks like traditional Japanese architecture. The sloping roof shows that look. The long eaves show it too. A plan of the grounds names several places. They include the Science Museum and the Tokyo National Museum of Modern Art. They include Kitanomaru Park and the Museum of Imperial Collections. They include the East Gardens and the Imperial Palace Outer Garden.

6They include the Imperial Palace and Nijubashi Bridge. The Imperial Palace grounds cover about 115 hectares (284 acres). Moats surround the grounds. Defensive stone walls stand there. Some of those walls are from the Edo period. Several museums have a home on the grounds. A picture shows Nijubashi Bridge. The Palace Grounds The palace grounds are divided into four sections. The sections are the Imperial Palace Outer Garden and the Imperial Palace inner grounds. They also include Kitanomaru Park and the East Gardens. The public can use the Imperial Palace Outer Garden, since it is a park. It has large grassy areas. It has groves of trees. The trees and grass give a variety of beautiful scenery with each season. The famous Nijubashi Bridge links the Outer Garden to the inner grounds. The view is very popular with tourists. It is popular with photographers too. In that view, the bridge stretches over the moat. A guard tower stands in the background. Nijubashi Bridge is opened only for special occasions. One occasion is when important guests attend events at the palace. It is open to the public twice a year. One opening is on January 2. That day lets the people and the emperor trade New Year's greetings. The other opening celebrates the emperor's birthday. The Imperial Palace itself contains 24,175 square meters of space. That is about 260,000 square feet. Four and a half soccer fields would take about the same space. The palace is two stories high. An additional level lies below the ground. Inside are rooms used for the state business of the emperor.

7It has audience rooms. It has a dining room. It has a banquet hall. It has drawing rooms where guests can relax. The rooms surround an open courtyard in the center. The emperor uses the palace for ceremonies. The ceremonies appoint prime ministers. They appoint Supreme Court justices. They appoint ambassadors. At the palace, the emperor also receives people who represent foreign governments. He treats them to elegant state dinners. Two times a year, the emperor and the empress greet the public. They do so from a palace balcony. A picture shows Emperor Akihito and Empress Michiko. The January 2017 photo shows them welcoming New Year visitors at the Imperial Palace. The building of the Imperial Household Agency lies near the palace. The agency oversees the schedules of the imperial family. It oversees their events. It maintains the palace grounds. The Imperial Cocoonery is also located in this part of the site. Empresses of Japan have been raising silkworms there since 1871. Silk taken from the empress's silkworms repairs kimonos that are ancient. The residence of the emperor and empress is in this area of the grounds too. Private Shinto shrines for the imperial family are there as well. A picture shows Empress Michiko in the Imperial Cocoonery. She attaches silkworm eggs to an oak twig. Kitanomaru Park is in the northern part of the site. It became a public park in 1969. The park offers visitors lovely scenery. The scenery is especially fine in spring. That is when the cherry trees are in bloom. The park is home to the Science Museum.

8It is home to the National Museum of Modern Art. These attractions offer an interesting contrast. Historic sites from the Edo period stand near modern exhibits in the museums. A scroll painting from the early seventeenth century shows Edo Castle. The stone foundation of the original main tower still stands today. The East Gardens are another public park. Entry to them is free. They feature picturesque ponds. They feature lawns. They feature many different trees, shrubs, and flowers. Japan's final garden from the Edo period is found in this area too. Along with the lovely views, the East Gardens hold many sites important to history. Guard houses from the Edo period are there. Walls and gates from that period are there too. The stone foundation of the former Edo Castle is in the East Gardens. The gardens also have the Museum of Imperial Collections. Visitors may look at parts of the art owned by the imperial family. One generation of the family has handed this art to the next, over and over. The passing down has gone on for many years. Masterpieces in the collection go back as far as the fourth century. The Imperial Palace Today In Japan today, the Tokyo Imperial Palace has a very important part to play. The emperor performs many of his state duties at the palace. He receives foreign officials there. He awards honors there. The palace is also a popular site for tourists. Tokyo residents like it too. Many people who jog like to run a loop around the palace grounds. The palace offers a quiet spot for reflection.

9That quiet sits in the middle of fast-paced city life. A Nature Sanctuary Emperor Hirohito was a dedicated nature lover. He reigned from 1926 to 1989. He did not allow his gardeners to use pesticides. He preferred that the gardens be inviting to insects. His choice left the grounds with more than 3,600 species of animals and insects. They are home to 1,366 plant species. They hold 20 percent of Tokyo's trees. Spring brings blossoms on more than 260 cherry trees. Their delicate pink flowers stretch over the Chidori-ga-fuchi moat. The moat is in the northwest area of the Imperial Palace grounds. This area is the most popular place for viewing cherry blossoms in Tokyo. Over a million people visit the moat each year. They come from late March to early April. Visitors can walk on a footpath beneath a canopy of cherry blossoms. They can also glide along the water in a rowboat and marvel at the beauty. A site this important must be maintained with great care. It is historic, cultural, and governmental. Directing the care of the palace grounds is the work of the Imperial Household Agency. About one thousand people on the agency staff give their work to these jobs. It spends billions of yen each year. That sum is millions of U.S. dollars. About 5.5 billion yen went to palace costs from the agency in 2016. That was $48 million U.S. A picture shows cherry trees in bloom in spring along the Chidori-ga-fuchi moat. The center of Tokyo is the place where the Imperial Palace stands. The city of Tokyo grew outward from the palace.

10A Site of Tranquility The Imperial Palace seems to be a place that time has not touched. It sits in the heart of bustling Tokyo. Its lush grounds contain forests that are thick. The forests are hard to pass through. Its serene gardens are a balm for weary souls. Its graceful wooden buildings are a balm too. The palace grounds have been home to shoguns for centuries. They have been home to emperors for centuries too. They are a cherished part of Japanese history. They are a cherished part of Japanese culture. They will no doubt be a beloved part of life in Tokyo for generations to come. Glossary A balm is something that comforts or restores. A parliament is a group of government officials who can make a nation's laws and change them. A cocoonery is a place where silkworms are raised. Picturesque means nice, pretty, or charming. A constitutional monarchy limits a ruler, such as a king or a queen, by a constitution or by a parliament. Shinto is a traditional religion of Japan. In Shinto, people worship various gods of nature. Shoguns were military rulers in ancient Japan. Imperial means having to do with royalty, or with an absolute ruler of an empire. Tatami is a floor covering made from rice straw. Kimonos are Japanese robes or gowns. People often wear them for formal occasions. The yen is the unit of currency in Japan. Mortar is a liquid mix of materials. It hardens as it dries. People use it to hold bricks or stones together.

63. The Holiday That Honors Work

1Marchers in a New York City parade carry a banner that honors union workers. The day is Labor Day. September's first Monday is the date the United States gives this holiday. For many American children it is the last burst of summer fun before school begins again. Banks close. Government offices close too, including post offices. Because so many people are off work, a backyard party is a common plan. Rest is only part of the meaning. The U.S. government set the day aside to recognize what American workers have contributed and achieved, both in the past and now. To see what the holiday honors, a reader needs the story of the labor movement. That movement is an organized push by workers. Joining together is the method. The demand is change. The goal is better economic conditions and better social conditions. The pages ahead follow that push. They look at machines and at hard jobs. They look at children who worked. They look at workers who joined together, at the honoring of labor, and at hopes for a better future. A word list comes at the end. Before machines were common, horses supplied much of the energy used on farms. The Industrial Revolution, from the late 1700s into the early 1800s, changed the tools of work. New technology let machines do many jobs faster and more efficiently than hands could.

2Planting and harvesting started to be done by machine. Some farms used machines in place of workers. Others used both. Profits often rose. Many small family farms, though, were driven out of business. Factories could now make cloth and other goods much more cheaply than small businesses run from homes. People left rural places and small towns because of those changes. They moved to larger cities and took factory jobs. In a picture from 1925, a tractor pulls a plow across a field while a farmer guides it. Factory owners often kept expenses down so the business could make more money. Wages stayed low, and the work was often dangerous. Recent immigrants were especially exposed to those bosses. So were people who had formerly been enslaved. Both groups were more likely to accept unsafe conditions and low pay. Time off was scarce as well. In the 1800s the United States had no law limiting how many hours a day or a week a business could demand. Employers used that gap. The average manufacturing worker put in 100 hours a week. Anyone who disliked the rules and spoke up could be fired and quickly replaced. Workers wanted a say in how bosses treated them. That wish is where the labor movement started. They wanted higher pay. They wanted fewer hours.

3They wanted safer conditions. A 1911 picture shows women and children working as spinners in a factory in Mississippi. Four children appear in a 1917 picture from a tobacco factory. Their pay was about $1.20 a day. Factories saw more child labor because of the Industrial Revolution. Most of the machines were simple enough for a child to run. Pay for a child could be set below an adult's pay. They were easier to control, and they could squeeze into tight spaces around the equipment. About two million children in the United States held jobs in mills or in factories. That count belongs to the early 1800s. Many came from families with little money. Some of those families had already lost their businesses in the Industrial Revolution. A job often started before a child's tenth birthday. Sometimes the age was six or seven. A week of work ran to six days. A day could last up to eighteen hours. Families often needed that income to survive. Rest was rare. School and play had no time left. Dangerous conditions and long hours made many children ill. Over time, workers began joining together to improve life on the job. They formed labor unions, organized associations meant to protect workers' rights and to widen them. Any union's goal is to bargain with employers for its members.

4Hours are on the table. So are wages, conditions on the job, and benefits. Unions sometimes call strikes. A strike protests an unfair situation, or it gives workers a stronger hand when they negotiate. Late in the 1800s the earliest labor unions were founded. In theory they welcomed every worker. Later the unions divided. Each job, or trade, tended to get a group of its own. Race and gender often divided those jobs. The labor movement became segregated because of that split. Professionals who operated machines, and who repaired them, were the people one group hoped to organize. An interracial union proved impossible for them, so they settled for a union open only to white workers. In 1902, Black workers were only 3 percent of all union members in the United States. A seal is something lots of unions put on the goods they make. The seal is a point of pride. It also tells shoppers which goods union workers made. President Ulysses S. Grant made an announcement in 1869. It was a promise aimed at people who worked for the government. An eight-hour day was part of the promise. A wage that stayed steady was the other part. He also urged private-sector workers to seek the same legal promise. New York City in 1872 is the setting of a picture. Marching workers are on strike, and the demand is a day of eight hours.

5Many employers hated the new day length. Illinois wrote an eight-hour day into law for every worker except people working on farms. Large numbers of employers still refused to go along. Chicago's Haymarket Square filled with people on May 4, 1886. Strikers and supporters together numbered eighty thousand. They were protesting that refusal. Stopping the rally took heavy force from the police. People remember the clash by the name Haymarket Affair. Since the 1980s, fewer workers across the United States have carried a union card. A change showed up starting in 2020. Strikes grew more common, and so did efforts to form unions. Government-worker unions, for their part, keep growing at a steady pace. Teachers have strong unions. Postal workers have strong unions as well. Firefighters do too, and so do police officers. About 9.9 percent is the share of United States workers in a union. The figure is for 2024. The early labor movement mostly kept women out. Some activists argued for a family wage. The idea was pay high enough for a husband to support everyone at home, so women would not have to go out to work. Around the turn of the century, the vote was one fight women were in. Fair conditions on the job were another. In New York City, people who made textiles took an important step.

6They organized, and the union they built was the Ladies Garment Workers Union. Labor activists found a listener in President Franklin Delano Roosevelt. The next result was a law from Congress. Its name is the Fair Labor Standards Act, shortened to FLSA. Lawmakers wanted to stop a pattern. Employers had been using low wages and poor conditions to take advantage of workers. A workweek under the act could run no longer than forty-four hours. In 1940 that limit changed to forty hours. It also set a minimum wage, the lowest pay an employer was allowed to give. When the act passed in 1938, that minimum was $0.25 an hour. Adjusted to the buying power of 2021, the same pay would be $5.03. By 2025 the federal floor on hourly pay stood at $7.25. States may set a higher figure. Thirty states have used that freedom. Washington, D.C., has used it too. A worker earns $15.00 an hour. In a workweek of forty hours, that worker earns $600. Add ten hours of overtime in a week and the pay is $825. The act also required extra pay for hours beyond the usual amount. That extra pay is called overtime. Once a single workweek passes forty hours, every extra hour earns one and a half times the worker's usual rate.

7The aim was to discourage bosses from overworking people. It was also meant to encourage hiring more workers, so the boss could avoid overtime costs. The act set safety rules for workplaces. Most forms of child labor were banned by the same act. The youngest age for work during school hours is sixteen. Certain jobs after school may begin at fourteen. Dangerous jobs must wait until eighteen. During the Pullman Strike of 1894, railroad workers stopped work for more than two months. Wage cuts were hurting their families. Several people shaped this movement. Mother Jones, whose name was Mary Harris Jones, lived from 1837 to 1930. In the early 1900s she helped coal miners. Miners in the union called her Mother. The name honored how hard she worked on their behalf. Her travels crossed the United States. Striking miners were one reason. Ending child labor was the other. A. Philip Randolph lived from 1889 to 1979. He was widely known as an advocate for the interests of Black working-class people in the United States. Ten years of steady work went into organizing a union called Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters. Those workers looked after passengers' needs on train trips. A march on Washington was another call Randolph made. He wanted to protest job discrimination in the armed forces.

8He stayed committed to protest without violence and to action by large crowds. That example helped spark the civil rights movement in the 1950s and again in the 1960s. Eugene Debs lived from 1855 to 1926. He helped found major unions for railroad workers and for industrial workers. Between 1900 and 1920 he sought the presidency five times. Workers who needed to bargain with a boss could find him on the road, crossing the country to help. Born in 1930, Dolores Huerta helped found the United Farm Workers Association. Her activist work focused on low-income families, on women, and on children. A 1965 strike of grape farmers drew 5,000 people, and she helped organize it. Safer conditions on the job were written into a contract she helped negotiate. Campaigns across the United States had her support. She promoted laws and policies aimed at equal rights. Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, is the city in a picture of marching workers. The celebration is Labor Day, and the year is 1882. New York City hosted the earliest Labor Day celebration. The year was 1882. The group that handled the organizing had a long name: Central Labor Union of New York. The aim was a day off for citizens who worked. The first state law making Labor Day official came from Oregon. The year was 1887. Similar laws then passed in thirty more states.

9Only after that, in 1894, did the national government make the holiday official for the whole country. Canada uses that same Monday, the first one in September, for its own Labor Day. A different date, May 1, is International Workers' Day. More than sixty other countries celebrate then. The spark for that May holiday was the Haymarket Affair in Chicago on May 4, 1886. Workers are the people both holidays celebrate. International Workers' Day shares that purpose with Labor Day. Labor activists teach people about their rights. Unfair practices on the job are something those activists try to stop. Ironworkers from Canada march side by side in a picture. The parade is for Labor Day, and the city is Toronto, Ontario. Founding year 1919 marks the start of the American Welding Society. Protection on the job is required for welders. Thick leather gloves are part of it. A special helmet is another part. Labor movements still work today to improve how workers are treated and how they are paid. Early 2020 is when the COVID-19 pandemic arrived in the United States. It drew attention to essential workers in healthcare, in food service, and in retail. Many people want the federal pay floor raised, as a way to support those workers. Federal workers saw their minimum lifted to $15 an hour.

10The United States made that change in 2022. Everyone outside federal employment kept the older floor, $7.25 an hour. Labor Day is a good moment for thanks. Honor the workers who make life better for their own households, for their communities, and for the whole country. A few words help. To negotiate is to try, through discussion, to reach a formal agreement. Economic describes things tied to buying and selling goods and services. Business that government does not run directly is called the private sector. Federal refers to a central government. That government shares power with states that stay separate. A regulation is an official rule. It tells how a thing should be done, or how it should be made. Guaranteed means promised or made sure. Manufacturing and transportation once depended on human power and animal power. The Industrial Revolution was the shift to machines. It began late in the eighteenth century. A right is a freedom, or a power, that a person can claim with justice. During a strike, workers stop doing their jobs. Sometimes they want to show they are unhappy. Sometimes they want to push a boss to meet their demands. Labor means hard physical work, or the people who do it. Wages are regular pay based on time worked. Minimum wage is the lowest hourly rate the law allows.

64. The Largest Bird Alive

1The parts of this book name the bird, then look from claw to small head. Later parts link it to dinosaurs, ask where it began, and visit the plains. Plants, stones, enemies, and group life come next. A closing look and a word list finish the book. How big is one? An ostrich can stand 9 feet tall, which is 2.74 meters. Weight can reach 350 pounds, which is 158.8 kilograms. A person in the same chart stands 6 feet, or 1.8 meters. That person weighs 175 pounds, or 79.4 kilograms. What kind of animal is this? Birds, in most minds, are small. They seem delicate. They fly. They sing sweet songs. They nest in trees, in homes that are tiny. Then you meet the ostrich. Hide the rest of the body and show only the legs. A viewer might guess reptile. A viewer might guess some animal from before written history. So what is an ostrich, exactly? It is the largest bird alive anywhere. Flight is not in its skill set. Small and fragile do not fit it at all. Its calls can be loud enough to raise the hair on your neck. Even so, the ostrich is a bird.

2Grown birds tower over the tallest people. These so-called little birds are strong. Fierce wild animals can meet a defense that works. A close look, from the claw up to a small head. Four toes is the usual count on a bird foot. An ostrich breaks that rule. Each foot has two toes. A hidden weapon sits on the inner toe. That weapon is a claw. The claw lets the bird dig into the ground. A firm grip helps it run. No other animal on two legs is faster. The legs are extremely powerful. A sprint can hit 45 miles an hour. That pace is 72.4 kilometers an hour. A longer run can hold 30 miles an hour. That pace is 48.2 kilometers an hour. One stride covers 10 to 16 feet. That reach is 3 to 5 meters. Feathers on the wing and on the torso set this bird apart in another way. Flying birds keep their feathers locked tight. Tight feathers are what make flight possible for them. An ostrich never flies, so its feathers stay soft. They are fluffy rather than stiff. Wings serve as balance. Balance makes the run smooth. Sharp turns become possible. Feathers also block sunburn.

3A picture shows a kick thrown at an enemy. The kick is powerful. A long neck helps in many ways. Extra height lets the head stay high. From up there the bird can scout new ground. It can search for food. It can spot danger coming. No land animal has larger eyes. Each eye measures 2 inches across. That is 5 centimeters. Long, thick lashes frame the eyes. Almost every part of an ostrich is oversized. The head is the exception. The brain is the other exception. Brain size is about the same as one eye. For a creature this strong, that brain is small. You could call the bird a little empty-headed. What puts an ostrich in the bird group? Its eyes are five times the size of a person's eyes. The neck is nearly half the bird's full height. Every bird has a backbone. Every bird has feathers. This bird cannot fly, yet the feathers still hold warmth. Wings help it stay balanced while it runs. Every bird has wings. Every bird has a bill. Every bird lays eggs. Every bird is warm-blooded. No bird egg is larger than an ostrich's. No bird egg has a thicker shell.

4Two toes, and only two, meet the ground on each foot. Running costs an ostrich about half the energy a person would spend. The reason sits in the leg tendons, which are tissues that connect parts. Those tendons are twice as springy as a person's. Ostriches and dinosaurs. Speed, size, and power are plain to see. Where the bird came from is not plain. Why flight was lost is not plain. How it grew so huge is not plain. Nobody truly knows. Theories are many. One recent idea looks back millions of years. Early relatives were much smaller then. They could still fly. Some scientists think these birds were a favorite dinosaur meal. Flight let the birds get away. That escape was their good luck. Dinosaurs later died out. Enemies grew fewer. More time was left for grazing. Across a long stretch of years, the birds changed. They became the huge flightless birds we know. And the winner is. Living relatives of T. rex do not get much closer than ostriches. An ostrich can average 30 to 45 miles an hour. That range is 48.3 to 72.4 kilometers an hour. T. rex was guessed at about 10 to 25 miles an hour.

5That range is 16 to 40.2 kilometers an hour. A newer study noticed how much an ostrich resembles Tyrannosaurus rex. A link seemed necessary to some scientists. Leg bones of the bird and leg bones of T. rex look extremely alike. Researchers wanted the dinosaur's speed, so they had an ostrich run on a moving belt. The study settled one point. A fit ostrich would beat a heavy T. rex in a race. Where ostriches live. A map shows the Atlantic Ocean, Africa, the equator, the Indian Ocean, Asia, and Europe. Shading marks the ostrich range. Ranches on many continents keep ostriches today. Africa is the only place they are native. Ostrich lands. Where the line began. The true starting place on Earth is still unsettled. The bird looks almost as if it came from another world. Fossils of ancient animals like ostriches have turned up in China. More have turned up in Europe. More have turned up in Canada. Those fossils let us make careful guesses. Could early relatives fly? Where did they start? How did they reach Africa? No one can answer for sure. Home on the plains. Today the birds live on the eastern plains of Africa.

6They also live on the southern plains. The land is dry. Scrubby grasses grow in plenty. Trees are few. That mix suits these birds. The savanna swings from one extreme to another. Days can be very hot. Nights can be quite cold. A year averages 68 to 86 degrees Fahrenheit. That range is 20 to 30 degrees Celsius. Winter runs a little cooler. Feathers become a fan in the daytime heat. The fanning keeps the bird cool. At night the feathers drop over the legs. That cover helps when the air turns cold. The Latin name is Struthio camelus. The words mean camel-like. A camel and an ostrich both carry a long neck. Both have eyes that stand out. Both can last a long time with no drink of water. Plants supply much of the water an ostrich needs. A long stretch can pass with no drinking. Greens, plus a side of stones. Almost any plant will do as food. Ostriches are omnivores. Most of the day goes to grazing. Leaves are on the menu. Seeds are on the menu. Fruit is on the menu. Roots are on the menu. An insect turns up now and then. A lizard turns up now and then.

7Teeth are missing, so stones do some of the chewing. An adult carries about 2.2 pounds of stones. That mass is 1 kilogram. The stones sit in the gizzard, which is an organ for digestion. Digestive fluids work with the stones. Food is ground before it moves on. The next stop is the intestines. Those intestines are astonishingly long. They stretch 46 feet, which is 14 meters. A person's intestines are about half that length. Enemies of the ostrich. Lions hunt them in the wild. Cheetahs hunt them. Leopards hunt them. Hyenas hunt them. Vultures steal eggs and eat them. Jackals do the same. A long neck and large eyes make the bird extremely alert. Danger can be seen from far off. Escape often follows that sighting. When a fight is the only choice, the bird has strong moves. A kick from those legs can do serious harm. The claws can do serious harm too. People once hunted ostriches for the plumes. The feathers were beautiful. Hats used them as trim. Dresses used them as trim. The hunting pushed the birds close to dying out. Plumes are used far less today. A male makes a deep booming call when a predator appears.

8The letters in one picture spell out that boom. Living on a large scale. An ostrich may live apart from others. It may also join a herd. A herd can hold five birds. It can hold fifty. It can hold still more. Time alone is what they prefer. They will still share grassland in peace with other grazers. Zebras are among those neighbors. Antelopes are among them too. The ostrich pays the neighbors back with noise. A loud call warns that danger is near. One herd usually has a single adult male in charge. That male is called the rooster. Several females, called hens, join him. Chicks join the group as well. The male courts more than one female. He decides which females may enter the herd. He also decides which ones may not. Once the herd is set, he digs. The dig is a shallow dent in the ground. That dent is the nest. The top female lays about six eggs there. No bird lays a larger egg. Each egg weighs about 3 pounds, or 1.4 kilograms. Other hens may share the nest, because the top hen allows it. Her own eggs stay safest in the center.

9Sitting on the eggs is shared work. Night duty goes to the top male. Day duty goes to the top female. A picture shows a male lifting his feathers in a mating dance. About forty-two days pass. A chick then hatches. The baby is about as big as a grown chicken. Running starts almost as soon as the shell opens. Wild-country skills pass from the male to the chicks. Luck can carry an ostrich to age fifty. Some live even longer. Six months is enough for a chick to stand near adult size. A myth says a scared ostrich buries its head in sand. The truth is different. The bird drops low. Its neck lies close to the ground. That pose hides it from predators. These birds are not cowards. They will fight when they must. On the plains, an ostrich keeps up with many other fast animals. An odd bird, and a wonder for science. Ostriches are grand. They are also mysterious. Their pace is quick. Their running skill is high. Predators do not automatically win. The land around them is hostile. It is dangerous. Flight was never their way of coping. They adapted anyway.

10Scientists stay fascinated for many reasons. The creature is swift. It cannot leave the ground. Studies will go on. They ask what makes this bird one of a kind. They also ask which traits it may have shared with Tyrannosaurus rex. That sharing, if it happened, was millions of years ago. Words to know. Adapted means changed so a living thing fits a new place or a special situation. To court is to try to win a mate. Defensive describes an action that protects the actor from harm or from attack. Dominant describes the one that is more important, more effective, or more powerful than the others. Grazing means feeding on grass and on other plants that grow in open land. Hostile means very unfriendly. An indentation is a shallow hole, or a dimple, in a surface. Omnivores eat plants and also eat animals. A plume is one feather. A group of plumes is a cluster worn by a bird. Prehistoric points to the time before people wrote history down. A savanna is flat grassland with few trees. The torso is the main part of an animal's body. Arms, legs, and the head are not part of the torso.

65. The Largest Lizards on Earth

1The parts of this book cover giant lizards, bodies built for a fight, a hot island home, deadly hunting, babies, dangers, a closing look, and a word list. Lizards of king size. Dr. Tim Jessop studies wild animals for a living. Komodo dragons are his specialty. His first wild dragon, in 2002, caught him off guard. He was just starting out. Could a lizard truly grow this big? That was the question in his mind. A huge male lay in the sun on a rock. Jessop watched. For a moment his eyes seemed to be tricking him. Years of watching, study, and handling came after that day. He now knows these giant reptiles are entirely real. How big is one? Length can reach 10 feet, which is 3 meters. Weight can reach 176 pounds, which is 80 kilograms. A person in the chart stands 6 feet, or 1.8 meters. That person weighs the same 176 pounds, or 80 kilograms. A younger dragon fights a stronger male. The prize is females. The prize is also food. Bodies made for battle. A fight is what these lizards are built to win. Their bodies show that purpose. Muscle makes up nearly the whole animal. Almost any rival can be overpowered. Two males may clash over a female.

2They rise up on their legs. Thick tails keep them balanced. Each one tries to throw the other down. Bony plates sit in the skin. Bites from a rival meet those plates. Scratches meet them too. Teeth are the greatest weapons. The teeth are sharp. The edges are serrated. Huge claws join the teeth as weapons. Prey dies by those tools. Other dragons meet them in a fight as well. Blood is a likely result when two of these lizards clash. What puts a Komodo dragon in the reptile group? Skin is rough. The color is black, or it is yellow-gray. Bony plates lie in that skin. About sixty sharp teeth are ready to tear flesh. The tail is long. Strong muscle runs through the tail. The tongue is forked. Claws are long. Claws are curved. Every reptile has a backbone. Every reptile has scales or bony plates. Lungs are how every reptile breathes. Eggs are what most reptiles lay. Most reptiles are cold-blooded. Where these dragons live. A map places them in Asia, on the Lesser Sunda Islands. Waters nearby include the Indian Ocean, the Flores Sea, and the Savu Sea. Indonesia is the country. Island names include Komodo, Flores, Padar, and Rinca.

3Gili Motang and Gili Dasami appear as well. One shade shows where dragons live now. Another shade shows where they lived in the past. A hot home. Every wild Komodo dragon lives in Indonesia. That country is in Asia. Five islands of the Lesser Sundas hold them. Those islands sit northwest of Australia. They also sit just south of the equator. The islands are small. Volcanoes built them. Hills are rugged. Forest mixes with grassland. Heat lasts all year. Humidity runs high from December through February. Those months are the rainy season. A typical day reaches about 91 degrees Fahrenheit, or 33 degrees Celsius. The high can touch 110 degrees Fahrenheit, or 43 degrees Celsius. Night averages 73 degrees Fahrenheit, or 23 degrees Celsius. Midday heat sends dragons into shallow burrows. Cool nights send them there too. A dragon may dig its own burrow. It may also use a burrow another dragon dug. Most of the time each dragon lives alone. Hunting fills the hours. Eating fills them. Napping fills them. Swimming is a strength. A dragon can cross to a nearby island. Even so, most stay on the island they call home. Beaches are a common walk. Dead fish washed ashore are what they seek. The old range was wider than the range today.

4Food has disappeared in places. Habitat has disappeared too. The living area has shrunk over time. Dragons on two islands are much smaller than the rest. Those islands are Gili Motang and Gili Dasami. Less food and a harsher home changed them. Their average weight is 44 pounds, or 20 kilograms. On the remaining three islands the average weight is 176 pounds, or 80 kilograms. Daytime cooling happens in the burrows. Night sleep happens there too. Many burrows are barely large enough for the animal inside. Prey includes Timor deer, water buffalo, and wild pigs. Animals follow game trails, old paths through the forest, to reach food and water. Hunters that kill. Komodo dragons are carnivores. The menu is wide. They hunt live animals. They also scavenge. Carrion is a clear favorite. The main foods start with deer. Wild pigs belong on that same short list. Water buffalo belong on it too. People brought all three of those animals to the Lesser Sunda Islands. Rats are eaten too. Snakes are eaten. Bird eggs are eaten. Dead fish are eaten. Young of their own kind are eaten as well. That makes them cannibals. About one-tenth of an adult's diet is young dragons. Scientists worked out that share.

5A chase is possible. Ambush is more common. The dragon hides beside a game trail. The wait can last hours. An animal passes, and the attack comes. Most predators fail more often than they succeed. Dragons are like that. A bite still lands often, and the bitten animal gets away. Death usually follows the bite. Sometimes death is quick. Sometimes death waits a few days. Bleeding from the injury alone can kill the prey. Harmful bacteria live in a dragon's mouth. A killing infection can grow from bacteria that live in the mouth. Hurt prey may later stand in dirty water where animals drink. Bacteria in that water can infect the wound and kill the animal. Dragons usually share a kill. Fights still break out at mealtime. Venom is a recent discovery. Venom is a kind of poison delivered in a bite. Evidence says the venom makes blood leave the body faster. It keeps blood from clotting as it should. It can also send the animal into shock. More study is needed. Scientists still need to sort out what venom does. They also need to sort out what the bacteria do. Wounded prey may wander off and die. A long forked tongue is the tool that finds the body.

6The tongue flicks out and tastes the air. Molecules floating in the air stick to it. The tongue pulls back into the mouth. Both tips touch a special organ. That organ sits on the roof of the mouth. Odor molecules from a nearby dead animal can be read there. Messages go to the brain. The brain compares the two tips. One tip holds a stronger dose of molecules. That tip points the way to the meal. Dr. Jessop once saw a dragon kill a water buffalo. He watched it eat. Other dragons arrived as time passed. They joined the feast. Several days later almost nothing remained. Bones were left. Horns were left. Hoofs were left. Those leftovers prove how huge the appetite is. One meal can pass three-quarters of an adult's own weight. Very little of a carcass is wasted. About 12 percent goes unused. Lions leave 25 to 30 percent unused. An extra hinge in the jaw lets the dragon swallow a piece bigger than its head. An egg is about 4 inches long and 2 inches wide. Those measures are 10 centimeters by 5 centimeters. At hatching, body length is just past the length of a ruler. Komodo babies. Females do not all use the same kind of nest.

7Some nests are dug in the ground. Some sit on a hillside. A mound built by a bird may be used instead. That bird is the orange-footed scrub fowl. It lives on the ground. Age decides how many eggs a female lays. The count runs from ten to thirty-five at one time. Laying takes a great deal of energy. It also takes responsibility. Six to nine months pass before hatching. The female must guard the eggs the whole time. Predators are the threat. Decoy chambers are sometimes built inside the nest. The false rooms trick predators. Other dragons are among those predators. A female does not lay every year. The off years let her regain energy. Babies break out of the eggs when the rains are finishing. The month is April. Insects are plentiful then, and the babies need that food. Mothers give no care. The young are on their own at once. Trees are the safe place. Adult dragons are the danger below. Hawks are a danger too. Other birds of prey hunt the babies. Two to four years can pass in the trees. Insects are food. Geckos are food. Rodents are food. Birds are food. Older young also take leftovers from adult meals.

8They stay careful. They do not want to become the meal. A common baby color is green. Black stripes and yellow stripes mark them. Spots mark them too. Males and females grow at the same pace at first. They stay the same size until adulthood. Adulthood arrives around age seven. Males then pull ahead in size. Males also live much longer. Sixty years is possible for a male. A female may live only about half that long. Nest building takes extra energy. Producing eggs takes extra energy. Guarding eggs takes extra energy. Scientists think that load makes females age faster. Dangers for the lizards. Wild numbers run from 3,000 to 5,000. Breeding females are few. The count of those females may be as low as 350. The conservation status is vulnerable. Vulnerable means the animal could become endangered. People compete with dragons for food. Wild dogs compete too. That contest threatens survival. Humans are also taking the habitat. Villagers sometimes kill a dragon that attacks livestock. Indonesian law protects the dragons. International law bans selling them. It also bans trading them. Poachers still kill some. People who study these lizards, in country after country, are trying to stop extinction. Indonesia set up Komodo National Park in 1980. The park shelters these rare reptiles.

9Dr. Jessop is Australian. Scientists from Italy joined him. Scientists from Indonesia joined him. The year 2007 is when their Komodo Survival Program began. The program studies wild dragons. It looks for ways to manage them. It looks for ways to conserve them and the land they need. Zoos in Europe keep captive dragons. Indonesia has zoos in the work. Canada has zoos in it. The United States has zoos in it. Their goal is a captive group with wide genetic variety. For a short burst, a Komodo dragon can reach 11 miles an hour. That pace is 17.7 kilometers an hour. Lizards of mammoth size. These reptiles are remarkable. They are supersized. No lizard in the world is larger. A zoo visit makes people stare. A video does the same. The body looks perfectly fitted to the life it leads. Tools of the hunt are always on the animal. Teeth are razor sharp. Claws are long and strong. Watch one move, and the damage it can do is easy to imagine. A meal can set it prowling. A mate can set it prowling too. Earth's biodiversity includes these dragons. They matter. Dr. Jessop asks people to help. Help can go to these lizards.

10Help can go to other wild animals as well. Support for conservation groups is one path. Another path is balance. People have needs. Other living things have needs. A balance between those needs can keep these huge lizards alive. Words to know. Solitary describes an animal that likes to be by itself. Serrated describes an edge cut into points, the way a saw is cut. Conservation is the work of guarding wild places and the creatures that live in them. Carrion is meat that is rotting after an animal has died. Clotting is the change of a liquid into a thicker or solid form. People use the word most often for blood. Scavengers search out animals that died already, then eat them. A molecule is the tiniest piece of a material that can stand alone. Two or more atoms join to build each one. Basking is a rest taken while sunlight warms the body. Genetically has to do with traits passed down, and with how living things differ. Bacteria are one-celled life. Some kinds make a body sick. A decoy pulls a threat away from the real goal. It can be a person or an object. Adapting is a change that helps a living thing fit a new setting.

66. The Leader from a Log Cabin

1Washington, D.C., holds the Lincoln Memorial. It is one of the monuments Americans love most. This book opens with his life, then follows the early years, law and politics, a nation split apart, the war, and a word list. A beginning. Few presidents matter more in the story of the United States than Abraham Lincoln. He led the country through the Civil War. Northern states and Southern states were fighting over what the nation would become. People call him the Great Emancipator. Enslaved people across the South gained freedom because of what he did. Peace left the country united once more. It has stayed one nation ever since. Pictures often show him tall. They show him lanky. They show him solemn. Memory paints him as a common man. Regular schooling was slight. A log cabin in Kentucky was his birthplace. Even so, he became a great lawyer. He became a great speaker. He became a great political leader. Speeches on freedom are cut into the stone of the Lincoln Memorial. So are speeches on justice. So are speeches on bringing all Americans together. Washington, D.C., is where that stone memorial stands. The belief he held was plain. He said he would not be a slave. He said he would not be a master either. That pair of refusals, he said, was his idea of democracy. A cabin in the picture is built of logs. People believe those logs came from the cabin where he was born. Visitors find the cabin at a national historic site named for his birth. Hodgenville is the town. Kentucky is the state. The early years. Thomas Lincoln and Nancy Hanks Lincoln were his parents. Birth came on February 12, 1809. The place was a small farm of log cabins near Hodgenville, in Kentucky.

2The family later moved to Knob Creek, which was nearby. Abe had an older sister named Sarah. The two children went to school only in short winter stretches. Abe was seven when the family left for Indiana. They hoped life would be better there. Tom built a new cabin of logs. Two years after that, Nancy grew ill. She died. Abe and Sarah grieved for a mother who had worked hard and loved them. Their father soon married again. The new wife was Sarah Bush Johnston. She was a widow. She already had three children. Tom had known her back in Kentucky. Love and care from her made a warm home for Abe. Sarah, his sister, shared that warmth. She encouraged Abe while he grew into a tall youth. The youth was awkward. Friends spoke of a moody quiet. Even so, Abe told stories that felt homey. The stories were funny. School still lasted only a few weeks each winter. The walk was 18 miles a day. That distance is 29 kilometers. Most of his learning came from books he borrowed. Newspapers were borrowed too. Neighbors lent them. Travelers lent them. Pioneer tales fed his mind. Daniel Boone was one of those pioneers. Stories of Johnny Appleseed did too. The books he read did the same. A world bigger than the backwoods began to seem real. A picture shows Abe on a flatboat bound for New Orleans. As a teenager he stood 6 feet 4 inches tall. That height is 2 meters. The flatboat rode the Mississippi River. New Orleans was the busy port at the end of the trip. There, for the first time, he saw Black men held in chains. He saw Black women in chains. He saw Black children in chains. White enslavers were buying them and selling them.

3Rivers of misery. His feelings about ending slavery changed across his life. Hatred of the institution itself never changed. A steamboat trip in the year 1841 carried him along the Ohio. That river was a border. Free states lay on one side of several stretches. Slave states lay on the other. A dozen enslaved people were on board. Shackles bound them together. Lincoln called the sight a torment that did not let up. Every later meeting with that river brought the same sight. The same sight met him at every line that separated free people from enslaved Black people. Work as a young man earned him the name rail splitter. At age 22 he moved to New Salem, in Illinois. Jobs came one after another. He kept a store. He worked as a surveyor. He worked as a carpenter. People knew him as a wrestler. They also knew him as a skilled speaker. That speaking club in New Salem was a debating society. A race for the state legislature of Illinois came next. The 1832 race was a loss. Two years later he won. John Todd Stuart was a lawyer. Stuart was also a legislator. Law study was the path Stuart urged. Books of law were what Abe read. March of 1837 is when the exams were behind him. He joined Stuart's law practice. Springfield became his new home. The Illinois legislature met there. Law and politics. Lincoln's views rested on one strong belief. Each person mattered. Wealth did not change that. Privilege did not change that. Respect came to him inside the Whig Party. Whigs wanted a strong central government. That government sat in Washington, D.C. Democrats were the other leading party. They wanted states to run their own affairs. They did not want Washington stepping in.

4At age 30 he met Mary Ann Todd. She would become his wife. The wedding came three years later, in 1842. A year after the wedding, their first son was born. The son's name was Robert. In 1846 Lincoln won an election. He would represent Illinois in the U.S. Congress. The family moved with him to Washington, D.C. A picture shows Mary Todd Lincoln in 1846. Lincoln sat in Congress while North and South grew more divided. Slavery was the issue. The North relied on workers who were paid. Those workers were in factories. They were also on small farms. A powerful government at the center was the Northern view. In those states, holding people as slaves was illegal. The Southern economy turned on King Cotton. Large plantations grew that cotton. Enslaved people did the labor. Ownership treated them as property. Daily life for most was very poor. Personal rights were denied. Civil rights were denied. Laws in the Southern states allowed slavery. Those laws protected it. The United States was growing. Western territories asked to join. Would a new state enter free? Would it enter with slavery? Atlanta, in Georgia, had a building where enslaved people were sold. Slavery was something Lincoln opposed. As Illinois's man in Washington, he still held a legal view. State law in the South, he believed, protected the practice there. He did fight the spread of slavery. The western territories were where he fought it. Two years in Washington ended. He went back to Springfield. For the next few years he shared a law practice. The practice did well. His partner was William Herndon. People came to know Lincoln's honesty. They knew his skill with the law. They knew his wit. They knew his fine public speaking. Early campaigns had already made him a skilled communicator.

5A nation split. Power was the prize in a fight between slavery's friends and slavery's foes. The year 1854 brought a law from Congress called the Kansas-Nebraska Act. An older law had banned slavery in those territories. The new act cancelled that ban. Residents could now choose. A territory might become a free state. It might become a slave state. Letting the people decide was called popular sovereignty. Stephen Douglas introduced that idea. Lincoln and Douglas had been rivals in politics for a long time. By then Douglas held a Senate seat. The state was Illinois. A map shows the United States after that act, in 1854. It marks the Nebraska Territory and the Utah Territory. It marks the Kansas Territory and the New Mexico Territory. It marks free states and free territories. It marks areas allowed to choose. It marks slave states. It marks unorganized territory. Lincoln decided the time had come to speak. He would speak against slavery's spread. A new try for office was part of the plan. Membership came in a young party called the Republicans. That party opposed slavery. In 1858 the party nominated him for senator. Facing him was Douglas, the senator who had long been his foe. The campaign included the Lincoln-Douglas debates. The whole country paid attention. Lincoln's speaking skill was great. A crisis for the whole nation, he said, was what slavery was creating. Split a house against itself, he warned, and it will not last. He did not believe this government could last forever half slave and half free. He argued that Black people were owed the right to life. They were owed liberty. They were owed the pursuit of happiness. White people already held those rights. In Douglas's reading, the Constitution offered equality to white people and to nobody else.

6Choice of slavery or freedom, he believed, belonged to each state. A picture shows Lincoln in 1858. The photo came two weeks before his last debate with Douglas. Another picture shows Stephen A. Douglas. Lincoln lost the race for the Senate. The debates still made him popular. The Republican Party felt that popularity most. By 1860 the party wanted him for president. Rallies and parades filled the campaign. People called him Honest Abe. They called him a homespun man of the people. Equality was his stand. Freedom was his stand. November of that year made him president. Joy broke out in the North. Western territories shared the joy. Outrage was the Southern answer. His inauguration was set for March 4, 1861. Even before that day, seven states of the South voted to quit the country. The word for that leaving is secede. Pro-slavery states set up their own government. They called it the Confederate States of America. Jefferson Davis was their president. They prepared for war. Lincoln took the oath on March 4, 1861. The place was the U.S. Capitol. Workers had not finished the building. Years of war. Lincoln still hoped to avoid war. His inauguration speech put a heavy question in other people's hands. He told unhappy fellow citizens that the huge issue of civil war was theirs. It was not his to settle alone. Events moved fast. April 14 arrived with a surrender. Northern troops left Fort Sumter in enemy hands. South Carolina had turned cannons on that fort. Speed marked what each side did next. The Union called for volunteers. The Confederacy called for volunteers. Both sides gathered weapons. Both sides gathered supplies. Lincoln's home and office were in Washington, D.C. That city stood with the Union.

7Across the river he could see Virginia. Virginia stood with the Confederacy. Southern generals were the stronger leaders at first. Bull Run was the first battle, and the Union lost it. Finding commanders with enough strength was a struggle for Lincoln. The search lasted through the war. General George B. McClellan led Union armies to some successes. By 1862 those armies were stopped. The stopper was Confederate general Robert E. Lee. Union forces did control New Orleans. They controlled the Mississippi River. Victories were still few. More of the war plans shifted into Lincoln's own hands. The North was calling for action. Huge numbers of young soldiers died. Others were wounded. Others went missing. The war moved into its second year. A picture shows President Lincoln talking with General McClellan. The place is Antietam. McClellan would soon be replaced. Personal loss hit Mary and Abraham Lincoln hard. Fever took Willie, their third son. The month was February 1862. Deep despair followed. Mary never fully recovered from the grief. Abraham carried his own sadness into meetings with families. Those families were mourning people killed in the war. Bull Run was fought a second time, and the Union lost again. Antietam brought the war's bloodiest clash, and both armies paid. Senators from the Republican Party, and powerful ones, pushed the president. They wanted ending slavery to become a goal of the war. A successful fight, they argued, required removing the issue that had caused the war. Lincoln at last became convinced. The presidency, he decided, gave him power to command abolition where the South held sway. New Year's Day of 1863 started the Emancipation Proclamation. Every enslaved person inside the Confederacy was declared free. The freedom was meant to last forever. Freedom for some. The proclamation freed many enslaved people.

8Some enslaved people were left out. Freedom on that January day covered enemy territory. Black men just freed inside Confederate land could join the Union fight. The North badly needed those soldiers. The war's meaning changed. It became a crusade against slavery. The order did not cover the border states. Delaware was one of those states. Maryland was another. Kentucky was another. Missouri was another. Why skip them? They held enslaved people, but they never seceded. Lincoln feared a different result if he freed people there. Joining the Confederacy was the risk he feared. A loss of the war would then be almost sure for the country. It would lose the South. It would lose the chance to end slavery in every state. Enslaved people who remained would wait two more years. A map of border states in 1863 uses four labels. One label is Union free state. One is Union slave state. One is Confederate slave state. One is territory. Names on the map include Maryland and Delaware. West Virginia is there. Missouri is there. Kentucky is there. Only West Virginia was created by breaking away from a state that had joined the Confederacy. That Confederate state was Virginia. From 1863 to 1865 the new Union state ended slavery bit by bit. Another people under oppression. Manuelito was a Navajo chief. The year was 1864. The land was taken, and his people had to leave. That land was in northeastern Arizona. Many people call Lincoln the Great Emancipator. Many Native peoples remember a harsher record. Westward growth was huge while he held office. His policies harmed Native peoples who already lived in those places. The Homestead Act came in 1862. The Pacific Railway Act came in the same year. A railroad across the continent followed from those laws.

9Land vanished for many Native peoples because of that railroad. It meant lost natural resources. It meant the loss of a whole way of life. Lincoln forced Native peoples onto reservations. In doing that, he continued harsh policies. The policies were discriminatory. Earlier presidents had used the same kind of policies. Fort Sumter fell, and free Black men hurried to sign up for the Union's army. At first they were turned away. By the middle of 1862 the need for volunteers was pressing. The government then began to take them. Men newly freed in the South signed up too. When the Civil War closed, Black men in uniform numbered nearly 200,000. Their service was as soldiers for the United States. A picture shows Company E of the 4th U.S. Colored Infantry. The company mixed newly freed men with other free Black men. Summer of 1863 brought a Union victory at Gettysburg. That battle was a turning point. President Lincoln dedicated a cemetery. Dead soldiers, and there were many, were the people that ground was meant to honor. His talk there is called the Gettysburg Address. Two minutes was the whole length. People remember it for simple beauty. They remember it for eloquence. He called the war a test of survival. Could the country remain a democracy? Living people, he said, had to complete what the dead had begun. The aim was a government of the people. It would be a government by the people. It would be a government for the people. That government, he said, must not perish from the earth. General Ulysses S. Grant led Union armies to victories. Those victories came in the West. They also came in the South. Lincoln began to hope the war would end. Confederate troops were beaten in Georgia late in 1864.

10They were beaten in Virginia in that same season. Voters re-elected him president. Early in 1865 he cheered a vote in Congress. The change was the Thirteenth Amendment. It was added to the Constitution of the United States. Slavery inside the country was banned. April 9, 1865, brought the end. The fighting had lasted four years. Lives lost came to 600,000. Survival went to the Union. Slavery was abolished. Six days after the peace, the president was gone. Abraham Lincoln had been killed. An assassin's bullet had killed him. John Wilkes Booth fired the shot. Booth sympathized with the Confederacy. Lincoln was at a play. The theater was Ford's Theatre. The city was Washington, D.C. A funeral train carried his body back to Illinois, the state he loved. Mourners along the road saluted in silence. They were saluting a great American hero. One of the last photographs of Lincoln was taken in February 1865. Words to know. Abolition means bringing something to an end. Here it means making slavery against the law. Momentous describes something of huge importance. An orator speaks in public, and the best ones speak with power and clarity. Civil rights cover the law, social life, and money matters. They exist so every citizen can have freedom and equal standing. A privilege is an honor, or a special gain that only some conditions allow. Eloquence is clear, strong speech or clear, strong writing. To secede is to leave a group in a formal way. An emancipator sets other people free. Solemn means grave, or full of sadness. Sovereignty means you are free to run your own affairs. Equality means all people hold the same rights. Homespun describes a humble person whose life began in a simple rural place.

67. The Living World of Fungi

1This book asks what fungi are and how many kinds exist. It looks at fungi that harm and fungi that help. It tells how to hunt mushrooms and how fungi can be fun. Word meanings and a topic list come last. White fuzzy mold on stale grapes and small brown mushrooms in a neighborhood park share something. Itchy, scaly skin on a person's feet shares something with yeast that makes bread rise. All four are organisms of the fungi kind. Flowers are often more colorful than fungi. Animals move around far more than fungi do. Fungi can still catch your eye in other ways. Shapes and sizes vary widely. Their ways of living are their own. They matter in health care. They matter in making food. They matter in other human work too. A common belief says fungi are plants. Plants make food by photosynthesis. That process uses sunlight, it uses water, and it uses carbon dioxide gas. Fungi cannot do photosynthesis. They must get food another way. Chemical study makes fungi look closer to animals than to plants. That likeness is why fungal diseases are hard to cure. A medicine that harms a fungus can harm a human. It can harm another animal too. Mycologists may study fungi with computers. Laboratory tools and indoor collections are other tools. Outdoor searches are another way. Food comes from chemicals called enzymes, which fungi release around themselves. Complex molecules nearby break down because of those enzymes. Simpler chemical nutrients are the result.

2Long, threadlike cells called hyphae then take the nutrients in. Most fungi share one more trait that many plants lack. They build tiny structures called spores. Wind can carry spores. Water can carry them. Animals can carry them. New fungi grow from the spores. A mycologist is a scientist who studies fungi. More than 100,000 species have been identified. Yeasts are fungi made of one cell each. Most other fungi are made of many cells. Molds, mildews, and mushrooms are in that many-celled group. A field of mushrooms is one kind. Mold on fruit is another. Bracket fungus on a tree is another. Athlete's foot on skin is another. The next sandwich you eat may deserve a thank-you to yeast. Yeast is a fungus of a single cell. Bread making uses it. Bubbles of carbon dioxide gas come out of the yeast. Bread rises into the soft, fluffy loaves you eat because of those bubbles. Beer and wine are made with yeast too. Some yeasts make new yeasts by forming spores. Others use budding. In budding, a small bulge called a bud forms on the cell. A hard wall grows around the bud. The bud then breaks away from the old cell. It becomes a yeast cell of its own. A picture shows a small bud on the side of a yeast cell. That bud will leave and grow into a new cell. A crusty patch on a rock may be gray, yellow, orange, or brown.

3The patch may be a lichen. Lichen can form where fungi and algae grow as partners. Algae make food the fungi use. Fungi take in water the algae can use. Rocks and tree bark are places lichens grow. Many lichens live where it is cold. Other life finds very little to eat in those places. Reindeer eat lichen. Caribou eat it. Other animals eat it too. A microscope can show mold on stale bread up close. Tiny sporangia may appear. Spores are made by sporangia. You may remember reaching for fruit, such as an orange, and finding blue-green and white fuzz. That fuzz was mold. Mold is one type of fungus. Grapes, peaches, and grapefruits can grow it. Bread, cheese, and other foods can grow it too. Many molds send hyphae straight up, like pins. Hyphae are what let fungi absorb nutrients. The pinhead tips are called sporangia. Spores come from those tips. The fuzzy look of mold comes from the pinheads. Mildews are parasitic fungi. They live in or on the organisms they eat. Powdery blotches on leaves are a common sign. Apple trees, cherry trees, rose bushes, and pea plants can show those blotches. Bathroom-wall scum is often called mildew. What bothers most bathrooms is actually bacteria, not a fungus. A picture shows fungi coating an apple that hangs in an orchard. Mushroom species number more than 5,000. Colors include white, yellow, orange, red, and brown. Most grow in woods or in grass.

4They live on dead matter that is decaying, such as dead grass. A mushroom's hyphae tangle into a mass called a mycelium. The mass sits underground, just under the surface. Years can pass while the mycelium grows and spreads down there. The umbrella-shaped parts above ground last only a few days. They last just long enough to make spores. Fly agaric mushrooms are poisonous. Enoki mushrooms, also called straw mushrooms, can be eaten. A blue whale may seem like the largest living thing. A giant redwood may seem largest instead. An underground fungus makes both look small. It grows in Malheur National Forest in Oregon. The mycelium covers 3.5 square miles, which equals 5.6 square kilometers. That spread is bigger than 1,600 football fields. Few people have looked at this giant. Only clusters of small golden-brown fruiting bodies rise above the soil. They appear now and then. A mushroom comes out of the ground on a stalk. Stalk height, depending on the kind, runs from 3/4 inch (1.9 cm) to 15 inches (38 cm). A round cap sits at the top. The biggest caps can reach 18 inches (46 cm) across. Stalk plus cap is the fruiting body. Under the cap, many mushrooms have rows of thin blades called gills. Fish use gills to breathe. These gills do not. Cells in the gills make spores. Some mushrooms make spores in tiny tubes under the cap. A diagram can name the cap, the gills, the annulus, the stalk, the volva, and the mycelium.

5A life cycle is the set of stages a species passes through. The stages run from first growth, through death, to the start of a new organism. Every fungus species has its own kind of life cycle. A typical mushroom's life cycle starts when a spore lands where food and water are enough for it to germinate. Hyphae branch out under the ground. A mycelium forms. Hyphae from two different mushrooms sometimes join inside one mycelium. Tiny knots called buttons grow on that mass. Buttons sprout and become fruiting bodies. After a heavy rain, those bodies may shoot up fast. Once spores are released, the fruiting body withers. The mycelium stays alive a long time. More fruiting bodies can be made. A cycle diagram can show a mature fruiting body, spores, and fungal spores. It can show a button sprouting after rain. It can show buttons starting to form, plus a button, hyphae, a mycelium, and a spore. Many fungi harm plants. They can harm animals, people included. They can harm things people make. In damp places, mildews and some other fungi grow in books, in clothing, and in wood. The items decay because of the fungi. Other parasitic fungi sicken crops. Cereal crops are at special risk. Wheat, rice, oats, and corn are examples. Spores sometimes enter the seeds of these grains. When grain falls, the spores move into the new plants that grow from those seeds.

6A fungus causes Dutch elm disease. Bark beetles, a kind of insect, carry it from tree to tree. A large elm can die in four to eight weeks. Chestnut blight, a similar fungus, killed nearly every chestnut tree in the United States. The early 1900s were when that happened. In the 1840s, blight, a fungal disease, killed most potato plants in Ireland. Potatoes were most of the food for people there. The blight was so wide that about one million people in that small country starved to death. Millions more left Ireland. They went to the United States, to Canada, and to England. Hot, sweaty feet do not look appealing, unless the viewer is a fungus. Some fungi too small to see prefer warm, moist skin. They grow between toes and on the soles. The disease they cause is athlete's foot, and it is infectious. Skin turns red, scaly, and itchy. Clean, dry feet help you avoid it. Socks that let fresh air through help too. Ringworm names several skin diseases caused by fungi. They show up as red, scaly rings. The neck, the back, the chest, or other skin can carry the rings. Spread from person to person is easy. Touching infected skin can spread it. Almost any object that touched the sore spot and then touched skin can spread it too. Red, itchy rings mark the skin of people who have ringworm. One picture shows ringworm over most of an ankle. Other fungal diseases hit the lungs, the kidneys, the throat, or other inner parts.

7Chemical solutions called fungicides can kill harmful fungi. Harm is not the whole story. Some fungi help doctors cure disease. Certain molds make chemicals used as antibiotics. An antibiotic is medicine that weakens or kills disease-causing bacteria. Penicillin is one of the more common antibiotics from fungi. It treats pneumonia. It treats many other bacterial diseases. Other molds go into cheese. Added mold sets off chemical reactions. Flavor changes. The cheese ripens. Fungi help food in further ways. Farmers count on fungi to decompose dead plant material. Chemicals released into soil become nutrients. New crops grow with the help of those nutrients. Blue cheese is one cheese made with blue mold. The mold makes the cheese ripen. Penicillin was the first antibiotic used on people with serious disease. The find was an accident in 1928. Sir Alexander Fleming, in England, made it. He saw green mold in a lab dish that also held bacteria. Every bacterium around the mold was dead. The mold was giving off a chemical that hurt the bacteria. Later researchers learned how to use that substance, penicillin, against bacteria in people. Going out to look for fungi is a fun way to learn more. Mold or mildew may turn up here and there. Hunting mushrooms is likely to be the most fun. Do not put any mushroom in your mouth. Wash your hands after you handle fungi. Some mushrooms are safe to eat.

8Others hold poisons that can make you very sick. Telling the safe kinds from the poisonous kinds is hard. Only a hunter with a great deal of experience can do it. Always go with a hunter who has that experience. The best hunting times are fall and spring, after heavy rain. Before you start, learn which mushrooms grow where you live. A library can help. A wider search can add facts about mushrooms near you. Mushrooms named at the end of the book show some of the many fungi of North America. People once killed pesky flies with sugar sprinkled on fly agaric mushrooms. Sugar drew the flies in. Once a fly landed and ate, poison in the mushroom killed it. Have any conclusions about fungi formed as you read? Did any fact surprise you? One discovery may be that fungi can be fun. Watch for fungi. See what else these special organisms can show you. You can grow mold of your own. Ask a parent or a guardian before you begin. A plastic sandwich bag should hold either one slice of bread or one piece of fruit. The food gives nutrients to mold spores. Add a moist paper towel to the bag. Close it. Moisture stays trapped. Mold needs that moisture if it is to grow. Repeat the steps with several foods. Wait until fuzzy mold appears. About 3 to 5 days is the usual wait. Do different foods grow different molds? Write what you see, or draw it.

9Some mushrooms are poisonous. The destroying angel, Amanita virosa, grows in woods under trees in eastern North America.
