The fly agaric, Amanita muscaria, grows in woods under trees through North America. The jack-o'lantern, Omphalotus olearius, grows in clusters on tree stumps. It glows in the dark. Its home is the eastern United States. The false chanterelle, Hygrophoropsis aurantiaca, grows on or near logs and stumps. Its home is northern North America. Some mushrooms are not poisonous. The oyster mushroom, Pleurotus ostreatus, grows in clusters on logs and stumps across North America. The shaggy mane, Coprinus comatus, grows on lawns, in fields, and beside roads across North America. The old man of the woods, Strobilomyces floccopus, grows under trees in eastern North America. The king bolette, Boletus edulis, grows under trees that bear cones. It grows in North America outside the central region. Buttons are knots on a mycelium that become a mushroom's fruiting bodies. A cap is the round top of a mushroom. To decompose is to break into simpler chemical substances. Enzymes are chemicals that cause or change reactions while staying unchanged themselves. A fruiting body is the mature part of a fungus, and it produces spores. Fungi are living things that take in nutrients by absorption. Fungicides are chemical solutions that kill fungi or slow their growth. To germinate is to start growing. Gills are mushroom parts whose cells make spores. Hyphae are long threads fungi use to absorb nutrients.

10Infectious describes a disease that can pass from one organism to another. A mycelium is a tangled mass of hyphae. Nutrients are chemicals a living thing needs in order to live. Organisms are living things. To reproduce is to make a new generation. A species is one specific type of living thing. Sporangia are structures on fungal hyphae that make spores. Spores are tiny fungus-made structures that can grow into new fungi. A stalk is the mushroom part that rises from the ground under the cap. Topics in this book include algae and the jack-o'lantern. They include antibiotics and the king bolette. They include athlete's foot and lichen. They include bacteria and the life cycle. They include the bark beetle and Malheur National Forest. They include blight and mildew. They include bread and mold. They include budding and the mushroom. They include the button and the mycelium. They include the cap and the mycologist. They include carbon dioxide and the old man of the woods. They include cheese and the oyster mushroom. They include the destroying angel and the word parasitic. They include Dutch elm disease and penicillin. They include enzymes and photosynthesis. They include the false chanterelle and ringworm. They include Sir Alexander Fleming and the shaggy mane. They include the fly agaric and sporangia. They include the fruiting body and the spore. They include the fungicide and the stalk. They include germinate and yeast. They include gills, the Great Irish Famine, and hyphae.

68. The Long Road to Rebellion

1A map of North America in 1750 shows who claimed the land. New France and British Canada sit in the north. The Atlantic Ocean lies to the east, and the Pacific Ocean lies to the west. Louisiana, the British colonies, and a disputed stretch appear on the map, along with Florida and New Spain. More than two hundred years ago, colonists in that claimed land went to war with an empire. They won. Those people lived in the place now called the United States. The empire they fought was Great Britain. Britain was already a strong, settled country. It wanted a larger empire, and it wanted land in the region Europeans of that time called the New World. Today that region is North America, Central America, and South America. Britain was not alone in that wish. Other countries in Europe wanted New World land as well. This book follows the quarrel that grew from those claims. It looks at Britain's colonies. It looks at the war for the continent. It looks at taxes passed without a colonial voice. It looks at angry answers and at the first shots. A word list comes last. Europeans saw the New World as a store of raw materials. They also saw open land for populations that were growing at home. Indigenous peoples were already there. Their history on that land stretched across thousands of years. Colonizing by Spain got underway in the 1400s. Spanish colonizers enslaved Indigenous people and killed them. Those peoples had been on the land for thousands of years. Come the 1700s, millions of Indigenous people had been killed by colonizers from Europe. Violence did part of that killing. Disease did the rest. In the east of North America, Britain seized Indigenous land by force. On that land Britain set up thirteen colonies. People who moved there were called colonists. An ocean, the Atlantic, lay between them and the country that ruled them. That distance let the colonists shape ideas of their own. It also let them shape their own habits of daily life. Every colony held a charter from the British king. Every colony also had a legislature.

2Property owners in the colony elected it. That habit of acting for themselves later fed the Revolutionary War. It did so even though the colonists and Britain had once stood on the same side. France and England spent much of the 1700s fighting over land in North America. They clashed more than once. Colonists joined Britain against the shared foe, France. During the 1750s, France wanted certain North American lands. Great Britain wanted those same stretches. The two kingdoms had already spent hundreds of years struggling for power in Europe. The struggle simply moved to North America. Explorers from France started at Newfoundland. They followed the St. Lawrence River downstream. That route arrived at the Great Lakes. It also reached the valley of the Ohio River. Fur trappers from France had set up trading posts along that route. Britain said those same lands belonged to Britain. Colonists went there to settle. Nations of Indigenous people in that region had traded with the French for a long time. Their ties to the French were better than their ties to the British. Settlers from Britain moved inland, leaving the East Coast behind them. They claimed ground where Indigenous people had lived for centuries. They also claimed hunting grounds used for centuries. Indigenous nations wanted those ancestral lands back. Many of them joined France. They hoped to guard their trade, their land, and their independence. War was coming between France and Britain. Some Indigenous nations chose Britain instead. The Cherokee did. So did the Catawba. The nations inside the Iroquois Confederacy did the same. In return, they were promised some of their land back. Other nations made the opposite choice. The Delaware sided with France. The Shawnee did too, and so did the Ottawa. Each camp began to build forts. They chose sites in the valley of the Ohio River. Each side wanted to protect its claim. Early in 1754 the French raised Fort Duquesne, a name said doo-KAYN. It stood where Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, stands now. The British had started a fort on that spot. French forces drove them off and finished the work themselves. The site mattered. Whoever held it could control the Ohio River Valley.

3Rivers met nearby, among them the Ohio, the Allegheny, and the Monongahela. Britain sent a young surveyor, George Washington, to ask the French to go. The French would not leave. Washington, his soldiers, and Seneca allies then struck a party of French scouts. Ten of those scouts were killed. Washington's men next built Fort Necessity. It stood about 60 miles, or 96.5 kilometers, from Fort Duquesne. In the summer of 1754 the French took Fort Necessity. Washington and his men gave up the fort, then got away. Washington later served as a volunteer aide to Britain's General Edward Braddock. Braddock meant to push the French out of the Ohio River Valley. He would start at Fort Duquesne. French soldiers hid in the woods beside the British columns. Indigenous allies hid with them. When the trap sprang, the British troops panicked and fled. Braddock was killed. Over half the men under his command died as well. Many historians call that clash the opening real battle. The wider struggle is known by the name French and Indian War. The larger conflict around it was the Seven Years' War. The North American fighting was one piece of that wider war. Colonists would later copy this kind of guerrilla warfare. In the American Revolution, they turned that same style of fighting on Britain's troops. A painting shows the Battle of Fort Duquesne as it was fought in 1756. The year 1756 was when Great Britain made the war with France official. Official fighting dates from that year. Fighting had already taken place in both worlds, the New and the Old, before that official start. Britain sent more soldiers to the colonies. France did the same. At the start, France looked likely to win. France had Indigenous allies. On the frontier, French fighters knew the style of war better. British troops and colonists knew it less well. The balance shifted by 1758. The British force in North America had grown to nearly 42,000 soldiers. The attacks hit Fort Niagara. They also hit Lake Champlain. Quebec was a third target. France could no longer reach the valley of the Ohio River.

4The Mississippi River was closed off too. So was the port at New Orleans. France had claimed all of that land. French forces depended on supplies that came out of those places. Without the supplies, they could not stay in North America. Britain won the war. A peace treaty signed in 1763 carried the name Treaty of Paris. It wiped out French claims on the eastern side of the Mississippi, across North America. Colonists from Britain could now move into land France had held, Canada included. For a short time the colonists were glad to belong to Great Britain. Many of them had fought beside British troops against a shared enemy. Once France was beaten, that feeling changed. Many colonists decided they no longer needed Britain's protection. They also decided they no longer needed Britain's oversight. What Britain did next made them angry. King George III and Parliament raised colonial taxes. The country was trying to shrink the huge debt left by the war. Britain also posted soldiers in the colonies to guard the larger empire. Colonists were expected to give those soldiers housing and food. A later map shows the result. British Canada remains in the north. The thirteen colonies sit along the Atlantic. Some of the British land is set aside. It is reserved so Indigenous peoples can use it. New Spain and Florida appear as well, with the Pacific Ocean on the far side. The cry of this chapter is taxation without representation. Parliament passed the Sugar Act in 1764. Only one year had passed since the Treaty of Paris. Lawmakers were widening an older law from 1733, the one called the Sugar and Molasses Act. It put a tax on molasses and sugar from Spain and from France when colonists bought them. It added taxes on coffee and on some textiles. It also limited the markets where colonists could sell what they made. Spanish and French sugar had been cheap. The tax made it so costly that colonists had to buy British sugar instead. The money helped Britain pay war debts. It also threw the colonial economy out of order.

5British leaders believed the support given to colonists had gone on longer than it should. Parliament's next law, in 1765, was the Quartering Act. After the Seven Years' War ended, some 10,000 British troops remained in America. The act told colonists to lodge those troops in private homes. The soldiers lived with colonial families. They did not have to pay rent. They did not have to help with the family's work. King George III had become king in 1760, when he was only 22. He was set on keeping the colonies loyal to Britain. Most colonies refused to obey the Quartering Act. New York would not supply food or lodging. As punishment, Parliament suspended that colony's governor and its elected council. The Stamp Act, passed in the same year, caused an even louder outcry. It was Britain's first serious try at showing full authority over the North American colonies. Every printed paper a colonist used required a stamp sold by Britain. Newspapers were taxed. Calendars were taxed. Playing cards and other paper goods were taxed. Hidden in the small print was an income tax as well. The Virginia Assembly stood at the center of the protest that followed. Colonists were furious about the taxes. They were just as furious about something else. The government taxing them gave them no say. A shout spread through the colonies. The words were these: No taxation without representation. Other English subjects had someone speaking for them in Parliament. Colonists wanted that too. King George disliked being told what to do by colonists. While he planned how to strike back at the rebels, the colonists began to act together against the taxes. Over many years they had already built ways to govern themselves. As early as 1619, an elected assembly in Virginia was already passing laws for that colony. Among all the colonies, that body was the earliest one voters had chosen. Its members debated whether the Stamp Act was fair. Other colonies took that debate as a model. A young lawyer, Patrick Henry, rose and made a claim. His claim was blunt. Only Virginians, he said, could tax Virginians.

6The assembly took his side. Some people still called him a traitor for speaking against King George. Newspapers carried his words. Protest against the Stamp Act soon spread through every one of the 13 colonies. Henry was not alone. Samuel Adams added his voice against the same tax. Colonists who backed their own colonies against the king were called Patriots. Colonists who stayed loyal to the Crown were called Loyalists. Some Patriots formed the Sons of Liberty. Others formed the Daughters of Liberty. They told neighbors to stop trading with Britain and to stop buying British goods. Colonists even attacked some of the British agents who sold the stamps. More laws from Parliament were still to come. More attacks were still to come. Nine of the thirteen colonies sent representatives to New York. The month was October, and the year was 1765. Those people met as the Stamp Act Congress. Women in the 1700s were mostly shut out of politics, yet they still served the Patriot cause. The Daughters of Liberty planned boycotts and took part in them. Many women bought the goods a household needed, or they ran small shops. Their refusal to buy hit British merchants hard. Women also formed sewing circles to keep the cause going. The Stamp Act Congress asked Parliament to repeal the Stamp Act, which means to cancel it. In 1766 King George agreed, and the act was repealed. A new set of laws arrived in 1767. They were the Townshend Acts. The taxed goods were glass and paint. Lead was taxed too. So were paper and tea. The anger looked familiar. Colonists had shouted down earlier taxes, and they shouted these down as well. They boycotted British goods, refusing to buy them. In 1770 Britain canceled every Townshend tax except one. Merchants in Britain were watching their income fall. Every Townshend tax was dropped except the one on tea. The strain kept growing. Patriots and Great Britain were pulling further apart. Soldiers spread through the colonies to make people pay. Each new tax deepened the anger. One night in Boston, anger turned into bloodshed. Once that war with France and its Indigenous allies was over, Boston still held a great many British soldiers.

7For a time they lived there in relative peace. Colonists resented them. Even so, the two groups shared the city for years. Then a date arrived: March 5, 1770. That night, noisy colonists in Boston picked a fight with some of the soldiers. The soldiers fired into the crowd. Five colonists died. Their only weapons had been snowballs, sticks, and stones. Patriot leader Samuel Adams treated the fight as a chance to pull more people toward independence. The friend he turned to was Paul Revere. Adams wanted a picture from him. Revere was a silversmith, and he engraved the scene. He printed the engraving and sold it as a poster. Adams named the fight the Boston Massacre, even though colonists had started it. The picture showed British soldiers shooting at calm, finely dressed colonists. Newspapers printed it too. The scene was not an honest report of what happened. It still did what Adams wanted. It filled many colonists with rage. The printed engraving is the picture people remember. Many people believe the Boston Massacre's first death was Crispus Attucks. Boston was his home. His job was whaling. The ships he sailed from worked out of Boston Harbor. Freedom from Great Britain mattered deeply to him. Speakers at the memorial returned often to his courage. By 1773 the tea tax was all that remained of the Townshend Acts. It was not a new tax. In 1773 the Tea Act was rewritten. Tea could be bought from one seller only. That seller was the East India Company, owned in Great Britain. They still had no representatives in Parliament. They were angry that the other taxes had not all been wiped away. A fed-up group of colonists acted in December 1773. They meant to show their hatred of the tea tax. They boarded a British ship. Into Boston Harbor went 342 chests of tea. They wore the dress of the Mohawk Nation so the blame would not fall on them. Britain was not fooled. Britain was not amused. Any leftover goodwill was finished. Later, the night took the name Boston Tea Party.

8Come summer in 1774, the king and Parliament answered with the Coercive Acts. Colonists gave those laws a new name, the Intolerable Acts. The laws were written to punish colonists who would not obey. One of them shut Boston Harbor to every ship. Many people in Boston lost their work. They feared they would starve. Colonists elsewhere felt sorry for Boston. They were furious at Great Britain. Colonial assemblies spoke up for Boston. The British governor of a colony often wanted them silent. They spoke anyway. General Thomas Gage received a new job from Britain. He would govern Massachusetts. He was sent to Boston to take the city in hand. He brought 4,000 troops. Colonists had to house them and feed them. The Intolerable Acts, like the Stamp Act before them, pulled the colonies together against Britain. In September 1774, delegates from 12 colonies met in Philadelphia. They called the meeting the First Continental Congress. Only one colony failed to come. That colony was Georgia. Repeal of the Intolerable Acts was the first demand. A second demand asked for a colonial voice whenever a tax law was made. Parliament refused. It declared that the colonies were in a state of mutiny. Members of the Continental Congress knew their demands might bring war with Great Britain. They agreed to gather again in 1775. In the meantime they urged people in Massachusetts to store up weapons. They also urged them to halt all trade with Britain. Massachusetts looked like the right place to start, because General Gage and his troops were in Boston. The Congress began training fighters for the struggle ahead. Those fighters were called militiamen, or minutemen. Colonists were getting ready to break from a country that many of them no longer trusted. The nickname minutemen came from a simple claim. A Patriot could seize a weapon and be outside within a minute. Most of those soldiers did not even have uniforms. In Boston, Gage grew worried. Reports said colonists were storing weapons at Concord, about 20 miles, or 32 kilometers, west of the city. His order went out on April 18, 1775, after dark.

9Seven hundred British soldiers were to seize the stored weapons. He also hoped to arrest the rebellion's leaders, Samuel Adams and John Hancock. They were in Lexington, a town close to Concord. A Patriot doctor, Samuel Prescott, learned what Gage intended. He warned the militia that British troops were on the way. Before the soldiers reached Concord, they met a group of militiamen. Lexington's village green was where those 70 fighters stood waiting. Britain's soldiers tried to pass them and keep walking. Then a shot rang out that nobody had ordered. Nobody knows which side fired it. That shot began the Revolutionary War. A famous name came later. People said it was the shot heard around the world. In the fight that followed, eight militiamen were killed and ten were wounded. The British losses were heavy. Even so, the British marched on toward Concord. Boston still tells a famous story about Paul Revere. The story says he warned the fighters at Lexington and at Concord that British troops were coming. That story is a tall tale. What is true is narrower. Revere did send a watcher. That person's job was to keep an eye on Britain's troops. The watcher was to hang lanterns in a church tower to show which way the troops would march. One lantern meant the soldiers were coming by land. Two lanterns meant they would cross the Charles River. That night Revere saw two lanterns. He left Boston on horseback with William Dawes, riding toward Concord to spread the warning. Samuel Prescott joined the pair on the road. British officers stopped Revere. They stopped Dawes as well. Prescott got away. The warning that reached the militiamen came from Prescott, not from the other two. Pictures still show the famous midnight ride. In Concord the British ruined some supplies. The colonists had already moved most of the weapons and hidden them. Patriot leaders Hancock and Adams were not arrested. Nearly 500 men of the Massachusetts militia reached Concord. At the North Bridge they attacked the tired British soldiers. The next day they kept up the attack while those soldiers marched back toward Boston.

10The British were in retreat. Militiamen fired from behind trees and from behind stone walls, straight into the lines of red-coated troops. Cover of that kind had already been used by French fighters and by Indigenous fighters during the earlier war over this land. Trained British professionals were humiliated. They had been beaten by colonists who were quickly trained and poorly equipped. The dead numbered 273 on the British side and 93 among the militiamen. The Revolutionary War was underway. A picture shows Patriot troops facing British soldiers on the village green at Lexington. These words come up often in the story. Allies are people or groups that join for a shared cause. A charter is an official paper that sets out the rights and duties of a person or a group. A colonist is a person living in a colony. The word also fits a person who founds a colony. Delegates are chosen people who speak and act for others. Economy means how money circulates. The word takes in workshops and trade. It also takes in how money is handled inside a country or a region. Frontier describes wild country at the edge of a settled region. Guerrilla warfare is irregular fighting, often a surprise attack, by small independent bands. A legislature is a body of elected officials who make or change laws. Migrated means moved on purpose from one region to another to live or to work. A militia is an army of ordinary citizens rather than full-time soldiers. Mutiny is a refusal to obey a government or another authority. Parliament makes the laws for the United Kingdom. Two houses form it. One is the House of Commons. The other is the House of Lords. Another useful word is raw materials. Those are basic stuff from which other things are made. Rebellious describes someone who tends to resist a government. A revolution removes a government by force and puts another in its place. Stationed means assigned to a place. To stockpile is to keep a large supply for later use. Textiles are cloth, fabric that has been woven.

69. The Man the Ice Kept

1The parts of this book come in this order. A scene set about 5,300 years ago. How people found the frozen man. Facts about the man himself. One idea calls the death an accident. Another idea calls it a killing over food. A third idea calls it a killing over power. A closing part says the true story stays hidden. A word list ends the book. About 5,300 years ago, a man prepared in his village. A small brown dog yapped beside his feet. He eased the puppy aside with a gentle push. A basket of grain sat in his arms. That push tipped the basket. Grain spilled. He told the puppy to look at the mess. The spill annoyed him. Even so, he smiled at the puppy. A hunt was coming. Much work still waited. Winter was drawing near. He had no spare time. A tall boy with dark hair came to the spilled grain. He began scooping the grain up. The man watched his son. Pride showed in that look. He told the boy to care for things while he was away. The boy answered, calling him Father. The boy said that he knew. Together they returned the grain to the basket. The dog played at their heels as they worked. The boy took the grain to a pit under the ground. The pit would guard the grain through the winter ahead. Father and son walked slowly back toward home.

2The man paused and rubbed his legs. He knew the weather would turn colder soon. Food would then grow scarce. Men who could not kill enough on the hunt would quarrel. The quarrel would be about food for their families. Tension in the community would run high. He needed to leave the village soon. He would hunt red deer, ibex, and wild boar. His family would live on that meat during winter. A later picture rebuilds Otzi and the belongings he carried on the journey. At home, the man gathered those belongings. He meant to be ready for almost anything. Then he left his family. The journey began. He traveled only a short distance from home. He killed an ibex. He carried the meat. Suddenly an arrow whizzed past his ear. Several more arrows flew. One struck hard into the back of his right shoulder. He clutched his arm. He moaned from the pain. His left hand reached behind him. He tried to pull the arrow free. He could not remove all of it. He walked slowly up a hill. Men behind him took the meat bundle he had dropped. He made it to the hilltop. He lay down. He shut his eyes for a final time. He did not know his body would freeze inside the ice. He did not know it would stay locked in time. Thousands of years afterward, people would know him as Otzi, the Iceman.

3This story is only one possible way he died. No one is sure how it happened. All anyone can do is theorize. To theorize is to guess from the facts. Scientists collect facts, the clues, before they make a theory. You can build a theory about his death too. Read the things that are known. Think the way a scientist thinks. Then form your own theories. Local people nicknamed the Iceman Otzi. The name honors Otztal. Otztal is a valley close to where he died. A picture shows people pulling Otzi from the ice. A map shows the place Otzi was found. The lands on the map are Switzerland, Austria, France, and Italy. Picture labels mark a dagger and a sheath. Other labels mark a grass cape fragment, a quiver, a birch-bark container, a bow, an ax, and a backpack frame. A compass marks the directions. In September 1991, two German hikers made an amazing discovery. They were Erika and Helmut Simon. They were high in the Tyrolean Alps. The height was more than 10,000 feet. The spot lay near the border of Austria and Italy. They found a frozen body that had no hair. Only the head rose above the ice. Part of the shoulders rose too. They first thought it was a modern climber's frozen corpse. A few days later, a different theory came from an Austrian scientist. His name was Rainer Henn.

4The corpse was yellowed and dried. He decided it had been frozen for a long time. He was right. Later tests put his age at about 5,000 years. A scientist examines the mummy of Otzi. That mummy is 5,300 years old. Scientists studied the well-preserved body to learn how he looked and how healthy he was. They used carbon dating. They used microscopic analysis. They used X-rays. They found that Otzi was short. He was only about five feet tall. He weighed about 110 pounds. He had wavy brown hair. He probably wore a beard. He lived to be about 46 years old. In that time, 46 years made him an elder. Several medical conditions bothered him. He had a bad back. He had arthritis. He had worn joints. He had a bad stomach. Scientists looked at Otzi's teeth and formed a theory about his diet. He probably ate mostly bread. His teeth were ground down. Only years of eating grains could wear teeth down that far. He probably also ate crab apples. He ate berries. He ate acorns. He ate hazelnuts. He ate the meat of animals he could hunt and kill. A food picture shows hazelnuts, acorns, a crab apple, an ibex, and berries. Using these clues and others, scientists began to theorize about how he may have died. Here is what was found with the Iceman, or learned from tests. A copper ax.

5A sloe berry. A bow. A stone disk on a leather string, and the string had fringe. Arrows. One arrow held blood traces left by two people. Mushrooms tied onto a leather string. A quiver made for arrows. Tests that show Otzi likely had arthritis and had back pain. A knife that held blood traces from a different person. A grass sheath for that knife. A long-sleeved jacket or vest made of animal hides, also holding blood traces from a different person. Strips of felt. A container of birch bark. Flint. A cloak woven from grass. A backpack with a wood frame. A leather pouch. A wooden stick tipped with deer antler. Leather pants. Shoes that were waterproof. A bone awl. A fur hat. Cuts on his hands and on his wrists. Socks made of grass. Meat of an ibex, which is a wild goat. Tattoos. A picture shows Otzi after he was pulled out of the ice. At first, investigators thought a storm had caught the Iceman. They thought he fell asleep. They thought cold caused his death. Later theories support a different idea. They support the idea that someone killed him. Blood was on his clothes. Wounds were on his body. A number of scientists believe the evidence fits one cause. An arrow wound to his back caused the death. Knife wounds marked his hands. But why? What reason would drive someone to kill Otzi? Several theories exist.

6The first theory calls it an accident. While Otzi hunted, other hunters shot him by mistake, and then he was buried. Scientists think he was hunting because of the clothes he wore. They also point to the equipment he carried when he was found frozen inside the glacier. Many scraps of material were on his body. Those scraps were leather, fur, grass, bearskin, cowhide, and tree bark. From the scraps, scientists think he wore leather pants. They think he wore a long-sleeved jacket or vest. The hides were deer, goat, and ibex. The fur side was turned out. He possibly wore a long cloak woven from grass. Scientists guess more about his clothes from the clues. His shoes were waterproof and wide. They seem designed for walks over snow. Bearskin made the soles. Cowhide or deer made the top panels. Netting of tree bark held the shoes together. Soft grass was wound around his feet. The grass worked like warm socks. Grass laces went through eyeholes. A leather flap kept those laces dry. The shoes held his size-six feet snug. Scientists also theorize about his hat. Separate cut pieces of fur were sewn into the hat. The fur was probably bearskin. Two leather straps were fixed to the hat. The straps might have served as a chinstrap. Scientists think these clothes match a long trek, such as a hunting trip. The equipment found with him strengthens that belief.

7Here is what scientists found. A copper ax. A bow. Arrows. A quiver. A tiny knife. Deer and ibex, they think, were hunted with his bow and his arrows. He used the knife to clean the animals. He used the ax to chop firewood. He used the quiver to hold the arrows. He also carried two strips of felt. He carried a small container made from birch bark. They think the felt may have been tinder for lighting fires. They think the container carried the felt. Beside the container was a soft leather pouch. The pouch held two pieces of flint. The flint was probably used to make tools. It was also used to strike sparks for a fire. A wooden stick four inches long had a tip of deer antler. It may have sharpened the flint chunks. From this evidence, and from knowledge of the time, some scientists theorize that he was hunting. Arrows from other hunters may have caught him by accident in a crossfire. An x-ray of his chest shows the arrowhead. A picture shows some of the items found with Otzi. The second theory says the death was not an accident. Hunters killed him on purpose in a fierce battle. Other scientists disagree with the accident idea. They think he was hunting ibex when he met starving hunters. Those hunters desperately needed a kill. They did not want him taking that kill.

8So they attacked and fired arrows. Otzi fired back. Dr. Tom Loy is director of the Queensland National Institute of Molecular Bioscience. He thinks the Iceman sent two arrows into two enemies. Each time, Otzi pulled the precious weapon out of the body. That theory explains why blood from other people was on his belongings. One trace came from his knife. Two traces came from the same arrowhead. A fourth trace came from his coat. Besides the arrows, the attackers may have used a knife. Cuts on his hands and wrist may show that he tried to defend himself. Many scientists hold this theory to be true. Some wonder if he was killed for yet another reason. The third theory says members of his community killed him. They saw him as a shaman who had become too powerful. Walter Leitner works at the Institute for Ancient and Early History. That institute is part of the University of Innsbruck in Austria. He thinks the Iceman might have been a shaman. A shaman is a healer of the body and of the spirit. People think a shaman can travel to the spirit world for medicine. People think a shaman can travel back again. When scientists examined the body, they found many mysterious tattoos. The tattoos included stripes. They included a cross. They included small bars. These were not decorations meant for others to see. They appeared only on parts that clothing would have hidden.

9Were these 57 crudely carved tattoos an old form of acupuncture? They were found on his ankles, knees, and calves. They sat on acupuncture points, or near those points. Those points would treat ailments he likely suffered. The ailments were arthritis and back pain. A picture shows one of his tattoos on his ankle. Some scientists believe one find might have been a necklace that Otzi wore. A small depression was found in his right earlobe. Did that mean he wore an earring? Some scientists think he may have worn jewelry as well. Near the body lay a leather string with a fringe. The string passed through a disk two inches across. The disk was white stone. Could this mysterious object have been a necklace for a medicine man like Otzi? Two mushrooms turned up as well, resting on a leather piece. This mushroom, scientists know, can help against sickness. Was he carrying them as medicine, something the hunters needed? Could this frozen man truly have been a shaman? These are only a few of the scientific theories about him. Theories change when the facts, the clues, change. Sometimes the clues remain the same, and scientists interpret the facts in a new way. What reading do you give these facts? What kinds of theories do you have now about how he may have died? The possible paths to his death are vast in number.

10The real account stays hidden from us, at least for the present. Word list. Acupuncture is a noun. It is care in which needles enter the skin at set places on the body so pain will ease. Arthritis is a noun. It is a disease in which joints swell and then stiffen. Carbon dating works as a verb in this list. It means using chemicals to find out how old something is. A corpse is a noun. It means a dead body. Evidence is a noun. It is information that can prove a claim true or prove it false. A glacier is a noun. It is a large build-up of ice plus compacted snow in a valley of mountains. Preserved works as a verb here. It means kept in the same condition. A shaman is a noun. It means a healer who works with the spirit and with the body. Tattoos are a noun. They are permanent marks put on the body with ink. A theory is a noun. It is one possible explanation. Index. Rainer Henn is tied to the find. Topics about the Iceman include his age, his appearance, his clothing, his condition, and his diet. Other topics include the discoverers, the fictional opening, his given name, his identity, the location, and his possessions. Walter Leitner is listed. Tom Loy is listed. Death theories listed here are accidental death, murder, and a death tied to weather.

70. The Normandy Landing

1This book begins with the morning itself, then the war behind it, then a plan called Operation Overlord. Five beaches follow in this order. The first is Utah. Then comes Omaha. Then comes Gold. Then comes Juno. Sword is last. A closing look and a word list come last. Hundreds of men crouched in dozens of small boats made for landing. Families far away filled their thoughts. The boats sat just off a coast. Germany occupied that part of France. Most of these men were not career soldiers. Lifelong military training was not their story. Some had been teachers. Some had been store clerks. Some had been housepainters. They were ordinary citizens. One home country was the United States. Another was the United Kingdom. Canada was another. A draft had pulled them into service. The war was World War II. Rough water rocked the landing boats. Seasickness hit many of them. Fear hit all of them. The mission started with a jump into cold water. Then came a run across open sand. German soldiers were shooting. Those German soldiers had been ordinary citizens too, before the war. The world these men knew had changed. Losing was not a choice they could accept. Planners had given the mission a code name. The name was Operation Overlord. For the Allies, this fight had to be won. This is the story of D-Day. What the letter D means. In military language, D stands for day. The code marked the date of any major operation. It was not limited to one battle. Days before that date, and days after it, used plus and minus signs. This particular day was June 6, 1944.

2D minus 3 meant three days earlier. That earlier date was June 3. D plus 3 meant three days later. That later date was June 9. A map of Europe in 1942 names Ireland and Prussia. It names England, the Netherlands, Poland, and Germany. Belgium and Czechoslovakia appear. Luxembourg, France, and Austria appear. Switzerland, Hungary, and Romania appear. Portugal, Yugoslavia, and Bulgaria appear. Spain, Italy, Albania, and Greece appear. Waters on the map are the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea. A key marks Axis control, neutral countries, and Allied control. The background. World War II was the biggest war of modern times. German troops marching into Poland were the start. The month was September 1939. Poland fell quickly. German troops then turned west. France was invaded in June 1940. Four years followed. Germany was not alone. Italy and Japan were the other Axis powers. Together they took most of Europe. They also took many islands in the Pacific. Allied nations tried to stop them. The United Kingdom was an Ally. The United States was an Ally. Canada was an Ally. The Soviet Union was an Ally. Many other nations stood with them. Freeing France would trap German troops. Allied-held France would lie on one side. The Soviet Union would lie on the other. Operation Overlord. For Allied forces, few dates in this war mattered more than June 6, 1944. Boats put men ashore on the beaches of Normandy, in France. That landing opened a long, brutal job. The job was to free Europe. The job was also to end the war. No earlier military operation had been this ambitious. More than 156,000 men had to cross the English Channel.

3Their equipment had to cross. Their tanks had to cross. The Axis could not be allowed to learn the plan in time. If they learned it, they could mass their forces. They could crush the landing. A map of the landing points names Portland and Southampton. It names Great Britain, Portsmouth, and Shoreham-by-Sea. Dartmouth is marked. The water is the English Channel. Marks show where U.S. forces, British forces, and Canadian forces would go. Utah is one beach on the plan. Omaha is another. Gold is another. Juno is another. Sword is the last. France is the far shore. Airborne troops would jump by parachute. Their zones lay across northern France. The jumps were set for early morning on June 6. Other soldiers would leave naval landing craft. They would storm the five beaches. German troops guarded those beaches. The hope was a foothold on the French coast. From there the advance into France could start. A Utah Beach map marks German positions. American spots on the map are shown for midnight. Counts for Utah Beach: 20,000 U.S. troops came ashore. Military vehicles that landed numbered 1,700. U.S. casualties numbered 589. The beaches. Utah Beach. The United States 4th Infantry Division was assigned here. So were the 82nd Airborne Division and the 101st Airborne Division. Landing time for the 4th Infantry was 6:30 in the morning. Five hours earlier, paratroopers had already jumped. They came from the 82nd and from the 101st. Drop points sat 2 to 5 miles inland. That span is 3.2 to 8.0 kilometers. One job was to hold the main road. The road ran from Valognes to Carentan.

4Say Valognes as vah-LOHN-yuh. Say Carentan as kah-rohn-TOHN. German troops could not tell what the paratroopers were. They might be the main attack. They might be a decoy, meant to pull eyes off a bigger assault. The beach landing at 6:30 was supposed to use that confusion. Those troops were to push inland and meet the paratroopers as fast as possible. Bad weather made strong currents. Amphibious boats therefore missed their beach targets. The miss was 2,200 yards, which is 2 kilometers. Men had to wade in from the water. Brigadier General Theodore Roosevelt Jr. was with them. He was the oldest son of Theodore Roosevelt, a former U.S. president. He told his men the war would begin from the spot where they stood. He ordered them forward. Luckily the beachfront was not heavily defended. American losses stayed small next to the losses on the other beaches. Afternoon brought a meeting. The 4th Infantry joined the American paratroopers. German defense there collapsed quickly. By night the Americans had moved about 4 miles inland. That distance is 6.4 kilometers. They were still about 1 mile, or 1.6 kilometers, from more paratroopers. Those paratroopers were the 82nd Airborne at Ste. Mere-Eglise. Say that town sahnt-MER-e-GLEEZ. The town sits some 6 miles north of Carentan. That gap is 9.7 kilometers. An Omaha map also shows Utah and Gold nearby. The key marks German resistance. American lines on this map are the ones held at midnight. Counts for Omaha: 34,000 U.S. troops came ashore. Military vehicles lost numbered 136. U.S. casualties numbered 3,686. Omaha Beach. The United States 1st Army fought here. This beach stretched 6 miles, or 9.7 kilometers.

5None of the other four beaches was bigger. Lieutenant General Omar Bradley led the 1st Army. From the start, his men were at a disadvantage. Cliffs 100 feet high looked down on the sand. That height is 30.5 meters. Attacking upward was very hard. The Germans had added dragon's teeth. Those were concrete obstacles shaped like teeth. Each stood 3 to 4 feet tall, or 0.9 to 1.2 meters. Mines packed the obstacles. The aim was to destroy landing craft. German gunners fired from the cliff tops. They also fired from thirteen resistance nests. A nest was a small defensive post that could fight on its own. Advantage did not sit with the American side. That was true before any shot. The attack was timed for 6:30 in the morning. The tide would be low. The dragon's teeth would show. Infantry would land with twenty-nine amphibious tanks. The tanks were Shermans. Armor was supposed to give the Allies a huge edge in firepower. Disaster came when the tanks left their boats too far out. All but two flooded. They sank to the ocean floor. Crews could not be saved. The tanks could not be saved. Men on the sand never got the armored cover they expected. Weather made things worse. Strong wind and a rising tide shoved many landing craft far off course. Confusion spread through the troops. German fire cut the Americans down at a frightening pace. Losses grew so bad that Lieutenant General Bradley thought about calling the whole operation off. The only path left was to keep going. A note on the picture says this beach runs 5 miles, or 8 kilometers.

6Rocky cliffs fence it in. Staying alive meant a sprint toward those cliffs. Heavy German gunfire had to be dodged the whole way. Men who reached the rock then had to climb. The cliffs towered over them. While they climbed, destroyers of the U.S. Navy came as near as they dared. The ships struck German fortifications. That fire was important relief. It pulled German attention off the Americans on the sand. Until then, the defenders had been fixed on beating those men. Night found the Americans gripping Omaha Beach. Storms had already forced the invasion to wait. The first chosen date was June 5. Allies picked it because they expected clear sight. They expected light wind from the northwest. They expected low tides. If that day failed, another two weeks would pass before conditions looked right again. June 5 turned stormy. Strong wind and high waves wrecked any chance of a landing from the sea. Clouds hung low. Pilots could not see targets. They could not drop paratroopers on the mark. They could not hit enemy positions. The next morning was not much kinder. Gold Beach. A map key marks German resistance. It marks British positions as of midnight. Counts for Gold: 24,970 British troops came ashore. Military vehicles that landed numbered 2,100. British casualties numbered 1,023. Britain's 50th Infantry Division fought here. Gold was one of two beaches taken by British troops. It sat in the middle of the five. Landing time was 7:25 in the morning. Weather struck at once as a major problem. Strong wind had let seawater cover German mines. Other beach obstacles were covered too.

7British engineers could not take the mines apart on the schedule they had set. Hidden mines damaged twenty armored cars. The day could have turned disastrous for the British. It did not, because naval guns and attacks from the air had already knocked out many German defenders. Afternoon found the British holding most of Gold Beach. They pushed inland quickly. They also took the fishing village of Arromanches. Say that name ar-roh-MAHNSH. Later, Mulberry harbor was built at this town. Allies used the harbor to unload supplies. Gold Beach counts as a tremendous success in strategy. British troops could then join the Canadians. Those Canadians had landed at Juno Beach. Mulberry harbor ran about 6 miles, or 10 kilometers. Flexible roadways of steel formed it. Steel pontoons held the roads up. Concrete pontoons held them up as well. Juno Beach. A map key marks German resistance. It marks Canadian positions as of midnight. Counts for Juno: 21,400 Canadian troops came ashore. Military vehicles that landed numbered 3,200. Canadian casualties numbered 961. Canada's 3rd Infantry had the job of taking Juno. Going inland was the aim. The inland move would tie together two British beaches. Gold was one. Sword was the other. Bad weather and a rising tide got in the way. German mines sat partly underwater. Canadian engineers who handled demolition could not destroy the mines. Damage from the mines was severe. Landing craft lost or hurt by them came to 30 percent. A picture shows a bulldozer tank. With a machine like that, American troops got through the dragon's teeth the Germans had built. Damaged boats left many Canadian soldiers struggling. They had to wade to the sand.

8Those who arrived met a powerful blast of German fire. In the first wave, survival was about a fifty-fifty chance. The Canadians refused to quit. They fought their way off the sand. They fought farther inland. Once clear of the beach, they took charge quickly. Losses were heavy. Even so, their inland advance beat the advance on each of the other four beaches. A number of towns fell to them. They linked up with the British who were at Gold. Sword Beach. A map key marks German resistance. It marks British positions as of midnight. Counts for Sword: 29,000 British troops came ashore. Military vehicles that landed numbered 2,603. British casualties numbered 630. Britain's 3rd Army raided this beach. It was the other British beach. The main aim was the town of Caen. Say Caen as KAHN. Caen lay 9.3 miles inland, which is 15 kilometers. Every main road in the region ran through that town. Allied success inland depended on holding those roads. The raid opened at 7:25 in the morning. British troops stormed the sand. Paratroopers landed inland. They came from the 3rd Parachute Brigade and the 5th Parachute Brigade. They joined the soldiers already on the beach. German resistance at Sword was light compared with the other beaches. The British were fortunate in that. After the landing, tanks in town streets became a common sight. Tour-La-Ville, in Normandy, was one such town. By 8:00 in the morning, most of the fighting on Sword was finished. By 1:00 in the afternoon, British commandos had met the paratroopers. The plan was working in every detail. Safety did not last.

9Germany launched a counterattack. By 8:00 at night a German unit was on the sand. It was the 192nd. Its title was Panzer Grenadier Regiment. The German gain was only temporary. Their vehicles sat in the open. Allied tanks were already at Sword. Allied fighter planes were there too. Those weapons could hit the German vehicles. The counterattack failed. It still blocked one planned link. British troops could not meet the Canadians from Juno on that same day. Caen stayed out of British reach for now. Even so, the Allies counted the mission a huge victory. The beach was made stable. Allied forces moved roughly 4 miles inland. That distance is 6.4 kilometers. The next day they met the Canadians. Caen itself fell six weeks later. The date was July 20, 1944. A closing look. Allied lives lost were many. Axis lives lost were many. Operation Overlord was still a tremendous success. The sacrifice bought a foothold. From that foothold, Allied forces could start pushing German forces back. Occupied France could be freed. The day was a huge military victory. Grief belonged to the day as well. So much happened that exact loss counts were hard to write down. Casualty is the word for every armed-forces loss. The count includes people killed. It includes people wounded. It includes people missing in action. It includes prisoners of war. Historians estimate German casualties somewhere from four thousand to nine thousand. Allied casualties that day passed six thousand. Fighting continued for about another year. Allied troops kept taking back lands in Europe that Germany held. May 8, 1945, is when Germany gave up. Japan's surrender came on August 15 of that year.

10That second surrender officially ended the war. D-Day was a major turning point in World War II. So was the later freeing of France. Allied soldiers gave work and sacrifice on D-Day. Take that away, and the war might have ended another way. Words to know. A paratrooper is a soldier trained to leap from an airplane and fight behind enemy lines. Panzer is the name for one German tank of this war. Mourning is grief, especially grief for someone who has died. Mines are bombs hidden under ground or under water. They explode when touched or moved. Liberation is the act of setting people free. Infantry are soldiers trained, armed, and equipped to fight on foot. Fortifications are defensive builds, including forts, meant to make a place harder to attack. A foothold is a first position from which a further advance can start. Drafted means ordered into military service, especially in wartime. A decoy is a person or an object that draws someone, or something, away from the real target. Commandos belong to a unit trained for fast raids inside enemy land. Casualties are people hurt, killed, or missing in a war, an accident, or a disaster. Axis powers were the countries lined up against the Allies during this war. Germany was one. Italy was one. Japan was one. Amphibious describes military moves in which troops enter enemy land from the water. Allies were nations that aided each other. Their enemies in this war were Germany, Italy, and Japan. Great Britain was among them. The United States was among them. France was among them. The Soviet Union was among them.

71. The Plan That Still Governs the Nation

1This book begins with a historic meeting. It then explains why a constitution was needed. A section asks what is inside the Constitution. Another section calls it a living document. The legacy of the Constitution comes next. A word list closes the book. A Historic Meeting. In the summer of 1787, delegates met as a group in Philadelphia. Their job was to write a constitution for the United States of America, a nation that had only just been formed. Leading figures were in the room. George Washington was one. Benjamin Franklin was another. James Madison was there as well, and he was the main author of the Constitution. Two other important figures were not in the room. Thomas Jefferson and John Adams were serving as ambassadors in Europe. A picture shows James Madison. When the delegates finished, they had a document that would last for centuries. Today the U.S. Constitution is the oldest written constitution anywhere that is still in use. Nothing in the land outranks it as law. The Constitution created a republic. Powers in that republic are separated and balanced. The aim is to protect majority rule and also to protect minority rights. After the Constitutional Convention ended, someone asked Benjamin Franklin a question. What sort of government had the delegates made? He knew the new nation might be fragile.

2His answer was that they had made a republic, if the people could keep it. The Need for a Constitution. The thirteen original states won independence from Great Britain in 1783. A different kind of government was soon obviously required. From 1781 on, the states used a constitution named the Articles of Confederation. That plan was not working. Most power stayed with the states. The Continental Congress was the nation's first legislature. It had very little authority. It could not force the states to send tax money to the government. It could not force them to send troops for the nation's defense. If even one state objected, the congress could do almost nothing. By 1786, the weakness of the government was plain. A stronger central government was required. That urgent need led people to call the Constitutional Convention in 1787. What Is a Republic? The United States is a democracy. It is not a pure democracy, which is also called a direct democracy. In a pure democracy, citizens themselves vote on proposed laws. Another name for this kind of democracy is a republic. Citizens choose representatives. In a republic, citizens vote for people who will represent them. Those people sit in a national legislative body. In this country, Congress is the body that does that work. Senators and representatives are the officials we elect.

3They pass bills. Those bills become the nation's laws. George Washington presided while the delegates debated through the hot summer. They chose to build a government of three branches. The legislative branch is Congress. The executive branch is the presidency. The judicial branch is the federal courts. By early 1789, eleven states had ratified the Constitution, which means they had approved it. It then became law. By the end of May 1790, the last two states had approved it as well. Those states were North Carolina and Rhode Island. George Washington won the first presidential election held under the Constitution. The election was in February 1789. A new era of the country began. A chart shows the three branches the Constitution created. The legislative branch makes laws and includes the Senate and the House of Representatives. The executive branch carries out laws and includes the president, the vice president, and the cabinet. Deciding the proper use of laws is the judicial branch's job. It includes the Supreme Court and other federal courts. The first three words of the Constitution are We the people. Those words have come to stand for the central idea of democracy. What's in the Constitution? The Constitution opens with a preamble. The preamble explains why the document was written. The reasons are these.

4The people wanted a more perfect union. They wanted to establish justice. They wanted peace at home. They wanted defense shared by everyone. They wanted to promote the general welfare. They wanted to secure the blessings of liberty for themselves and for the generations that would follow. Seven articles, or sections, organize the Constitution. The first three articles explain how the three branches are set up and how they operate. Article I is about Congress. Congress is split into two chambers. They are the House of Representatives and the Senate. Members of the House are to be elected every two years. Members of the Senate are to serve terms of six years. Tax collection is a power this article grants to Congress. It also gives Congress the power to provide for the defense of the nation. That power includes the right to declare war. A note names George Washington as president number one. It names Thomas Jefferson as president number three. Pictures show both men. Early presidents, including Washington and Jefferson, helped shape ideas about presidents. Those ideas covered how a president should act. They also covered how much power a president should have. Article II is about the presidency. The Constitution grants the president certain powers. Command of the armed forces is one of those powers.

5Eligibility starts with birth as a citizen of this country. The person must also be at least thirty-five years old. People called electors choose the president. State legislatures choose those electors. That rule later became the basis of the Electoral College. The system is still used today. It is now combined with a popular vote. The founders created the Electoral College because they thought most citizens would know little about people running for president. Planes, trains, and automobiles did not yet exist. A candidate could not easily cross the country to meet voters. Citizens who never heard a candidate in person relied mainly on newspapers. There was a second important reason. The founders did not trust a direct vote by the people. Some of them linked that kind of vote with mob rule. So the job of electing a president, and a vice president, would go to electors. Those electors were thought to be more knowledgeable. They were also thought to be more levelheaded. Each state would choose its own. Article III sets up the federal court system. It says the judiciary includes lower-level courts and a Supreme Court. In federal legal cases, the last word belongs to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court of the United States has nine justices. A justice is a judge. The other articles cover several topics.

6They deal with how the states relate to one another. They deal with how to amend the Constitution. They deal with national debts and with treaties. They deal with how the Constitution itself was to be ratified. The Constitution holds a set of ideas. Those ideas aim at a government that works properly and a society that is just. The framers followed one guiding idea. Government should run under checks and balances. That system would limit each branch so no branch could dominate the others. States feared the federal government might become too powerful. States' rights mattered to them a great deal. The Constitution answers that fear by splitting powers. Some stay with the states. Some go to the federal government. Protection of individual citizens is written into the Constitution and into its amendments. An accused person cannot lose life, liberty, or property unless due process of law is given. Someone charged with a crime may have a jury trial. The jury must be impartial. Excessive bail is forbidden. Cruel and unusual punishment is forbidden too. Free speech and other liberties are also protected. A Living Document. Because the Constitution can be amended, it is a living document. It changes as times change. It changes as American society needs new things. Amendments began even before every state had ratified the document.

7Some states feared that citizen rights were not protected well enough in the first seven articles. James Madison drafted suggested amendments so that gap would be filled. The First Congress approved twelve of his suggestions in late 1789 and sent them to the states. The states approved ten of them. Those ten became part of the Constitution. They are called the Bill of Rights. The most important addition is the First Amendment. It guarantees freedom of speech and freedom of religion. It guarantees freedom of the press. It guarantees the right of people to assemble in a peaceful way. The Bill of Rights guards many rights people here treat as essential. Free speech lets people say what they think in the open. That is true even when the view is unfavorable to the federal government. The right is not absolute. A threat to harm someone is not protected. A lie told under oath in a court of law is not protected either. The First Amendment also says Congress may not make a law that sets up an official religion. Congress may not make a law that stops people from freely practicing religion. People may follow any religion they choose. They may follow none at all. Religion and government must stay separate. Freedom of the press means journalists can work freely.

8The government may not interfere. Journalists may report on government wrongdoing. They may criticize policies and officials. They may criticize the president. The right of assembly guarantees that citizens may meet in peace. They may talk about issues that concern them. Being free to assemble is a major liberty guarantee. A picture shows thousands of Americans gathered in peace in Washington, D.C., in 1963, to hear Martin Luther King Jr. speak. More protections for citizens sit in the Fourth, Fifth, and Sixth Amendments. The Fourth Amendment guards people against unreasonable searches of their home. The Fifth and Sixth Amendments set out protections for people accused of crimes. Under the Tenth Amendment, powers not specifically handed to the federal government stay with the states. That is why so many laws differ from state to state. Public education is one example. State taxes are another. Over the years, seventeen more amendments have joined the Constitution. Some of them ended slavery. Some gave the vote to African Americans and to women. One set up a federal income tax. Repeal has happened for just one amendment. The Twenty-First Amendment, in 1933, wiped out the Eighteenth Amendment. The Eighteenth Amendment had been adopted in 1919. It banned the manufacture, the sale, or the transport of alcoholic beverages. It began an era known as Prohibition.

9Adding an amendment, or repealing one, can affect society in a large way. Pocket-size printed copies of the Constitution make the text easy to reach. People can study it and look back at it. The Legacy of the Constitution. Many other constitutions around the world have used the U.S. Constitution as a model. The document is not without flaws. One major shortcoming is that it kept the institution of slavery in place. Only after the Civil War was slavery ended for good. The amendment process was the path. Other criticisms have been raised as well. Many people say it is unfair that every state gets two votes in the Senate. They say states with fewer people get a voice in Congress far beyond what their number of citizens would merit. Another criticism focuses on the Electoral College. A presidential winner needs more than half of the electoral votes. Under this system, a candidate can win the popular vote and still lose the election. That has happened five times. The elections of 2000 and 2016 are two of those times. A 1915 picture shows a march by women through New York streets. They were marching for the right to vote. Ratification of the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920 finally gave women that right. Given the circumstances, the framers produced the best plan they could.

10They produced a document that has lasted well over two hundred years, even with its imperfections. Today the Constitution still defines how the national government is organized. It still defines how that government functions. If modern needs outgrow the text, amendments are the tool for bringing it up to date. People hope this living document will keep guiding the country for centuries. Word list. A confederation is a loosely joined group of states, provinces, or other groups, with only a limited central authority. A legislature is a group of elected officials whose job is to make laws or to change them. A constitution holds the basic laws of a state or a nation. Those laws explain how government operates. Populous means having many people in an area. A preamble is the opening of a document. It states the purpose and the reasons for what follows. Contenders are people who compete against others. Dominating means controlling or overpowering. Prohibiting means forbidding something by a law or a rule. Due process means a citizen may have a fair trial before a court. Ratifying means approving through an official process. Impartial means treating people, groups, or situations fairly and without bias. Repealed means ended, removed, or reversed, when the thing ended is a law or a policy.

72. The Scientist behind the Polio Shot

1This book begins with a summer of terror. It tells how one person tried to make a difference. It shows him doing the work his own way. It asks whether a virus in a vaccine should be dead or alive. The first tests come next. Then comes the trial. The book also tells what went wrong. New challenges close the story. A glossary explains hard words. Signs told people to keep away from places where polio had struck. Parents across the United States got ready in spring 1953. Another season of terror was coming. The disease is called poliomyelitis, or polio. The summer before, it had sickened nearly fifty-seven thousand people. That same year, twenty thousand people were left with trouble walking, or with no walk at all. Most of those people were children. Another three thousand people died. In most cases the poliovirus caused symptoms like a cold. Arms and legs lost the power to move in some of those cases. In the worst cases it paralyzed the muscles of the chest. Those people could not breathe. Crowds were something people stayed away from. Police quarantined homes. They took sick children to hospitals. A stay there could last months. It could even last years. One hope remained. Doctor Jonas Salk told the nation that a polio vaccine was coming. Jonas Salk was born in New York in 1914. He was a good student. At twelve he entered Townsend Harris Hall.

2That school was a high school for gifted students. By age sixteen he had moved on to City College of New York. He wanted his work to help humanity. He wanted to be a medical researcher who fought diseases. His studies ended at the moment World War II began for the United States. Soldiers needed protection from influenza, also called flu. They also needed protection from other illnesses of the breathing system. A flu epidemic in World War I had killed more than forty thousand soldiers from the United States. The military wanted a vaccine. Doctor Thomas Francis worked at the University of Michigan. He received money to research a flu vaccine. He hired Salk for the lab. In 1943 the United States Army started influenza vaccinations. A diagram can show how antibodies work. It can mark a binding site on a virus. It can show an antibody next to a virus. Antibodies attach to viruses. That attachment stops the viruses from infecting the body. A virus stuck to an antibody cannot break free. It also cannot latch onto other healthy cells. Exposure to a virus makes the body protect itself. The body makes special proteins called antibodies. Those antibodies bind with viruses. They bind with bacteria too. The binding helps the body fight illness. A vaccine pushes the body to make antibodies. In most cases the vaccine does this without giving the person the disease.

3Salk built a test that counted antibodies in the blood. Researchers could then judge a vaccine without waiting for someone to fall ill. Making the vaccine meant killing the flu virus with great care. Damage to the virus's outer shape would be a problem. The body would not recognize that virus. It would not make antibodies against it. The team succeeded. Their killed-virus flu vaccine saved thousands of lives. Salk was thirty-two when he took a new post. He became head of the Virus Research Laboratory. The lab was at the University of Pittsburgh. The National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis is also called the NFIP. It raised money for people who had survived polio. It wanted to fund research toward a polio vaccine. Basil O'Connor led the foundation. Salk's eagerness to get things done impressed him. O'Connor gave Salk money for the research. A first step was to learn how many types of poliovirus existed. The common cold virus has dozens of types. If polio were like that, one vaccine could not protect people. Working with the poliovirus was difficult. Only humans catch polio in nature. In a laboratory, monkeys can be infected with it. The old way of counting strains took months or years. Researchers gave monkeys one type of polio. They then waited months to see sickness or recovery. Only after that wait did they try new strains.

4Salk wanted a different test. A monkey would receive only a light dose. The strain would be one nobody had named yet. The monkey would not get sick. It would still make antibodies against that type. Later the monkey would receive a known type of polio. If the monkey was immune, its blood would flood with antibodies. If the virus grew instead, the strain was a different type. An NFIP conference was held that year. Most scientists there scoffed at the new idea. Doctor Albert Sabin was among them. Sabin was a well-known polio researcher. He was vocal about his views. The NFIP chose to fund the traditional way of typing the virus. Back in his lab, Salk worked extra hours. He tried both methods. The new method worked. It was faster. It needed far fewer monkeys. He then looked for antibodies in tissue cultures. A tissue culture is living material grown outside the body. Those tests succeeded. With the new methods, the team found only three types of polio. The work took one year. People had expected three years. A picture can show virus samples growing in glass plates. Those plates are called petri dishes. They fit under microscopes. A chart can show polio in the United States across the years. By 1950, most scientists held one belief. Only a live-virus vaccine, they thought, could give people protection from polio that would last.

5In a live-virus vaccine, scientists prepare a weak virus. That weak virus goes into the vaccine. Once injected, it makes the body produce antibodies. In most cases it does not cause the disease. Salk believed a killed-virus vaccine could work just as well. He and Francis had already made that kind of vaccine for the flu. A killed virus had another advantage. It was safer. A virus that is already dead can never give someone polio. Money from the NFIP went to both methods. Salk went to work with a team of fifty researchers. Killing the poliovirus without damaging it was not easy. They used the same chemical that had killed the flu virus. They tried different temperatures. They tried different strengths. The method had to be perfect. Viruses are tiny. A million of them can line up inside one inch. A single live poliovirus left in the vaccine could cause the deadly disease. While the team worked, the hospital above the lab filled its beds. The patients were sick children. Monkeys were protected by a vaccine Salk had ready in 1952. He still had to decide whether he dared to try it on children. Polio vaccines tried in the 1930s had devastating effects. Children who received those vaccines developed polio. Salk's first tests used children who had already survived polio. Those children could not catch the disease again. The test worked.

6Antibodies in their blood increased. He next vaccinated children who had never had polio. Those children developed antibodies that could protect them. They showed no ill effects. Salk got ready to present the results. The next NFIP meeting would be the place. A picture can show Jonas Salk in his Pittsburgh lab. He is checking hundreds of vials of vaccine. The lab belongs to the University of Pittsburgh. A picture can show Albert Sabin with his staff. They worked at the University of Cincinnati. News of Salk's work leaked out. People began visiting the lab to learn more. The visits made concentration hard. O'Connor urged a different plan. Salk should explain the project on the radio once. That would replace many separate interviews. People were thrilled that a vaccine seemed close. Salk became famous overnight. Sabin was furious. Other researchers were furious too. Salk had mentioned other people's research in the interview. Even so, the others thought he wanted all the credit. They said real scientists share research at formal scientific meetings. They said the radio was not the place. Salk ignored the complaints. He returned to the work. In 1953 polio sickened another thirty-five thousand people. Once Salk felt sure the vaccine was safe, he took it himself. His family took it too. So did the workers in the lab. O'Connor pushed for a huge field trial. He wanted it before the next summer.

7Hundreds of thousands of children would be vaccinated. Salk agreed. A delay would likely mean polio for thousands more children. O'Connor set out to find children for the vaccine. He organized thousands of healthcare workers. He raised money. Salk's own lab could not make enough vaccine in time. He taught large drug makers the exact way to kill the virus. They could then produce the vaccine. So hard was the process that readiness came to just two makers. Five manufacturers had been asked. Only those two succeeded in time for the trial's start. Almost two million children took part. Some received the vaccine. Some received a placebo. The rest were tracked as a control group. A picture shows children lined up for the polio trials. The year is 1954. An hour passed, then forty more minutes, before Thomas Francis finished speaking. Only then did he announce that Salk's vaccine worked. Months of waiting had come before that day. Francis had been Salk's old boss. He collected the results. He analyzed them. Salk was about to be a national hero. He might instead be seen as a villain. On April 12, 1955, millions of people listened. They listened on the radio. They listened on speakers in department stores. Francis made the announcement at the NFIP meeting. He said the vaccine worked. He called it safe. He called it effective. He called it potent. Reporters rushed off to spread the news.

8Church bells rang. People in the streets cheered. Salk stood up quietly to speak. He thanked polio researchers who had come before him. He thanked the volunteers. He thanked people who had given money. He forgot to name the members of his own team. That missed thanks angered many other scientists. Some of them never forgave him. Most people, though, treated Salk as a hero. Radio stations interviewed him. Newspapers interviewed him. People sent money. People sent gifts. He turned every gift and every sum over to the NFIP. Then he went back to the lab. His aim was to improve the vaccine. Summer was coming. The NFIP started giving out free vaccine. All five manufacturers supplied it. Trouble showed up quickly. Some children who got the vaccine came down with polio. Distribution was suspended. Salk did not panic. He knew a properly prepared vaccine was safe. Investigators traced the problem to one manufacturer. That company had not killed the virus properly. Its vaccine was pulled. The vaccinations then went on. By 1962, polio cases in the United States had fallen below one thousand. Salk's vaccine worked. Producing it cost a great deal. That same year the United States approved Sabin's vaccine. Sabin's version used a live virus. It cost less than the killed-virus vaccine. It was given on a sugar cube. It did not require a series of shots.

9By 1979, only a few polio cases remained. Most of those cases were traced to the live-virus vaccine. After 2000, the United States chose the killed-virus vaccine alone. Salk had made the first polio vaccine. In the end, his vaccine eliminated the disease in the United States. A picture from 1967 shows a boy taking Sabin's vaccine. The dose sits on a sugar cube. Salk moved on to new challenges. In 1960 he founded the Salk Institute. He wanted a place where scientists could work for the good of humanity. He studied diseases such as cancer. He studied HIV/AIDS as well. That research continued until his death in 1995. Today the Salk Institute does medical research at the cutting edge. Several winners of the Nobel Prize have come from it. Salk himself did not receive a Nobel Prize. Many scientists of that time agreed with Sabin. Sabin described Salk's work as pure kitchen chemistry. Sabin said Salk had not discovered anything. Among major polio researchers, Salk alone was never elected to the National Academy of Sciences. His country thanked him. The world thanked him. Thousands of children had been saved from the deadly disease. That saving was the reason for the thanks. Time magazine placed him on a list. One hundred people from the twentieth century were judged the most important. His name was on that list. He pulled together discoveries from decades of polio research.

10He also used new ideas. Those ideas helped him develop the first polio vaccine. Signs told a cheerful story about vaccination. People who got the vaccine were rewarded with lollipops. Salk reached his goal. He made a difference for humanity. Devastating describes great damage, of the body or of the feelings. A placebo is a pill or other substance. It has no physical effect on a patient. Experiments often use it as a control while another substance, such as a drug, is tested. An epidemic is a disease spreading fast inside a community. Polio is an acute disease caused by a virus. It attacks skeletal muscle and the spinal cord. A field trial tests a new product or process where it will really be used. The test asks how well that product works. To have been quarantined is to have been kept apart. The aim is to stop a disease from spreading. To fund something is to supply money for a cause, a group, or a purpose. Strains are groups of viral organisms that belong to the same species. Immune means protected from a disease. A vaccine is a medicine made from weak or dead microbes. From it, the body learns how to fight tougher microbes. Those microbes are the same kind.
