Paralyzed means one or more body parts were made unable to move. Vocal means outspoken. A vocal person expresses strong opinions.

73. The Water Hidden Under Our Feet

1Ten days after her well went dry, a woman in California received 300 gallons of drinking water. That is 1,136 liters. The month was August 2014. Picture a morning when the faucet gives only a gurgle. That is what happened in 2014 in a California region famous for fruit and for vegetables. Drought had lasted years, so rain was scarce. To water their crops, farmers pulled huge amounts of groundwater up from under the land. Some two thousand wells ended up dry. The county government answered by setting up centers. People could get drinking water there, and they could take showers. Experts warn that rain alone will not end the shortage soon. California is not the only place in a water crisis. Groundwater is water sitting underground. It fills the spaces and the cracks among rocks, sand, and soil. This book asks what that water is and where it lies. It looks at too many straws in one supply, at fights over water, at staying out of trouble, at smarter farming, and at choices still ahead. A word list closes the book. A chart of all the water on Earth, based on the U.S. Geological Survey, splits the supply into a few shares. Salt water is 97 percent. Fresh water is 3 percent. Of the fresh water, ground ice and permafrost lock up 70 percent. Surface water is only 0.3 percent. A glance at a globe fools many people into thinking the planet holds plenty of water for every need. Oceans contain that 97 percent, and the salt makes it unfit to drink.

2It is also useless for watering crops. Fresh water is what keeps us alive. It quenches thirst, and it lets us grow food. Earth's water includes a fresh share, and that share is under 3 percent. Almost 70 percent of that small fresh share is locked in polar ice caps and in glaciers. Rivers, lakes, and ponds are the fresh water we notice first. They are surface water, and they make up just 0.3 percent of the fresh supply. Scientists estimate that groundwater is a whopping 99 percent of the usable water on Earth. It is fresh water, and it moves slowly beneath the ground. Most of it sits in aquifers. Rock, gravel, and sand, stacked underground, are what an aquifer is made of. They hold groundwater the way colossal sponges hold liquid. Rain and melting snow are called recharge water. They percolate very slowly through the soil and rock at the surface. That trickle feeds the aquifers. Depth can run to thousands of feet. It can stretch for thousands of miles. Rivers, lakes, and wetlands are fed by aquifers in turn. Irrigation for the world's best farming regions comes from those same layers. Billions of gallons have been pumped from underground. People have been doing it for more than a century. They drink it, grow crops with it, and meet other needs that cannot wait. Even in a drought, a town or a farm sitting above an aquifer can draw that water, survive, and thrive. Hunger and thirst stay away from much of humanity because of this source.

3The trouble is the speed of the pumping. People take water far faster than nature puts it back. Researchers see an alarming trend. Levels of groundwater are falling fast. Food supplies are threatened by these crises, and so is peace. Experts around the world warn about the danger of using up this life-giving resource. Research now shows the rate of use cannot last. Almost two-thirds of wells across the United States show a drop in water level. The U.S. Geological Survey is the source of that finding. The records start in 1995. Experts predict a hard future for the Ogallala Aquifer, which lies under the Great Plains. By 2060 it could be 70 percent depleted. Another name for it is the High Plains Aquifer. It waters America's wheat fields, but the water cannot last forever. A map tracks changes in its water level, state by state, across about sixty years, from 1950 to 2010. Wyoming is down 0.4 feet, or 0.12 meters. South Dakota shows 0 feet, which is 0 meters. Nebraska is down 0.9 feet, or 0.27 meters. Colorado is down 13.2 feet, or 4.02 meters. Kansas is down 22.8 feet, or 6.95 meters. New Mexico is down 15.1 feet, or 4.6 meters. Oklahoma is down 12.3 feet, or 3.75 meters. Texas is down 36.7 feet, or 11.19 meters. In some places today's level is largely unchanged. In others the drop is dramatic. A single Texas well has fallen farther than 120 feet. That is 36.6 meters.

4A depth scale starts at ground level. It is marked in steps of 20 feet and continues until 140. Vineyards made Sonoma Valley, in California, renowned. In some farming areas, competition for groundwater is turning into conflict. Winemakers in Northern California, for example, grow acres of grapes. Grapes take a large amount of water. Many of those growers have drilled deep wells so they can be sure of a supply. Lose the water, and the business might fail. Smaller farmers nearby are worried, and so are homeowners. They call the practice water grabbing. The shared groundwater, they say, is being pulled up in excess by the vineyards. Their own shallower wells go dry. Deeper drilling costs more than many of those smaller owners can pay. Picture everyone with a straw in the same drink. Paying for extra straws, and for longer ones, is something some farms and businesses can do. Big questions follow. Who owns groundwater? How much use is fair? A chart compares water use in India, China, the United States, and Pakistan. A single cubic kilometer holds one trillion liters. In gallons that is 264,172,052,358. That volume would fill about 400,000 swimming pools of Olympic size. The chart's figures include 251 cubic kilometers, two separate totals of 112 cubic kilometers, and 65 cubic kilometers. One population figure is 1,341 million. Another is 1,225 million. A third is 310 million. A fourth is 174 million. Per person, one yearly figure is 373,600 liters. Another is 361,300 liters. A third is 205,000 liters.

5A fourth is 83,500 liters. Population can change how much water a country uses overall. Even so, these countries do not use the same amount per person. Pakistan's dependable water is down by almost 75 percent. The place is halfway around the world from the California story. The drop covers the last sixty years. Many people in Pakistan blame India, the neighbor to the south. Dams built by India are the accusation. Those dams, people say, stop river water that would otherwise reach them. Farmers in Pakistan say the blocked rivers left them one choice. They pump more from underground. Officials in India answer that Pakistan itself is to blame, because it manages the water it has poorly. Both countries are longtime rivals. Four wars already mark their shared past. Today both face water shortages, and the competition for fresh water is increasing. The United Nations predicts that crises like these will only grow more severe. Officials there estimate a grim result if nothing changes. The year 2030 is the deadline in that estimate. The shortfall would be 40 percent of needed water. Severe water shortages could reach nearly two billion people around the world. Food shortages and famine could follow. Experts warn that such crises can feed conflict and war. Homes and lands have already been left behind by large numbers of people in some places, because water ran short. Syria is one case. People from the countryside moved into cities because of drought. A civil war began in 2011. Evidence suggests the movement into the cities helped set it off.

6Many Syrians have died in it. A picture shows two Syrian refugee children standing outside their shelter. Importance on that scale is what groundwater has in many places. Green farms stand on one side of that difference. Dusty fields stand on the other. The stakes are life or death. Safe supplies that people can rely on, reaching as many people as possible, ought to rank as a worldwide priority. Ignore the crisis and the results pile up. People clash. Violence follows. Suffering is great. That suffering threatens to spread as people keep fighting over water. An old saying fits the world's groundwater. Staying clear of trouble is easier than escaping trouble later. Act while the aquifers still hold water. Waiting until they are depleted will make the crisis much harder. Keeping the supply means planning ahead. It also means careful management of how water is used today. Harder challenges are what many experts see ahead. Climate change is one growing threat to groundwater. Scientists who study Earth are nearly united on one basic fact. Average temperature on this planet is going up. Records of yearly heat put the ten hottest years in one stretch. Every one of them falls after 2000. Weather patterns may also shift on a large scale because of climate change. Climatologists predict one example. Some regions count on rainy seasons that arrive on a regular schedule. Those seasons may shift. The amount of precipitation they bring may change too. Major breaks in the water people can count on would likely follow.

7Population growth is another huge challenge. The planet's population now stands above eight billion. By 2100 the expected population is eleven billion. Drinking water will be a need for each of them. Water for growing food will be a need as well. Groundwater has to be managed now. It can be. Supplies that last depend, more than anything, on using less water. That means finding ways to use less, and practicing them, so more groundwater stays in the ground. No step matters more than a change in farming. Irrigating crops takes about 65 percent of what America pumps. The water in question is fresh groundwater brought up to the surface. That share comes from the U.S. Geological Survey. Studies show that many kinds of irrigation waste water. Spraying and sprinkling leave water on the surface. Evaporation then takes much of it. A growing number of farmers accept a limit. Pumping at the old volume cannot continue. They are taking up new ideas and new technology so that every drop counts. Tensiometers are now in use on some farms. Moisture in the soil is what these sensors watch. They switch the irrigation on and off by themselves, which wastes less water. Many orchards of fruit and of nuts are changing too. They bury the irrigation pipes so water arrives closer to the tree roots, and less water is wasted. A picture shows almond trees in bloom. A view from space marks Europe, Asia, Africa, the Indian Ocean, and the Atlantic Ocean.

8Some aquifers are losing water rapidly. Others are gaining water. NASA has watched groundwater change from orbit. That watch began in 2002. GRACE is the short name. The full name is Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment. Earth's gravity field is what the pair of satellites responds to. They can measure shifts in how much water sits on the surface and under it. Data gathered across ten years, from 2003 to 2013, show trends for the planet's largest aquifers. The share in dangerous depletion is about one-third. Another large saving comes from planting crops of a different kind. Kansas is one state where some farms are switching crops. Iowa is another. Corn is giving way to wheat and to sorghum. Corn needs much more water than those other two crops. Corn also earns more money, so other farmers stay reluctant to switch. Choice is one path to saving water. Emptied aquifers are the other, and they will force the change. Record drought pushed California to save water. The year 2014 brought a state law, the Sustainable Groundwater Management Act. It required that water levels in aquifers be monitored. It gave the state power to enforce stronger conservation if a community did not write its own plan. Five hundred dollars a day is an example of the fine a city could charge. The fine would follow a broken rule about washing cars or watering lawns. Rules like these worked. Per-person use plummeted across a span that began in June 2014 and ended in December of that year. On average, Californians went from as much as 140 gallons a person each day down to just 67 gallons.

9Those amounts are 530 liters and 254 liters. Groundwater is the supply for 57 percent of households in the nation. In rural areas the share is more than 90 percent. Hundreds of gallons a week can be saved in an average American home. The tools are small plumbing changes and small changes in habit. Low-flush toilets help. So do shorter showers. Another small effort is to run washing machines and dishwashers only when the load is full. A chart of water inside the house gives daily gallons per household, with liters in parentheses. One figure is 33.1 gallons, or 125.3 liters. Another is 31.7 gallons, or 120 liters. A third is 26.3 gallons, or 99.6 liters. A fourth is 23.9 gallons, or 90.5 liters. The last figure is 22.7 gallons, or 86 liters. The uses shown are the clothes washer, the dishwasher together with leaks and other uses, the faucet, the toilet, and the shower and bath. Nothing else in the house uses more water than the toilet does. A study in 2016 looked at indoor water use. It covered 23,749 homes across the United States. A similar study in 1999 found higher use. Less water reaches the sewer from newer toilets, because they are built to be more efficient. Selective flushing is another habit some families use. They do not flush every time they use the toilet. Large volumes can also be saved by the people who own the property.

10Lawns of thirsty grass can come out. Landscaping that asks for less water can go in. California has a catchy motto for lawns that are allowed to die. The words are Brown is the New Green. Keeping groundwater has no fix that is both quick and easy. People need to drink. Farmers need to irrigate crops so we have food. Smarter use is still possible. It matters now, and it will matter far ahead. A few words are worth keeping. An aquifer is a buried layer. Rock, sand, and other material in that layer can hold groundwater and can soak it up. Climate change means long-lasting shifts in weather patterns, for Earth or for a region. Conservation is careful use of resources so they are not wasted, used up, or destroyed. A crisis is a dangerous or unstable time that demands attention. Depleted means emptied, or used up for the most part. A long spell with little rain, or with none, is a drought. The shortage of water comes from that missing rain. Water stored under the ground, in soil or in rock, is groundwater. Wells are often fed by it. Irrigating means putting water onto land. Helping crops grow is the usual reason. Per capita means for each person. To percolate is to trickle slowly through something full of tiny openings. Sensors are devices that notice signals, or changes in conditions, and react. Unsustainable describes something that cannot last at the current rate, or a practice that permanently damages a resource.

74. The Young King and His Tomb

1British archaeologist Howard Carter found the tomb of King Tut. A picture shows him examining the golden sarcophagus during the dig. The parts of this book come in this order. Finding Tut. His homeland. His family. The boy who ruled. The end of a ruling family. His tomb. The suspects. The body. Is the mystery solved? A word list. In 1922, a British archaeologist made a fantastic discovery in Egypt. The word archaeologist is said AR-kee-OLL-oh-jist. Egyptian workers helped him. He found the tomb of Tutankhamun, said toot-an-KAH-muhn. Most people know him as King Tut. More than 3,300 years ago, Tut was a ruler of ancient Egypt. He became pharaoh, said FAIR-oh, at the age of nine. He ruled for less than a decade. Then he died suddenly at about age nineteen. In all the years since his coffin was opened, many people have wondered how the young king died and why. Archaeologists work like detectives. Mysteries get solved, in their work, by studying evidence and by asking questions. Where did Tut live? What was his health like? Who were his family and his friends? Did he have enemies? Answers to questions like these may help with the largest question. Why did King Tut die so young? One picture offers a guess at Tut's face, and his funeral mask sits behind him. About three thousand years of rule in ancient Egypt came from thirty dynasties, meaning ruling families. Four historical periods hold the first twenty dynasties. Four period names follow in order. First is the Early Dynastic Period. Next is the Old Kingdom. Then comes the Middle Kingdom. Last is the New Kingdom. King Tutankhamun belonged to the 18th Dynasty. That family was the first ruling family of the New Kingdom. This period began around 1550 BCE. That was almost two hundred years before Tut was born. A map shows ancient Egypt. Religious belief mattered deeply in daily life in ancient Egypt. People then worshipped many different deities, meaning gods and goddesses. To understand King Tut's life, and maybe his death, a reader must learn the history behind this belief.

2At the start of the New Kingdom era, two of Egypt's most important gods were Ra, said RAH, and Amun, said AH-muhn. Ancient Egyptians believed Ra lived inside the Sun. In images, he was often shown as a falcon. Amun was usually shown as a man with a tall crown. During the New Kingdom, some Egyptians began to worship the Sun in a new way. They no longer saw the Sun only as Ra's home. They saw the Sun as a god itself. They called this new god Aten, said AH-tuhn. They showed him as a golden disk. Rays of light reached from the disk toward Earth. Other gods received less and less worship as Aten grew more important to the nobility. In Egypt, religion touched daily life, yet the rules could bend. To most people, Aten was just one more god among many. He did not threaten their beliefs until a young man became pharaoh. That man was Amenhotep, said ah-muhn-HO-tep, the fourth of that name. He was Tut's father. A picture shows Amenhotep IV. People usually picked a small set of major and minor gods and goddesses from hundreds of deities. One reason Egyptians worshipped certain deities was to get help with their work. Thoth was the god of writing and of knowledge. Seshat was the goddess of writing and of measurement. Craftspeople looked to Ptah as their god. Embalmers looked to Anubis as their god. Amenhotep IV began his rule in 1352 BCE. In Egyptian artwork he has unusual features. He has a long face. He has thin calves. He has a belly that sticks out. He had been raised in the new Aten religion. He truly believed in the Sun god. He saw Aten as a universal god. That means a god of all people in the world, not only of Egyptians. The pharaoh believed Aten created the world at the start of time.

3He believed Aten ruled it alone. He believed Aten kept giving life to the world through bright rays of light. Because of this, Amenhotep IV has been called the world's first monotheist. A monotheist believes in a single god who holds all power. A drastic step came from the new pharaoh after about five years. He began a religious revolution. That means a sudden and complete change in Egypt's official religion. He declared that Egyptians could worship only Aten. He changed his own name to Akhenaten, said ahk-eh-NAH-tuhn. The name means He Who Serves Aten. He closed temples where people worshipped the other gods. He tried to destroy those temples. His actions upset people who were used to many gods. His actions angered the priests of the old gods. People in several parts of Egypt tried to halt the ruin of their temples. The pharaoh's military was able to control them. He also ordered a new capital city. He moved the capital away from Thebes. He called the new city Akhetaten, said ahk-eh-TAH-tuhn. The name means Horizon of Aten. Today this area is called Amarna. His revolution is called the Amarna Revolution. King Tut was born in this new capital of Egypt in about 1345 BCE. He was named Tutankhaten. The name means the Living Image of Aten. Only recently, researchers used genetic tests to identify mummies of his parents and grandparents with confidence. DNA samples taken from bones established the mummy most likely to be Akhenaten as Tut's father. The tests also gave a family tree of five generations for the boy king. Tut's mother is known to be one of Akhenaten's sisters. Which sister is uncertain. Members of Egyptian royal families often married close relatives. Land, and the power joined to that land, was what they hoped to keep. A carving from a temple at Amarna shows Akhenaten and Nefertiti, who was possibly Tut's stepmother, with three of their children. Seventeen years of rule ended when Akhenaten died in 1336 BCE.

4The next events puzzle people as much as the other mysteries of Tut's life and death. Apparently two rulers had very brief reigns after Akhenaten died. A brother of Tutankhaten may have been one of those rulers. The other may have been Akhenaten's favorite wife, Nefertiti. No one knows for sure. In any case, three or four years after Akhenaten's death, Egypt's throne was empty again. Nine-year-old Tutankhaten became pharaoh. Nefertiti, said neh-fer-TEE-tee, is the best-known queen of Egypt apart from Cleopatra. Pharaoh Akhenaten favored her above his other wives. After the young prince's mother died, Nefertiti was likely stepmother to Tutankhaten, later called Tutankhamun. Death came to Nefertiti in her early thirties. Before his reign and during it, Tut lived as a wealthy person. He wore jewelry. He wore linen clothes. He used perfumed oils and makeup. All of these items were in the tomb when archaeologists opened it. Hunting beside members of his royal court was expected of him once he was pharaoh. The hunt usually used a bow and a chariot. Nearly fifty bows were placed in his tomb. Chariots were placed there too. So was senet, a board game. These things were for his use in the afterlife. A picture shows King Tutankhaten. During his reign he married his half-sister Ankhesenpaaten, said AHNK-eh-suhn-PAH-ah-tuhn. She was a daughter of Nefertiti. Her name means She Lives Through Aten. Tut fathered at least two daughters. Neither daughter lived. Several servants served King Tut inside the court. One personal attendant was named Tutu. Tutu had served the family since Tut's grandfather had been king. Other servants, some even younger than the king, helped him with even the smallest tasks. One example is his cupbearer. That job was to keep everyone's drinking cups full, especially the young king's cup. Because the pharaoh was so young, others mostly did the military work and the political work of the court. Two men in particular did that work. One was an aging military officer and adviser named Ay.

5The other was a great army general named Horemheb, said HOR-ehm-heb. Both had served Akhenaten. Even so, they strongly disliked his religious reforms. A return to the old worship was what the two men hoped King Tut would make. A wall painting shows Horemheb, an army general and an adviser to King Tut. Tut was persuaded to stop Aten worship through the influence of Horemheb and of Ay. They especially wanted him to return Amun to his old glory as chief god. The young king did so. He changed his name from Tutankhaten to Tutankhamun. The new name means the Living Image of Amun. The queen also took a new name, Ankhesenamun, said AHNK-eh-suhn-AH-muhn. The main push behind changes in King Tut's reign, historians are sure, came from Ay and from Horemheb. His young age, they believe, is why the pharaoh obeyed. The royal court went back to Thebes while the old ways returned. Amarna had once thrived for the god Aten, yet it was left to rot under the Egyptian sun. Remains still show Akhenaten's city of Akhetaten, built around 1348 BCE. In 1327 BCE, when he was about nineteen, King Tutankhamun died. How he died was not written down in an official record. That gap created a mystery. The young pharaoh was mummified. His tomb stood in the royal burial ground called the Valley of the Kings. That valley is a large royal cemetery near Thebes. Tut had no living children. The throne was open to someone outside the royal family. Ay, who had long experience in the court, became Egypt's next pharaoh. He married Tut's widow. Ay ruled for just four years. His death came in 1323 BCE. Horemheb then became pharaoh. Pharaohs had more than one name, much as a person today might have a first name, a middle name, and a last name. They had one name at birth. When they became pharaohs, they received other names. Often these names appeared inside an oval called a cartouche, said car-TOOSH.

6Names, ancient Egyptians believed, held great power. They thought that writing a person's name on something and then breaking it could hurt that person. They even thought it could kill the person. Archaeologists who dig in Egypt's Valley of the Kings always hope to find a ruler's tomb that no one has touched. To show devotion to Amun, and to break with earlier leaders, Horemheb ordered destruction. He wanted everything linked to the Aten religion and to Akhenaten destroyed. His men tore down the empty Aten temples that stood in Amarna. They smashed statues of Akhenaten and of his family, including statues of King Tut. They even cut the names and the faces out of wall art. Later, workers took the stone blocks that held the wall art out of the city buildings. Horemheb ruled for twenty-seven years. He died in 1295 BCE. The 18th Dynasty closed when he died. Ramses II, a great pharaoh of the 19th Dynasty, later completed Amarna's destruction. Drifting sand covered the broken remains of Akhenaten's once-splendid capital. The city was forgotten. Many archaeologists from Britain and from Europe traveled to Egypt in the 1800s. They studied the writing on many walls and monuments. This Egyptian writing is called hieroglyphics, said hy-uh-ruh-GLIF-iks. It revealed much about the customs of the pharaohs. A pharaoh's tomb, archaeologists learned, would contain everything a person might need after death. Hoping to make money from these sacred objects, they dug up many tombs. They were always disappointed. Other treasure seekers had robbed the tombs first. Scholars had long puzzled over hieroglyphics, the old Egyptian language. In 1798, Napoleon brought his army to occupy Egypt. One of his soldiers found something that lasted longer than the occupation. It was a flat black rock. Writing in three languages was carved into its surface. Two of the languages were forms of ancient Egyptian. The third was Greek. Over the next twenty-five years, scholars translated the other languages.

7They used the Greek text as a key. They also used knowledge of the Egyptian language Coptic. A breakthrough came when one scholar realized a difference. Ancient Egyptian was not simple picture writing. Its symbols stood for sounds, not for whole words. The find of this rock, the Rosetta Stone, still ranks among the most critical discoveries in archaeology. By the early 1900s, archaeologists believed they had found the tomb of every known pharaoh except one. The missing tomb was Tutankhamun's. The search by British archaeologist Howard Carter lasted more than five years. He had no success. In 1922, he persuaded Lord Carnarvon, the man paying for the search, to pay for one more season. Later that year, Carter found Tut's tomb. It was in almost undisturbed condition. It held a wealth of artifacts. The finds included thrones, jewelry, weapons, and statues. The mummy of Tutankhamun lay inside three coffins nested together. A large gold mask covered the mummy. The innermost coffin was made of about 242 pounds, or 110 kilograms, of pure gold. Carter's discovery created a sensation. Tut became the most famous pharaoh in history. Who received Tut's treasure? Howard Carter opened the tomb. The Egyptian government still had rules for archaeologists from other lands. One rule said that if an intact tomb was found, every artifact had to stay in Egypt. Carter argued with the government. His claim was that the tomb had already been disturbed. Half the treasure, he hoped, would go with him to England. Egypt kept every piece when the argument ended. Today the Egyptian government works with researchers from other countries. It allows artifacts from Tut's tomb to go on tour. The Egyptians have the final say about this Egyptian treasure. Early death was nothing unusual in ancient times. About thirty years was an average life span in ancient Egypt. Many people did not live that long. Still, some historians first believed teenage King Tut was murdered. They thought disease and genetic disabilities had weakened him.

8More than one person had a motive for his death. Ay and Horemheb controlled many of his decisions. Both became pharaohs after he died. There was no natural heir to his throne. If they wanted to seize power, the time to act was before Tut had children who lived. The window also closed if he grew up and set the two men aside. Some ancient Egyptians must have suspected Horemheb. A statue in his tomb carries carved words that claim he took no part in foul play. A wall painting of Ay was found in Tut's tomb. Ay and Horemheb were the most likely suspects. They were not the only ones. Some researchers named two of Tut's servants as possible killers. One was the cupbearer. The other was his personal attendant, Tutu. They were among the few people allowed into the king's bedroom. Either man could have murdered the pharaoh. Perhaps one struck his head with a heavy object while he slept. Perhaps one pushed him down stairs. For many years, people theorized that a blow to the head killed Tut. X-ray studies of the mummy were the basis of that theory. The studies were made in 1968 and in 1978. The X-rays showed damage to the back of Tut's skull. Experts said the damage was strong evidence. They said someone had hit the back of his head with a heavy object. A detail from his Golden Shrine shows King Tut hunting birds with a bow. Egyptian archaeologist Dr. Zahi Hawass stands with Tut before the mummy enters a CT scanner. In 2005, researchers in Cairo, Egypt, decided to test the old idea. A top Egyptian archaeologist, Dr. Zahi Hawass, led the group. The researchers studied the mummy with an advanced X-ray method called CT scanning, also called CAT scanning. A CT scanner takes many X-rays of an object from different angles. The X-ray information goes to a computer. The computer uses it to produce images. CT images are much more detailed than images from regular X-ray machines.

9Hawass announced a clear result. A blow to the head was definitely not how King Tutankhamun died. The damage to the skull, he said, came only after Tut had died. He said it probably happened during mummification, when King Tut was embalmed. The CT scans also showed several physical problems that young King Tut lived with. He had a cleft palate. He had a club foot. The club foot required him to walk with a cane. The tomb held many canes. Other clues to a possible cause of death also turned up. The scans showed a broken leg shortly before his death. The leg had not healed properly. An infection from the injury, Hawass said, may have taken hold in the king. He may have died a few days later. From 2007 to 2010, researchers, including Hawass, studied the remains further with genetic tests. The new tests showed two important conditions they had not seen before. They found evidence of multiple attacks of severe malaria. Malaria was common in Egypt. The disease alone probably would not have killed Tut. It may have left him very weak. They also found evidence of bone necrosis. That is a breakdown of the bones in his left foot. It may have left the young king open to other infections not yet discovered. Scientists reveal the face of King Tut's mummy. Is the mystery finished? Did the young king die from a mix of body troubles, an accident, a disease, and an infection from a broken leg, or from only some of those? Maybe, or maybe not. After reading the CT scans, some members of Hawass's group offered another view of the broken leg. They said the break might also have happened while Tut was being embalmed. Others felt sure that Howard Carter's team caused the break. They think it happened years ago when the team took the body out of its inner coffin. It is still possible that Tut was poisoned.

10A failed attempt on his life could still be the moment the leg broke. Definite proof, and the name of any attacker, may stay out of reach if either idea is true. New scientific research and DNA evidence make theories about the young king's life and death more provable. Different experts might still interpret the evidence in different ways. What is your interpretation? A picture shows Carter's team removing artifacts from the tomb. Word list. An archaeologist is a noun. It means someone who studies the remains of ancient cultures. Artifacts are a noun. They are any objects that humans made or used long ago. Deities are a noun. In religions with one god, the word can mean the supreme beings and creators. In a religion with many gods, it means gods or goddesses. Depicted is a verb. It means represented something, or portrayed it. Deterioration is a noun. It is the process of becoming worse over time. Dynasties are a noun. A dynasty is a line of rulers who come from one family in a country. Embalmed is a verb. Embalmed means a dead body was treated so that decay would not begin. Genetic is an adjective. It has to do with heredity and with variation in living things. Hieroglyphics are a noun. They are a writing system that uses pictures or symbols. The symbols can stand for words, for syllables, or for sounds. Ancient Egyptians and others used this system instead of alphabet letters. An inscription is a noun. It means words carved into stone or into metal. A monotheist is a noun. It means a person who believes in one god. Mummified is a verb. It means made into a mummy. A pharaoh is a noun. It means a ruler in ancient Egypt. Protruding is an adjective. It means sticking out. Remnants are a noun. They are small parts left after the rest is gone. A picture shows examples of Egyptian hieroglyphics from the Temple of Amun.

75. Three Cities and the Fires That Remade Them

1Fire can serve people, and fire can harm them. This book tells that double story. One great fire happened in Rome. Another is the Great Fire of London. A third is the Chicago Fire. The close looks at what later cities learned. Safety rules come after that, along with meanings of hard words. People learned to use fire thousands of years ago. Warmth was one use. Cooking food was another. Since those early days, fire has sometimes slipped free of human hands. Homes have been torn apart by it. Cities have been torn apart by it. People who start fires on purpose are called arsonists. Hundreds of deaths each year come from their fires. Property damage from those fires reaches millions of dollars each year. Fire has also been a weapon. Parts of Jerusalem were burned during the Crusades. German cities were hit with firebombs during World War II. Even so, accidents by people start most city fires, whether the fires are large or small. Unsafe conditions start many of them too. Ways to fight fire were worked out by the Egyptians. They did that work only after a destructive fire had already struck. Bad luck, sadly, often teaches the clearest lesson. People who lived through city fires saw the need for fire safety only once the flames were gone. Fire prevention and firefighting became clear needs only then. After a great fire in ancient Egypt, a water pump was invented there. Bucket brigades were organized too. Volunteers in a bucket brigade passed water buckets along a line of people toward the fire. Rome, London, and Chicago each suffered a terrible fire. The destruction was huge. New ways to stop fires, and to fight them, came out of those same fires. In the year 64, Rome had the good sides of a large city.

2It had the not-so-good sides too. Libraries, art galleries, and markets were open to visitors. Chariot races could be watched at the Circus Maximus. Rome's stadium could seat more people than most football stadiums of modern times. Indoor plumbing belonged to the rich. Their homes were comfortable and full of space. Most citizens of Rome did not live like that. The city's people numbered more than a million. Cramped, stuffy apartment buildings held most of them. Some buildings rose as high as six stories. The buildings were poorly made. Wood made them easy to burn. A bathroom on the first floor was shared by everyone in the building. Open flames were used for cooking. Open flames were used for light. The summer of the year 64 brought horrible heat to Rome. The city was dry. Fires were a common event. July 19 was the day a fire began. It began in a shop near the Circus Maximus. Warm breezes helped the flames travel. The marketplace burned. Parts of the stadium burned. Nearby homes burned. Roman firemen fought with hand pumps and leather hoses. Their best effort was not enough. The fire moved too fast. Crowds in a panic blocked them. Unruly mobs blocked them too. Emperor Nero was not in the city when the fire began. Heat had sent him to a home on the coast. A picture shows citizens of Rome in a panic while homes and temples burn. Nero returned so he could direct the fight. Bucket brigades got to work. People cleared firebreaks. A firebreak is ground in the fire's path with everything burnable taken away. Across nine days the fire died down and flared up several times. Firebreaks, together with plain good luck, finally ended it. Homes were gone for thousands of people. Ways of earning a living were gone too.

3The number of dead is not known for sure. Nero set up help for people without homes. Temporary shelters went into his own gardens. Public buildings and parks were used as well. Extra food came in from outside Rome. Merchants were ordered by Nero to drop the price of grain. Many Romans still thought Nero himself had lit the fire. They believed he wanted a new city built to honor himself. To shift the blame, he steered people toward a story that Christians had set the blaze. That story became an excuse to persecute the Christians. To persecute is to mistreat. Rome did take lessons from the fire. A large water supply would always be kept close by. New buildings would be stone, not wood. Burned debris was even used to fill marshy ground. A new city stood where the old one had been. Streets were wider. Homes were safer. Reading and writing in Latin and in Greek were taught in Roman schools. Students learned a Latin word, flamma. Flamma is one of many Latin words that mean fire. English words that grow from flamma include flame and flammable. Sixteen hundred years went by. In other parts of the world, daily life had not improved very much. Fire prevention had not improved very much either. London in 1666 dumped its garbage in the streets. Bathing was thought unimportant. Rats that carried bubonic plague filled most buildings. Flea bites from those rats spread the disease. In the years before the fire, the plague had already killed thousands. Wooden buildings with thatched roofs stood packed together. Upper stories jutted over the narrow streets. They nearly met in the middle. Life in London could still feel exciting. A rider in the street might be the king, Charles II. A good play might be seen.

4A coffeehouse might offer rest among local celebrities. A few pennies could buy a fresh, warm roll. The shop belonged to Thomas Farynor, baker to the king, on Pudding Lane. Evening on September 1, 1666, was when Thomas Farynor finished his work. He believed the cook fires were out. They were not. Around one in the morning, a spark left an oven and landed on a pile of wood. The pile caught fire. Thomas woke to someone crying Fire. His family and his servants tried to get out. Smoke rose up the stairs in clouds. They left through an attic window. They jumped to the roof of the next house. Neighbors took buckets from a building close by. They tried to kill the flames. Control was soon lost. People grabbed what they could carry. They led their families to safer ground. Stopping the fire, or at least slowing it, was still possible. A fire hook is a long pole. It could yank building material out of the fire's path and open a firebreak. Mayor Thomas Bludworth did not see the fire as serious enough for so drastic a step. The flames kept moving. Samuel Pepys was a Londoner. He lived through the plague and through the Great Fire. People remember him among the greatest keepers of diaries in the world. His diaries tell a great deal about England in the 17th century. A picture shows people of London rushing away from the fire. Flames roared, and wind roared with them. People fleeing must have been terrified. Warehouses full of rope, paper, and other burnable goods were reached by the fire. A maid warned a government official named Samuel Pepys. She told him the fire was spreading. Alarmed, Pepys hurried to the king. Soldiers and militiamen were sent by King Charles to fight the flames.

5He set up fire posts stocked with food, water, and equipment. Trained militiamen gathered at the posts to help. Charles placed the Duke of York over the firefighting. The duke's men pulled down houses that stood in the fire's path. That work made firebreaks. Gunpowder was used to blow up large buildings. At last the fire burned itself out and stopped. London lost many buildings from medieval times. Records list only nine deaths in the fire. One of those dead was a maid who worked for Thomas Farynor. The true count is probably much higher. Many people in London had no home left. They had no job left. Eighty percent of the city was destroyed. The loss included 87 churches. It included more than 13,000 homes. Where fleeing people gathered, tent cities rose. Organized charity such as the Red Cross did not exist yet. Help came from family, from neighbors, from churches, and from employers. King Charles gave the rebuilding job to two architects. They were Christopher Wren and John Evelyn. Wood was replaced with brick. Streets were made wider. More space was left between houses. Years passed before the work was finished. St. Paul's Cathedral was still unfinished in the years right after the fire. It was completed in 1712. That was 46 years after the fire. New laws told businesses and owners of property to keep garbage off streets and walkways. Improving how 100,000 Londoners lived cost a terrible price. That price was the fire. The Thames River runs through London. It was one of the few places that stayed safe. Before its own great fire, Chicago was huge and booming. In the late 1800s the city really bustled. Livestock was slaughtered at its stockyards and turned into meat. Much of the nation's food came from those yards.

6Travelers crossing the country often stopped to visit. Fine restaurants and hotels were a point of pride. So were entertainment, big stores, and museums. Families could use a beach along Lake Michigan. They could watch cattle arrive from the West at the stockyards. Chicago, like Rome and like London, had slums. Those neighborhoods held poorly built wooden houses set close together. Inspection of housing was lax. Warehouses did not have to follow fire codes. They held all sorts of materials that could burn. Chicago did have a professional fire department. The department was badly overworked. Few people could recall a summer as dry as 1871. From the Fourth of July to early October, the rain that fell measured about 3.8 centimeters, or 1.5 inches. Dying trees dropped dead leaves. Small fires kept springing up, and firefighters grew exhausted putting them out. Evening on October 8, 1871, brought a spark into the hay of a barn. The barn belonged to Catherine O'Leary. It stood on DeKoven Street. Mrs. O'Leary earned a modest living by selling milk. A later story said a cow kicked over a lamp and started the blaze. That story was never proved. A quick end to the fire should have been possible. That night the firefighters went to an address that was wrong. Other buildings were soon burning. Winds that earned Chicago the name Windy City carried the fire onward. No one stopped it in time. The Chicago River itself caught fire. An oily film lay on the water. Then flames took the gasworks. That plant pumped gas used for heat and for light. Hotel guests fled. Parents gathered their children. Many headed for Lake Michigan, hoping to get away. Fleeing crowds packed the bridges. Hot cinders and sparks dropped from the sky. The fire's horrible noise mixed with church bells.

7Bells warned other parts of town. Smoke grew so thick that even one block ahead was invisible. People in a panic blocked many of the city's bridges. Wind joined with fire and made a firestorm. A firestorm is super-heated wind. Wherever that wind blows, flame spreads. Burning chunks were lifted and thrown onto buildings. Those buildings held oil, fabric, and kerosene. Each of those would feed the fire. Brave people stayed to fight the flames and to save the helpless. Some were professional firefighters. Some were ordinary citizens. Even the station that pumped water was destroyed. The fire department's work was blocked by that loss. Hotels of luxury fell into the flames. Plain houses fell too. Three days passed while the fire burned. Buildings not yet burning were blown up so firebreaks could be made. Rain came on October 10. Firefighters used that rain to put the flames out. The fire ended at last. Relief came first. Then the loss became clear. About 300 people were dead. Others were still missing. Homes, possessions, and workplaces were gone. Dust and ash still hung in the air. Some parts of the city were still too hot to enter. Federal troops came to stop looting. General Philip Sheridan was in command. Supplies and volunteers were sent to Chicago. Survivors who still had enough gathered food and clothing for people without homes. Shelters were opened by the Chicago Relief and Aid Society. Later the society gave materials so small temporary houses could be built. Owners of businesses set up tables or carts and went back to work. Some people left the city as soon as they could. Most remained and rebuilt. Rebuilding moved rather slowly. Changes that might prevent another fire met resistance. Bit by bit, people saw the need for stricter rules on buildings. They saw the need for stricter rules on preventing fire.

8Safer housing went up. Officials made the fire department better. The lesson was hard, and it was learned again. A view from above shows how large the Chicago fire was. Pictures of Chicago in ruins reached the front pages of news across the country. Peshtigo, Wisconsin, burned on that same night. Its fire was even more destructive than Chicago's. That summer, Peshtigo and the towns around it had the same drought Chicago had. Forests had been cleared by farmers and by railroad workers. Piles of dry wood and dry leaves were simply left on the ground. On the night of October 8, a huge firestorm swallowed the whole region. The ground shook under the townspeople. Tornado-force winds pushed a wall of flame at the town. Less than one hour later, the whole town was gone. Peshtigo had 1,700 citizens. Eight hundred of them died. Deaths in the forest fire are estimated at 1,200. The fire jumped Green Bay. Parts of Michigan burned as well. Among natural disasters in U.S. history, this fire is one of the deadliest. Survivors carried terrible scars on their bodies. They carried terrible scars in their minds. The Peshtigo fire is almost forgotten. It fell on the same night as the Chicago fire, which is more famous. Chicago's fire killed fewer people. Even a very small town today has a fire department with good equipment. Good fortune puts us in an age that treats fire safety as very important. Strict fire codes cover every area of the country. Professional fire departments train to prevent fires, to fight them, and to save lives. Volunteer departments train in those same skills. Fire alarms and sprinkler systems are built into buildings. Firewalls stand between houses. Schools and the media teach people how to keep fires from starting.

9They teach how to plan for an emergency. Terrible fires still happen, even with all this work. Modern prevention and modern firefighting give us a hope. We hope never again to see fires like those of Rome, London, and Chicago. Reports of fires in the United States reach almost two million every year. A fire can kill, so these safety rules should always be followed. Do not play with matches or lighters. Do not play with materials that burn easily, such as gasoline. Leave cooking and the stove alone until you are allowed, and until an adult stays to watch. Keep blankets, clothes, and every other object off lamps, radiators, and heaters. A covering like that could catch fire fast. Your home should have at least one smoke detector on each floor. Detectors near bedrooms matter most of all. They can wake you if a fire starts. Check smoke alarms every six months. Change the batteries at least once each year. Keep a household fire extinguisher near any heat or any flame in or near your home. Your family needs a plan for getting out of a fire. Walk through the home and learn at least two exits from every room. An exit may be a door. It may be a window on the first floor. It may be a window that has a safe escape ladder. Pick a meeting place that is easy to find. It must sit a safe distance from the building. Name one person to count family members so you know all are safe. Name a different family member to reach a neighbor's house and call 911. Practice the escape plan together. Knowing the steps saves time when an emergency comes. It may save your life. If fire starts in your home, these rules help your family get out fast and stay safe.

10Leave as fast as you can. Go to the meeting place you chose. Leave your belongings behind, even when they are very valuable. Objects can be replaced. You cannot be replaced. As you leave, try to warn the rest of the family. Yell the word Fire. Bang on doors you pass. Poisonous gases are in smoke. Smoke can be hot enough to scorch lungs. Smoke gathers near the ceiling, so keep low. Stay in a crouch, and crawl when you must. A damp towel or cloth held at your mouth can work as a mask. Do not return to a burning building, whatever the reason. If your clothes catch fire, stop at once, drop, and roll. If another person's clothes catch fire, that person should stop, drop, and roll right away. A towel, a blanket, a rug, or a cloth can cover the person and help kill the flames. A bucket brigade is a line of people passing buckets, one person to the next, from water to a fire. Militiamen are volunteers who carry out police duties. To persecute is to mistreat one specific group. Firebreaks are areas cleared of fuel and of anything that can burn. Refugees are people who flee trouble and have nowhere to go. A fire hook is a long, heavy hook that pulls structures down to open a firebreak. Slums are poor, crowded parts of a city. Stockyards are places where livestock is killed and made into meat. A firestorm is super-heated wind that carries fire across a wide area. Thatched roofs are roofs built of straw. A gasworks is a factory that processes fuel and pumps it. Unruly means hard to control, or disobedient. Lax means relaxed, or not strict. Looting means robbing on a wide scale.

76. True Story or Clever Trick?

1A 1952 photo by an amateur photographer showed something many people believed was an alien spacecraft. Was that picture genuine, or was it a fake? Imagine hearing that huge, hairy, smelly giants live in wild places, or that beings from other worlds draw shapes in wheat. Imagine a friend saying an old curse can kill, or that a stretch of the Atlantic can swallow ships and planes. How would you test those stories? Did a curse guard a king's tomb? Who or what pressed such detailed patterns into fields? Can anyone account for ships and planes that vanish? This book sets out evidence on four open mysteries. You can then judge each one to be real or false. For hundreds of years, Native Americans in remote parts of the Pacific Northwest have told of meeting gigantic, apelike creatures that keep to themselves. Reclusive means solitary and shut away from other people. Canada's Salish peoples named them Sasquatch, or wild man of the woods. Other tribes use other names. English speakers usually say Bigfoot. A map of sightings marks Washington, Oregon, and the United States, and its key stands for one sighting. A puzzling 1967 photograph by Roger Patterson shows a figure like this.

2Railway workers, forest workers, hikers, travelers, and people in remote country have also reported meetings. Most of them had never heard the Native American stories, so those older accounts had not shaped their reports. A Bigfoot is said to stand as much as 8 feet, or 2.4 meters, with hair covering its body. Footprint depth leads to a weight guess of 350 to 800 pounds, or 160 to 360 kilograms. Witnesses often mention high screams and a terrible smell. A chart puts a grizzly at 9 feet, or 2.74 meters, a Bigfoot at 8 feet, or 2.44 meters, and a human at 6 feet, or 1.83 meters, with lower marks at 4 feet, or 1.22 meters, and 2 feet, or 0.61 meter. Bigfoot is pictured as shorter than a grizzly and taller than an average human. Cryptozoologists, scientists who study animals that might or might not be real, have spent much time and money on the question. Thousands of eyewitness reports still have not produced proof. In 1998, Doctor John Bindernagel studied a nest he believed a Bigfoot had made. In 1924, lumberjack Albert Ostman went alone into the mountains to search for gold.

3On the third night, something huge and smelly carried him off inside his sleeping bag. Hours later it set him down in a clearing. Four huge, hairy, apelike beings stood around him, seeming to be a father, a mother, and two children. He got away after almost a week, badly shaken and unharmed. Many other meetings have been reported, and not every one was so calm. A cast of a footprint looks far larger than a man's foot. In the vast empty forests and glaciers of the northwestern United States, a dead body does not last. To decompose is to decay and rot until matter breaks into small parts. Insects and animal scavengers also eat remains. Scientists say that if Bigfoot is real, a body, a skeleton, or fossil remains should turn up. None has ever been found. In 1977, a sighting in northern Washington proved to be a hoax, something meant to mislead or trick. Three young men had used gorilla suits and walkie-talkies. That trick leads some people to treat other reports as fakes too. Are the Bigfoot sightings genuine, or are they a hoax?

4In tall crops, circles of flattened plants were reported as early as 1590. Farmers blamed the wind. During the 1980s the number of circles rose sharply, and simple rings gave way to complex designs. Intricate means very detailed, complicated, and complex. Most circles appear mysteriously at night. A few people say they watched spaceships or whirlwinds form them. Lights may show in the sky. Humming or music may be heard. Radiation is sometimes found inside. One very large formation held 149 circles and showed up near Stonehenge within 20 minutes, in full daylight. Plants inside are not crushed. They bend at the lowest node, the place on a stem where a leaf or a branch grows. Bent plants often grow better than straight plants outside the circle. Experiments suggest that strong microwave beams could lay crops down this way. A microwave is an electromagnetic energy wave shorter than a radio wave and longer than infrared radiation. Heating and radar devices often use it. Where would such beams come from, and who would aim them? Some people read the shapes as messages from beings on other planets.

5Overnight watchers say a detailed pattern can appear in only a few minutes. Bent stalks inside a circle can form a spiral. Humans make many crop circles, for several reasons. Some want to show that the work can be done. Some want to play tricks. Some crop artists say a divine impulse guides their designs. In 1991, Englishmen Doug Bower and David Chorley said they had made every circle since 1978. Some listeners accepted that claim of one gigantic hoax. Others questioned whether the two men had the skill and strength to build huge patterns at night without being seen. Seven years later, Doug retracted his confession. Retracted means he took it back and withdrew it. He then said unknown forces made the circles. He has also shown a method for flattening a field by hand. A fake is possible, yet the labor is heavy. Tornadoes sweep a wide path and wreck a broad area. Circle designs look guided and intricate, so a tornado is a weak match. Another weather idea uses an electrically charged whirlwind called a plasma vortex. Plasma is gas formed of charged particles, and it can conduct electricity.

6A plasma vortex could explain reported lights and humming. It can hover, which means it stays in one place in the air, or it can shift as if a remote control steered it, so it might be mistaken for a UFO. Some researchers suggest that the military of the United States and of Britain is testing a secret high-energy weapon powered by microwaves, and that practice shots create the circles. Are crop circles genuine, or are they a hoax? In 1922, Howard Carter, aided by local Egyptian workers, found the tomb of the pharaoh Tutankhamun. A pharaoh was a ruler in ancient Egypt. People now call him King Tut. The tomb held treasures of stunning worth. That same year, newspapers spread a story of a curse painted on a wall: They who enter this sacred tomb shall swift be visited by wings of death. Early Egyptians held that cobras protect the pharaohs. On the opening day, a cobra swallowed Carter's canary. Lord Carnarvon had paid for the search. In 1923 he died in Egypt, and newspapers said a pharaoh's curse had killed him. They also said his dog in England howled and fell dead at the same minute.

7Papers claimed that twenty-six people connected to the find died during the next ten years, many in ways called suspicious. The tale has since shaped movies, books, and games. Carter is shown opening a door of the tomb in 1922. In the early 1900s, reporters sometimes made up details so a story would feel more exciting. Lord Carnarvon had already been ill for twenty years, so the date of his death may have been a coincidence. Research finds that only six people connected to the discovery died during those ten years. Carter kept working at the tomb for at least ten years. He lived seventeen more years after the find. The curse said to be written inside was not there at all. A photo places him with Lord Carnarvon, who funded the dig in Egypt's Valley of the Kings. Dead bodies can give off bacteria, and those bacteria might bring sickness and death. Might that have played a part in Carnarvon's death? Archaeologists today, scientists who study the remains of ancient cultures, wear rubber gloves and protective clothes. People who robbed tombs long ago may have fallen ill in this way, and that illness may have started the curse stories.

8Early Egyptians worked hard to ready a king for burial. They believed he needed riches in the next life. Tales of danger may have been spread to hold people back from the tombs. Pyramids were burial places for these pharaohs. Is the mummy's curse genuine, or is it a hoax? For years, odd events have struck ships and planes in an Atlantic region lying generally between Florida, Bermuda, and Puerto Rico. A map of that region also shows Canada, the United States, the Bahamas, Miami, San Juan, Mexico, and Puerto Rico. In 1965, Vincent Gaddis published Invisible Horizons about these events. He was first to name the region the Bermuda Triangle, and he also called it the Triangle of Death. Many planes and ships vanish and leave no trace. Crews vanish from ships. Thick fog can form without warning. Compasses and other navigation tools can fail. On a clear day in 1945, Flight 19 was on an ordinary training flight when all five Avenger bombers lost their bearings and vanished. The rescue airship sent after them vanished too.

9In 1881, the merchant ship Ellen Austin found a ghost ship with nobody aboard and with no sign of a struggle. A crew went aboard to sail it to port. Thick fog then wrapped both ships, and they lost touch during the night. The next day the ghost ship was found again, and the second crew was gone too. A crew that brought an empty ship into port could claim a reward. The USS Cyclops vanished in 1918 with 306 people aboard. That loss is among the earliest tied to the Bermuda Triangle. In 1966, Captain Donald Henry's tug, the Good News, was towing a cargo barge from Puerto Rico toward Florida. Dense fog suddenly spun around the barge. The tug lost every instrument and part of its power. For five minutes it strained in a pull against the fog bank, then drew itself and the barge clear. Some people say a mysterious power lies behind the many losses of ships and crews. Strange lights lead some to think UFOs seize people and carry them off. Others point to harsh weather that is common there. Hurricanes and violent waterspouts rise without warning, and tidal waves are frequent.

10A wrecked vessel could be carried off and leave nothing behind. Some missing crews, saved later, say storms forced them off damaged ships. Others say the region is not unusual at all. They note that some losses blamed on the Triangle happened hundreds of miles away, and that some vessels reported lost appeared again later. In so huge an ocean, violent weather could wreck a ship and leave no evidence. Are the Bermuda Triangle stories genuine, or are they a hoax? Mysteries, events we cannot yet explain, will always be with us. On Rapa Nui, also called Easter Island, people still ask how the moai statues were carved and moved. At Stonehenge, people still ask why and how the structures were built. Some listeners will call such stories nonsense. Others will call them real. Some sources deserve more trust than others. Evidence should come before any claim is accepted, whether the claim is extraordinary or ordinary. Weigh what you have read, and decide what you believe. What is your view of these mysteries, and which further mysteries can you track down?

77. Two Brothers and the First Flight

1A map of early balloon trips near Paris, France, marks several dates and places. On August 27, 1783, a flight ended at Gonesse. On September 19, 1783, another began at Versailles. On November 21, 1783, a flight left the edge of Paris. On December 1, 1783, a flight left the Tuileries Garden. Belleville and Saint Denis appear on the map as well. England and Germany lie to the north and east. Spain and Italy lie farther south, with the Mediterranean Sea between them. The Atlantic Ocean borders the west. The scale is marked in miles and in kilometers. September 19, 1783, fell on an afternoon when excitement ran high. A crowd of 130,000 packed the grounds. The place was the Palace of Versailles, said vair-SYE, just outside Paris. The draw was a test. The machine was a large balloon lifted by hot air. Two French brothers had built it, Joseph-Michel and Jacques-Etienne Montgolfier, a name said mon-GOLF-yay. From the palace courtyard, the king and queen watched. He was Louis XVI. She was Marie Antoinette, said an-twon, then ET. Beauty came from silk and from paper. Gold designs sat on a background of blue. Tension hung in the air. Nobody yet knew how dangerous flight might be, so the passengers were not people. A wicker basket hung under the balloon. A sheep rode inside. So did a rooster. So did a duck. The animals were part of a scientific experiment, and each one had a reason for being there.

2The sheep's body was judged close enough to a human body to make a fair test. The rooster was a bird, yet it could not fly very high, so it was included too. High flight was something the duck could do. Its job was to test what dangers flight might hold. A fire burned in a pit. Hot air, full of smoke, went from that fire into the balloon. Release came shortly after 1:00 in the afternoon. The crowd watched in wonder as the balloon rose about 460 meters, or 1,500 feet. Earth received it again eight minutes later. The landing spot was 3.2 kilometers off, which is 2 miles. The animals were unharmed. A dream as old as humanity, the age of flight, had begun. People could now head for the clouds, and much of the credit belonged to the Montgolfiers. A small town in the south of France was home to Pierre and Anne Montgolfier. Sixteen children were theirs. Joseph and Etienne were two of them. Pierre manufactured paper with success. Official stationery for King Louis XVI's court came from his factories. That contract gave the family financial security. The 1770s were when Joseph and Etienne took the family business into their own hands. Free time was plentiful, and they used it on other interests. Joseph was in his early forties when flight began to intrigue him.

3From the 1600s onward, scientists explored a craft that would be lighter than air. Buoyancy was the principle that would let it fly. Building that vehicle was a problem nobody had solved yet. The ancient Greek mathematician Archimedes, said ark-uh-MEE-deez, was the first to understand buoyancy. It compares densities. Density is an object's weight for a given volume, set against the fluid the object is immersed in. Here, fluid can mean liquid. It can also mean gas. If the object is less dense than the fluid around it, an upward force acts on the object. A light gas inside a lightweight enclosure might, Joseph suspected, push upward with real force. He read about a gas that several earlier researchers said they had produced. The gas was hydrogen. People of that time called it inflammable air, because it could explode. Hydrogen was already familiar to scientists across many years. The year 1766 is when Henry Cavendish, a chemist from England, showed that the gas was an element. The name he gave it was inflammable air. A new name, hydrogen, came in 1783 from the French chemist Antoine Lavoisier. Say his name la-VWAH, then zee-ay. Small spheres of paper got a fill of the gas. Joseph then let them go. The results disappointed him. The spheres rose only a few meters, then came down. The atoms of hydrogen were tiny enough to slip through paper.

4Outside air is where they escaped. Chemistry builds the universe from elements. Atoms make up every element. They are the smallest particles that still keep that substance's properties. Oxygen is an element. Hydrogen is an element too. Water's molecule can be built from two hydrogen atoms plus one oxygen atom. Another route was needed. Joseph wanted a machine that could ascend, which is the name he used. Shirts hung over a fire full of smoke, drying, caught his eye one day. The shirts puffed upward. Chimneys sending smoke upward were a sight he knew, as most people did. Smoke, he decided, was the answer. Early in 1783 the brothers began burning different materials, hunting for the ones that made the most smoke. Damp straw mixed with wool that had been chopped up produced more smoke than anything else in their tests. It also made a terrible stench. The smoke did give buoyancy to any light container. Some unknown thing inside smoke, the brothers decided, must be able to lift. They gave that marvelous substance a name: Montgolfier gas. No such substance existed. Hot air itself caused the lift. When air is heated, the molecules in it move faster. The air expands and becomes less dense. Put that lighter air in a balloon and the balloon goes up. Joseph and Etienne kept believing in Montgolfier gas, and they kept making foul-smelling smoke, even though they did not understand the real science of hot-air balloons.

5They had no reason to think the idea was wrong. Their test balloons were working. Silk was one material they tried for the envelope. Paper was another. Linen was a third. As the work went on, the balloons grew larger. They rose ever higher. Attention followed the experiments. June 4, 1783, brought a crowd into a town square. The town was Annonay, in France. Say it AN, then on-ey. The test used a large balloon of cloth lined with paper. No one rode in it. Watchers were amazed as it soared some 2,000 meters, or 6,560 feet, into the sky. After a flight of ten minutes, it landed about 2 kilometers, or 1.2 miles, away. France caught a craze for balloons after successes of that kind. The machines that excited the French were called ascending machines, and later aerostats. History was already made by the Montgolfiers before anyone called the machine a balloon. The word arrived later. French already had the word ballon. It named the big ball people use when they play games. The new name was adapted from that. Official recognition was what the brothers requested from the French Academy of Sciences. Inventors gained from an academy seal that said the work was approved. It raised their prestige, earned admiration, and, they hoped, won the king's support. The academy withheld approval. Waiting seemed wiser. Someone else might invent a balloon that worked better.

6A physicist led the rivalry. His name was Jacques Charles, said ZHOCK, then SHARL. He proposed a hydrogen balloon. Hydrogen was a path the Montgolfiers had abandoned a long while back. Hot air was the choice they kept. Charles saw great possibilities in hydrogen. No element is lighter than hydrogen. Its weight is only one-fourteenth that of air. A first glance makes it look perfect for balloons. Danger sits in that gas. Fire catches in it easily, and so do explosions. Helium, the second-lightest element, is a much better gas. Fire does not catch in helium, and it does not explode. Lighter-than-air flight can use it in complete safety. Discovery of helium waited until the 1880s. Makers of balloons in the 1700s therefore had none. July 1783 was when Charles started building his balloon. The academy had approved the work. Public donations paid for it. Help came from two brothers, both named Robert: Nicolas-Louis and Anne-Jean. Say the surname roh-BEAR. Both were professional engineers. The three built a small test balloon of silk. Rubber coated the surface so the hydrogen would stay inside. Reports of the Montgolfier experiments reached King Louis. He invited the brothers to Paris. Glory, shown to all of France, was what he wanted from a dazzling balloon. Government money now backed the brothers, because the king favored them. Each team wanted to be first to launch a balloon carrying human passengers.

7A race had begun. The rivalry, even so, stayed reasonably friendly. Summer was fading. The Montgolfiers were nearly ready to show a balloon. Charles was nearly ready too. August 27, 1783, drew a large crowd to a grassy area in Paris. The Eiffel Tower stands on that spot today. They came to see the Charles balloon launch. Benjamin Franklin stood among the onlookers. The famous American was serving France as ambassador for the United States. Size was modest. Across, it measured about 4 meters, which is 13 feet. Red stripes alternated with white. Yellow had replaced the white in the stripes. A rubber solution on the silk caused the stain. Both teams were chasing one question. Is it possible to build a device lighter than air that will let people fly? They followed a procedure called the scientific method. The steps run in this order. Pose a question. Study what is already known. Build a hypothesis. Check it by watching, or by running experiments. Study the data and decide what it shows. Share the findings. Release came late in the afternoon. Nobody was aboard. The rise was quick. The path ran northeast, and the flight lasted under an hour. Gonesse was the village where it came down, about 15 kilometers off, or 9 miles. Pitchforks came out. Terrified villagers struck at the strange monster that had fallen from the heavens.

8Paris was ready to be amazed again, and the turn belonged to the Montgolfiers. Versailles was the launch site on September 19. Animals rode in the test balloon. A safe landing for the animals meant the next trial could carry a person. Danger would be extreme. The king thought the riders should be prisoners already condemned. Two volunteers stepped forward instead. One was a science teacher, Jean-Francois Pilatre de Rozier, said ROZE-ee-ay. A soldier volunteered as well, the Marquis d'Arlandes. Say it mar-KEE, then dar-LOND. November 21 was the date of their historic flight. This time the start was on the outskirts of Paris. Impressiveness went beyond the balloon that had flown before. It towered 23 meters, or 75 feet, high. Various golden designs covered it. Louis's monogram was one design, a pair of capital L's intertwined. Another design was fleurs-de-lis arranged in a circle. Say that flur-duh, then LEES. They are stylized lilies, a mark of French royalty. Sun disks decorated it too. So did the signs of the zodiac. So did eagles, wings spread. Blimps are one kind of modern airship. Gas pressure alone holds their shape. Dirigibles are another kind. An internal structure holds them. De Rozier was aboard, and so was the marquis. The aerostatic globe then rose. Landing came twenty-five minutes later, about 8 kilometers off, or 5 miles. Two windmills stood outside the city, one on each side of the landing spot.

9Heroes is what people called the two men. Benjamin Franklin watched the historic flight. Another spectator asked what the balloon was good for. Franklin's reply is still quoted. What good is a newborn baby? Only ten days after the Montgolfier triumph, December 1 arrived. A hydrogen balloon carried people upward for the first time. One flier was Jacques Charles. The other was Nicolas-Louis Robert. They took off from the Tuileries Garden in Paris, said TWEE-luh-reez. More than two hours passed in the air. The town where they came down was about 36 kilometers off, or 22 miles. Several further balloons left the Montgolfiers' hands in later years. The French Academy of Sciences honored the brothers. King Louis made their father, Pierre, a nobleman. Passion for ballooning soon spread through Europe. The risks became clear before long. June 1785 brought a fatal attempt to cross the English Channel. De Rozier died, and so did his copilot, Pierre Romain. Risks did not stop the pioneers. They kept improving balloon designs well after the late-1700s craze had faded. Rudders were added to lighter-than-air vehicles in the 1800s. Motorized propellers were added too. Passenger trips across the Atlantic, in both directions, were being made by huge airships by the 1930s. An abrupt end came in 1937 for the golden age of airships. Fire broke out on the German airship Hindenburg. It crashed during a landing in New Jersey.

10Advertising is the main use of airships today. Large sporting events often have them overhead, above stadiums open to the sky. Gas balloons are mostly used to gather weather data. Recreation is the main use of balloons lifted by hot air. Festivals in many areas, held each year, send hundreds of colorful balloons into the sky, all lifted by hot air. Those events can make it seem that balloon mania never ended. A few words belong with the story. Immersed describes something dipped into a fluid, or set down inside one. It can also mean being surrounded completely by something else. Airships are wingless, steerable aircraft that can fly under power, using bodies filled with gas to stay lighter than air. Inflammable means able to catch fire easily and burn quickly. Atoms are the smallest parts of an element. Intrigued means very curious or interested. Buoyancy is the ability or the tendency to float. Alone, the smallest part a substance can still be is a molecule. One or more atoms make it. Chemical elements, and the ways chemicals interact, are what a chemist studies. Energy and matter, their nature and their properties, are what a physicist studies. An envelope is the outer bag of an airship, a hot-air balloon included. Gas or heated air is what that bag holds. Prestige is a high level of standing or respect. An experiment is a scientific test or trial.

78. Two Ways People Get Their Energy

1This book starts with different styles, then defines the terms. It looks at strengths and challenges for introverts and for extroverts. It clears up myths, tells how to honor a temperament, and ends by valuing diversity. A word list comes last. Angela and Lisa are sisters. A picture shows that they differ in some ways. Two years separate their ages. Angela likes to stay home. She reads, or she does art projects in her room. She also likes writing stories. She likes playing with her pet hamster. Outside, she likes being in nature. She likes watching plants and wildlife with care. Lisa would rather be with friends than do anything else. She likes games with them. Parties for birthdays appeal to her. So do other gatherings with people. Her pet rabbit is a frequent playmate when she is home. Friends receive jewelry from her, including bracelets that stand for friendship. She talks a lot. She keeps asking Angela to join the play. Angela would rather be alone. In some ways the sisters are alike. Both are creative in art. Both love animals. They differ in a basic way. Angela is an introvert. Lisa is an extrovert. Introvert and extrovert are terms for different styles. The styles cover how a person feels energized, how a person deals with other people, and how a person handles information.

2The biggest difference is about social time. That time tends to tire introverts. It tends to energize extroverts. A chart lists more traits. These are broad patterns. They may not fit every person. Most people mix the two types. The types form a continuum. Many people are ambiverts. An ambivert has clear qualities of both types. The situation decides which side of an ambivert's temperament shows up. The line runs from introvert to ambivert to extrovert. Introverts get energy from time alone. Extroverts get energy from time with other people. Introverts tend to notice their inner world more. That world is the mind and the feelings. Extroverts tend to notice the outer world more. That world is people and activities. One-to-one talk is what introverts prefer. Large groups can feel uncomfortable to them. Extroverts prefer talk in groups. Large groups feel comfortable to them. Introverts have fewer friendships, and those friendships are closer. Extroverts have more friends. Casual ties are part of that larger friend group. Introverts often listen more. Extroverts often talk more. Introverts do not like the attention on them. Extroverts like attention. Introverts are comfortable when they focus on several things at once. That skill is called multitasking. One task at a time is the focus extroverts prefer. Introverts prefer to watch a new task before they do it.

3Extroverts learn best by doing. Introverts take time when they decide. Extroverts often decide quickly. Distractions disrupt introverts. Distractions do not bother extroverts. Introverts share opinions when someone asks. Extroverts offer opinions freely. Brain structure may differ between the two types. Scientists are looking into that possibility. They are also studying differences in brain chemistry. The evidence points to a trait people have when they are born. It is not learned. Temperament is a person's basic nature. Personality is different. Experiences shape personality. Education can influence personality. Upbringing can too. So can many different events. None of those change temperament.
