The words introvert and extrovert come from Carl Jung. Say his name YOONG. He lived from 1875 to 1961. He was a Swiss psychologist. He built a theory of psychological types. People still use that theory widely. The theory has four pairs of contrasting qualities. The introvert-extrovert pair is seen as the most important. Surveys have taken in those qualities. One survey is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator, or MBTI. It names sixteen different combinations of qualities. Many people find these profiles useful for understanding themselves. Jung's list pairs the qualities this way. Extroverted, marked E, means a stronger focus on the outer world. Introverted, marked I, means a stronger focus on the inner world.

4That pair is about preferred focus. Intuitive, marked N, means a stronger focus on impressions and meanings. Sensing, marked S, means a stronger focus on physical reality. That pair is about how a person receives information. The letter F stands for Feeling. It means paying more attention to people's cares and to how a decision changes their lives. Thinking, marked T, means a stronger focus on logic and on pros and cons. That pair is about making decisions. Judging, marked J, means a structured and orderly way of living, with a preference for certainty. Perceiving, marked P, means a flexible way of living, with more comfort around uncertainty. That pair is about how a person lives life. One style is not above the other. Both styles are equally healthy. Both are useful in certain circumstances. A culture may still prize one style more than the other. Take the United States as an example. People there place a higher value on extroversion. People often treat it as normal. Some Americans treat introverts as if something is missing, or as if they are lesser. This culture often pushes introverts to copy extrovert behavior. That means more outgoing, more assertive, and more interested in group activities. Japan is one country where introversion gets more acceptance. It is even encouraged. Both types have strengths.

5Both have challenges. The descriptions that follow are broad. They do not fit every person. Among Americans, introverts are as few as one-quarter of the people. They are as many as one-half. Extroverts are as few as one-half. They are as many as three-quarters. Introverts tend to focus inward. Extroverts tend to focus outward. Introverts tend to be independent. They tend to be self-motivated. They work well alone. They solve problems in creative ways. They think things through with care. They are often well prepared. They pay attention to detail. Some situations and settings can overwhelm them. They do not like interruptions. Background noise often distracts them. A sudden demand for an answer is something they dislike. Speaking up in class may be hard. Speaking up at work may be hard too. Solitude is a need that friends and family may miss. A first meeting often goes well for an extrovert. They make friends easily. Links with other people come easily to them. They work well in groups. Working alone may be hard for them. They may get bored easily. Boredom may make them very uncomfortable. Too many words is another risk. They may not notice that other people need space or quiet. Trouble can come when parents, or other relatives, stand on the opposite end of the spectrum.

6It helps to talk about differences in an open and respectful way. It helps to find a balance that meets everyone's needs. Extroverts have an advantage in many modern classrooms of this country. Desks may sit in pairs or in small groups. Group work is emphasized. Students may not get room or minutes for work they do alone. Public speaking may be required. All of that can challenge introverted students. Some schools have changed classrooms to meet these issues. One solution is a quiet zone. Another is some quiet time each day for students. Another is a quiet choice instead of the usual recess. Teachers can also urge students to learn independent work. They can urge work in pairs as well as work in groups. Certain jobs gain a great deal from either type. Writing, art, and science are careers that often attract introverts. Those jobs often require working alone. They often require deep work on one task at a time. Teaching often attracts extroverts. So do sales and politics. Those jobs move fast. Those jobs call for quick decisions. They call for frequent contact with other people. Both types are misunderstood at times. Wrong ideas about them are widespread. A common myth says introverts are shy. Introversion and shyness can overlap. They are still distinct. They do not always go together.

7A shy person feels nervous, or ill at ease, when people are around. Shy people often want very much to socialize. They avoid it because they fear rejection. Fearing social time is not the same as caring little about it. Little interest is often true of introverts. Shy people cannot turn shyness off whenever they wish. When they choose to, introverts can often behave in an extrovert way. Another wrong idea says introverts must be antisocial or insecure. The idea comes from the fact that they join fewer social events. They are neither. They get overstimulated easily. They seek solitude so they can take care of themselves. A picture shows introversion on top and shyness below. They are very different. A common wrong idea about extroverts says life is easy for them. It says they are happier than introverts. In a social setting, an extrovert often seems more at ease than an introvert. They still have challenges, just as everyone else does. An extrovert may feel as uncomfortable as an introvert in some situations. The extrovert may hide it better. A further myth calls extroverts pushy people who listen poorly. The truth is that connection with other people delights extroverts. They can often befriend people in very effective ways. They draw people into conversation. Introverts can feel flooded by that lively outreach.

8A third myth says extroverts do not like to be alone. Often they do like it. They just need shorter periods to recharge. The alone time they need may differ in kind from an introvert's. Friendship between the two types is possible. They often enjoy similar things. They do those things in different ways. Are you an introvert, an extrovert, or an ambivert? If you are not sure, look back at the chart. Does one column fit you far more than the other column? Maybe your fit is midway. Knowing where you sit on that three-part spectrum is useful. Knowing yourself will help you feel more confident about who you are. It will help you understand your moods and your preferences. Choices that feed you become easier with that knowledge. It can also help you talk with others so they can respect your needs better. An introvert's wish to be alone is less likely to be heard as an insult once others understand. An extrovert's wish for company is easier for others to accept, even when they cannot come along. Tips for introverts follow. Being an introvert is fine, even where the culture does not fully value it. Give yourself regular time alone so you can recharge. Tell friends, family, and teachers why you need time alone.

9Pick hobbies that leave room to think, to reflect, and to daydream. New people and new activities may require extra time before you feel at ease. Take that time. Do not worry if you do not have a lot of friends. A few good ones matter more. Tips for extroverts follow. Pick hobbies that put you with other people. Plan pleasant solo activities for times when no companion is free. High activity may leave you needing a wind-down. A wind-down need not be silent or motionless. Find what works best for you. If you are an ambivert, call on your introvert qualities and your extrovert qualities as you need them. Enjoy having both. Each sister picked work that fits her temperament. A picture shows them as adults. Success also comes in jobs that fit a temperament only partly. Those jobs may take more energy. They may be more stressful. Introverts and extroverts offer different skills and different perspectives. All of those gifts are valuable. Understanding different temperaments matters for good communication and teamwork. That is true in families, in schools, and in workplaces. Acceptance and shared respect grow in that setting. When a group splits tasks by temperament, it uses different people's strengths well. Remember Angela and Lisa. They are adults now. Angela is an artist and a research assistant.

10She works from home. Lisa is an event planner. She also works as a receptionist. Her office is a busy medical one. For these sisters, knowing their own temperaments lets each one honor her nature. It lets them respect their differences. Wise choices follow, and those choices support lives that satisfy them. Anxiety means worry or nervousness, usually about what is unknown or about what has not happened yet. An assertive person has a bold style, or a confident one. Circumstances are conditions, facts, or events that affect a situation. An impression is an opinion, a belief, or a notion that forms about a person or a thing. Insecure means lacking self-confidence or certainty. People interact when they work as a team, or when they talk and act with one another. Misconceptions are ideas that are wrong because they rest on information that is inaccurate or incomplete. Too much activity, or too much excitement, can leave a person overstimulated. The feeling is mental or physical anxiety, or a sense of being overcome. Social means having to do with society, with community, or with a connection between individuals. Solitude is the experience of being alone. A spectrum is a range. A trait is a feature or a quality. Animals, plants, things, and groups all have them.

79. When Many People Solve One Problem

1This book begins with gamers who came to the rescue. It then tells of a prize for finding longitude and a prize for keeping food. It shows people working together, then crowdsourcing in our time, including supercomputers and games. It covers tests of ideas, raising money, times the crowd goes wrong, and a better future. A word list ends it. Scientists spent ten years on one mystery: the way proteins fold. Many microbes that cause disease are built from proteins in an important way. If researchers understood that structure, they might find cures. Years passed with no success. Science then asked an unlikely helper: people who play computer games. Foldit is a computer game. The University of Washington created it in 2008. The task for a player is to design proteins that are new. Within three weeks, the players had figured out a protein's structure. That protein was in a deadly virus. Scientists had been stuck on it for years. Thousands of gamers used their brains together. Even the brightest scientists, working alone, had less power than that group. Asking so many minds to help at one time is called crowdsourcing. One task, or one problem, can be handed to the general public by a person or by an organization.

2The help may be ideas. It may be services. People often volunteer because each person's share of the project is small. A small effort still adds up when hundreds or thousands of people join in. One of the world's first crowdsourcing efforts fixed a problem that had worried people for centuries. Sailors who are far from land need to know exactly where they are. The difference can be life or death. A ship that loses its position can hit shoals or other dangers and sink. Sailors have long found their latitude, which is how far north or south they are. They watch the Sun's position at noon with care. East-west position is called longitude. In earlier ages, sailors could only guess it. In 1714, Britain's government offered cash to anyone who found a reliable way to know longitude at sea. People all over the country worked on the problem for years. A clockmaker named John Harrison found a solution in 1741. He knew longitude could be worked out from the Sun's position if the correct time was known. The best clocks of the 1700s used pendulums. Timekeeping came from a weight that swung one way and then the other. Those clocks failed at sea. Wind and waves make ships toss and turn.

3Harrison invented a new kind of clock. It could keep time at sea. Sailors could then work out longitude at any hour of the day. Crowdsourcing also helped with problems on land. Napoleon Bonaparte was France's greatest general. He once said that an army's march depends on its stomach. He meant that soldiers cannot fight if they have nothing to eat. In 1795, France's government offered a prize. Someone had to invent a way to keep food safe for a long military campaign. Nicolas Appert made candy for a living. After fourteen years he had a method that worked. He sealed food so no air could get in. He used empty champagne bottles. The prize money paid for a factory. It was the first one that canned food. People everywhere still use the method he perfected. Modern machines make canning fast and easy. A contest is not the only way to put many minds on one problem. The public can chase one goal together. They do not have to compete. In 1849, Joseph Henry asked for help. His job as a scientist was at the Smithsonian Institution. About 150 volunteers were asked to gather facts about the weather. The places were all over the United States.

4People tracked local weather with care. Each month they sent reports by telegraph. The project kept growing for the ten years that followed. Canada sent weather watchers. Mexico joined in. Latin America joined in. The Caribbean joined in. A book in 1861 printed what the volunteers had learned about storms and about weather. The climate record came to depend on that book. Joseph Henry lived from 1797 to 1878. The Smithsonian Institution had him as its earliest leader. Today the Smithsonian includes centers for research and for education. Museums are part of it. Galleries, gardens, and a zoo are part of it too. Crowdsourcing has kept changing as new technologies have appeared. The Internet made it easier for people to work on projects together than it was in the past. Wikipedia is an online encyclopedia built by a crowd. Members of the general public may write its articles. They may check facts. They may edit. Millions of users share more experience and knowledge as a group than any old encyclopedia staff could. Science is one topic. History, sports, and television shows are others. Wikipedia launched in 2001. It now has more than five million articles. On the Internet, no general reference is more popular. Supercomputers are very powerful machines.

5Scientists have used them for a long time. Those machines crunch numbers and do complex calculations. Supercomputers cost a great deal. Getting time on one can be hard. Crowdsourcing on the Internet let scientists build huge networks. Thousands or millions of ordinary computers, in homes, offices, and schools, now do work that once needed a supercomputer. A teenage girl watches a screensaver called SETI@home. It studies radio signals from space, looking for signs of alien life. SETI is a short form of Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence. For decades, scientists have collected electromagnetic signals from space. The search looks across the galaxy for hints that alien life is there. A screensaver came out in 1999. Its name is SETI@home, which means SETI at home. Millions of resting computers lend their processing power to the program. Each machine studies a small unit of the collected data. The same method is now used for testing software, for math, for biology, and for more. Leave your computer, and it might spend that time helping science. One of the most exciting crowdsourcing methods uses computer games. Foldit's success led scientists to release more games. Ordinary people become lab helpers in those games. In Eyewire, gamers map the brain's neurons. Planet Hunters players located forty planets that resemble Earth.

6Professional astronomers had missed those planets. Phylo shows patterns of colored squares. Tetris, the game of puzzle blocks, is what they resemble. What they really do is line up sequences of DNA. Their play aids research into diseases that genetic disorders cause. Fraxinus has the look of a game made of puzzles. A set pattern is shown, and players match shapes of color to it. Ash-tree DNA is in the game. So is DNA from a fungus. That fungus is killing the trees. The goal is real protection for the trees, and players hunt for new methods. Quantum Moves asks players to shift an atom. The tool is a beam of light, and the methods are new. Computer games let scientists crowdsource important research of every kind. Crowdsourcing is not only for science. In 2008, Lego began asking the crowd for ideas. New sets were the goal, both for the toy bricks and for characters. Anyone age thirteen or older could suggest a new Lego set. People could also vote for ideas they liked. Lego would think about building and selling a set if a year of voting reached at least ten thousand. Fans could invent far more ideas than the company's designers could.

7Fans could point the company toward sets people would want. A person from the public offered a set idea. The year was 2016. It would celebrate women who worked at the space agency NASA. Her idea shot up in the voting. The next year, Lego released a set of 231 pieces called Women of NASA. It became a best seller at once. The set shows astronomer Nancy Grace Roman. It shows computer scientist Margaret Hamilton. Sally Ride, an astronaut, is in the set. Mae Jemison, also an astronaut, is in it too. Money for a cause can be raised by a group. That is another form of crowdsourcing. An invention can cost more than one person has. So can a movie. So can a political campaign. A few dollars from each of thousands of people, or from millions, grows quickly. Crowdfunding of this kind has paid for new albums of music. It has paid for films and for video games. The sums reach thousands of dollars, and sometimes millions. Star Citizen is an online game set in space. In 2014 it gathered over $150 million so it could be developed. Nobody had raised that much for such a project before then. Crowdfunding has also served many charitable causes.

8AdoptTogether is a website. It lets people donate money to families who want to adopt a child. AdoptTogether was founded by Hank Fortener. A picture shows him speaking at a fund-raiser. Children who need homes are the reason for the event. After an adoption, donors hear news about the child. People are more likely to give money when they feel more involved. YouTube hosted a 2014 fund-raiser. People called it the Ice Bucket Challenge. It went viral. Movie stars and ordinary kids alike made videos of themselves. They dumped ice water on their heads. Each video asked people to give money to help cure ALS. The nervous system is what ALS attacks. ALS is a disease. The challenge brought in $115 million. Doctors used part of it to help identify the gene that causes the disease. Ordinary people helped by the millions, and a cure is now one step nearer. Hainan is a province in China. Young people there joined the challenge with ice buckets. The day was World ALS Day in 2017. Crowdsourcing is a powerful tool. A crowd, once its power is released, is not easy to steer. Britain's government learned that in 2016. They let the public vote on a name for a new ship for polar research.

9The ship cost $287 million. They expected a name after a famous polar explorer such as Ernest Shackleton. A naturalist was another expected namesake. David Attenborough, who films nature, was the example. Internet voters grabbed a less scientific name instead. The winner was Boaty McBoatface. The organizers would not accept the winning name, silly as the vote was. David Attenborough got the ship's name in spite of the vote. He speaks in a picture taken when the ship's keel was laid. The ship carries his name as an honor. The public was disappointed. To soothe them, the silly name went to a drone that does research for the ship. That drone is a submersible. Antarctic waters are already being explored by Boaty McBoatface. The people who ran the naming campaign learned a lesson. If you hand a choice to a crowd, you may not get the result you hoped for. Failure happens, but progress can still come from this powerful tool. Future years will probably see it grow still more popular. Projects already use crowdsourcing to help the environment, to cure disease, and to explore space. A history-changing project could include you. Two physics-based computer games help researchers measure and catalog how humans perform at various tasks.

10One game, shown at the top, is Potential Penguin. The other, shown at the bottom, is Skim Racer. Charitable means generous toward people in need. Pendulums are weights that hang from points that do not move, and they swing from side to side. Collective means several people, or several things, are treated as a single group. To preserve is to stop decay, or to keep something in its first state. A living thing's genes are stored as information in a code. That code is DNA. It is short for deoxyribonucleic acid. Proposals are ideas shared so others may consider them and discuss them. Electromagnetic refers to electrical fields and magnetic fields acting on each other, or to something that comes from that action. A screensaver is a computer program. The computer is on, but nobody is using it. The program puts images on the screen, and those images change or move. Microbes are microscopic living things. A shoal is high ground beneath the water. Boats are in danger there. Neurons are nerve cells. Information moves inside the brain on these cells. It also moves between the brain and the rest of the body. Viral describes something shared quickly and widely over social media.

80. Why Fresh Water Is Precious

1Young tadpoles hurry against a shrinking puddle on bare rock. In many places, people treat water as something that will always be on hand. Daily life is full of water. Faucets release it on demand. After rain, sidewalks hold puddles. Lakes stand full. Rivers stand full. Stores sell water in bottles. Public fountains give people a drink. Lake Baikal lies in Russia. Among freshwater lakes, none on Earth is deeper. None is older either. By volume, Baikal is the largest lake. By surface area, the record belongs to Lake Superior. Picture a glass whose width matches the United States. All the water on the planet goes into it. A height of 145 kilometers would be required to hold that water. The same height is 90 miles. A supply that large can seem like more than enough. Even so, drinking water is still out of reach for many people. Fresh water is growing more precious than gold. It is growing more precious than oil as well. Usable water on this planet falls short of what people need. Salt water makes up most of the supply. Drinking it is not possible. Crops cannot be watered with it. Fresh water is only about 3 percent of the total. Polar ice caps lock away most of that fresh share. Glaciers lock away more of it. Aquifers, which are rock layers underground, lock away still more.

2Salt water in the oceans accounts for 97 percent. The fresh share is the other 3 percent. Of all fresh water, ice caps and glaciers hold 68.7 percent. Groundwater holds 30.1 percent. Surface water holds 0.3 percent. Of fresh water on the surface, lakes hold 87 percent. Rivers hold 2 percent. Swamps hold 11 percent. Drinking water worldwide draws 25 percent to 40 percent from groundwater. Food crops draw an even bigger share from groundwater. Those underground supplies are getting smaller. Water is scarce across Saudi Arabia. People there can still obtain it. The country has a high income. Across the planet, water is not shared out evenly. A few countries hold more than the rest. People’s needs can still be met in most countries. The missing piece is often a way to deliver the water. Hard-to-reach sources are easier to tap where income is high. Wells are costly to dig where income is low. Dams that form reservoirs are costly to build there too. Today, reachable usable fresh water is only 1 percent of the fresh total. Stress sits on that 1 percent. One cause is pollution. Another cause is demand, which climbs as population climbs. Climate change is a third cause. On many continents, polluted water is a serious trouble. The Amazon rainforest in South America spreads across 7 million square kilometers.

3In square miles, that spread is 2.7 million. Roughly thirty million people make their homes there. Plant species there number more than thirty thousand. Untreated human waste has entered the Amazon River for decades. Toxic chemicals have entered it as well. The jungle’s fragile ecosystem is slowly being wrecked by these poisons. Brazil’s Amazon River receives many kinds of waste. Elsewhere, in low-income places, fresh water is often left untreated. Organisms that carry disease then multiply. Sickness follows in other forms. Running water is missing for many households. Indoor plumbing is missing too. Rivers and streams then receive waste loaded with bacteria. Drinking draws on those toxic waterways. Cooking draws on them. Bathing draws on them. A report from the United Nations Development Program states a grim share. Patients with waterborne illnesses fill half of hospital beds worldwide. Dimock, Pennsylvania, was home to a resident who, in 2014, raised a jug of fouled water. Washington, D.C., was where an official viewed the jug. Residents there, including him, wanted fracking on nearby land halted. Oil and gas can be obtained by fracking. Other pollution troubles face high-income countries, including the United States. Clean drinking water is available to most people there. Farm runoff is the challenge seen most often. Rain carries chemicals off fields and into waterways.

4Rain also carries animal waste off farms. U.S. waters face an old sewage treatment system. They face oil spills. They face wastewater left by fracking for oil and gas. They face radioactive waste. Several kinds of water pollution are limited by the Clean Water Act. Wider protections have been the goal of some administrations. Narrower protections have been the goal of others. A mobile phone is more common worldwide than a toilet. A human milestone arrived in 2011. An infant girl was born on October 30. Her birthplace was the Philippines. She became person number 7 billion. By 2050, experts expect the walking population to reach 9.7 billion. Food will be sought by each of them. Energy will be sought by each of them. Land will be sought by each of them. Water will be sought by each of them. Each person then has a smaller water share as population grows. Earth’s population in 1950 was 2.5 billion. Fresh water used then was only a third of today’s use. Water was widely seen then as a resource without a limit. Safe drinking water is missing for 1 in 9 people, research now shows. A daily supply under 8 liters is what many of them live on. Two gallons is that same daily amount. Water-stressed regions are expected, by 2050, to hold over half the world’s people.

5Poverty helps explain polluted water in Bangladesh. Overpopulation helps explain it too. A population of 250 million is possible there by 2050. Compared with 2020, that count would add more than 85 million people. Polluted drinking water is a far smaller threat in high-income countries. Purifying water is something they can often afford. Human waste can often be handled properly there. Shortages can still follow population growth where income is high. Water use per person is higher in those countries. Yearly human water use is charted in trillion cubic meters. A single cubic meter equals 264 gallons. Population, in billions, appears on the same chart. A four-person family in the United States averages 1,514 liters of water in a day. Four hundred gallons is that family total. One person accounts for roughly 379 liters. One hundred gallons is that personal share. A few users could keep using water at this rate without emptying the supply. Limited sources now support ever more people. By 2050, Los Angeles County is expected to pass thirteen million residents. Local water there can support only one million people. Distant rivers supply Los Angeles. The same practice serves many other cities of the western United States. The cost of moving that water is high. Enough river water for every user is gone. People around the world already feel climate change.

6Extreme weather is one result. Storms belong to that pattern. Floods belong to that pattern. Nothing may threaten the global water supply more. A forecast from scientists looks ahead to 2050. Severe shortages may then face more than five billion people. Climate change would be the cause. Too much carbon dioxide in the air is behind climate change. Other greenhouse gases add to the problem. A large share of those gases comes from burned fossil fuels. Heat from the Sun stays near the surface because those gases trap it. Heat stays inside a greenhouse in much the same way. Earth’s temperature rises overall as a result. Climate change follows from that warming. The water cycle is disrupted by the extra heat. Evaporation and precipitation must stay in a delicate balance. That balance is the water cycle. Surface water evaporates faster when temperatures rise. The atmosphere receives that extra vapor. Places do not all feel the same effect. Some areas may dry out. Other areas may receive too much precipitation. A drought is a long spell of precipitation that is abnormally low. Water then runs short. Drought risk is especially high around the Mediterranean. The Middle East shares that high risk. Most scientists in the United States blame climate change for an extreme drought. The Southwest is hit.

7California is hit. Problems from the Southwest drought date to 1999. Lake Mead’s water has plunged. Nevada and Arizona meet at the lake’s border. Feeding the lake is the Colorado River. Fresh water from the lake serves twenty-five million people. Rationing is likely for desert residents if rains stay low. A drought contingency plan produced agreed cuts in 2019. Those cuts were a first. Arizona took part. Nevada took part. Mexico took part. The Colorado River supports nearly forty million people. It fades to a trickle and never reaches the sea. Melting has struck glaciers that stand high among the Himalaya mountains. Scientists blame climate change for that melt. Those glaciers help supply 1.5 billion people with fresh water. India is home to many of them. Pakistan is home to many of them. Six other countries in Asia are home to many of them. Melting used to happen slowly. Tributaries of the Indus received the melt. Tributaries of the Ganges received it. Tributaries of the Brahmaputra received it. The stored water is now being used up by rapid melt. Severe flooding has come from the extra melt at the same time. All three rivers have flooded. Energy production has less water as climate change worsens. Livestock raising has less water. Crop growing has less water. Wildlife is harmed. Natural ecosystems are harmed.

8The best claim to water is now a fight among cities. States join that fight. Countries join that fight. India and Pakistan feel growing tension over water. India and China feel it too. Dams are going up in a race among all three. Himalayan headwaters are the sites. Important rivers below are fed by those headwaters. The Nile is another river under argument. Some African countries disagree on the strongest claim. Few places on Earth are drier than the Middle East. Water, some experts say, will be the cause of the next war there. One person’s choice to conserve can still have an effect. A state can conserve as well. California’s driest recorded year was 2013. A voluntary reduction of 20 percent was requested by the governor. Residents did reduce use. The dry spell was over in 2017. Use rose once the dry spell ended. Shut off the tap while brushing your teeth. Keep showers short. A bath is a choice if you prefer to linger. Repair leaks. Repair drips. Meat can be a smaller part of meals. Potatoes of equal amount need far less water than beef. The gap is 125 times, on average. Used items can replace new ones when that choice is open. Recycled products can replace them too. A rain barrel can catch water and hold it for plants.

9Yards do better without added chemicals. Pollution comes from plastic. Plastic use can be cut when a choice exists. A bottle you can refill can stand in for bottled water. A bicycle ride is one way to help stop climate change. Walking helps that effort. Public transit helps that effort. Competing water uses appear on one chart. High-income countries are one group on it. The world as a whole is another. Low- and middle-income countries are the third. UNESCO published the figures in the World Water Development Report. Domestic use in high-income countries is 11 percent. Industry there is 59 percent. Farming there is 30 percent. Domestic use worldwide is 8 percent. Industry worldwide is 22 percent. Farming worldwide is 70 percent. Domestic use in low- and middle-income countries is 8 percent. Industry there is 10 percent. Farming there is 82 percent. National governments also need to hunt for answers. Salt water is turned into fresh water by workers in Saudi Arabia. Desalination is the name of that process. The cost is high. Desalination plants are beyond the budget of many countries. Wastewater is purified in Singapore, an island nation. Dishwashing sends some of that wastewater. Toilets send some of it. Baths send some of it. Showers send some of it. Purifying wastewater is done in a few other countries as well.

10This method supplies one-third of Singapore’s water. Around 70 percent of water worldwide goes to farming. Lower use is a goal some farmers are reaching. Some ranchers are reaching it too. Cities that grow quickly could take the water that is saved. A simple fix for the planet’s water trouble does not exist. Conserving this precious resource is still everyone’s job. Our generation is not the only one with that need. Generations not yet born share it. People cannot see carbon dioxide, because it is an invisible gas. Fossil fuels, when burned, often create it. Lasting shifts in Earth’s weather patterns are what climate change means. Guarding a natural place, or a resource, so it lasts longer is what conserve means. Spread or scattered across an area is what distributed means. Living things plus their habitat form an ecosystem. Coal, oil, and natural gas are fossil fuels taken out of the ground. Water that is not salty is fresh water. Harmful substances put into air, water, or soil count as pollution. The harm that follows counts as pollution too. All members of one species in one area form a population. Purify means to cleanse. Dirt and bad things are removed. Short supply is when rationing limits how goods are portioned. A resource that is not used up completely can be called sustainable.
